units.la: Cardinalis Bellarmini Opufculum De Officio Principis Christiani omnium fere manibus versatur: quo de argumento (Principum optime) Serenissimus Rex noster olim scripserat ΔΩΡΟΝ [?] illud vere βασιλικον Fratri tuo HENRICO PRINCIPI (ad miraculum usque omni virtutum genere illustri) datum; & Pietati T. iam factum haereditarium. Quod incomparabilis Regis opus tam divinum & absolutum iure debuit Bellarmino omnem scribendi ansam praeripuisse: eoq; magis, quia, licet Principes opus vel maximè habeant ut de officio piè moneantur, Bellarminus tamen seipsum longè indignissimum fecerit, qui hoc munere defungatur. Quamuis enim Principes [?]ssle Dei Pro-reges, Vicarios, Præfectos, à Deo secundos, Subditorum geniculis adorandos fateatur ultrò, vix ut quisquam suspicetur Eum Principum illorum dignitatem ire imminutum, quos tantis effert, ornatq; elogijs; tamen (en hominum strophas[?]!) in hoc eodem Opusculo, Principi dicato, Principibus, parum hoc est; Regibus, hoc quoque parum; imò Imperatoribus omnibus planissimè imposuit, & fucum fecit. Quos singulos, quotiescunque vel præsidendi, vel præcedendi, vel (quod leuissimum) præbibendi occasio tulerit, non tantum in Templis, sed & in Palatijs; nec in Conciliis solum, verumetiam in Conuiuijs, plateisque infra non Pontifices modò, atque Episcopos (quamuis hoc per se intolerabile) sed Presbyteros, & sacri ordinis infimum quemque deijcit detruditq;
units.tr: Cardinal Bellarmine's little work On the Duty of a Christian Prince is in almost everyone's hands. On this subject our most serene King, the best of princes, once wrote a gift (ΔΩΡΟΝ) which was truly royal (βασιλικόν), given to your brother Prince Henry, who was distinguished in every kind of virtue almost to a miracle, and which has now become a hereditary possession of your piety. This work of an incomparable King, so divine and perfect, ought rightly to have snatched from Bellarmine every occasion for writing. Moreover, although princes most of all need to be piously instructed in their duty, Bellarmine has shown himself very unworthy to discharge this office. For although he freely admits that princes are God's pro-kings, vicars and prefects, second to God, to be adored by their subjects on their knees, yet, so that no one would suspect that he diminishes the dignity of those princes whom he so exalts and adorns with praises, nevertheless (behold the stanzas of men!) in this same little work, dedicated to a prince, it is too little for princes; it is too little for kings too; indeed he has most plainly deceived and deluded all emperors. Whenever the opportunity of presiding, of precedence, or (the most trivial matter) of drinking first arises for each of them, he thrusts down and degrades not only the popes and bishops (though this is intolerable in itself) but also the presbyters and every person of the lowest sacred order, not only in churches but also in palaces; not only in councils but also at banquets and in the streets.

units.la: Nec tamen hoc mirum in ea Ecclesia, in qua Cyprianus tyrannicum tumorem, Hieronymus supercilium, Augustinus, & alij Africani Episcopi fumosum seculi typhum, Basilius odiosum fastum antiquitus glisc ere conquesti sunt; in ea, (inquam) decursis plusquam mille Annis, Dominationis superbiam indies ita intumescere, ut Principibus ipsis dominari gestiat. Cui vomicae iam latius excrescenti virus infudit, prae alijs, Bellarminus.
units.tr: Yet this is no wonder in that Church, in which Cyprian long ago complained of tyrannical swelling, Jerome of arrogance, Augustine and the other African bishops of the smoky pride of the age, and Basil of hateful haughtiness; in which (I say) after more than a thousand years have passed, the pride of domination swells daily to such an extent that it longs to lord it over princes themselves. Among others, Bellarmine has poured poison into this sore, which is now growing ever more widely.

units.la: Hunc Romanum Achillem plurimum suspiciendus Episcopus Eliensis, idem nunc Wintoniensis, (quo post renatas literas non extitit ingeniosior aut doctior) Serenis. Regem in acie ducem auspicemque sequutus, iudicij pondere feliciter debellauit: post insigniter eruditus Episcopus Roffensis conglobato omne genus Testium agmine obruit: tandem Reuerendissimus Archiepiscopus Spalatensis solidis insuper argumentis transfixit: vix ut Mihi (post tam illustres pugiles) quicquam negotij superfit, nisi, quùm Sacerdotes prætextu quodam Spiritualitatis evehendos, & Principes. Ipsorum humilitatis obtentu deprimendos esse docuerit, ut Ego larvam, hanc Illi detrahaṁ[?], quo vulnus Eius Principibus baudquaquam benignus appareat: ac deindè Eum, in hac Causa, erroris convincam, ex ipsis Sociorum suorum confessionibus, imò suis. Quos non parum torqueri certum est, quoties sentiunt se (quod genus pugnæ exhorruisse dicitur Lulianus) pœnis[?] proprijs vulnerari. Inde enim est, quòd alicubi Maldonatus Iesuita fateri cogatur, Se impeditum esse, quo minùs acriter & vehementer in Protestantes invehatur, quia Catholici quidam ijs se junxerant.
units.tr: This Roman Achilles, to be greatly respected, the bishop of Ely, now of Winchester (than whom no one has been more ingenious or learned since the revival of letters), following our most serene King as leader and auspicious commander in the battle, successfully routed him with the weight of his judgment. Afterwards the learned bishop of Rochester overwhelmed him, marshalling every kind of witness into a single column. At last the most reverend Archbishop of Spalato pierced him through with solid arguments in addition. Scarcely anything remains for me to do after such illustrious champions, except that, since he has taught that priests are to be raised up under a certain pretext of spirituality, and princes are to be depressed under the pretext of their humility, I shall tear off this mask from him, so that his wound against princes may appear by no means kind; and then I shall convict him of error in this cause from the confessions of his own associates, indeed from his own. It is certain that they are not a little tormented whenever they feel themselves wounded by their own weapons (a kind of fighting which Lulian is said to have dreaded). Hence it is that somewhere the Jesuit Maldonatus is forced to confess that he was hindered from attacking the Protestants more sharply and vehemently, because certain Catholics had joined themselves to them.

units.la: Hasce qualescunque lucubratiunculas Tibi potissimùm (inclytissime Princeps) consecrare causæ plurimæ me impulerunt. Bellarminus Librum, quo Principum omnium dignitatem & splendorem obfuscauit, Illustrissimo PRINCIPI VLADISLAO dicare non est veritus: Egone Responsum meum, quo Principum honor a tam alto despectu, pro viribus, vindicatur, dignissimo PRINCIPI CAROLO inscribere, & illo magnifico nomine munire reformidarem? Aut quum Ille, in Epistola Dedicatoria, Principem suum ad funesta bella gerenda accenderet: ut non Ego potius BEATE-PACIFICI Regis filium (quoad fieri potest) ad pacem inter Christianos colendam fouendamque impensius adhorter? Tempora ipsa loquantur, Templa Pacis semper magis gloriosa & diuturna, quam trophaea Victoriae. Paci vero hostis capitalior nullus, quam spiritus ille, qui, Religionis ergo Turcae propensior quam nominis Christi Professoribus, tanto odio in Principes Protestantes exarsit, ut Caesarem, & Galliae Regem incusaret, quod illi cum Protestantibus amicitiam conclusissent, quandò ipse cum Turca ( Alexandri Pontificis Prædecessoris sui exemplo) occultum commercium habuisset.
units.tr: Many reasons have impelled me to dedicate these little works, such as they are, to you above all, most renowned Prince. Bellarmine did not hesitate to dedicate to the most illustrious Prince Vladislaus the book by which he has obscured the dignity and splendour of all princes. Should I fear to inscribe my reply, in which the honour of princes is defended, as far as my strength allows, against so lofty a contempt, to the most worthy Prince Charles, and to fortify it with that magnificent name? Or, when he in his dedicatory epistle stirred up his prince to wage deadly wars, should I not rather urge, as earnestly as I can, the son of the blessed and peaceful King to cultivate and foster peace among Christians more zealously? The times themselves speak: temples of peace are always more glorious and lasting than trophies of victory. Truly no enemy of peace is more deadly than that spirit which, more inclined to the Turk for the sake of religion than to the professors of the name of Christ, has blazed with such hatred against the Protestant princes that it accused the Emperor and the King of France of having made friendship with the Protestants, when the Pope himself (following the example of his predecessor Alexander) had carried on a secret dealing with the Turk.

units.la: Quin & (uti spero) Celsitudini T. non ingratum videbitur huius Operis patrocinium, quod Paternæ Maiestatis iussu (cui, post Deum, Me meaque omnia debeo) susceptum & peractum fuit. Caussam ipsam, (si quæ alia) Principis cognitione imprimis dignam attexam. Hic, nimirum, Controuersia inter Regnum & Sacerdotium, inter Coronam & Mitram, inter Pedum & Sceptrum agitatur. Summa est ; Etsi Sacerdotium tantum præcellat Regno, ex parte mediorum, quæ sunt spiritualia, quantum spiritus carni; & ex parte finis, qui salus est, & pax æterna, quantum cœlum terræ ; tamen quoad [illegible, ~3 letters], siue Suprematum externum, bonoris & authoritatis Regno Sacerdotium subest ; idq; ex [illegible, ~4 letters] id est, ordinatione Dei, qui OMNEM ANIMAM aliam potestati huic subijci & subesse. voluit. Hæc hæc Causa est potissima, cur Romanæ hierarchiæ Assertores Doctores Protestantes tam contemptim habeant; nimirum, quùm hi, si Papismo se addicere vellent, præsidere, præcedere, imperitare Regibus ad nutum Pontificis pofsent; tamen propter Deum stulti facti, vt fiant sapientes, parere malint; nec Principes ludibria fieri, & quasi bruta animalia tractari patiantur.
units.tr: Moreover, as I hope, this patronage of the work, which was undertaken and completed by the command of your Paternal Majesty (to whom, after God, I owe myself and all that is mine), will not seem unwelcome to Your Highness. I shall add the cause itself, if any other, most worthy of the Prince's attention. Here, namely, the controversy between the kingdom and the priesthood, between the Crown and the Mitre, between the Crosier and the Sceptre, is debated. The sum is this: although the priesthood surpasses the kingdom as far as spiritual means are above the flesh, as the spirit is above the body, and as far as the end, which is salvation and eternal peace, is above the earth, as heaven is above earth, yet as regards external supremacy, of honour and authority, the priesthood is subject to the kingdom; and this by the ordinance of God, who willed that every soul be subject to the higher power. This is the chief cause why the defenders of the Roman hierarchy despise the Protestant teachers so contemptuously: namely, since these, if they wished to embrace Popery, could preside, take precedence, and command kings at the nod of the Pope; yet, made fools for God's sake that they might become wise, they prefer to obey, and they do not allow princes to be made into mockeries and handled like brute beasts.

units.la: Quid igitur? Non multi Nobiles &c. Te autem, (nobilissimorum religiosissime, & religiosorum nobilissime Princeps) Ecclesia Euangelica illius fidei religionisque DEFENSOREM expectat, quæ cœlestem coronam annuncians, terrenam etiam defendit. Et quia inter tribus ludæ & Leui maxima semper cognatio intercessit; hæc Tribus, quæ Dei, Regisque CAVSSAM ex animo propugnat, demississimè humilimé Clementiam Tuâ rogat, vt suos, tanquam Dei Angelos [illegible, ~18 letters], id est, in longè charissimorū loco habere pergat, idque idque propter opus suum; ac Eosdem à contumelioso prophanorum hominum contemptu asserere, ac vindicare. Quùm enim Euangelizantium pedes non modo speciosi sint, sed & adeo minabundi, ut vel ijs excussus puluis ad iudicium, & vindicam apud Deum valeat; eorum certè preces ad gloriam tuam temporalem in hac vita stabiliendam, & ad coelestem in futura impetrandam haud dubiè valebunt. Quam utramque Pietati T. ex animo humillimè à Deo Opt. Max. precatur
units.tr: What then? Not many nobles, etc. But you, most religious of the noble and most noble of the religious Prince, the Evangelical Church expects as the defender of that faith and religion, which, while proclaiming the heavenly crown, also defends the earthly one. And because between the tribes of Judah and Levi there has always been the closest kinship, this tribe, which wholeheartedly champions the cause of God and of the King, most humbly and most lowly begs Your Clemency that you continue to hold its men, as the angels of God, in the place of your most dear ones, and to protect and vindicate them from the insolent contempt of profane men, on account of their work. For since the feet of those who preach the gospel are not only beautiful but so dusty that even the dust shaken from them has power before God for judgment and vengeance, surely their prayers will undoubtedly avail to establish your glory in this temporal life and to obtain the heavenly glory in the future. May the Most Good and Most Great God humbly grant both of these to your Piety, which I pray for from my heart.

units.la: Tutum fuisse nonnullis Christianis, absque omni satis dispendio, Pontificibus Rom. non subjici; exemplis luculentis. Ecclesiarum celeberrimarum ostenditur tàm antiquæ, quàm posteræ ætatis. §. 4.
units.tr: That it has been safe for some Christians, without any serious loss, not to be subject to the Roman Pontiffs; this is shown by brilliant examples from the most famous Churches of both ancient and later times. §. 4.

units.la: Hanc, quam obtrudút, Vnionem cùm hoc velillo[?] Pontifice Rom.ceu visibili Capite Ecclesiæ, tanquam Notam verae Ecclesiæ, membris ipsius Rom.Ecclesiæ summo esse præiudicio. §. 5.
units.tr: That this union which they impose, with this or that Roman Pontiff as the visible Head of the Church, held up as a mark of the true Church, is greatly prejudicial to the members of the Roman Church itself. §. 5.

units.la: De I. Titulo Pontificis, viz. PATER.
units.tr: On the first title of the Pontiff, namely FATHER.

units.la: Elogia S. Patrum cùm Pontificum Rom. Titulis æquâ lance trutinantur. §. 6.
units.tr: The eulogies of the holy Fathers are weighed in equal balance with the titles of the Roman Pontiffs. §. 6.

units.la: Paternam curam Ecclesiæ universæ non soli Pontifici Rom. incumbere. §. 7.
units.tr: That the paternal care of the whole Church does not rest on the Roman Pontiff alone. §. 7.

units.la: Complures Pontifices non pacis filios, sed belli incentores esse. §. 8.
units.tr: That many Pontiffs are not sons of peace but instigators of war. §. 8.

units.la: Conc.African.aliud Titulum hunc (PATRIS PATRUM) Papæ attribuere, rem verò aliud negare. §. 9.
units.tr: The African Council ascribes this title (FATHER OF FATHERS) to the Pope in words, yet in reality denies it. §. 9.

units.la: Nomen PAPAE non ad solum Rom. Pontificem restringendum esse. §. 10.
units.tr: That the name POPE is not to be restricted to the Roman Pontiff alone. §. 10.

units.la: Restrictionem hanc novam, & nuper exortā esse. §. 11.
units.tr: That this new restriction is recent and of recent origin. §. 11.

units.la: Secundum modum (colligendi Primatum Pont. ex nomine PAPAE) pariter inanem esse. §. 12.
units.tr: The second method (of collecting the Primacy of the Pontiff from the name POPE) is likewise empty. §. 12.

units.la: Papam Rom. dum fraternitem despicit, Paternitatem suam amittere. §. 13.
units.tr: That the Pope of Rome, while he despises brotherhood, loses his fatherhood. §. 13.

units.la: Pontificios ipsos, de nomine PAPAE, inter se flucture, & collidere invicem. §. 14.
units.tr: That the Papists themselves waver over the name POPE and clash with one another. §. 14.

units.la: Titulum SANCTITATIS, contrà primæuam nominis institutionem, frustrà & iniquè traductum esse, Ex Iª. Comparatione, factà inter ipsos Pontifices, probatur. §. 15.
units.tr: That the title of HOLINESS, contrary to the original institution of the name, has been wrongly and unjustly transferred; this is proved from the first comparison, made between the Pontiffs themselves. §. 15.

units.la: Ex IIª. Comparatione Pontificum cum aliis Episcopis, idem probari. §. 16.
units.tr: From the second comparison, of Pontiffs with other bishops, the same is proved. §. 16.

units.la: Ex Comparatione IIIª. inter Pontifices & Imperatores, de SANCTITATIS atq; PIETATIS vocabulis, Idem cuinci[?]. §. 17.
units.tr: From the third comparison, between Pontiffs and Emperors, concerning the words HOLINESS and PIETY, the same is shown. §. 17.

units.la: Cautela Principibus necessaria. §. 18.
units.tr: Caution is necessary for princes. §. 18.

units.la: Bellar. mentem (sub vocabulo Patris delitescentem) perquàm infestam Regibus comperi. §. 19.
units.tr: I have found Bellarmine's intent, lurking under the word Father, to be exceedingly hostile to kings. §. 19.

units.la: Verborum Christi Luc. 14. [SIQUIS VENIT AD ME &c.] sensus germanus enucleatur. §. 20.
units.tr: The true sense of the words of Christ, Luke 14 [IF ANYONE COMES TO ME, etc.], is set forth. §. 20.

units.la: Pactum illud Baptismi, quod Sanderus 1°. commentus est, Pacto, quo Christus ab omnibus Christianis obedientiam stipulatur, diametro tota repugnare. §. 21.
units.tr: That baptismal covenant which Sanders first devised is wholly contrary to the covenant by which Christ demands obedience from all Christians. §. 21.

units.la: Bellarminum, vi Principiorum suorum, ad palinodiam vel invitum trahi. §. 22.
units.tr: That Bellarmine, by the force of his own principles, is dragged, even against his will, toward a recantation. §. 22.

units.la: Illud Baptismi pactum religioni Pontificiæ obesse vel maximè. §. 23.
units.tr: That this baptismal covenant is most harmful to the Papist religion. §. 23.

units.la: Pacti illius consequentiâ (quâ Bellar. Reges vrget, atque devincit) universæ antiquitati ignotum penitùs fuisse: Atque etiam ab ullo Episcopo rectiùs quam à Rom. Pontifice de Principibus exigi posse. §. 24.
units.tr: That the consequence of that covenant (by which Bellarmine presses and binds kings) was wholly unknown to all antiquity, and that it could be demanded of princes more correctly by any bishop than by the Roman Pontiff. §. 24.

units.la: Paulinum exemplum à Bellar. prauè inverti, & aliorsum trahi. §. 25.
units.tr: That the Pauline example is wrongly inverted by Bellarmine and drawn to another purpose. §. 25.

units.la: Absurdè statui, Papam filios gignere tantùm per Vicarios. §. 26.
units.tr: That it is absurdly maintained that the Pope begets sons only through vicars. §. 26.

units.la: Primum reverà Petrum inter Apostolos, non Primatem fuisse. §. 27.
units.tr: That in truth Peter was first among the Apostles, but not their Primate. §. 27.

units.la: Paulum æquè Patrem fidelium ac Petrum fuisse. §. 28.
units.tr: That Paul was as much the Father of the faithful as Peter was. §. 28.

units.la: Ritus Pontificios subinde mutabiles esse, & nonnunquam significationis inertes. §. 29.
units.tr: That Papist rites are changeable from time to time and sometimes without meaning. §. 29.

units.la: Novellum Coronationis Pont. Ritum Paternitatis antiquitatem malè confirmare. §. 30.
units.tr: That the novel rite of the Pontiff's coronation poorly confirms the antiquity of the paternity. §. 30.

units.la: Coronatio Pontificis quàm noviter cœperit in usu haberi. §. 31.
units.tr: How recently the coronation of the Pontiff began to be in use. §. 31.

units.la: Pontificem coronam ostentare, ut Principes facilius coronis suis exuat. §. 32.
units.tr: That the Pontiff displays a crown, so as more easily to strip princes of their crowns. §. 32.

units.la: Qualia solet esse Romæ, & quæ visenda spectacula. §. 33
units.tr: What sort of spectacles are customary at Rome, and what is to be seen there. §. 33

units.la: Reverentia, Pontificibus Rom. exhibita, qualis & quanta sit. §. 34.
units.tr: What reverence is paid to the Roman Pontiffs, and how great it is. §. 34.

units.la: Putidæ Bozij Rationes, pro osculo pedum Pontificis, diluuntur. §. 35. Eundem ritum osculandi Pontificum pedes ab ipsis Pontificijs reprehendi. §. 36. Quò tendat immodica Pontifici habita Reuerentia §. 37. Pontifices olim eandem Principum[?] reuerentiam præstitisse, quam nunc ab ipsis exigunt. §. 38. Nimiam istam Pontificis Reuerentiam triplici de causa vituperandam esse. §. 39. Papa iure tantum humano posse se Patrem-familias venditare. §. 40. Papam Ecclesiæ filium, forsan, Patrem pariter non esse censendum. §.41. Quàm durum & difficilem Pontifex in Cardinales fratres, tùm etiam in Patres prædecessores se præbuerit. §. 42. Papa non Principum Pater, sed superciliosus & fastidiosus Dominus. §. 43. Reges reuerà Patres esse, quibus honor externus à Pontificibus & Sacerdotibus deferendus sit; qui tamen dedecori sibi esse ducunt Regum manus osculari. §. 44.
units.tr: The foolish arguments of Bozius in favour of kissing the Pontiff's feet are refuted. §. 35. That the same rite of kissing the Pontiffs' feet is criticised by the Papists themselves. §. 36. Where immoderate reverence shown to the Pontiff leads. §. 37. That Pontiffs formerly showed princes the same reverence that they now demand from them. §. 38. That this excessive reverence for the Pontiff is to be condemned on three grounds. §. 39. That the Pope may claim to be father of a family only by human law. §. 40. That the Pope is perhaps not to be regarded as the father, in the same way, of the Church's son. §. 41. How harsh and difficult the Pontiff has shown himself toward his brother cardinals, and also toward his predecessors the Fathers. §. 42. The Pope is not the father of princes but a haughty and disdainful lord. §. 43. Kings are truly fathers, to whom external honour is to be paid by Pontiffs and priests, who nevertheless think it a disgrace to kiss the hands of kings. §. 44.

units.la: In CAP. II. De II. Tit. Pontificis uz. PASTOR.
units.tr: In CHAP. II. Concerning the title of the Pope: PASTOR.

units.la: PASTORIS titulo sensum pernitiosum inuolui. §. 1. Dependentiam omnium aliorum Pastorum à Papa caduco niti fundamento. §. 2. Pontificis Ius dirigendi & corrigendi omnes alios Pastores antiquitùs inauditum fuisse. §. 3. Bellar. in distinctione Ouium & Agnorum. §. 4. Hieronymum nihil causæ Pontificiæ prodesse. §. 5. Eundem Pontificiæ Caussæ obesse plurimum. §. 6. Distinctionem Bellar. de LVPIS & ARIETIBVS, impropriam atque incommodam esse. §. 7. Vtrum pernitiosior an insulsior sit Ratio Bellarmini (de Lupis) difficilè esse dicere. §. 8. Indirectam Pontificis potestatem Temporalem è regio Christi officio, nullo artificio elici posse. §.9.
units.tr: That the title of Pastor conceals a pernicious meaning. §. 1. That the dependence of all other ministers upon the Pope rests on a shaky foundation. §. 2. That the Pope's right to direct and correct all other ministers was unheard of in antiquity. §. 3. Bellarmine on the distinction between sheep and lambs. §. 4. That Jerome is of no help to the Papist cause. §. 5. That the same Jerome greatly harms it. §. 6. That Bellarmine's distinction concerning WOLVES and RAMS is improper and inconvenient. §. 7. That it is hard to say whether Bellarmine's argument (concerning wolves) is more pernicious or more foolish. §. 8. That the indirect temporal power of the Pope cannot be drawn from the kingly office of Christ by any artifice. §. 9.

units.la: Potestatem hanc Coactiuam, vt per se iniustam, ita per multas Annorum centurias ignotam penitus fuisse. §.10.
units.tr: That this coercive power, being unjust in itself, was also entirely unknown through many centuries of years. §. 10.

units.la: Ex veræ Ouis notâ primariâ ostendi, Papam non Pastoris, sed tyranni partes agere. §.11.
units.tr: From the chief mark of the true sheep it is shown that the Pope plays not the part of a minister but of a tyrant. §. 11.

units.la: In arietibus debellandis infeliciter Bellarminum aciem struere. §.12.
units.tr: That Bellarmine draws up his battle line unsuccessfully in attacking the rams. §. 12.

units.la: Formulam Bellarm. (<bl>Reclvdendi</bl> Principes) atrocES in Principes iniurias innuere; cui typus pastoralis Pedi reclamat. §.13.
units.tr: That Bellarmine's formula (that princes are to be shut up, Reclvdendi) hints at atrocious injuries against princes, to which the pastoral type protests. §. 13.

units.la: Causas deponendi Principes plures indignas, multas ineptas, iustas esse nullas. §.14.
units.tr: That the reasons for deposing princes are many and unworthy, many are inept, and none are just. §. 14.

units.la: Causæ superiores, propter quas Principes deponendos censent Pontificij, sigillatim recensentur; & eorum omnium Pontificum ipsi rei peraguntur. §.15.
units.tr: The higher reasons, on account of which the Papists think princes should be deposed, are listed one by one, and all of them are pursued against the Popes themselves. §. 15.

units.la: Papam negotijs multis à prædicandi munere impediri; otiosè obtendi. §.16.
units.tr: That the Pope is hindered from the office of preaching by many affairs; this is idly alleged. §. 16.

units.la: Papam per Vicarium, non per se concionantem, omni iudicio tam humano quàm diuino damnandum: & ex ipsis verbis Christi [Pasce Oves] Pastoris nomine indignum probari. §.17.
units.tr: That the Pope, not preaching in person but through a vicar, deserves condemnation by every judgment, human as well as divine; and from the very words of Christ [Feed my sheep] it is proved that he is unworthy of the name of Pastor. §. 17.

units.la: Quo sensu Principes Sacerdotum, adeoque Pontificum ipsorum Pastores iure haberi debeant. §.18.
units.tr: In what sense the princes ought by right to be regarded as pastors of the priests, and therefore of the Popes themselves. §. 18.

units.la: In CAP. III.
units.tr: In CHAPTER III.

units.la: De III. Tit. Papæ, vz. Doctor, vel Iudex.
units.tr: On the Third Title of the Pope, namely Teacher or Judge.

units.la: Titulum Doctoris, communem Alijs, Pontifici proprium Monarchiam stabilire non posse. §.1.
units.tr: That the title of Teacher, which is common to others, cannot establish a monarchy proper to the Pope. §.1.

units.la: Papam in Conc. Florentino speciem magis quàm vim authoritatis habuisse. §.2.
units.tr: That at the Council of Florence the Pope had the appearance rather than the force of authority. §.2.

units.la: Papam Concilio subesse. §.3.
units.tr: That the Pope is subject to the Council. §.3.

units.la: Sensum verborum Christi [Confirma Fratres] celebriorem & veriorem Bellarminianæ expositioni adversari. §.4.
units.tr: That the more famous and truer sense of the words of Christ, Confirm your brethren, is opposed to Bellarmine's exposition. §.4.

units.la: Illud [Non deficiat] Non uni Petro proprium, sed alijs Apostolis charisma commune esse. §.5.
units.tr: That the words that his faith may not fail were not peculiar to Peter alone, but a gift common to the other apostles. §.5.

units.la: Personale Petri privilegium nullo jure transferri in Papam.§.6.
units.tr: That Peter's personal privilege is not transferred to the Pope by any right. §.6.

units.la: Bernardi judicium sæpè etiam ab Aduersariis contemni.§.7.
units.tr: That Bernard's judgment is often despised even by our adversaries. §.7.

units.la: Cypriani authoritate, de more suo rhetoricantis, abuti Bellarminum.§.8.
units.tr: That Bellarmine abuses the authority of Cyprian, rhetorizing in his usual manner. §.8.

units.la: Cypriannm[?] dictis factis Rom. Cathedræ acerrimum oppugnatorem fuisse.§.9.
units.tr: That Cyprian, by his words and deeds, was a most fierce opponent of the Roman See. §.9.

units.la: Bellarminú in interpretatione Eccles.12.&c. falli.§.10.
units.tr: That Bellarmine is mistaken in his interpretation of Ecclesiastes 12, etc. §.10.

units.la: Sacerdotis Vet.Testamenti judicio, nisi juxta legem acquiescendum non fuisse.§.11.
units.tr: That, by the judgment of the priests of the Old Testament, one was bound to submit only in accordance with the law. §.11.

units.la: Per [Mosis Cathedram] non propriam Judicis sententiam, sed doctrinam Mosaicam indicari.§.12.
units.tr: That by [the seat of Moses] is meant not the judge's own sentence but the doctrine of Moses. §.12.

units.la: Expositiones Pontificiorum deliramentis Rabbinorum insulsorum perquam esse similes, ad cæcam obedientiam inducendam.§.13.
units.tr: That the expositions of the Papists are very like the absurd fancies of the foolish rabbis, aimed at inducing blind obedience. §.13.

units.la: Lutherum Pontificiorum partes, propter impiam Pontificis doctrinam, in novis fidei Articulis condendis, jure deseruisse.§.14.
units.tr: That Luther, on account of the impious doctrine of the Pope, rightly deserted the Papists' side in framing new articles of faith. §.14.

units.la: Principes Protestantes Bellarminum vituperando laudare.§.15.
units.tr: That Protestant princes praise Bellarmine by blaming him. §.15.

units.la: Lutherum ovem innocentem, tum Pastorem bonum agnosci posse.§.16.
units.tr: That Luther can be recognised as an innocent sheep and also as the good Shepherd. §.16.

units.la: Summam regulam interpretandi legem non esse absolutè penes Pontificem Rom.§.17.
units.tr: That the supreme rule of interpreting the law does not rest absolutely with the Roman Pontiff. §.17.

units.la: De Luthero reo, deque occasione, & modo iniquo aduersus illum procedendi.§.18.
units.tr: Concerning Luther as the accused, and concerning the occasion and the unjust manner of proceeding against him. §.18.

units.la: Indulgentiarum doctrinam longè abesse à veritate, antiquitate, pietate.§.19.
units.tr: That the doctrine of indulgences is far removed from truth, antiquity and piety. §.19.

units.la: Bellarmini, de Aquilone, sarcasma contra Prophetæ mentem perperam deprauari.§.20.
units.tr: That Bellarmine's sarcasm about the North is distorted wrongly against the mind of the Prophet. §.20.

units.la: Lutheri doctrinâ Principum incolumitatem & dignitatem maximè muniri.§.21.
units.tr: That Luther's doctrine especially safeguards the security and dignity of princes. §.21.

units.la: Titulum Apostoli Caluino nos nullum tribuere, quem Papæ prærogativam esse adulatorie astruunt Pontificii.§.22. Caluinum, ut Miracula ederet, nunquam prorsus attentasse. §.23.
units.tr: That the title of Apostle is not granted by us to Calvin, which the Papists flatteringly claim as the prerogative of the Pope. §.22. That Calvin never at all attempted to work miracles. §.23.

units.la: Pontificiorum miraculosa figmenta, seu fictitia Miracula. §. 24.
units.tr: The miraculous fabrications of the Papists, or fictitious miracles. §.24.

units.la: Aduersarios non sine summa peruersitate à Caluino, aut Protestantibus miracula exigere. §. 25.
units.tr: That our adversaries demand miracles from Calvin or the Protestants only with the greatest perversity. §.25.

units.la: Ex ipsius Pont. decreto, fidem Pontificibus plurimis abrogari, quos Ecclesia Rom. tanquàm Iudices suos venerata est. §. 26.
units.tr: That by the Pope's own decree, faith is taken away from very many Pontiffs whom the Roman Church has revered as its judges. §.26.

units.la: Pontifices Rom. subtractis omnibus intelligendi medijs, Principes ut sapiant insulsè [?] monere. §.27.
units.tr: That the Roman Pontiffs, having removed all means of understanding, foolishly advise princes to be wise. §.27.

units.la: Interpretatione Bellar. de Petra, omne genus testium nube obscurari. §. 28.
units.tr: That by Bellarmine's interpretation of the rock, every kind of witness is obscured by a cloud. §.28.

units.la: Pont. Rom. nisi sanctitatem Petri verè imitetur, nullum ex promissis Petro factis sibi asserere posse. §. 29.
units.tr: That the Roman Pontiff cannot claim for himself any of the promises made to Peter unless he truly imitates the holiness of Peter. §.29.

units.la: Papam tùm quà priuata persona, tum etiam quà publicus Doctor in hæresin incidere posse. §. 30.
units.tr: That the Pope can fall into heresy both as a private person and also as a public teacher. §.30.

units.la: Catholicam Ecclesiam Rom. sedi non itâ esse affixam, ut non Roma ipsa possit esse Babylon Apocalyptica. §. 31.
units.tr: That the Catholic Church is not so attached to the Roman See that Rome itself cannot be the Apocalyptic Babylon. §.31.

units.la: In CAP. IV. De IIII. Pontificis Tit. vz. SPECVLATOR.
units.tr: In CHAPTER IV. On the Fourth Title of the Pontiff, namely WATCHMAN.

units.la: SAnctum Augustinum Bonifacio Papæ fastigium concessisse; fastum adimisse. §. 1.
units.tr: That Saint Augustine granted to Pope Boniface the highest rank, but took away his pride. §.1.

units.la: Speculandi officium, Episcopis omnibus æquè impositum, nullum esse Papalis dominationis argumentum. §. 2.
units.tr: That the duty of watching, laid equally upon all bishops, is no argument of papal domination. §.2.

units.la: Pontifices, ad suam tyrannidem stabiliendam, scripturam hanc Hier 1. [Ecce constitui te, &c.] egregiè peruertere; idque ex Bernardi, Bellarmini, aliorumque antithesi [?] demonstrari. §. 3.
units.tr: That the Pontiffs, to establish their tyranny, have grievously perverted this passage of Jeremiah 1, [Behold, I have set you, etc.]; and that this is shown from the antithesis of Bernard, Bellarmine and others. §.3.

units.la: Prophetam (Ezechielem) & Papam, quoad officium speculandi, longo interuallo inter se distare. §.4.
units.tr: That the Prophet (Ezekiel) and the Pope are far apart from each other as regards the office of watching. §.4.

units.la: Papam,quà (ex interpretatione Pontificiorum) Caput dicitur, reliquis membris heterogeneum; & a corpore Ecclesiæ, quum ratio tulerit, amputandum esse.
units.tr: That the Pope, insofar as (by the interpretation of the Papists) he is called the Head, is unlike the other members; and that, as reason dictates, he must be cut off from the body of the Church.

units.la: Papam, etiamsi Speculatorem præ se ferat, speculam tamen ipsam jam olim deseruisse.
units.tr: That the Pope, even if he presents himself as a watchman, has nevertheless long since abandoned the watchtower itself.

units.la: Ambrosij diuinissimi viri exemplum [?] esse. ejicere, & reiicere.
units.tr: That the example of the most divine man Ambrose is to cast out and reject.

units.la: Vniuersum orbem Pontificis esse dioecesin, totius orbis omni praxi & suffragijs refragari.
units.tr: That the whole world is the diocese of the Pontiff, and that every practice and vote of the whole world opposes this.

units.la: Odiosum Oecumenici, seu Vniuersalis Episcopi Titulum à Gregorio Papa damnatum probari.
units.tr: That the odious title of Ecumenical, or Universal, Bishop, condemned by Pope Gregory, is shown to be proper.

units.la: Pontifices nihil minus quàm docendo Monitores agere.
units.tr: That the Pontiffs, far from acting as admonishers by teaching, do nothing of the kind.

units.la: Pontificibus Rom. nimis adhærere, fatale Principibus nonnunquam fuisse.
units.tr: That to cling too closely to the Roman Pontiffs has sometimes proved fatal to princes.

units.la: Pontifices ipsos omnium maximè ad sua monita audires, & pectora obturare.
units.tr: That the Pontiffs themselves should most of all listen to admonitions of their own, and stop their ears.

units.la: Bellarmini Precationem neque hic vndequaque ver-ram; & eius generis aliam tantùm non blasphemam esse.
units.tr: That Bellarmine's prayer is not wholly true here, and that another prayer of this kind is almost blasphemous.

units.la: Reges Christianos, quoad curam subditorum, speculatores habendos esse.
units.tr: That Christian kings, as regards care of their subjects, are to be regarded as watchmen.

units.la: In C A P. V. De V. Tit. Papæ, vz. Sacerdote Magno, &c.
units.tr: In CHAPTER V. On the Fifth Title of the Pope, namely High Priest, etc.

units.la: HISce titulis, [Summus, & Maximus Pontifex] aliorum Episcoporum ordinem & dignitatem æqualem non imminui.
units.tr: By these titles, [Supreme, and Greatest Pontiff], the order and equal dignity of the other bishops are not diminished.

units.la: Immodica Pontificiorum, de Papis, Elogia & Christianis hominibus horrori, & ipsi Christo dedecori esse.
units.tr: That the immoderate eulogies of the Papists concerning the Popes are a horror to Christian men and a disgrace to Christ himself.

units.la: Formam regiminis politici, sub vet. Testamento, Principe noui Test. exemplo proponi posse.
units.tr: That a form of political government under the Old Testament can be set forth as an example for a prince under the New Testament.

units.la: Mosen, & Iosuam, qua Principes, Sacerdotibus præfuisse.
units.tr: That Moses and Joshua presided over the priests as princes.

units.la: Idemius[?] Salomoni in Abiatharum, Iosiæ in Sacerdotum tribum vindicari. §. 5.
units.tr: That the same right was asserted for Solomon against Abiathar, and for Josiah against the tribe of the priests. §.5.

units.la: Idem ius Principum, in Sacerdotes vet. Testamenti, confessionibus aliorum Aduersariorum, confirmari. §. 6.
units.tr: That the same right of princes over the priests of the Old Testament is confirmed by the confessions of other adversaries. §.6.

units.la: Bellarminum Liberati testimonium, pro libitu suo, accipere, & reijcere. §. 7.
units.tr: That Bellarmine accepts and rejects the testimony of Liberatus as he pleases. §.7.

units.la: Patarensem Episcopum, sensu minimè Pontificio, totius Ecclesiæ præfecturam Pontifici concessisse. §. 8.
units.tr: That the Bishop of Patara, in a sense by no means Papal, granted the headship of the whole Church to the Pope. §.8.

units.la: Iustinianum in causa Syluerij (non obstante Patarensis Episcopi [illegible, ~3 letters]) de iure suo neutiquam cessisse. §. 9.
units.tr: That Justinian, in the case of Silverius (notwithstanding the Bishop of Patara's [illegible]), by no means yielded his right. §.9.

units.la: Non defectum humanarum virium, sed diuinum mandatum antiquos Christianos in subiectionis officiis erga Ethnicos Principes continuisse; contra quam blasphemè docent Pontificij. §. 10.
units.tr: That it was not a lack of human strength but the divine command that kept the ancient Christians in the duties of subjection toward heathen rulers; contrary to what the Papists teach blasphemously. §.10.

units.la: Bernardum ipsum, vbi accuratius textum hunc (Rom. 13. Omnis Anima, &c.) pensitâsset, sensum & explicationem Protestantium confirmâsse. §. 12.
units.tr: That Bernard himself, when he had weighed this text (Romans 13, Let every soul, etc.) more carefully, confirmed the sense and explanation of the Protestants. §.12.

units.la: Patres illos multos, quos citari posse ait Bellar. in contrariam planè sententiam abijsse. §. 13.
units.tr: That those many Fathers whom Bellarmine says can be cited had clearly gone over to the contrary opinion. §.13.

units.la: Spiritus S. præcepto, de subiectione Omnis anima, omnes etiam Ecclesiasticos necessariò constringi. §. 14.
units.tr: That by the precept of the Holy Spirit concerning subjection, every soul, all ecclesiastical persons too are necessarily bound. §.14.

units.la: S. Bernardum potestatis Regiæ assertorem esse satis luculentum. §. 15.
units.tr: That Saint Bernard is a quite clear defender of royal power. §.15.

units.la: Pontifices Rom. Petro meritis ac doctrinâ dispares atque discordes, eidem successores haut aptè constitui. §. 16.
units.tr: That the Roman Pontiffs, unlike Peter and at odds with him in merit and doctrine, were not aptly appointed as his successors. §.16.

units.la: Papæ potestatem, neque quà vinctus, neque quà vicarius, vllo modo stabiliri. §. 17.
units.tr: That the power of the Pope is established in no way, neither as one bound nor as a vicar. §.17.

units.la: Causam Regiam demonstrari ex suffragijs Pontificum Rom. per LXX. annorum curriculum, qui reverentiam Imperatoribus vltrò professi sunt. §. 18.
units.tr: That the Royal Cause is demonstrated from the votes of the Roman Pontiffs over a course of seventy years, who of their own accord professed reverence to the emperors. §.18.

units.la: Eosdem Pontifices, in causis Ecclesiasticis, eandem obedientiam factis quoque præstitisse. §. 19.
units.tr: That the same Pontiffs, in ecclesiastical matters, likewise rendered the same obedience to the emperors in deeds. §.19.

units.la: Imperatorum authoritatem tam ex nominum in Decretis ipsorum præpositione, quàm ex eorum in Conciliis præsidentia demonstrari. §. 20. Priscos Imperatores Pontificibus ipsis authoritate, & potestate eminuisse, ijsque leges imposuisse. §. 21.
units.tr: That the authority of the emperors is demonstrated both from the placing of their names before the Pontiffs' own decrees and from their presidency in councils. §.20. That the ancient emperors excelled the Pontiffs themselves in authority and power, and imposed laws upon them. §.21.

units.la: Eandem authoritatem succedentes Imperatores super Pontifices exercuisse. §. 22.
units.tr: That the emperors who succeeded exercised the same authority over the Pontiffs. §.22.

units.la: Francorum etiam Reges contra violentiam Pontificis legem Pramaticam sanxiuisse, obseruasseque. §. 23.
units.tr: That the kings of the Franks also enacted and observed the Pragmatic Sanction against the violence of the Pontiff. §.23.

units.la: Parem sanctionem Hispaniae & Lusitaniae Reges, simili causa, aduersus Pontifices tulisse. §. 24.
units.tr: That the kings of Spain and Portugal likewise issued a similar sanction against the Pontiffs in a similar cause. §.24.

units.la: ELENCHUS DISSERTATIONIS.
units.tr: ELENCHUS DISSERTATIONIS.

units.la: In CAP. VI. vz. De Officio Principis Christiani erga proprium Episcopum
units.tr: On CHAPTER VI, namely On the Duty of a Christian Prince towards his own Bishop

units.la: Inconsultò[?] Bellarminum Principes pios rixarum ad-versus Episcopos, insimulare. §. 1.
units.tr: Bellarmine rashly accuses godly princes of quarrelling against bishops. §. 1.

units.la: Ex Scripturis sacris, à Bellarmino praeter sensum detortis, Principes superbiae denotari. §. 2.
units.tr: Princes are shown to be denoted by pride from Scripture, which Bellarmine has twisted beyond its sense. §. 2.

units.la: Ut Principes deprimantur, Relativorum (ut potè Pastoris, Patris, Doctoris, &c.) nomina & habitudines inverti. §. 3.
units.tr: To bring princes down, Bellarmine inverts the names and relations of correlative terms (such as minister, father, teacher, etc.). §. 3.

units.la: Celsiorem in Ministerio locum externam dignitatis celsitudinem non probare. §. 4.
units.tr: An external display of dignity does not prove a higher place in the ministry. §. 4.

units.la: Ex speciosis Patrum nominibus Bellarminum velitari. §. 5.
units.tr: Bellarmine is skirmished with by means of the splendid names of the Fathers. §. 5.

units.la: Argumentum à similitudine ductum illustrare magis quàm probare. §. 6.
units.tr: The argument drawn from similitude illustrates rather than proves. §. 6.

units.la: Celebrem illam Carnis & Spiritus aduersus Principes detortam similitudinem ab ipso Nazianzeno membratim refutari. §. 7.
units.tr: The famous similitude of flesh and spirit, twisted against princes, is refuted point by point from Nazianzen himself. §. 7.

units.la: Eandem similitudinem & Rationibus, & Pontificiorum principijs manifesto convelli. §. 8.
units.tr: The same similitude is plainly overturned both by reasons and by the principles of the Papists. §. 8.

units.la: Sacerdotes Regibus externa potestate non praecellere, licet Sacerdotium Regno (obiecto, & fine) praemineat. §9.
units.tr: Priests do not surpass kings in external power, although the priesthood excels the kingdom in its object and end. §. 9.

units.la: Veram Chryfoftomi sententiam, de Regum suprematu, omnes Sophistarum distinctiones confundere. §. 10.
units.tr: The true opinion of Chrysostom concerning the supremacy of kings confounds all the distinctions of the sophists. §. 10.

units.la: Ambrosij, de Auro, similitudinem Bellarminum mifcrere adulterasse. . §. 11.
units.tr: Bellarmine has corrupted Ambrose's comparison in the treatise On Gold. §. 11.

units.la: Ambrosium aduersus Imperatorem nullum procefsum forensem tentaffe. §. 12.
units.tr: Ambrose attempted no legal proceeding against an emperor. §. 12.

units.la: Frigidum & ieiunum esse, quod Bellarminus de lege condenda, & de cancellis interdicendis obiicit. §. 13.
units.tr: What Bellarmine objects concerning the enacting of a law and the forbidding of the chancels is cold and feeble. §. 13.

units.la: Ambrosium recte intellectum sublimitatis Regiae propugnatorem fortissimum, cultoremque humillimum suisse. §. 14.
units.tr: Ambrose, rightly understood, was the most valiant defender of royal majesty and the most humble of its servants. §. 14.

units.la: Citatam Gregorij, de Medardi monasterio, Epistolam spuriam esse,& indignam Gregorio prolem. §. 15.
units.tr: The letter of Gregory about the monastery of Medardus, which is cited, is spurious and unworthy of Gregory's offspring. §. 15.

units.la: Inanissimam Bellarmini Rationem esse,dicentis,solius esse inferioris reuerentiam alteri exhibere. §. 16.
units.tr: Bellarmine's reason, which says that reverence is owed to another only by the inferior, is most empty. §. 16.

units.la: Gregorium Mauritij iussionibus obtemperasse,non solum ex necessitate, sed ex conscientiae vinculo.. §. 17.
units.tr: Gregory obeyed the commands of Maurice not only from necessity but from the bond of conscience. §. 17.

units.la: Nullum omnium Pontificum tàm infensum Regiae Maiestatis hostem fuisse, quam fuit Gregorius propugnator feruidus.. §. 18.

units.la: QVùm multa & ingentia Card. Bellarmini volumina, quibus peruoluendis nonnihil operae impendi, plurimis Eius Consequutionum repugnantium, Distinctionum [?] ... Opinionumque quarundam portentis me in reformata religione confirmationem reddiderint: tùm sanè Opus hoc De Officio Principum, eodem conducere videatur. In quo etsi [illegible, ~6 letters] quae veram pietatem redolent; at [illegible, ~5 letters] quae Recognitione eius egere videntur: sed non illa iam antea edita; in qua [illegible, ~4 letters] corriguntur plurima; sed candidiore aliquà, & minimè corrigendâ. Nec tamen Ego omnia in Eo examinare proposui, sed ea tantum quae in Causla hac Regia ad inebriandos Principes miscuit hic noster [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: Although the many large volumes of Cardinal Bellarmine, through which I have spent some effort reading, have, with the monstrous contradictions of his consequences, distinctions [?] … and certain opinions, confirmed me in the reformed religion, this work On the Office of Princes seems to serve the same end. In it, although [illegible, ~6 letters] breathe true piety, yet [illegible, ~5 letters] seem to need his revision. But it is not the earlier edition; in it [illegible, ~4 letters] many things are corrected, though in a more candid manner, and one that needs no correction at all. Nor, however, have I proposed to examine everything in it, but only those things which our author here [illegible, ~10 letters] has mixed into this royal cause to intoxicate princes.

units.la: Bellarmini NOMEN Principibus nimis odiosum merito suo fieri.
units.tr: Bellarmine's NAME is rightly made too hateful to princes.

units.la: INomni hortan- i ac instituendi Alios munere Quis Cui loquatur multùm sanè interest. Author hic noster, in suo De Officio Principum libro, nomen proprium extare voluit, {a}ROBERTVS BELLARMINVS. ingenuè factum, fateor; sed & nimis inconsulto, nisi forte affinitatem omnem cum illo Roberto Bellarmino penitus abiuret, qui non ita pridem librum edidit {b}De Potestate summi Pontificis (nempe supra Principes) inscriptum, authoritate Senatus {c}Parisiensis proscriptum ilico, Gallicaeque na-{d} tionis hominibus interdictum, quod {d} Doctrinam contineret ad euersionem potestatum supremarum à Deo constitu-tarum pertinentem, ad rebellionem mouentem, & ad machinandum in Principum capita ditionésque, ac ad perturbandam pacem publicam, incitantem. Rectius itaque nomini causæque suæ consuluisset, si sub Torti, vel Schulkenij, aut alterius cuiusquam tenebrionis nomine fictitio delituisset, quàm vt sic, larua abiecta, dum Principes blandè alloquitur, indolem suam heu! nimis infestam Illis prodidisset.
units.tr: The difference between the one who addresses and the one who instructs others by the duty of exhortation, To whom one speaks, is certainly very great. Our author, in his book On the Office of Princes, wished his own name to stand: {a}ROBERT BELLARMINE. I confess this was done openly; but also very unwisely, unless perhaps he wholly disowns any kinship with that Robert Bellarmine who not long ago published the book {b}On the Power of the Supreme Pontiff (namely over princes), which was condemned at once by the {c}Parisian Senate and forbidden to men of the French nation, because it {d}contained a doctrine pertaining to the overthrow of supreme powers established by God, stirring up rebellion, and inciting men to plot against the heads and dominions of princes, and to disturb the public peace. Therefore he would have served his name and his cause better had he hidden under some fictitious name, such as Tortus or Schulkenius, or that of some other obscure fellow, rather than, with his mask thrown off, while he flatteringly addresses princes, reveal to them his disposition, alas! all too hostile to them.

units.la: Titulum CARDINALIS apud Principes haud magnam mereri gratiam.
units.tr: The title of CARDINAL does not earn much favour with princes.

units.la: NEc equidem video cur Bellarminus in animum suum induxerit se Cardinalis titulo beneuolentiam facilius apud Principes conciliaturum, cùm quibus ausus erat, quà {a} Cardinalis, improbà se lance componere: qui procul dubiò existimarent Eum digniorem gratiâ suâ, ni ipse se illà nimis dignum esse censuisset.
units.tr: Nor indeed do I see why Bellarmine has persuaded himself that by the title of Cardinal he would more easily win the goodwill of princes, when he had dared to weigh them, as a Cardinal, in a dishonest balance: men who would undoubtedly judge him unworthy of their favour, unless he himself had judged himself all too worthy of it.

units.la: Quid quod Cardinalis honori sibi ducit istius se quondam scholæ{f} Alumnum fuisse, quam Societatem Iesu indigitant. Factio hominum, qui (fatente Massonio){g} Videntur soli societatem contraxisse cum Iesu, in eo sanè nimium sapientes, quod putant se cœlo ipsi aliquando imperaturos. Nec hoc solum, sed {h}Penes quos (ut ipsi iactant) est Imperium literarum. En Iesuitarum modestiam! Nos verò hoc in loco non de Literatura Imperio, sed de obsequio Principibus debito ab his novis [illegible, ~8 letters] spreto effractoque litem intendimus. Multò scilicet tolerabiliori in loco res constaret Christiana, si tantum imperia litera-rum.
units.tr: What of the fact that the Cardinal counts it an honour to have been a pupil of that school which they call the Society of Jesus? A faction of men who (as Massonius admits) seem alone to have entered into partnership with Jesus, and are certainly very wise in this, in that they think they will one day rule heaven itself. Nor is this all: those in whose hands (as they boast) lies the empire of letters. Behold the modesty of the Jesuits! But in this place we are not pressing a suit about the empire of letters, but about the obedience owed to princes, which these newcomers have spurned and broken. Certainly Christendom would stand in a much more tolerable position if there were only empires of letters

units.la: {f} Bellar. epist. dedic. ante lib. de Arte m riendi: vocat hanc Piam matrem suam. [?] rum[?], & non Imperiorum litera & arcana penes Iesuitas essent. Quae enim secta, post hominum memoriam, magis [illegible, ~6 letters] quae magis, cum seculum abiurauerit, seculi pedisequa, ne dicam magistra ac Domina? Ipsa quae (vt Pontificij ipsi querúntur) Formidolosa Regibus esse {i} coepit: Cuius primus fundator Ignatius Loyola praditor fuit{k} aduersus auum Regis Nauarreni: & Filij patrissant heu! satis bene, sequitur enim apud Oratorem; Nec igitur mirum (inquit) si hic pater tot perfidos filios genuerit. Haec ille de spiritu Ignatiano, quem Thuanus Consiliarius Regius, & Curiae Parisiensis nuper Praeses, suis in Parricidas Elegijs eleganter in hunc modum perstrinxit;
units.tr: {f} Bellar. epist. dedic. ante lib. de Arte m riendi: he calls this his Pious Mother. ...rum[?], and the letters and secrets of empires were not in the hands of the Jesuits. For what sect, within living memory, has been more ... than this one, which, though it has renounced the world, is more the servant of the world, not to say its teacher and mistress? This is the very order which (as the Papists themselves complain) has begun to be feared by kings. {i} Its first founder, Ignatius Loyola, was a commander {k} against the grandfather of the King of Navarre; and the sons, alas, have followed their father all too well, for the orator goes on: Nor is it surprising, then (he says) if this father has begotten so many treacherous sons. Thus he wrote of the Ignatian spirit, which Thuanus, royal counsellor and recent president of the Parisian court, neatly lashed in his elegies against the regicides, in these words:

units.la: {1}Atque utinam nunquam tibi crus, dux Loyola secta, Icisset Leuâ missa sagitta manu. Quàm bello plus pace noces! & ad otia versus Crudelis animum vertis ad insidias.
units.tr: {1}Would that the crossbow bolt launched by a left hand had never struck your leg, Loyola, leader of the sect! How much more harm you do in war than in peace! And in your leisure you turn your cruel mind to plots.

units.la: Sed fustibus Illi potius quàm versibus profligandi, nonne? dicant igitur (si possunt) cur Galli primum, deinde Veneti, post Hungari, Bohemi, aliaeque Respublicae Christianae, caeteris Pontificiae religionis Sacerdotibus intrà fines suos acceptis retentisque, hos solos regnis & ditionibus suis exegerunt? Quoties igitur apud me cogito, (Bellarmine) Te doctrinam istam tàm exosam & planè exitiosam Regibus, quam olim in isthac Societate puer imbiberas, alijs postea propinâsse, duplici de causa dolore afficior; tùm quòd Tu Societatem istam vnquàm noueras, tùm quòd Illa Te.
units.tr: But these men are to be overthrown with cudgels rather than with verses, is it not so? Let them then say (if they can) why the French first, then the Venetians, afterwards the Hungarians, Bohemians, and other Christian commonwealths, while they admitted and kept the other priests of the Papist religion within their borders, drove out these alone from their kingdoms and dominions. So whenever I consider within myself, Bellarmine, that you have poured out to others that doctrine, so hateful and utterly ruinous to kings, which as a boy you had once soaked up in that Society, I am troubled by a twofold grief: first, that you ever knew that Society, and then that it knew you.

units.la: Bellarmini de suis Principibus simulatam gratulationem esse, & gloriationem inanem.
units.tr: Bellarmine's own princes claim that their congratulation was feigned and his boasting empty.

units.la: TAm blanditèr se insinuat Cardinalis in Principum benevolentiam, vt Suada ipsa, puto, si vel maximè vellet maiori artificio in Eorum animos influere non posset: “iactat enim Se merito gloriari posse Ecclesiam Rom. “ hâc « hāc nostrā ætate Reges aliusque Principes primarios omnes « tàm omninò Egregios, tamque tund quo[?] pietate ac iusti« tiâ conspicuos habere, quasi Admonitione nulla indigeant; & proinde scripsisse tantùm vt eis optimum regimen gratularetur. Egregium profecto Bellarmini de Principibus præconium, si liceret Nobis isthoc non credenti Illi credere: qui etiam in his de officio Principis libris secum submurmurantes, {n}Vtinam (inquit) non quotidie audiremus Principes cum Episcopis rixantes, &c. Sic Ille. Hæccine vero gratulantis gloriantisque vox est, an non potius exprobrantis, & penitus indignantis? non quidem quòd Episcopi cum Principibus, sed quòd Principes cum Episcopis, idque quotidie, rixantur. Itâ prima Eius Gloriatio nouâ hac deploratione obruitur. Tantumne vero Tibi ocij, Bellarmine, fuit, vt aut gloriabundus tecum ipse luderes; aut idonei Tibi Principes vestri videntur, quibus ementita gratulatione tàm aperte illuderes? Quanquam (nam nihil Nos quicquam de Principis cuiusquam laude debità detractum volumus) Opus hoc Bellarmini non tàm Principibus gratulandi, quàm Pontificibus & Episcopis gratificandi studio elaboratum atque editum fuisse, liber eius, vel me tacente, satis profitetur.
units.tr: Cardinal Bellarmine insinuates himself so flatteringly into the goodwill of princes that I think even Eloquence herself could not do it more artfully if she tried with all her skill. For he boasts that the Roman Church may rightly glory that in our age kings and all the other chief princes are so thoroughly outstanding and conspicuous for piety and justice that they seem to need no admonition at all; and that he therefore wrote only to congratulate them on the best rule. A remarkable eulogy of princes indeed, if we could believe him when we do not believe him: he who even in these books On the Office of a Prince, muttering to himself, says, Would that we did not every day hear of princes quarrelling with bishops, and so on. Thus he. But is this the voice of one congratulating and boasting, or rather of one reproaching and deeply indignant? Not indeed that bishops quarrel with princes, but that princes quarrel with bishops, and daily at that. So his first boast is overwhelmed by this new lament. Did you have so much leisure, Bellarmine, that you either played with yourself in self-glorification, or do your princes seem to you fit subjects on whom to mock so openly with feigned congratulation? Yet (for we do not wish any prince's due praise to be taken away) that this work of Bellarmine was laboured over and published less with the zeal of congratulating princes than of currying favour with Pontiffs and bishops, his own book makes plain enough even if I say nothing.

units.la: Bellarminorum de Regnorum iure assignando varium & incertum Arbitrium esse: Bozdam vero aduersus Principes iniquissimum.
units.tr: Bellarmine's assignment of the right to kingdoms is varied and uncertain, and his view of it against princes is most unjust.

units.la: {o}CUr Sereniss. Principi Vladislao opus suum Cardinalis dicauerit, caussam præcipuam attexit, Quia nimirum unus is in prima iuuentutis flore, ac si veteranus Imperator esset, exercitum sapienter duxit, bella grauissima gerit, &c. Quòd tanti Principis res tàm præclarè gestas tantis effers laudibus, amicè factis & benignè; quòd autem Regi Suecie, & Moscouiæ Ducì, aliisque Regibus bella, armaq; subministaris[?], animumq; Principis ad bellum gerendum tantoperè accendis & instigas, in eo nomen men tuum, Bellarmine, fere syllabice exprimis: idque in ea causa, in qua nemini magis quam Tibi ipsi bellum iudicere videare. Verba tua recognosce, obsecro. "{p}Tibi (inquis) regna multa & maxima acquirenda, deinde iniuste erepta recuperanda sunt, &c. Sic hoc in loco Orator, qui alibi disputator plane contrarium. "{q}Etiamsi (inquis) qui regna initio constituerunt, fuerint invasores ut plurimum, tamen successu temporis vel ipsi, vel successores eorum fiunt legitimi Principes, quia populi paulatim consentiunt. Hoc modo regnum Francorum, nunc omnium consensu legitimum, licet initio Franci iniuste Gallias occupaverint: atque idem dici potest de regno Hispaniae, & Anglorum. Quamuis autem, in causis huiusmodi, Praescriptionis & communis consensus ius obtinere debere Theologi omnes agnoscant, nihilominus Galliarum & Hispaniarum Regibus communi populi consensu multis iam seculis feliciter stabilitis; Vobis tamen integrum est, in Regum fere omnium praeiudicium, inductae Praescriptionis lege omni spreta atque excusa, docere, "{r}Ad Pontificis Rom. liberalitatem, scilicet, confugiendum esse; cuius est (inquit Bozius vester) ligare & soluere, Regna transferre & imperia. Ita Papae arbitrio interuenient "{s}(Vae vae) nigra candida, distorta recta, infera supera fiunt. Nonne vos pudet dogma tam portentosum tamque Principibus perniciosum astruere? Miseros Principes, si mala sua intelligant; miseriores si incauti non intelligant. Iners malorum remedium ignorantia.
units.tr: Why he dedicated his work to the most serene Prince Vladislaus, the Cardinal gives as the chief reason: because this prince, in the first flower of youth, has led his army wisely as if he were a veteran emperor and wages the most serious wars, and so on. That you praise so highly and so kindly the so brilliant achievements of so great a prince is fine. But that you supply wars and arms to the King of Sweden, the Duke of Muscovy and other kings, and so eagerly stir up and urge the prince to wage war, in this you almost spell out your own name, Bellarmine, in a matter where you seem to be judge of war for no one more than yourself. Recall your own words, I beg you: "For you (you say) many great kingdoms are to be acquired, and then those unjustly snatched away are to be recovered, etc." So here speaks the orator; elsewhere the disputant says quite the opposite: "Even if (you say) those who first established kingdoms were for the most part usurpers, nevertheless with the passage of time they, or their successors, become lawful princes, because the peoples gradually consent. In this way the kingdom of the Franks, now lawful by the consent of all, although the Franks at the beginning unjustly occupied Gaul; and the same can be said of the kingdoms of Spain and England." Although all theologians acknowledge that in causes of this kind the right of prescription and of common consent ought to prevail, nevertheless, with the kings of France and Spain happily established for many centuries by the common consent of the people, it is open to you, to the prejudice of almost all kings, to scorn and cast aside the law of prescription and teach that "one must flee to the liberality of the Roman Pontiff, whose office (says your Bozius) is to bind and loose, to transfer kingdoms and empires." Thus by the Pope's judgement "(woe, woe) black becomes white, crooked straight, low high." Are you not ashamed to assert a dogma so monstrous and so pernicious to princes? Wretched princes, if they understood their evils; more wretched if, being careless, they do not understand. Ignorance is a sluggish remedy for evils.

units.la: Bellarmini monitis plerumq; eruditionis satis, equitatis pa- rum inesse; ubi se ipsum facit scripturarum interpretem.
units.tr: Bellarmine's admonitions have commonly plenty of learning but little fairness, where he makes himself the interpreter of Scripture.

units.la: e Suarez Tom. 2 a. in Thom. disp. 46. Sect. 1 n. 12. humanioris literaturae eruditionem eius exquisitam agnoscimus; & modo quis Illi Theologiae scholasticae accuratam intelligentiam tribuat, minimè repugnamus: at {B}llarminum cum esse Sacerdotem, ex cuius ore Principes officij sui momenta requirere debeant, id vero iustis de causis pernegamus. Quale enim, Deus bone! Os illud est, quod saepissime non Divini oraculi genuina interpretamenta, sed ingenij sui deliramenta refudit? Talia enim sunt ea (vt saltem gustum aliquem Lectoris capiat) quibus a Christum in Papam: x Omnes in Solos: y Iudicem in personam iudicandam: z Manducationem in Monarchiam: * Praeceptum in permissionem: * tributi pensionem (quae est subiectionis nota exploratissima) in Praelatura praerogatiua nouis & insigniter distortis glossematis transformauit. O nos obtusos Protestantes, quibus non licet tam cernere acutum. Immensi operis esset, omnes eas Interpretationes persequi, quas emisit non solum praeter, sed etiam contra vnanimem consensum Patrum. Vt nihil discam de Contradictionibus, quibus Labia eius in infinitum diffident atque dissentiunt [?].
units.tr: e Suarez, vol. 2a on Thomas, disp. 46, sect. 1, n. 12. literature, and we acknowledge his exquisite learning in it; and if anyone credits him with an accurate grasp of scholastic theology, we do not strongly object. But that he is a priest from whose mouth princes ought to seek the essentials of their office, this we deny for good reasons. For what sort of mouth is that, good God, which very often has poured out not the genuine interpretations of a divine oracle but the ravings of its own wit? For such are those (so that the reader may at least get a taste) by which he has turned a: Christ into the Pope; x: all into only; y: a judge into a person to be judged; z: eating into monarchy; *: a command into a permission; *: the payment of tribute (the most certain mark of subjection) into a prerogative of prelacy, by new and remarkably twisted glosses. O us dull Protestants, to whom it is not granted to see so sharply! It would be an immense task to pursue all the interpretations he has put out, which are not only beyond but even against the unanimous consent of the Fathers. Not to mention the contradictions in which his lips endlessly differ and dissent.

units.la: Bellarminum Principes suos Legendis futilibus, tanquam siliquis, pascendos curare.
units.tr: Bellarmine has his princes fed on trifling legends, as on husks.

units.la: Quanto in precio apud Pontificios habeantur historiae, quas (honoris causa) Legendas aureas vocant, lippis & tonsoribus notum; etiamsi viris quibusdam cordatis & veritatis amantibus plane plumbeae esse videantur; b Monstra continentes ... & fabularum plena, quibus veritas ipsa labefactatur. Cuius furfuris fabellis, veluti opiparis bellarijs, se nimium oblectat c Bellar. quem non dispuduit obiectum, ex Beda, visionem de viridi & florentissimo prato apud inferos, à Serenissimo Rege nostro festiuè religiosèque explosam, seriò d regerere denuo. Quam tamen Suarius Iesuita (in hoc diuersus à Bellarmino, --- cetera penè gemellus) nisi e Metaphoricè intellectum, fide omni indignam censuit. De visione alia verisimillima, scilicet, quid dicam? nempe {f}Uallis apud Inferos, in qua miserae[?] animae coguntur ingiter prosilire in medium frigoris intolerabilis, & in ardentem[?] reflire in medium flammae inextinguibilis.
units.tr: How highly the Papists value the histories which they call, by way of honour, the Golden Legends is known to bleary-eyed men and barbers, although to some sensible men who love the truth they seem utterly leaden, containing monsters ... and full of fables by which truth itself is undermined. With the bran of these fables, as with rich sweetmeats, the Cardinal delights himself too much. He was not ashamed to throw at us, taken from Bede, the vision of a green and flourishing meadow among the dead, which our most serene King had wittily and devoutly exploded, and he seriously rehashes it again. Yet the Jesuit Suarez (in this differing from Bellarmine, otherwise almost his twin) judged it unworthy of all belief unless understood metaphorically. As for another, most probable vision, namely, what shall I say? A valley among the dead in which wretched souls are forced continually to leap out into the middle of intolerable cold and to flee back into the middle of inextinguishable flame.

units.la: O dura lectorum; vel certe scriptorum illa! Id genus quisquilias si quis cupiat, habet hic {b}liber Bellarmini quod det, & quidem largiter; Nobis nunquam visas visiones obtrudens Animae deportatae in caelum. Multum splendentium se apud sedem Apostolicam procuratoris honorem caelestem Sancto defuncto: Petri Apostoli locum (ubi nunc Westmonasteriense templum est situm) proprijs consecrantis manibus. De huiusmodi historiis nihil Ego aliud dicam, quam quod de similibus, ex Ludovico, Canus vester; {i}Eos, qui pietatis loco duxerunt mendacia pro religione fingere, nihil aliud egisse videri, quam ut veris propter falsa admittat fides.
units.tr: O hard-hearted readers, or rather writers! If anyone wants trifles of this kind, this book of Bellarmine has something to give, and generously too, obtruding visions never seen by us: the soul carried off into heaven. Much splendid heavenly honour, a procurator presenting himself at the Apostolic See for a saint who had died, consecrating with his own hands the place of the Apostle Peter (where the Westminster church now stands). About histories of this kind I will say nothing else than what your Canus said of similar ones, quoting Ludovicus: Those who thought it a pious act to invent lies for religion seem to have done nothing other than make faith accept true things for the sake of false ones.

units.la: Perge uero Lector, nisi molestum est, & intelliges à Leone Pontifice {k}Edwardi Regis Votum, ut Deo gratum & laudabile approbari, & mox Eum ab eiusdem Voti peccato absolui: Satyrum dixeris, qui ex eodem ore simul [illegible, ~9 letters] exhalat. Aliquando {l}Pauperes Regi Stephano barbam bono animo euellere; & S. Regem subinde B. Mariam invocare, & in hunc modum exclamare; Ecce Regem, quem Tu constituisti, sic honorant milites tui; quae si mihi ab hoste aliquo illata esset iniuria, tuo fultus adivtorio, non sinerem inultum abire. Divi te (Chartuici) Divaeque donent tonsore, pro hoc, de Stephani barba, tam lepido commento. Pedem vix progrediere, & providentiae exemplum accipies ad unguem factum; nam idem {n}Sanctus Stephanus Eremita cuidam Regni sui curam demandat, qui liberalitate (de re nempe aliena) in pauperes res omnes Aulae exinanit. In Eremita vero nihil non sanctum: non illud Aegypti Eremita, qui {o}Solitudinem ingressus est, ut pacem inter Deum & Diabolum componeret, sed nihil à Daemone obtinere potuit. Mitto misericordiae specimen, quod Alredus Monachus Bellarmino persuasit, in exemplo S. Edwardi Regis, qui;
units.tr: Go on, reader, if it is not tiresome, and you will learn from Pope Leo that King Edward's vow, as pleasing and praiseworthy to God, was approved, and soon he was absolved from the sin of that same vow. You might call it satire, which from the same mouth breathes out [illegible, ~9 letters]. At one time paupers plucked King Stephen's beard with good intentions; and the holy king repeatedly invoked the Blessed Virgin and cried out in this way: Behold the King whom you have set up; thus your soldiers honour him. If any injury had been done to me by some enemy, supported by your help, I would not have let it go unavenged. May the saints (you Carthusians) and saintly women reward you, along with the barber, for this charming fiction about Stephen's beard. Scarcely will you advance a foot before you receive an example of providence made to the nail; for the same Saint Stephen the Hermit entrusts the care of a certain part of his kingdom to a man who, out of liberality (with other people's property, namely), empties all the court's goods upon the poor. But in the hermit there is nothing that is not holy: not that Egyptian hermit who entered solitude to make peace between God and the Devil, but could obtain nothing from the Demon. I pass over the specimen of mercy which the monk Alred persuaded Bellarmine of, in the example of Saint King Edward, who;

units.la: {†}Ut spiritualis asinus, miraculi causâ, claudum humeris portabat. Cui forte quis rectius, quod de claudo clamoso populus apud Poëtam, Quare peregrinum. Hæc (ut alia multa omittam) satis ostendunt ex quàm turbidis fontibus quam cœnosos riuulos Bellarminus in Tractatum suum deriuauerit: de quibus illud Theologi Pontificij merito vsurpem.; {q}Dolenter dico potiùs quam contumeliosè, multò à Lactio[?], & ethnicis Historicis Philosophorum vitas seueriùs scriptas, quàm à Christianis vitas Sanctorum. Cum itaque, ne frustra sint libri, inter Authorem ac Lectorem semper supponatur proportio, insignem certè Principibus intulit Bellarminus contumeliam, dum huiusmodi fabulatorum quisquilias ijs apponit, quasi muscas à cæcis devorandas.
units.tr: As a spiritual donkey, for the sake of a miracle, it carried the lame man on its shoulders. To him one might more fittingly apply what the people say in the poet about the lame man who cries out: "Why a foreigner?" These examples (to leave out many others) sufficiently show from how muddy a spring and how filthy a stream Bellarmine has drawn his treatise. Of these things I may rightly borrow the words of a Papist theologian: "I say with sorrow rather than with insult that the lives of philosophers have been written more severely by Laertius and the pagan historians than the lives of the saints have been written by Christians." Since, so that books are not written in vain, a proportion must always be presumed between author and reader, Bellarmine has certainly inflicted a notable insult on princes, in that he sets such trifles of these fabulists before them, as if they were flies to be devoured by the blind.

units.la: Applicationem Exemplorum, de Principum humilitate, ad ipsorum honorem imminuendum, egregiè à Bellarmino peruerti.
units.tr: The application of the examples about the humility of princes, to diminish their honour, is cleverly perverted by Bellarmine.

units.la: Sunt quos Exemplis, sunt quos Præceptis erudiri iuuat: ab exemplis facilior & tritior, à præceptis tutior firmiorque discendi ratio proponitur. Bellarminus pietatis iustitiæque regulam absolutam constituit in Sanctorum suorum duntaxat Exemplis; {r}Quæ (inquit) qui Princeps sequitur errare non poterit. At qui ad hominum, quamuis Sanctorum, Exempla mores aliorum fingi & efformari volunt, perinde mihi facere videntur (nam quot in sacra pagina sanctorum Patriarcharum, Sacerdotum, Prophetarum, Regum, & Apostolorum commemorantur:) acsi dent operam vt imitentur Ethnicorum quorundâ insaniam; inter quos Poëtæ bibacitatem Ennij; Philosophi contractos Platonis humeros, Aristotelisque balbutiem; Milites Alexandri Imp. proiectam ceruicem, leuitatem oculorum, & vocis quandam asperitatem agrestem; Subditi denique (vt apud Aethiopes) Regum suorum morbos imitati sunt. Sanctos igitur vltra humanam fortem sanctissimos esse oportet, quos Sine errore quisquam sequi poterit; quales Sanctos tuos non fuisse, praeter eos, quos dedimus, instantiae multae demonstrent.
units.tr: Some people like to be taught by examples, others by precepts: the method of learning from examples is easier and more familiar, while the method from precepts is safer and firmer. Bellarmine sets up an absolute rule of piety and justice in the examples of his saints alone. "A prince who follows these," he says, "cannot go astray." But those who want the morals of others to be shaped and formed by the examples of men, however holy, seem to me to act as if they were trying to imitate the madness of certain pagans: among them, the poet Ennius's drunkenness; the philosophers Plato's hunched shoulders and Aristotle's stammering; the soldiers of Emperor Alexander his stiff neck, the wandering of his eyes and a certain rustic roughness of voice; and finally subjects (as among the Ethiopians) imitated the diseases of their kings. The saints, then, must be most holy beyond human frailty if anyone can follow them without error; that they were not such saints as yours, apart from those we have given, many instances demonstrate.

units.la: Ad Exempla veniamus, quae sunt Causae ipsi propria, quibus Bellarminus Principes suos ad Humilitatem erudiit, praesertim erga Sacerdotes. Nobis, ut experiamur aquam marinam esse falsam, non necesse est mare totum ebibere; nec, ut Bellarmini mentem assequamur, multa Exempla reperire opus est. Liber integer De officio Principis inscribitur: Exempla huius Officii proponuntur Principum pedes Pontificis exosculantium; Imperatoris semel, non sedentis, nisi annuentibus Episcopis: deinde Regis non bibentis, priusquam Presbyter poculum delibasset. Haec & similia Bellarminus Exempla in praecepta vertit, & actiones liberae devotionis & zeli trahit in legem officii; tandemque concludit, Sacerdotes esse Regibus superiores. Sed, Nil agit exemplum quod exemplo dissonitur; nam posito, quod quae Sancti ex humilitate liberè fecerint, necessario sint facienda, tum sequetur (nam haec quoque Exempla humilitatis profert) quoties Regi cum{f} Imperatore conferendum est, Imperatorem potius ad Regem, quam Regem ad Imperatorem honoris causa debere accedere: {t}Reges suis ipsos manibus vinum Sacerdotibus inter sacra libare, & thura subministrare; Imperatorem{u} Ecclesiarum hospitia visere, aegrotis in lecto decumbentibus curationem{x} adhibere, tractare ollas, elucre pocula, omniaque praestare, quae servi & ancillae exequi solent: Denique duces, Monacho iubente, *ex equis desilire: Imo (ne de Pontificibus exempla desint) Pontificem Se humi coram Abbate prosternere: & Archiepiscopo benè literato, **sequestrato illo Romani supercilii factu, honoris causa, dignanter assurgere. Iccirco (ut uno verbo dicam) Lex ab Exemplis est Regula lesbia.
units.tr: Let us come to the examples, which are proper to the cause itself, by which Bellarmine has trained his princes to humility, especially towards priests. For us, to find out that sea water is salty, it is not necessary to drink up the whole sea; nor, to grasp Bellarmine's mind, is it necessary to find many examples. An entire book is entitled On the Office of the Prince: the examples of this office are set forth as princes kissing the feet of the Pontiff; an emperor who did not sit down except when the bishops nodded assent; then a king who did not drink until the priest had tasted the cup. Bellarmine turns these and similar examples into precepts, and draws actions of free devotion and zeal into the law of duty; and at last he concludes that priests are superior to kings. But "an example achieves nothing if it disagrees with an example"; for granting that what the saints freely did out of humility must necessarily be done, it would then follow (for these examples of humility also bring forth this) that whenever a king is to be compared with an emperor, the emperor ought, for the sake of honour, to approach the king rather than the king the emperor: that kings should pour wine for priests with their own hands during sacred rites and serve incense; that an emperor should visit the hospices of the Churches, apply care to the sick lying in bed, handle pots, wash cups, and perform all the things that male and female servants usually do; finally, that dukes, at a monk's command, should dismount from their horses: indeed (lest examples of Pontiffs be lacking) that a Pontiff should prostrate himself on the ground before an Abbot, and that he should graciously rise, as a courtesy, for a learned archbishop, having set aside that haughtiness of Roman pride. Therefore, to say it in one word, the law drawn from examples is a Lesbian rule.*

units.la: S. IX. Illorum vanitas amplius illustratur.
units.tr: IX. Their vanity is further illustrated.

units.la: {y}Iosephi Stephani Valentini Doctoris Theologi, Canonici Ecclesiæ Segobricensis; De potestate coactiva quam Rom. Pontifex exercet in negotiis secularibus. Ad Sanctiss. D. Sixtum V. Pont. Ex authoritate superiorum. Romæ 1586.
units.tr: Joseph Stephen Valentine, Doctor of Theology, Canon of the Church of Segovia; On the coercive power which the Roman Pontiff exercises in secular affairs. Dedicated to the most holy Lord Sixtus V, Pope. By the authority of superiors. Rome, 1586.

units.la: x Cap.12.pag. 357.
Pontificiorum Sacerdotum præposteram esse honorum supra Principes affectationem.
units.tr: The preposterous ambition of the Papist priests for honours above princes.
