units.la: IN hac Controuersia Sacerdotes Pontificij omni industriæ, eruditionis, ingenijque aucupio honorem suum amplificare, etiam supra Principes, conantur; sed tamen tam præposterè, tam inconditè, tam monstroseid [?] faciunt, vt quiuis intelligat Eos, vbi maximè scientiam suam ostentant, maximè perdidisse scientiam sui. Inter quos{7} Stephanus Valentinus, in libro de coactiua Pontificis potestate, quem Sixto Quinto Pont. nuncupauit, se Helenam hanc in Vtopia reperisse gestit; {2} Apud Vtopienses insulanos (inquit) Sacerdotes nulli subsunt, omnibus præsunt, vt ait Thomas Morus lib. 2. Vtopiæ.
units.tr: In this controversy the Papist priests, by hunting for every kind of industry, learning and talent, try to enlarge their honour, even above princes; but they do it so preposterously, so inelegantly, so monstrously, that anyone can see that they lose their own self-knowledge most of all just where they display their learning most. Among them, Stephen Valentine, in his book on the coercive power of the Pontiff, which he dedicated to Pope Sixtus V, rejoices to have found this Helen in Utopia: "Among the Utopian islanders," he says, "priests are subject to no one, and preside over all, as Thomas More says in book 2 of Utopia."

units.la: Atque Hactenus [illegible, ~8 letters]. Quæ in Opere sequuntur multò copiosiùs ostendunt, Eos, qui ex rasis capitibus omnem terrenarum cupiditatum, ceu Retium, abiectionem profitentur; plurimùm accendi gloriæ studio, & præcellentiæ suæ imaginem quodammodò deperire. Nunc Cavssam ipsam REGIAM [illegible, ~6 letters] aggrediar, quam Bellarminus in tribus Capitulis, De officio principis, erga Tres eius Superiores complexus est; I. Erga summum Pontificem, II. Erga Episcopum proprium: III. Erga proprium Confessorem...
units.tr: And so far [illegible]. What follows in the work shows much more fully that those who profess, from shaven heads, the renunciation of all earthly desires, as if it were a net, are greatly inflamed with the zeal for glory and in some way lose the image of their own pre-eminence. Now I shall take up the royal cause itself [illegible], which Bellarmine, in three chapters, On the Office of the Prince, has embraced in relation to his three superiors: I. towards the supreme Pontiff; II. towards his own bishop; III. towards his own confessor...

units.la: IN TRACTATUM IPSUM Cardinalis BELLARMINI, De Officio Principis Christiani, ANIMADVERSIONES. CAP. I.
units.tr: Animadversions on the Treatise of Cardinal Bellarmine, On the Duty of a Christian Prince. Chapter I.

units.la: Partitio totius Operis.
units.tr: The division of the whole work.

units.la: "Diuiditur in quatuor Considerationes,
units.tr: "It is divided into four considerations,

units.la: "pro numero; videlicet, Relationum, si-
units.tr: "by number; namely, of the relations, or habitudes,

units.la: "ue habitudinum,quas habent Principes ad 1 Superiores, 2 Inferiores, 3 Pares; deuls[?] 4 Seipsos.
units.tr: "which princes have toward (1) superiors, (2) inferiors, (3) equals, and (4) themselves.

units.la: In fine Præf. ad Lect. & initio Lib.
units.tr: At the end of the Preface to the Reader and at the beginning of the Book.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: First Animadversion.

units.la: Partitionem hanc nonnullam sinistra mentis su- spicionem ingerere.
units.tr: That this division suggests some sinister suspicion of mind.

units.la: Vereor equidem, nec sanè immeritò, ne Partitio hæc omnibus Principibus inuidiosa, atque etiam, ex amphibolia huius vocis [Svperiorvs] insidiosa nimis videri possit; vtpote quâ à Republica ciues germani; à Regibus natiui Subditi, ceu vel [illegible, ~3 letters] ac germana membra à Corpore, vel à capite partes subiectæ[?] distrahantur prorsus atque diuellantur. Agè vero (Te obsecro,) Bellarmine; dicito ecquem in suis Regnis Principibus ipsis omninò Superiorem constituere vobis fas erit, præter Regem Regum immortalem solum Deum?
units.tr: I indeed fear, and not without reason, that this division may seem to all princes hateful, and even too insidious, on account of the ambiguity of this word [Superior]; by which fellow citizens are separated from the Commonwealth, natural subjects from kings, as true and kindred limbs are torn and utterly pulled away from the body, or subject parts from the head. Come now, I beg you, Bellarmine, tell me: will it be lawful for you to set any superior over princes themselves in their own kingdoms, apart from God alone, the immortal King of kings?

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Duty.

units.la: “ Princeps quatuor agnoscere debet Superiores, sive verè Christi-
units.tr: "A prince ought to acknowledge four superiors, if he wishes to be and be considered truly a Christian;

units.la: “ anus dici & haberi velit; Deum optimum maximum, Pontificem summum, Episcopum proprium, & proprium Confessorem. — Pag.1.
units.tr: "God, the best and greatest, the Supreme Pontiff, his own Bishop, and his own Confessor. — Page 1.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Scopum Animadversionum sequentium praecipuum, Mai- estatis Principum defensionem esse.
units.tr: First Animadversion. The chief aim of the following animadversions is the defence of the majesty of princes.

units.la: NOlo ego huius distributionis membra curiosius perscrutari, nec enim dubito quin Tu iam non Logici, sed Theologici Professoris munere fungare: & sanè nostri instituti erit ea potissimum notare, atque connectere, in quibus Principibus omnem salutis spem penitus eripuisse; vel sanctitatis opinionem deflorasse; vel etiam obfuscasse dignitatis splendorem ac reuerentiam; vel denique ipsissimam Authoritatem Regiam debilitasse, ac plane labefactasse videare. Dum haec persequor, Bellarmine, ordinem tuum sequar, tuisque vestigiis insistam. Vt igitur à Pontifice Superiore auspicemur.
units.tr: I do not wish to examine the parts of this division too closely, for I do not doubt that you now act less as a logician than as a professor of theology. It will certainly be my business to note and connect especially those points by which you seem to have utterly snatched away from princes all hope of salvation, or to have plucked the reputation for holiness, or even to have darkened the splendour and reverence due to their dignity, or finally to have weakened and plainly undermined the very authority of kings. As I pursue these matters, Bellarmine, I will follow your order and tread in your footsteps. Let us begin, then, with the Supreme Pontiff as superior.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Duty.

units.la: “ Princeps Pontificem summum Superiorem agnoscere debet, “ si verè Christianus dici & haberi velit. — Pag. 1.
units.tr: "A prince ought to acknowledge the Supreme Pontiff as superior, if he wishes to be and be considered truly a Christian. — Page 1.

units.la: Explicatio mentis Bellarmini.
units.tr: Explanation of Bellarmine's meaning.

units.la: Hoc est quod dixi, Te Principibus omnibus salutis spem omnem eripere, si forte Pontificis tui plusquam adamantino iugo colla sua subtraxerint; id quod Tu alibi liquidius docuisti.{a} NVLLVS cum Ecclesia communicat, qui non subest Pontifici, licet alioqui fidem Catholicam profiteatur. Unio enim cum Capite est nota Ecclesiae.
units.tr: This is what I said: that you take away from all princes every hope of salvation, if perhaps they withdraw their necks from the yoke of your Pontiff, which is more than adamantine; a point you have taught more plainly elsewhere.{a} NO ONE communicates with the Church who is not subject to the Pontiff, even if he otherwise professes the Catholic faith. For union with the Head is the mark of the Church.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Dogma Bellarminianum novum, & ex maligna, adversus Principes, Pontificis mente primo profectum esse.
units.tr: First Animadversion. That the Bellarminian dogma is new, and that it arose first from the malice of the Pontiff against princes.

units.la: PAtrissas[?], Bellarmine, sat bene, jamdudum enim Pater ille tuus Pontifex Bonifacius VIII. circa Annum MCCC id prius decreuerat. {b}Subesse (inquit) Romano Pontifici omnem humanam creaturam declaramus, dicimus, definimus, & pronunciamus esse de necessitate salutis. Satis pro imperio. hoc enim decretum istius Pontificis maximi ex maximo in Principes odio profectum esse, & de insano & virulento pectore ebullisse, historiae vestrae luculenter ostendunt; quae nimirum Bonifacium istum sic definiuisse aiunt, quando {c}Ille maiori incensus odio mittebat in Galliam quendam Clericum Romanum, & Archidiaconum Narbonensem cum literis, quas publicari iubebat; illa autem continebant diras in Philippum Pulchrum Galliae Regem, nisi in temporalibus aeque ac in spiritualibus Subditum se Pontifici profiteretur: Quandoque {d}Ipse Bonifacius Pontificiâ auctoritate (Historici vestri verba repeto) in perniciem Christianorum abutebatur. Quid porro? Ipsus Rex Regum num Eorum iura violari, ac fulmine dispelli, & Christianae Reipub. membra istius Pontificis decreto tam horrido discindi & lacerari impune passus est? non opinor; quid enim Bonifacio paulo ante mortem contigerat ex vestro Massonio discas velim. {e}Bonifacius ex dolore animi (inquit) in morbum tam violentum incidit, ut ipse sibi membra roderet. Ecce Nemesin Dei, & [illegible, ~6 letters]! quodammodo juxta legem talionis.
units.tr: You speak well enough, Bellarmine, for long ago that Pontiff of yours, Boniface VIII, had decreed this around the year 1300. "We declare, say, define, and pronounce," he says, "that it is altogether necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff."{b} That is enough for his empire. Your own histories clearly show that this decree of that most high Pontiff arose from the greatest hatred toward princes and boiled up from his mad and venomous breast. They say that Boniface defined it in this way when "inflamed with the greatest hatred, he sent into France a certain Roman clergyman and Archdeacon of Narbonne with letters, which he ordered to be published; these letters contained dire threats against Philip the Fair, King of France, unless he professed himself subject to the Pontiff in temporal matters as well as in spiritual ones"{c}; and at another time "Boniface himself, by papal authority (I repeat the words of your historian), was abusing it to the ruin of Christians."{d} What is more? Did the King of kings himself suffer the rights of those princes to be violated, and their thunderbolts scattered, and the members of the Christian commonwealth torn and mangled by this most horrid decree of the Pontiff, and go unpunished? I think not. I would like you to learn from your Masson what happened to Boniface shortly before his death: "Boniface, from the grief of his mind (he says), fell into so violent a sickness that he gnawed at his own limbs."{e} Behold the vengeance of God, and [illegible]! It is, in a sense, according to the law of retaliation.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: Second Animadversion.

units.la: Tutum fuisse nonnullis Christianis, absque omni Salutis dis- pendio, Pontificibus Rom. non subiici; Exemplis lucu- lentissimis Ecclesiarum celeberrimarum ostenditur, tam antiquae, quam posteriore aetatis.
units.tr: That it was safe for some Christians, without any loss of salvation, not to be subject to the Roman Pontiffs; this is shown by the clearest examples of the most celebrated Churches, both ancient and of later times.

units.la: TAntum abfuit ut prisci Christiani hanc Pontificis praerogatiuam agnoscerent, qua dicitur, Subesse Rom. Pontifici esse de necessitate salutis, ut ipsius Pontificis Rom. Excommunicationem habuerint contemptui. Primi enim (ut ex concessis causam hanc expediam) Graeci (quorum Ecclesia Reip. Christianae diu pars potissima fuit, nec reuerà vnquàm Romanae Ecclesiae subdita) Diu.si fuerunt ab Ecclesia Romana annis octingentis. Etiam, {g}Omnes Ecclesiae Asiae à Victore Pontifice (vt dicitis) excommunicatae fuerunt: Nec hae solùm, (quamuis {h}Multi ex Episcopis eorum Christi Martyres fuerunt) sed etiam {i}Aliquot Ecclesiae Occidentales eodem Anathemate Pontificis percussae. Quod Pontifex superbè admodùm & superciliosè; nec posteà mutauit factum, qui {k}Excommunicationem hanc suam non legitur mutasse. Ab Asianis ad Carthaginenses descendo.
units.tr: So far were the early Christians from acknowledging this prerogative of the Pontiff, by which it is said that being subject to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation, that they held even the excommunication of the Roman Pontiff in contempt. For first (to clear up the matter from what is granted) the Greeks (whose Church was for a long time the chief part of the Christian commonwealth, and never truly subject to the Roman Church) were cut off from the Roman Church for eight hundred years. Even all the Churches of Asia were excommunicated by Victor the Pontiff (as you say). Nor were these alone (although many of their bishops were martyrs of Christ), but also some Western Churches were struck by the same anathema of the Pontiff. The Pontiff did this most haughtily and disdainfully; nor is it read that he afterwards changed what he had done, since he did not withdraw this his excommunication. I pass from the Asians to the Carthaginians.

units.la: Secundò igitur quomodò Carthaginenses, tempore Cypriani, sese gesserint aueo scire. {l}Carthaginensibus Episcopis (octoginta septem) Stephanus Papa Romanus poenam excommunicationis comminatus est. Verum est; hanc tamen Pontificis Excommunicationem Carthaginenses non pluris fecerunt quàm inclytissimi nominis Carthaginis Praesul Cyprianus: nam {m}Cyprianum quoque Pontifex, quantùm in se erat, à Communione sua repulit, & praecepit vniuersae fraternitati, ne quis eius Legatos in domum receiperet. Quid ergo? ergonè Cyprianus ex Catholicorum albo expungendus fuit? * quo nemo vnquàm potuit Pontificem Stephanum magis contemnere; quùm praesertim {n}Cyprianus, (vt inquitis) semper est habitus in numero Catholicorum: idque merito suo, quia {o}Martyrio posteà coronatus fuit. {p}Nec tamen eius Retractatio vnquàm inuenitur. Ad Africanos festino, tempore Augustini, qui consilio Eorum interfuit.
units.tr: Second, I am eager to know how the Carthaginians behaved in the time of Cyprian. Stephen, the Roman Pope, threatened the Carthaginian bishops (eighty-seven in number) with the penalty of excommunication. That is true; yet the Carthaginians valued this excommunication of the Pontiff no more than did Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, of most illustrious name; for the Pontiff, as far as lay in him, also cast Cyprian out of his communion and ordered the whole brotherhood not to receive his envoys into their houses. What then? Was Cyprian therefore to be struck off the roll of Catholics? No one could ever have despised Pope Stephen more; especially since Cyprian (as you say) has always been counted among the number of Catholics; and this on his own merit, because he was afterwards crowned with martyrdom. Nor is any retraction of his ever found. I hasten to the Africans in the time of Augustine, who took part in their council.

units.la: Tertiò, {q}Africani Patres in Concilio restiterunt Papae Celestino, quòd contrà Conc.Niccenum venire voluit. Numquid vero impunè tulerunt Sanctissimi Patres tantum erga Pontificem contemptum? {r}Illos per centum annos Pontificis excommunicationem pertulisse, Bonifacij Papae epistola certissimè testatur. Quodsi forte quis eos Excommunicationem pertulisse negauerit, at perferre tamen voluisse nemo inficiabitur, qui illos Coelestino Papae, cum ppellationis praeiu-
units.tr: Third, the African Fathers in council resisted Pope Celestine, because he wished to act against the Council of Nicaea. But did the most holy Fathers really bear such contempt toward the Pontiff with impunity? That they endured the excommunication of the Pontiff for a hundred years is most certainly attested by the letter of Pope Boniface. But if anyone should deny that they endured excommunication, no one will deny that they were willing to endure it, who knows how sharply they resisted Pope Celestine when he falsely claimed the prerogative for himself, and who granted that from the time of Cyprian the African bishops began to be separated from the Roman Church. Among these, however, our adversaries themselves freely admit that innumerable cohorts of martyrs arose, and that in the Vandal persecution, at the hands of pagans, they won the palm of martyrdom.

units.la: {q} Cusan.Card.Cusanus ord.Caib lib.1.cap.20.
units.tr: {q} Cusanus the Cardinal, ord. Caib., lib. 1, cap. 20.

units.la: {r} Lindan.Panop.l.4 cap.48 & Cofirr. Enchirid.Tract. de Pont.p.159. & Salmeron.Ief quo infrà & Sander. de viib.monar.lib. 7.c.369. prærogatiuam falso sibi vendicanti, tam acriter restitisse nouerit; quique concesserit quod {f}A tempore Cypriani Africani Episcopi seperari cœperunt ab Ecclesia Romana. Inter quos tamen innumeras cohortes Martyrum extitisse, & in persecutione Vandalica per manus Paganorum Martyrij palmam consequutas esse, {t} Aduersarij nostri fatentur vltro.
units.tr: {r} Lindanus, Panopl., lib. 4, cap. 48; and Cofirr., Enchirid., Tract. de Pont., p. 159; and Salmeron, Ief quo infrà; and Sander, De visibili monarchia, lib. 7, cap. 369. Who knows how fiercely he resisted the prerogative falsely claimed for himself, and who conceded that {f}from the time of Cyprian, bishop of Africa, they began to be separated from the Roman Church. Among them, nevertheless, there existed countless companies of martyrs, and in the Vandal persecution they won the palm of martyrdom at the hands of the pagans; our opponents themselves freely admit this.

units.la: Quartò (nam natale me solum ad se inuitat) {u}Anti-qua Britannorum Ecclesia à communione Romanæ Sedis multo tempore fuerunt diuisa. Nempè intelligis tempus Gregorij Magni Papæ; quandò tamen {x}Eorum mille ducenti contra Northumbros infideles vno die Martyrio decorati regni cœlestis adepti sunt sedem. Quandò de Britannis loquor, non excipio {y}Scotos, qui (vt est apud Bedam) propter morem obseruandi Paschæ, non minus quàm Angli, Romanæ Ecclesiæ aduersati sunt. His pensitatis, nemo tàm excors est, qui tantarum Ecclesiarum tot myriades Martyrum diris iure deuoueri ideò censeat, vt (nec id quidem optimi) Pontificii articulus vnus, præsertim tàm nouus & execrabilis obtineat.
units.tr: Fourthly (for my native land invites me to it), {u}the ancient Church of the Britons was for a long time divided from communion with the Roman See. Clearly you understand the time of Pope Gregory the Great; yet {x}of them, twelve hundred, adorned with martyrdom in a single day by the unbelieving Northumbrians, obtained a seat in the heavenly kingdom. When I speak of the Britons, I do not exclude {y}the Scots, who (as is recorded in Bede) opposed the Roman Church no less than the English, on account of their custom of observing Easter. With these things weighed, no one is so foolish as to think that the countless myriads of martyrs of such great Churches should rightly be devoted to dreadful curses, so that (and not even this is the best course) one article of the Papists, especially one so new and detestable, should prevail.

units.la: Posteræ ætatis Exempla Aduersarij nostri non pauca recensent {a}Græcorum, Armenorum, {b}Ruthenorum, Ægyptiorum, Æthiopum, aliarumque remotiorum orbis partium; quos tamen Pontificij non audent asseuerantèr {c}Hæreticos dicere; quamuis Illi Pontificem Romanum non magis suum Superiorem, quàm Protestantes agnoscant: quorum sunt innumeri, qui iam Germaniam, Calliam, Britanniam, Poloniam, Daniam, Bohemiam, Hungariam, Helueiam, Sueuiam, Siletiam, Moraviam, Transilvaniam, aliasque orbis Christiani partes plurimas incolentes, Romanam hierarchiam, veluti Antichristianam tyrannidem auersantur. Neminem igitur esse arbitror, in quo vel mica Christiani salis inest, cui persuaderi possit omnium vndique Nationum populos tàm infinitos, qui Christum Iesum etiam cùm vitæ suæ dispendio profiteri sacro-sanctū Baptismi voto sese obstrinxerunt, Christia-
units.tr: The adversaries of ours recount not a few examples from later times: of Greeks, Armenians, {b} Ruthenians, Egyptians, Ethiopians, and other more remote parts of the world; whom the Papists do not dare to call confidently {c} heretics, although they acknowledge the Roman Pontiff no more as their superior than do the Protestants. Of these there are innumerable people who, now inhabiting Germany, France, Britain, Poland, Denmark, Bohemia, Hungary, Switzerland, Swabia, Silesia, Moravia, Transylvania, and many other parts of the Christian world, shrink from the Roman hierarchy as an Antichristian tyranny. I think therefore there is no one in whom even a grain of Christian salt remains who can be persuaded that such infinite peoples of all nations everywhere, who bound themselves by the sacred vow of Baptism to profess Christ Jesus even at the cost of their lives, are Christians...

units.la: {a} Azorius Inst. part. 1. lib. 8. cap. 20.
units.tr: {a} Azorius, Inst. part. 1, lib. 8, cap. 20.

units.la: {b} Bellarm. lib. 1. de verbo Dei cap. vlt. in fine.
units.tr: {b} Bellarm. lib. 1, de verbo Dei, cap. vlt., in fine.

units.la: {c} Azor. quo iam supra. nos iam amplius non esse, quia Romano Pontifici, tanquam suo Superiori, subijci nolunt; vel, vt fides vnius Ecclesiae stabiliatur, putet actum iam esse de salute plurimarum.
units.tr: {c} Azor., as above. They say we are no longer [members of the Church] because we refuse to be subject to the Roman Pontiff as our superior; or else, so that the faith of the one Church may be made firm, they think the salvation of very many people is already lost.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Hanc, quam obtrudunt, Vnionem cum hoc vel illo Pontifice Romano seu visibili Capite Ecclesiae tanquam Notam verae Ecclesiae; membris ipsius Romanae Ecclesiae summe esse praeiudicio.
units.tr: This union which they press upon us, with this or that Roman Pontiff, or visible Head of the Church, as a mark of the true Church, is extremely prejudicial to the members of the Roman Church itself.

units.la: NOn defuit inter viros Pontificios, qui in ipsa etiam Romana Ecclesia {d}Schismata viginti obseruauit; quorum decimum-octauum Annis viginti nouem durasse fatetur. Etenim hic parcius nobiscum egit; Eum potius consulendum duximus, qui (iuxta Aduersariorum nostrorum elogium) {e}Historiam Ecclesiasticam indefesso labore peruoluit. Ille; {f}Vnum, inquit, Schisma erat quadraginta sex Annorum: Alterum, in quo {g}Tota Resp. Christiana diuisa est; Clemens enim à Gallis, Hispanis, Scotis veneratus est; Italia vero, Hungaria, Germania, & Anglia Urbani partes sequuti sunt: durabat hoc Schisma Annis continuis quadraginta, vsque ad electionem Martini Quinti, Anno MCCCCXVII. Apagite igitur cum isthac Capitis vestri Vnione, quae fuit non solum tot Schismatum occasio, quibus Romanae Ecclesiae corpus miserè lacerabatur, sed & causa etiam iam extat istius Schismatis, quo Ecclesia Catholica hodierno die grauissime laborat.
units.tr: Among Papist writers there has not been lacking one who has noted twenty schisms within the Roman Church itself, of which he admits that the eighteenth lasted twenty-nine years. This writer dealt more sparingly with us, so I thought it better to consult the one who, by the testimony of our adversaries, has read through Church history with tireless labour. He says: "One schism lasted forty-six years. The other, in which the whole Christian commonwealth was divided: for Clement was venerated by the French, Spanish and Scots, but Italy, Hungary, Germany and England followed the party of Urban. This schism lasted for forty continuous years, until the election of Martin V in the year 1417." Away, then, with that union of your Head, which was not only the occasion of so many schisms, by which the body of the Roman Church was wretchedly torn apart, but is also now the cause of that schism by which the Catholic Church is suffering most grievously today.

units.la: De Pontificis Rom. Titulis in genere.
units.tr: On the Titles of the Roman Pontiff in general.

units.la: Bellarminus de Officio.
units.tr: Bellarmine on the Office.

units.la: "De officio Principis Christiani erga Summum Pontificem. "Quia Summus Pontifex officio fungitur in Ecclesia vniuersa Patris, Pastoris, Doctoris, Speculatoris, & summi Sacerdotis. --- Pag. 25.
units.tr: "On the office of a Christian prince toward the Supreme Pontiff. Because the Supreme Pontiff, in the whole Church, performs the office of Father, Pastor, Teacher, Overseer and Chief Priest." --- Pag. 25.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Est verò vbi Tu, de Pontificis authoritate suprema in spiritualibus agens, & {a} Argumentum sumens (vt ais) à nominibus Episcopi Romani, nomina Quindecim enumeras, videlicet; Papa, Pater Patrum, Pontifex Christianorum, Princeps Sacerdotum, Vicarius Christi, Caput Ecclesiæ, Fundamentum, Pastor ovilis Domini, Rector domus Dei, Pater, & Doctor omnium Christianorum, Sponsus Ecclesiæ, Apostolica Sedis Episcopus vniuersalis. Quorsum verò hæc tàm gloriosa nominum istorum iactantia? {b}Ex his omnibus & singulis (inquis) aperte colligitur Pontificis Primatus. At quousque, obsecro, Primatus iste se extendit? {c}Vt Papa (inquis) à nemine iudicetur: {d}Nec (licet hæreticus fuerit) ab Ecclesia, aut Principibus coactiue deponatur.
units.tr: And there is a passage where you, treating of the supreme authority of the Pontiff in spiritual matters, and taking your argument (as you say) from the names of the Bishop of Rome, list fifteen names, namely: Pope, Father of Fathers, Pontiff of Christians, Prince of Priests, Vicar of Christ, Head of the Church, Foundation, Pastor of the Lord's fold, Ruler of the house of God, Father and Teacher of all Christians, Spouse of the Church, Bishop of the Apostolic See, universal. To what end, then, this so glorious boasting of these names? From all these and each of them, you say, the primacy of the Pontiff is plainly gathered. But how far, I ask, does that primacy extend? That the Pope, you say, is judged by no one: nor, even if he be a heretic, is he deposed by the Church or by princes by coercion.

units.la: Elogia Sanctorum Patrum cùm Pontificum Titulis aequâ lance trutinantur.
units.tr: The praises of the holy Fathers are weighed in equal balance with the titles of the Pontiffs.

units.la: VAh! quàm in Paparum titulis stupet Bellarminus, qui si suos Pontificios Theologos, Iesuitas quoq; penitùs consuluisset, sensisset haud dubiò multos Ecclesiæ Patres antiquitùs tàm eximijs laudum præconijs celebratos fuisse, vt in multis aliqui Episcopo Romano nulli cedere; in aliquibus, omnes superare videantur.
units.tr: Ah, how Bellarmine is astonished at the titles of the Popes! Had he consulted thoroughly his own Papist theologians, the Jesuits too, he would undoubtedly have perceived that many Fathers of the ancient Church were celebrated with such distinguished praises that in many respects some seem to yield to no Bishop of Rome, and in some seem to surpass all of them.

units.la: I. {c}Athanasium Gregorius Nazianzenus vocauit Egregium Ecclesiæ columen, cuius dogmata pro orthodoxæ fidei lege habeantur. {f}Cui creditur Populi Alexandrini præsidentia, quod perinde est (inquit) ac si dicam, totius Orbis præfectura: id est, sic vniuersis prafuit, quia fides, quam ille sartam tectam defendit, ad omnes spectat: quem Damascenus {g}Ecclesiæ Dei fundamentum appellat. II. {h}Origenes, à Didymo, Secundus post Apostolos Ecclesiarum magister dictus est: ab Hieronymo, Sacrorum omnium Expositorum victor: à Seuero is censetur, qui, {i}In quâ parte probatur, neminem post Apostolos habuit æqualem. III. {k}Cyprianus non solum Ecclesiæ Africanæ (vt ait Nazianzenus) sed etiam toti Occidenti praefuit; imo Orienti fere ipsi, & meridiei, ac septentrioni, & quocunque ille sui admiratione peruenit: {1}Praeclarissimus Doctor (vt ait Augustinus) & Martyr gloriosissimus. IV. Basilius à Nazianzeno appellatur{m} Oculus Orbis; &, {n} Doctrina palatium; Sol inter sydera; & unum caelum complexu suo coercens: necnon à Gregorio Nisseno, {o} Os Ecclesiae.
units.tr: I. Gregory Nazianzen called Athanasius the distinguished pillar of the Church, whose dogmas are held as the rule of orthodox faith. To him is entrusted the presidency of the people of Alexandria, which (he says) is just as if I were to say the government of the whole world; that is, he presided over all, because the faith which he defended whole and untouched concerns everyone. Damascene calls him the foundation of the Church of God. II. Origen was called by Didymus the second teacher of the churches after the Apostles; by Jerome, the victor over all expounders of sacred things; by Severus he is counted as one who, in whatever part [of learning] he is tested, had no equal after the Apostles. III. Cyprian presided not only over the African Church (as Nazianzen says) but also over the whole West, nay almost over the East itself, and the South and North, and wherever his fame has reached: a most distinguished Doctor (as Augustine says) and most glorious Martyr. IV. Basil is called by Nazianzen the eye of the world; the palace of doctrine; the sun among the stars; and one who restrains the heaven within his embrace; and also by Gregory of Nyssa, the mouth of the Church.

units.la: V. Chrysostomus per Innocentium primum Pont. indigitatur{p} Magnus totius Orbis Doctor: — cuius iactura Orbis sub Sole totus ad orbitatem redactus est. VI. Gregorium Nazianzenum non dubitauit Basilius{q} Vas electionis, & os Christi dicere. Ruffinus eum Solum sensit, de cuius fide nec diffidentes quidem inter se disputare potuerint, sed obtinuisse eum id apud Dei Ecclesias meriti, ut manifestum esset indicium non esse rectae fidei omnem, qui in fide Gregorij non concordat. De quo Hieronymus; {r}Praeceptor hic meus (inquit) à quo[?] divinas Scripturas explicare didici. Et Eusebius; {s}Columna aurea, & totius Ecclesiae fundamentum. Qui denique{f} Ab omnibus Graecis, ob singularem authoritatis suae excellentiam, primus post Johannem Evangelistam Theologi, ac Magni cognomento illustratus est. Saepè à multis celebratur illud, de (VII) Ambrosij praestantia, Theodosij Imperatoris{t} Encomium, quando, eius virtutum celsitudine commotus, publice in summo templo Constantinopolitanae urbis exclamabat; ΑΜΒΡΟΣΙΟΝ ΟΙΑΑ[?] ΜΟΝΟΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΝ ΑΞΙΩΣ ΚΑΛΟΤΜΕΝΟΝ[?], hoc est, Ambrosium novi solum Episcopi nomine dignum.
units.tr: V. Chrysostom is designated by Innocent I, Pontiff, as the great Teacher of the whole world, by whose loss the whole world under the sun has been reduced to orphanhood. VI. Basil did not hesitate to call Gregory Nazianzen a vessel of election and the mouth of Christ. Rufinus thought him the only one, whose faith not even those who disagree with one another could dispute; and he had obtained such merit in the churches of God that it was a plain sign that whoever does not agree with the faith of Gregory does not have the right faith. Of him Jerome says: This man was my teacher, from whom I learned to explain the divine Scriptures. And Eusebius: a golden pillar and foundation of the whole Church. Finally, by all the Greeks, on account of the singular excellence of his authority, he was the first after John the Evangelist to be honoured with the surname Theologian, and Great. (VII) Often is cited that saying about the preeminence of Ambrose, the encomium of the Emperor Theodosius, when, moved by the loftiness of Ambrose's virtues, he publicly cried out in the great church of the city of Constantinople: ΑΜΒΡΟΣΙΟΝ ΟΙΑΑ ΜΟΝΟΝ ΕΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΝ ΑΞΙΩΣ ΚΑΛΟΤΜΕΝΟΝ, that is, Ambrose alone is worthy of the name of bishop.

units.la: VIII. Priscae antiquitatis Patres certatim contendunt {a}Augustinum laudibus efferre quantis potuerint maximis; de quo Hieronymus, "Conductorem antiquae fidei Augustinum omnes venerantur atq; suspiciant: & rursus, Dilexi in Augustino habitantem Dominum Salvatorem. Remigius, Sicut Sol in lumine excedit omnes planetas, ita {w}Augustinus omnes Theologos in exponendis Scripturis. Paulus Nolanus, Sal terrae Augustinus, & lucerna digne super candelabrum Ecclesiae posita. Apis Dei. Prosper Rhegiensis, Sui temporis Sacerdotum praecipui portio Augustinus: Hilarius, {y}Augustinus excellentissimus Doctor: Rupertus Abbas, Erat Augustinus columna & firmamentū veritatis: Bernardus, Habet Ecclesia Augustinum Validissimum malleum Haereticorum. Scite igitur & eleganter Erasmus, {*}Augustino nihil habet Christianus Orbis augustius. Haec habui, quae Tibi, Bellarmine, de Titulorum praestantia opponerem; ut siquam voluptatem, coactas nimis & undique accersitas Pontificum horum laudes efferendo, conceperis; eam, syncera & genuinas patrum audiendo, amittas. Hactenùs de Titulis in genere.
units.tr: VIII. The Fathers of antiquity vie with one another in extolling Augustine with the greatest praises they can. Of him Jerome says: All venerate and look up to Augustine, the guide of the ancient faith; and again, I have loved the Lord the Saviour dwelling in Augustine. Remigius: As the sun in light surpasses all the planets, so Augustine surpasses all theologians in expounding the Scriptures. Paulinus of Nola: Augustine, the salt of the earth, and a lamp rightly set upon the lampstand of the Church. A bee of God. Prosper of Regium: Augustine, the chief part of the priests of his time. Hilary: Augustine, most excellent Doctor. Rupert the Abbot: Augustine was the pillar and firmament of truth. Bernard: The Church has Augustine, a most powerful hammer of heretics. Rightly and elegantly, Erasmus: The Christian world has nothing more august than Augustine. These are the things I have set against you, Bellarmine, concerning the excellence of the titles; so that if you have taken any pleasure in extolling these Pontiffs' praises, which are forced and gathered from everywhere, you may lose it by hearing the sincere and genuine praises of the Fathers. So far on titles in general.

units.la: De Titulis Pontificum Rom. Tractatus peculiaris.
units.tr: On the Titles of the Roman Pontiffs: a separate treatise.

units.la: Quos enumerat {*}alibi Bellarminus Quindecim Pontificum Rom. Titulos; in hoc Tractatu reduxit ad quinque, viz.
units.tr: Bellarmine elsewhere lists fifteen titles of the Roman Pontiff. In this treatise he reduces them to five, namely:

units.la: 1. PATRIS.
units.tr: 1. FATHER.

units.la: 2. PASTORIS.
units.tr: 2. SHEPHERD.

units.la: 3. DOCTORIS.
units.tr: 3. TEACHER.

units.la: 4. SPECULATORIS.
units.tr: 4. WATCHMAN.

units.la: 5. SUMMI SACERDOTIS.
units.tr: 5. HIGH PRIEST.

units.la: PATRIS Titulū, tanquam proprium Papæ vendicat, non quidem simpliciter, sed partim ex: Attributis; Rationibus eius, seu Consequentijs.
units.tr: He claims the title Father as belonging to the Pope, not simply, but partly from its attributes and partly from its grounds or consequences.

units.la: Attributa tria observat; quòd sit Pater, viz. Christianæ plebis. Patrum. Sanctus.
units.tr: He notes three attributes: that he is Father of the Christian people, Father of the Fathers, and holy.

units.la: Titulus primus, Pater; eiusq; Attributum primum, Christianæ plebis.
units.tr: The first title, Father; and its first attribute, of the Christian people.

units.la: Bellarminus de Officio:
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office:

units.la: “ De officio Patris loquitur {*}Augustinus in Epist. ad Glo-rium & Eleusium, in qua de S. Miltia loquens vocat eum filium Christianæ pacis, & patrem Christianæ plebis. — Pag. 25.
units.tr: "The office of Father is spoken of by Augustine in his letter to Glorius and Eleusius, in which, speaking of St Miltiades, he calls him the son of Christian peace and the father of the Christian people. — p. 25."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Paternam curam Ecclesiæ universæ non soli Pontifici Rom. incumbere.
units.tr: I. Animadversion. That the paternal care of the whole Church does not rest on the Roman Pontiff alone.

units.la: QUomodò, quaeso, Christiana plebis Pater Pontifex Miltiades dicendus? an ut toto studio & solicitudine incumbat in commune bonum plebis Christianae? at hoc est omnibus Episcopis cum Pontifice commune. an quod nulla Plebs verè Christiana dici aut haberi debeat, quae non Rom. Ecclesiae gremio foveatur? at haec ratio (si tamen ratio dicenda est, quae tum cum incredibili salsitate, tum etiam cum Christiana plebis fere vniuersae intolerabili iniuria coniuncta est) iam antea excussa & protrita euanuit. Tertium quid somnias; age igitur, &, quod alibi habes, nunc exhibe. {a}Argumentum certissimum est principatus Romani Pontificis, quod nimirum ex quavis o: bis Christiani parte ad Rom. Pontificem legitimè provocatur; ab eius vero sententia nulla conceditur appellatio. Nunc nobis Augustinus adest, Author oppido quam idoneus & opportunus, qui Te suo testimonio obruat; Is enim in eadem, quam allegas, Epistola celebrem illam Causam commemorat, quae Caeciliano cum Donatistis intercesserat. Summa est, Constantinum Imp. 1°. Causam hanc ad Miltiadem Papam detulisse: 2°. Episcopos alios etiam ei, tanquàm Collegas & Delegatos, in illo iudicio assignasse. 3°. Re tandem per Miltiadem, eiusque Collegas iudicata atque definita, Imperatorem denuò (Donatistis ab illo iudicio non sine maxima peruersitate prouocantibus) eandem Causam apud Episcopum Arelatensem diligentius examinandam terminandamque curasse. Quo uno exemplo (nam hic à Pontificis sententia Appellatio conceditur) tuum, pro Pontificis principatu, Argumentum certissimum, scilicet, certissimè apertissimèque refellitur.
units.tr: How, I ask, is Pope Miltiades to be called father of the Christian people? Is it because he gives all his zeal and concern to the common good of the Christian people? But that is common to all bishops together with the Pope. Or is it because no people ought to be called or held truly Christian unless it is cherished in the bosom of the Roman Church? But this argument (if it is to be called an argument, being joined both with incredible silliness and with an injury almost intolerable to nearly the whole Christian people) was long ago examined, worn threadbare, and has vanished. You dream up a third thing; come then, and now produce what you have elsewhere: {a}The most certain argument for the primacy of the Roman Pontiff is that from every part of the Christian world an appeal is lawfully made to the Roman Pontiff, and from his judgment no appeal is granted. Now Augustine stands by us, an author exceedingly suitable and opportune, who will overwhelm you with his testimony. For in the same Letter you cite, he recalls that famous cause which had arisen between Caecilian and the Donatists. The sum is this: first, Constantine the Emperor referred this cause to Pope Miltiades; second, he also assigned other bishops to him, as colleagues and delegates, in that judgment; third, when the matter had at last been judged and settled by Miltiades and his colleagues, the Emperor, when the Donatists appealed from that judgment (not without the greatest perversity), took care that the same cause be examined and concluded more carefully before the Bishop of Arles. By this one example (for here an appeal from the Pope's sentence is allowed) your most certain argument for the papal principate is clearly and most manifestly refuted.

units.la: Respondes vero (nec enim ignoro) {b}Miltiadem hac permisisse. Quae sane Responsio exigua nimis rima est, & paulò arctior, quàm ut per eam elabi possis: nam (praeterquam quòd Constantino non licuit, per leges à se sancitas, Causam Ecclesiasticam iudicare) nihil apud Augustinum occurrit, quo significetur, Constantinum impetrando magis quàm imperando peregisse omnia; nihil, in quo Miltiades non tàm permittentis, quàm obsequentis, ac obtemperantis partes obiisse ac praestitisse. Quanquam Miltiadem id permisisse fingamus; si tamen Paulus Quintus Pont. qui nunc rerum potitur, Imperatorem sineret pro arbitrio suo non solum viris Ecclesiasticis iudicandi prouinciam destinare, sed sibi etiam, prae aliis, imponere; atque una secum Episcopos aliquos, non ut Consiliarios, sed ut Iudices; nec assumptos, ut subditos; sed assignatos, ut Collegas adiungere, qui cum eo Sedntes de illa Causa, quod iustum videretur, statuerent; ac demum, post prolatam à se integerrimam sententiam, Archi-episcopo Remensi causam examinandam rursus determinandamque committere: quotus, quaeso, quisque est ex toto vestro Cardinalium coetu qui Paulo Quinto suffragaretur, & non potiùs isthoc [Permittere] esse plane Principatum suum prodere interpretaretur; illudque ingereret, (quod Bernardo, tempore Eugenij Papae, valde displicuit;) {e} Absit! non Maiestati convenit: quam geras personam attendito? Videtisne Papa Papae quid interfit, sed antiquo recens; sed pacis filio turbarum pater? Redeo ad Augustinum.
units.tr: You reply (for I am not unaware of it) that {b}Miltiades permitted this. Certainly this answer is a very narrow crack, and somewhat too tight for you to slip out through. For (apart from the fact that it was not permitted to Constantine, by laws he himself had enacted, to judge an ecclesiastical cause) nothing in Augustine occurs by which it is indicated that Constantine accomplished everything by entreaty rather than by command; nothing in which Miltiades played the part, not so much of one permitting, as of one complying, obeying and submitting. Yet let us suppose that Miltiades did permit it. If Paul V, the Pope, who now holds the reins of affairs, were to allow the Emperor at his own discretion to assign the province of judging not only to churchmen, but to impose himself above the rest; and to join with himself some bishops, not as counsellors but as judges, not taken as subordinates but assigned as colleagues, who, sitting with him, would decide in that cause whatever seemed just; and finally, after his most upright sentence had been pronounced, were to commit the cause to the Archbishop of Reims to be examined and determined again: how many of your whole College of Cardinals, I ask, would support Paul V, and would not rather interpret that [permitting] as plainly a betrayal of his own principate, and hurl at him what displeased Bernard in the time of Pope Eugene: {e}Far be it! It is not fitting for majesty: consider what person you bear. Do you see what difference there is between Pope and Pope, the one recent, the other ancient; the one a son of peace, the other a father of disturbances? I return to Augustine.

units.la: Augustinum itaque, quem hactenus illius contentionis (coram Miltiade) narratorem audiuistis, nunc moderatorem attendite; nec enim praetermittendum duxi quod vester Card. Cusanus ex eadem Epistola Augustini, de Causa eadem, tanquàm observatu dignissimum, retulit. {d}Augustinus (inquit) ad eos, qui Papae Miltiadis sententiae se opposuerunt, dicentes, malos Iudices perpessi sumus; respondit, Ecce putemus eos, qui Romae iudicârunt, malos fuisse, restat[?] Concilium, in quo cum ipsis Iudicibus posset agitari causa. Ergo non iam Supra Concilium Papa [illegible, ~8 letters] fuit, à cuius sententia (dicis) nullam Appellationem concedendam esse.
units.tr: So, Augustine, whom until now you have heard as the narrator of that contest before Miltiades, now attend to as its moderator. For I thought it not to be passed over what your Cardinal Cusanus reported, as most worthy of notice, from the same Letter of Augustine about the same cause. {d}Augustine (he says) answered those who opposed the sentence of Pope Miltiades, saying that they had suffered bad judges: suppose, he says, that those who judged at Rome were bad; there remains a Council, in which the cause could be debated with the judges themselves. Therefore it is no longer a Council above the Pope [illegible, about eight letters] who, as you say, is not to be granted any appeal from his sentence.

units.la: {e} Reading of the marker in the text is uncertain; the marginal note carries the same mark.
units.tr: {e} The reading of the marker in the text is uncertain; the marginal note carries the same mark.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. Animadversion.

units.la: Complures Pontifices non pacis filios, sed Belli incentores esse.
units.tr: That several popes were not sons of peace but instigators of war.

units.la: Eodem omnino spiritu Augustinus Miltiadem Papam filium pacis, quo Patrem Christianae plebis vocauit; & jure id quidem: erat enim Miltiades pacis studiosissimus. de nonnullis aliis Papis, scio, non idem tulisset judicium. Quomodo enim pacis filium dixisset Papam Victorem, quem, tanquam {e}Pacis perturbatorem, Pater Irenaeus obiurgabat? Aut Gregorium VII, quem {f}Leodienses, nouello Schismate regnum & Sacerdotium scindentem, Sacerdotalem lanceam contra Imperij diadema leuasse, & se, suoque[?] exemplo alios Pontifices contra Principes gladio accinxisse, belloq; hereditario quasi insurrexisse conquesti sunt? Aut Urbanum VI, quem alij propter grauissimas turbas, quas concitauit, non illepide Turbanum appellarunt?
units.tr: In exactly the same spirit Augustine called Pope Miltiades a son of peace, just as he called him Father of the Christian people, and rightly so, for Miltiades was most devoted to peace. I know that concerning some other popes he would not have passed the same judgement. For how could he have called Pope Victor a son of peace, whom Father Irenaeus rebuked as a disturber of peace? Or Gregory VII, whom the people of Liège complained had, by splitting kingdom from priesthood in a new schism, raised the priestly lance against the imperial diadem, and by his example girded other popes with the sword against princes, rising up as it were in hereditary war? Or Urban VI, whom others, on account of the very grave disturbances he stirred up, not unwittily called Turban?

units.la: Quid multa? si Papae subsequentes non Decessorum suorum temporibus, potius quàm moribus Successores fuissent, quorsum attineret illa tàm grauis querela & deploratio Theologi non ignobilis? {g}Tales quidem fuerunt (inquit) in utroque Dei populo Sacerdotum inermium, & pacificorum erga seculi dominos fideles & infideles, mites & barbaros victoria non minùs gloriosè quàm incruenta; quibus non contenta posteritas, veteris Gentilis ritu, togas in sagos mutauit, postquàm exlex semel necessitas Clero ad praelia non tantùm animum, sed & manum etiam exercuit; factum est, ut, cùm tempore omnia deterente, eundem ludum exercerent, simulatq; receptum est, ut profanas cùm sacris ministeriis ditiones & tenerent & gererent: nec tantùm contrà barbaros & incredulos, sed eiusdem quoq; nunc sanguinis, nunc patriae, aut certè fidei Principes. Haec ille; qui praeterea aegrè admodùm fert, eos Vicarios Dei pacis se indigitare, qui minùs Pacifici bella indicare & gerere solent: {h}Exemplo (inquit ille, Gregorium VII innuens) scandalis infinitis gravido, & nulla Scripturarum aut Canonum authoritate
units.tr: What more need be said? If the later popes had been successors not in the times of their predecessors but rather in their morals, what point would there be in that very grave complaint and lament of a not undistinguished theologian? Such indeed (he says) were, in both peoples of God, the priests who were unarmed and peaceable towards the lords of the world, faithful and unbelieving, gentle and barbarous, victorious no less gloriously than bloodlessly. Not content with these, posterity, after the old pagan custom, exchanged togas for cloaks, once necessity, lawless, had exercised the clergy for war not only in mind but also in hand. It came about that, as time corrupts all things, they practised the same game as soon as it was accepted that they should both hold and govern secular dominions alongside their sacred ministries: and not only against barbarians and unbelievers, but also against princes now of the same blood, now of the same country, or at least of the same faith. So he. He moreover takes it very badly that those should designate themselves Vicars of God of peace who are less accustomed to proclaim and wage war peacefully. By the example (he says, alluding to Gregory VII), pregnant with infinite scandals, and with no authority of Scripture or canons

units.la: {g} Espen in 1. Tim. Digest.[?] l.2.q.8.273
units.tr: Van Espen on 1 Tim.; Digest, bk. 2, q. 8, p. 273.

units.la: {e} Agrippa de vanit. scient. ex hist. Eccles.
units.tr: Agrippa, De vanitate scientiarum, from Ecclesiastical History.

units.la: {f} Leodiens. Epist. ad Paschal. 2. ritate probato. Itá vt non possit Miltiades non gratus admodùm nobis accedere, quocum fi posterę ætatis Pontifices conferantur, non tàm plebis Christiane Patres, quàm non Pacis filij meritiffimò existimari debent. Hæc de primo Attributo Patris.
units.tr: Liège writers, Letter to Paschal II, ... (the text is garbled in the scan). Thus Miltiades cannot seem other than most welcome to us; if the popes of later ages are compared with him, they ought to be judged not so much Fathers of the Christian people as by no means sons of peace. These things concerning the first attribute, Father.

units.la: Attributum fecundum est Pater Patrum.
units.tr: The second attribute is Father of Fathers.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office.

units.la: “ De hoc officio loquitur * Conc. Africanum in Epistola ad Damafum Papam, cùm S. Damafum appellat Patrem Patrum: & mos, &c. — Pag.25.
units.tr: "Of this office the African Council speaks in its letter to Pope Damasus, when it calls St Damasus Father of Fathers; and the custom, etc." — Page 25.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. Animadversion.

units.la: Concilium Africanum aliud Titulum hunc Papæ attribuere; rem verò aliud negare.
units.tr: The African Council grants this title to the Pope, but in fact says otherwise.

units.la: VNum Conc. Africanum inscribit Damasum Patrem Patrum: hunc Tu titulum arripis, tanquàm Primatus Pontificis insigne aliquod documentum. At aliud Conc. Africanum (cui ipse Augustinus interfuit) Appellationem ad Romam prohibet. Hoc cùm primum obiectum fuit Stapletono tuo, ipse protinus stomachatus ilicò, & in Sanctissimos Africani Concilij Patres procaciter debacchatus est. {i}Huius Concilij Decreta (inquit) pro suo iure temerè sanxiuerunt. Vide, obsecro, quò iam res redijt. Tu ex vno Concilio Africano obtrudis nobis hoc Attributum[Pater Patrum:] Nos ex altero Concilio Africano opponimus vobis non minoris authoritatis iudicium omnium Patrum. In illo titulum videmus sine re; in hoc verò rem ipsam habemus, id est, expressum Concilij Decretum, quo illud, quod Tu stabilire tantoperè cupis, Ius Pontificale abrogatur. Postremò (nam non opus est, in hac quæstione, diutiùs immorari) habemus ipsissimum Papam Damasum Patribus vestris Papis hodiernis aduersantem, qui, {k}In causa Bonasi, negabat iudicium illud sibi competere. Non competere (inquam) non solum nonconuenire.
units.tr: Indeed the Council of Africa entitles Damasus Father of Fathers; this title you snatch up as some notable proof of the Primacy of the Pontiff. But the other African Council (in which Augustine himself took part) forbids appeal to Rome. When this was first put to your Stapleton, he at once flew into a rage and raged insolently against the most holy Fathers of the African Council. The decrees of this Council (he says) were rashly enacted on their own authority. See, I beg you, where the matter has now come. From one African Council you thrust upon us this attribute [Father of Fathers]; from another African Council we set against you the judgement of all the Fathers, of no less authority. In the former we see the title without the thing; in the latter we have the thing itself, that is, an express decree of the Council by which what you so eagerly wish to establish, the pontifical right, is abrogated. Lastly (for there is no need to linger longer on this question) we have Pope Damasus himself, opposing your Popes of today, who in the case of Bonosus denied that this judgement belonged to him. Does not belong (I say), not merely does not agree.

units.la: {i} Stapleton. Doctr. Prim. Controv. 3. q. 7.
units.tr: Stapleton, Doctr. Prim. Controv. 3, q. 7.

units.la: {k} Cusan. quo supra. At nè Te forte praetereat solenne Pontificis tui nomen, Papa, quod, à Pappas deductum, idem quod Pater Patriae; seu (ut alij Iesuitae) Patrum sonat: ex quo vos hodiè Papistae auditis; & de quo non mediocriter gloriamini, tanquàm quod amplissimam Primatus Papalis Prærogatiuam designet; reuoco Tibi in memoriam quod alibi de hoc nomine tradidisti, vt mens tua Lectori facilius innotescat.
units.tr: Cusanus, as above. But lest the solemn name of your Pontiff, Papa, escape you, which, derived from Pappas, means the same as Father of the Fatherland, or (as other Jesuits have it) Father of Fathers, from which you Papists today hear your name, and of which you boast not a little, as if it signified the very ample prerogative of papal primacy, I recall to you what you taught elsewhere about this name, so that your meaning may become more readily known to the reader.

units.la: Mentis Bellarminianæ explicatio, in no- mine Papæ, triplici modo. De modo 1°. Bellarminus alibi.
units.tr: Explanation of Bellarmine's meaning in the name of Pope, in a threefold way. Concerning the first way, Bellarmine elsewhere.

units.la: {1}Primum, communissimum, & antiquissimum nomen Episcopi Rom. est PAPA. B. Ignatius vocat Linum Papam. — quod nomen Latinè Pater Patris significat: quodq; quamuis tribuatur à veteribus cuilibet Episcopo (nàm Hieronymus Augustinum Papam vocat; & quilibet Sacerdos dicitur Pater) nihilominus tribus modis colligitur ex hoc nomine Episcopi Rom. Primatus, 1°. quia per Antonomasiam, quùm absolutè dicitur Papa, ipse solus intelligitur, vt in Conc. Chalcedonensi Act. 16. de Leone Pontifice, Beatissimus & Apostolicus vir Papa hoc nobis præcepit, &c.
units.tr: First, the most common and most ancient name of the Roman Bishop is POPE. St Ignatius calls Linus Pope. This name in Latin signifies Father of the Father; and although the ancients attribute it to any bishop (for Jerome calls Augustine Pope, and any priest is called Father), nevertheless three marks of primacy are gathered from this name of the Roman bishop. First, because by antonomasia, when he is called simply Pope, he alone is understood, as in the Council of Chalcedon, Act 16, concerning Pope Leo: "The most blessed and apostolic man, Pope, has commanded us this," etc.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Nomen Papæ non ad solum Rom. Pontificem re- stringendum esse.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO. The name Pope must not be restricted to the Roman Bishop alone.

units.la: Papæ nomen, vt verum dicis, Communissimum & antiquissimum, id est (ut ego interpretor) communitatem antiquissimum, & Antiquitate communissimum Episcopis aliis iuxtà cùm Pontifice Rom. non vllo modo huic, apud Antiquos, proprium. Testis est Baronius Cardinalis; {m}Constat hoc nomen Papa, olim fuisse commune reliquis Episcopis. Testis Onuphrius; {n}Hanc vocem, Papa, omnes antiquæ Christianorum Episcopi pro Patre seu Maiore frequentarunt, præsertim magnarum & insignium urbium, vt Romæ, Carthaginis, Antiochiæ, Hierosolymorum, & similium. Itàdilutum & plane ridiculum est, quod de Antonomasia occinis; nam, si externum tantum loquendi modum quis spectet, Cypriano Martyri est tributum, quando (ut refert Pontius) {o} In eius passione Proconsuli quaerenti ab eo, An tu is es, quum Christiani suum Papam vocant? respondit Cyprianus, Ego. Nihil fere ab hac dissonat Card. Baronij narratio;{p} Proconsul dixit, Is ne tu es, qui Christianis hominibus te Papam praebuisti? Cyprianus, Ego. Quod si, quum de nomine Papa agebatur, illud, Ego, quod quondam a strenuo Athleta Cypriano geminatum, ab aliquo Rom. Pontifice prolatum fuisset unquam, Papa! qualem Papistae triumphum canerent.
units.tr: That the name Pope is, as you say, very common and very ancient, that is (as I interpret it) common to many and, by its antiquity, most common among the bishops, and in no way belonged to the Roman Pontiff alone among the Ancients. Cardinal Baronius is a witness: {m} It is established that the name Pope was once common to the other bishops. Onuphrius is a witness: {n} All the ancient bishops of the Christians used this word, Pope, for Father or Greater, especially those of great and famous cities, such as Rome, Carthage, Antioch, Jerusalem and the like. So what you sing about Antonomasia is watered-down and plainly ridiculous. For if one looks only at the outward manner of speaking, the name was given to the martyr Cyprian, when (as Pontius reports) {o} at his passion, the proconsul asked him, "Are you the man whom the Christians call their Pope?" and Cyprian answered, I am. Cardinal Baronius's account hardly differs from this: {p} The proconsul said, "Are you the one who presented yourself to the Christian people as their Pope?" Cyprian: "I am." But if, when the name Pope was under discussion, some Roman Pontiff had ever uttered that "I am", which the valiant athlete Cyprian once repeated, and had said Pope!, what a triumph the Papists would sing.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Restrictionem hanc novam, & nuper exortam esse.
units.tr: That this restriction is new and only lately arisen.

units.la: QUòd dicimus huius vocis usum communem olim suisse, Antiquitas nobis iam suffragata est: quod vero contendis illum antiquitus Rom. Pontifici per Excellentiam proprium tribui, vel novitas ipsa Te confutabit: nam, ut Onuphrius (quem agnoscitis {q} Historias Ecclesiasticas diligenter pervoluisse) palam asseruit;{r} Post Gregorij (Magni) tempora nomen hoc, Papa, reliquis Episcopis ademptum, soli Pontifici Rom. attributum esse. At quando tandem, & quo Authore? hoc duo fratres tui{f} Iesuitae expedient. Papa nomen (inquiunt) peculiariter attributum est Rom. Pontifici, ex decreto Gregorij VII, in Synodo Rom. Anno Christi MLXXIII. Proinde, quum ita disseris, Antiquus Episcopus Rom. per Antonomasiam, Papa, solus vocabatur; Ergo, obtinuit Primatum in Ecclesia: Antecedentis falsitatem Fratrum tuorum diserta confessio; Consequentis futilitatem Patris Cypriani ad Proconsulem responsio facile arguet. Taceo, interim, hodie apud Graecos (ut fertur) quemlibet Parochum παπᾶς[?] appellari.
units.tr: THAT we say the use of this word was once common, antiquity has already supported us. That you contend it was in ancient times attributed to the Roman Pontiff as his own by eminence, the very novelty of the claim will refute you. For, as Onuphrius (whom you acknowledge to have diligently perused the Ecclesiastical Histories) plainly asserted: {r} After the time of Gregory (the Great) this name, Pope, was taken from the other bishops and attributed to the Roman Pontiff alone. But when at last, and on whose authority? Your two brothers, the Jesuits, will explain this: The name Pope (they say) was attributed peculiarly to the Roman Pontiff by the decree of Gregory VII, in a Roman Synod, in the year of Christ 1073. Therefore, when you argue that the ancient Roman Bishop was called Pope alone by Antonomasia, and therefore obtained the Primacy in the Church, the falsity of the antecedent is proved by your brothers' plain admission, and the futility of the consequent will easily be shown by the reply of Father Cyprian to the proconsul. I say nothing, meanwhile, of the fact that today among the Greeks (so it is said) any parish priest is called [παπᾶς].

units.la: Modus II. colligendi Primatum Pontificis, ex nomine Papae.
units.tr: The second way of inferring the Pontiff's Primacy from the name Pope.

units.la: {q} Posterius. Apparet ad supra §. 5. lit e. Onuphr. vbi supra ad lit. a.
units.tr: {q} Later. It appears above at §. 5, letter e. Onuphrius, as above, at letter a.

units.la: {f} Lorinus [?] in Act. 16. & Azorius Instit. part 2. l. 5. cap. vlt.
units.tr: {f} Lorinus [?] on Acts 16, and Azorius, Institutes, part 2, book 5, last chapter.

units.la: Bellarminus.
units.tr: Bellarmine.

units.la: {e}Secundus modus est, quia solus Episcopus Romanus totius Ecclesiæ Papa dicitur, ut ibidem patet.
units.tr: {e} The second way is that the Roman Bishop alone is called Pope of the whole Church, as is clear in the same place.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Secundum modum pariter inanem esse.
units.tr: That the second way is equally empty.

units.la: PAtet omninò, Pater quoad curam & solicitudinem, quemadmodum Cyprianus (indefinitè) {*}Christianorum Papa. Par pari refero;ecquid te mordet? facessant igitur istæ nugæ næniaeque.
units.tr: IT is entirely clear that Father refers to care and concern, just as Cyprian (indefinitely) was {*} the Pope of Christians. I return like for like: what bites you? Away then with these trifles and dirges.

units.la: Tertius modus colligendi Primatum, ex nomine Papæ.
units.tr: The third way of inferring the Primacy from the name Pope.

units.la: {u}Ipse Rom. Pontifex ab aliis salutatus neminem vocat Patrem, sed omnes filios, vel fratres.
units.tr: {u} The Roman Pontiff himself, when greeted by others, calls no one Father, but all sons or brothers.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Papam Rom. dum Fraternitatem despicit, Pater- nitatem suam amittere[?].
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO. The Roman Pope, while he despises brotherhood, loses his fatherhood[?].

units.la: HÆc est eiusdem ferculi placēta peræq; insipida;nam (vobis etiam fatentibus) {x}Cornelius Episcopus Rom. & alij multi Cyprianum Carthaginensem Episcopum Papam, & Papatem vocárunt:& Epiphanius Epistolam ad Hormisdam Rom. Episcopum sic inscribit, {y}Sanctissimo & beatissimo Domino fratri comministro Hormisdæ salutem. Tu itaque, Bellarmine, qui Patris appellatione, indefinitè sumptâ, Pontificis Primatum demonstrari putas; Fratris autem (si forte illi attribueretur) attenuari atque diminui; has, quas retulimus, salutationes æquâ iam lance perpende. Nam si in voce, Pater, tanta vis inest, vt Primatum evincat, tùm, ex sententia Rom Pontificis, iste Primatus Cyprianus est deferendus; quia Cornelius Pontifex, aliíque multi Cyprianum Papam, idèst, {z}Patrem Patrum voca-runt. runt. Si deinde etiam hoc nomen, Frater, Primatui obest, tum primatus dignitas Rom. Pontifici detrahenda est: nam Epiphanius Hormisdam Pontificem (tantum) Fratris, & Comministri nomine salutabat.
units.tr: THIS is a dish of the same course, and quite insipid; for (even by your own admission) {x} Cornelius, Bishop of Rome, and many others, called Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, Pope and Papa; and Epiphanius addresses his Letter to Hormisdas, the Roman Bishop, thus: {y} To the most holy and most blessed lord, brother and fellow minister Hormisdas, greetings. So you, Bellarmine, who think the Primacy of the Pontiff is shown by the title Father taken indefinitely, but that Brother, if it were perhaps applied to him, would weaken and diminish it, weigh these greetings we have cited on an even balance. For if there is so much force in the word Father that it proves the Primacy, then by the Roman Pontiff's own judgment that Primacy must be transferred to Cyprian, since Cornelius the Pontiff and many others called Cyprian Pope, that is, {z} Father of Fathers. Again, if even the name Brother stands in the way of the Primacy, then the dignity of the primacy must be taken away from the Roman Pontiff, for Epiphanius greeted Pontiff Hormisdas (merely) with the names Brother and Fellow Minister.

units.la: At Pontifex Rom. (inquis) neminem vocat Patrem, sed omnes Filios. Respondeo, si antiquos Pontifices intelligis, erras; nam (ut iam {*}liquet) Cornelius Pontifex Cyprianum Episcopum Papam; & {*}Bonifacius Augustinum Sanctum Patrem vocauit: sin Successores, inique facis, qui à nobis exigis, ut rationem reddamus, cur Romanis Episcopis alto quodam aliorum omnium despectu adeò superbis & fastuosis esse licuerit.
units.tr: But the Roman Pontiff (you say) calls no one Father, but all sons. I reply: if you mean the ancient Pontiffs, you are wrong; for (as is now clear) Pontiff Cornelius called Bishop Cyprian Pope, and Boniface called St Augustine Holy Father. But if you mean the successors, you act unfairly in demanding that we give an account of why Roman bishops have been permitted to be so proud and haughty, with a certain lofty contempt for all the others.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. REMARK.

units.la: Pontificios ipsos de nomine [ Papa,] inter se fluctuare, & collidere inuicem.
units.tr: The Papists themselves waver and clash with one another over the name [Papa].

units.la: VOX, Papa, tanquàm à nomine Pappas, quod significat Patrem Patris, vel, Patrum, deduci verum est: cui consentit etiam {a}Glossa. Sed si haec Etymologia vocis ad Pontificis primatum euincendum per se valeret, nihil opus fuisset vobis, relicto nomine Pappas, ab interiectione Papae! tanquàm à nobiliore atque augustiore stemmate originem petere: nam {b}Papa (ut habet eadem Glossa) Admirabilis; & dicitur à Papa, quod est interiectio admirantis; & verè admirabilis Papa, quia vices Dei in terris gerit. Inde dixit ille Angelicus in poëtria noua; Papa stupor mundi: --& circa finem; --- Quia maxima rerum, nec Deus es, nec homo; quasi neuter inter vtrumque. Haec illa. Sed lingua quò vadis, ex qua nihil magis nobis admirabile videtur, quam horum hominum stupor, qui in amplificanda Romani Pontificis potestate nec modum, nec modestiam tenent vllam. Sed esto; Nec Deus, Papa, quia non potest; nec homo, quia non vult: quid ergo est Papa? --Illud quod dicere nolo. Verùm cùm de praecipuo Prosessionis suae Titulo, nimirùm Papa, Papistae circa etymon eius, & vim, & vsum antiquum adeò hallucinentur; quis speret fore ut aliis aliquandò unanimes consentiant? Hæc de secundo Attributo.
units.tr: It is true that the word Papa is derived from Pappas, which means Father of the Father, or of the Fathers. The Gloss agrees with this. But if this etymology of the word could by itself establish the primacy of the Pope, you would have had no need, leaving aside the word Pappas, to derive its origin from the interjection Papae, as if it sprang from a nobler and more august lineage! For Papa, as the same Gloss has it, is admirable; it is said to come from Papa, which is an interjection of wonder, and the Pope is truly admirable because he bears the place of God on earth. Hence that Angelic poet in his new poetics said: Papa, the wonder of the world; and near the end: Because he is the greatest of things, he is neither God nor man, but as it were neither of the two. So far the Gloss. But where are you heading, tongue? Nothing seems to us more admirable than the wonder of these men, who in magnifying the power of the Roman Pontiff keep no measure or moderation at all. But grant it: he is not God, Papa, because he cannot be; nor man, because he does not wish to be. What then is Papa? That which I am unwilling to say. But since the Papists are so badly mistaken about the etymology, the meaning, and the ancient use of their very title Papa, the principal title of their profession, who could hope that they will ever agree among themselves about other things? So much for the second attribute.

units.la: Tertium Attributum est Pater Sanctus.
units.tr: The third attribute is Holy Father.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: “ Et mos est Christiani populi, ut summum Pontificem Patrem sanctum appellet. Quâ appellatione non vulgus tantùm, sed omnes Principes Christiani, etiam summi utuntur, cùm ad Pontificem Romanum scribunt, atque ad eum loquuntur? Pag.25.
units.tr: “And it is the custom of the Christian people to call the supreme Pontiff Holy Father. This form of address is used not only by the common people but by all Christian princes, even the highest, when they write to the Roman Pontiff and speak to him.” Page 25.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Titulum Sanctitatis, contra primeuam nominis institu- tionem, frustrà & iniquè traductum esse, Ex I. Com- paratione factâ inter ipsos Pontifices probatur.
units.tr: FIRST REMARK. It is shown, from the comparison made among the Popes themselves, that the title of Holiness has been transferred vainly and unjustly, contrary to the original institution of the name.

units.la: VIs, vel potiùs vanitas huius Obiectionis, de Sanctitatis Attributo, ex triplici comparatione facilè decernitur. Prima est Pontificum cum ipsis Pontificibus. Nam, primò, Primos Ecclesiæ Pontifices hoc titulo caruisse, Iesuitæ ipsi haud inuiti dabunt. (ait Azorius) Sanctissimus, & Beatissimus Leoni primo (nimirum circiter Ann. Domini ccccx l.) cœperunt tribui. Secundò, Prima ascriptionis ratio tunc, in Episcopo Leone, respiciebat hominis, non Pontificis; vel, vt planiùs dicam, morum, non muneris . An igitur quod nonnisi Pontificibus, summâ Sanctitate præditis, conuenit, sceleratis quoque competere possit? Credo equidem, Nauarre, Tibi; (inquis) tam vocantes Papas, Sanctissimos; imò & vocati, si hæc velint ratione personarum, quas norunt non esse tales. Fuisse sanè priscæ ætatis Pontifices egregiâ Sanctitatis laude celeberrimos, liberè fatemur; sed heu! fuisse: nam multis iam retrò seculis transactis, veluti degeneres filij, qui tantùm Maiorum stemmate; nobilitatisque inani titulo, & insignibus gaudent, quorum tamen virtutibus sunt exhæredes: hæredes: ità fit ut succedentes Pontifices proprijs suorum vitiorum sordibus volutantes, ijsdem tamen Sanctitatis & dignitatis titulis & appellationibus fruantur, quas eorum Prædecessores eximiâ & planè admirabili virtute suâ conciliârunt. De quo pluribus suo loco.
units.tr: The force, or rather the emptiness, of this objection concerning the attribute of Holiness is easily judged from a threefold comparison. The first is of the Popes with the Popes themselves. For first, the Jesuits themselves will not be unwilling to grant that the first Popes of the Church lacked this title. Azorius says that Most Holy and Most Blessed began to be given to Leo I (about the year of the Lord 450). Second, the original reason for ascribing it to Bishop Leo regarded the man, not the Pontiff; or, to speak more plainly, it regarded his character, not his office. Can it then be that what suits only Pontiffs endowed with the highest holiness can also belong to the wicked? I believe, Navarre, that you will say to me: they call the Popes Most Holy, and indeed they are called so if these titles are meant of the persons, whom they know not to be such. Indeed we freely confess that the Pontiffs of an earlier age were most famous for their outstanding praise of holiness; but, alas, were: for many centuries have passed since then, and like degenerate sons who rejoice only in the lineage of their ancestors and the empty title and insignia of nobility, while being disinherited of their virtues, so it comes about that the succeeding Pontiffs, wallowing in the filth of their own vices, nonetheless enjoy the same titles and appellations of holiness and dignity which their predecessors won by their remarkable and altogether admirable virtue. More on this in its proper place.

units.la: Quæstio, quæ inpræsentiarum vos acriùs vrgeat, est, quo iure Successores nequissimi pijssimorum Prædecessorum Sanctitatis titulum vsurpent? Ex his angustijs mirum quanto conamine vos expedire satagitis. Nauarrus {g} Non peccat (inquit) Papa volendo se vocari Sanctissimum, nec Rex volendo se vocari Christianissimum, nec ij, qui sic eos vocant, secundum hunc sensum; quod habent dignitates, quorum possessores debent esse tales. Exemplum ab Extravagantibus petere licet, non illepidum illud quidem, Bonifacy IX. Pontificis, qui (vt Bonifacy VIII. Prædecessoris sui memoriam colere videretur) Eum Bonæ memoriæ prædecessorem suum vocabat. Indè Glossa Papalis commentandi ansam sibi arripiens, quærenti, {b} Nunquid Papa, qui improbis actionibus, Simonijs, ac turpiloquijs Ecclesiam fœdauit, dici potest Pontifex male memoriæ? Responsum reddit; {i} Dic (inquit) quod non, quid respicere debet non ad id quod fecit, sed ad id quod facere ipsum decuit. Sic ille. Qualis laus (vt cum Bernardo loquar) vituperio est proxima; quia hac ratione quis est tàm perdite improbus, qui non Sanctissimus habeatur? Iesuita Azorius aliquanto modestius; {k} Licet (inquit) hæc nomina, Sanctissimus, & Beatissimus, Leoni primo ceperint tribui, tanquàm præsidi cuidam vitæ, & morum dignitate Sanctissimo, posteà verò sunt ea nomina retenta ratione Muneris & officij, quod Pontifex gerit: vt Christianissimi nomen vni Francorum Regi dari cœpit Christi filem & religionem egregiè tuenti, quod posteà alijs mansit hereditarium; & Catholici nomen Regibus Hispaniæ, ob fidei Catholicæ patrocinium. Quo hæc faciant, quæris, Bellarmine? dicam, vt pudorem tibi incutiant, tùm quia (vt Pontifices tuos non modò Episcopis, sed etiam Imperatoribus authoritate Superiores esse [?]suaderes) [Sanctus] usum Antiquissimum esse docueris; qui tamen à Leone 1o. cœperat: tum etiam quià proprium & genuinum eius sensum, quo morum probitas commendabatur, ad alienum & coactum, de Muneris & officij honore, traduxeris; itâ ut illud in vestros Pontifices optimè quadret, quod ad Eugenium Papam Bernardus; {1}Ecclesiasticus zelus solum pro dignitate tuendâ honori totum dat, Sanctitati aut nihil, aut parum.
units.tr: The question which now presses you more keenly is: by what right do the most wicked successors usurp the title of Holiness belonging to their most pious predecessors? You labour with great effort to extricate yourselves from this difficulty. Navarre says: The Pope does not sin in wishing to be called Most Holy, nor does the King in wishing to be called Most Christian, nor do those who so call them sin, in this sense, because they hold dignities whose possessors ought to be such. One may take an example from the Extravagantes, not an unpleasant one, of Pope Boniface IX, who (as if to cherish the memory of his predecessor Boniface VIII) called him his predecessor of good memory. Hence the Papal Gloss, seizing an occasion to comment, when someone asks: Can a Pope who has defiled the Church by wicked deeds, by simony and by foul speech, be called Pontiff of ill memory? it replies: Say that he cannot; one must look not to what he did, but to what it befitted him to do. So it speaks. Such praise (to use Bernard's words) is close to blame; for on this principle who is so utterly wicked as not to be considered Most Holy? The Jesuit Azorius is somewhat more modest: Although these names, Most Holy and Most Blessed, began to be given to Leo I as to a man of holy life and of a character most holy, afterwards these names were retained on account of the function and office which the Pontiff performs; just as the name Most Christian began to be given to the single King of the French, who was excellent in guarding the Christian faith and religion, and afterwards remained hereditary to others; and the name Catholic to the Kings of Spain on account of their defence of the Catholic faith. Why do you ask, Bellarmine, what these things achieve? I will tell you, so that they may shame you: first, because although you taught that the use of Holy [Sanctus] is most ancient, you tried to persuade us that your Popes are superior by authority not only to bishops but even to emperors; yet this use only began with Leo I. Second, because you transferred its proper and genuine sense, by which the probity of character was commended, to an alien and forced sense, the honour of office and function; so that what Bernard said to Pope Eugenius fits your Popes most aptly: Ecclesiastical zeal gives everything to the defence of dignity and nothing, or very little, to holiness.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Ex II^a. Comparatione Pontificum cum aliys Episco- pis, Idem probari.
units.tr: From the Second Comparison of the Popes with other Bishops, the same point is proved.

units.la: QVod si vero titulum Sanctitatis non tam hominis quàm ordinis Pontificij insignem Notam esse voleris, sequetur, neminem prorsus esse sacris ordinibus inauguratum, quem non, ratione tàm diuini muneris, Sanctum existimemus; eòque magis quanto quis cœlesti mysteriorum Dei cognitione est instructior. Ad hanc rem sat erit vnicum Augustini exemplum attexere, cui Bonifacius hàc inscriptione Epistolam suam nuncupauit; {m}Domino beatissimo, & venerabili, Sancto Patri Augustino Episcopo. Et in eundem modum Hieronymus; {*}Domino vere sancto, & beatissimo Papae Augustino. Hinc verò colligere (quod Tu, Bellarmine, doces) Augustinus Primatum obtinuisse per vniuersos Christianos, esset, vt itâ dicam, crassa subtilitas, & ad euertendam Rom. Pontificis Monarchiam propè fatalis. Nec sane quicquam iuuat Morem cuiusquam nobis objcere, nam {n}Gregorij Turonensis Archiepiscopi (inquit Possevinus) mos erat, vt omnes viros, pietate insignes, nominaret Sanctos. Hæc est alia ratio vocandi Sanctos, quæ est ab hac causa remotior; in qua, ex splendido Sanctitatis titulo, Pontifices tantùm Primatus & honoris opinionem aucupantes, virtutem ipsam & Sanctitatem suisque deque habent.
units.tr: But if you would have the title of Holiness be a mark distinguishing not so much the man as the Papal office, it will follow that no one at all who has been inaugurated into the sacred orders should fail to be regarded as holy, given the great divine office he holds, and all the more so the more fully he is instructed in the heavenly knowledge of God's mysteries. One example of Augustine will be enough for this matter: Boniface addressed his letter to him with this inscription: To the most blessed and venerable lord, the holy father Augustine, Bishop. And Jerome in the same way: To the truly holy and most blessed Pope Augustine. But to infer from this (as you, Bellarmine, teach) that Augustine held the Primacy throughout all Christians would be, so to speak, a gross subtlety, and almost fatal to overturning the Monarchy of the Roman Pontiff. Nor does it help at all to object to us the custom of any one man; for (says Possevinus) it was the custom of Gregory of Tours, Archbishop, to name all men distinguished for piety saints. This is another and more remote reason for calling men saints, one in which, from the splendid title of Holiness, the Popes, grasping only at the reputation of Primacy and honour, hold virtue itself and holiness in contempt, both for themselves and for others.

units.la: Posteriorum enim seculorum Pontifices cuius tribus fuerint, facilè erit ex eo dignoscere, quòd antiquum illud obseruantiæ {o}Shibboleth ( si vnquàm nouerunt ) iamdiu dedidicerunt: nunc autem, Sanctitate ipsa spretâ atque contemptâ, Sanctitatis Titulos duntaxat vendicant. Melius sanè profanus ille apud {p}Poëtam (quanquàm peßimè omninò) qui solebat orare, — O pulchra La-serna, — Da iustum, sanctúmque videri, saltem; Illi verò tantùm audire, & appellari cupiunt. Hæc de Comparatione secunda.
units.tr: For it will be easy to tell from this what sort of Popes the later centuries have had: they have long since unlearned that old Shibboleth of observance (if they ever knew it). Now, having scorned and despised holiness itself, they claim only the titles of holiness. Far better was that worldly man in the Poet (though a very bad one altogether), who used to pray: O lovely Laserna, grant that I may seem just and holy, at least; but these men desire only to hear and to be called so. So much on the second Comparison.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Ex Comparatione IIIª inter Pontifices & Impera- tores, de Sanctitatis atque Pietatis vo- cabulis, Idem eiusdem.
units.tr: From the Third Comparison between the Popes and the Emperors, concerning the words Holiness and Piety, the same author's point.

units.la: Quin & Principes Christiani etiam Summi {*} (inquis) cùm ad Pontificem scribunt & loquuntur, cum Sanctum vocant.
