Mitte quod scio, dic quod rogo; ergonè Principes Pontificem (hoc enim intendis) seipsis, etiam in Temporalibus, Superiorem esse agnoscunt? {q}Reges gentium (ait Christus Dominus) dominantur eorum, & qui potestatem habent super eos εὐεργέται[?] vocantur, id est, magnificis ornantur titulis. Rationem huius Iansenius reddituru- rus est; {r}Significatur (inquit) eos affectare huiusmodi titulos & nomenclaturas, quibus commendatur eorum munificentia & liberalitas; magisque vocari huiusmodi nominibus, quàm esse quod vocantur. In hoc speculo Pontificibus veritis vultus suos contemplari licebit, nisi quod Regum Gentium hypocrisin atque tyrannidem non imitari modò, sed & longè superare maluerint; qui, quùm se Seruos Seruorum Dei inscribunt, nihil tamen magis affectant quàm Dominari, non tantùm in Spiritualibus, sed, more Regum Gentium, vtique in temporalibus; nec populo modò, sed (sicut Tu vis) ipsis Regibus; nec solùm Christianorum, sed & Gentium; idque vsquèadeò, vt eos Regnis suis exuant, nisi pro Pontificum arbitrio se eorum potestati per omnia mancipauerint. Siccinè imperitare Regibus solent Christi Vicarij; non obstante quòd (Christus[?] id Apostolis suis interdixerit, dicens, Vos autem non sic?
units.tr: Moreover, you say, Christian princes, even the highest, when they write to or speak with the Pope, call him Holy. Set aside what I know; tell me what I ask: do princes acknowledge the Pope (for this is your aim) to be superior to themselves, even in temporal matters? The kings of the nations (says Christ the Lord) lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors [εὐεργέται], that is, they are adorned with magnificent titles. Jansenius will give the reason for this: It is signified (he says) that they aim at titles and forms of address of this kind, by which their generosity and liberality are commended; and that they would rather be called by such names than be what they are called. In this mirror the Popes may look upon their own faces, except that they have preferred not merely to imitate the hypocrisy and tyranny of the Kings of the Gentiles, but to far surpass them; who, while they write themselves the Servants of the Servants of God, nevertheless aim at nothing more than to Lord it over, not only in spiritual matters, but, after the manner of the Kings of the Gentiles, certainly in temporal ones; not only over the people, but (as you would have it) over the very Kings themselves; not only over Christians, but also over Gentiles; and to such a degree that they strip them of their kingdoms unless they have surrendered themselves entirely to the power of the Popes at their discretion. Is this how the Vicars of Christ are accustomed to rule over kings, notwithstanding that Christ forbade this to his Apostles, saying, But you shall not be so?

units.la: Nè tamen obstrepat nobis illud, quod Tu seriò nimis oggannis, Pontificem à summis Principibus Sanctum dici; quasi ex eo Pontifex Principibus summis, vt ita dicam, Summior constituatur: habeo ad manum literas Antiquorum, non modò Imperatorum, quibus Episcopi alij Sanctissimi salutantur; sed & etiam Episcoporum, quibus {*} Imperatoris persona, semel Diuinitas, interdùm Beatitudo, nonnunquam Maiestas, frequentissimè verò Pietas appellatur. Nec hoc solùm, sed & Mandata eius scriptis obsignata, (nescio an à Sancto) Sanctiones; Literæ, sacræ Leges, ac Syllabæ diuinæ vocantur. Nec sanè desunt Pontifices verè Sancti, qui nobis in hac parte plurimùm suffragantur. Martinus I.ᵐᵒ[?] Papa inscribit Imperatorem Dominum pissimum; Hadrianus I.ᵗᵘ[?] Papa, Pissimum Dominum; Anastasius Papa Anastasio Imperatori {ƒ}Pietatis titulum tribuit; an forte minùs honorificum altero vocabulo Sanctitatis? eundem Pontificem consulamus. {‡}Sicut (inquit) praecelsum PIETATIS tua vocabulum per vniuersas Gentes toto Orbe praefulget, &c.
units.tr: Yet lest that point clamour against us, which you so earnestly and repeatedly press, that the Pope is called Holy by the highest Princes; as if from this the Pope were set up, so to speak, as higher than the highest princes: I have at hand the letters of the Ancients, not only of Emperors, in which other bishops are greeted as most holy; but also of bishops, in which the person of the Emperor is called once Divinity, at times Blessedness, sometimes Majesty, and most often Piety. And not only this, but his commands, sealed with his writing, are called (I know not whether from holy) sanctions; letters, sacred laws, and divine rescripts. Nor indeed are there lacking Popes who were truly holy, who lend us very great support on this point. Pope Martin I addresses the Emperor as Lord most pious; Pope Hadrian I as most pious Lord; Pope Anastasius gives the title of Piety to the Emperor Anastasius; or is perhaps the other term, Holiness, more honourable? Let us consult the same Pope. As (he says) your most exalted title of PIETY shines forth through all the nations throughout the whole world, etc.

units.la: Ad Conclusionem festino. Tu, Summorum Imperatorum (inquis) mos fuit summos Pontifices Sanctos appellare; Indè alibi Concludis, Ergò Pontifices Primatum habent, quo vel ipsos Imperatores deponant. Respondeo; Mos pariter fuit summorum Pontificum summos Imperatores Pissimos vocare. Ergo possunt Pontifices ab Imperatoribus deponi. Huius consequutionis, pro Principibus, vim aliquam percipis? Hanc ampleˇere igitur: Non percipis? ergò expunge, pro Pontificibus, tuam; quâ perinde contendis, ac si statuas inter Pietatem ac Sanctitatem ταυτὸν ἐστιν[?] excitare. Nullus Princeps tàm obesæ naris, cui mens tua non suboleat, Ergo si sipis[?] (nam morem populi iactas) — Ad populum has phaleras. Hucúsque de Tribus Attributis ipsius nominis [Pater.] Sequuntur de Rationibus & Consequentijs alijs, quas Tres esse video: quarum I. à Potestate gignendi filios spirituales; II. à Ritibus celebratis in solenni creatione Pontificis. III, ex Principum honorifica congratulatione deducitur.
units.tr: I hasten to the conclusion. You say, it was the custom of the highest Emperors to call the highest Popes Holy; and then elsewhere you conclude, Therefore the Popes hold the Primacy, by which they may even depose the Emperors themselves. I reply: it was equally the custom of the highest Popes to call the highest Emperors most pious. Therefore the Popes may be deposed by the Emperors. Do you perceive any force in this consequence, as regards princes? If you do not, then grasp it: if you do not perceive it, then strike out your own, as regards Popes, by which you contend just as if you were to set up Piety and Holiness as the same thing [ταυτὸν ἐστιν]. No prince is so thick-nosed that your mind does not smell him out. Therefore, if you are not wise (for you boast of the custom of the people)—Take these trappings to the people. Thus far on the Three Attributes of the name itself [Father]. There follow the other Reasons and Consequences, which I see are three in number: the first derives from the power of begetting spiritual sons; the second from the rites celebrated in the solemn creation of the Pope; the third is deduced from the honourable congratulation of Princes.

units.la: Rationes Bellarminiana, pro Titulo Patris.
units.tr: Bellarmine's Arguments for the Title of Father

units.la: Ratio prima, & planè palmaria, quâ Bellarminus aduersus Ius & dignitatem Regiam pugnat nequiter; dum obtendit vniuersalem Paternitatem Pontificis colligi ex pacto Baptismatis.
units.tr: The first argument, and a thoroughly outstanding one, by which Bellarmine wickedly attacks the right and dignity of kings, is that he contends that the universal fatherhood of the Pope is inferred from the covenant of Baptism.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: “ Iure autem Summus Pontifex Pater omnium Fidelium, quià ipse est, qui vel per se, vel per alios, per verbum Dei, & Sacramentum Baptismi filios spirituales gignit. Pag. 25.
units.tr: "By right, the Supreme Pontiff is the Father of all the faithful, because he is the one who begets spiritual sons, either himself or through others, by the Word of God and the Sacrament of Baptism." Page 25.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Cautela Principibus necessaria.
units.tr: First Observation: A Caution Necessary for Princes

units.la: Verba ista, [Pater omnium fidelium, qui gignit (id enim Bellarminus intendit) Principes per verbum, & per Sacramentum Baptismi, filios nimirum spirituales,] singula singularem quandam & omninò spiritualem Pontificem erga Principes Paternitatem spirare videntur. Ecquis enim Princeps Christianus tam sagacis acuminis est, qui in Patre hostem; in hoc Gignere perdere; in Baptismo Christi, videlicet Sacramento & sigillo mysterij fidei, & pietatis, mysterium aliquod Antichristianæ perfidiæ subolfacere possit? At auscultent, oro, Principes parumper, & fraude Bellarmini patefactâ protenus obstupescent; Is enim erit sui appositissimus interpres.
units.tr: These words, "the Father of all the faithful, who begets (for this is what Bellarmine means) Princes through the Word and through the Sacrament of Baptism, namely spiritual sons," each and every one seem to breathe a peculiar and wholly spiritual paternity of the Pontiff towards Princes. For what Christian prince is so keen-sighted that he could scent, in this "Father", an enemy; in this "begetting", a loss; in the Baptism of Christ, that is, the Sacrament and seal of the mystery of faith and piety, some mystery of Antichristian perfidy? But let Princes, I beg, listen a little longer, and once Bellarmine's trickery is exposed they will be astonished at once; for he will be his own most fitting interpreter.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Bellarmini mentem (sub vocabulo Patris delitescentem) perquàm infestam Regibus comperi.
units.tr: Second Observation: I have found Bellarmine's mind, lurking under the word Father, to be very hostile to Kings.

units.la: Quando {a}Reges & Principes ad Ecclesiam veniunt, ut Christiani fiant, recipiuntur cum paucis expresso, vel tacito, ut sceptra sua subiiciant Christo, & pollicentur se Christi fidem seruaturos & defensuros, etiam sub poena regni perdendi. Ergo, quando fiunt Haretici, aut religioni obsunt, possunt ab Ecclesia iudicari, atque etiam deponi a Principatu: nec ulla eis iniuria fiet, si deponantur; nam non est idoneus Sacramento Christi, qui non est paratus Christo seruire, & propter ipsum amittere quicquid habet. Ait enim Dominus Luc.14. Si quis venit ad me, & non odit Patrem & Matrem, non potest esse meus Discipulus.
units.tr: When Kings and Princes come to the Church so that they may become Christians, they are received on the understanding, expressed or tacit, that they will submit their sceptres to Christ, and promise that they will keep and defend the faith of Christ, even under penalty of losing their kingdom. Therefore, when they become heretics, or stand in the way of religion, they can be judged by the Church, and even deposed from their principality; nor will any injury be done to them if they are deposed; for he is not fit for the Sacrament of Christ who is not ready to serve Christ and, for his sake, to lose whatever he has. For the Lord says in Luke 14: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, he cannot be my disciple."

units.la: Hæc Bellarminus adfert ad confirmandam Conclusionem, quam præmiserat; Papam nimirùm habere potestatem temporalem indirectè, quâ Principes deponat. Et vix dici potest quantopere in hoc argumento, tanquàm summo causæ suæ propugnaculo, exultet. Hoc enim semel posuit in controuersijs suis de Pontifice: idem iterùm in Torto suo (dixissem semet-ipso) repetit: in Responso demùm ad Barclaium cramben ter coctam reponit. Quod tamen, si à nobis accuratiùs discutiatur, nihil eo videbitur magis vel à Christi mente abhorrere; vel Bellarmini ipsius principijs repugnare; vel Patrum suorum Pontificum religioni obesse; vel Antiquitati aduersari: Addo; id etiam Papārum minùs quàm aliorum Episcoporum authoritatem iuuare.
units.tr: Bellarmine brings these things forward to confirm the conclusion he had laid down before: namely that the Pope has a temporal power, indirect, by which he deposes Princes. And it can hardly be said how greatly he exults in this argument, as in the highest bulwark of his cause. For he has put this forward once already in his controversies concerning the Pope; he repeats it again in his Tortus (I should have said, in himself); and finally in his Response to Barclay he serves up cabbage boiled three times over. Yet if this is examined by us more closely, nothing will appear more remote from the mind of Christ, or more opposed to Bellarmine's own principles, or more harmful to the religion of his Fathers the Popes, or more contrary to antiquity. I add that it also supports the authority of the Popes less than that of other Bishops.

units.la: III ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: Third Observation.

units.la: Verborum Christi Luc. 14. [Si quis venit ad me &c.] sen- sus germanus enucleatur.
units.tr: The true sense of the words of Christ in Luke 14 [If anyone comes to me, etc.] is set out.

units.la: Argumenti tui vis omnis istis Christi verbis nititur, Si quis &c. nostri muneris erit, verborum Christi sensum germanum expiscari; qui (vt facilius nobis innotescat) Aduersarium certis quibusdam quaestionibus & responsis, tanquàm tormentis, ad veritatem agnoscendam adigemus. I. Quaerendum esse visum est, Quemnam Christus instruere & erudire his verbis voluerit? dico quemlibet Christianum. Patet; Si quis (inquit) venit ad me: Vbi loquitur (secundùm Augustinum) {b}de Omnibus Christianis. II.* Ecquem vero odisse cuiquam Christiano liceat? Imò quemuis Christianæ fidei aduersantem, id quod satis innuitur verbis proximis, [Odit Patrem, & Matrem.] III. Hoc autem [Odisse Patrem, aut Matrem] quid sibi vult? an vt Parentes nostros, aut amicos alioqui Nobis charissimos, religionis causâ, hostili odio prosequamur? nullo pacto, nam (fatente Iesuitâ) {c}Est hæc hyperbolica locutio, vt illa Matt.18. Si manus tua te scandalizauerit, abscinde; non quòd manus abscindendas sit, sed quòd quæuis occasio mali fugienda sit. Odisse ergò Parentes nihil aliud est, quàm eis, quando fidei nostræ, & Dei obedientiæ[?] debitæ abuersantur, non obedire. Quærit Gregorius; {d}Parentes odisse iubemur, qui præcipimur Inimicos diligere? elegantèrque respondet; Si Pater, ait, aduersatur in via Domini, per odium diligitur, qui carnaliter sapiens est, dum cùm prauis nobis ingeri non auditur.
units.tr: The whole force of your argument rests on these words of Christ, "If anyone comes to me," etc. It is my task to draw out the true sense of the words of Christ. So that it may become clearer to us, I shall press our opponent, as with certain tortures, through definite questions and answers, to acknowledge the truth. I. It seems right to ask: whom did Christ wish to instruct and teach with these words? I say, any Christian. This is plain: "If anyone comes to me," he says, where he speaks (according to Augustine) {b} of all Christians. II. But may any Christian hate anyone at all? Indeed, any opponent of the Christian faith, as the words that follow sufficiently indicate, [He hates his father and mother.] III. But what does this, to hate father or mother, mean? Are we to pursue our parents, or other friends otherwise dearest to us, with hostile hatred for the sake of religion? By no means. For (as the Jesuit admits) {c} this is hyperbolical speech, like that at Matt. 18, "If your hand offend you, cut it off": not that hands are to be cut off, but that every occasion of evil is to be shunned. Therefore to hate parents is nothing other than not to obey them when they oppose our faith and the obedience owed to God. Gregory asks: {d} are we bidden to hate parents, when we are commanded to love our enemies? And he answers elegantly: If a father, he says, opposes us on the way of the Lord, he is loved through hatred, since he who is wise in the flesh is not heard when he forces wicked things upon us.

units.la: IV. At hoc Christi mandatum quenquam Odio habendi quoüsque se extendit? an ita alios constringit, vt nosipsos solutos & immunes relinquat, qui Alios odisse iubemur? Imò verò nosipsos premit vel maximè. patet; Nisi (inquit) odio habeat etiam animam suam. Vbi (vt rectè Augustinus) {e}Per animam, vitam significat: & sensus est, Qui non odit vitam suam (cùm opus est Martyrium obire) non potest esse meus Discipulus. Postrema; Quam pœnam tandè minatur Christus ei, qui pacti sui reus, à fide Christiana, mortis timore, defecerit; temporalemne ac corporalem, an dûtaxat spirituale & æternam? Proculdubiò prorsus æternâ, id quod Euangelista Matthæus, Christi doctrinam referens, plenius ostendit. {f}Qui inuenerit animam suam, perdet eam, qui autem perdiderit animam suam meâ causâ, inueniet eam. In quê locum vester Maldonatus. {g}Nomine Animæ vitæ, Christus ambiguè, quod in similibus ambiguis vocabulis non solùm sine vitio, sed etiam cum elegantia & emphasi fieri solet, vt Mat. 8.22. in priore accipit Animam pro vita Hebræorum idiomate; in posteriori pro anima, quæ aut in vitam æternam recipienda, aut in ignem æternum mittenda est. Potui ego hanc nostram Expositionem Iansenij, Abulensis, Salmeronis, plurimumque aliorum Pontificiorum testimonijs per omnia confirmare: sed quia nullus omnium est, quod sciam, qui huic refragatur, ab his Præmissis ad Bellarmini consequutionem reuertor.
units.tr: IV. But how far does this command of Christ to hate extend to anyone? Does it so bind others that it leaves us ourselves free and exempt, when we are bidden to hate others? Indeed it presses hardest upon ourselves. It is plain: "unless he hate even his own soul." Here (as Augustine rightly says) {e} "soul" signifies life; and the sense is: he who does not hate his life (when it is necessary to undergo martyrdom) cannot be my disciple. Last point: what punishment does Christ at last threaten against one who, bound by his covenant, falls away from the Christian faith through fear of death: a temporal and bodily one, or only a spiritual and eternal one? Assuredly wholly eternal, as the evangelist Matthew shows more fully when reporting the teaching of Christ. {f} He who finds his soul will lose it, but he who loses his soul for my sake will find it. On this passage your Maldonatus {g} says: Christ speaks ambiguously with the name "soul," which is done not only without fault but even with elegance and emphasis in similar ambiguous words, as at Mat. 8.22, where in the first case he takes "soul" for life, in the Hebrew idiom; in the latter case for the soul, which is either to be received into eternal life or sent into eternal fire. I could confirm this our exposition by the testimonies of Jansen, Abulensis, Salmeron, and very many other Papists in every respect. But since there is, so far as I know, none of them all who disagrees, I return from these premises to Bellarmine's conclusion.

units.la: SECT. XXI.
units.tr: SECT. XXI.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Pactum illud, quod Sanderus primò commentitum est, Pacto, quo Christus ab omnibus Christianis obedientiam stipulatur, diametro tot à repugnare.
units.tr: That pact which Sander first invented is diametrically at odds with the pact by which Christ requires obedience from all Christians.

units.la: PActum, quo Bellarminus (siue id tacitum, siue expressum fuerit) Reges obligari in Baptismo comminiscitur, ita Eos Pontificis potestati obnoxios reddit, vt si quandò vel Ipsi in Hæresin incidërint, vel Subditos ad Hæresin pertraxerint, regnis suis necessariò deturbentur. Nunc, si placet, huius Pacti scopum cum Christi scopo; pœnam cum pœna; Odij dicti modum cum modo; Authoritatémque denique mandandi cum authoritate conferamus; & in his singulis Bellarmini Pactum à Pacto Christi non minùs quàm lucem à tenebris, verùm à falso distare deprehendemus.
units.tr: The pact by which Bellarmine (whether tacit or express) imagines that kings are bound in baptism makes them so subject to the power of the Pope that, if they themselves fall into heresy or draw their subjects into heresy, they are necessarily thrown from their kingdoms. Now, if you please, let us compare the aim of this pact with Christ's aim, its penalty with his penalty, the manner of the said hatred with his manner, and finally the authority of commanding with his authority. In each of these we shall find that Bellarmine's pact differs from Christ's pact no less than light from darkness, or rather truth from falsehood.

units.la: I. Christi scopus erat ita discipulum suum instituere, vt semper animo paratus fit * voluntariam, & spontaneam Patria, atque adeò vitæ propriæ amissionem subire, quo Christianorum religionem afferat atque defendat. At Pactum Bellarminus tale colligit, quo Principes, si forte fidem deseruerint, Regnis suis velint nolintue discedere cogantur. II. Christus in suo Pacto pœnam tantum *æternam: Bellarminus autem suo Regni amissionem, quæ est pœna prorsus temporalis, delinquenti denunciat. III. Alium illud aduersus *Parentes, ex mente Saluatoris, tantùm significat Nolle obedire Parentibus in eis, quæ contra veram fidem impiè persuaserint, aut mandauerint; non autem (quod Bellarmini Pactum infert)
units.tr: I. Christ's aim was to instruct his disciple so that he is always ready in mind to undergo a voluntary and spontaneous loss of his homeland, and indeed of his own life, in order to bring forward and defend the religion of Christians. But Bellarmine infers a pact of such a kind that princes, if perhaps they abandon the faith, are compelled to leave their kingdoms whether they will or no. II. Christ in his pact threatens the offender only with eternal punishment; but Bellarmine threatens the offender with the loss of his kingdom, which is a wholly temporal penalty. III. That other precept concerning parents, in the mind of the Saviour, signifies only refusing to obey parents in those things which they have impiously urged or commanded against the true faith; it does not mean (as Bellarmine's pact infers)

units.la: b Nam hoc Argumentum Bellarminus Sandero debet, ex quo mutuatus est; in lib. 2. de vi.sib. Monarch. cap. 4. pag. 71.
units.tr: b For this argument Bellarmine owes to Sander, from whom he borrowed it; in book 2 of On the Visible Monarchy, chapter 4, page 71.

units.la: * Vid. Quæst. 4. supra.
units.tr: See Question 4 above.

units.la: * Supra quæst. 1.
units.tr: See Question 1 above.

units.la: * Vid. quæst. 3. fert) Parentes nostros possessionibus suis spoliare. Postremò Authoritatem, quam exercet Christus in supplicio æterno irrogando, omnes Directam esse nôrunt. Eam autem, quam Bellarminus Pontifici in temporalibus tribuit, tantùm Indirectam esse, multis Ipse Rationibus confirmare satagit. Quis igitur non peruersè cœcus iam non clarè videt, quantum Bellarminus à Christiani Pasti[?] vero & destinato scopo aberraverit? Coactam enim Regni amissionem cum spontaneâ; Temporalem pœnam cum Æterna; positiuum Odium cum Priuatiuo; Authoritatem denique Indirectam cum Directa confundere perinde est atque polum Arcticum cum Antarctico copulare.
units.tr: See Question 3 above. ...[the sentence continues:] to strip our parents of their possessions. Finally, all know that the authority which Christ exercises in inflicting eternal punishment is direct. But the authority which Bellarmine grants to the Pope in temporal matters, he himself labours to show by many arguments is only indirect. Who then, unless perversely blind, does not now clearly see how far Bellarmine has strayed from the true and intended aim of the Christian pastor? For to confuse a forced loss of a kingdom with a spontaneous one; a temporal penalty with an eternal one; a positive hatred with a privative one; and, finally, indirect authority with direct authority, is just as absurd as joining the Arctic Pole to the Antarctic.

units.la: V. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: V. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Bellarminum, vt Principiorum fuerum, ad palinodiam, vel invitum trahi.
units.tr: That Bellarmine, as the author of his own principles, is dragged back to a recantation, even against his will.

units.la: TRia extant apud Bellarminû principia, ex quibus Eum revinci necesse est. Primum cernitur collatione habitâ inter Principes Ethnicos & Christianos. II. Inter Magistratum Ecclesiasticum, & Politicum. III. Inter Principes ipsos & Pontifices. Primi generis Principium est huiusmodi. {i} Ex Scripturarum testimonys colligitur, (nempe contrà Anabaptistas) Politicum Magistratum apud Christianos: nam si ex adductis testimonijs licet subesse Regi Ethnico, cur non Regi Christiano? & si licet Christiano subesse, cur non præesse? Consequentiâ hâc nihil solidius aut firmius, quâ posità, eiusdem Argumenti vim in Bellarminum intorqueo. Si enim Ethnicus iam factus Christianus virtute Christianitatis, ceu Baptismatis, magis præesse debet; tùm profectò non itâ ex Pacto Baptismatis subjiciuntur Pontificibus, vt ex eorum authoritate (quod est minus quàm præesse) facilius Regnis suis priuari possint; nisi, secundùm vestram Dialecticam, idem locus Topicus obsit Regibus maximè, quem produxti, vt eorum potestati inseruiat.
units.tr: There are three principles in Bellarmine by which he must necessarily be refuted. The first is seen from the comparison made between heathen and Christian princes; the second between the ecclesiastical and the political magistrate; the third between the princes themselves and the Pontiffs. The principle of the first kind is this: {i} From the testimonies of Scripture it is gathered (namely against the Anabaptists) that there is a political magistrate among Christians; for if from the testimonies adduced it is lawful to be subject to a heathen king, why not to a Christian king? And if it is lawful for a Christian to be subject, why not to be set over others? Nothing is more solid or firm than this inference; granting it, I turn the force of the same argument against Bellarmine. For if a heathen, now made a Christian, ought to rule all the more by virtue of Christianity, as by baptism, then assuredly they are not thus made subject to the Pontiffs by the pact of baptism, so that by their authority (which is less than ruling) they may more easily be deprived of their kingdoms. Unless, by your dialectic, the very topical argument which you have produced to serve the power of the Pope is especially harmful to kings.

units.la: Secundum principium exploremus. Vbi proponitur Quaestio, vtrum Christianus, ex pacto Baptismatis, quo se addicit Deo in seruitutem, liber sit factus ab omni humana seruitute, siue Ecclesiastica ea sit, siue politica? Tu, ex dictis Christi, iubentis docere Baptizatos seruare omnia praecepta eius, Respondes, {k} Christianos per Baptismum non liberari ab obligatione legis Ecclesiasticae, quia unum est ex praeceptis Christi, vt eis obediamus, quando Dominus ait, Qui vos audit, me audit. Quod ad Politicas leges attinet; Apostolus (inquit) passim imperat vt obediant, post Baptismum, serui Dominis, filij Parentibus, priuati Magistratibus. Vnde haec ratio emergit? (vt Dialecticorum viribus pugnemus.) Qua vi Politica potestas stabilitur, eadem nullo modo diminui censenda est: sed potestas politica in temporalibus, vi Pacti in Baptismo suscepti, eadem qua potestas Ecclesiastica Christi authoritate stabilitur. Proinde ex eodem Pacto minime minuitur aut debilitatur.
units.tr: Let us examine the second principle. The question is put: whether a Christian, by the pact of baptism, by which he dedicates himself to God in servitude, is made free from every human servitude, whether ecclesiastical or political? From the words of Christ commanding that the baptized be taught to keep all his precepts, you answer that Christians are not freed through baptism from the obligation of ecclesiastical law, because it is one of Christ's precepts that we obey the Church, when the Lord says, He who hears you hears me. As for political laws: the Apostle (he says) everywhere commands that after baptism servants obey their masters, children their parents, and private persons their magistrates. From what reasoning does this come? (Let us fight with the strength of the dialecticians.) By the same power by which political authority is established, that authority is in no way to be judged diminished; but political power in temporal matters, by the power of the pact received in baptism, is established by the same authority of Christ as ecclesiastical power is. Therefore it is in no way lessened or weakened by the same pact.

units.la: Tertium aggredimur. Ex Christi Pacto quilibet cuiuscunque fuerit temporis, sexus, aetatis, ordinis Christianus, quoties postulauerit occasio, Patrem & Matrem odisse tenetur: Institutio enim Christi est {*}vniuersalis; Si quis venit ad me, & non odit Patrem & Matrem, &c. Tu vero, cum asseris vi huius Pacti Reges subiici debere Ecclesiae, vsque ad Regnorum amissionem; tamen {l}Pontificem posse renunciare Papatui suo, absque consensu Ecclesiae, plane negas. Nec hoc solum, sed si Ecclesia aliqua de causa Pontificem deposuerit, negas porro Pontificem posse se subiicere coactiuae potestati Ecclesiae. Disputo. Quum Pontifex eadem Pacti religione, qua erat baptizatus, constringatur, si eius naufragium fecerit, poteritne ab Ecclesia deponi, vel non? Si potest, tum falso dicis Pontificem non subiici coactiuae potestati Ecclesiae. Si non potest, tum falso asseris Principes, ex Pacto Baptismatis, ab Ecclesia debere deponi. De Principibus autem quid (inquies) nihil ratio valet, quum iusta adest causa Depositionis? At Depositionis causa (inquam) nulla iusta fingi potest, vbi ius Deponendi nullum est.
units.tr: Let us come to the third. By the pact of Christ, any Christian of whatever time, sex, age or rank is bound, whenever occasion demands, to hate father and mother, for Christ's institution is universal: If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, etc. You, indeed, when you assert that by the power of this pact kings ought to be subject to the Church, even to the loss of their kingdoms, nevertheless plainly deny that the Pope can renounce his papacy without the consent of the Church. Not only this, but if some Church for some reason deposes the Pope, you further deny that the Pope can submit himself to the coercive power of the Church. I argue: since the Pope is bound by the same religion of the pact by which he was baptized, if he has suffered shipwreck, can he be deposed by the Church or not? If he can, then you falsely say that the Pope is not subject to the coercive power of the Church. If he cannot, then you falsely assert that princes, by the pact of baptism, ought to be deposed by the Church. But what (you will say) of princes? Nothing of the argument holds, since there is a just cause of deposition. But a just cause of deposition (I say) cannot be feigned where there is no right to depose.

units.la: VI. ANIMADVERSIO. Illud Baptismi Pactum Religioni Pontificiæ obesse vel maximè.
units.tr: VI. ANIMADVERSIO. That the baptismal covenant is above all harmful to the Papist religion.

units.la: VI illius voti, in sacro Baptismate suscepti, siue taciti, siue expressi, omnes Christiani illam Religionem auersari atque vitare arctè tenentur, quâ veritas Evangelica oppugnatur; & in hac causa nullius hominis mandatis, ad extremum vsque halitum, non obsistere: quod significare Christus voluit, cùm mandauit {*}Odisse Patrem,&c. ipsum, licet, Patrem vestrum Papam intelligamus. Ad hoc confirmandum Te, Bellarmine, Aduocatum deposcimus. {n}Si Pontifex (inquis) præciperet manifestum vitium, aut prohiberet manifestam virtutem, dicendum est cùm Petro obedire oportet magis Deo quàm hominibus.
units.tr: By that vow taken in holy Baptism, whether tacit or expressed, all Christians are bound to turn away from and avoid that religion by which the Gospel truth is assailed. In this cause they must not yield to any man's commands, even to their last breath. Christ meant this when he commanded us to hate "the Father", etc., and we understand this to mean our Father the Pope. To confirm this we call upon you, Bellarmine, as our advocate. You say: If the Pontiff should command a manifest vice, or forbid a manifest virtue, we must say that we ought to obey God rather than men, as Peter did.

units.la: Optimè, nihil Nos optamus amplius. Nobis igitur ignoscere debetis, si per legem solennis illius Pacti, quo Christo fidem astrinximus, religioni isti assentire renuamus, quâ (Papâ partim imperante, partim annuente) Dei nostri Zelotis Cultus publicus varia votorum, invocationum, genu-flectionum multiplici Idololatriâ polluitur; eius Nomen vel execrandâ arte eludendi iuramenta, vel nefariâ præsumptione relaxandi, contra ius & fas, impiè profanatur; Eius Sigilla, salutis humanæ mysteria, sacrilegâ mutilatione, contra Christi institutionem, deformantur; eius Templa, quæ sunt corpora Christianorum, incestorum coniugiorum, fœdissimorum prostibulorum patrocinijs, vel potiùs lenocinijs contaminantur; eius, in terris, Proreges immanibus parricidijs è medio tolluntur; eius Christi Saluatoris nostri Prophetia cùm humanarum Traditionum, nouorumque ac falsorum Articulorum pari affectu & veneratione suscepta adulteratur; eius Sacerdotium, ex sanguinis Christi immaculati ac infiniti pretij cùm Martyrum (hominum tamen) sanguinis fœcati nefariâ commixtione, per Indulgentiarum doctrinam, conspurcatur; & eius denique Regnum immensâ Ceremoniarum, & Decretorum infinitâ multitudine atque congerie, quibus hominum conscientiæ miserè cruciantur, dirâ tyrannide obruitur. Quæ omnia si quis se videre posse negauerit, eâdem operâ vel mediâ luce solem ipsum se videre posse neget.
units.tr: Excellent! We desire nothing more. You must therefore forgive us if, by the law of that solemn covenant by which we bound ourselves to Christ, we refuse to assent to that religion, in which (with the Pope partly commanding and partly consenting) the public worship of our God, the zealous one, is polluted by manifold idolatry of various vows, invocations and genuflections; in which his Name is impiously profaned, either by the accursed art of evading oaths or by the wicked presumption of relaxing them, contrary to right and law; in which his Seals, the mysteries of human salvation, are deformed by sacrilegious mutilation, contrary to the institution of Christ; in which his Temples, which are the bodies of Christians, are contaminated by the patronage, or rather the pandering, of incestuous marriages and most foul brothels; in which, on earth, his Proreges are removed from the midst by monstrous parricides; in which the Prophecy of our Saviour Christ is corrupted, when human Traditions and new and false Articles are received with equal devotion and reverence; in which his Priesthood, by the wicked mingling of the blood of the immaculate Christ, of infinite price, with the blood of Martyrs (yet only men), is defiled through the doctrine of Indulgences; and in which, finally, his Kingdom is overwhelmed by a dire tyranny of immense Ceremonies and an infinite multitude and heap of Decrees, by which the consciences of men are miserably tormented. If anyone should deny that he can see all these things, he may just as well deny that he can see the sun itself in the midday light.

units.la: VII. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: VII. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Pacti illius Consequentia, (quà Bellarminus Reges vrget atque deuincit) vniuersa Antiquitati ignotam peni- tùs fuisse: Atque etiam ab vllo Episcopo rectiùs, quàm à Pontifice Romano, de Principibus exigi posse.
units.tr: That the consequence of that covenant, by which Bellarmine presses and binds the Kings, was entirely unknown to all antiquity; and that it can be demanded of Princes more rightly by any bishop than by the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: SAcrosanctum illud Pactum Baptismatis, quod iam exposuimus, Nos, cùm toto Orbe Christiano, agnoscimus, colimus, profitemur. At consequentiàm, quam Tu, Bellarmine, infers; quâ Reges premis, quos religione istius voti teneri, ais, Sceptra sua Pontificibus submittere, merito reijcimus & execramur: tùm quia Baptismi pacto & fœderi, quod cùm Christo iniuimus, ex aduerso repugnat; tum quia Pactum, quod inculcas, fuit antehàc adeò omninò Tacitum, vt & vniuersa Antiquitas illud penitùs tacuerit; vtque Tu, omni aliorum patrocinio destitutus, necesse haberes hoc, veluti, Achilleum tuum Argumentum tuâ solius authoritate, scilicet, promulgare.
units.tr: We acknowledge, cherish and profess that sacrosanct covenant of Baptism, which we have now set forth, together with the whole Christian world. But the consequence which you, Bellarmine, draw, by which you press the Kings, whom you say are bound by the obligation of that vow to submit their sceptres to the Pontiffs, we rightly reject and execrate. This is because it conflicts with the covenant and compact of Baptism which we have made with Christ; and because the covenant which you urge was until now so entirely unspoken that all antiquity has wholly passed it over in silence. Thus you, deprived of all support from others, had to put forward this argument, as your Achilles' heel, on your own authority alone.

units.la: Postremò à Pontifice Sergio III.{*} (vel, vt alij, IV.°) iam, per mille plus minùs Annos, omnes feré{o} Pontifices nomina sua Christiana, quæ in sacro Baptismate susceperant, expunxerunt. Ab hoc enim Sergio{P} Manauit dein (inquit Polydorus) mos ad posteros, vt qui Pontifices crearentur, omisso priore nomine, eligerent sibi vnum aliquod ex Pontificum, qui antea fuerant, nominibus. Istosnè igitur non ineptissimos Baptismatis Pacti ab aliis exactores putemus, qui nomina sua, solenni baptismo ante imposita & consecrata, tanquàm perpetua sacri illius Pacti [illegible, ~6 letters], suapte sponte deleuerunt? In qua Christiani nominis renunciatione an aliquod Antichristiani mysterij lateat, ipsi Pontifices viderint. De Ratione Paternitatis Pontificia diximus, quàm dupliciter confirmare ex Scripturis eniteris.
units.tr: Lastly, since the time of Pope Sergius III (or, as others have it, IV), for about a thousand years and more, almost all the Pontiffs have erased the Christian names which they had received in holy Baptism. For from this Sergius, as Polydore says, a custom then arose among the successors that those who were created Pontiffs, setting aside their former name, should choose for themselves one of the names of the Pontiffs who had been before them. Shall we then think that these men, who erased of their own accord their names, imposed and consecrated in solemn baptism, as if they were the perpetual covenant of that holy compact [illegible, about six letters], were not the least fitting exactors of the Baptismal covenant from others? Whether some mystery of Antichrist lies hidden in this renunciation of the Christian name, the Pontiffs themselves must see. We have spoken of the basis of Papal fatherhood, which you strive to confirm from the Scriptures in two ways.

units.la: Confirmatio I. universalis Paternitatis Pontificia.
units.tr: Confirmation I. Of the universal fatherhood of the Pope.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: “ Quod enim B. Paulus * dicebat Corinthiis, si decem millia “ Pædagogorum habeatis, sed non multos Patres, in Christo “ Jesu per Evangelium vos genui ; Idem dicere potest “ summus Pontifex fidelibus omnibus. Atque ad hoc &c. Pag. 28.
units.tr: "For what the blessed Paul said to the Corinthians, If you have ten thousand instructors, yet not many fathers, for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel, the same can be said by the supreme Pontiff to all the faithful. And to this, etc." Page 28.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Paulinum exemplum à Bellarmino prave inverti, & aliorsum trahi.
units.tr: That the Pauline example is wrongly inverted by Bellarmine and drawn to another purpose.

units.la: IN verbis praecedentibus asseruisti Pontificem omnium fidelium Patrem esse, quia per Verbum Dei alios filios spirituales gigneret, vel per se (inquis,) vel per alios. Ad hoc probandum, subinde attexis, [Quod enim B. Paulus &c.] Prius igitur nos de Paulo, post de Papa videbimus. Paulum vero per se, non per alios, id est, sua, non aliorum praedicatione hosce Corinthios ad fidem genuisse tam certum esse, quam quod certissimum, vestrum Thomam testem appello. {q}Considerandum est (inquit) quòd Pater est, qui primò genuit, Pædagogus autem, qui natum nutrit, atque erudit: Apostolus igitur dicit se Patrem, quia primo eis Evangelium praedicabat, [In Christo, inquit, vos genui.] --- Alios autem Pædagogos vocat, qui Christiani, postquam fidem receperunt, eos adjuvârunt. Et intelligit eandem esse Comparationem hoc in loco Pædagogi ad Patrem, quae supra cap. 3. Rigatoris ad plantatorem ; & super-edificatoris ad fundatorem. Hæc ille. Quæ ille quidem ab Hieronymo discere potuit, [Ego vos genui, ] id est, (inquit) {r}Me predicante vos in nouam vitam reformati estis. Omnes vero, qui ab alio geniti (nempe Pædagogi) ministrant, Patres dici non possunt. Proinde dum Tu Papam, quia gignit per Alios, fidelium Patrem esse contendis, ab exemplo Pauli, qui genuit per se, contra distertissimam Pauli sententiam: Patrem cum Pædagogo; Plantatorem cum Rigatore; Fundatorem cum Super-edificatore; Primum cum Secundo; Unum cum Alio perperam absurdeque confundis.
units.tr: In the preceding words you asserted that the Pope is the Father of all the faithful, because he begets other spiritual sons through the Word of God, either by himself or through others. To prove this you add, from time to time, [For what the blessed Paul said, etc.] Let us therefore first look at Paul and afterwards at the Pope. That Paul begot these Corinthians to the faith himself, not through others, that is, by his own preaching and not by that of others, is as certain as anything most certain; I call your Thomas as witness. He says: It must be considered that the father is the one who first begets, but the instructor is the one who nourishes and educates the born child. The Apostle therefore says that he is their father, because he first preached the Gospel to them, [In Christ, he says, I begot you.] But he calls the others instructors, who, after the Christians had received the faith, assisted them. And he understands the comparison in this passage of the instructor to the father to be the same as that, above, in chapter 3, of the waterer to the planter, and of the superstructor to the founder. So he. Jerome could have taught him what he says: [I begot you], that is (he says), through my preaching you have been reformed into a new life. But all those who minister to those born of another (namely instructors) cannot be called fathers. Therefore, while you contend that the Pope is the father of the faithful because he begets through others, you foolishly and absurdly confuse, against Paul's most express judgment and by the example of Paul, who begot through himself: the father with the instructor; the planter with the waterer; the founder with the superstructor; the first with the second; and the one with the other.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: SPaulus prædicabat per se, & Fidelium Pater iure dici potuit: Papam autem prædicatorem ac Concionatorem per aliquot retrò secula vix sanè ullum historiæ vestræ meminerunt: ac propterea Tu, catus homo scilicet, eum Per alios gignentem introducis Patrem. Id quod nobis portenti simile videtur, uti & * Hieronymo, qui aliorum Ministros Patres dici posse planè negat. Sed apud vos licet Confessario{c} Imponere pœnitentiam pœnitenti, per se, vel per alium implendam; ita ut unus pro alio ieiunet. Licet populo vestro in Sacramento{t} Spiritualiter comedere per Sacerdotem, tanquàm per os suum. Licet Papa spiritualiter gignere per alios. Denique vestra Affica[?] quid monstri non alit? De Pontificis officio prædicandi per se, & non per alium, pleniùs * differemus, cùm ad Pastoris Titulum discutiendum devenerimus.
units.tr: Paul preached in person, and could rightly be called Father of the faithful. But the Pope as preacher and sermon-giver is hardly mentioned in your history for some centuries past. Therefore you, clever fellow that you are, introduce him as Father while he begets through others. This seems to us a portent, as does Jerome, who flatly denies that the ministers of others can be called fathers. But among you it is lawful for a confessor to impose penance on a penitent, to be performed by himself or by another, so that one man may fast for another. It is lawful for your people, in the sacrament, to eat spiritually through the priest, as through his own mouth. It is lawful for the Pope to beget spiritually through others. In short, what monster does your Affica not nourish? We shall discuss more fully the office of the Pontiff, to preach in person and not through another, when we come to examine the title of Pastor.

units.la: Confirmatio II. Paternitatis Papalis, ab exemplo Petri.
units.tr: Confirmation II. of Papal Paternity, from the example of Peter.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: “ Atque ad hoc significandum voluit Deus ut primus om“nium, qui tam ex Iudæis[?] quàm ex Gentilibus filios spiri“tuales
units.tr: “And to signify this, God willed that Peter should be the first of all who begot spiritual sons, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles,

units.la: “ tales per verbum & baptismum genuit, S. Petrus fuerit : “ ipse enim primus, accepto Spiritu sancto, * die Pentecostes “ Euangelium praedicauit Iudeis, & conuersos ad fidem baptizari iussit, & ipse idem primus Cornelio Gentili & eius familia praedicauit, & credentes iussit baptizari. Pater ergo Petrus fuit. --- Pag.26. --- Hoc autem quid sibi velit alibi dilucidius explicas.
units.tr: “such through the word and baptism. For he himself, first, having received the Holy Spirit, on the day of Pentecost preached the Gospel to the Jews and ordered those who were converted to the faith to be baptized. And he himself first preached to the Gentile Cornelius and his household, and ordered the believers to be baptized. Peter therefore was the father.” --- Page 26. --- What this means, you explain more clearly elsewhere.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: {a}* Praerogatiua Petri decima-tertia est, quod primus * Euangelium promulgans, tria millia hominum conuertebat. x Decima-septima, quod primus omnium incepit * praedicare Gentilibus in domo Cornelij, sicut ante Iudeis. † Ex quibus Petri Primatus confirmatur; etiam in ipsos ⌣Apostolos.
units.tr: Peter's thirteenth prerogative is that, as the first to proclaim the Gospel, he converted three thousand men. His seventeenth is that he was the first of all to begin to preach to the Gentiles, in the house of Cornelius, just as before to the Jews. From these points Peter's primacy is confirmed, even over the Apostles themselves.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Primum reuerà Petrum inter Apostolos, non verò proprie Primatem fuisse.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. That Peter was indeed first among the Apostles, but not properly their Primate.

units.la: HÆc tua illatio nullo cùm negotio refellitur; nam quoties Petrus in Scripturis vel in {a}nomenclatura Apostolorum, vel in muneris Apostolici executione Primus nominatur, Primatus quidem eius intelligitur; sed ex prioritate ætatis, aut vocationis, aut zeli, aut denique Ordinis: at Authoritatis, aut Iurisdictionis in Apostolos alios nequaquàm. Dicam, si potero, expressiùs. Petrus Inter, non In ipsos ⌣Apostolos primatum habuit. Hæc distinctio quoties objicitur à nostris, solet esse vobis [illegible, ~6 letters]; hàc semel audità, Aduersarius obmutescit ilicò: citiùs clauam extorquebit Herculi, quàm hanc è manibus nostris excutiat eorum quispiam. Quî n.possit? {b}quùm præsertim Petrus Apostolatus sui sæpius meminerit, Pap.tus vero, aut Pōtifi:atus, aut etiam supremi Vicariatus nusquàm; sed nè Primatus quidem, quamuis hi tituli ad Primatum eum, quem neoterici Pontifices crepant, corroborandum facerent maximè.
units.tr: This inference of yours is refuted without any difficulty. For whenever Peter is named first in the Scriptures, or in the list of the Apostles, or in the carrying out of the apostolic office, his primacy is indeed understood, but it arises from priority of age, or of calling, or of zeal, or finally of rank. It is by no means a priority of authority or jurisdiction over the other Apostles. I will say this more plainly, if I can. Peter had primacy among, not over, the Apostles themselves. Whenever our side raises this distinction, it is usually met with [illegible] by you; but once it has been heard, the adversary falls silent at once. Sooner would someone wrest the club from Hercules than snatch this from our hands. How could he? Especially since Peter often mentions his apostleship, but nowhere his papacy or pontificate, or even a supreme vicariate. He does not even mention primacy, although these titles would most of all support the primacy which the modern Pontiffs boast of.

units.la: Hæc obiectio in causæ ipsius visceribus hæret: solutionem igitur, si placet, attende (Lector) & si forte quid inter Petrum, & Papam interfit antea ignores, nunc à Salmerone Iesuita discas. {c}Cùm Petrus (inquit) non tantùm esset Pastor universalis Ecclesiæ, sed etiam Apostolus, cuius proprium erat munus, universum orbem illustrare, & Evangelio illuminare, maluit tamen perfungi Apostolico munere, discurrendo per omnes Provincias, erigendo Ecclesias, & Ministros, & Episcopos ordinando (quæ munia scilicet erant Petro cum cæteris Apostolis communia) quàm pastoratu, in quo tantùm erat Coryphæus, & universarum Christi ovium Iudex, & sub se peculiarium Pastorum; itàque videretur quodammodò Pastoratum suum negligere, & primatum: & cùm cæteris Apostolis tanquàm fratrem & æqualem se gerere elegit, non autem ut maiorem, & ipsorum caput, & Rectorem. Nam si Petrus, ut Rom. Pontifex, & Christi Vicarius scripsisset, videretur in suis scriptis ius Ecclesiasticum, seu, quod idem est, Pontificium dictâsse, potiùs, quàm divinum. Hæc ille. Bellarminus vi disputationis, veluti tempestatis æstu, in transversum actus, Primatum Pontificis supra omnes Apostolos, ex gestis Petri colligit: Iesuita Salmeron tranquillo animo, veluti aëre sereno & liquido omnia propiciens atque perpendens, ipse etiam Bellarmino antiquior, Petrum gessisse[?] se, imò vel etiam scripsisse ut Pontificem diserte negat. Non est igitur cur deinceps quis dicat Petrum vnquàm Papâ gravidum fuisse, sed potiùs Papam ventosâ de Petro opinione tumidum atque inflatum, nil aliud quam [illegible, ~9 letters] suâ hâc paternitate genuisse.
units.tr: Let the reader attend to the answer to this objection, which lies in the very heart of the cause. If you do not know what difference there is between Peter and the Pope, learn it now from the Jesuit Salmeron. Since Peter (he says) was not only the universal pastor of the Church but also an Apostle, whose proper office was to enlighten the whole world with the Gospel, he nevertheless preferred to discharge the apostolic office, travelling through all the provinces, founding churches, and ordaining ministers and bishops (duties which were of course common to Peter with the other Apostles), rather than the pastorate, in which he was only the coryphaeus and judge of all Christ's sheep, and of the special pastors under him. So he would seem in some measure to neglect his pastorate and primacy, and chose to behave towards the other Apostles as a brother and equal, not as their greater, head and ruler. For if Peter had written as Roman Pontiff and Vicar of Christ, he would seem in his writings to have dictated ecclesiastical, or what is the same, papal law, rather than divine law. So he says. Bellarmine, driven by the force of the argument as by the heat of a storm, is carried off course, and from the deeds of Peter infers the Pontiff's primacy over all the Apostles. The Jesuit Salmeron, with a calm mind, surveying and weighing everything as if in clear, serene air, and himself older than Bellarmine, expressly denies that Peter acted or even wrote as Pontiff. There is therefore no reason for anyone to say that Peter was ever pregnant with the Pope. Rather, the Pope, puffed up and swollen with the windy opinion about Peter, has begotten nothing but [illegible] by this paternity of his.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Paulum æquè Patrem fidelium ac Petrum fuisse.
units.tr: That Paul was equally the Father of the faithful as Peter was.

units.la: Jam verò, ad Conversos[?] quod spectat, Petrus (inquis) primus Iudeorum & Gentilium quærundam convertsor fuit. Quid ergò? an proptereà (id enim indè colligis) om-
units.tr: Now, as far as the converts are concerned, Peter (you say) was the first converter of certain Jews and Gentiles. What then? Is he therefore (for that is what you infer) the father of all

units.la: {c} Salmer. Tef.[?] Com. in 1.Pet. 1. disp. 1. in ua.& §. Dicen-dum itaque, Tom. 16. nium fidelium conversorum vel per se, vel per alios Pater Petrus fuit? An Paulus, qui (ut ipse {d} alibi fateris) plures gentes ad fidem perduxit, quàm Petrus, filios Petro genuit? Errauit igitur Apostolus Paulus, quùm non modò erga conversos Corinthios, sed etiam erga Timotheum, & Titum Paternitatem sibi soli vendicavit. De Corinthijs. {c}Patres (inquit) non multos habuistis, in Christo Jesu, per Evangelium, Ego vos genui. Timotheum etiam & Titum vocat {f}γνήσια τέκνα [?], germanos suos filios, secundùm fidem. Nisi igitur eo peruersitatis deuenieris, ut Petrum (quod à Graeco πάτερα [?] significat Patrem Patris) Papam Pauli constituas, erroris manifestò reuinceris.
units.tr: {c} Salmeron, Tef.? Comm. on 1 Peter 1, disp. 1, and §. Dicendum itaque, Vol. 16. of the faithful converts, whether directly or through others? Or is Paul, who (as you yourself admit elsewhere) brought more nations to the faith than Peter, to be counted as having begotten sons to Peter? The Apostle Paul therefore erred when he claimed fatherhood for himself alone, not only over the converted Corinthians, but also over Timothy and Titus. To the Corinthians: "For you have not many fathers in Christ Jesus through the Gospel; I have begotten you." He also calls Timothy and Titus his genuine children [γνήσια τέκνα], his own sons according to the faith. Unless, therefore, you have sunk to such perversity as to make Peter (which in Greek [πάτερα] means father of a father) the Pope of Paul, you are manifestly refuted in your error.

units.la: Ratio II. ad probandum Papam esse Principum Pa- trem; sumitur ex Ritibus Papalibus.
units.tr: Argument II, to prove that the Pope is the Father of Princes, taken from the Papal rites.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: «« Quod ipsum ritus declarat, qui in coronatione Pontificis adhibetur, cùm Decanus Cardinalium eraus pro Pontifice vocat eum Patrem Regum, & Principum Christianorum.» pag.26.
units.tr: "Which the rite itself declares: the rite used at the coronation of the Pontiff, when the Dean of the Cardinals, calling him forth, addresses him as the Father of Kings and Christian Princes." p. 26.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: FIRST ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Ritus Pontificios subinde mutabiles esse, & nonnunquam significationis inertis.
units.tr: That the Papal rites are from time to time changeable, and sometimes of inert significance.

units.la: AIn' Ritus? etiam declarat? adeòque idipsum? qui deinceps Ritus in coronatione Pontificis adhibetur per Decanum quóque? inque eum finem, ut Papam Regum Patrem esse demonstret? In his singulis jugaris strenuè: Quasi verò Rom. Ecclesiæ Ritus perpetui esse, solerent; & non, veluti alati & volatiles essent, hodiè in usu, paulò post evolent perpetim. Ecclesiæ Romanæ, tempore Gregorij I. Ritus obtinuit, ut, quùm Missarum solennia celebrarentur, {h}Diaconus clamaret, si quis non communicet,{g} det locum. Qui Ritus à prima usque (christi institutione, per mille Annos, in eadem Ecclesia celebratus, nunc planè exoleuit & exulavit. Neque etiam sunt omnes Ritus vestri liquidi & Declarantes: nam ille Ritus, quem,{h} (Contra quàm à Christo fuit institutum) Concilium Tridentinum ore sacrilego decreuit,{i} Vt submissa voce verba Consecrationis proferantur; totus mutus est, nec declarat (quod sciam) quicquam. Quin insuper complures apud vos frequenti sunt in vsu Ritus, qui nihil minus declarant, quàm idipsum, ad quod significandum instituuntur: vt facile esset ostendere ex Abulensi, Holcotto, Durando, atque aliis, de quibusdam Ritibus, qui apud vos pro veris habentur Sacramentis. Sed solennis illa Pontificis vestri Coronatio me ad se inuitat; hæc minora relinquere hortatur.
units.tr: AIn Ritus? Does it declare? And so the same? Which then Ritus, in the coronation of the Pontiff, is used by the Dean as well? And to what end, that it shows the Pope to be the Father of Kings? On all these points you labour vigorously. As if the rites of the Roman Church were wont to be perpetual, and not, as if they had wings and could fly, in use today and flown away shortly afterwards. In the Roman Church, in the time of Gregory I, a Ritus prevailed that, when the solemnities of the Mass were celebrated, the Deacon would cry out, "If anyone does not communicate, let him give place." This Ritus, celebrated in the same Church from the very institution of Christ for a thousand years, has now quite faded and vanished. Nor are all your Rites clear and declaratory: for that Ritus, which the Council of Trent decreed with a sacrilegious mouth (contrary to what was instituted by Christ), that the words of consecration be pronounced in a subdued voice, is entirely mute, and declares (as far as I know) nothing at all. Moreover, several Rites are in frequent use among you which declare nothing less than that same thing for which they were instituted, so that it would be easy to show from Abulensis, Holcot, Durand, and others, concerning certain Rites which among you are held to be true Sacraments. But that solemn coronation of your Pontiff invites me to itself; it urges me to leave these minor matters aside.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. SECT. XXX. Nouellum Coronationis Pontificis Ritum Paternitati[?] an- tiquitatem male confirmare.
units.tr: SECOND ANIMADVERSION. SECT. XXX. That the novel rite of the coronation of the Pontiff badly confirms the antiquity of his fatherhood.

units.la: Apud Antiquos de Consecratione, aut (si minùs hæc vox tibi arriserit) de Creatione Pontificis sæpè legitur; de Coronatione (quod sciam) nusquam: id quod non ægrè concedit Balbus I.C.us vester.{k} Nec coronandi Pontificis consuetudo, inquit, admodum est vetusta, olim à Clero populoque Rom. Pontifices electi (vbi intercesserat Imperatoris authoritas) Cathedrae D. Petri insidebant, nullis aliis ceremoniis adhibitis: demùm increbuit vsus, in hunc vsque diem obseruatus, vt simul ac quis designatus est Pontifex, inter missarum solennia per Præsulem Ostiensem coronetur. Hæc ille, de Ritu minimè vetusto. Erras igitur, si ex nouo Coronationis ritu Pontificis Paternitatem veterem declarari magis putes, quàm ex prima barbæ lanugine senectutem. Forsan hic Ritus eò celebrior & honorificentior tibi, Cardinali, videtur; quòd Decanum Cardinalium præconem habet. Noli tu nimium de re isthac gloriari; nam{l} In Pontificia domo marmorea sella spectatur cæca medium inanis, in qua nouus Pontifex continuò ab eius exaltatione residet, vt ab vltimo Diacono (Cardinale sc.) sedentis, &c. Reliqua proloqui me pudor prohibet, includitque vocem.
units.tr: Among the ancients, the consecration, or (if that word is less pleasing to you) the creation of the Pontiff, is often read of; of a coronation (as far as I know) nowhere. Your jurist Balbus does not reluctantly concede this: "Nor is the custom of crowning the Pontiff", he says, "very ancient; formerly Pontiffs chosen by the clergy and people of Rome (where the authority of the Emperor had intervened) sat in the chair of St Peter, with no other ceremonies employed. At last the custom grew, and is observed to this day, that as soon as anyone is designated Pontiff, he is crowned during the solemnities of the Mass by the Bishop of Ostia." So he; and he speaks of a rite by no means ancient. You are wrong, therefore, if you think the old fatherhood is declared more by the new rite of coronation of the Pontiff than old age is shown by the first down on a beard. Perhaps this rite seems to you, a Cardinal, more celebrated and more honourable, because it has the Dean of the Cardinals as herald. Do not boast too much about this matter; for "in the Pontifical house a marble seat is seen, hollow in the middle and empty, on which the new Pontiff sits continually from his exaltation, so that from the last Deacon (that is, a Cardinal) sitting," etc. Shame forbids me to set out the rest, and it locks up my voice.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. Animadversion.

units.la: Coronatio Pontificis quàm nouiter cœperit in vsu haberi.
units.tr: That the coronation of the Pope has only recently come into use.

units.la: ADhuc hærerem, nec satis perciperem quomodo non soloecismũ faceret Pontifex coronâ indutus æq; ac Bos ephippijs; nisi legissem {n}Papam consecrari ut Sacerdotem, coronari ut Regem. Unde Innocentius III. Papa dicit Rom.{m} Pontificem in signum Imperij uti regno (id est Coronâ) in signum Pontificij, uti mitrâ. Si Papa, Idem, & Rex, tùm Romanus Rex iuxta ac Papa appellari posset. Sed Rex esto; huius tamen Regnum non valdè antiquum, cuius arx ipsa, Roma, non ante Annum millesimum quadringentesimum Illi contigit: nam, Balbus vester affirit, {o}Ex Pontificibus primum Bonifacium IX. Anno MCCCC. urbis Romæ dominatum sibi vendicare tentavisse; ipsum enim urbem ingressum, munita mole Hadriani mœnibus & turribus, dominatu urbis sensim potitum esse. De Regno aut Titulis nullam facessam vobis amplius negotium. De Corona, & Regijs Insignijs agemus. Durantum (cuius {a}Libros perèruditos, & antiquæ veritatis plenos dicitis) consulere liceat: apud quem tàm immensam Rituum farraginem esse video, ut Religio vestra, velut omni varietate colorum picta vestis, corporis tamen expers esse videatur.
units.tr: I was still puzzled, and could not clearly see how the Pontiff, crowned, does not commit as much of a solecism as an ox wearing saddles, unless I had read that the Pope is consecrated as a priest and crowned as a king. Hence Pope Innocent III says that the Roman Pontiff uses a kingdom (that is, a crown) as a sign of empire, and a mitre as a sign of the pontifical office. If the Pope is also a King, then the Roman King could be called Pope just as well. But grant that he is a King; his kingdom is not very ancient, and its very citadel, Rome, did not come to him before the year 1400. For your Balbus affirms that Boniface IX was the first of the Pontiffs to try, in the year 1400, to claim lordship of the city of Rome; for, having entered the city and fortified it with the mass of Hadrian's walls and towers, he gradually gained control of the city's rule. I shall give you no further trouble about kingdom or titles. We shall deal with the crown and the royal insignia. Let us consult Durantus (whose very learned books, full of ancient truth, you say they are). In him I see such an immense jumble of rites that your religion, like a garment painted with every variety of colour, seems to lack a body.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. Animadversion.

units.la: Pontificem Coronum ostentare, ut Princeps facilius Coro- nis suis exuat.
units.tr: That the Pope displays crowns so that a prince may more easily be stripped of his crowns.

units.la: AD Coronationem quod attinet. {b}Summus Pontifex (inquit; quod & {c}Durandus notandum esse monuit) non solum Mitrâ, sed & Coronâ uti solet. Innocentius III. Papa, (serm.1. in Festo S. Syluestri) Romanus Pontifex, inquit, in signum Imperij vtitur regno (id est, Corona, quæ regnum dicitur,) & in signum Pontificis vtitur mitrâ: sed mitrâ semper vtitur & vbique; coronâ verò nec vbique, nec semper; quia Pontificalis authoritas est prior & digniòr, & diffusior quàm Imperialis. Et (in serm. de consecrat. Pont.) in signum Spiritualium donorum datur mihi mitrâ; in signum Temporalium, Corona; Mitra pro Sacerdotio, Corona pro Regno. Pontifex antiquitùs Sacerdos; post Rex; tandem factus Imperator; qui, quasi ex Imperiali fastigio, Dictatu suo statuit, {d}Quòd solus Rom. Pontifex posset uti Imperalibus Insignijs. Sic Gregorius VII. (circiter Ann. Domini MLXXIII: aliter autem visum erat Sylvestro I. Pont. (circiter Annum cccxiv.) {e}Qui, teste Platinâ, concessum sibi Diadema aureum distinctum gemmis aspernatus est, tanquàm religioso capiti minimè convenientes. O tempora! quid facitis? Hic aspernatus est Diadema; ille arripit, vel arrogat potius: ita ut in eo, quod {*}Durandus notandum dixit, hoc occurrat Notatu sanè dignissimum, nimirùm; solenne esse Pontificibus (à Gregorij VII. temporibus in hunc usque diem) ut per iejunas Cæremonias, & à se confictas, in Regum possessiones vafrè callidèque irreperent. Huius exemplum minimè obscurum esse potest, quod (ut Balbus vester, non sine irrisione, obseruat) {f}Canonista (id est, vt ego interpretor, Pontificis assecla) Imperij iura, inquit, labefactare studentes, non legitimum Imperatorem censebant sine Pontificis coronatione.
units.tr: As for the coronation: the Supreme Pontiff (he says, as Durandus also rightly warned) uses not only a mitre but also a crown. Pope Innocent III (Sermon 1 on the Feast of St Silvester) says: the Roman Pontiff uses a kingdom (that is, a crown, which is called a kingdom) as a sign of empire, and uses a mitre as a sign of the pontifical office; but he always and everywhere uses the mitre, whereas the crown he uses neither everywhere nor always, because the pontifical authority is prior, more worthy and more widely extended than the imperial. And (in the sermon on the consecration of the Pope) the mitre is given to me as a sign of spiritual gifts, the crown as a sign of temporal ones: the mitre for the priesthood, the crown for the kingdom. The Pontiff was of old a priest; afterwards a king; at last he became emperor, and, as if from the imperial summit, by his own dictate he decreed that the Roman Pontiff alone could use the imperial insignia. So Gregory VII (about the year of the Lord 1073), though it had seemed otherwise to Sylvester I (about the year 314), who, as Platina testifies, scorned a golden diadem set with gems that was offered to him, as not fitting a religious head. O the times! What are you doing? The one scorned the diadem; the other snatches it, or rather arrogates it. So in what Durandus said was to be noted, there occurs something most worthy of notice: that it has been the custom for Pontiffs (from the times of Gregory VII down to this day) to creep craftily and cunningly into the possessions of kings by empty ceremonies of their own devising. An example of this can be no obscure one, which (as your Balbus observes, not without mockery) a canonist (that is, as I interpret it, a follower of the Pontiff), striving to weaken the rights of the empire, held that a lawful Emperor could not be recognised without the Pontiff's coronation.

units.la: Papa igitur vah [?] quantus repentè prodijt Imperator, qui Regna aliena auferendi iuxta & conferendi ius sibi vendicat: Conferendi, ut Papa, (risum contine, Lector, si potes) qui nè redderet quod ipse iniustè abstulerat, dedisse dicitur {g}Regnum Scilia & Apulia Comiti Richardo; sed eâ lege, & conditione, ut Comes illud suis viribus acquireret: proinde Comes respondit, Hoc idem esse, ac si quis diceret, vendo, vel do tibi Lunam, ascende, & apprehende eam. Regna verò auferendi potestatem sibi Papam arrogare, nimis compertum habemus: imò Bellarminus ipse de numero {h}Pontificum, qui Imperatores, & Principes regnis suis priuârunt, non mediocriter gloriatur. Quam Pontificum tyrannidem primò ex Cæremonialibus huiusmodi obseruationibus ortum habuisse, Historici vestri Confessio diserte{*} docebit. Orat igitur Decanus vester Cardinalium pro Pontificibus; eosque Regum & Principum Patres appellitet; Ego Deum Opt. Max. oro, nè Reges aut Principes insidiosis Pontificum Ritibus, tanquàm retibus capiantur & implicentur. Ita secundam Rationem excusimus; sequitur Tertia.
units.tr: Behold, then, how great an emperor suddenly came forth, who claims for himself the right both to take away and to bestow alien kingdoms! To bestow, as the Pope does (restrain your laughter, reader, if you can): he is said to have given the kingdom of Sicily and Apulia to Count Richard, so that he should not give back what he had unjustly taken away; but on this condition, that the Count should win it by his own strength. Accordingly the Count replied that this was the same as if someone said, "I sell or give you the moon; climb up and seize it." As for the power of taking away kingdoms, we know well enough that the Pope arrogates it to himself; indeed Bellarmine himself boasts not a little of the number of Pontiffs who have deprived emperors and princes of their kingdoms. Your historians' Confession will clearly show that this tyranny of the Pontiffs first arose from such ceremonial observances. Let your Dean of the Cardinals therefore pray for the Pontiffs, and call them fathers of kings and princes; I pray to God Most Good and Most High that kings and princes be not caught and entangled by the crafty rites of the Pontiffs, as in nets. Thus we have dealt with the second reason; the third follows.

units.la: Ratio III. pro Pontificis dignitate amplificandâ, ex factis Principum deducitur.
units.tr: Reason III: for enlarging the Pontiff's dignity, deduced from the acts of princes.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: “Atque hac etiam causa est, cur Reges Christiani, in creatione novi Pontificis, Legatos, sive Oratores mittant; qui reverentiam & obedientiam Pontifici recens creato promittant, tanquam Patri spirituali. pag.26.27,
units.tr: "And for this reason too, Christian kings, when a new Pontiff is created, send legates or envoys, who promise reverence and obedience to the newly created Pontiff as to a spiritual father." pag. 26, 27.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Sic hoc in loco; alibi vero explicatius. {i}Quod autem Principes orthodoxi ista velint etiam à populis sibi subiectis inrari, ut simul velint suam Pontifici Max. fidelitatem & obedientiam conservari; ex ipsâ reverentiâ, & obedientiâ, quod nuper, de more, huic ipsi summo Pontifici Paulo V. publicè per Legatos suos exhibuerunt, hoc clarius demonstratur. Vidimus enim, totâ spectante Româ, Legatos Reip. Lucensis, Genuensis, ac Venetæ cum splendidissimo Comitatu ad urbem advenire, summi Pontificis pedes deosculari, Latinâ & perelegante oratione reverentiam & obedientiam totius Reip. exhibere. Vidimus Regem Hispaniarum, & post, per aliquod tempus, Regem Francorum Christianissimum per Oratores suos cum eo procerum comitatu, eaque nobilium virorum multitudine, quæ tantorum Regum magnificentiam decuit, summi Pontificis deosculari pedes, eiq; amplissimis verbis per eloquentissimos Oratores suos, Reverentiam & obedientiam præstare, quæ S. Petro, eiusq; Successoribus iure debetur.
units.tr: Thus in this place; elsewhere, however, more fully. {i}That orthodox princes wish these things to be sworn also by their subject peoples, so that they also wish their own fidelity and obedience to the Supreme Pontiff to be preserved, is shown more clearly by the reverence and obedience which lately, according to custom, they publicly rendered through their envoys to this very Supreme Pontiff, Paul V. For we have seen, with all Rome looking on, envoys of the Republics of Lucca, Genoa and Venice arrive in the city with most splendid retinues, kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff, and in a Latin and most elegant speech offer the reverence and obedience of the whole Republic. We have seen the King of Spain, and afterwards, for some time, the most Christian King of France, through their envoys, with a company of nobles and a crowd of distinguished men fitting the magnificence of such great kings, kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff and render to him, in the most generous words through their most eloquent envoys, the reverence and obedience which is rightly owed to St Peter and his successors.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Qualia sint Roma, & quàm visenda Spectacula.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. What sort of things Rome is, and how well worth seeing its spectacles are.

units.la: Videmus Roma, ais Bellarmine? quid tùm postea? vidit Bernardus (nè Bozius vester amplius queratur, nos male animatos offendi, quando videmus pompam, quà sepè insolentibus apparatibus incedit Pontifex Rom.) & minimè gavisus est Videndo, Papam purpuratum, gemmis ornatum, & cæteram pompam; in quibus Papa (inquit) successit Constantino, non Petro. Vidit Platina, & vehementer ingemuit, Paulum II. Papam mitram gestantem, in quam multas opes contulit, coëmptis undique, ac magnis pretijs, adamantibus, sapphiris, smaragdis, chrysolitis, iaspidibus, unionibus, & quicquid gemmarum in pretio est; quibus ornatus, tanquàm alter Aaron, in publicum prodibat, inspici & ab hominibus volebat, & admirari. Denique cùm Roma (ut Baronius vester vult) Theatrum mundi sit, quid non visibile Roma? Cùm vero etiam solennia isthæc spectacula,[illegible, ~8 letters] quæ vobis visu[?] iucundissima videntur, ita sint per se lugenda; quid illic non lachrymabile cernas?
units.tr: We see Rome, you say, Bellarmine? What then? Bernardus saw it (lest your Bozius complain further that we are ill-temperedly offended when we see the procession in which the Roman Pontiff often advances with unusual display), and was by no means glad at seeing the Pope clothed in purple, adorned with gems, and the rest of the pomp; in which (he says) the Pope has succeeded Constantine, not Peter. Platina saw this and groaned vehemently at Paul II, wearing a mitre, into which he had gathered much wealth, buying from everywhere and at great prices diamonds, sapphires, emeralds, chrysolites, jaspers, pearls, and whatever gems are prized; adorned with these, like another Aaron, he came forth in public and wished to be looked at and admired by men. Finally, since Rome (as your Baronius wishes) is the theatre of the world, what is not visible in Rome? But since indeed these solemn spectacles, which seem most pleasant to you to see, are in themselves to be lamented, what is there that you would not see with tears?

units.la: Enimverò vidimus, inquis; ut videnti Tibi Cardinali pronior fit fides. quasi Cardinales etiam non viderint {o}Stephanum Papam tantâ rabie sævientem in corpus Papæ Formosi defuncti, ut extractum è tumulo, & habitu Pontificali spoliatum, ac seculari indutum, Laicorum sepulchro mandaret, abscisisque prius dextræ eius duobus digitis: Aut {p}Christophorum Papam Leonem V. prædecessorem suum in Tiberim conjicientem; Aut {q}Sergium Papam eundem Christopherum, in arctâ custodiâ vinctum, tenentem: Aut {r}Bonifacium VII. Cardinalem oculis privantem: Aut {s}Urbanum VI. unum Cardinalem (Esto vero Tu bono animo, Bellarmine; non enim erat hoc crimen, quale {*}Tuum, in Principes seculares, sed in ipsum Pontificem perpetratum) læsæ Maiestatis damnatum, in mare projci[?] mandantem. Sed quid turba Remi? Hoc, totâ spectante Româ, factum dicis; Esto, Atque eadem Roma spectavit, atque etiam coluit {t}Stephanum VII. Papam, qui Petri sedem (fatente Baronio) nefando & inaudito sacrilegio deturpauit: Nec potuit non spectare proximis hisce temporibus (ut nôstis) à {u}Sixto V. nobile admodum lupanar Roma extru-ctum.
units.tr: "Indeed we have seen," you say, so that faith is more readily inclined to you, the seeing Cardinal. As if the Cardinals themselves had not seen {o}Pope Stephen raging with such fury against the body of the dead Pope Formosus that, dragging it from the tomb, stripping it of its pontifical dress, clothing it in secular garb, he committed it to a layman's grave, after first cutting off two of its right-hand fingers: or {p}Pope Christopher throwing his predecessor Leo V into the Tiber; or {q}Pope Sergius holding the same Christopher bound in close custody; or {r}Boniface VII depriving a cardinal of his eyes; or {s}Urban VI condemning one cardinal to death for treason, and ordering him thrown into the sea. (Be of good cheer, Bellarmine; for this was not a crime of the kind yours, against secular princes, but was committed against the Pontiff himself.) But what of the crowd of Remus? This, you say, was done with all Rome looking on; be it so. And the same Rome saw, and even honoured, Pope Stephen VII, who (as Baronius admits) defiled the seat of Peter with an abominable and unheard-of sacrilege. Nor could Rome have failed to see, in these most recent times (as you know), the very noble brothel built by Sixtus V.

units.la: Quæ verò solennia Roma spectet, quid refert; quæ Ipsa facta est tam fœdum, per se, spectaculum, ut qui eam spectabat, testis oculatus, non potuerit non grauiter vicem eius dolere & deplorare. {x}Urbs (inquit) deformatissima; ubi sub sole maior malorum licentia, clamor, iniqui-tas; ne dicam, infamia, impudentia talis sanè at tanta, ut nemo credat, nisi qui VIDERIT, negat nemo, nisi qui NON VIDERIT.. Idem Author oblatâ sibi spe Cardinalatus, exclamat; {y}Quid Roma faciam, mentiri nescio. Ubi, propter Meretricum multitudinem, viri aliquot graues coacti sint fateri, dicendo; {z}Nullâ in urbe hac corruptionem VIDIMUS, præterquam in hac (Româ,) omnium exemplari: Necnon {a}Alius (quod cecinit Poëta de Ethnicis;) Nunc, sub Petri Successoribus, ----Urbs est jam tota Lupanar. Denique Baptista veiter Mantuanus;
units.tr: But what solemn spectacles Rome beholds matters little; for she herself has become such a foul spectacle in herself that whoever looked upon her, as an eyewitness, could not but grievously lament and deplore her plight. "The city (he says) is most deformed; where under the sun there is greater licence of evils, clamour, iniquity; not to mention infamy and impudence of such a kind, yet so great, that no one believes it unless he has SEEN it, and no one denies it except he who has NOT SEEN it." The same author, when hope of a cardinal's hat was offered to him, cries out: "What shall I do in Rome? I do not know how to lie." Where, because of the multitude of harlots, some grave men have been compelled to confess, saying: "In no other city have we SEEN corruption, except in this one, the model of all." And another (as the poet sang of the heathens): "Now, under the successors of Peter, the whole city is already a brothel." Finally, Baptista Mantuanus again:

units.la: {b}Roma vale, vidi, satis est vidisse; reuertar? Cum leno, meretrix, scurra, cinaedus ero.
units.tr: Farewell, Rome; I have seen; it is enough to have seen. Shall I return, when I shall be a pimp, a harlot, a buffoon, a catamite?

units.la: Nonne igitur horrendum spectaculum iam Roma ipsa visa est? at heu! quantò horribilius & execrabilius, quùm (fatentibus etiam {c}duobus Iesuitis) posthàc ipsius Antichristi Sedes necessario spectanda fuerit. Nihil igitur pensi habemus, quid hic Populus Romanus spectet, magis quàm Romanus ille multò antiquior, de quo, Theatrum spectante, Poeta; ---- Populi frons durior Imius.
units.tr: Was not Rome herself already seen to be a horrible spectacle? But alas! how much more horrible and detestable, when (as even two Jesuits admit) the very seat of Antichrist must needs hereafter be seen. We therefore have no concern what the Roman people looks upon, rather than that older Roman, of whom the poet spoke when the theatre was watching: the brow of the people harder than that of Imius.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Reuerentia Pontificibus exhibita; Qualis & quanta sit.
