units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. Reverence shown to the Pontiffs: what it is and how great.

units.la: REuerendissimus, &c, propter eximiam eruditionem, plurimùm suspiciendus Episcopus Eliensis, hoc Tuum, de Reuerentia Pontificibus exhibita, tanquàm pompæ quàm palestræ aptiusd exagitat. Næ ego imprudens essem, si illam vestram [illegible, ~12 letters] imaginem, quàm hic nostèr Apelles tàm singulari artificio depinxit, penicillo meo adumbrare aggrederer? Nostri instituti est, suffragijs vestris, (vt alia fere omnia) itâ hoc caducum Argumentum profligare; eámque tùm Reuerentiam,tùm Obedientiam (quam Tu Pontificibus deberi astruis) vestris viribus expugnare.
units.tr: Most reverend, etc., the Bishop of Ely, deservedly held in high esteem for his outstanding learning, criticises your work on Reverence shown to the Pontiffs, saying it is better suited to a procession than to a wrestling-ground. Indeed I would be foolish to undertake to sketch with my little brush that image of yours [illegible], which our Apelles here has painted with such singular skill. It is my purpose, as with almost everything else, to overthrow this unstable argument with your votes, and to assail with your strength both that reverence and that obedience (which you maintain is owed to the Pontiffs).

units.la: Primo autem in loco Lectori vt constet, par est, quæ, quantáque fit ista Reuerentia, quam Papa sibi, tanquàm honoris fui Symbolum proprium, asciscunt? De hac copiosissimè scripsisse videtur Bozius, Congregationis Oratorij Presbyter: quem Ego (licet indignissimus sit) in scenam producam. (inquit) maximos honores exhiberi, illi vnà cùm Pharisæis volunt Christum cruci affixum. At quem Tu, Conuiciator vanissime, maximum honorem esse somnias? perge, quid dices? fQuid dicam? faciunt impij isti Christo se maiores, qui ad pedes Apostolorum se abiecit, abstersit illos, & verisimiliter illos exosculatus est. O ridiculum caput! Sed quid porrò? In hoc exemplum dans nobis, vt quod ipse fecit, & Nos faciamus; ampliusque affero, peccaret Pontifex si honores istos non admitteret: teste ipsa Christo, qui Petro dixit, non habiturum eum partem secum, nisi à Christo acciperet hunc honorem, vt ad pedes eius se abiceret. Nempè, quod personale fuit Petro, id commune omnibus Pontificibus esse vis, etiam sub necessitate salutis: quasi actum iam esset scilicet de Pontificis anima, nisi quam Obedientiam Christi mandato Petrus præstitit, eandem ille ab omnibus exigat Christianis. En hominis amentiam! quid concludes tandem? g Papa Christi Vicarius in Cælo regnantis, cui subiecta esse debent omnia, nullos non honores, quandiu tenet illius personam, iure potest vendicare. O apertam blasphemiam! quam nullus Christianus non horreat execretur: & tamen in eandem fere sententiam Lorinus Iesuita.
units.tr: First, so that the reader may be clear, it is right to say what and how great is this reverence which the Pope claims for himself as the proper badge of his honour. Bozius, a presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, seems to have written most fully on this, and I shall bring him onto the stage (though he is most unworthy). He says that they wish the greatest honours to be paid to him, just as the Pharisees wished Christ to be fixed to the cross. But what do you, most vain slanderer, dream to be the greatest honour? Go on, what will you say? "What shall I say? Those impious men make themselves greater than Christ, who threw himself at the feet of the Apostles, wiped them, and probably kissed them. O ridiculous head! But what further? Giving us an example, so that we also do what he did; and I add more: the Pontiff would sin if he did not admit these honours, Christ himself being witness, who told Peter that he would have no part with him unless he received this honour from Christ, namely that he should throw himself at his feet." Namely, what was personal to Peter you wish to be common to all Pontiffs, even under necessity of salvation, as if the soul of the Pontiff were already lost unless he demanded from all Christians the same obedience Peter rendered at Christ's command. See the madness of the man! What will you conclude at last? "The Pope, Christ's Vicar reigning in heaven, to whom all things ought to be subject, can rightly claim every honour whatsoever, as long as he holds that person." O open blasphemy! which no Christian does not shudder at and curse; and yet the Jesuit Lorinus says much the same.

units.la: d Rifponf. ad Apo-log.Card. Bellar.
units.tr: d Reply to the Apology of Cardinal Bellarmine.

units.la: e Bozius de signis Tom.1.l.11.c.10. pag.913.
units.tr: e Bozius, De signis, Tom. 1, lib. 11, cap. 10, p. 913.

units.la: f ibid. verbis seqq.
units.tr: f Ibid., in the words that follow.

units.la: g Haec Conclusionem præmisit, pag. 906. Iesuita. {h}Nos (inquit) in quolibet Pontifice agnoscentes Christum ipsum, cuius vices in terris gerit, ad illius pedes exosculandos proni prouoluimur: & in hunc finem sacris Scripturis insigniter abutitur.
units.tr: g He prefaced this with a conclusion, p. 906, Jesuit: "We (he says) recognising in any Pontiff Christ himself, whose vicar he is on earth, prostrate ourselves to kiss his feet", and to this end he grossly abuses the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Hæc ipsi Paparum assecla. quid Domini Papæ ipsi? Illinè vt æquis animis hanc crassam, pro sua honorificentia, adulationem sustineant? sustineant vero? imò eundem honorem, tanquàm proprium sibi vendicant etiam imperantque. Nam Gregorius VII. Papa, inter priuilegia Rom. Pontificis, nono loco recensuit, quòd {i}Solius Papa pedes omnes Principes exosculentur. Ità vt inter Pontifices iam nec, ob tyrannidem, Nerones; nec ob luxuriam, Heliogabali; nec, ob insolentiam, Tarquinij superbi deesse videantur. Denique in Libro Caremonialium Papalium praescribitur, quòd {k}Omnes Mortales, cuiuscunque sint dignitatis & praeeminentiæ, cùm primùm in conspectum Pontificis veniunt, ter debeant ante Illum genuflectere, & pedes eius osculari, in honorem Iesu, cuius vicem gerit. Quamuis apud Lectorem ingenuum hanc tam intolerabilem Pontificum arrogantiam denotâsse, difflâsse[?]; & penitùs dissipâsse sit: nihilominus Argumenta Aduersariorum conuellam, nè se despectos magis quàm non refutatos esse queritentur.
units.tr: These are the words of the Pope's followers. What of the Lord Popes themselves? Do they bear this gross flattery with equanimity, as due to their honour? Bear it? Indeed they claim the same honour as their own and even command it. For Pope Gregory VII, among the privileges of the Roman Pontiff, listed in ninth place that the feet of all princes should be kissed by the Pope alone. So that among the Pontiffs there seem to be no lack of Neros for tyranny, of Heliogabaluses for luxury, or of proud Tarquins for insolence. Finally, in the Book of Papal Ceremonies it is prescribed that all mortals, of whatever dignity and eminence, as soon as they come into the presence of the Pontiff, must kneel before him three times and kiss his feet, in honour of Jesus, whose vicar he is. Although it is clear to a candid reader that this intolerable arrogance of the Pontiffs has been pointed out, scattered and utterly dissipated, I will nevertheless refute the arguments of the adversaries, lest they complain that they have been despised rather than refuted.

units.la: III ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Putida Bozÿi Rationes, pro Osculo pedum Pontificis, diluuntur.
units.tr: The silly reasoning of Bozius in favour of kissing the Pontiff's feet is refuted.

units.la: DVobus praecipuè fundamentis Bozij vestri defensio niti videtur; authoritate, scilicet, Christi, & dignitate eius Vicarij. In vtroque refellitur. I.° enim Christus, vbi lauàssel[?] pedes Discipulorum, Exemplum (ait) dedi vobis, vt vos similiter faciatis. Sensus est (expositore Maldonato Iesuita) {1}Dum contentio facta est inter Discipulos, {*}Quis eorum esset maior, præuenit Christus, & hoc exemplo suo, & exhortatione eos ad humilitatem prouocat: & persequitur {†}Argumentum proximis verbis; {†}Amen, dieo vobis, non est servus maior Domino suo, neque ◡Apostolus maior eo, à quo mittitur. Hæc Ille. Obseruanda imprimis est Domini nostri Logica; Quod si Ego (ait Christus) Dominus & Magister vester laui pedes vestros, debetis vos alter alterius pedes lauare. Dictis factisque suis Discipulos instituit & erudit ad humilitatem, & ex Reuerentia, quam suâ sponte in eos, vt Dominus inferuos, contulit, docuit, Reuerentiam inter Servos debere esse mutuam atque reciprocam: Debetis (inquit) alter alterius pedes lauare; Id est; indicia & testimonia mutui obsequij praestare. At Papæ metaphysica multò sublimior; {*}Solius Papæ pedes exosculandi sunt. Sic Seruus Seruorum Dei scilicet. Deinde itâ causam hanc tractant Pontificij ac si quicquid externi honoris dabatur Christo, eius etiam {*}Vicario debeatur; quia honos Vicario exhibitus in Christum redundat, cuius ille personam gerit; parùm considerantes (quod tamen Nauarrus docere eos potuit) quòd licet honor exhibitus Vicario principaliter exhibetur. Eius est Vicarius (non ei, qui est Vicarius, nisi per quandam dam redundantiam) nihilominùs {m}Etiamsi Vicarius, inquit, honorandus sit, tanquam vicem tenens & locum principalis Domini, tamen non eodem honore. Et, exempli causa, insistit in hoc Ritu osculandi pedes Pontificis: Osculamur (inquit) pedes Papæ honoris gratia; non tamen id facimus eius gratia; etiam à latere minus eius delegato. Sic ille. Apudhosce homines consequentia eiusdem honoris, quæ à Legato Pontificis ad ipsum Pontificem non valet; tamen à Vicario Christi ad (infinite maiorem) Christum ipsum valebit. O Stagirita, vt Tu nunc vapulas?
units.tr: Two chief foundations seem to support the defence of your Bozius: namely the authority of Christ and the dignity of his Vicar. Both are refuted. First, when Christ washed the feet of the disciples, he said: I have given you an example, that you should do likewise. The sense is (the Jesuit Maldonatus being the expositor): "While a contention arose among the disciples, who of them should be greater, Christ anticipated it, and by his example and exhortation provokes them to humility; and he pursues the argument of the words that follow: Amen, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than him by whom he is sent." So he. "The logic of our Lord must above all be observed: For if I (says Christ) your Lord and Master have washed your feet, you ought to wash one another's feet." By his words and deeds he instructed and trained the disciples in humility, and from the reverence which of his own accord he showed them as Lord to servants, he taught that reverence among servants ought to be mutual and reciprocal. You ought (he says) to wash one another's feet: that is, to render tokens and proofs of mutual service. But the metaphysics of the Pope is far more lofty: the feet of the Pope alone are to be kissed. Thus, no doubt, the Servant of the servants of God. Next, the Papists handle the matter as if whatever external honour was given to Christ were also due to his Vicar, because honour shown to the Vicar redounds upon Christ, whose person he bears; little considering (which Navarrus could have taught them) that although honour shown to the Vicar is principally shown to him whose Vicar he is, not to him who is Vicar except by a certain overflow, nevertheless even if the Vicar, he says, is to be honoured as one holding the place and standing in for the principal Lord, yet not with the same honour. And, for example, he insists on this rite of kissing the feet of the Pope: We kiss (he says) the feet of the Pope for the sake of honour; yet we do not do it for his sake, even of his less-than-delegate. So he. Among these men the consequence of the same honour, which does not hold from the Legate of the Pontiff to the Pontiff himself, will nevertheless hold from the Vicar of Christ to Christ himself (infinitely greater). O Stagirite, how you are now being whipped!

units.la: Summa est. Papam Christi Vicarium (vt ita eum esse demus) Domini ipsius exemplo superbiæ non mediocris damnari. Huc etiam facit celebre illud {n}Petri Exemplum, qui Cornelium ad pedes eius procidentem, & adorantem leuauit, dicens, surge, & ego Homo sum. Causam, cur Petrus hanc Cornely demissionem recusauerit, præcipua & fere sola, quæ reddi ab Antiquis solet; hæc est; vt Petrus nimiam Cornelij de ipso opinionem corrigeret; non quòd opinionem aliquam Diuinitatis de Petro conceperit. Vos testes appello. ◦ Non est (inquit Iesuita) verisimile Cornelium, qui religiosus dicitur, & timens Deum, cultum Deo debitum in creaturam transtulisse. Cur igitur honorem istum repudiauit Petrus, verus (licet non solus) Christi Vicarius? Respondent Iesuitae & fatentur (sed sensu suo) {p}Petrum hoc praemium honoris tenere Ecclesiae principijs reiecisse (quasi seruiisset tempori Petrus, donec tempus Illi seruiret) vt ille doctrinam vitandae ambitionis Successoribus suis traderet. At quàm egregiè profecerint isti Petri successores, tàm Legatorum Principum, quàm Regum ipsorum exempla, à quibus haec Reuerentia Pontifici exhibita fuit, satis declarant. Petrus enim oblatum sibi tantùm honorem respuit; Pontifex verò maiorem affectat, exigit, &(si opus est) exrorquet. Petrus Cornelium [illegible, ~8 letters] seu Centurionem ad pedes suos procumbere non siuit: Pontifex Chiliarchas, & Chiliarcharum Dominos ipsos Reges, & summos Monarchas, totâ spectante Româ, & applaudentibus Cardinalibus, ad pedes suos osculandos adegisse serio gestit. {q}Petrus exurgit in medio Discipulorum, nempè, {r}Reuerentiam eis exhibens: Papa autem, vbi semel sedem occupauerit (quantum ego intelligo) in medio licet Principum Christianorum choro, non magis assurgere, aut curuare se, quàm Elephas, potest. Neque sanè expectandum, vt ille obiectum sibi à Petro conseruo Humilitatis exemplum sequatur, qui Domini eius exemplum praeceptúmque contemnit.
units.tr: In sum, the Pope, granted to be Christ's Vicar, is condemned for no small pride by the example of his Lord. The famous example of Peter also bears on this, who raised up Cornelius when he fell at his feet and worshipped him, saying: rise, I too am a man. The chief and almost only reason the Ancients usually give why Peter refused Cornelius's humble obeisance is this: that Peter wished to correct Cornelius's excessive opinion of him, not that Peter had conceived any notion of divinity about himself. I call you to witness. It is not likely (says the Jesuit) that Cornelius, who is called religious and God-fearing, transferred to a creature the worship due to God. Why then did Peter, the true (though not the only) Vicar of Christ, reject that honour? The Jesuits answer, and admit (but in their own sense), that Peter rejected this prize of honour on the principles of the Church, as if he had served the times until the times served him, so that he might hand down to his successors the teaching on avoiding ambition. But how splendidly those successors of Peter have profited, the examples both of the legates of Princes and of the Kings themselves, by whom this reverence was shown to the Pontiff, sufficiently declare. For Peter spurned the honour offered to him alone; the Pontiff, however, seeks more, demands it, and (if need be) extorts it. Peter did not allow Cornelius, or the centurion, to fall down at his feet; the Pontiff eagerly compels chiliarchs, the lords of chiliarchs, the Kings themselves and the greatest Monarchs, to kiss his feet, with all Rome looking on and the Cardinals applauding. Peter rises up in the midst of the disciples, namely showing them reverence; the Pope, however, once he has occupied his seat (as far as I understand), cannot stand up or bow himself any more than an elephant can, even in the midst of the choir of Christian princes. Nor indeed should we expect that he, set before him as an example of humility by Peter his fellow-servant, would follow it, since he despises the example and command of his Lord.

units.la: VI. ANIMADVERSIO. Eundem Ritum, osculandi Pontificum pedes, ab ipsis Pontificijs reprehendi.
units.tr: VI. ANIMADVERSION. That the same rite of kissing the feet of the Pontiffs is itself condemned by the Papists.

units.la: EXigant Pontifices licet hunc à Principibus honorem, & eum sibi quasi *peculiarem arrogent; non deerunt tamen etiam qui huic morbo medicam manum adhibeant, vomicámque aperiant. Polydori Virgilij vestri verba sunt clarissima. {f}Voluit proculdubiò (inquit) Cornelius pedes Apostoli Petri exosculari, sed pater mansuetudinis plenus id fieri non est passus, dicens, Surge, nam & ego homo sum. O vocem memorabilem atque salutarem! Si bene multi hodie se quoque homines esse perpenderent; qui propterea, quia Sacerdotio prediti sunt, planè se reliquorum mortalium longè, post hominum memoriam, imperiosissimos Dominos prebent, non communes Patres, uti fieri deberet: ita usu venit, ut nos Pontificum nostrorum pedes exosculemur; illudque institutum à Romanis Pontificibus dixerim. Hæc Polydorus. Quam linguam [illegible, ~2 letters] {t}Pontificij Inquisitores Expurgatorij radicitùs euulserunt; haud mitius cùm Erasmo acturi, qui pariter non raro nimis prodigus solet esse veritatis.{a}Maximinus Senior (inquit) nunquam ad pedum suorum osculationem quenquam admisit, nam [Absit, ait, ut pedibus meis oscula quis figat.] Vbi sunt igitur qui non modo ingenuos verumetiam summos Monarchas ad oscula, non pedum dico, sed calceorum, non admittant modò, sed quodammodò cogant? Hæc ille. Et dubio procul Massonius Historicus vester in eandem spongiam delectilem olim incumbet; quæ tamen Ille notatu digna censuit, ego minimè reticebo. {b}Notabo (inquit) Iacobi Fabri prudentissimi iuris verba, vz. [Papa in verbis dicit se Seruum Seruorum Dei, de facto tamen se adorari permittit, quod Angelus in Apocalypsi refugit.] Videtur autem id dicere, quasi damnans consuetudinem morem eorum, qui demississimè procumbunt ad pedes Pontificis, ut signum Crucis in superficie calcei intextum deosculentur: qui mos, an sit antiquissimus, nescio, nondum enim omnia legi; sed hoc scio, Consuetudinem illam Cisalpinis populis minus probari, quàm Italicæ genti, ad huius generis obsequia & demissiones natæ. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Let the Pontiffs demand this honour from princes, and claim it as though it were their own; yet there will not be lacking men who apply a healing hand to this disease and lance the abscess. The words of your Polydore Vergil are most clear: "Cornelius (he says) certainly wished to kiss the feet of the Apostle Peter, but the father full of gentleness did not allow it, saying, 'Rise, for I too am a man.' O memorable and wholesome word! If only many today would weigh that they too are men, who, because they are endowed with the priesthood, present themselves as far more imperious lords than other mortals, and not as common fathers, as ought to be the case. Thus it has come about that we kiss the feet of our Pontiffs; and I would say this custom was introduced by the Roman Pontiffs." Thus Polydore. This tongue [illegible] your Papist Inquisitors of the Index have torn out by the roots; they would not act more gently with Erasmus, who likewise is not seldom too lavish with the truth. "Maximinus the Elder (he says) never admitted anyone to kiss his feet, for [Far be it, he says, that anyone should plant kisses on my feet.]" Where then are those who not only do not admit free men, but even the highest monarchs, to kisses, I do not say of the feet but of the shoes, and who in a way not only permit but compel them? Thus he. And doubtless your historian Massonius will in time lay his hand upon the same sponge; yet what he judged worthy of note I will by no means pass over. "I will note (he says) the words of the most prudent jurist Jacobus Faber, namely, [The Pope in words calls himself the servant of the servants of God, yet in fact permits himself to be adored, which the Angel in the Apocalypse refused.]" He seems, however, to say this as though condemning the custom of those who prostrate themselves most humbly at the feet of the Pontiff, in order to kiss the sign of the Cross woven into the surface of his shoe. Whether this custom is very ancient I do not know, for I have not yet read everything; but this I know, that the custom is less approved among the peoples on this side of the Alps than among the Italian nation, to whose kind of servility and abasement it was born. Thus he.

units.la: Quod Maximinus dixit accepimus; Absit, inquit, ut quisquam pedibus meis oscula figat. Pontifex contrà, Absit ut non oscula figant Papæ solius pedibus Mortales omnes. At Papa quamuis Maximini maior, scilicet, maior tamen Magno Gregorio (qui idem Papa) profecto non est. quid ille? ille? Lorinus Iesuita narrabit :{c} Gregorius Magnus, Is (inquit) qui cum celsitudine Pontificiæ Maiestatis Christianam humilitatem summopere coluit, & vt prius cognominis, Petri illam modestiam celebrauit; Ioannem Abbatem Perf.m (vt est in prato spirituali) adse adorandum in medio vrbe (Romā igitur spectante) progredientem præuertit, prosternendo se humi coram Illo, negans se surgere prius, quam illum surrexisse vidisset. Bonum factum. At vt nunc sunt hominum mores, citius quis Camelum volantem cernat, quàm Pontificem Romanum ad cuiusquam vel Imperatoris pedes procumbentem. His de hoc Reuerentiæ genere sic expositis, ad Obedientiam accedamus.
units.tr: What Maximinus said we have heard: "Far be it," he says, "that anyone should plant kisses on my feet." The Pontiff, on the contrary: "Far be it that all mortals should not plant kisses on the feet of the Pope alone." But the Pope, though greater than Maximinus, is surely not greater than Gregory the Great (who was himself a Pope). What did he do? Lorinus the Jesuit will tell us: "Gregory the Great, who (he says) cultivated Christian humility above all, together with the loftiness of the Pontifical majesty, and who celebrated that modesty of Peter, as was said before, when John, the Abbot of Persia (as is in the Spiritual Meadow), came forward to meet him in the middle of the city (with Rome therefore looking on) to be adored, anticipated him by throwing himself prostrate on the ground before him, refusing to rise until he had seen him risen first." Well done. But as men's manners now are, one would sooner see a flying camel than a Roman Pontiff prostrating himself at the feet of any emperor. Having thus set out this kind of reverence, let us come to obedience.

units.la: De Obedientia Legatorum Principum, & Rerumpubl. Rom. Pontifici exhibita.
units.tr: On the Obedience of the Legates of Princes and of the Commonwealths Shown to the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: “ {*}Vidimus & isthic Rerumpublicarum & Regum Legatos exosculantes pedem Pontificis, & Dominorum suorum nomine Reuerentiam & Obedientiam exhibentes, eiusque Successoribus promittentes &c. Pag. 26.27.
units.tr: "We have seen there also legates of commonwealths and kings kissing the foot of the Pontiff, and in the name of their lords offering reverence and obedience, and promising to his successors, etc." Pp. 26–27.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Quo tendat immodica Pontifici habita Reuerentia.
units.tr: Whither the Immoderate Reverence Shown to the Pontiff Tends.

units.la: Vidistis igitur, quod Solem vidisse pudeat: sed veniat insuper vobis in mentem illud, quod, in omni negotio, humana diuinaque iura plurimum efflagitant, Videndum est quatenus. Tu igitur etiam atque etiam Vide quoúsque: nam (vt eos memorem, in quibus Tu maximè insistis) Dux, & Respubl. Venetorum nonne Interdicto Pontificis vestri, De bonis emphyteuticis, parere renuerunt? Henricus IIII. nuperus Rex Francorum an persuaderi sibi passus est vnquàm Concilij Tridentini decreta amplecti, aut in Regnum suum admittere? Hispaniarum Regem Philippum III. in eâ causa, (quam Baronius Cardinalis itâ vehementer vrget) de Regno Siciliæ, noluisse cedere, orbi Christiano notum est. Et quàm parùm conuenit olim inter Regem Hispaniæ, & Papam, {d}Bellum illud inter Philippum II. & Paulum IV. Pontificem palàm testatur. Vtcunque, permagni sanè sua interesse Principes existimabunt, si ex nimijs illis officijs, & exuberantibus, erga Pontificem, obsequijs aliquid amputetur; siquidem apud se diligentiùs perpenderint, quàm exiguo compendio quantum dispendij Pontifices interdùm Imperatorum dignitati, ex istiusmodi Papalium rituum obseruatione, attulerint.
units.tr: You have therefore seen what it would shame the sun to have seen. But let there come to your mind besides that saying which, in every matter, human and divine law strongly demand: It must be seen how far. You too, then, again and again, see how far, for (to mention those cases on which you chiefly insist) did the Doge and Commonwealth of Venice not refuse to obey the Interdict of your Pontiff concerning the emphyteutic goods? Did Henry IV, the recent King of France, ever allow himself to be persuaded to embrace or admit into his kingdom the decrees of the Council of Trent? It is known to the Christian world that Philip III, King of the Spains, in that dispute (which Cardinal Baronius urges so vehemently) concerning the Kingdom of Sicily, was unwilling to yield. And how poorly the King of Spain and the Pope once agreed, that war between Philip II and Pope Paul IV openly bears witness. However that may be, princes will surely judge it of great importance to their interests if something is cut away from those excessive duties and overflowing services of obedience toward the Pontiff; since they will weigh more carefully within themselves how small a gain, and how great a loss, the Pontiffs have at times brought to the dignity of emperors through the observance of such Papal rites.

units.la: {e}Quâ de re Thuanum audiendum censeo. * Otho Tertius cùm Gregorio V. Pontifice, quem in (Papalem) sedem restituerat, posteris æquè damnosâ ac ignominiosâ pactione transfegit, vt nimirum qui Rex Romanorum ab Electoribus deinceps crearetur, non priùs Imperator & Augustus haberetur, quàm Eum Romanus Pontifex inaugurâsset. Itâ Rom. Pontifex ab Imperatoribus Rom.priùs creari, atque constituì solitus, arbitrium summi inter Christianos principatus constituendi adsè paulatim traxit. Idcirca Ann. Domini MCCCCXVII. accidit: posteà Carolus VI. eandem legem renouauit, sub bullæ aureæ nomine, Anno MCCCLVI. publicatæ, quæ & hodiè magnâ religione inter Germanos seruatur. Is suo periculo, sed ferò, sensit quorsum pertineret Ius illud, quod sibi in augurandis Romanis Imperatoribus Romanus Pontifex sumpsit, vt scilicet liceret ei à quo accipere debuerit leges, quas vellet, pro inaugurationis pretio imponere. Siquidem Innocentius VI. non aliter per Ministros Coronam imponi passus est, quàm Ille se iurciurando obstrinxisset, Romæ, aut in Italia, iussu Pontificis, diutiùs non moraturum. Itâ vt non immeritò Franciscus Petrarcha, qui tunc temporis floruit, indignabundo animo miratus sit, quænam ista superbia esset, Principem Romanum, publicæ libertatis auctorem libertate priuare; vt cuius esse debent omnia ipse non sit suus. Hactenùs Historicus vester. Exemplum hoc (vt & illud, quòd supra *attigimus) satis de-
units.tr: On this matter I think we should hear Thuanus. Otho III, when he had restored Gregory V to the (Papal) see, transferred to his successors a compact as damaging as it was disgraceful: namely, that he who should afterwards be created King of the Romans by the Electors should not be regarded as Emperor and Augustus until the Roman Pontiff had inaugurated him. Thus the Roman Pontiff, who had customarily been created and appointed before the Roman Emperors, gradually drew to himself the right of establishing the supreme princedom among Christians. For this reason it happened in the year of the Lord 1417; afterwards Charles VI renewed the same law under the name of the Golden Bull, published in the year 1356, which is still kept today among the Germans with great reverence. He learned at his own peril, though late, to what end that right tended, which the Roman Pontiff had taken to himself in appointing Roman emperors, namely that he from whom he ought to receive laws might impose whatever laws he wished as the price of inauguration. For Innocent VI did not allow the crown to be placed by his ministers unless he had bound himself by oath, at Rome or in Italy, on the Pontiff's order, not to delay longer. So that Francis Petrarch, who flourished at that time, was not unjustly moved to wonder with indignant mind what kind of pride this was, that a Roman prince, the author of public liberty, should be deprived of liberty; since he himself should not be his own, to whom all things ought to belong. Thus far your historian. This example (as well as that which we touched upon above) sufficiently de-

units.la: * rid. supra §.32. lib.f.g. clarat, Pontifices ambitiosâ Rituum solennitate, tanquàm vafro quodam aucupio vsos esse; & hoc pacto ad Temporalem Monarchiam viam sibi munijsse.
units.tr: See above §32, book f.g. It makes clear that Pontiffs used the ambitious solemnity of their rites as a kind of crafty fowler's snare, and by this means paved their way to temporal monarchy.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Pontifices olim eandem Principibus Reuerentiam praestitisse, quam nunc ab Ipsis exigunt.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. The Popes formerly showed the same reverence to princes that they now demand from them.

units.la: LEctori fortassis opus non minus vtile, quàm Nobis non difficile videbitur ostendere, tum antiquos Pontifices Reuerentiam, & Obedientiam Imperatoribus exhibuisse; tùm Imperatores ipsos hæc officia sibi debita à Pontificibus suo iure postulâsse. Circà primum satisfacere nobis debet, quod Leo I. Gregorius I. Agatho I. Anastasius I. aliique nonnulli, qui in Romano Episcopatu, si non primæ, at certè quidem secundæ magnitudinis stellæ resplenduerunt, suæ ætatis {*}Imperatores Dominos suos, seque illis Subditos palàm agnouerint: quibus nimirum Supplicare; quos veneratione debitâ prosequi; quorum mandatis, iußis, iußionibus obedire se, quasi flexo mentis poplite; & tanquàm eorum vestigijs prouolutos vltrò professi fuerint. Secundum autem. Utrum syncerioris Antiquitatis Imperatores in ipsos Pontifices authoritatem aliquam exercuerint, extra omnem dubitationem ponendum est; modò quid Constantinus Magnus, Theodosius, Valentinianus, Iustinianus, & quiuis Imperator religiosus fecerint, accuratiùs attendamus: quorum authoritatem non solùm ex Imperatorum Actis, sed etiam ex Pontificum litteris, & Pontificiorum ipsorum ingenuis Confessionibus probatam & stabilitam hoc in loco complexus essem; nisi hisce locum alium magis oportunum destinâssem.
units.tr: The reader will perhaps find it no less useful than we find it easy to show, first, that the ancient Popes showed reverence and obedience to the emperors, and second, that the emperors themselves rightly demanded these duties as owed to them by the Popes. On the first point, Leo I, Gregory I, Agatho I, Anastasius I and several others, who shone in the Roman bishopric as stars of the second, if not the first, magnitude, openly acknowledged the emperors of their own age as their lords and themselves as their subjects. To these emperors they freely professed that they would supplicate; honour with due veneration; obey their commands, orders and injunctions, as if with the knee of the mind bent; and fall prostrate at their feet. On the second point, it must be put beyond all doubt that the emperors of purer antiquity exercised some authority over the Popes themselves, provided we attend more carefully to what Constantine the Great, Theodosius, Valentinian, Justinian, and any religious emperor did. I would have gathered their authority in this place, proved and established not only from the Acts of the emperors but also from the letters of the Popes and the frank confessions of the Papists themselves, had I not assigned these matters to another, more suitable place.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO. Nimiam istam Pontificis Reuerentiam triplici de causa vituperandam esse.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION. That excessive reverence of the Pope is to be condemned on three grounds.

units.la: QUodsi vero quis, ut alias externæ venerationis species, inter quas numeratur Apertio capitis, corporis inclinatio, genuflectio; ita hanc quoque, quæ est abiectissima demissionis formâ, osculationem pedum inter Adiaphora collocandam censuerit; nihilominùs Tria observare licet, in Papæ adoratione, quæ in Christianorum reprehensionem merito incurrant. Primum est, quòd hanc honoris tesseram vt Soli Sibi propriam Papæ vendicat. Secundum, quòd hoc demissionis genus, tanquàm Subiectionis & Obedientiæ testimonium, Regibus & Imperatoribus imponit. Tertium, quòd plerique omnes, qui in hoc genere Reverentiæ Papam colunt, ciuilis cultus modum egressi, Pontificem tanquàm (sic enim {f}Eum vocant) numen quoddam in terris nefandâ superstitione adorant.
units.tr: But if someone, like other outward marks of respect, among which are counted uncovering the head, bowing the body and kneeling, judges that this too, the form of most abject submission, the kissing of feet, should be placed among the Adiaphora, nevertheless three things may be observed in the adoration of the Pope which rightly expose Christians to blame. The first is that he claims this token of honour as his own alone. The second is that he imposes this kind of submission on kings and emperors as a testimony of subjection and obedience. The third is that almost all who worship the Pope in this kind of reverence, going beyond the measure of civil honour, adore the Pope as a (for so they call him) divinity on earth with impious superstition.

units.la: Miror igitur Aduersarios nostros, alioqui mirae subtilitatis ac perspicaciae viros, adeò coecutire atque defipere vt non intelligant, quando tantam à Regibus, alijsque Mortalibus Pontifici Obedientiam & Reverentiam exhibitam esse gloriantur; se non obseruare in Summo suo Pontifice Bestiam illam Apocalypticam, de quâ Spiritus Sanctus; {g}Cui, inquit, Reges vires & potestatem suam tradunt. Haec de Obedientia; vide de Reverentia; {h}Et omnes adorabunt eam. Eius locum vis? {i}Babylon, id est, (ex Pontificiorum ipsorum communi iudicio) Roma, disertissimè expressa: Ex situ; {k}Super septem montes. Nec, vt alij volunt Ethnica Roma, quæ iamdiu extincta est, sed futura alia (vt {l}Iesuitæ duo luculenter demonstrant) Roma nouissima. Nec deest illi Nomen, vocatur enim Mysterium. Atque in Romana Ecclesia omnia scatent Mysteriis plena, vsque ad Templorum situs, angulos, campanulas, & ipsos Campanarum funes: non Exosculationes excipiam, de quibus Durandus vester. {m}Creditur non vacare mysterio, quòd summus Pontifex septem modis accipit osculum, videlicet, ad os, ad pectus, ad humerum, ad manum, ad brachia, ad genu, & ad pedes: Quos, praecipuè in tanta varietate, malè morati homines (quùm Os, vel dextram poterant) Pedes porrigunt Principum & Imperatorum osculis. Ita Pontifi-cij, cij, cùm maximè Pontificiū nomen celebrare volunt, vel maximè dedecorant, eiqué notam quandam Antichristianismi imprudentes inurunt: neque enim maior excogitari potest contrarietas, quàm vt quantum {a}Christus Deus de cœlo se humiliauit in terris; tantum ille Vicarius scil. in terris sese efferat in cœlum vsque, super omnem mortalem Deum, & [illegible, ~5 letters]; quocum Scortari Spiritus Sanctus Christianos seuerè prohibet. Mitte igitur blanda hæc, sed meretricia Basia, & — habeat iam Roma pudorem. Dicito potiùs quorsum spectet hæc tua, de Pontificis Paternitate, tam insolens & importuna Iactantia?
units.tr: I am therefore amazed at our opponents, otherwise men of wonderful subtlety and insight, that they are so blinded and infatuated that they do not notice, when they boast of such great obedience and reverence shown by kings and other mortals to the Pope, that in their supreme Pontiff they are not observing that Apocalyptic beast, of which the Holy Spirit speaks: To whom, he says, the kings give their power and authority. So much for obedience; now see about reverence: And all will worship it. Do you see its place? Babylon, that is (by the common judgment of the Papists themselves) Rome, plainly expressed. From its situation: upon seven mountains. It is not, as others wish, pagan Rome, which has long been extinct, but another, future one (as the Jesuits clearly demonstrate in two works), the newest Rome. Nor does it lack a name, for it is called Mystery. And in the Roman Church everything is full of mysteries, down to the positions, corners and little bells of the temples, and even the ropes of the bells. I will not mention the kisses, about which your Durandus says: It is believed not to be without mystery that the supreme Pontiff receives a kiss in seven ways, namely on the mouth, on the breast, on the shoulder, on the hand, on the arms, on the knee, and on the feet. Since there is such great variety, ill-mannered men, when they could offer the mouth or the right hand, stretch out their feet for the kisses of princes and emperors. Thus the Papists, when they most want to celebrate the name Pontifical, disgrace it most, and unwittingly stamp upon it a certain mark of Antichristianism. For no greater contrast can be imagined than that, as much as Christ God humbled himself from heaven on earth, so much should his Vicar exalt himself on earth, even up to heaven, above every mortal God; with whom the Holy Spirit strictly forbids Christians to play the harlot. Put aside, then, these flattering but harlot's kisses, and, let Rome now have shame. Tell me rather, to what does this so insolent and unseemly boasting of yours about the Paternity of the Pope tend?

units.la: Bellarmini Conclusio; quâ Papam Patrem-famil- ias facit.
units.tr: Bellarmine's conclusion, by which he makes the Pope the father of the household.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On Duties.

units.la: « Vt omnes intelligant, eos quoque ad familiam Christi pertinere, quæ est Ecclesia Catholica, cui vice Christi Pontifex Maximus, vt Paterfamilias præsidet, &c. — pag. 27.
units.tr: "So that all may understand that they also belong to the family of Christ, which is the Catholic Church, over which the supreme Pontiff presides in the place of Christ, as father of the household, etc." — p. 27.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Sic Tu; Nos hoc in loco vocem hanc Catholicam nihil moramur; de quâ alibi opportuniùs. Id, quod nunc in quæstionem vocatur, est, quo iure Papa Pater-familias dici debeat; siuè Ecclesiam Catholicā, siuè in Eâ Catholicos Principes spectemus. In vtroque; mentis tuæ expressionem desideramus. Respectu Ecclesiæ, Nilus Archiepiscopus Thessalonicensis contra Rom. Pontificem Pobijcit, Intolerabile esse quòd Romanus Papa Sanctorum Patrum Canonibus subijci nolit, cùm ipse à Patribus dignitatem suam habuerit; Imò quòd etiam Ipse Canones ediderit: Esse Ergò Papam indignum, qui tanquàm Pater honoretur. Hæc ille; quid Tu? Respondeo (inquis) Pontificem non à Patribus, sed à Christo authoritatem habere: & quòd ipse Canones condat, signum est, cum esse Legislatorem, nec Principem habere Superiorem: Non potest autem Principiis suis legibus obligari; si tanquam Pater ab omnibus honoretur, non habet ille Patrem, sed omnes filios; at filij Patri subiici debent.
units.tr: Thus you; we do not here dwell on this word Catholic, which will be treated more fittingly elsewhere. What is now called into question is by what right the Pope ought to be called father of the family, whether we consider the Catholic Church, or within it the Catholic Princes. In either case we desire an expression of your meaning. With respect to the Church, Nilus, Archbishop of Thessalonica, charges the Roman Pontiff that it is intolerable that the Roman Pope is unwilling to be subject to the canons of the holy Fathers, since he himself received his dignity from the Fathers; indeed, that he has even issued canons himself. Therefore, he says, the Pope is unworthy to be honoured as a father. Thus he. What do you say? I answer (you say) that the Pontiff has his authority not from the Fathers but from Christ; and that he makes canons himself is a sign that he is a lawgiver and has no superior prince. But he cannot be bound by his own laws. If he is honoured by all as father, he has no father himself, but all are his sons; yet sons ought to be subject to a father.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Papam iure tantum humano posse se Patrum-familias vendere.
units.tr: That the Pope may sell himself as Father of the family only by human right.

units.la: QVæstio est, vtrum Rom. Pontifex Authoritatem (non dico tantam, quantam nunc sibi vendicat, sed quantam vetustas in eo agnoverit) Diuino, an solùm Humano iure obtinuerit. Bellarminus Diuino asserit. Cùm igitur hoc sit primum imùmque fundamentum illud, super quod immensam illam molem, quam Potestatis Pontificiæ plenitudinem vocant, superstructam cernimus; hoc demùm labefactato, quæ de Papa vel Monarchico Regimine, vel de Iudicij eius infallibilitate Pontificij decantant, corruant omnia necesse est. Nostri muneris esset, hanc basin imprimis demoliri atque subuertere, nisi iamdiù innumeris Patrum suffragijs, tanquàm totidem manibus machinisque funditus subrutum iacuisset. Exempli causa. Anno Domini ccccl. Concilium Chalcedonense, in Phrygia congregatum (quod Gregorius Magnus numerat inter illa Concilia, quæ dicit se venerari, & totâ devotione amplecti) communi Centum & quinquaginta Patrum censensu (in Act. 16. Can. 28.) statuit atque decernit, Ecclesiam vrbis Constantinopolitanæ Æquali bus cum Rom. vrbis Ecclesia privilegijs frui, & non secus ac Illam extolli, as magnifieri.
units.tr: The question is whether the Roman Pontiff has obtained authority (I do not say as great as he now claims for himself, but as great as antiquity acknowledged in him) by divine right or only by human right. Bellarmine asserts divine right. Since this is the first and most fundamental foundation, on which we see that huge mass which they call the fullness of papal power is built, it must follow that once this is overthrown, everything the Papists sing about the Pope, whether his monarchical rule or the infallibility of his judgment, must collapse. It would be our task to demolish and subvert this base first of all, were it not that it has long lain thoroughly undermined by the countless votes of the Fathers, as if by so many hands and machines. For example: in the year 450, the Council of Chalcedon, assembled in Phrygia (which Gregory the Great counts among those councils which he says he venerates and embraces with all devotion), by the common agreement of one hundred and fifty Fathers (Act. 16, Can. 28), decreed and ordained that the Church of the city of Constantinople should enjoy equal privileges with the Church of the city of Rome, and be exalted and magnified no less than it.

units.la: Cuius Decreti Rationem si quæramus propriam, & (vt ita loquar) fundamentalem, Illa profectò statim nobis occurrat necesse est, quam vester assignat Binius, nimirum, Supponit Synodus illa (inquit) quod Romana sedes non Diuino, sed humano iure Caput Ecclesiarum effecta fuerit. Nec sanè, vlla alia Ratio esse potuit, cur, ante hoc, in Conc. Carthaginensi sub Cypriano lxvii. Episcopi, de Baptizandis Hæreticis, Rom. Pontificis decreto plane contrarium statuerent : aut in Conc. Africano (cui interfuit Augustinus) Patres ccxvii Appellationem ad Rom. Pontifi- cem suis interdicerent. Impie id quidem Sanctissimi illi Episcopi factitassent, siquidem Pontificem Rom. Divino iure Patrem familias sibi constitutum agnouissent: quippe quo iure filij Eum Patrem appellant, codè pariter ad eundem Appellare tenentur. Sed quid multis opus est? Deus Opt. Max. cuius solius virtute è Brutis oratio, ex tenebris lux, & ex summo hominis malo (viz. Peccato) summum eius bonum, æterna nempe salus emanauit, ex ipsa Ecclesia Rom. in Concilio Constantiensi ccxi. Episcopis consentientibus (Cui Conc. Basileensis Patres multi suffragati sunt) veritatem hanc extraxit, quòd nimirum *Primatus Pontificis non diuino sed tantum humano iure constit. Vsque adeò igitur certum & indubitatum est, nostros Neotericos in Romano suo Petro fingendo & fabricando non cùm Petro, in ipsa Petra, sed, cùm stolido & imperito architecto, fundamentum in Arena posuisse.
units.tr: If we ask for the proper and, so to speak, foundational reason for this decree, it must immediately occur to us, the one your Binius assigns, namely: That council (he says) presupposes that the Roman see became the head of the Churches by human right, not divine. Indeed, there could be no other reason why, earlier, in the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, sixty-seven bishops decreed concerning the baptism of heretics something plainly contrary to the decree of the Roman Pontiff; or why, in the African council (at which Augustine was present), two hundred and seventeen Fathers forbade appeals to the Roman Pontiff. Those most holy bishops would have acted impiously indeed, if they had acknowledged the Roman Pontiff as constituted Father of the family by divine right; for by that same right, sons who call him "Father" are equally bound to appeal to him. But why need there be many words? God, the Best and Greatest, by whose power alone speech came from brute beasts, light from darkness, and from man's greatest evil (namely sin) his greatest good, eternal salvation, drew out this very truth from the Roman Church itself, at the Council of Constance, when two hundred and eleven bishops agreed (to which many Fathers of the Council of Basel also assented): that the primacy of the Pontiff was established not by divine but only by human right. So certain and indubitable is it, then, that our modern writers, in feigning and fabricating their Roman Peter, did not place the foundation on Peter, on the rock itself, but like a foolish and unskilled builder placed it on sand.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Papam Ecclesiæ filium forsan, Patrem pariter non esse censendum.
units.tr: That the Pope, perhaps a son of the Church, is likewise not to be regarded as a father.

units.la: AEnæas Syluius, (qui post Rom. Pontifex nomine Pij II. constitutus est) quíque in componendo, de Theologorum iudicijs, qui in Conc. Basileensi claruerunt, Commentario certè quidem egregio plurimùm elaborauit; nonnihil habet huic Causæ explicandæ oppidò necessarium, quod non me pigebit eius verbis referre. x Si mater omnium fidelium est Ecclesia, Romanum etiam Episcopum filium habet ; alias verò, sicut Beatiss. prædicat Augustinus, nunquam habebit Deum Patrem, qui non habet Ecclesiam Matrem. Quod Anacletus (Papa) intelligens, vniuersalem Ecclesiam Matrem suam appellat: & Calixtus (Papa) ait; Sicut filius (Christus) venit facere voluntatem Patris ; ita & nos debemus implere voluntatem Matris nostræ, quæ est Ecclesia. Papa igitur debet subesse Concilio, quod est Ecclesia: unde & Petrus alio nomine est Simon appellatus, quae Hebraica vox (ut Rabano placet) interpretatur Obediens, ut intelligerent omnes, etiam in Rom. Pontifice necessariam esse obedientiam. Haec ille. Quod testimonium revera causae ipsius iugulum petit. Iam igitur non modo ex Pontificiorum Theologorum, verum etiam ex ipsorum Pontificum iudicijs perspicuè satis constat, Papam, dum nimirum se venditat Ecclesiae Patrem, ab ipsa Matre Ecclesia penitus esse desertum, & derelictum. Haec de Papae Paternitate, respectu Ecclesiae.
units.tr: Aeneas Silvius (who afterwards became Roman Pontiff under the name Pius II), who certainly labored greatly in composing his commentary on the judgments of the theologians who flourished at the Council of Basel, has some things most necessary for explaining this cause, which I shall not be sorry to report in his words: If the Church is the mother of all the faithful, then the Roman Bishop too has the Church as his mother; otherwise, as the most blessed Augustine proclaims, he will never have God as Father, who does not have the Church as Mother. Pope Anacletus, understanding this, calls the universal Church his mother; and Pope Callixtus says: As the Son came to do the will of the Father, so we too ought to fulfil the will of our Mother, who is the Church. Therefore the Pope ought to be subject to the Council, which is the Church; whence also Peter was called by another name, Simon, which Hebrew word (as Rabanus pleases) means Obedient, so that all might understand that obedience is necessary even in the Roman Pontiff. Thus he. Which testimony truly attacks the very throat of their cause. Now, therefore, it is quite clearly evident not only from the judgments of the Papist theologians but also from the judgments of the Pontiffs themselves, that the Pope, while he indeed boasts himself to be Father of the Church, has been utterly deserted and abandoned by the Mother Church herself. So much for the Pope's paternity with respect to the Church.

units.la: Quo sensu Pontifex Bellarmino Pater familias esse videtur, respectu Principum maximè.
units.tr: In what sense the Pontiff seems to Bellarmine to be Father of the family, chiefly with respect to princes.

units.la: Bellarminus alibi.
units.tr: Bellarmine elsewhere.

units.la: {i}Pontificem supremam authoritatem sibi vendicare, quod est Asserere, libenter admittimus: sic tamen, ut per[Authoritatem] non despoticum Imperium, sed paternam, sine Pastorale intelligamus.
units.tr: {i}We gladly admit that the Pontiff claims supreme authority, which is to assert; yet so that by "authority" we understand not a despotic empire but a paternal and pastoral one.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Quàm durum & difficilem Pontifex, cùm in Cardinales, Fratres, tùm etiam in Patres, vz. Predecessores s[?]e prabuerit.
units.tr: How harsh and difficult the Pontiff has shown himself to be, both toward cardinals and brothers, and also toward the Fathers, that is, his predecessors.

units.la: NIsi Bzouij, Bozij, aliorúmque id genus Adulatorum Euge (quibus minimum Pontificum screatus & ructus cinamomum & opobalsamum redolet) quàm vestrorum (inter quos Massonius, Platina, Onuphrius) Historicorum Ecce plus apud Te valeret, non de illo Paterno Pontificum ingenio dictata toties decantares. Quippè Nos vestrorum Historicorum oculis vidimus à Pontificibus vestris {z}Cardinales duos veneno extinctos: Alium {a}oculis privatum: praeterea etiam Duos miserè multatos, vtpote, quorum {b}Alteri manus; alteri nasus abscissus fuerit: Quinque item alios {c}Faedissimo carcere clausos, & post feré, & plusquàm barbarâ immanitate occisos.
units.tr: Unless the "Euge" of Bzovius, Bozius, and others of that sort of flatterers (to whom the spittle and belch of the Pontiffs smell of cinnamon and balsam) had weighed more with you than the "Ecce" of your historians (among whom Massonius, Platina, Onuphrius), you would not so often have sung of that paternal disposition of the Pontiffs. For we have seen with our own eyes, as your historians report, that two cardinals were extinguished by poison by your Pontiffs; another was deprived of his eyes; moreover two others were cruelly mutilated, one having his hand cut off, the other his nose; likewise five others were shut up in a most foul prison and afterwards killed with a cruelty almost barbarous, and more than barbarous.

units.la: {b} Idem in vita Joh.13.
units.tr: {b} Idem in vita Joh. 13.

units.la: {c} Maffon. in vita Urbani.
units.tr: {c} Maffon. in vita Urbani.

units.la: Eisdem oculis cernere nobis licuit à Pontificibus ipsis etiam Pontifices miris dirisque tractatos modis; {d} Fornosum mortuum e sepulchro extrahi, in sede Pontificali collocari, & vestimentis Pontificalibus in lutum decollari, & in Tiberim præcipitari. Breuitatis causâ prætereo tùm nefarium odium Sabiniani, tum etiam Christophori, Bonifacij VI. Stephani VI. ipsiusque Formosi, aliorumque complurium crudelitates. {e}Qui (vt de quibusdam Onuphrius) nihil aliud cogitabant, quàm vt nomen & dignitatem Praedecessorum extinguerent. Hæc, quæ illi certè quidem [illegible, ~8 letters], an proinde etiam [illegible, ~7 letters] tibi fecisse videntur?
units.tr: We have also been able to see with the same eyes Pontiffs themselves treated by Pontiffs in strange and dreadful ways: {d}Formosus, dead, was dragged from his tomb, placed on the pontifical throne, beheaded in his pontifical vestments, and hurled into the Tiber. For the sake of brevity I pass over the unspeakable hatred of Sabinian, and also the cruelties against Christopher, Boniface VI, Stephen VI, Formosus himself, and many others. {e}Who (as Onuphrius says of some of them) thought of nothing else than to extinguish the name and dignity of their predecessors. Did those things, which they certainly [illegible, ~8 letters], seem to you to have done likewise [illegible, ~7 letters]?

units.la: Imò verò cùm tantas exercuerint crudelitates non modò in Cardinales, {f}Primarios, scilicet, Pontificis, & Ecclesiae Romanae Consiliarios, ac veluti canes, super quos Deus posuit orbem; sed etiam in Praedecessores Pontifices, & Patres suos ita immaniter saeuierint, vt Eos, quorum pedes sunt exosculati, collo suspenderent: credibilene est Eos (modò iure suo uti queant) cum infensis sibi Principibus (quos pro Vassallis habent) remissiùs, & (itâ didam) [illegible, ~7 letters] esse acturos?
units.tr: Indeed, since they have exercised such great cruelties not only against cardinals, {f}the chief men, namely, the counsellors of the Pontiff and of the Roman Church, and like dogs, over whom God has placed the world; but have also raged so monstrously against their predecessor Pontiffs and their own Fathers, that they hanged from the neck those whose feet they had kissed: is it credible that they, provided they can use their own right, will act more mildly, and (so to say) [illegible, ~7 letters] toward princes who are hostile to them (whom they hold as vassals)?

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Papa non Principum Pater, sed superciliosus & fastidiosus Dominus.
units.tr: The Pope is not the Father of princes, but a haughty and disdainful Lord.

units.la: QVid Tu per Paternum illud & Pastorale Pontificis Imperium significare velis, Nemini dubium esse potest, qui scripta tua vel extremis, quod dicitur, labijs degustauit: nam siquidem Principes Pontificis tui nutibus non obtemperant, tùm (Te suadore) Excommunicationis fulmine feriendi; sicubi verò resistant, Regnis suis deturbandi; quin etiam porrò, si vim adhibent, proteniùs conclamatum est, ferro, flammáque ad extremum spiritum persequendi sunt. Quid hic (malum) Paterni Imperij sit, nequeo satis decernere. Possem ego ex Germania, Gallia, Anglia, Hispania, Bohemia, aliisque Regnis exempla Principum plena manu producere, in quos Despoticum suum Imperium Pontifices exercuerunt; si quidem bella Illis indicere; si Regnis deturbare; si procurare, & ludibrio eos habere Despoticum aliquid in se habeat.
units.tr: What you mean by that paternal and pastoral empire of the Pope can be doubtful to nobody who has tasted your writings even with the tips of the lips, as they say. For if princes do not obey the nods of your Pope, then (at your urging) they are to be struck with the thunderbolt of excommunication; and if they resist anywhere, they are to be cast down from their kingdoms. Moreover, if they use force, it has been loudly proclaimed that they are to be pursued with sword and flame to the last breath. What evil this paternal rule is, I cannot sufficiently determine. I could bring forth from Germany, France, England, Spain, Bohemia and other kingdoms examples of princes in plenty, against whom their Popes exercised their despotic rule, if to wage war upon them, to cast them down from their kingdoms, and to procure their ruin and hold them up to mockery is anything despotic in itself.

units.la: Sed quia nullum tibi spectaculum videtur iucundius, quam in quo Imperatoria Maiestas, Totâ spectante Româ, fasces suos Pontifici submiserit, omissis alijs, tantùm in duobus Henrico,& Frederico Impp.insistam. Imperatorem Henricum IV. Pontifex Gregorius VII. non nisi nudis pedibus ad se venientem, & per quatriduum ieiunantem, ad colloquium admisit. Fredericum Barbarossam Caesarem Pontifex Alexander III. Inclinatâ cervice collum pedi suo submittere compulit, dicens, Super aspidem & basiliscum ambulabis, conculcabis Leonem & Draconem. Respondet Imperator; Non tibi, sed Petro hunc honorem exhibeo: Regerit Pontifex, Et mihi, & Petro. Haec vester Historicus. Quae mala bestia, vel si se ruperit, huic fatui par erit? Istinè sunt, qui (vt ais) Tam Petrum, quàm Paulum Patrem & Praedecessorem suum habuerunt? Sint pariter, oportet, etiam Illi, in quos Bernardi querimonia perquàm commodè quadrabit, Scilicet, inquit, sic faciebat Petrus, sic Paulus ludebat. Iactes igitur, per me licet, Principes nonnullos Patres tam tetricos coluisse; ego facilè credam, sed tamen eo animo id fecisse, quo Ethnici nonnulli dicuntur adorare Deum Veiovem, scilicet, ne noceat. Ad exitum festino,
units.tr: But because no spectacle seems to you more pleasing than the one in which the Imperial Majesty, with all Rome looking on, lowered its fasces before the Pope, I shall leave out the others and dwell only on two emperors, Henry and Frederick. Pope Gregory VII admitted the Emperor Henry IV to an audience only when he came to him barefoot and fasting for three days. Pope Alexander III forced Frederick Barbarossa to submit his bowed neck to his foot, saying, "You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk; you shall trample the lion and the dragon." The Emperor replied, "I pay this honour not to you, but to Peter." The Pope retorted, "And to me and to Peter." So says your historian. What evil beast, even if it burst itself, would be a match for this fool? Are these the men who, as you say, had both Peter and Paul as their Father and Predecessor? They must equally be those of whom Bernard's complaint fits very neatly: "Thus Peter used to act, thus Paul used to play the fool," he says. Boast, then, if you like, that some princes worshipped Fathers so grim; I will readily believe it, but they did so with the same intent with which some heathens are said to worship the god Veiovis, namely, "so that he may not harm them." I hasten to the end.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Reges reuerà Patres esse, quibus honor externus à Pontifi- cibus & Sacerdotibus deferendus sit; qui tamen dedecori sibi esse ducunt Regum manus osculari.
units.tr: Kings are indeed fathers, to whom external honour is to be paid by the Pontiffs and priests, yet they count it a disgrace to kiss the hands of kings.

units.la: Pontifices tamen ratione Sacerdotali, quo funguntur, muneris Patres dici posse, vltrò concedimus; sed eâ lege, vt Tu vicissim Principes Patres esse agnoscas. Sunt, inquis, etiam Reges Patres. At Pontificem insuper Papam, id est, Patrem Patris appellari iactitas. Esto; quanquàm est etiam vbi{m}Regem Patrem patriæ esse largiris non inuitus. At Pontificibus Reuerentia debetur. De Regibus autem, quid? Regem quoque adorandum esse, Exemplo demonstrat. Quid iam igitur inter Principem & Pontificem interfit, aueo scire. {k}Princeps (inquis) vt personam Dei gerens geniculis hominum adoratur; nempè Laicorum. At, {*}Papa Christi vicem tenens (inquitis) osculatione pedis solus est honorandus à mortalibus omnibus. Tantum verò abest vt vllius Principis pedem attingat, vt nec Episcopo cuiquam id liceat. Imò si Princeps quispiam Episcopis aut Sacerdotibus manus exosculandas porrexerit, vix quidem reprehensionem effugiet: obseruat enim Nauarrus à nonnullis Pontificijs reprehendi {l}Reges Castellæ, quòd manum Sacerdotibus osculandam porrigant: & subinde ipse gestit, Donnam Iohannam Principem Portugalliæ gloriosissimam, in honorem Sacerdotij, ipsi manum osculandam denegâsse.
units.tr: We freely concede that Pontiffs may be called fathers in the sacerdotal sense, by reason of the office they discharge; but on this condition, that you in turn acknowledge princes to be fathers. Kings too are fathers, you say. But you boast that the Pope is even called the father of the father, that is, Father of the Father. Be it so; although you also grant, not unwillingly, that the king is Father of the fatherland. But reverence is owed to Pontiffs. And what of kings? You show by example that the king too is to be adored. What, then, lies between the Prince and the Pontiff? I am eager to know. The Prince (you say), bearing the person of God, is adored on the knees of men; namely, of laymen. But the Pope, holding the place of Christ (you say), is alone to be honoured by all mortals with the kissing of his foot. Yet so far is he from touching the foot of any prince that it is not lawful for any bishop either. Indeed, if some prince should offer his hands to bishops or priests to be kissed, he would hardly escape rebuke. For Navarrus observes that the kings of Castile were reprehended by some Papists because they offer their hands to priests to be kissed; and afterwards he himself rejoices that Donna Joanna, most glorious princess of Portugal, in honour of the priesthood, denied her hand to be kissed by him.

units.la: Ex his insolens hominum fastidium quis non videt? cùm præsertim quod Cives omnes bene affecti, tanquàm gratiæ & honoris symbolum interpretantur, ambitiosuli[?] nostri Pharisæi, vel à Gloriosissimo oblatum, dedecori sibi esse putant; & in istis rebus delicias sibi faciunt. O tempora! Superbiam hanc tamen contundet sana Cusani Cardinalis modestia. {m}Non exaltat Papam (inquit) Imperialis spontanea propter Christum humilitatis reuerentia, qui eum nominat & honorat vt Patrem; --sed potius aduertat, quòd humiles Imperatores Catholici Rom. Pontificem scriptis & operibus, vt spiritualem Patrem & custodem animarum venerabantur: multò etiam plures Scripturæ inuenirentur, quomodò Rom. Pontifex Imperatores honorare multo ampliore gradu solitus fuerit, vt superius Agathonis Papæ epistola declarat. &c. Hæc vester Cusanus Cardinalis; Tibi, Bellarmine, dignitate par, ætate prior, & candore animi (vt mihi quidem videtur) longè superior: cuius iccirco verissimam & difertissimam consessionem, in Titulo [PATER] discutiendo, ad vindicandam Principum dignitatem Coronidis vice esse volui.
units.tr: From these things, who does not see the insolent disdain of men? Especially since all well-disposed citizens interpret it as a symbol of grace and honour, our rather ambitious Pharisees think it a disgrace to be offered it by the most glorious king, and they make delights for themselves in such matters. O the times! Yet the sound modesty of the Cardinal of Cusa will crush this pride. The imperial voluntary reverence of humility for Christ does not exalt the Pope (he says), who names and honours him as Father; but rather let it be noted that humble Catholic emperors venerated the Roman Pontiff in writings and works as spiritual father and guardian of souls: much more numerous writings would be found showing how the Roman Pontiff was accustomed to honour emperors to a much greater degree, as the letter of Pope Agatho above declares, etc. So says your Cardinal of Cusa. To you, Bellarmine, he is equal in dignity, earlier in age, and (as it seems to me) far superior in candour of mind. I wished, in discussing the title [FATHER], to add his most true and eloquent confession as a kind of finishing touch, for vindicating the dignity of princes.

units.la: Hactenus de Titulo primo; sequitur Secundus.
units.tr: So much for the first title; the second follows.

units.la: CAP. II. Secundus Titulus, qui Papæ ascribitur, est PASTOR.
units.tr: CHAP. II. The second title that is ascribed to the Pope is PASTOR.

units.la: Vt partes, alioqui dissolutas, in Methodum reducam; agitur de Pontificio Iure Vniuersali in Laicos; Episcopos, & Sacerdotes omnes; quos Bellarminus Oues vocat. Ciues Reipublicae; quos Agnos. Hæreticos; quos Lupos:
units.tr: To reduce the parts, which are otherwise scattered, into order: the subject is the Papist universal right over the laity; over bishops and all priests, whom Bellarmine calls sheep; over the citizens of the commonwealth, whom he calls lambs; and over heretics, whom he calls wolves.

units.la: De Officio Pastoratus Pontificij vniuersali, praesertim su- pra Sacerdotes vniuersos.
units.tr: On the Office of the Papal universal pastorate, especially over all priests.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: FIRST ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Pastoris Titulo sensum perniciosum innolui.
units.tr: A pernicious sense lurks in the title of Pastor.

units.la: CVm dulce sit imprimis Patris spiritualis nomen, quod maximum charitatis officium in se complecti videtur; tùm certè quidem nomen Pastoris pergratum nobis videri posset: quùm praesertim sicut Patris officium est Gignere filios Deo; itâ Pastoris sit alere filios iam natos. Sed heu! priscam Pastorum fidem, quam à seculis aliquot è terris sublatam plurimi non abs re questi sunt. Quum enim in Pontifice Rom. sub nomine Patris, tantam ὑπόκρισιν[?] atque ἀγχάθιαν[?] latere iam experti sumus: sub Pastoris larua iam Lupum tegi non immerito subuereamur. Nec vanam hanc nostram suspicionem, imò nè suspicionem quidem, sed firmam & ratam veritatem esse, quiuis facilè intelligat, qui apud se perpenderit, quot vos, ex hoc uno Pastoris officio, quámque Christianæ Reip. noxias & perniciosas Argumentorum strophas deducere & colligere soletis. Exempli gratiâ. Papa Pastor est Ecclesia. Ergo I. Papa non subjicitur Concilio. II. Ergo Potest Papa authoritate sua Pastores alios omnes iudicare, & Pastoratu remouere. III. Ergo Ecclesiastici omnes, a Papa dependentes, exempti esse debent à foro seculari. IV. Ergo Penes Papam erit Principes & Imperatores deponere. Quo magis Tu Consequentias hasce subdolas Principes in hoc libro astutè celas; eò impensius Nobis, pro virili nostrâ, innitendum erit, ut Pastores, Populum, Principes Christianos, adeoque Ecclesiam ipsam ab istis tuis insidijs liberemus.
units.tr: Although the name of spiritual Father is especially sweet, since it seems to embrace the greatest office of charity, the name of Pastor might well seem very pleasing to us as well, especially since, just as it is the office of a Father to beget children for God, so it is the office of a Pastor to feed children already born. But alas! the old faithfulness of Pastors has been taken from the earth for some centuries, and many have not without reason complained of it. For since we have already learned that under the name of Father, in the Roman Pontiff, such great hypocrisy [ὑπόκρισιν] and guile [ἀγχάθιαν] lie hidden, we may rightly fear that under the mask of Pastor a wolf is now concealed. And anyone who weighs this in his own mind will easily understand that our suspicion is not an empty one, nay not even a mere suspicion, but a firm and established truth: how many harmful and pernicious chains of arguments you are accustomed to draw and gather from this one office of Pastor, and how noxious and destructive they are to the Christian commonwealth. For example: The Pope is the Pastor of the Church. Therefore I. the Pope is not subject to a Council. II. Therefore the Pope can by his own authority judge all other pastors and remove them from the pastorate. III. Therefore all ecclesiastics who depend on the Pope ought to be exempt from the secular court. IV. Therefore it will rest with the Pope to depose princes and emperors. The more you cunningly conceal these deceitful consequences against princes in this book, the more earnestly we must strive, each to the best of his powers, to free pastors, the people, Christian princes, and so the Church itself, from your snares.

units.la: Vniuersalem Pastoratum, vt Petri in Apostolos omnes asserit; ita Papa in omnes Episcopos
units.tr: He asserts a universal pastorate, as Peter's was over all the Apostles; so the Pope's is over all bishops.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office.

units.la: “Quamuis enim multi sunt in Ecclesia Pastores, qui verbo “ & Sacramento fideles pascunt, tamen omnes à Principe Pastore pendent. — pag.27.
units.tr: "Although there are many pastors in the Church who feed the faithful with word and sacrament, yet all depend on the Prince Pastor." — p. 27.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Hæc Tu; hoc in loco; Alibi verò explicatiùs. {a}Passim docent veteres, à Rom. Ecclesia omnes Episcopos habuisse consecrationem suam, quod non videtur esse verum, nisi in eo sensu, quòd Petrus qui fuit Episcopus Rom. omnes ⌣Apostolos, omnésque alios Episcopos vel per se, vel per alios ordinavit. ⌣Alioqui enim, cum omnes ⌣Apostoli Episcopos alios in variis locis constituerint, certè (si Apostoli ipsi non fuissent facti Episcopi à Petro) maxima pars non deduceret originem à Petro: nec recte diceretur ab Anacleto Epist. 1. Sacerdotalem ordinem post Christum cæpisse à Petro, si omnes Apostoli immediatè à Christo ordinati fuissent,
units.tr: You say this here; elsewhere you explain it more fully. {a} The ancients everywhere teach that all bishops received their consecration from the Roman Church. This does not seem true, except in the sense that Peter, who was bishop of Rome, ordained all the Apostles and all the other bishops, either himself or through others. For otherwise, since all the Apostles appointed other bishops in various places, surely (if the Apostles themselves had not been made bishops by Peter) the greater part would not derive their origin from Peter. Nor would Anacletus, in his first Epistle, be rightly said to have taught that the sacerdotal order began with Peter after Christ, if all the Apostles had been ordained immediately by Christ.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Dependentiam omnium aliorum Pastorum à Papa caduco niti fundamento.
units.tr: SECOND ANIMADVERSION. The dependence of all other pastors on the Pope rests on a tottering foundation.

units.la: Conclusionem repete. Omnes (inquis) Ecclesiæ Pastores pendent ab uno Pastore Rom. Pontifice. Conclusio hæc quùm tanti sit momenti, solido certè aliquo fundamento niti debet: hoc subjice; Quia omnes (inquis) Apostoli consecrati & ordinati sint Pastores à Petro. At fundamentum hoc suo eget fundamento, Tu illud substerne; Quia (inquis) Anacletus dixit Sacerdotalem ordinationem cœpisse à Petro. Hanc telam facilè retexam. Ultimum fundamentum nimis est caducum; quia Epistola ⌣Anacleti vestro Cardinali adulterina & suppositititia esse videtur. {b}Ego (inquit Cusanus) has Epistolas ⌣Anacleti Apocryphas esse credo. Quæ, ut veræ & genuinæ sint, tamen (teste vestro Victoria) {c}non significant id quod huius (nempe Tuæ) sententia Authores volunt.
units.tr: Repeat your conclusion: all the pastors of the Church (you say) depend on one Pastor, the Roman Pontiff. Since this conclusion is of such weight, it must surely rest on some solid foundation. You add this: because all the Apostles (you say) were consecrated and ordained pastors by Peter. But this foundation needs a foundation of its own, and you supply it: because (you say) Anacletus said that sacerdotal ordination began with Peter. I shall easily unravel this web. The last foundation is too tottering, because the Epistle of Anacletus seems to your Cardinal to be spurious and supposititious. {b} "I (says Cusanus) believe these Epistles of Anacletus to be apocryphal." And even if they were true and genuine, nevertheless (as your Victoria testifies) {c} they do not signify what the authors of this opinion, namely you, want them to.

units.la: Nihilominùs hoc solo fundamento innixum est Alterum, nimirùm; ⌣Apostolos omnes ordinationem suam habuisse à Petro: quod, tanquàm absonum & putidum Paradoxon , Schola vestra jamdiu explosit. Nam Azorius Iesuita defendit, {d}Omnes Apostolos à Christo Domino proximè fuisse Sacerdotes & Episcopos ordinatos ; & ab eo potestatem non solùm ordinis, sed etiam iurisdictionis accepisse, arctè tenet, accuratèque defendit : {*}Quia (inquit) omnes Apostoli sunt à Christo electi, uti ex Euangelio constat, & ipse Paulus aperte tradit, Gal.1.& 2. se non esse ab hominibus, neque per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum Apostolum institutum. Matthias autem non erat ab Apostolis, sed à Deo creatus : at Apostolica potestas continebat in se non solùm ordinis potestatem, sed etiam Iurisdictionis : & ideò Apostoli ubiq; terrarum Episcopos & Presbyteros constituebant ; omnibusque dictum, Accipite Spiritum Sanctum ; & Omnibus plenissima Iurisdictio data est, Matth.18. illis verbis, [Quaecunque alligabitis, &c.] Omnibus dictum est, Euntes in universum mundum praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae ; etiam de Iuda dictum est : Episcopatum eius alter accipiat. Hæc ille; Cui Iesuita Vasquez succinens, Conclusioni tuæ vel maximè aduersatur : {e}Dico (inquit) Episcopos omnem potestatem ius dicendi, quæ dicitur actiua Iurisdictio, & quasi radicalis, non accepisse à Pontifice, sed proximè à Christo, idcoque iure etiam Diuino, hoc ipso, quod Episcopi sunt, accepisse potestatem leges condendi. Atque etiam Scholasticos, qui à tua opinione abhorruerint, citari video à {f}Vestris; Caietanum, Sotum, Cordubensem, Bannez: Necnon {g}Maiorem, Victoriam, Petrum de Soto, de Castro, affirmantes, Opinionem suam esse omnium Doctorum sententiam. Sic ille. Vestris igitur lacertis Argumentū Tuum retorquebimus, in hunc modum. Maior. Nisi Apostoli omnes ordinati Pastores fuerint à Petro, nulla ratio est cur Episcopi dicantur à Pontifice pendere. Consequentia hæc Tua est. At Apostoli omnes immediatè à Christo, non à Petro constituti ordinatique fuerunt. (Hæc fuit communis Assumptio Tuorum.) Ergò Episcopos alios non pendere à Papa, Conclusio erit cuiusuis hominis Academico sole vel leuiter colorati. Ut unda undam ; sic absurdum unum aliud trudit.
units.tr: Nevertheless the other foundation rests on this one alone, namely that all the Apostles had their ordination from Peter. Your own School has long since rejected this as an absurd and stinking paradox. For the Jesuit Azorius defends, {d} that all the Apostles were ordained priests and bishops immediately by Christ the Lord, and received from him not only the power of order but also of jurisdiction, and he holds this firmly and defends it carefully: {*} Because (he says) all the Apostles were chosen by Christ, as is clear from the Gospel, and Paul himself plainly teaches, Gal. 1 and 2, that he was instituted an Apostle not by men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ. Matthias, however, was not from the Apostles but was created by God; but apostolic power contained in itself not only the power of order but also of jurisdiction. Therefore the Apostles everywhere on earth appointed bishops and presbyters; and to all of them it was said, Receive the Holy Spirit; and to all of them the fullest jurisdiction was given, Matt. 18, in those words [Whatsoever you shall bind, etc.] To all it was said, Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature; and it was also said of Judas: let another take his bishopric. So he. The Jesuit Vasquez, echoing him, is very much opposed to your conclusion: {e} I say (he says) that bishops have not received from the Pontiff the whole power of judging, which is called active jurisdiction, and which is as it were radical, but have received it immediately from Christ; and therefore by divine right, by the very fact that they are bishops, they have received the power of enacting laws. And I see that the Schoolmen who shrank from your opinion are also cited by your people: Cajetan, Soto, Cordubensis, Bañez; and also {g} Major, Victoria, Peter de Soto, and de Castro, affirming that their opinion is the view of all the Doctors. So he. Therefore we shall turn your argument back upon you with your own arms, in this way. Major premise: unless all the Apostles were ordained pastors by Peter, there is no reason why bishops should be said to depend on the Pontiff. This consequence is yours. But the Apostles were all constituted and ordained immediately by Christ, not by Peter. (This was the common assumption of your people.) Therefore the conclusion that the other bishops do not depend on the Pope will be one that any scholar of even slight wit could draw. As wave follows wave, so one absurdity thrusts forth another.

units.la: {*} Pastores omnes ab illo Pastorum Principe (Pontifice) diriguntur, & si non bene fungantur officio, ab illo remoueri à munere Pastoritio possunt. — Pag.27.
units.tr: {*} All pastors are directed by that Prince of Pastors (the Pontiff), and if they do not discharge their office well, they can be removed from the pastoral office by him. — p. 27.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. Animadversion.

units.la: Pontificis Ius dirigendi & corrigendi omnes alios Pasto- res, antiquitus inauditum fuisse.
units.tr: That the Pontiff's right to direct and correct all other ministers was unheard of in antiquity.

units.la: QVemquamnè, Bellarmine, Tu adeò hospitem & peregrinum in Ecclesiasticis historijs putas (modò vestigium saltem aliquando in ijs posuerit) cui persuadeas Omnes Pastores à Papa, tanquam à Principe Pastorum, dirigi deberi; aut exauctorari munere suo Pastoritio posse, si minus illi obsequantur? quotus, quaeso, quisque est omnium, qui non explorate didicit, Pontifices vestros, quamuis satis imperiosos, & contrà nitentes, parùm aut nihil in Ecclesijs alijs antiquitùs valuisse. Non enim (haud ignota loquar) apud Asianos receptam Paschae observationem mutare; non duo vocabula, nempè, [illegible, ~2 words] à Conc. Chalcedonensis Patribus fancita, delere; non per Conc. Carthaginensis Patres excommunicatos restituere; non ab Africani Conc. Patribus ius Appellationis obtinere; nec inultam sibi Falsi notam vitare; non in Conc. Constantinopolitano impositam ipsi Romanae Ecclesiae Ieiunij legem abrogare; non, in causa Bulgariae, Episcopos à Iustino ordinatos remouere; non postremis seculis in Conc. Florentino (vbi tamen maximè dominari videri voluerunt) electionem Patriarchae impetrare. Tot & tanta {*}argumenta Nullitatis Pontificiae publicis Historicorum monumentis consignantur. Iuuentus est tamen, ex schola Societatis Iesu, Bellarminus, ausus Principes docere; quòd omnes Episcopi à Pontifice, tanquam Pastore suo pendent, à quo dirigendi, & nisi ex arbitrio eius officio fungantur Pastoritio, munere remouendi sunt, scilicet: hoc nouo eget fulcimento ; nam hoc, quod nunc posuisti, fragile est, caducum, & putridum.
units.tr: Is there anyone, Bellarmine, whom you consider so foreign and such a stranger to ecclesiastical history (provided he has ever set foot in it at all) that you could persuade him that all ministers ought to be directed by the Pope, as by the Prince of Pastors, or that they can be deprived of their pastoral office if they do not obey him? How few, I ask, are there of all who have not thoroughly learned that your Popes, however domineering and however much they strove against others, had little or no authority in the other churches in antiquity. For (I speak of things well known) they did not change the observance of Easter received among the Asians; did not delete two words sanctioned by the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon; did not restore the excommunicated by the Fathers of the Council of Carthage; did not obtain the right of appeal from the Fathers of the African Council; did not escape the stigma of falsehood unpunished; did not, at the Council of Constantinople, abrogate the law of fasting imposed on the Roman Church itself; did not, in the case of Bulgaria, remove bishops ordained by Justin; and in the last centuries, at the Council of Florence (where nevertheless they especially wished to seem to dominate), did not obtain the election of the Patriarch.
