So many and such great proofs of the nullity of the Papacy are recorded in the public monuments of the historians. Yet it is a young man from the school of the Society of Jesus, Bellarmine, who has dared to teach princes that all bishops depend on the Pope as their pastor, by whose direction they are governed, and unless they perform their pastoral office according to his judgement, they are to be removed from office, forsooth. This needs a new prop, for what you have now put forward is fragile, perishable, and rotten.

units.la: Confirmat priorem suam Conclusionem
units.tr: He confirms his earlier conclusion.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Offic.

units.la: “ Neque solum Pastores ceteri Principi Pastorum subiecti esse debent, sed etiam oues dici possint summi Pastoris: nam ea causa est, cur Dominus Petro non solum Agnos, sed etiam Oues, agnorum matres, pascendas commiserit. &c. — Pag. 27.
units.tr: Not only must the other pastors be subject to the Prince of Pastors, but the sheep too may be called the sheep of the chief Shepherd; for this is the reason why the Lord committed to Peter not only the lambs but also the sheep, the mothers of the lambs, to be fed, etc. — p. 27.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Intelligis nimirum (aut ego fallor) Apostolos alios, quamuis alioquin praecipuos Ecclesiae Pastores, tamen Petro, veluti Oues, fuisse subiectos. Hoc tam crassum Paradoxon ut vel specie aliquâ Argumenti suadeas, Alibi citas illud {h}Ioh. 21. [ Dixit Christus Petro, Pasce oues meas. Unde nobis (inquis) certum exploratumque est (quod Lutherani negant) omnes omninò Christianos, etiam Apostolos, Petro tanquàm ouiculas commendari. Est enim obseruandum Christum bis dixisse [ Pasce agnos, ] & semel [ Pasce oues, ] vt est vulgata editione; & debuit ita esse in Graecis, vbi librariorum vitio Graecè ponitur pro ἀρνία [?] ; oues pro ouiculis. His probatis, ex hac variatione, quae mysterio non videtur carere, probamus Petro omnes Christianos debere esse subiectos: nam si per ouiculas intelligimus Agnos, dicemus Agnos bis repetitos, ad significandum populum Iudaicum & Gentilem; harum curam commisit Petro; & etiam Ouium, quae agnos peperint in Christo, qui sunt Apostoli & Episcopi.
units.tr: You understand, surely (unless I am mistaken), that the other apostles, though otherwise the chief ministers of the Church, were nevertheless subject to Peter as sheep are to a shepherd. So that you may at least lend some semblance of argument to this crass paradox, you cite elsewhere John 21. [Christ said to Peter, Feed my sheep. From this, you say, it is certain and clear to us (which the Lutherans deny) that all Christians without exception, even the apostles, are committed to Peter as little sheep. For it must be observed that Christ said "Feed the lambs" twice and "Feed the sheep" once, as in the Vulgate edition; and it must have been so in the Greek, where through a scribal error the Greek is put for arnia [ἀρνία]; sheep for little sheep.] Having established these points, we prove from this variation, which does not seem to lack a mystery, that all Christians must be subject to Peter: for if by little sheep we understand the lambs, we shall say that the lambs are repeated twice to signify the Jewish and the Gentile people, whose care he committed to Peter; and the sheep, who brought forth lambs in Christ, are the apostles and bishops.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Anim. Bellarmini, in distinctione Ouium & Agnorum, refelli.
units.tr: I. Animadversion. Bellarmine's distinction between sheep and lambs is refuted.

units.la: CHristus Pasce Oues semel, Agnos vero bis: Ergo per Agnos duos populos; Per Oues Apostolos significaut, v-treftrosque Petro subiectos. Agutè admodùm. Ad hoc Commentum nostrer {i}Beza nonnihil excanduit; Nec sanè immeritò; nam (vt nullam de Translatione Tibi litem intendam) quod Tu tanquàm certum & exploratum prorsus putas, diuinique cuiusdam Mysterij nomine dignum, id compatri tuo Maldonato Iesuitæ perridiculum videtur.
units.tr: Christ says "Feed the sheep" once and "the lambs" twice: therefore by the lambs he signifies two peoples, and by the sheep the apostles, both of which are subject to Peter. Very sharp indeed! Our Beza grew somewhat heated at this invention, and not undeservedly; for (not to press any quarrel with you over the translation) what you think quite certain and clear, and worthy of the name of some divine mystery, seems perfectly ridiculous to your fellow Jesuit Maldonado.

units.la: {k}Non subtiliter disputandum est (inquit) cur Christus Agnos potiùs quam Oues appellauerit; quod qui fecerit, videat etiam atque etiam ne doctis hominibus Risum prabeat: satis enim constat, eosdem nunc Agnos, verf.17. nunc Oues appellari. quod si quicquam discriminis est inter Oues & Agnos, id non in re, sed voce est; quod cùm idem sint, tamen vocabulum ⌣Agni[?] blandius est, & maiorem amorem prae se fert.
units.tr: It is not necessary to dispute subtly why Christ called them lambs rather than sheep; whoever does so should take care that he does not give cause for laughter to learned men: for it is well established that the same ones are now called lambs, now sheep (verse 17). But if there is any difference between sheep and lambs, it lies not in the thing but in the word; since they are the same, yet the word "lamb" is more tender and shows greater love.

units.la: Assertio confirmari potest ex collatione Euangelistæ Matthæi cap.10.16. & Lucæ cap.10.3. vbi Christus dicit, Mitto vos vt agnos in medio luporum: apud Matthæum est [ὡς πρόβατα][?] Oues, apud Lucam vero [ἄρνας][?] Agnos, in vtroque discipulos suos, id est, Pastores ipsos alloquitur: vbi subtilitati tuæ locus nullus esse potest, nisi cùm semel Apostolos, id est, Pastores in Oues (respectu Petri) conuertisti; noua aliquâ metamorphôsi, aut (vt Tu dicis) Mysterio velis quasi Medeæ potentibus herbis Eos, iam Oues, rursùs in Agnos, id est, Populum transmutare. Dux greges inter oues agnus medicamine fiet. {l}Quin insuper recognosce, quæso, verba tua. Commissi Petro sunt tàm Agni, seu oniculæ; quàm{m} Oues, quæ sunt Agnorum matres; {n}qui sunt Apostoli & Episcopi. Quibus, Te Authore, distinguntur Apostoli à populo, vt oues ab oniculis: nihilominùs, in eodem capite, {*}Nobis exploratum est (inquis) Apostolos Petro, tanquàm oniculus commendari. Animaduerte. Apostoli distinguuntur vt oues ab oniculis; & ipsi Apostoli sunt oniculæ: nonne Te deprehensum vides? nonne membra distinctionis concidere cernis? Quis iam Illum distinguentem feret, qui seipsum confundit? Siquis huius Paradoxi confutationem amplorem desideret. Pontificiorum multorum suffragia in memoriam reuocet, quibus paulò ante {*}demonstrauimus, Apostolos non à Petro, sed à Christo Ecclesiae Pastores constitutos fuisse. Petrum Te deseruit, ad Papam conuerteris; & Scripturae testimonio destitutus, Hieronymum in praesidium vocas.
units.tr: This assertion can be confirmed by comparing Matthew 10.16 and Luke 10.3, where Christ says I send you as lambs in the midst of wolves. In Matthew it is hōs probata [ὡς πρόβατα], sheep; in Luke it is arnas [ἄρνας], lambs; in both he addresses his disciples, that is, the ministers themselves. Here there is no room for your subtlety, unless you have once converted the apostles, that is, the ministers, into sheep (with respect to Peter), and by some new metamorphosis, or (as you say) by a mystery, wish to change them again, from sheep into lambs, that is, into the people, as if by the potent herbs of Medea. Among the flock the lamb will become the leader by the medicine. Moreover, please recognise your own words again: Lambs, or little sheep, are committed to Peter, and so are the sheep, who are the mothers of the lambs; who are the apostles and bishops. By your own authority the apostles are distinguished from the people as sheep from little sheep; yet in the same chapter you say, It is certain to us that the apostles are committed to Peter as little sheep. Note this: the apostles are distinguished as sheep from little sheep, and the apostles themselves are little sheep. Do you not see that you have been caught? Do you not see the members of your distinction collapsing? Who will now tolerate a man making a distinction who confounds himself? If anyone desires a fuller refutation of this paradox, let him call to mind the testimonies of many Papists, by which a little earlier we showed that the apostles were established as ministers of the Church not by Peter but by Christ. You desert Peter and turn to the Pope; and, deprived of the testimony of Scripture, you call Jerome to your aid.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, de Offic.

units.la: “ Et {°}S. Hieronymus, qui Sacerdos & Doctor insignis {•}in “ Christiano orbe habebatur, à S. Damaso Pontifice pabulum “ spirituale petens, dicebat; A pastore praesidium Ouis effla-“ gito. Et in Epistola sequenti, Flagito (inquit) vt paruum “ Magnus aspicias, & dimes Pastor morbidam non contemnas “ Ouem. --- Pag.27.28.
units.tr: "And S. Jerome, who was regarded as a priest and an outstanding teacher in the Christian world, seeking spiritual food from S. Damasus the Pope, said: From the shepherd let the sheep seek protection. And in the following letter: I beg (he says) that you, great one, look upon the little one, and that you, shepherd, do not despise the sickly sheep." --- Pag. 27, 28.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. Animadversion.

units.la: Hieronymum nihil causae Pontificiae prodesse.
units.tr: That Jerome does nothing to help the Papal cause.

units.la: HIeronymus reuera toto orbe Christiano celebris & insignis Doctor, idque merito suo, habitus est: attamen tanti tamque illustris Doctoris authoritatem Bellarminus, quoties ei lubitum est, tantilli faciet, vt non dubitet interdum dicere, {p}Falsa est haec sententia Hieronymi, quae refelletur in suo loco. Sed ad rem. Causam Petitionis Hieronymi ad Damasum Canus vester copiose retulit, his verbis. {q}Ab Arianis trium hypostaseon (inquit Hieron.) nouellum à me nomen exigitur: interrogamus quid per tres Hypostases intelligant? Tres subsistentes personas, aiunt: Respondemus, Nos ita credere; non sufficit sensus, nomen efflagitant, & quia nescio quid veneni in syllabis lateat; Haeretici indicamur. Sic recitantem verba Hieronymi Canum audisti; Commentantem ausculta. {r}Ex quibus verbis (inquit) intelligas Hieronymum non sibi, in recta & sana intelligentia, à crimine Haereseos timuisse, nouam vocem, vbi venenum sub melle latere suspicabatur, formidasse. Sic Canus. Cur autem venenum formidauerit, Ribera Iesuita explicat: {f}Hieronymus (inquit) quoniam videbatur concedere tres Hypostases in Deo, ne videretur tres concedere substantias; Tota, inquit, secularium literarum Schola nihil aliud per Hypostasin nouit, quam usiam; verùm communi usu Conciliorum & Patrum Hypostasis pro persona accipitur, & quidem valde proprie. Sic Ribera.
units.tr: Jerome is indeed a famous and outstanding teacher throughout the whole Christian world, and he has been held in that esteem on his own merits. Yet Bellarmine, whenever it pleases him, makes so little of the authority of so great and so illustrious a teacher that he does not hesitate at times to say: "This opinion of Jerome is false, and it will be refuted in its place." But to the matter. Your Canus has set out at length the reason for Jerome's request to Damasus, in these words: "(Jerome says) a new name for the three hypostases is demanded of me by the Arians. We ask what they mean by three hypostases. They say, three subsisting persons. We reply that we believe this too. Their sense is not enough; they demand the name, and because I know not what poison lies hidden in the syllables, we are judged heretics." So you have heard Canus reciting the words of Jerome; now listen to his commentary. "From these words (he says) you may understand that Jerome, in a right and sound understanding, did not fear the charge of heresy for himself, but feared the new word, in which he suspected poison under honey." So Canus. Why he feared the poison, the Jesuit Ribera explains: "Jerome (he says), since he seemed to concede three hypostases in God, lest he seem to concede three substances. The whole school of secular letters, he says, knows nothing else by hypostasis than essence; but by the common usage of the Councils and the Fathers, hypostasis is taken for person, and indeed very properly." So Ribera.

units.la: Consuluit igitur Damasum Hieronymus, non de sensu, sed de libero usu istius vocis [Hypostasis]; nec quærebat utrùm sine errore, sed utrùm sine scandalo illud tam nouellum vocabulum usurparet. Quid igitur? ergonè Damasus in orbe Christiano uniuersalem pastoratum, ac Primatum obtinuit? si sic argumentari liceat, Hieronymum vicissim Damaso Pastorem efficies ilico; quià Damasus exactissimo Hieronymi iudicio cùm in aliis, tùm in hac ipsà Causà plurimùm nitebatur. Primùm in aliis. Hieronymus (cuius {t} tu testimonium allegas,) Ante annos plurimos (inquit) cùm in chartis Ecclesiasticis iuuarem Damasum Rom. vrbis Episcopum, & orientis atque occidentis Synodicis consultationibus responderem. Deinde,de hac ipsa Causa (vestro Espencæo teste) Hieronymus Damasum consulit, ymò Damaso consulit, vocem Hypostasis non esse recipiendam, quia sub melle venenum latebat. Istæne, cedo, partes Tibi pecoris meri; annon Doctoris potiùs præcipientis videntur?
units.tr: Jerome therefore consulted Damasus, not about the meaning but about the free use of that word [hypostasis]; he did not ask whether he could use it without error, but whether he could use that very new term without scandal. Well then? Did Damasus obtain universal pastorship and primacy in the Christian world? If we may argue in this way, you will at once make Jerome in turn a pastor of Damasus; because Damasus, by Jerome's most exact judgment, leaned very heavily both on other matters and on this very cause. First, on other matters. Jerome (whose testimony you cite) says: "Many years ago, when I was helping Damasus, Bishop of the city of Rome, with ecclesiastical papers, and answering the synodal consultations of East and West." Next, about this very cause (your Espencaeus being witness), Jerome consults Damasus; indeed he consults Damasus that the word hypostasis is not to be received, because poison lay hidden under honey. Tell me, are these the parts of a mere sheep, or do they not rather appear to be those of a teacher giving instructions?

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Hieronymum Pontificiæ causæ obesse plurimum.
units.tr: II. Animadversion. That Jerome greatly hinders the Papal cause.

units.la: VBi sensit Hieronymus Romæ Diaconos Presbyteris anteferri, vehementer stomachatus; {x} Quid mihi profers (inquit) vnius vrbis consuetudinem? quid paucistatem, ex qua ortum est supercilium, in leges Ecclesiæ vendicas? Addit; Si authoritas quæratur, orbis maior est quàm vrbis. Quid hoc ad tempora nostra pertinet, quæris? Respondebunt Tibi Conc. Basileensis Theologi, qui in hoc Hieronymi testimonio, tanquàm in agro fertili, versati, quodammodò exultant. {y} Quid tum, obsecro, Hieronyme? (Aiunt) An magnus est Papa, quia Romanæ præest Ecclesiæ? magna eius authoritas, maior tamen est Vniuersalis Ecclesia, quæ non vrbem vnam duntaxat, sed totum complectitur[?] ditur Orbem. Hæc Ille. Tu autem in vno Pastore Damaso Ecclesiam vniuersam, tanquam Orbem in vrbe, compingi velles. Quod si Hieronymus antea Rom. Ecclesiæ Presbyter, nunc autem in palestina degens, pristinum Damasi Pastoratum non illibenter agnoverit; ex eo non innuit potestatem aliquam Iurisdictionis vniuersalem; sed in hoc Pastore D.Damaso fidem ac vigilantiam commendat: haud idem laturus iudicium de Pontifice alio, cuius aut deficeret fides, aut industria languesceret.
units.tr: When Jerome perceived that deacons at Rome were placed above presbyters, he was greatly vexed: "Why do you bring forward (he says) the custom of one city? Why do you claim as church law what arises from the pride of a few? He adds: If authority is to be sought, the world is greater than the city." What has this to do with our times, you ask? The Basel Council theologians will answer you; they rejoice, as it were, and in a way exult, as in a fertile field, over this testimony of Jerome. "What then, I beg you, Jerome? (they say) Is the Pope great because he presides over the Roman Church? His authority is great, but the universal Church is greater, which embraces not only one city but the whole world." So they. But you would have the whole Church compacted in one pastor, Damasus, as the world is in one city. But if Jerome, who was once a presbyter of the Roman Church and now lives in Palestine, gladly acknowledged the former pastorate of Damasus, he does not thereby imply any universal power of jurisdiction; rather, he commends faith and vigilance in this pastor, Damasus, and would not pass the same judgment on another Pope, whose faith might fail or whose diligence might flag.

units.la: Quippè de Hieronymo Aeneas Syluius, tunc quidem Papatus capax, mox Papa Pius II. {a}En, inquit, clarum est Hieronymi testimonium, [projiciatur foràs] id est, inquit, Deponitur; & loquitur de Prælato, qui Petri locum tenet, & sic de Rom. Pontifice, quem in præcipitando insipidum, ac fatuum in delinquendo ex gradu dignitatis deponendum affirmat; nec, vt aliqui delirant, propter solam haeresin. Hæc Aeneas. Quid iam inter Hieronymum & Bellarminum interest? Hieronymus,{b} parua ouis Damasi, docet; Papam deponendum esse ob alias causas, quàm propter haeresim: At, {c} Papam cogi non posse ab Ecclesia, defendit nutantis Cathedræ operosus sustentator Bellarminus. Cuium pecus? Hæc de Pastoris vestri, in Pastores, Authoritate: sequitur in Principes.
units.tr: Indeed, concerning Jerome, Aeneas Silvius, then capable of the Papacy and soon Pope Pius II, wrote: "Behold, the testimony of Jerome is clear: [let him be cast out]. That is, he says, let him be deposed; and he speaks of a prelate who holds the place of Peter, and so of the Roman Pontiff, whom he declares must be removed from the rank of dignity when he has become foolish in his stumbling and worthless in his offending; and not, as some rave, on account of heresy alone." So Aeneas. What difference now is there between Jerome and Bellarmine? Jerome, the little sheep of Damasus, teaches that the Pope must be deposed for other causes than heresy; but Bellarmine, the busy supporter of the tottering Chair, defends that the Pope cannot be compelled by the Church. Whose flock is this? So much for the authority of your Pastor over Pastors; it follows now as to Princes.

units.la: De Pastorali Pontificis potestate in Seculares; tàm Principes, quàm Populum in- seriorem.
units.tr: On the pastoral power of the Pope over secular rulers, both princes and the lower people.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: Quod si Pastores & Doctores à summo Pontifice Pastore pabulum aliquando petunt, non mirum esse debet, si Principes seculi, qui inter oues, vel potius inter arietes gregis Christi numerantur, ab eodem Principe Pastorum, Christique in terris Vicario doctrinam pabulum libenter accipiant, &c.— pag.28.
units.tr: But if pastors and teachers sometimes seek their food from the Supreme Pontiff, the shepherd, it should be no surprise if the rulers of the world, who are counted among the sheep, or rather among the rams, of Christ's flock, gladly receive doctrine as their food from the same Prince of Shepherds and Christ's Vicar on earth, etc. — p. 28.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Imò verò Hieronymus, quem Tu insignem Doctorem in toto Orbe habitum esse dixti inter Pastorem insipidum & sapientem; inter pascua vrbis, & latifundia orbis; & (vt alibi) inter pabulum nouum Traditionum humanarum, & vetus diuinarum Scripturarum distinguere nos docuit. Ad Principes quod attinet, quos Tu, hic Arietibus assimulas; valdè metuo (ita Tu es erga Principes afsectus) nè aliquid diri & sinistri ominis portendat. Scribe vero, vt Te videamus. {d}Papam habere potestatem (inquis alibi) Indirectè; — {e}Probatur Rationibus. — {f}Quin-ta Ratio est, cùm dictum est Petro [Pasce oues meas,] Ioh. 21. data est ei facultas omnis, qua Pastori necessaria est, ad gregem tuendum. At Pastori necessaria est triplex potestas; vna circa Lupos, secunda circa Arietes, tertia circa Oues. Vna circa Lupos, id est, Principes eos, qui ex Christianis fiunt Haeretici: Secunda circa Arietes, id est, Principes Catholicos, sed suriosos; & destruentes ouile. Tertia circa Oues, (in genere) tàm Principem, quàm Populum.
units.tr: Indeed, Jerome, whom you say was regarded as an outstanding teacher throughout the whole world, taught us to distinguish between the foolish shepherd and the wise one; between the pastures of the city and the broad estates of the world; and (as elsewhere) between the new food of human traditions and the old food of divine Scriptures. As for the princes, whom you here compare to rams, I greatly fear (given how you are disposed toward princes) that this portends something of dire and ominous omen. But write on, so that we may see you. You say elsewhere that the Pope has power indirectly; this is proved by reasons. The fifth reason is that when it was said to Peter [Feed my sheep,] John 21, he was given every faculty that a shepherd needs to guard the flock. But a shepherd needs a threefold power: one over wolves, a second over rams, a third over sheep. The first over wolves, that is, those princes who from Christians become heretics; the second over rams, that is, Catholic princes who are furious and who destroy the fold; the third over sheep (in general), both prince and people.

units.la: Primo loco, arcem quasi defensionis tuæ, distinctionem Ipsam adoriemur.
units.tr: First, let us attack the very foundation, as it were, of your defence: the distinction itself.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: First Animadversion.

units.la: Distinctionem Bellarmini, de Lupis, & Arietibus, im- propriam atq; incommodam esse.
units.tr: The distinction of Bellarmine, concerning wolves and rams, is improper and inconvenient.

units.la: DIstinguis Principes in Lupos, Arietes, & Oues, : Principes autem ouile destruentes inter petulcos Arietes; obsequentiores denique inter proprie dictas Oues recensés. Quasi vero solos Haereticos, Lupos; aut Ecclesiam turbantes, ac gregem laedentes Principes, & Magistratus Arietes dici oportuerit. Quae si vera essent, insigniter errarunt 1o. {f}Patres, nempè Hieronymus, Augustinus, Basilius, qui Apostolos & primi ordinis Ecclesiastici Praelatos inter Arietes numerâmerárunt. 2°. Toletus Ief. qui{g} Lupum Ioh.20.non solùm Hæreticos, aut Tyrannos, & nominis Christiani persecutores à Christo intelligi ait; sed etiam quoscunque fideles, qui eos à iustitiâ arcere conantur. 3°. Frater Baronius Cardinalis, qui Venetos (opinione vestrâ nihil minùs quàm Hæreticos) {h}Leonibus assimulauit. Imo etiam Pater ille vester Alexander III. qui Fredericum Imperatorem (nempè vnum ex tuis Arietibus) {i}Aspidem & basiliscum appellauit. Adeòne igitur Tu putas coecutiuisse Pontificem, nimirùm Pastorem tuum, vt Arietem à Basilisco non dignosceret? aut quenquam tuorum Collegarum ita delipere, vt, in animalibus decernendis, Tibi Ouì, potiùs, quàm Pastori tuo fidem habeat? Hactenùs distinctionem Tuam inualidam esse probauimus; nunc singula eius membra penitiùs introspiciamus.
units.tr: You distinguish princes into wolves, rams, and sheep; you count princes who destroy the fold among the wanton rams, and finally the more obedient among the strictly so-called sheep. As if only heretics were to be called wolves, or princes and magistrates who disturb the Church and injure the flock were to be called rams! If these things were true, the following would have gone badly wrong. First, the Fathers, namely Jerome, Augustine, Basil, who counted the Apostles and the prelates of the first ecclesiastical order among the rams. Second, Toletus the Jesuit, who says that by wolves in John 20 Christ means not only heretics, or tyrants, and persecutors of the Christian name, but also any faithful who try to keep them from justice. Third, Brother Baronius the Cardinal, who compared the Venetians (in your opinion anything but heretics) to lions. Indeed, even that father of yours, Alexander III, called the Emperor Frederick (one of your own rams) an asp and a basilisk. Do you then think that the Pontiff, your shepherd, was so blind that he could not tell a ram from a basilisk? Or that any of your colleagues is so foolish that, in deciding about animals, he would trust you the sheep rather than your shepherd? So far we have shown that your distinction is invalid; now let us look more closely into each of its parts.

units.la: De Triplici potestate Papæ in tria genera Principum.
units.tr: On the threefold power of the Pope over three kinds of princes.

units.la: I. in Principes Hæreticos, tanquam in Lupos
units.tr: I. Over heretical princes, as over wolves.

units.la: Bellarminus alibi.
units.tr: Bellarmine elsewhere:

units.la: {k}Triplex potestas Papæ necessaria est, vna circà Principes Hæreticos, ceu in Lupos, vt eos arceat OMNI RATIONE QVA POSSIT. Si ergò Princeps aliquis ex oue, vel Ariete fit Lupus, possit Pastor eum arcere: per Excommunicationem, ac simul subere populo, nè eum sequantur, & proindè priuare Eum dominio in Subditos.
units.tr: The threefold power of the Pope is needed: one over heretical princes, as over wolves, so that he may keep them away BY EVERY MEANS POSSIBLE. If therefore some prince becomes a wolf from a sheep or a ram, the shepherd may keep him away by excommunication, and at the same time bind the people not to follow him, and thus deprive him of dominion over his subjects.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Vtrùm perniciosior an insulsior sit hæc Ratio Bellarmini difficile esse dicere.
units.tr: First Animadversion. It is hard to say whether this reasoning of Bellarmine is more pernicious or more silly.

units.la: Pontifex igitur, Tesuafore[?], debet Principes omnes, opinione vestrâ Hæreticos, tanquam Lupos arcere OMNI (inquis) RATIONE QVA POSSVNT. Quibus verbis Principes Orthodoxos (quos Tu falso Hæreticos vocas) mones(si sapiant) vt diligenter sibi caueant à vestris pugionibus, sclopetis, catapultis, alijsque omnibus machinis, quibus Eos plusquam hostili odio prosequimini: Nam cum OMNEM RATIONEM adijcis, nemo non videt quid velis; vel potius quid nolis dicere. Sed ita nimirum hæsitanter & obscurè Eos loqui maximè decuit, qui confictis calumnijs, fucatis interpretamentis, crassis sophismatis, adulationibus portentosis OMNIQ; RATIONE Papalem tyrannidem stabilire moliuntur. Quid ni verò ista OMNI RATIONE? cùm præsertim hæc ipsa Tyrannis iam summa, & ferè sola Ratio sit Protestantes oppugnandi?
units.tr: So the Pope, your Tesuafore[?], must keep away all princes, which in your opinion are heretics, as wolves, BY EVERY MEANS (you say) POSSIBLE. By these words you warn the Orthodox princes (whom you falsely call heretics), if they are wise, to take careful heed of your daggers, muskets, catapults, and all the other machines with which you pursue them with more than hostile hatred. For when you add BY EVERY MEANS, no one fails to see what you wish, or rather what you do not wish, to say. But it was especially fitting that those who by invented calumnies, painted interpretations, gross sophisms, and monstrous flatteries strive to establish papal tyranny by every means should speak so hesitantly and obscurely. Why not indeed by every means, since this very tyranny, already supreme and almost the only method, is for opposing the Protestants?

units.la: Quod enim ad Hærefin attinet. Si, vt olim Pontifices vestri quemuis vel {1}affirmantem Christum nihil priuatum habuisse; vel asserentem esse {m}Antipodes; vel etiam {n}humaniorís literaturæ studiosum Hæreticum esse censuerint: Ita nunc hodiernus Pastor vester Paulus V.ᵉᵘˢ[?] decreuerit, omnes eos esse Hæreticos, qui aut neglecta imagine oculos ad cœlum orantes attollunt; aut Eucharistiam suis fumant manibus; aut Petrum Pa[illegible, ~2 letters] meritis præferunt; & (quod de Leone fertur) Aures cornua esse iudicauerit; num propterea de Illis actum erit? Num iccirco OMNI RATIONE perimendi? Reuera iuxta tecum sensit Pater vester Eugenius, qui nimirùm istiusmodi Dracones non pascendos, sed omnibus potius viribus expugnandos esse monuit: Cui multò sanctius vir verè Sanctus;{o} Propter hoc (inquit) eos aggredere, sed verbo, non ferro; aut, vt alibi elegantius; {p}Haretici (inquit) capiuntur non armis, sed argumentis, conuince, vt conuertas. Enimuero Te miserè coecutire, Bellarmine, quis non videt, quòd Protestantes Principes tanquam Lupos æstimes, & non Oues potius, saltem errantes; vel (vt verius dicam) nè errantes quidem: quùm præsertim in eorum numero sint, qui (de quibus vester Agrippa) {q}Scripturæ testimonijs se tueri conantur; quos Inquisitores, Sacram Scripturam veluti mortuam literam, & non nisi veritatis umbram ater-
units.tr: As for heresy. If, as your Pontiffs of old judged that anyone who maintained that Christ had nothing of his own, or who asserted that there were Antipodes, or even a man devoted to the study of humane literature, was a heretic, so now your present shepherd Paul V has decreed that all those are heretics who lift their eyes to heaven while praying with the image neglected, or who handle the Eucharist with smoking hands, or who prefer Peter to Paul on the basis of merits, and who (as is said of Leo) judged ears to be horns, would it therefore be all over for them? Would they for that reason be destroyed by every means? Indeed, your father Eugenius thought as you do, when he warned that such dragons are not to be fed but attacked with all one's strength. Far more holy was the advice of a truly holy man: Attack them for this reason, he says, but with the word, not the sword; or, as he puts it more elegantly elsewhere: Heretics are taken not by arms but by arguments; convict them so that you may convert them. Truly, Bellarmine, you are miserably blind: who does not see that you regard the Protestant princes as wolves, and not rather as sheep, at least straying ones, or (to speak more truly) not even straying? This is especially so since they are among those who (as your Agrippa says of them) try to defend themselves by the testimonies of Scripture; whom the Inquisitors, treating Holy Scripture as a dead letter, and nothing but the shadow of truth, leaving it behind their backs, persecute not with arguments or Scriptures but with fire and faggots. Even though Christ the Lord wished the mark of his sheep to be stamped not so much on the tongue or the skin, much less on the horns, but on the ear, saying my sheep hear my voice, lest anyone allow himself to be deceived in judging Christ's sheep either by the flattery of men, or by the outward paint of holiness, or by the headlong zeal of some who are not according to knowledge. Since, then, your Pontiff can be satisfied with the blood of no sheep but such as these, who may not easily understand what sort of animal he is? Certainly the wolf has devoured the sheep, and the shepherd has not devoured the wolf.

units.la: {m} Ioh. Auentinus l.3. Annal. refert quendam German.ũ Pastorem(Virgilio vocatum) à Zacharia Pont.ro nomine accusatum.
units.tr: {m} Johann Aventinus, in Annals book 3, reports that a certain German minister, called Virgilius, was accused by Pope Zachary.

units.la: {n} Paulus II. apud Plat.
units.tr: {n} Paul II, cited in Platina.

units.la: {o} Bern. de consid. ad Eugen. l.4. c.3.
units.tr: {o} Bernard, On Consideration, to Eugenius, book 4, ch. 3.

units.la: {p} Idem. in Cant. s.1. serm.16.
units.tr: {p} Idem. in Cant. s.1. serm.16.

units.la: {q} Agrippa de vanit. scient.[?] c.96. initio, & seq. à tergo relinquentes, non argumentis aut scripturis, sed igne & fasciculis perseq̃untur. Etiamsi Christus Dominus Ouis suæ notam non tam in lingua aut pelle, nedum cornibus, quàm in aure imprimi voluerit, Oues meæ (inquiens) vocem meam audiunt: nè forte in dijudicandis Ouibus Christi vel adulatione hominum, vel externo sanctitatis fuco, vel præcipiti quorundam zelo (qui non est secundum scientiam) decipi se quisquam patiatur. Quùm igitur non nisi huiusmodi Ouium sanguine satiari Pontifex vester possit; quale animal ille sit, quis non facilè intelligat? Certè quidem Ouem Lupus, non Lupum Pastor comesit.
units.tr: {q} Agrippa, De vanitate scientiarum, c.96, at the beginning and following: leaving them behind their backs, they pursue them not with arguments or Scriptures, but with fire and faggots. Although Christ the Lord wished the mark of his sheep to be stamped not so much on the tongue or the skin, still less on the horns, but on the ear, saying, "My sheep hear my voice", so that no one may allow himself to be deceived in judging Christ's sheep, whether by the flattery of men, by the outward paint of holiness, or by the headlong zeal of some who is not according to knowledge. Since, therefore, your Pontiff can be satisfied only with the blood of such sheep, who would not easily understand what kind of animal he is? Certainly it is the wolf that devours the sheep, not the shepherd that devours the wolf.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Indirectam Pontificis potestatem Temporalem, è Regio Christi officio elici nullo artificio posse.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. That the indirect temporal power of the Pope cannot be drawn from Christ's kingly office by any artifice.

units.la: AC non modò non necessarium esse, vt in Principes Coactiuam illam potestatem temporalem exerceat Pastor quispiam spiritualis; verum-etiam necessarium esse, vt non exerceat, Rationibus addicam necessarijs. Prima. Supremus Pastor noster Christus Iesus, (qui, propter singularem excellentiam, dicitur Pastor ille, propter summam bonitatem, Ille bonus; propter immensam & infinitam potestatem Pastor & Episcopus animarum) profeßus est, teste Abulensi, Se nolle exercere opus Iurisdictionis coactiuæ. Nec mirum; nam Is, qui dicitur Ille Pastor, vocatur etiam Agnus ille, ad patiendum, non ad vim faciendam natus. Propterea hic Pastor (vt non insciteè Lutherus) Asino insidebat, non autem equo, qui est animal bellicosum. Sed cùm Bellarminus ex illis verbis Christi, [Pasce oues meas] Colligi ait authoritatem imperandi Regio more; Papamque, vt Pastorem Ecclesiæ, post Petrum accepisse potestatem coactiuam temporalem, saltem Indirectè, ad Reges deponendos; hic locus à nobis effiagitat, vt probemus hanc Coactiuam potestatem temporalem nè quidem Christo, vt eit summus Pastor, competere. Quod quamuis multa Argumenta à Theologis Pontificijs porrecta & quasi in manus nostras tradita abundè præstét, malui tamen, breuitatis causâ, vno illo esse contentus, quo Bellarminus ex ipsius dictatis facillimè refellitur.
units.tr: Not only is it unnecessary for some spiritual Pastor to exercise that coercive temporal power over Princes; it is actually necessary that he not exercise it. I will support this with necessary arguments. First, our supreme Pastor, Christ Jesus (who, on account of his singular excellence, is called that Shepherd, on account of his supreme goodness, the Good One, and on account of his immense and infinite power, the Shepherd and Bishop of souls), declared, according to Abulensis, that He was unwilling to exercise the work of coercive jurisdiction. This is no surprise, for He who is called that Shepherd is also called that Lamb, born to suffer, not to use force. Therefore this Shepherd (as Luther rightly observed) sat upon an ass, not upon a horse, which is a warlike animal. But when Bellarmine says that from those words of Christ, [Feed my sheep], he gathers an authority to command in the royal manner, and that the Pope, as Pastor of the Church, after Peter received coercive temporal power, at least indirectly, for deposing Kings, this passage requires of us that we prove this coercive temporal power does not belong even to Christ as the supreme Pastor. Although many arguments put forward by the Papist theologians, and handed over, as it were, into our hands, amply establish this, I preferred, for the sake of brevity, to rest content with the one by which Bellarmine is most easily refuted from his own dictates.

units.la: Is in Recognitionibus, vbi exprimit suas [illegible, ~12 letters] , de Christi Regno copiosè disserit, & distinguens docet Quatuor esse Regna, quorum Tria Christo conueniunt. {x}Primum est (spirituale, quod per passionem in cruce sibi peperit, de Diabolo triumphans, quo superato, capit Christus regnare in cordibus fidelium per fidem, & obedientiam Dei. Alterum regnum est diuinum vniuersale, quod Christo conuenit ratione Vnionis hypostaticæ cum diuinâ naturâ. Tertium est regnum gloriæ, quod in perfecta corporis & animæ beatitudine & felicitate consistit. Quartum autem, quod proprie temporale dici debet, qualia sunt regna Principum terrenorum, nos quidem in Scripturis & in Patribus non inuenimus Christo conuenire. Hactenùs Bellarminus. His præmissis, Quæsitu quidem procliue est, ecquo Trium Regnorum potestas illa Pontificis Coactiua Temporalis nitatur? an Spirituale? Hoc regnum (inquis) Christo Messiæ proprium est. An igitur, Diuino vniuersali? imò hoc, inquis, Christo cum Patre commune est, nec potest communicari cum vlla creatura. An verò Tertiò, quod in perfecta beatitudine anima & corporis consistit? Et Hoc regnum (inquis) adeptus est Christus in resurrectione; de quo Luc.23. Memento mei cum veneris in Regnum: quod tum datum est Christo homini, vt non amplius subiectus esset vlli Creaturæ, neque famè, neque siti, neque morti. Hoc igitur nulli homini competit, dum viuit in corpore mortis huius. Restat Quartum, quod proprie temporale, quale est Principum terrenorum. Hoc, inquis, non inuenimus Christo tributum; & Papa non habet vllam temporalem Iurisdictionem directè.
units.tr: In his Recognitions, where he sets out his [illegible] and discourses at length on Christ's Kingdom, he distinguishes and teaches that there are four kingdoms, three of which belong to Christ. The first is the spiritual kingdom, which He won for himself by his passion on the cross, triumphing over the Devil; once that is overcome, Christ begins to reign in the hearts of the faithful through faith and obedience to God. The second is the divine universal kingdom, which belongs to Christ by reason of the hypostatic union with the divine nature. The third is the kingdom of glory, which consists in the perfect blessedness and happiness of body and soul. The fourth, which ought properly to be called temporal, such as the kingdoms of earthly princes, we indeed do not find in the Scriptures or the Fathers to belong to Christ. So far Bellarmine. With these premises laid down, the question naturally arises: on which of the three kingdoms does that coercive temporal power of the Pope rest? On the spiritual? This kingdom (you say) is proper to Christ the Messiah. On the divine universal? Indeed, you say, this is common to Christ with the Father, and cannot be communicated to any creature. Or thirdly, on that which consists in the perfect blessedness of soul and body? This kingdom (you say) Christ obtained in the resurrection, concerning which Luke 23: Remember me when you come into your kingdom. That was then given to Christ as man, so that he would no longer be subject to any creature, neither to hunger, nor thirst, nor death. Therefore this belongs to no man while he lives in this body of death. There remains the fourth, which is properly temporal, such as that of earthly princes. This, you say, we do not find attributed to Christ; and the Pope does not have any temporal jurisdiction directly.

units.la: Nullam igitur adhuc inuenimus in regio Christi ossicio Pontificij Regni similitudinem; sed nè vmbram quidem. Quod verò alibi oggeris, Pontifici tribui potestatem, quam habet Christus vt erat homo mortalis tantum; nec tamen omnem, quia Christus ut Deus & homo mortalis habuit potestatem excellentiæ instituendi Sacramenta & miracula faciendi propriâ authoritate &c. sed solam illam potestatem Pontifici communicavit, quæ puro homini communicari poterat: Frustrà es, nec enim adhuc causam ipsam attingis. Nam quæstio est, utrum illa Pontificis potestas Regÿ, an Sacerdotalis muneris sit? Si Sacerdotalis tantùm, tùm nihil ad Christi regnum: sin prorsus Regÿ, tum nihil ad Sacerdotem. Et profectò Sacerdotale Christi officiū totum spirituale fuit, temporale verò nullo modo, nè indirectè quidem; cuius Pastoratus partem potissimâ exercuit, non quidem Actiuâ,in Deponendis Principibus; sed potius Passiuâ illâ, quâ ipse {a}Pastor bonus vitam dedit pro ovibus suis. Denique Regnum & potestas Christi, quod{b} Extendit se ad temporalia, quatenus ad spiritualia ordinantur, ut omnes Theologi (inquis) fatentur, non erat spirituale, quatenus spirituale, à divino distinguitur (ut Tu, mirus sed &, ut{c} vestri confitentur, Infelix distinctionum Architectus{c} commentus es) sed planè diuinum, Christi hominis, ratione Hypostaticæ Unionis: quod est secundum membrum diuisionis tuæ, quo dominia temporalia non tolluntur, sed reguntur, & diriguntur ipsius numine & nutu, qui{ d} Rex Regum, & Dominus Dominantium tam in corda, quàm in corpora hominum; cuius in Pauli conuersione exemplum luculentum habemus, in quo Theologos omnes, quibus veritas est cordi, adstipulatores me habere nullus dubito. Certè vester Tolosfanus affirmat{x} Christum, eiiciendo vendentes & ementes è templo, Regis potestatem gessisse; Sacerdotis autem, sese in hostiam offerendo. rendo. III. ANIMADVERSIO. Potestatem hanc Coactiuam, ut per se iniustam, itâ per multas Annorum centurias ignotam penitus fuisse. PRimo in loco tempora Apostolorum recole, & tunc (fatente vestro Abulensi) constabit{4} Apostolos neque {a} Ioh.10.11. {b} Bellar.Recog. quæ supra. {d} Apoc.19.16. {x} Tolosfan. de Re-pub. lib.7. cap.1. pag.381. {4} Abulens.Tom.11. in Matth.20. pag.304. criminaliter, neque ciuiliter habuisse exercitium Iurisdictionis coërcitionum.Hic Author preterea occurrit ijs obiectionibus, {b} quæ afferri solent in contrarium. II. Apostolicorum virorum ætatem revolue, de quibus S. Paulus vaticinatus est; {c}Scio, inquit, quod post discessum meum ingredientur LVPI RAPACES, non parcentes GREGI.
units.tr: Therefore we have so far found in Christ's kingly office no likeness of the Papist kingdom, not even a shadow of one. As for what you throw in elsewhere, that the Pope has been granted the power that Christ had as mortal man only, yet not all of it, because Christ as God and mortal man had the power of excellence to institute sacraments and to work miracles by his own authority, etc., but only that power was communicated to the Pope which could be communicated to a mere man: you labour in vain, for you do not yet touch the matter itself. The question is whether that papal power belongs to the kingly office or to the priestly one. If only to the priestly, then it has nothing to do with Christ's kingdom; but if wholly to the kingly, then it has nothing to do with the Priest. And indeed Christ's priestly office was wholly spiritual; it was in no way temporal, not even indirectly. Of this pastoral office he exercised chiefly that part which is passive, not active in deposing princes: that by which the good Shepherd gave his life for his sheep. Finally, the kingdom and power of Christ, which extends itself to temporal things insofar as they are ordered to spiritual ones, as all theologians (you say) confess, was not spiritual insofar as it is distinguished from the divine (as you, a marvellous but also, as your own people admit, unhappy architect of distinctions, have devised), but plainly divine, belonging to Christ the man by reason of the hypostatic union. This is the second member of your division, by which temporal dominions are not abolished but are ruled and directed by his divine power and will, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, over hearts as well as bodies of men. We have a notable example of this in the conversion of Paul, and I do not doubt that all theologians, to whom truth is dear, will side with me. Certainly your Tolosanus affirms that Christ, in driving the buyers and sellers from the temple, exercised the power of a King; but in offering himself as a sacrifice, that of a Priest. III. ANIMADVERSION. That this coercive power, as unjust in itself, was thus wholly unknown through many centuries of years. First, let us recall the times of the Apostles, and then (as your own Abulensis admits) it will be established that the Apostles had neither criminal nor civil exercise of coercive jurisdiction. Here the author also meets the objections that are usually brought to the contrary. Second, let us revolve the age of the apostolic men, concerning whom St. Paul prophesied: I know that after my departure grievous wolves will enter in, not sparing the flock.

units.la: Nunc igitur, si unquam, istius Ecclesiæ Pastorem Timotheum coactitam potestatem meditari oportuit; vires temporales comparare, moxque exercere, saltem Indirectè, nempe ad abarcendos Lupos, qui actus ordinem habes ad Spiritualia. Et reuerà Apostolus Timotheum armis instructum, & potestate munitum consultò voluit; Temporalia verò lædendo quempiam? imò omninò Spirituali, quod exercetur ἀ τὶ ἐχρῆν[?]; sic enim ibidem Apostolus,{d} Νῆφε ἐν πᾶσι, κακοπάθησον[?] — In omnibus iniuriam perfer.
units.tr: Now, then, if ever, Timothy, the pastor of that Church, ought to have contemplated coercive power, to acquire temporal forces and at once exercise them, at least indirectly, namely to drive off the wolves, since that act has relation to spiritual matters. And indeed the Apostle deliberately wished Timothy not to be equipped with arms and fortified with power. Was he to injure anyone in temporal matters? Rather, everything was to be done entirely by spiritual means, which must be exercised [...]. For thus the same Apostle says: Be sober in all things, endure hardship [Νῆφε ἐν πᾶσι, κακοπάθησον]. That is: endure injury in all things.

units.la: Sed quid Ego argumentis contendo? Res in confesso est. nam Primo de Christo Bellarminus;{e} Potestas Regia non erat Christo necessaria. De Apostolis, Apostolicisque Pastoribus Sanderus;{f} Petrus (inquit) in Neronem, Domitianum, & Tyrannos Gentium nullam potestatem accepit. Duplex enim fortitudinis potestas, altera in faciendo res arduas animosè, altera in patiendo res aduersas constanter: cùmque illa virtus, quæ in patiendo consistit, sit præstantior; --- hanc patiendi potestatem sibi, & suis Christus elegit, vt mundum in admirationem potentiæ suæ converteret. --- iccirco Apostoli, & primi Apostolorum Successores, hoc mysterium non ignorantes, ab armis pro fide sumendis abstinuerunt. Quid Confessione hac ad causam accommodatius? quid difertius dici potuit? An propterea iam è Syrtibus emersimus? an Principes Christiani, quos Romana Ecclesia pro Lupis habet, in portu navigant? Nihil Illis deinceps de Pontificis coactiua potestate timendum? Imò Regibus infidelibus hac Ratione Pax alma oblata est; quam tamen, nempe fax ipsa Rebellionis in Hibernia, Sanderus Christianis Principibus inuidet: Discriminis causa, vnicum allegat Pactum illud Baptismi, quo (vt ait) omnes Christiani obligantur Christo, adeóque Vicario eius Rom. Pon-tifici, ita vt possint ab Eo deponi. Quod figmentum, Reipub Christianæ ita perniciosum, post mille quingentos annos (sicut Ille fraterculus ad exitium humanum natus, Bombarda inuentor) Nicholaus Sanderus (gentis no-stræ opprobrium) primus excogitauit; quóque post Bellorum instigator Bellarminus statim arripuit, & Alumnorum Societatis suæ animis insculpit atque instillauit. Sed hoc Telum {*}suprà è manibus Aduersariorum extorsimus. Impræsentiarum perpende, Lector, quantum hinc absurdi consequetur; sic enim Sanderus disputat, ac si Pastorum omnium Princeps Christus Dominus maiorem curam haberet posteræ sub Christianis Tyrannis, quàm primatiuæ Ecclesiæ sub infidelibus: ita vt (quasi Lupus albus nè an ater sit Pastorum quid referat) Principes infideles Gregem destruentes tolerandi sint, fideles autem, qui esse desiuerunt, OMNI RATIONE è medio tollendi. ꞁredite posteri; imò posteritas veniens negabit.
units.tr: But why do I labour with arguments? The matter is conceded. For first, of Christ, Bellarmine says: Royal power was not necessary to Christ. Of the Apostles and the apostolic pastors, Sanders says: Peter (he says) received no power against Nero, Domitian, and the tyrants of the Gentiles. For there are two kinds of power of fortitude: one, in doing difficult things boldly; the other, in suffering adversities constantly; and since that virtue which consists in suffering is the more excellent... Christ chose this power of suffering for himself and his own, so that he might turn the world to astonishment at his power... Therefore the Apostles and the first successors of the Apostles, not ignorant of this mystery, abstained from taking up arms for the faith. What could be more suited to our cause than this confession? What could have been said more plainly? Have we therefore now emerged from the Syrtes? Are the Christian princes, whom the Roman Church holds to be wolves, sailing into harbour? Are they to have nothing further to fear from the Pope's coercive power? Indeed, this peaceful offer is made to unbelieving kings on this ground; yet Sanders, the very spark of rebellion in Ireland, grudges it to Christian princes. As the ground of the difference, he alleges only that covenant of baptism, by which, as he says, all Christians are bound to Christ, and therefore to his Vicar, the Roman Pontiff, so that they can be deposed by him. This fiction, so pernicious to the Christian commonwealth, was first devised after fifteen hundred years by Nicholas Sanders (the shame of our nation), a man born to the destruction of mankind like that little brother who invented the bombard; and Bellarmine, the instigator of wars, immediately seized upon it and impressed and instilled it into the minds of the pupils of his Society. But we have already wrested this weapon from the hands of our adversaries above. For the present, reader, weigh how much absurdity follows from this; for Sanders argues as if Christ, the Prince of all shepherds, had greater care for the posterity under Christian tyrants than for the primitive Church under unbelievers: so that (as if it mattered little whether a white or black wolf were among the shepherds) unbelieving princes destroying the flock are to be tolerated, but faithful ones, who have ceased to be such, are to be removed from the midst by every means. Believe it, posterity; nay, coming posterity will deny it.

units.la: Apostolicis Pastoribus qui successerunt, quamuis tempore quidem longè illis, at fide & constantia tamen nihilo posteriores fuerunt. De quibus Tolosanus vester.{h} A Christo passo (inquit) per interuallum propè trecentorum Annorum, etsi innumera crudelisque tormenta Christiani passi fuerint, & clades atrocissimas; semel viginti millibus necatis; tamen nusquam omninò legitur eos aduersus leges, Magistratum, Imperatorem, securitatémque eius vel tantillum molitos fuisse, vel rebellasse. Quin hoc ius fere argumento se suamá religionem omnibus anteferri debere, colendam, & amplectendam, quòd nullâ dominandi cupiditate, nullo studio honorum partium ductâ, in eâ tàm pertinaciter atque obnixè perduraverent; & unico amore Dei, & Diuini cultus Christianos se ab eo dicerent appellari, cuius sit hoc pijssimum dogma, vt Magistratibus pareant. Hoc ille. Quod antiquitatis praeclarum sane testimonium egregio omninò{i} exemplo illustrat; pergit enim.{k} Cùm (inquit) Nicomedie proponeretur edictum Diocletiani & Maximiani Imperatorum crudele adversus Christianos, nimirum, quo templa solo aequarentur, divina Scriptura comburerentur, ut servi, & alii Christianismum abiurarent, & pleraque huiusmodi alia gravia statuerentur: quidam, illeque primus Christianorum extitit, qui tantae severitatis indignatione motus, ausus est, cum etiam uterq; Imperator Nicomedie moraretur, edictum manu capere, discerpere, conscindere in minutissimas partes: atq; cum in eum extremo supplicio esset animadversum, (Averte Bellarmine) reliqui etiam Christiani iure eum casum esse pronunciant.
units.tr: They were followed by apostolic ministers who, though far later in time, were in faith and steadfastness no inferior to those first ones. Your Tolosanus writes of them: From the passion of Christ, through nearly three hundred years, although the Christians suffered countless and cruel torments and most atrocious slaughters, once twenty thousand being put to death, yet nowhere is it read that they ever plotted or rebelled, even in the slightest degree, against the laws, the magistrate, the emperor or his safety. Indeed, from this very fact they argued that their religion ought to be preferred to all others and embraced, because they persevered so stubbornly and resolutely in it, without any lust for power and without any desire for office, and because they called themselves Christians out of the sole love of God, and this most pious doctrine belongs to the one who bids them obey the magistrates. So he. He illustrates this splendid testimony of antiquity with an excellent example; for he goes on: When the edict of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian against the Christians was published at Nicomedia, a cruel edict ordering that the churches be levelled with the ground, the divine Scriptures be burned, that slaves and others be made to renounce Christianity, and several other grave measures of this kind, one man, the first of the Christians, was moved by indignation at such severity. Though both emperors were staying at Nicomedia, he dared to take the edict in his hand, tear it, and rip it into the smallest pieces. When he was executed with the utmost punishment (take note, Bellarmine), the other Christians too declared that he had rightly suffered this fate.

units.la: Decurso dein longo multorum sequentium seculorum spacio Principum eorum, qui ex Paeto[?] baptismatis sese Christo devouerunt, usque ad Gregorium VII. Pontificem, circiter Ann. Domini MLXXXIII. sinfert[?] idem Authorem testimonium Ottonis Frisingensis, {k}(Cuius cum laude meminit Aeneas Syluius, qui postea Pius II. Pontifex, in oratione Francofurdia habita.) Is in suis Chronicis; {l}Lego (inquit) & relego Regum & Imperatorum gesta, & nusquam invenio quemquam Eorum ante hunc (scil. Henricum IV. Imperatorem) à Pontifice excommunicatum, vel Regno privatum. Qui memoriâ rectè tenent, quæ iam in Confesso habemus, (Christum nimirum Summum Pastorem animorum (nam Pilatum & Herodem, Lupos taeterrimos, vel levissimo oris sui sibilo subita morte prosternere potuisset) potius tamen Agni lenitatem & innocentiam suscepisse, humiliando se, & ferendo iniurias usque ad mortem: Deinde Apostolos in Pastorata ipso primarios Christi Vicarios, quibus data esset, si necesse foret montes movendi potestas Neroni tamen, aliisque immanissimis Lupis, tanquam Oves iugula sua dedisse potius quàm hostili aliquâ molitione pacem & securitatem illorum interturbare voluisse: Atque etiam porrò Pastores subsequentis aetatis per Annos à Christo trecentos, glisccente[?] tùm rapacissimorum Luporum rabie, nullâ Pastoratus vi constituâ usos, tanquam Oves Christi tantùm vel fugiendo declinâsse, vel vicisse patiendo. Postremò Pastores omnes alios, quamuis à Iuliano, Valente, multisque alijs (qui tamen Christianitatis pacto quandóque constricti tenebantur) Apostatis & Haereticis Imperatoribus Depositiones saepè perpessos, nihilominus Principes deposuisse, à Legente, & relegente Regum & Imperatorum res gestas nusquam esse inuentos; Quis non potius arbitretur Rom. Pastores (quod Pastoribus accidere posse {m}Gregorius docet) in Lupos degenerasse, quam illam potestatem Coercitiuam temporalem, quam nunc nequiter exercent, iure illis competere. Hactenus de Lupis.
units.tr: Then, after a long passage of many following centuries, from those princes who had dedicated themselves to Christ by the pact of baptism down to Pope Gregory VII, about the year of the Lord 1083, the same author cites the testimony of Otto of Freising (whom Aeneas Silvius, afterwards Pope Pius II, mentions with praise in his oration delivered at Frankfurt). Otto says in his Chronicles: I read and re-read the deeds of kings and emperors, and nowhere do I find that anyone before this man (namely Henry IV, emperor) was excommunicated by a pope or deprived of his kingdom. Those who keep in memory what we already have as admitted, namely that Christ, the supreme Shepherd of souls (for he could have struck down Pilate and Herod, most foul wolves, with a sudden death by the slightest hiss of his mouth), nevertheless took on the gentleness and innocence of a lamb, humbling himself and enduring injuries even to death; and then that the apostles, the chief in the ministry itself and Christ's vicars, to whom was given the power, if need be, to move mountains, yet gave their throats like sheep to Nero and to the other most savage wolves, rather than wishing to disturb their peace and security by any hostile enterprise; and moreover that the ministers of the following age, through the three hundred years after Christ, while the rage of the most rapacious wolves was growing, used no force of ministry at all, but as sheep of Christ merely avoided them by fleeing or conquered them by suffering. Finally, all the other ministers, though they were often subjected to deposition by Julian, Valens and many others (apostate and heretical emperors, who nevertheless were bound by the pact of Christianity at some point), did not on that account depose princes, and are not found in the deeds of kings and emperors as read and re-read: who would not rather suppose that the Roman ministers (which Gregory teaches can happen to ministers) have degenerated into wolves, than that the coercive temporal power, which they now wickedly exercise, belongs to them by right? So much concerning the wolves.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Ex vera & Quiu[?] nota primaria ostendi, Papam non Pastoris, sed potius Tyranni partes agere.
units.tr: From a true and primary mark it is shown that the Pope plays the part not of a shepherd but rather of a tyrant.

units.la: Indirectam illam Pontificis Potestate Temporalem fraude, vi, armis, aperta molitione, vel cuniculis, vel quacunque ratione Protestantes Principes, eorumque fautores Deponendi, & ut Lupos profligandi; ita saepè serióque inculcas, ac si totam Pontificii Pastoratus praesidium in eâ solâ constitutum esset. nunquid metior? Pastorem vestrum Paulum Pont. Iudice appello, qui A.° MDLIX[?] senio effoetus, "Cardinales in cubiculū accersiuit, — Postremū eos hortatus est, ut Sanctissimū (sic ille vocabat) Inquisitionis officiū, quo vno S.S. authoritatem niti affirmabat, comendatum haberent. Sic Papa. Inquisitorum autem ingeniū vester {o}Agrippa scitè admodum descripsit: Quorû (inquit) Iurisdictio, cum tota in Theologicis traditionibus & sacris paginis fundata esse deberet, ipsi tamen ex iure Canonico, & Pontificis decretis crudelissime eam exercent's, ipsam sacram Scripturam, veluti mortuam literam, & nonnisi veritatis umbrâ à tergo relinquentes, quin & Hereticorum scutum (ut aiunt) & propugnaculum procul reiciunt; — sed unam Rom. Ecclesiam, quae (ut dicunt) errare non potest, cuius caput Papa est, eiusque Curiae stylum caput fidei praefigunt. — Quodsi Inquisitus Scripturae testimoniis, aliisque rationibus se tueri conetur, interrumpentes strepitu iratis buccis dicunt, non esse illi negotiū cum Scholaribus ad Cathedram, sed cum Iudicibus ad tribunal: simpliciter igitur respondendum, si velit stare decreto Rom.Ecclesiae, sin minus fasciculos & ignes ostendunt, inquientes, non cum Argumentis aut Scripturis, sed fasciculis & igne decertandum. Expedite sane; in hunc enim modum cum Germanis egere: {p}Quibus diu se pressos cum quererentibus, per eos, qui maiorum suorum simplicitate abusi essent, vicissim gladios, fasciculos minabantur, qui potius docere & pugnare gladio spiritus. Vultis Bellonae filium germanum? Audite Stapletonum {q}Theologum (ut vobis videtur) atate sua optimum. {r}Eo sane loco (inquit) haeretes nunc sunt, ut non tam arte, & industria, quam Alexandri gladio dissoluende, quasi clava Herculis feriende sint.
units.tr: You so often and so earnestly press that indirect temporal power of the Pontiff, by which Protestant princes and their supporters are to be deposed, by fraud, force, arms, open enterprise, mines, or any means whatever, and are to be put down like wolves, as if the whole protection of the Papist ministry were established in that alone. Am I measuring wrongly? I call upon your shepherd Paul IV as judge, who, worn out with age in the year 1559, summoned the cardinals to his bedchamber. Finally he exhorted them to commend to their care the most holy (so he called it) office of the Inquisition, on which alone, he affirmed, the authority of the Holy See rests. So the Pope. Your Agrippa has aptly described the character of the inquisitors: Although their jurisdiction ought to be founded wholly on theological traditions and the sacred pages, they nevertheless exercise it most cruelly from canon law and the decrees of the Pontiff, casting aside Scripture itself as a dead letter, leaving only a shadow of the truth behind them, and even rejecting, as they say, the shield and bulwark of the heretics; and they put forward the one Roman Church, which (as they say) cannot err, whose head is the Pope, and the style of its Curia as the head of faith. And if the accused tries to defend himself by the testimonies of Scripture and other arguments, they interrupt with noise and angry mouths, saying that he has no business with the scholars at the chair but with the judges at the tribunal; therefore one must simply answer, if one wishes to stand by the decree of the Roman Church; but if not, they show bundles of faggots and fire, saying that the contest is to be fought not with arguments or Scriptures but with faggots and fire. Certainly they dealt in this way with the Germans; when these complained that they had long been oppressed, the men who had abused the simplicity of their ancestors threatened in turn swords and faggots, which should rather teach and fight with the sword of the Spirit. Do you want the true son of Bellona? Hear Stapleton, the theologian (as it seems to you) the best of his age: In that situation, he says, heretics are now to be dissolved not so much by skill and diligence as by the sword of Alexander, and struck as with the club of Hercules.

units.la: Ex his Te miserè coecutire, Bellarmine, quis non videt; qui nec inter Principes Protestantes Oues, nec inter vestros Pontifices Lupos discernere possis? Errantnè ipsi Protestantes? Ergò nondum adhuc absolutè & omninò Lupi, sed errantes Oues censendi sunt; nec iam, ut Tu vis, omni ratione abigendi: sed, ut Bernardus, pascendi potius, omnique ratione in septa Domini redigendi. Non errant autem? Ergò genuinae Christi Oues sunt, quos ita esse, res ipsa demonstrat, quia (teste {*}Agrippa) Sacram Scripturam, quam Aduersarij ipsorum tanquam Literam mortuam contemnunt, illi (Panoplia Dei armati) tanquàm gladium spiritus induunt, atque distringunt, quo haereses omnes succrescentes iugulent atque propulsent; sicut Annis abhinc mille circiter & trecentis praescripsit Tertullianus, {t}Coge (inquit) Haereticos, ut ad solas Scripturas opiniones suas sistant, & stare non possunt.
units.tr: From these things who does not see that you, Bellarmine, are miserably blind, you who cannot discern among the Protestant princes the sheep, nor among your own Pontiffs the wolves? Are the Protestants themselves in error? Then they are not yet absolutely and wholly wolves, but are to be counted erring sheep; nor are they now, as you wish, to be driven away by every means, but rather, as Bernard says, to be fed, and brought into the fold of the Lord by every means. But are they not in error? Then they are genuine sheep of Christ, and the thing itself shows that they are so, because (as Agrippa testifies) they, armed as the panoply of God, put on Sacred Scripture, which their adversaries despise as a dead letter, as the sword of the Spirit, and draw it, so that they may slay and repel every heresy as it springs up; just as Tertullian prescribed about a thousand three hundred years ago: Compel the heretics to confine their opinions to the Scriptures alone, and they cannot stand.

units.la: Porrò iurent, licet, Aduersarij in Decreta Pontificum, Protestantes verò Scripturarum testimonijs acquiescunt; nolunt Imagines colere; nolunt honorabilis coniugij torum impolluti Actum pollutionem dicere; nolunt in Missa creare suum Creatorem; & in Satisfactionibus merita Christi & Martyrum, id est, immaculati Agni Dei sanguinem cum polluto hominum sanguine, sacrilegâ superstitione, commiscere; nolunt Testamenti Iesu Christi sigilla diuclere. Charta me potius quàm oratio deficeret, si recensere vellem singulos Pontificiæ Religionis errores, quibus Protestantes implicari & inquinari nolunt, ut scil. Summi Pastoris Christi Iesu voci fideliter[?] constantérque obediant, atque obtemperent: quâ quidem nulla potest esse verâ Ovis nota certior & exploratior.
units.tr: Furthermore, let the adversaries swear by the decrees of the Pontiffs, while the Protestants rest on the testimonies of Scripture. They are unwilling to worship images; they are unwilling to call the act of the honourable marriage bed of the undefiled pollution; they are unwilling to create their own Creator in the Mass; and in satisfactions they are unwilling to mix the merits of Christ and of the martyrs, that is, the blood of the spotless Lamb of God, with the polluted blood of men, in sacrilegious superstition; they are unwilling to break the seals of the Testament of Jesus Christ. The paper would fail me rather than my speech, if I wished to list each of the errors of the Papist religion, by which the Protestants refuse to be entangled and defiled, namely so that they faithfully and steadfastly obey and submit to the voice of the supreme Shepherd, Jesus Christ; and indeed no surer or more certain mark of a true sheep can exist than this.

units.la: De Catholicis ( quos vocat ) Principibus, veluti Arie- tibus; quorum duo genera ponit Bellarminus: Primum Eorum, qui laedunt Gregem, Alterum Eorum,qui non adiuvant.
units.tr: On the Catholic (so-called) Princes, as Rams; of whom Bellarmine lays down two kinds: first, those who harm the flock; second, those who do not help.

units.la: Bellarminus alibi.
units.tr: Bellarmine elsewhere.

units.la: {1}Altera potestas, quæ est Pastori necessaria, circa Arietes versatur, qui sunt Principes Catholici, ut quando cornibus gregem laedunt, eos recludat, & prohibeat, ne ultrà procedant. Possit Pastor Arietes furiosos, & destruentes ovile separare, & recludere; talis Aries est Princeps, Catholicus fide, sed adeò malus, ut multùm obsit religioni & Ecclesiæ. Sic de primo Arietum genere; de Altero adiungis. Et debet Pastor iubere Reges Deo servire defendendo Ecclesiam, & punicndo Hæreticos & Schismaticos, & nisi fecerint, etiam cogere per excommunicationem, aliasque COMMODAS RATIONES.
units.tr: {1}The other power, which is necessary to the shepherd, concerns the rams, who are the Catholic Princes, so that when with their horns they harm the flock, he may shut them up and restrain them, lest they go further. The shepherd may separate and shut up furious rams that destroy the sheepfold. Such a ram is a prince, Catholic in faith, but so bad that he greatly harms religion and the Church. Thus of the first kind of rams. Of the second you add: And the shepherd ought to order kings to serve God by defending the Church and punishing heretics and schismatics, and if they do not, even to compel them by excommunication and other CONVENIENT MEANS.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: In Arietibus debellandis infeliciter Bellarminum aciem struere.
units.tr: Bellarmine wrongly deploys his battle line against the rams to be crushed.

units.la: TRiplex igitur bellum iam denunciavit strenuus hic buccinator Bellarminus; unum inter Arietes & Lupos; excitat enim Regem Catholicum ad Reges Hæreticos puniendos: Alterum est inter ipsos Arietes, quia Rex innocens debet Arietes furiosos, & schismaticos prohibere: Tertium Pastoris adversus omnes; Eius enim est, I. Lupos OMNI RATIONE abigere. II. Arietes furiosos recludere. claudere. III. Arietes pacificos & innocentes ad Gregem defendendum cogere. Eho, bellum Arietis cum Lupo? imparcongressus. An etiam Arietis cum Ariete? fieri potest, & etiam solet; sed num instinctu aliquo, quo Gregem, & non se potius defendat? III. An vero etiam fando vnquam auditum est, Pastorem vllum cum suis belligerasse Arietibus? nec tamen negari potest Pastores Rom. Ecclesiæ sæpè non modò Principes Pontificios cum Protestantibus, aut Pontificios inter se commisisse; sed etiam ipsum cum vtroque atrocia bella gessisse, & vicissim Religionis Principes in Pastores illos vestros arietasse. Quod tamen non de vetustioris notæ, vsque ad millesimum post Christum Annum, Pastoribus, sed de eorum Successoribus intelligi volumus; de quibus vester Espencæus: {u}Moribus antiquis (inquit) non contenta posteritas, veteris Gentilis ritu, togas in sagas mutaunt, quando Clericus ad prælium non tantum animum, sed & manum exercuit; cumque non tantum contra barbaros, sed eiusdem quoque nunc sanguinis, nunc patriæ, aut certè fidei Principes Domini nostri Dei pacis quidam minus pacifici Vicarij bella indicerent, & gererent, exemplo nullâ Scripturarum aut Canonum authoritate probato. Hæc ille; Itâ vt nunc planè constet, quàm immenso hiatu tuæ similitudinis protasis ab apodosi differiat. Hæc in genere de ipsa Similitudine.
units.tr: So this vigorous trumpeter Bellarmine has now declared a threefold war. One is between the rams and the wolves, for he incites the Catholic King to punish heretic kings. The second is between the rams themselves, since an innocent king must restrain furious and schismatic rams. The third is the shepherd's war against all. For it belongs to him: (1) to drive off the wolves BY ALL MEANS; (2) to shut up furious rams; (3) to compel peaceful and innocent rams to defend the flock. Come now, a war of the ram against the wolf? An unequal encounter. And of the ram against the ram? That can happen, and often does; but by what instinct, which defends himself rather than the flock? And has it ever been heard, even by report, that any shepherd waged war on his own rams? Yet it cannot be denied that the shepherds of the Roman Church have often not only set Papist princes against Protestants, or Papists against one another, but have themselves waged savage wars against both, and in turn princes of the religion have butted against those your shepherds. Yet we want this understood not of the shepherds of older note, down to the year one thousand after Christ, but of their successors. Of these your Espencaeus says: {u}Posterity, not content with the ancient customs, after the rite of the old Gentiles, changes togas into cloaks, when the cleric has exercised in battle not only his mind but also his hand; and when some less peaceful vicars of our Lord, the God of peace, declared and waged wars not only against barbarians but against princes of the same blood, now of the same country, or at least of the same faith, a practice approved by no authority of Scripture or canons. So he. Thus it is now plainly clear how vast a gap separates the protasis of your comparison from its apodosis. These things in general concern the comparison itself.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Formulam Bellarminianam, Recludendi Principes, atro- cem in Principes iniuriam innuere: cui Typus pastoralis Pedi reclamat.
units.tr: The Bellarminian formula of shutting up princes hints at atrocious injury to princes; the pastoral type of the crook protests against it.

units.la: INtàm graui in vestros Principes Catholicos censurâ duo præcipuè expendenda exagitandáque, Pœna, & Causa. Quoad Pœnam, Principes ledentes Gregem Recludendos esse ais: negligentes verò ad Gregem defendendum per Excommunicationem, aliásque COMMODAS RATIONES cogendos. Hæc phrasis [Recludere Principes] Alijs peregrina & insolens videtur; Ego verba non capto, modò[?] sensum capiam: nec tam offendit, quòd absona & inufitata, quàm quòd ita obscura sint, quasi malueris Te potiùs Nobis non intellectum, quàm Principibus reprehensum propinare. Quanquàm de mente tua coniectura non levis, ex verbis sequentibus, emergit; quibus asseris, Eos, vltrà Excommunicationem, per ALIAS COMMODAS RATIONES esse cogendos. Quod tamen quid sibi velit facilius quis ex Pontificum factis palpare, quàm ex dictis vestris expiscari potuerit. Iesuita {a}Azorius laetà admodùm memoriâ recolit exempla Principum Pontificiæ Religionis, quos Romanos Pastores vel Regnù suis cedere; vel collum pedibus subijcere; armorumque vi voluntati imperióque suo concedere coegerunt. Atque nullam videri Illis viam magis compendiosam,non paucæ Pontificum {b}Bulla ferali more vociferantur, imperantes, ut, veluti Oves in Arietes, Subditi in Reges suos Armis insurgant, eorum fautores persequantur, & Regnis & dominijs eorum expellant. At quid, quaeso, Tela lethalia sibi volunt? quis sensus Armorum? quae in hostili odio Ratio commoda? nonnè hæc omnia perduellionem, cædem, & sanguinem spirare videntur?
units.tr: Two things especially must be weighed and examined in so grave a censure of your Catholic princes: punishment and cause. As to punishment, you say that princes who harm the flock are to be shut up, while those who neglect to defend the flock by excommunication and other CONVENIENT MEANS are to be compelled. This phrase [to shut up princes] seems strange and unusual to others. I do not grasp the words, but I grasp the sense. It offends not so much because it is absurd and unusual as because it is so obscure, as if you preferred to serve us up not an understanding but a reproach against princes. Yet a not slight conjecture about your mind emerges from the following words, in which you assert that they are to be compelled, beyond excommunication, by OTHER CONVENIENT MEANS. What this means, anyone could more easily grasp from the deeds of the Pontiffs than extract from your words. The Jesuit {a}Azorius, with quite joyful memory, recalls examples of princes of the Papist religion whom the Roman shepherds forced either to yield their kingdoms, or to submit their necks to their feet, and to concede to their will and command by force of arms. And since no way seems to them more expeditious, not a few Bulls cry out in deadly fashion, commanding that, like sheep against rams, subjects rise up in arms against their kings, pursue their supporters, and drive them from their kingdoms and dominions. But what, I ask, do deadly weapons mean? What sense do arms have? What convenient reason lies in hostile hatred? Do not all these things seem to breathe treason, slaughter and blood?

units.la: Eodem planè, quo Tu animo, nuper Baronius vefster aduersus alios Arietes, nimirùm Venetos, Pontificis Potestatem charitatium scilicet, re autem verò coactivam (id est, vafro & callido) venditavit. {c}Duplex, Beate Pater, (inquit) ministerium Petri, Pascere, & occidere ac manducare, Dixit enim Dominus Petro, Pasce Oves; & audivit etiam è cœlo vocem, Occide & manduca:-- Nempè, quando cùm Leonibus & feris animalibus agendū; iubetur Petrus occidere; obsistere sc. pugnare, & expugnare &c. In hac igitur causa Venetorum illud [Pasce] Baronio nimis spissum verbum videtur; occidere, & manducare arrident magis: nec satis Illi est, si Recludantur, nisi etiam Expugnentur. Nec sane mirum; non enim iam in Venetiis (etiamsi eiusdem Religionis cultoribus) Arietes, sed Leones, nempè, fera animalia discernit.
units.tr: In exactly the same spirit as you, lately your Baronius, against other rams, namely the Venetians, flaunted the Pontiff's power of charity, but in truth coercive, that is, cunning and crafty. {c}Double, Blessed Father, he says, is the ministry of Peter: to feed, and to kill and eat. For the Lord said to Peter, Feed my sheep; and he also heard a voice from heaven, Kill and eat. Namely, when he must deal with lions and wild beasts, Peter is ordered to kill, that is, to resist, fight, storm and so on. In this case of the Venetians, the word [feed] seems too thin a word to Baronius; kill and eat please him more. Nor is it enough for him that they be shut up unless they are also overthrown. Nor is this surprising, for in Venice (though its people are worshippers of the same religion) he discerns not rams but lions, that is, wild beasts.

units.la: Quid igitur mirum, si is Pontifici persuadeat, vt Pastoris persona exuta, Lanij induat. Christianos Principes (etsi Dracones essent) pascendos esse {d}Bernardus monuit, ferro autem aggrediendos negauit. Chrysostomus etiam negat Licere Pastoribus tanta authoritate homines curare, quantâ Oues Pastor curat; {e}Cui liberum est eos à pabulo arcere, vrere, secare. ---- Christianis enim (inquit) minimè omnium licet peccantium lapsus vi corrigere.
units.tr: What wonder, then, if he persuades the Pontiff to lay aside the person of the shepherd and put on that of the butcher. {d}Bernard advised that Christian princes (even if they were dragons) should be fed, but denied that they should be attacked with iron. {e}Chrysostom also denies that it is lawful for pastors to care for men with as much authority as the shepherd cares for sheep; for to whom is it free to keep them from pasture, to burn and to cut? ---- For (he says) it is least of all permitted to Christians to correct the lapses of sinners by force.

units.la: Antiquorum Patrum testimonijs, & Pontificiorum ipsorum suffragijs plurimis hoc in loco superseden-dum, & in Massonij vestri iudicio accurato acquiescendum duxi. Hic de {f}Bonifacio VIII. qui Philippum Pulchrum Principem miris modis diuexabat; Non putent Pontifices (ait) se à Deo datos Regibus vt eos cohibeant, veluti equos intraætatos[?] ; admoneant, precentur; minari autem, terrefacere, arma ciere Episcopos non decet. Hæc ille. Eodem spectare videtur officij Pastoralis typus solennis, & (vti vos iactitatis) ab Apostolicis deductus temporibus, nimirum, Baculus ille, seu virga, quam Pedum {§}dicitis, Episcopis proprius, Recurvus in summo, rectus in medio, & in fine acutus. Cuius hæc à vobis panduntur mysteria, nempe, Pastorem debere colligere vagos, regere debiles, & pigros pungere. Iccirco Pastores meminisse oportet, sibi (vt omne genus Ouium regant) Baculum tradi, non fustem; Virgam, non sclopetum; Pedum denique, non gladium, aut pugionem; vt, colligere, regere, & (si ratio tulerit) ad summum pungere possint, non autem corporaliter vulnerare, transfigere, confodere.
units.tr: I have thought it best here to pass over the testimonies of the ancient Fathers and the many suffrages of the Papists themselves, and to acquiesce in the accurate judgment of your Masson. Here is {f}Boniface VIII, who harassed Philip the Fair in marvellous ways: Let not the Pontiffs think they have been given by God to Kings to restrain them as unbroken horses; let them admonish and pray; but it is not fitting for bishops to threaten, terrify, or raise arms. So he. The solemn pastoral type seems to aim at the same thing: that staff or rod, which you call the {§}crook, you say is proper to bishops, derived from apostolic times, curved at the top, straight in the middle, and sharp at the end. Its mysteries you expound thus: the shepherd must gather the wandering, guide the weak, and prick the lazy.
