Therefore ministers should remember that a staff is given to them, so that they may rule every kind of sheep: not a cudgel (Baculum, not fustem); not a gun (Virgam, not sclopetum); in short a crook (Pedum), not a sword (gladium) or a dagger (pugionem). Thus they may gather, guide, and (if reason requires) prick at the top, but not wound, pierce or stab the body.

units.la: III ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Causas deponendi Principes plures indignas, multas inept.as, iustas esse nullas.
units.tr: The causes given for deposing princes: many unworthy, many inept, none just.

units.la: PRincipes non modò Excommunicandi, sed etiam Regnis & Dominijs suis per Pontifices exuendi, causæ plurimæ obtendi solent; (Exempli gratiâ) in k Rege Sicilia, quod Episcoporū & Abbatum Electiones ad[illegible, ~2 letters], contra Canones traxerat: in{k} Berengario, quòd nimia erat potentia eius à quo Pontifex multa indignè passus est: In Frederico Imp. quòd{m} Sui iuris esse dixit causam iudicare in Schismate quod inter Papam & Antipapam intercesserat: In Frederico II. quòd{n} Periurus erat & sacrilegus: In Childerico Francorum Rege,{o} Non tam profuis iniquitatibus, quàm quòd tanta potestati erat inutilis, vbi coadiutor adhiberi potuit: Denique in quouis Principe, qui ({p}Bellarmini vox est) vel Regigioni multùm obfuerit, vel Episcopatus vendiderit, vel Ecclesiam diripuerit. &c.
units.tr: Not only are princes excommunicated, but many causes are commonly alleged for stripping them of their kingdoms and dominions through the Pontiffs. For example: against the King of Sicily, that he had drawn the elections of bishops and abbots to himself contrary to the canons; against Berengar, that his power was excessive, and by it the Pontiff had suffered many indignities; against the Emperor Frederick, that he claimed it was his right to judge the schism that had arisen between the Pope and the Antipope; against Frederick II, that he was perjured and sacrilegious; against Childeric, King of the Franks, not so much for his wicked deeds as because he was useless in so great a power, where a coadjutor could have been employed; and finally against any prince who (in Bellarmine's words) either has greatly harmed the kingdom of Christ, or has sold bishoprics, or has plundered the Church, etc.

units.la: Hoc Bellarmini [&c.] quo plenam periodum cautè figit, Principem quemuis Regno suo spoliari certum est, si vel Canones, quæ ad Electionem Abbatis spectent, violauerit; vel Nimiâ potentiâ Pontificem læserit; vel se componendo Paparum schismati immiscuerit; vel Periurij, aut Sacrilegij vllius Reus fuerit; vel animi impotens, & tanto oneri impar exiterit; vel denique Ecclesiam diripuerit, [ET CAETERA] vt ait Bellarminus, — incedens per ignes suppositos cineri dolosò. Nam Causas cæteras quis mortalium augurari coniecturâ potest, cùm tot causæ esse possint, quot Pontifici, ex plenitudine potestatis, apud Se fingere libuerit: forte, si Princeps se Cardinali dignitate anteferat; certè, nisi se Papæ arbitrio & imperio mancipauerit.
units.tr: By this phrase of Bellarmine's, "etc.", which he cautiously leaves to finish the sentence, it is certain that any prince whatever may be despoiled of his kingdom, if he has violated the canons concerning the election of an abbot; or has injured the Pontiff by excessive power; or has mixed himself into the schism of the Popes by taking a side; or has been guilty of perjury or sacrilege of any kind; or has been unable to control his mind and has proved unequal to so great a burden; or finally has plundered the Church, and the rest, as Bellarmine says, walking over fires hidden under deceitful ash. For who among mortals can guess the other causes, since there can be as many causes as the Pontiff, out of the fullness of his power, chooses to invent for himself? Perhaps, if a prince puts himself before a cardinal in rank; certainly, unless he surrenders himself to the will and command of the Pope.

units.la: Expedit igitur Principibus apud se perpendere, quàm lubrico in loco iam sacro-sancta eorum maiestas versetur, ex illo, de Coactiua Pontificis in Principes Potestate Temporali; nouo, & plusquàm mille retro seculis inaudito paradoxo, quo Pastor Romanus aliquandiù Illis fucum fecit. Chrysostomus sui temporis Laicos multis argumentis vehementer hortatus est, vt in sacrarum Scripturarum lectionem incumberent. Nonnulli verò male-sani homines, sic se excusarent, Hoc Pastoris officium est, Nos Oues sumus: Quibus Sanctus ille Pater:{q} Oues reuerà estis, (inquit) verùm non irrationales, sed Rationales. Quemadmodùm in isthac Causa, de Lectione Scripturarum, Oues illas,
units.tr: It is therefore useful for princes to consider how slippery the ground is on which their sacred majesty now stands, through that new paradox, unheard of for more than a thousand years, concerning the Pope's coercive temporal power over princes, by which the Roman Pastor for some time deceived them. Chrysostom earnestly urged the laity of his own day, with many arguments, to devote themselves to reading the Holy Scriptures. But some ill-disposed men excused themselves thus: "This is the office of the shepherd; we are the sheep." To them that holy Father replied: "You are indeed sheep (he says), but not irrational ones, but rational." {q}

units.la: {k} (Per Iohannem XII Papam. itàin[?] hac quæstione, de Principum depositione, hos Arietes, sed Rationales. existimare par est; nec igitur habendos esse tanquàm pecudes meras: nam omnia ferre si possint, & debent, pulsandum Pontificis pedi præbendum quandóque Caput. Vt de Causis omnibus, quas pro deponendis Principibus Pontifex fingere possit, breuiter concludam; Vbi Principibus pœnam Temporalem infligendi Ius non est, ibi eidem pœnæ Causa prætexi iusta nulla potest. At vbi in Scripturis de Principibus dicitur, {z}Noli tangere vnctos meos, ibi non hominis vox sonat, sed oraculum planè diuinum, quod vetus Theologia per totum Orbem Christianum docuit & celebrauit: quódque antiqui Pontifices sanctè coluerunt, qui, in Arietibus cogendis, semper ad Anathemata, tanquam ad arma vltima, confugerunt. * confugerunt.
units.tr: {k} (By John XII, Pope.) So in this question, on the deposition of princes, it is fitting to regard these as rams, but rational ones, and therefore not to be held as mere cattle. For they can and must bear all things, except that at some time they must offer the Pope's foot a head to be struck. To conclude briefly regarding all the causes which the Pope may devise for deposing princes: where there is no right to inflict temporal punishment on princes, no just cause can be pretended for that same punishment. But where Scripture says of princes, {z}Touch not my anointed, there it is not the voice of a man that sounds, but a plainly divine oracle, which the old Theology taught and celebrated throughout the Christian world, and which the ancient Popes devoutly observed; these, when gathering the rams, always had recourse to anathemas as to their last weapons. * had recourse.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Causæ superiores, propter quas Principes deponendos ce- nsent Pontifices, sigillatim recensentur; & earum omni- um Pontifices ipsi Rei peraguntur.
units.tr: The higher causes for which the Popes judge princes should be deposed are listed one by one, and the Popes themselves are shown to be the authors of all of them.

units.la: EX causis, quas attulistis, pro deponendis Principibus Catholicis, prima fuit iuris vsurpatio in Electione Episcoporum, & Abbatum; quùm tamen Pontifices Rom.diù Impertores[?] Constantinopolitanos pacificè tulerint, etiamsi {a}Absq; eorum[?] confirmatione, & nisi solutâ prius pro Confirmatione pecuniâ Pontifices ordinari non poterant: tandem Agatho I. Papa An.Dom.DCLXXXIX.[?] hoc priuilegium ab Imperatore abtinuit, vt hàc pessimâ consuetudine sublatâ, Pontifex electus non sine Imperatoris assensu consecraretur, quæ ille gratis dare tenebatur.
units.tr: Of the causes you have advanced for deposing Catholic princes, the first was the usurpation of right in the election of bishops and abbots. Yet the Roman Popes long tolerated the Constantinopolitan emperors quietly, even though, without their confirmation, Popes could not be ordained, and unless money was first paid for the confirmation. At last Pope Agatho I, in the year of our Lord 689, obtained from the Emperor this privilege: that, with this most wicked custom abolished, a Pope elected should be consecrated without the Emperor's assent, which the Emperor was bound to give freely.

units.la: Secunda est Iniuria in Papam, qui sæpè sine causa quiritatur; quid igitur? Cùm Princeps aut à Papa ad Concilium prouocandū censuerit; aut Calceū Pontificis exosculari recusauerit: si Papa de illata sibi iniuria vehementius postulauerit; an propterea Coronâ suâ spoliandus est Princeps? * Iniusta oratio; cùm præsertim complures Pontifices nefarias & immanes iniurias in suos Prædecessores exercuisse confteant, nec tamen Pontificatu abdicati sint.
units.tr: The second is the wrong done to the Pope, who often complains without cause. What then? When a prince has thought fit to summon the Pope to a Council, or has refused to kiss the Pope's slipper, if the Pope has demanded more vehemently for the injury done to him, is the prince therefore to be stripped of his crown? * An unjust argument, especially since many Popes are known to have inflicted wicked and monstrous injuries on their own predecessors, and yet were not deposed from the papacy.

units.la: Tertia, Arrogatio Iuris in tollendo Schismate tum gliscente inter Papa atq; Antipapa. Otho Imperator facinus perperrauit insigne, qui Iohannem XII. Papam omnibus probris contaminatu&, & scortis deditum Pontificatu deiecit: & tamen fæliciter regnauit, ab omnibus Pontificijs celebratus tanquam Vir optimus, & Ecclesia Rom. defensor acerrimus.
units.tr: The third is the assumption of right in ending the schism which then flared up between Pope and Antipope. The Emperor Otto committed a notable crime when he deposed John XII, a Pope defiled with every disgrace and given over to harlots; and yet he reigned happily, celebrated by all the Papists as a most excellent man and a most zealous defender of the Roman Church.

units.la: Quarta est Periurii; quasi vero quisquam mortalium sit, vel etiã esse possit magis *periurus Pontifice ipso, qui non modò in se periurus, cum suo iuramento dispensat, sed etiam se egregiû nefarijs aliorû periurijs Patronû praestitit; Subditorum praecipuè, quos à iuramento fidelitatis Principib° debitæ absoluit. Respòdebunt Aduersarij (quæ est ipsorû detestanda subtilitas) Papa in his casibus non dispensare cum periurijs, sed declarare Hac non esse Periuria. At Ego non tàm Domino Pontifici vice-deo credendû puto, quâ Pontificis Domino verè Deo; nõ illi, qui Declarat istas Iuramenti violationes periuria non esse; sed huic, qui eas Periurij esse demõstrat, cosq; per vindictâ suam Reos ostendit, quos Papa absoluit, nec tàm praeceptis suis, quàm iustissimis in perfidos Rebelles supplicijs. Cuius exemplum extare voluit in Rodulpho Suevia Duce; d Huic (excomunicato prius Henrico Imp.) Gregorius VII. Papa Regnû Teutonicorum confirmat, ei adhærentibus absolutionê omniû peccatorum concedit; benedictionemq; in hac vita, & in futura. Sicut enim Henricus (inquit) pro sua superbia & inobedientia a Regni dignitate iuste abiicitur, ita Rodulpho pro sua humilitate & obedientia potestas & dignitas regni conceditur. Agite nunc quaeso, (Beate Petre, & Paule) Patres & Principes sanctissimi, ut omnis mundus intelligat & cognoscat, quia * si potestis in coelo ligare & soluere, potestis in terra Imperia, Regna, Principatus, Ducatus, & omnium hominum possessiones, pro meritis tollere unicuique, & concedere. Et paulo ante. Henrico dignitatem Regiam tollo, itaque ut nullus Christianorum Ei, sicut Regi, obediat interdico; omnesque, qui ei iurauerunt, vel iurabunt, de Regni dominatione a Iuramenti promissione absolvo. Sic Papa. At Deus, qui sedit in caelis, & huiusmodi Gigantum tàm nefanda consilia pro-
units.tr: The fourth is perjury; as if any mortal were, or could be, more perjured than the Pope himself, who not only is perjured in himself, when he dispenses with his own oath, but also has shown himself an outstanding patron of the perjuries of others, chiefly of his subjects, whom he absolves from the oath of fidelity owed to their princes. The adversaries will answer (such is their detestable subtlety) that the Pope in these cases does not dispense with perjuries, but declares that these are not perjuries. But I think that we must believe not so much the Lord Pope, as vice-god, as the Lord Pope, truly God; not him who declares that those violations of oath are not perjuries, but him who shows that they are perjury, and by his vengeance shows guilty those whom the Pope absolves, and this not so much by his precepts as by the most just punishments against faithless rebels. He willed that an example of this should stand in Rudolph, Duke of Swabia. To him (Henry the Emperor having been excommunicated beforehand), Pope Gregory VII confirms the kingdom of the Germans, grants absolution of all sins to those adhering to him, and a blessing in this life and in the next. For, he says, just as Henry is justly cast down from the dignity of the kingdom for his pride and disobedience, so to Rudolph is granted power and dignity of the kingdom for his humility and obedience. Come now, I beg you, (blessed Peter and Paul), holy Fathers and Princes, so that the whole world may understand and know that, if you can bind and loose in heaven, you can also, on earth, remove from each man, and grant, empires, kingdoms, principalities, duchies, and the possessions of all men, according to their merits. And a little before: "I take away the royal dignity from Henry, and so I forbid any Christian to obey him as king; and I absolve from the promise of the oath all who have sworn, or shall swear, to him concerning the rule of the kingdom." Thus the Pope. But God, who sits in the heavens, and so the most impious counsels of such Giants ...

units.la: * Gregorium 13, infigniter periurij* iussisse in adoptione Papatus, offendit Maffeius in vita Gregor.
units.tr: * Maffeus, in the life of Gregory XIII, shows that he notably ordered perjury in the adoption of the papacy.

units.la: d Binius To.3.pa.2. pag 1288 & Baron. Tom.11.An.1080, num.12.
units.tr: d Binius, To. 3, pt. 2, p. 1288; and Baronius, Tom. 11, An. 1080, num. 12.

units.la: * O bellam dialecticam, non solum, sed caelo dignam! deridiculo habet, iam partes suas agit. {c}Rodulphus bello cecidit, fertúrque in extremis positus, & abscissam in prælio manum dexteram intuitus, ad Episcopos, qui forte aderant, graviter suspirans dixisse; Ecce hæc est manus, quâ Dominus meo Henrico fidem Sacramentaliter firmauit: ecce ego iam eius (Imperatoris) regnum & vitam relinquo præsentem; vide te, qui me solium eius conscendere fecistis, vt rectâ via vos monita vestra sequentem duxeritis. Hæc Rodulphus; Manus (inquit) dextra abscissa, quâ Iuramentum firmauit. Nullum verò esse possit Iudicij diuini luculentius aut expressius indicium & argumentum, quàm quod à lege talionis deducitur. Et, vt manifestius constaret, Papam diuinæ Maiestati magis adhuc esse ludibrio, Gregorius Pontifex, (ante mortem Rodulphi) {f}Quasi sibi diuinitùs reuelatum prædixit, falsum Regem hoc Anno esse moriturum: & verum quidem prædixit, sed fefellit eum coniectura de Rege; nam ille, secundum velle suum, id interpretatus est de Henrico, qui tunc contra Saxones graui prælio decertans, Regem falsum, scilicet Rodulphum, interfecit. Eodem planè modo quo Deus prophetiam veram extraxit ex mente salsa, & blasphemo oré {g}Caipha, quùm dixit Ioh. 11. Oportet vnum mori pro populo: ] {*}Vbi, vt ait Chrysostomus, Cor eius non erat motum à Spiritu Sancto, sed lingua, quia recta mala mente loquebatur. Matthæus Parisiensis Exemplum aliud diuinæ vindictæ mirandum sanè stupendumque prodidit aduersùs Alemanicum Comitem, eiusdem Henrici Imperatoris Persecutorem grauissimum, & Rebellem perfidum: {h}Quem ad mensam residentem cæterùa quaedam multitudo (qui nullis domesticis eorum fustibus depelli potuerant) terribiliter corroso laniarunt.
units.tr: * O what a fine dialectic, not only, but worthy of heaven! He mocks, now he plays his own part. {c} Rudolph fell in battle, and is reported, lying at the point of death, and looking at his right hand cut off in the fight, to have said with a deep sigh to the bishops who happened to be present: "Behold this is the hand with which I sacramentally confirmed my faith to my lord Henry; behold, I now leave his (the Emperor's) kingdom and life; see to it, you who made me climb his throne, that you may lead those following your admonitions by the straight way." Thus Rudolph: the right hand, he says, cut off, with which he confirmed the oath. Yet no clearer or more express indication and proof of divine judgment could be given than that which is derived from the law of retaliation. And, so that it might be more plainly established that the Pope was still more a plaything to the divine Majesty, Pope Gregory, before Rudolph's death, as if divinely revealed to him, foretold that the false king would die this year; and indeed he foretold the truth, but a guess about the king misled him; for Rudolph, according to his own wish, interpreted it of Henry, who then, fighting a grievous battle against the Saxons, killed the false king, namely Rudolph. In exactly the same way God drew a true prophecy out of the impure and blasphemous mouth of {g} Caiaphas, when he said (John 11): "It is expedient that one man die for the people." {*} Where, as Chrysostom says, his heart was not moved by the Holy Spirit, but his tongue, because he spoke with a wicked mind. Matthew Paris recorded another remarkable and truly astonishing example of divine vengeance against the Alemannic Count, a most grievous persecutor of the same Emperor Henry and a faithless rebel: while he sat at table, a certain crowd (who could not be driven off by any of their domestic clubs) tore him to pieces terribly, having been gnawed away.

units.la: Quinta exceptio est Impotentia, & ignaua quædam inutilitas in regnando. Quis autem inutilior Eo (Iohanne nimirùm XV. Papâ) qui {i}Pontificatum adeptus humana diuinaque omnia affinibus suis largiebatur, posthabito Dei honore, & Romanæ sedis dignitate: quem errorem (ait Onuphrius) ita posteris tradidit vt ad nostram vsque ætatem peruenerit; quo quidem nihil perniciosius dici potest, cùm non ob religionem aut Dei cultum appetere Pontificatum nostri Sacerdotes videantur, sed ut fratrum, nepotum, famulorum ingluviem & avaritiam expleant, nec tamen Pontificatu abdicantur.
units.tr: The fifth exception is impotence, and a certain lazy uselessness in ruling. Yet who was more useless than John XV, who, having obtained the papacy, bestowed all human and divine things on his relatives, setting aside the honour of God and the dignity of the Roman see? This error (says Onuphrius) was handed down to posterity in such a way that it has come down to our own age; and nothing more harmful can be said of it, since our priests seem to seek the papacy not for religion or the worship of God, but to satisfy the gluttony and greed of their brothers, nephews and servants, and yet they are not removed from the papacy.

units.la: Vltima est Episcopatuum venditio, & Ecclesiarum direptio. At nullæ magis execrabiles venditiones, quàm illæ Pauli II. Papæ, quibus (nouo quodam aucupio, &, vt {k}Platina loquitur, Lenocinio) beneficia ferè omnia facta sunt venalia; nullæ Direptiones magis calamitosæ, quàm illæ quas Pontifices perpetrárunt. Nolo ego Cameram Apostolicam (quam vocant) ceu Camarinam mouere; nec etiam Granamina, quibus Franci & Germani succubuerunt. Nostratium Anglorum anhelitus & eiu'atus[?] repetere me sinant, quorum direptiones, & portentosas Pontificum exactiones {l}Matth. Parisiensis omni posteritatis nostræ memoriæ tradidit. Anno MCCXXIX. Tanta fuit (inquit) Gregorij IX. Pontifi.is exactio, vt Præliati cogerentur calices, phiolas, phylacteria Altaris, alia vendere, alia in pignus sub fœnore pònere. Anno MCCXL. {m}Exactio alia, quâ Papa infinitam pecuniam miserus[?] Anglis emunxit, quam Abbates clamabant impossibilem esse, & toto mundo detestandam. Anno MCCXLVI. {n}Statuit Innocentius IV. Pont. vt bona omnia Clerici, qui intestatus moreretur, in vsum Domini Papæ conuerterentur. — Et denunciauit, vt omnes beneficiati, in suis beneficijs residentes, tertiam partem bonorum suorum; non residentes verò dimidiam Papæ persoluerent; additâ illâ adiectione, [NON OBSTANTE,] quæ omnem extinguit iustitiam. Hæc Historicus. Quæ igitur immanior charybdis aut insatiabilior istis Pastoribus vestris, qui non tondere gregem suum, sed deglubere voluerunt, &, veluti harpyæ, seu alata dæmonia omnia sibi arripere & deglutire.
units.tr: The last is the sale of bishoprics and the plunder of churches. But no sales were more detestable than those of Pope Paul II, by which almost all benefices were made saleable, through a new kind of fowling and, as Platina puts it, pimping. No plunderings were more calamitous than those the popes committed. I do not wish to stir up the Apostolic Chamber (as they call it) like the proverbial Camarina, nor the grievances to which the French and Germans succumbed. Let me pass over the groans and [?] of our own English, whose plunderings and monstrous exactions of the popes Matthew Paris handed down to the memory of all posterity. In the year 1229: So great was the exaction of Pope Gregory IX that prelates were forced to sell chalices, flasks, and the reliquaries of the altar, some outright, others to pledge at interest. In the year 1240: Another exaction, by which the Pope drained an infinite sum of money from the English, which the abbots cried out was impossible to bear and to be detested by the whole world. In the year 1246: Innocent IV decreed that all the goods of a cleric who died intestate should be turned to the use of the lord Pope. And he proclaimed that all beneficed clergy residing in their benefices should pay a third of their goods to the Pope, and those not residing half; adding that clause, [NOTWITHSTANDING], which destroys all justice. So the historian. What monster, then, is more savage than Charybdis, or more insatiable than those shepherds of yours, who wished not to shear their flock but to flay it, and, like harpies or winged demons, to snatch up and swallow everything for themselves?

units.la: Ad Principes redeo, cum quibus iniquissimè actum, quis non videt? quùm præsertim sicut Oues cum Lupo, de caussa turbandæ aquæ, isti Arietes cum hisce Pastoribus de causis destruendi Gregis expostulare aut contendere velint, nihil aliud expectandum quàm vt statim fiant eiusdem fabulæ [illegible, ~3 letters]. Simile quid Historico vestro, alijsque viris diuini atque humani iuris peritissimis accidisse legimus, qui conquestus apud Papam, quòd Ille, indistâ causâ, eos legitimâ possessione suâ spoliauerit, {o}Petebat vt causa ipsa Iudicibus (quos Rote auditores vocant) committeretur: Tum Papa illum toruis oculis aspiciens; Et nos, inquit, ad Iudices reuocas? ac si nescias omnia iura in scrinio pectoris nostri collocata esse: sic stat sententia (inquit) loco cedant, cant quo volunt.
units.tr: I return to the princes, with whom most unjustly dealt, who does not see it? Especially since, just as sheep with the wolf argue about the cause of muddying the water, so these rams, with these shepherds, wish to dispute or contend about the causes of destroying the flock, and one can expect nothing else than that at once they become [illegible] of that same fable. Your historian and other men most skilled in divine and human law, we read, suffered something similar: when they complained to the Pope that he had despoiled them of their lawful possession without any cause, they asked that the case be committed to judges (whom they call auditors of the Rota). Then the Pope, looking at him with grim eyes: And do you summon us to judges? As if you did not know that all laws are stored in the casket of our breast. Thus stands the sentence (he says): let them yield and go where they wish.

units.la: Bellarminus alibi.
units.tr: Bellarmine elsewhere.

units.la: {p}In istis verbis Ioh.21. [Pasce oues meas] data est potestas Petro eiusque Successoribus regendi gregem. Potest enim Pastor ac debet ouespascere.
units.tr: In these words of John 21 [Feed my sheep] power was given to Peter and his successors to rule the flock. For a shepherd can and ought to feed his sheep.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. Animadversion.

units.la: Primum Excusationis genus; Papam negotijs multis à prædicandi munere impediri; quod ociosè obtendi probatur.
units.tr: The first kind of excuse: that the Pope is hindered from his preaching office by many affairs; which is shown to be idly pleaded.

units.la: CIrcà hoc Pastoris officium Pastoris vestri cor (nisi omnino excors sit) pupugit, atque acriter momordit Caluinus; {q}Ipse Pontifex (inquit) quid omninò habeat Episcopale scire velim: primum enim in munere Episcopi caput est, plebem Verbo Dei docere; Istocnè[?] Papa facit, imo aut facere se simulat? soluant hunc nodum mihi Romanenses. {r}Lutheri quoque stylus in eodem Pontificis vlcere, tanquàm vnguis aculeatus inhæsit. Vosque huic muneri Papas per se deesse non quidem negatis; sed huius defectus labem, quam eluere non potestis, duplici responso incruitare satagitis: quorum vtroque, si æquo perpendatis animo, non tam dissoluitur nodus quàm distringitur.
units.tr: Concerning this office of the pastor, your Pastor's heart (unless he is utterly senseless) was pricked and sharply bitten by Calvin: "I would like to know what the Pontiff should know about the episcopal office at all. For the first point in the office of a bishop is to teach the people the Word of God. Does the Pope do this, or even pretend to? Let the Romanists untie this knot for me." Luther's pen, too, stuck in the same sore of the Pontiff like a barbed claw. And you do not deny that the Popes themselves fail in this duty; but you labour to cover the stain of this defect, which you cannot wash away, with a twofold answer. If you weigh each of these with an even mind, the knot is not so much loosened as drawn tighter.

units.la: Vnum est, Papas alijs negotijs impediri. {f}Etiamsi (inquis) plerisque eorum non concionantur, tamen exercent multos alios actus Pastorales, dum ligant & absoluunt, controuersias iudicant. Esto; sed quærimus quid sit in Pasto[?]rali officio praecipuum? Concilium Tridentinum Seff.V. definit Praedicationem esse praecipuum munus Episcoporum. Et rursus Seff.24. eiusdem Synodi Patres statuunt, Praedicationem esse munus Episcoporum praecipuum: & hàc ratione ducti, utrobique huius muneris functionem Episcopis imponunt, Nisi legitimè impediantur. Nisi igitur ostendere possis Pontifices vestros ab hoc ministerio legitimè impeditos fuisse, Eos neglectae praecipua partis officij, & quodammodò deserti muneris Pastoralis reos esse fateare necesse est.
units.tr: The first answer is that the Popes are hindered by other business. "Even if" (you say) "most of them do not preach, they still perform many other pastoral acts, while they bind and loose and judge controversies." Granted; but we ask what is chief in the pastoral office. The Council of Trent, Session 5, defines that preaching is the chief duty of bishops. And again, in Session 24, the Fathers of the same Synod decree that preaching is the chief duty of bishops; and led by this reasoning, in both places they impose the performance of this duty on bishops unless they are lawfully hindered. Unless, therefore, you can show that your Popes were lawfully hindered from this ministry, you must admit that they are guilty of neglecting the chief part of the office and, in a sense, of deserting the pastoral duty.

units.la: Nos sanè nec possumus, nec debemus negare Pontifices complures ab hoc Pascendi munere saepissimè retardatos, & impeditos fuisse: an autem propter causas necessarias & legitimas? imò verò leuissimis nequissimisque de causis. Nam si quantum temporis Pontifices (vt Historici, & Authores vestri testantur) tribuerint (I) Ignauiae: (II) venationi, aucupijs, & omni oblectationis generi: Si quantum (III.) Pompis, & spectaculis: Si quantum (IV) Medecinae; vel (V) Columnarum, Obeliscorum, fastuarum erectioni; aut etiam (VI) arti Diabolicae: Si quantum (VII) Immensis exactionibus; (VIII) Bellis; (IX) Caedibus; (X) Adulteriis; Aliisque; (XI) Sceleribus: Tantum in Praedicandi curam ministeriumq; contulissent; Excusationis, fortassis, speciem aliquam praetexere possent. At quùm iam constet Eos, potiùs quàm huic tàm sacro muneri vacarent, vel nihil, vel aliud, vel male agendo, omni socordiae, atque vitiorum genere tam animorum, quàm corporum vires consumpsisse, quisquis Eos necessarij impedimenti obtentu excusare nititur, seipsum vaecordem aut inverecundum praebeat necesse est. Ad Causam accedam propius.
units.tr: We certainly can neither deny nor ought to deny that many Popes were very often delayed and hindered from this duty of feeding. But were the causes necessary and lawful? Indeed, they were most trivial and most wicked. For if the Popes (as your historians and authors bear witness) had devoted as much time (I) to idleness; (II) to hunting, fowling and every kind of amusement; if as much (III) to pomps and spectacles; if as much (IV) to medicine; or (V) to the erection of columns, obelisks and palaces; or even (VI) to the diabolical art; if as much to (VII) immense exactions; (VIII) wars; (IX) slaughters; (X) adulteries; and others; (XI) crimes: had they given as much to the care and ministry of preaching, they might perhaps have put forward some semblance of excuse. But since it is now established that they, rather than devoting themselves to this so sacred office, have spent the strength of both mind and body on nothing, or on something else, or by doing evil, in every kind of sloth and vice, whoever tries to excuse them under the pretext of a necessary hindrance must show himself either mad or shameless. I shall come closer to the cause.

units.la: Etsi semel, atque iterum fieri possit, vt vnus aut alter Pontifex per aliquot Menses, vel (si ità vultis) etiam duos aut tres Annos, aliorum negotiorum necessariâ im-
units.tr: Although it may happen once or twice that one Pope or another is drawn away from preaching for some months, or (if you like) even two or three years, by the necessary im-

units.la: IX. Alexander sextus, apud Massum.
units.tr: IX. Alexander VI, in Massus.

units.la: X. Benedictus nonus, apud Onuphrium: & Iohannes decimus, apud Baronium.
units.tr: X. Benedict IX, in Onuphrius; and John X, in Baronius.

units.la: XI. Bonifacius septimus, apud Onuphrium. portunitate, & quasi impetu à Prædicatione abstraheretur (sicut in rebus humanis interdum usu venit:) At ut unumquemque Pontificem per ætatem integram tot, tamque necessariis negociis implicatum fuisse credamus, qui sibi vel maximè credi cupit, suadebit prorsus nemo. Ratio est, quià cùm in omni hominum professione, tùm maximè in hac Pastoritia, quæ accidunt occupationes, vel etiam legitimæ, illegitimæ sunt; quibus id, quod est in suo cuiusque officio præcipuum munus, frustratur.
units.tr: XI. Boniface VII, in Onuphrius. portunity, and as if by a sudden onslaught (as sometimes happens in human affairs). But that every Pope was entangled for his whole life in so many and such necessary affairs, no one will persuade, least of all one who wishes above all to be believed. The reason is that in every profession of men, but most of all in this pastoral one, whatever occupations arise, even lawful ones, are illegitimate in so far as they frustrate that which is the chief duty of each one's office.

units.la: Hoc exemplo suo nos docuit sanctus Apostolorum coetus, quando communi pauperum curæ inservire recusauit, quùm hæc erat impedimento prædicationi verbi Dei; {u}Non æquum est, relicto verbo Dei, ministrare mensis: Rursus & Paulus suo, quando nè quidem {x}Baptizare voluerit, ut magis sedulò Evangelizaret. {y}Martha, sit licet erga Christum nimis officiosa, minùs tamen grata Christo, quandò partem reliquit meliorem. Id quod nunc probare contendimus; in naturali Pastoratu (ut non aliunde similitudines accersamus) vel maximè illustratur: Pastor enim Oves suas educit è caulis, nunc reducit, atque cogit, nunc insuper lauat, & ungit, nunc denique ligat, & urit; & si quæ alia opera Ovibus necessaria sint, diligenter curat & exequitur. Si verò ita totus in hæc munia incumbat, ut, (quod est præcipuum Pastoris ministerium) Oves pascere, pabulum ad vitam tolerandam necessarium suppeditare negligat, imò si totos dies dormiat, aut perpetuum moduletur ărundine carmen, quomodo, obsecro, impastarum omnium vērum[?] Pastor dici aut haberi potest?
units.tr: The holy company of the Apostles taught us this by their own example, when they refused to serve the common care of the poor, since this was a hindrance to preaching the Word of God: "It is not right, leaving the word of God, to serve tables." Again Paul, who did not even wish to baptize, so that he might evangelize more diligently. Martha, however attentive she was in serving Christ, was less pleasing to Christ, when she left the better part. What we now contend to prove is most clearly illustrated in the natural pastorate (so as not to fetch comparisons from elsewhere). For the shepherd leads his sheep out of the folds, now brings them back and gathers them, now also washes and anoints them, now finally binds and cauterizes them; and whatever other works are necessary for the sheep he diligently attends to and performs. But if he so wholly devotes himself to these tasks that he neglects what is the chief ministry of a shepherd, to feed the sheep and supply the food necessary to sustain life; indeed, if he sleeps whole days or endlessly plays the same tune on his reed, how, I ask, can he be called or considered a true shepherd of the flock?

units.la: De secundo Excusationis genere; Papa per alios concionari.
units.tr: On the second kind of excuse: the Pope preaches through others.

units.la: Bellarminus alibi.
units.tr: Bellarmine elsewhere.

units.la: {a}Non tenentur Pontifices per se concionari, & sacra administrare, satis est si curent per alios ista præstari. Et rursus: {b}Quod concionando non faciunt per se, faciunt per alios.
units.tr: {a} Popes are not bound to preach and administer the sacraments in person; it is enough that they see to it that these things are done through others. And again: {b} What they do not do in person by preaching, they do through others.

units.la: {a} Bellarm. lib. 3. de Pont. cap. 24. §. Adde.
units.tr: {a} Bellarm. book 3 on the Pope, ch. 24, section "Adde."

units.la: {b} Idem.lib.de Pont. c.15.§.Deinde.
units.tr: {b} The same, book on the Pope, ch. 15, section "Deinde."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: First Animadversion.

units.la: Papam per Vicarium, non per se concionantem, omni iudicio tàm humano, quàm diuino damnandum; & ex ipsis verbis[PASCE OVES]Pastoris nomine indignum probari.
units.tr: That the Pope, who does not preach in person but through a vicar, is to be condemned by every judgement, human as well as divine, and by the very words [FEED MY SHEEP] is shown to be unworthy of the name of Pastor.

units.la: Mirum sanè nobis videri non debet, si vos, quibus persuasum est vnum, in satisfactionibus praestandis, {c}Per alium teinunare ; in Eucharistia vnum {d}Per alium ( nempè Sacerdotem ) bibere ; in Conuersione Infidelium vnum {e}Per alium gignere : sic {f}Pastorem vnum per Alium pascere posse doceatis. possibile quidem esse Pastorem Oues per Alium pascere, quis negat? debere etiam, vbi necessitas effagitat, vltrò fatemur. Vt autem Pontifex Vicaria doctrina aliorum contentus, ipse personalem exuat prorsus, aut non aliquando exerceat, id Christi Vicario, Pastoriue legitimo conuenire posse pernegamus. Etenim, vt primo de officio Episcoporum in genere dicamus, Te (Bellarmine) testem locupletissimum habemus in praeclara illa quidem Admonitione tua ad Nepotem tuum Episcopum Theanensem. {f}Pastor (inquis) nec nomen Pastoris meretur, si non personaliter intendat gregi suo. --- Neque enim quilibet omnium Dominus, sed ille tantum, qui pascit suas, vocatur Pastor, iuxta verbum Domini ad Petrum, Pasce oues meas. {g}Tenetur Episcopus ad curam animarum, mediantibus his actibus personalibus, scilicet doctrina, ministratione, Sacramentorum, visitatione, &c. Episcopo dicitur, Vade, praedica populo Dei: {h}Etin ordinatione non dicitur, Mitte ad praedicandum. {i}Immo Concilij Tridentini verba sunt, sess. 5. 24. Quia praedicatio est praecipuum munus Episcopi, statuit & decernit S.Synodus, omnes Episcopos & Prelatos Ecclesiae teneri per seipsos, si legitimè impediti non fuerint, ad praedicandum; Quia & dixit Dominus Petro, [Pasce oues meas;] non dixit, Cura vt alij pascant. Haec Bellarminus, quibus dum patruus nepotem monet, Patrem suum, viz: Papam, non leuiter tangit & angit.
units.tr: It should not seem strange to us if you, who have persuaded yourselves that one man can {c} fast through another in performing satisfactions; that in the Eucharist one man can {d} drink through another (namely a priest); and that in the conversion of unbelievers one man can {e} beget through another; likewise teach that a single {f} pastor can feed through another. That it is possible for a pastor to feed his sheep through another, who denies it? We even freely confess that he ought to, where necessity demands it. But that a Pope, content with the teaching of others, should altogether strip off the personal office himself, or never exercise it at any time, this we deny can befit Christ's Vicar or a lawful pastor. For, to speak first of the office of bishops in general, we have as a most weighty witness you, Bellarmine, in your famous Admonition to your nephew, the Bishop of Teano. {f} "A pastor," you say, "does not even deserve the name of pastor if he does not attend to his flock in person. For not every lord, but only he who feeds his own, is called a shepherd, according to the Lord's word to Peter, Feed my sheep." {g} A bishop is bound to the care of souls through these personal acts, namely teaching, ministering, the sacraments, visitation, etc. To a bishop it is said, Go, preach to the people of God. {h} And in ordination it is not said, Send to preach. {i} Indeed these are the words of the Council of Trent, session 5, 24: Because preaching is the principal office of the bishop, the holy synod decrees and orders that all bishops and prelates of the Church are bound to preach themselves, unless they are lawfully hindered; because the Lord also said to Peter, [Feed my sheep;] he did not say, See that others feed. These are Bellarmine's words, by which the uncle, admonishing his nephew, does not lightly touch and sting his own father, namely the Pope.

units.la: {f} Bellar.admonit.ad Episc.Theanen. pa.10.
units.tr: {f} Bellarmine, Admonition to the Bishop of Teano, p. 10.

units.la: {g} Ibid.pag.11.
units.tr: {g} Ibid., p. 11.

units.la: {i} Ibid.pag.12.
units.tr: {i} Ibid., p. 12.

units.la: Amplissima hic quidem dicendi seges exoritur; sed plurima paucis complecti libet. vester Cl. Espencæus acerbè admodùm inuehitur in aliquot Rom. Ecclesiæ Episcopos, iam, post Conc. Tridentini reformationem scilicet: ab ipso Authore causam addiscamus. {k}Quotusquisq; (inquit) Prælatorum maiorum minorumé populum suum docere videtur? an illi ipsi decreti huius (nempe in Concilio Tridentino) Authores unquàm docuerunt, quorum exemplo aly ad munera sua facienda excitarentur? Certè ex nostratibus Episcopis, qui Tridenti, & Bononiæ pars aliquota fuerunt, nemo per se (quod quidem audiverim) docet. Ludimusne in re adeo seria? an potius hæc Decretorum specie reformationem posterioribus illudimus? Hæc Espencæus. Addit, nouisse se quosdam Episcopos, qui ut se adiistam docendis seruitutem demittant (generosi & excellenti viri!) teneri præstare negent: Quos (ait) cùm omnis omnium temporum historia Ecclesia, Concilia, Pontifices, Cesares, Superi, inferi, accusent, damnentq;, quis est qui absoluat? Hactenus Ille.
units.tr: Here indeed a vast field of discussion opens up, but I prefer to embrace most of it in a few words. Your famous Espencaeus inveighs quite bitterly against some bishops of the Roman Church, namely since the reformation of the Council of Trent; let us learn the reason from the author himself. {k} How few of the greater and lesser prelates, he says, seem to teach their people? Did those very authors of this decree (namely at the Council of Trent) ever teach, by whose example others might be stirred to perform their duties? Certainly among our own bishops, of whom some part were at Trent and at Bologna, no one (as far as I have heard) teaches in person. Are we playing at so serious a matter? Or rather do we mock later generations with this show of decrees? So Espencaeus. He adds that he knew some bishops who, lest they demean themselves with the servitude of teaching (noble and excellent men!), deny that they are bound to perform it. Whom (he says), when all the history of all times, the Church, the councils, the popes, the emperors, the heavens and the underworld accuse and condemn, who is there that absolves them? Thus far he.

units.la: Adeste igitur quotquot estis ex quonis[?] hominum ordine, Romanæ religionis professores, mecumq;[?] etiam animaduertite, quot, & quantis Iudicibus Pastor vester Rom. Pontifex damnetur, & nihil minus quàm Pastor esse convincitur. Iudice enim Espencæo; Episcopus non prædicans ab omnibus damnatur. Iudice {*}Bellarmino; Non meretur nomen Pastoris, qui necessariis officij actibus (talis est doctrina) non perfonaliter agit. {m}Iudice Hilario; {n}Ecclesiæ Episcopus, officij necessitate, hoc prædicationis ministerium debeo. Iudice Ambrosio; {o}Effugere non possumus docendi officium, quod nobis imposuit Sacerdotij necessitudo. Cui Hieronymus, Augustinus, Chrysostomus, (& quis non Patrum?) suffragatur. Iudice, (ex antiquorum Pontificum Senatu) 1o. Symmacho in Synodo Romanâ sibi, & Successoribus suis præiudicante; Væ erit nobis, si prædicare neglexerimus: 2o. Nicolao; Dispensatio cœlestis feminis nobis inuncta
units.tr: Come forward then, all of you, of whatever rank of men you are, professors of the Roman religion, and consider with me how many and how great judges condemn your Pastor, the Roman Pontiff, and how completely he is shown to be no pastor at all. For in the judgement of Espencaeus, a bishop who does not preach is condemned by everyone. In the judgement of {*} Bellarmine, he does not deserve the name of pastor who does not act in person in the necessary acts of his office (such is the doctrine). {m} In the judgement of Hilary: {n} As bishop of the Church, by the necessity of my office, I owe this ministry of preaching. In the judgement of Ambrose: {o} We cannot escape the duty of teaching, which the necessity of the priesthood has laid upon us. Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom (and who among the Fathers not?) support him. In the judgement (from the senate of the ancient Pontiffs) of 1. Symmachus, who in the Roman synod prejudged himself and his successors: Woe will be upon us if we have neglected to preach. 2. Nicholas: The heavenly dispensation of the seed has been enjoined upon us

units.la: {*} Paulo supra lib.f. est, vt si non sparserimus: Et 3°. In Ecclesia Romana{e} (vtor Espencæi verbis) Leo primus, Gregorius primus, & Innocentij duo, & si qui tales Romæ alij fuerunt Episcopi ijdem, & Ecclesiastæ, vt ex homilijs eorum patet. Leo sane adeo huius s. seruitutis deb.torem agnouit, vt sibi libertatem n.egaret tacere, aut fidelibus populis sermonis ossicium subtrahere. Hæc Espencæus; qui colophonem attexens: Tunc (inquit) adeo portenti instar habitum fuisset, si quis se pro Episcopo habuisset, qui non etiam re ipsa verum & proprium hoc Episcopi munus exhibuisset; quod hodie plusquam monstri loco haberetur, si quis exhiberet. Porrò Iudice Ecclesiâ Romanâ, in Synodo Tridentina, quâ decreuit, ideò Episcopos teneri Perseipsos prædicare, quia hoc est proprium eorum officium. Iudice etiam (qui idem decreuit, & confirmauit) Pontifice ipso. Imò etiam (nè se forte quisquam vel tanquàm innocentè excuset, vel tanquàm peccantem absoluet) Iudice Eo, qui est nostrâ conscientiâ maior, Immortali Deo, in veteri Testamento per Prophetas, qui Pastoribus non prædicantibus * VAE multiplex denunciauit; tum etiam in nouo Testamento per filium; quandò dixit aliis Apostolis, Pascite (Cuius mandati verba Pauli ad Timotheum, [* Prædica Tu verbum, insta tempestiuè, intempestiuè; &, VAE mihi nisi prædicauero] instar Commentarij esse possunt:) tum etiam peculiariter Petro, * Pasce oues meas, id est (interprete Bellarmino) * Pasce Tu, non per alios: vt intelligamus Pontificem ex ipsdem verbis demonstrari non esse Pastorem, ex quibus ipse Pastoratus sui fundamentum primum posuit.
units.tr: {*} as Paul said above, so that if we have not sown: and 3. In the Roman Church {e} (I use Espencaeus's words), Leo I, Gregory I, and the two Innocents, and whatever other bishops there were at Rome of this kind, were both bishops and preachers, as their homilies make plain. Leo indeed acknowledged himself so much a debtor of this sacred service that he denied himself the liberty to keep silent or to withhold the office of preaching from the faithful peoples. So Espencaeus; who, adding the finishing touch, says: Then it would have been so much a portent that, if anyone had called himself bishop without in fact exhibiting the true and proper office of bishop, it would be held as more than a monster today if anyone did so. Moreover, in the judgement of the Roman Church, in the Council of Trent, by which it decreed that bishops are bound to preach in person, because this is their proper office. Also in the judgement of the Pontiff himself, who decreed and confirmed the same. Yes, even (lest anyone excuse himself as innocent, or be absolved as a sinner) in the judgement of Him who is greater than our conscience, the Immortal God, who in the Old Testament through the Prophets pronounced manifold woes upon pastors who did not preach; then also in the New Testament through the Son, when he said to the other Apostles, Feed (the words of this command are like a commentary in Paul's words to Timothy, Preach the word, be instant in season, out of season, and Woe to me if I do not preach); and then especially to Peter, Feed my sheep, that is (in the interpretation of Bellarmine) Feed thou, not through others. So that we understand the Pontiff is shown by these very words not to be a pastor, the very words on which he laid the first foundation of his own pastorship.

units.la: Ite nunc, viri Pontificij, & Eum vniuersæ Ecclesiæ Pastorem, summum præcipuumque vendicate, qui vniuersalis Ecclesiæ tot tantisque testimonijs Pastoris nomine indignus esse conuincitur, quia præcipuum Pastoratus officium nequiter deseruit: atque ita dùm tanti gregis Dominus esse vult, certè quidem omninò (nam nomen hoc à præstantiori, nempè: verbo tanquam pabulo, Pascere, ortum habet) Pastor esse desinit. Non est igitur Papa verus Pastor. Qualis ergò? qualem Propheta describit, Zach. 11. [Ego suscitabo Pastorem in terris, qui derelicta non visitabit.] {a}Id est, (Ribera Ies.Commentatore) Pastorem, qui tantùm suæ vtilitati & ambitioni studebit, [oues non visitabit] id est, non curabit. Pastoris autem nomine significatur ANTICHRISTVS, quoniam & PASTOR, & DOCTOR, & REX, imo & DEVS haberi volet. --- [O Pastor, & idolum!] nempè qui præter figuram nihil habet Pastoris; qui Pastor videri & vocari cupit, quùm sit certissima pecorum pernicies, & vt idolum adorari ab illis velit. Hæc Iesuita; atque hæc de Pontificibus erga Reges.
units.tr: Go now, Papists, and claim for yourselves the chief and principal Pastor of the whole Church, when by so many and such great testimonies of the universal Church he is proved unworthy of the name of Pastor, because he has wickedly deserted the principal office of the pastorate. And so, while he wishes to be Lord of so great a flock, certainly he altogether ceases to be a pastor (for that name comes from the more excellent thing, namely feeding with the Word as with fodder). Therefore the Pope is not a true pastor. What then is he? Such as the Prophet describes in Zech. 11: Behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, who will not visit those that are forsaken. {a} That is (in Ribera's commentary), a shepherd who will study only his own advantage and ambition; will not visit, that is, will not care. By the name of Pastor is signified ANTICHRIST, since he will want to be held both PASTOR, and TEACHER, and KING, and even GOD. --- O Pastor and idol! That is, one who has nothing of a pastor but the outward appearance; who wishes to be seen and called a pastor, since he is the most certain destruction of the flocks, and wishes to be adored as an idol by them. Thus the Jesuit; and thus the Papists' attitude towards Kings.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Quosensu Principes ipsi Pontificum ac Sacerdotum Pa- stores iure haberi debeant.
units.tr: II. Animadversion. In what sense the princes themselves ought rightly to be regarded as the shepherds of the pontiffs and priests.

units.la: PRincipes seculi inter Oues, vel potiùs Arietes sub Pontifice Pastore ideo numerandos esse contendis, vt Reges eius ductui pareant; seu minùs, velint nolint, coactioni eius subdantur: qui clauus clauo pari facilè pellitur. Nam {b}Josua,& {c}Dauid, Principes longè illustrissimi, diuino oraculo Ecclesiæ Israëliticæ Pastores renunciati & constituti fuerunt: sed nec Tu, Bellarmine, vel in hoc De Principum officio Tractatu, Pastoris titulum Principibus inuides.
units.tr: You contend that the princes of the world are to be counted among the sheep, or rather the rams, under the Pontiff as shepherd, so that kings may obey his leading, or at least, whether they will or not, be subject to his compulsion. One nail is easily driven out by another of equal size. For Joshua {b} and David {c}, most illustrious princes, were declared and appointed shepherds of the Israelite Church by divine oracle. But you, Bellarmine, do not even in your treatise On the Office of Princes grudge princes the title of shepherd.

units.la: “ {d}Princeps (ais) non solùm caput in corpore, sed etiam quasi Pastor inter oues, sic enim loquitur Deus in Psal. 77.[Elegit Dauid seruum suum, & sustulit de gregibus ouium pascere Iacob seruum suum, & Israël hereditatem suam, & p.suit eos in innocentia cordis sui.] Vbi Dominus dicit (inquis) se exercuisse Dauidem in arte pastoritia ouium irrationalium, & deinde eum transtulisse ad officium pascendi populos ratione præditos. Nec solùm Dauidem Regem Hebræorum, sed, quod magis mirandum est, Cyrum ipsum Regem Persarum, apud Isaiam, vocat Pastorem suum, vum, “um, [Dico Cyro, Pastor meus es.] Denique (vt alia praetermittam) apud Ezechielem conqueritur Deus de Pastoribus Israël, id est, de Regibus, qui cùm essent ipsi deterrimi, populum ad exitium perduxerunt: & tandem subjicit, [Et suscitabo super Eos (oues scilicet gregis sui) Pastorem vnum seruum meum Dauid, ipse pascet eos, & ipse erit in Pastorem.] Haec Tu, rectè admodùm, & perquàm opportunè, præsertim quùm Sanctum Dauid (inquis) speculum Luciditsimum esse poterit Christianis Principibus omnibus. Bene est.
units.tr: “{d}You say that the prince is not only the head in the body but also, as it were, the shepherd among the sheep. For God speaks thus in Psalm 77: [He chose David his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds; from following the ewes great with young he brought him, to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance. So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart.] Here, you say, the Lord says that he trained David in the pastoral art with irrational sheep, and then transferred him to the office of feeding peoples endowed with reason. And not only David, king of the Hebrews, but, what is more remarkable, Cyrus himself, king of the Persians, he calls his shepherd in Isaiah: [Who says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd.] Finally (to pass over other things) God complains in Ezekiel about the shepherds of Israel, that is, the kings, who, being themselves most wicked, led the people to destruction; and at last he adds: [And I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.]” You say this quite rightly and very aptly, especially since you say that holy David could be a most luminous mirror for all Christian princes. Good.

units.la: Vtinam igitur omnes Principes Christiani suarum animarum oculos in hoc speculo diligentiùs defigerent, in quo cùm pietatis, prudentiæ, sanctitatis, innocentiæ, atque etiam authoritatis, curæque Pastoralis specimen egregium & luculentum facilè cernant; tum profectò tuam, Bellarmine, (vt leuissimè dicam) Incogitantiam discernant. Suprà enim in obscuro Pastoratus Papalis speculo Pontifices in Principes Christianos omnes Coactiuam potestatem temporalem intuitus es, quia scilicet Principes, respectu Papæ, in Ecclesia Christi sunt puræ putæ oues, quos Arietes dicis, id est, minorum Ouium ductores. Nunc autem in purissimo Dauidis speculo cernis Omnes Christianos Principes Pastores esse populi Dei, hereditatis Dei, & Gregis Domini. Pastores igitur Principes esse agnoscamus oportet, quos Deus, optimus imposuit, hoc nomine indigitat.
units.tr: Would that all Christian princes therefore fixed the eyes of their souls more diligently on this mirror, in which they may easily discern a remarkable and clear example of piety, prudence, holiness, innocence, and indeed of authority and pastoral care. Then they would surely discern your inconsistency, Bellarmine (to speak most gently). For above, in the dim mirror of the papal pastorate, you looked upon all Christian princes as subject to the pope's coercive temporal power, because, you say, with respect to the Pope, princes in the Church of Christ are mere sheep, whom you call rams, that is, leaders of the lesser sheep. But now in the most pure mirror of David you see that all Christian princes are shepherds of the people of God, the inheritance of God, and the flock of the Lord. Let us acknowledge, then, that princes must be shepherds, since God, the best and greatest, has set them over his people and designates them by this name.

units.la: Nec hic locum habet exceptio tua, quùm dicis, quòd Princeps omnis est Sacerdotis spiritualis, sed Sacerdos omnis Principipis nullo modo dici potest, quoniam omnes Clerici suam beneficiale potestatem (spiritualem à Papa, à quo non solùm in spiritualibus, sed etiam in temporalibus regunter. Quid ais? Clerici habent suam potestatem à Pastore spirituali, à quo non modò spiritualiter, sed etiam temporaliter regantur? Absurdè, quid enim Pastori, omninò spirituali, cum regimine temporali? hoc certè perinde est, ac si quis dixerit; Voluntas humana rationalem facultatem habet à luà lumine animæ rationalis, quâ non modò rationaliter, sed etiam irrationaliter & sensualiter regitur. Quodsi candidè & accuratè causam hanc tractare velles, distinguendum Tibi esset, (in quo sanè Causæ totius cardo vertitur) nimirùm Sacerdotes, respectu muneris spiritualis, Principum Pastores; at, respectu facultatis temporalis coæ̃tiuæ, quâ vel protegunturtemporaliter, vel etiam corriguntur, omninò Principum Oues esse censendas.
units.tr: Your exception has no place here either, when you say that "every prince is subject to the spiritual priest, but no priest can be said to be subject to a prince, since all clerics have their power (spiritual) from the Pope, by whom they are governed not only in spiritual but also in temporal matters." What do you say? Clerics have their power from a spiritual shepherd, by whom they are governed not only spiritually but also temporally? Absurd! For what has a purely spiritual shepherd to do with temporal government? This is just as if someone should say: "The human will has its rational faculty from the light of the rational soul, by which it is governed not only rationally but also irrationally and sensually." If you wished to treat this cause candidly and accurately, you would have had to distinguish (and on this distinction the whole matter turns): priests, with respect to their spiritual office, are shepherds of princes; but with respect to their temporal coercive power, by which they are either protected or even corrected in temporal matters, they must be judged to be altogether the sheep of princes.

units.la: Protectionem Principum tantùm abest ut Sacerdotes, aut etiam ipsi Pontifices non agnoscant, vt eam non nunquàm etiam vehementer efflāgitent. quod agnoscunt, Azorius Iesuita palàm facit; Imperatori (inquit) Clerici sunt commissi, ut Patrono, Protectori, & Propugnatori Ecclesiæ. De Papis autem: Erant (inquit Idem) Imperatores iuris & privilegij Pontificij Patrons & conseruatores. Audin', Bellarmine? An Eos, qui sunt Pastorum tuorum Patroni & Protectores, Tu tantùm Arietes dixeris? an etiam Arietum præsidio ipsos Pastores indigere censes? Indigere verò Pontifices interdùm Imperatorum & Principum auxilijs, illa Baronij sanè vehemens querela declarat, vbi dicit; Non sine summo dedecore Christianorum Principum, Iohannem VIII. Papam eorum Præsidio destitutum; atque adeò, vt se liberaret ab Ingruentibus Saracenis, pacemque suam redimeret, ad Tributum ingens eisdem (Saracenis) annuatim soluendum coactum fuisse. Et certè Turca, ceu Aper sylvestris, & nocturnus Lupus, Romanos Pontifices saepè iampridem devorâsset, nisi Imperatores & Principes immanissimo huius belluæ furori sese agmine facto obiecissent. Nec tamen postmodùm Papas puduit Coactiuâ potestate temporali Principes, Patronos suos, indignissimè coërcere atque affligere (ô ingratos ventres!) adeòque in hos Arietes scilicet ferocire, tanquàm qui habeant imperium in meras belluas.
units.tr: So far are priests, or even the pontiffs themselves, from failing to acknowledge the protection of princes, that they not infrequently even vehemently demand it. The Jesuit Azorius plainly admits this. To the emperor (he says) the clerics have been entrusted, as to a patron, protector, and defender of the Church. Concerning the popes, he says: The emperors were patrons and conservers of the papal right and privilege. Do you hear this, Bellarmine? Will you call only rams those who are the patrons and protectors of your shepherds? Or do you think the shepherds themselves need the defence of the rams? That the pontiffs at times need the aid of emperors and princes is shown clearly enough by that vehement complaint of Baronius, where he says: Not without the greatest disgrace of Christian princes, Pope John VIII was left without their protection; and so, to free himself from the attacking Saracens and to buy back his peace, he was forced to pay them an enormous tribute every year. And certainly the Turk, like a wild boar of the woods or a nocturnal wolf, would long ago have devoured the Roman pontiffs often, had not emperors and princes thrown themselves in a body against the savage fury of this beast. Yet afterwards the popes were not ashamed to coerce and afflict most shamefully, by temporal coercive power, their patrons, the princes (O ungrateful bellies!), and to rage against these rams, as if they had dominion over mere beasts.

units.la: Quod ad Correctionem attinet; Historiæ plenæ sunt Exemplorum eorum Imperatorum, qui Pontifices &c. impios castigârunt authoritate suâ, & in ordinem redigerunt. Bellarminus factum Eorum non negat; Ius vero coactiuum Illorum in Papas exagitat: quod tamen Mosis, Hezechiæ, Iosuæ, aliorumque sanctissimorum Regum exemplis (à Bellarmino collectis) etiam magni nominis Doctores Pontificij (vel nobis tacentibus) diserte {*}confirmabunt. {l}Gregorius VII. Pontifex cogebat Clericos barbas suas radere. quis vetat? at nè Papæ Principes cogant, vel pilum eorum attingant, {m}Diuino iure prohibetur.
units.tr: As for correction: histories are full of examples of those emperors who, by their authority, punished impious pontiffs etc. and brought them into order. Bellarmine does not deny the deed, but he attacks their right of coercion over the popes. Yet even the Papists' own teachers of great name will clearly confirm this (even if we keep silent) by the examples of Moses, Hezekiah, Joshua, and the other most holy kings collected by Bellarmine. Pope Gregory VII compelled the clerics to shave their beards. Who forbids it? But that princes should compel the popes or touch so much as a hair of theirs {m} is forbidden by divine right.

units.la: CAP. III. DE TERTIO TITULO PAPAE, VIDELICET, DOCTOR, vel IUDEX.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. ON THE THIRD TITLE OF THE POPE, NAMELY, TEACHER OR JUDGE.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office.

units.la: Tertium est nomen Doctoris, quo nomine usum esse Conc. Florentinum, cum in Decreto suo Romanum Pontificem appellandum censuit Doctorem omnium Christianorum. ---Pag.28.
units.tr: The third is the name of Teacher, which the Council of Florence used when, in its decree, it judged that the Roman Pontiff should be called the Teacher of all Christians. ---Page 28.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Quid Concilium censuerit, postea videbimus: quo vero sensu atque animo Tu hunc Titulum vrgeas, exponere, quaeso, ne grauere. {a}Rom. Pontificem succedere Petro, in Monarchia Ecclesiastica, probatur. {b}Ex nominibus quae Rom. Pontifici tribui solent; Duodecimum est Pater, & Doctor omnium Christianorum: ita habemus in Conc. Florent. Sess. ultima.
units.tr: What the Council judged we shall see later. But in what sense and with what intention you press this title, please explain, and do not hesitate. That the Roman Pontiff succeeds Peter in the ecclesiastical monarchy is proved. Among the names usually given to the Roman Pontiff, the twelfth is Father and Teacher of all Christians; so we have it in the Council of Florence, last session.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Titulum Doctoris, communem Aliis, Pontifici propriam Monarchiam stabilire non posse.
units.tr: I. OBSERVATION. That the title of Teacher, which is shared by others, cannot establish a monarchy peculiar to the Pope.

units.la: Sacerdotes Christi Ecclesia semper eximiis titulis decorauit atque ornauit, quibus tamen Ministerij Eorum virtutes varias, non autem vnius Dominij praepotentiam praestantiamque designari voluit. Nomen igitur Patris Illis, tanquam charitatis; Pastoris, tanquam vigilantiae, atque industriae; Doctoris item, tanquam scientiae nota & symbolum tribuebatur: at, tanquam Iurisdictionis Monarchicae indicium, nè per somnium quidem. Pontifex Rom. (inquis) dicitur Pater Patrum: dicitur Pastor ovilis Dominici: dicitur Doctor omnium Christianorum. Ergo in Monarchia Ecclesiastica successit Petro. Mirus Tu sanè artifex, Bellarmine, qui veluti ex quovis ligno Mercurium, ità ex singulis nominibus, quae Episcopo Romano tribui solent, Monarcham tuum fabricasti. Sed dic, amabò, Bellarmine, num Doctor omnium Christianorum cum Monarcha idem plane sonat? {*}Origenes à Didymo, Ecclesiarum Magister, Chrysostomus à Greg. Nisseno, Magnus totius orbis Doctor; Cyprianus, ab Augustino, Praclarissimus Doctor; Gregorius Nazianzenus (vt ait Ruffinus) ab omnibus Graecis primus, post Evangelistam Ioannem, Theologus vocatus est. Si igitur in isto Doctoris Titulo tanta vis sit, vt Monarcham demonstret, quot (quaeso) iamdū[?] Monarchas simul Respub. Christiana praeter, nè dicam supra Romanum Pontificem habuisset? Tu vero ad Conci-lium Florentinum provocas.
units.tr: The Church has always adorned and decorated the priests of Christ with distinguished titles, yet by these it meant to designate various virtues of their ministry, not the power and pre-eminence of a single lordship. So the name of Father was given to them as a mark of love, that of Pastor as a mark of watchfulness and diligence, and likewise that of Teacher as a mark and token of learning. But as a sign of monarchical jurisdiction, not even in a dream. You say: the Roman Pontiff is called Father of Fathers; he is called the Pastor of the Lord's flock; he is called Teacher of all Christians. Therefore he succeeded Peter in an ecclesiastical monarchy. You are indeed a clever craftsman, Bellarmine, who, as though from any wood whatever, have fashioned your monarch from the individual names usually given to the Bishop of Rome, as one might make Mercury from any block. But tell me, pray, Bellarmine, does Teacher of all Christians mean exactly the same as monarch? Origen was called by Didymus Teacher of the Churches; Chrysostom by Gregory of Nyssa, Great Teacher of the whole world; Cyprian by Augustine, a most distinguished Teacher; Gregory Nazianzen (as Rufinus says) was called Theologian by all the Greeks, first after the Evangelist John. If, then, there is such force in this title of Teacher that it proves a monarch, how many monarchs (I ask) would the Christian commonwealth have had at the same time, not to say above the Roman Pontiff? Yet you appeal to the Council of Florence.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Papam in Conc. Florentino speciem magis quam vim authoritatis habuisse.
units.tr: II. OBSERVATION. That at the Council of Florence the Pope had the appearance of authority rather than its force.

units.la: VErum est, Doctor vester Eugenius IIII. Pontif. Concilio Florentino Iudex praefuit, eodem tempore, quando quandò in Conc. Basileensi idem Doctor {c}Eugenius, tanquàm contumax Violator Canonum Synodalium, vnitatis Ecclesiæ turbator, Simoniacus, periurus, Schismaticus, & à fide deuius, pertinax hereticus, à Pontificatu depositus declaratus est. Ecce Christianorum omnium Doctorem, scilicet! Qui, qualem vel Doctorem, vel Monarcham in Florentino Conc. se præstiterit, argumento nobis luculentissimo esse potest eius, in illo Concilio, cum Græcis transactio; apud quos, authoritate suâ, cùm parum valeret, {d}Sententiabat rem commodè aliter quàm per disputationes finiri non posse. Cùmque rationibus, pollicitationibusque magnopere instaret, vehementiúsque vrgeret, vt ipse Patriarcham quendam, ab illis Electum, confirmaret, nec obtineret; ægrè repulsam tulit, & {e}Se suauissimis verbis excusans, Græcos demisit. Nempè, vt possumus agendum, quandò vt volumus non licet. Quid igitur nos verba audimus, cùm facta vidimus? Hæc de Concilio Florentino. nunc quanta vobis videatur esse Doctoris & Iudicis vestri authoritas, explica.
units.tr: It is true that your Teacher, Pope Eugenius IV, presided over the Council of Florence as judge, at the same time when, in the Council of Basel, the same Teacher Eugenius, as a stubborn violator of synodal canons, a disturber of the Church's unity, a simoniac, a perjurer, a schismatic, and one who had strayed from the faith, a obstinate heretic, was declared deposed from the papacy. Behold the Teacher of all Christians, forsooth! What sort of teacher or monarch he showed himself to be in the Florentine Council can be shown by the most evident proof, namely his dealings with the Greeks at that council; among whom, since his own authority counted for little, he judged that the matter could not conveniently be settled otherwise than by disputations. And when he pressed hard with arguments and promises, and urged most vehemently that he himself should confirm a certain patriarch elected by them, and did not prevail, he took the rebuff ill, and excusing himself in the sweetest words, he dismissed the Greeks. Clearly, we act as we can when we may not act as we wish. Why then should we listen to words when we have seen deeds? So much for the Council of Florence. Now explain how great you think the authority of your Teacher and Judge is.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office.

units.la: “ Pontificem Doctorem omnium Christianorum dici, proprie “ locum habet in Doctrina fidei Catholica, quam non solùm “ docere, sed etiam definire cum potestate debet, vt simul & “ Doctor & Iudex haberi debeat. --- Pag.28.
units.tr: "That the Pontiff is properly called Teacher of all Christians has its place in the doctrine of the Catholic faith, which he must not only teach but also define with authority, so that he ought to be held both Teacher and Judge at once. ---Page 28."

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Id est (vt Tu alibi liquidiùs) Pontifex est absolutè supra Conc. generale, & nullum in terris supra se iudicium agnoscit; & contraria sententia non est toleranda.
units.tr: That is (as you say more clearly elsewhere): The Pope is absolutely above a general council, and acknowledges no judgment on earth above himself; and the contrary opinion is not to be tolerated.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. OBSERVATION.

units.la: Papam Concilio Generali subesse.
units.tr: That the Pope is subject to a General Council.

units.la: IMò aut toleranda est contraria sententia, aut Ecclesiæ Romanæ Doctores sanè egregij tollendi sunt, qui Eam acerrimè defenderunt, vt (nimirùm) {*}Card. Cameracensis, Nicolaus Campanus, Panormitanus, Card. Florentinus, rentimus, & alij Concilij {a}Basileensis Patres; Qui (Te fatentur) statuerunt generale Concilium esse supra omnem potestatem in terris. Nec hoc solùm, sed Basileenses Patres Eum Haereticum esse definiuerunt, qui huic sententiae pertinaciter se opposuerit. Quam praeterea etiam Schola Sorbonica. Professores in hunc usque diem constanter defenderunt. Quam etiam {o}Conc. Constantiensis Patres Mille suis suffragijs publicis unanimiter comprobárunt. Quam {p}Card. Cusanus, ex Dimes, Zozimo, Leone Papa fusè copiosèque confirmauit. Priùs igitur vos de Iudicio vestri potestate aptiùs inter vos consentire, quàm Nos illius iudicio subijcere debuistis. Tu humanae Traditionis auxilio destitutus, diuinum praetexis: pergis enim.
units.tr: Indeed, either the contrary opinion must be tolerated, or the outstanding teachers of the Roman Church must be removed, those who defended it most fiercely: namely the Cardinal of Cambrai, Nicolaus Campanus, Panormitanus, the Cardinal of Florence, Rentimus, and the other Fathers of the Council of Basel. These (as you yourself admit) decreed that a general council is above every power on earth. And not only this: the Fathers of Basel defined that he is a heretic who obstinately opposes this opinion. Besides, the Sorbonne faculty has constantly defended it down to the present day. The Fathers of the Council of Constance, a thousand of them, unanimously confirmed it by their public votes. Cardinal Cusanus, drawing on Dionysius, Zosimus and Pope Leo, set it forth and confirmed it at length and in full. Therefore you ought to agree among yourselves more fittingly about the power of your Judge than we ought to submit to his judgment. Since you lack the support of human tradition, you put forward the divine; for you go on.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office.

units.la: “Quia Dominus S. Petro Luc. 22. dixit; [Ecce Satan expetiit vos cribrare sicut triticum, Ego autem rogavi pro Te, ne deficiat fides tua; & tu aliquando conversus confirma fratres tuos:] Ideo in dubiis ad sedem Petri recurrendum omnibus est. — pag. 28.”
units.tr: "Because the Lord said to St Peter, Luke 22: [Behold, Satan has sought to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.] Therefore in doubtful matters everyone must have recourse to the seat of Peter. — p. 28."

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Vt & alibi. {q}¶ Quibus verbis clarissimè Dominus ostendit, Petrum fore Principem, & Caput fratrum suorum: sic enim exponunt Patres Graeci, & Latini.
units.tr: As also elsewhere. {q} ¶ By these words the Lord most clearly shows that Peter will be the Prince and Head of his brethren; for so the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, expound them.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. OBSERVATION.

units.la: Sensum verborum [Confirma Fratres] celebriorem & veriorem Bellarminiana expositioni adversari.
units.tr: That the more common and truer sense of the words [Strengthen the brethren] runs counter to Bellarmine's exposition.

units.la: PEtrus Confirmator fratrum, Ergo (inquis) supra reliquos Apostolos Iudex destignatus est. Argute: distinguendum Tibi fuit, hic, nimirum, intelligi non authoritatis, sed experientiae Confirmationem; nec à iudicio, sed ab exemplo Petri deducendam. At Patres (inquis) Graeci & Latini sic (nempè sicut Tu) expenunt: vnde quis non putet te iam Patrum omnium authoritatem pro expositione tua vendicare? Vafrè hoc admodùm; nam, ex vniuersis Græcis, tantum Theophylactum: ex Latinis, Leonem duntaxat allegas: & tamen Expositionis nostræ veritatem etiam Theophylactus tuus docere te potuit. [Confirma fratres.] {e} De omnibus fidelibus (inquit) vsque ad consummationem seculi futuris dictum est, quod confirmatum fuerint à Petro: [Tu conuersus,] Id est, Tu bonum exemplum Poenitentiæ eris omnibus, vt nullus credentium in te respiciens desperet. Patres alij testes aut muti sunt, aut tibi reclamantes.
units.tr: Peter is the strengthener of the brethren; therefore (you say) he was marked out as judge over the other Apostles. Cleverly argued! You ought to have distinguished here: the strengthening meant is not one of authority but of experience, and it is to be derived not from judgement but from Peter's example. But the Fathers, Greek and Latin (you say), expound it thus, that is, just as you do. From this, who would not think you were already claiming the authority of all the Fathers for your exposition? A very sly move indeed. For out of all the Greeks you cite only Theophylact, and out of the Latins only Leo; and yet your own Theophylact could have taught you the truth of our exposition. [Strengthen the brethren.] {e} It was said of all the faithful, to be future until the end of the world, that they were to be strengthened by Peter. [When thou art converted,] that is, you will be a good example of repentance to all, so that no believer, looking to you, will despair. The other Fathers are either silent witnesses or speak against you.

units.la: Sed quid Patres morer? cùm præsertim nonnulli è fratribus tuis nobis astipulentur. [Confirma fratres] {f} Id (Sà Iefin cum le-est, (inquit Emanuel Sà) Sicut ego orando Te protexi, ne deficeres; tu infirmiores exemplo pænitentiæ tuæ conforta, ne à venia desperent. Rursus, [Confirma fratres.] Id est (ait Arias Montanus) oratione & exemplo; ita demum fiat, vt Satanas studium irritum cuadat, cùm tuam ruinam fratrum tuorum confirmationem esse viderit. Denique Aquinas, præceptor tuus, in hanc sententiam Bedam, & Theophylactum profert; quæ quidem clarior est, quàm vt authoritate aut confirmatione aliquâ indigeat. Hanc ad nonnullos Rom. Pontifices (quos * supra citauimus) accommodemus; qui suis fœdissimis flagitiosissimisque Exemplis peccatores alios in sacrilegijs, parricidijs, periurijs, aliisque scelerebus obfirmare facilè possint, Pœnitentium animos in spe veniæ confirmare non possunt. Hoc de illis verbis, [Confirmi fratres,] in quibus Petrum vidimus, Papam verò nondum. Hoc præsta.
units.tr: But why should I dwell on the Fathers, especially since some of your own brethren support us? [Strengthen the brethren] {f} This, says Emmanuel Sá, means: as I protected you by prayer lest you fail, so you, by the example of your repentance, strengthen the weaker, lest they despair of pardon. Again, [Strengthen the brethren.] That is (says Arias Montanus), by prayer and example; in this way at last Satan's attempt is made void, when he sees that your fall has become the strengthening of your brethren. Finally, Aquinas, your own teacher, brings in Bede and Theophylact in support of this view; and that view is clearer than to need any authority or any support. Let us apply this to some of the Roman Pontiffs (whom we cited above*), who by their most foul and shameful examples can easily confirm other sinners in sacrileges, parricides, perjuries and other crimes, but cannot confirm the minds of penitents in the hope of pardon. So much for those words, [Strengthen the brethren], in which we have seen Peter, but not yet the Pope. Make good on this.

units.la: Bellarminus alibi vrget verba reliqua Luc. 22.
units.tr: Bellarmine elsewhere presses the remaining words of Luke 22.

units.la: [Orauì prote, nè deficiat fides tua.]
units.tr: [But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not.]

units.la: {a} Vera expositio est, quod Dominus duo priuilegia Petro impertierit, unum, vt ipse non possit vnquam veram fidem amittere; Alterum, vt ipse tanquam Pontifex non possit vnquam docere aliquid contra fidem. Primù fortasse non manauit ad Posteros: & secundum sine dubio manauit ad Successores, ut Pontifices, tanquam Pontifices, nunquam possint docere aliquid contra fidem.
units.tr: {a} The true explanation is that the Lord bestowed two privileges on Peter: first, that he himself could never lose true faith; second, that he, as Pontiff, could never teach anything against the faith. The first perhaps did not pass down to posterity; but the second undoubtedly passed down to successors, so that Pontiffs, as Pontiffs, can never teach anything contrary to the faith.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Illud [Non deficere] non uni Petro proprium: sed Aliis Apostolis charisma commune fuisse.
units.tr: I. OBSERVATION. That [not to fail] was not peculiar to Peter alone, but was a gift common to the other Apostles.

units.la: DUo illa beneficia, in Petrum collata, (quae Tu Priuilegia vocas) quid aliud significant (nam eò spectat ratio vestra) quàm haec duo uni Petro propria & peculiaria fuisse, ut nec ipse in se deficere, nec Alios decipere unquam posset; Coeteros autem Apostolos nulla tali praerogatiuà munitos fuisse? Hanc enim vim habet vox, Priuilegium, ut significet priuatam & singularem gratiam, quia {b}Priuilegia, ait A.Gellius, sunt priuatá iussa, ad singulares homines pertinentia, quae veteres Prima dixerunt, quae nos singula dicimus. Tale autem Priuilegium Petro proprium fuisse? Hoc deliramehtum fortasse ex tuis ipsius verbis hausit vester Bzouius, sic enim Ille, Pro Petro unico Christus orauit, ne eius fides deficeret, ut ipse unicus fratres omnes accuratius solidaret. Quasi vero Christus non orauerit praecipuè pro alijs, quùm diceret, [{d}Pater pro his rogo, quos mihi dedisti:] aut non eadem Priuilegia alijs promiserit, vbi ait, [c Cùm venerit Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem,] Id est(inquit Toletus Iesuita) Apostoli cdocti & illustrati erant in ijs siue quae ad dogmata, siue quae ad mores, siue quae ad regendam Ecclesiam pertinebant. Id quod disertè etiam Salmeron Iesuita testatur, Hoc pie & magnâ ratione putandum est(inquit) Apostolos omnes non modò deficere non potuisse, sed necerrare in fide.
units.tr: These two benefits conferred on Peter (which you call privileges) what else do they signify (for your argument aims at this) than that these two were proper and peculiar to Peter alone, so that he himself could never fail in himself nor deceive others, while the remaining Apostles were not fortified by any such prerogative? For the word privilege has this force, to signify a private and singular grace, since {b} privileges, says Aulus Gellius, are private laws, pertaining to particular men, which the ancients called prima, and which we call singula. But was such a privilege peculiar to Peter? Your Bzovius perhaps drew this nonsense from your own words, for he says: Christ prayed for Peter alone, that his faith might not fail, so that he alone might more diligently strengthen all the brethren.
