As if Christ had not prayed especially for the others, when he said, [{d}Father, I pray for those whom thou hast given me], or had not promised the same privileges to the others, where he says, [When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth]. That is (says the Jesuit Toletus), the Apostles were taught and enlightened in those things which pertained either to doctrine, or to morals, or to governing the Church. The Jesuit Salmerón also clearly attests this: It is to be piously and with great reason believed (he says) that all the Apostles not only could not fail, but could not even err in the faith.

units.la: Quod denique Apostolus Paulus asseuerantèr professus est, vbi (scribens ad Corinthios), tanquàm ex impossibili infert; h Tum comperimur falsi testes. Hæc pro Apostolis; nunc contra Pontificem.
units.tr: Finally, the Apostle Paul asserted this earnestly, where (writing to the Corinthians) he infers, as from an impossibility: Then we are found false witnesses. So much for the Apostles; now against the Pontiff.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Personale Petri priuilegium nullo iure transferri in Papam.
units.tr: II. REMARK. The personal privilege of Peter is not transferred to the Pope by any right.

units.la: Dixit Christus Petro, Rogaui pro te, ne deficiat fides tua.] Quibus verbis duplex priuilegium Petro concessum fuisse, nullus non concesserit: Vnum respectu sui, nè ipse aberraret à fide; Alterum respectu Ecclesiæ, nè alios seduceret. Quorum neutrum vi huius Textus ad Papam Romanum promanare, non asserere solum, verum etiam illæsa conscientia iurare quiuis potest. Nec dubito quin Bellarminus in hanc sententiam, ex concessis suis, necessario cogatur.
units.tr: Christ said to Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. From these words, no one fails to grant that a twofold privilege was given to Peter: one with respect to himself, that he himself should not go astray from the faith; the other with respect to the Church, that he should not lead others astray. Neither of these can be derived from this text to the Roman Pope. Anyone can not only assert this but also swear to it with a clear conscience. Nor do I doubt that Bellarmine, from his own concessions, is necessarily compelled to this opinion.

units.la: Prima Ratio. Omnes Pontificij duplicem personam in Petro considerant, vnam publicam, quoad Ecclesiam; vnde est quod acceperit priuilegium non deficiendi à fide, nempe quatenus erat Apostolus; nec decipiendi alios: Alteram priuatam, quoad animam suam, quo respectu obtinuerat Priuilegium, quatenus erat priuatus Doctor, nè ipse seduceretur errore aliquo in fide. Si iam vtrumque priuilegium per verba Christi, hoc in loco, in Petrum collatum, Petro omninò personale fuisse constiterit, certè quidem vicimus; quia, ex omnium confessione, quibus verbis donum aliquod personale in quempiam intenditur atque confertur, ex verborum eorum vi, idem in personam aliam, absque summa Textus iniuria, transferri nequit. Vtrumque autem hisce verbis in Petrum collatum Petro personale, & singulare, siue quoad personam publicam, nè doctrinis aut Decretis suis Ecclesiam in errorem induceret; siue quoad personam priuatam, nè ipse opinionis suæ errore seductus à fide deficeret, verba ipsa perspicuè demonstrant.
units.tr: First reason. All the Papists consider a twofold person in Peter: one public, as regards the Church, whence he received the privilege of not failing in the faith, namely in so far as he was an Apostle, and of not deceiving others; the other private, as regards his own soul, with respect to which he had the privilege in so far as he was a private teacher, so that he himself would not be led astray by some error in the faith. If it is now established that both privileges, conferred upon Peter in this passage by the words of Christ, were wholly personal to Peter, then we have certainly won; for, by the admission of all, when a personal gift is intended and conferred upon someone by words of this kind, by the force of those words it cannot be transferred to another person without great injury to the text. That both privileges conferred on Peter by these words were personal and singular to him, whether as regards his public person, so that he would not lead the Church into error by his doctrines or decrees, or as regards his private person, so that he himself, seduced by an error of opinion, would not fall from the faith, the words themselves clearly demonstrate.

units.la: Ad Bellarminum ipsum provoco. {i}Quia Dominus (inquit) vnam tantùm personam designauit, dicens; Simon, Simon; & addens toties pronomen secundæ personæ, videlicet, Pro Te, & fides Tua, & Tu conuersus, & confirma fratres Tuos : Certè si intellexisset de tota Ecclesia, Dixisset, Rogavi pro vobis. Hæc ille. Nihil profecto rectius dici potuit, nihil aptius ; neque enim illud Privilegium non errandi, quod alibi acceperunt Apostoli, hoc Textu innuitur. Eodem plane Argumento Nos ; Quià Dominus unam tantùm personam, idque singulariter totidem verbis designavit, [Simon, Simon ;] addens toties pronomen secundæ personæ, Te, Tua, Tu, Tuos ; certè si subintellexisset in Petro reliquos eius Successores, non tantùm dixisset, [Rogavi pro Te,] verùm etiam pro Tuis : nam hac voce, Simon, Simon, quà (ut ipse vis) Paulus Apostolus, eàdem pariter Paulus V. hodiernus, & quivis alius Episcopus Rom. excluditur : ad quem, ex vi huius Textus, omen Simonis, non magis quàm nomen, ad Paulum vestrum manavit. Hoc confirmatur ex natura personalis Privilegij, {k}Quod (ut inquit Salas Ief.) veluti adhæret personæ immediatè, quod vel singulare est, vel commune ; singulare, quod alicui personæ individuo tantùm concedebatur, expressò eius nomine, & hoc in iure absolutè vocatur personale, & cùm persona incedit, durat & finitur. Sic ille verè accuratèque docuit. Hæc ad Causam accommodemus. Hoc Privilegium, in his Christi verbis nominatim Simoni Apostolo, non vlli Bonifacio, Clementi, Paulo Pontifici concedebatur. Ergò Privilegium non deficiendi à fide, quod Papa sibi concessum putat, ex his Christi ad Petrum verbis, Petro moriente, expiravit.
units.tr: I appeal to Bellarmine himself. Because the Lord (he says) designated only one person, saying, Simon, Simon; and adding so often the pronoun of the second person, namely, For thee, and thy faith, and when thou art converted, confirm thy brethren. Certainly, if he had meant the whole Church, he would have said, I have prayed for you. Thus he. Nothing more correct could be said, nothing more apt; for that privilege of not erring, which the Apostles received elsewhere, is not implied by this text. By the very same argument we say: because the Lord designated only one person, and that singly, with so many words, [Simon, Simon,] adding so often the pronoun of the second person, Thee, Thy, Thou, Thy brethren; certainly, if he had intended to include in Peter his other successors, he would not have said only, [I have prayed for thee,] but also, for thine. For by this name, Simon, Simon, by which (as you yourself wish) the Apostle Paul is excluded, in the same way Paul V, the present one, and any other Bishop of Rome is excluded too; to whom, by the force of this text, the name of Simon has no more passed than the name has passed to your Paul. This is confirmed from the nature of a personal privilege, which (as Salas the Jesuit says) adheres immediately to the person, and is either singular or common; singular, which was granted only to some individual person, with his name expressly stated, and this in law is called absolutely personal, and when the person goes, it lasts and ends. Thus he taught truly and accurately. Let us apply this to our cause. This privilege, in these words of Christ, was granted by name to Simon the Apostle, not to any Boniface, Clement or Paul the Pope. Therefore the privilege of not failing in the faith, which the Pope thinks was granted to himself, from these words of Christ to Peter, expired when Peter died.

units.la: Ratio secunda. Quicquid erat Privilegij sivè non errandi in se, in quæstione fidei, sive non implicandi alios in errore, in S. Petrum collatum, illud totum Christus absque omni distinctionis notà eodem verborum tenore complexus est. Ergò ex his aut utrumque Privilegium Petri Successoribus competere ex Christi verbis elici potest ; aut neutrum. Quod ad Assumptionem attinet, Ego rursus Bellarminum appello. {1}Primum privilegium (inquit) ut nunquàm fidem veram amitteret, fortasse non manavit ad Successores. [Fortasse non manauit:] tum falso, tam etiam hæsitanter dictum, multò verò rectius, quandò addis ; {m}Conuenient omnes Catholici (inquis) in hoc, quòd Pontifex, vt priuatus Doctor, poßit errare, etiam in quæstionibus iuris universalibus tam fidei, quàm morum, idque ex ignorantia, vt alijs Doctoribus interdum accidit. Sic Tu; in quo sensu habes Protestantes tecum Catholicissimè sentientes; qui credunt Pontifices vestros adeò erroribus obnoxios, vt non possint interdùm non perniciosè errare; eóque facilius hoc credimus, quòd in expositione huius loci, in quo Privilegij huius præcipuum fundamentum posuit, turpissimè erraui. Nam si eadem verba Petro iuxta & Papæ dicta fuerunt, qui fit, vt quibus verbis duo privilegia concedantur Petro, unicum duntaxat in Papam conferatur? quæ malum! hæc peversitas, sensum eum divellere, quem Spiritus S. coniunxit; contra universale illud Axioma, quod humanarum & divinarum legum omnium nigro rubróque habetur, Ubi lex non distinguit, nec Nos distinguere debemus? Contráque Privilegiorum omnium verba interpretandi Regulam, à Jesuita allatam, nempè, {n}Quando verba Privilegij sunt clara, nec restringenda, nec extendenda sunt?
units.tr: Second reason. Whatever privilege there was, either of not erring in itself in a question of faith, or of not involving others in error, was conferred on St Peter; Christ embraced all of it, without any mark of distinction, in the same tenor of words. Therefore either both privileges of Peter can be drawn from the words of Christ as belonging to his successors, or neither. As for the assumption, I again appeal to Bellarmine. The first privilege (he says), that he should never lose the true faith, perhaps did not pass to the successors. [Perhaps it did not pass.] This is said falsely, and also hesitantly; but much more correctly when you add: All Catholics (you say) agree in this, that the Pope, as a private teacher, can err, even in universal questions of law, both of faith and of morals, and that through ignorance, as sometimes happens to other teachers. Thus you; in which sense you have the Protestants with you, who feel most Catholically; who believe that your Popes are so liable to errors that they cannot sometimes fail to err in a harmful way. We believe this all the more easily because, in the exposition of this passage, on which he laid the principal foundation of this privilege, he has erred most shamefully. For if the same words were spoken to Peter and equally to the Pope, how does it come about that by the words by which two privileges are granted to Peter, only one is conferred on the Pope? What a perversity, alas, to tear apart that sense which the Holy Spirit joined together; contrary to that universal axiom, held by all human and divine laws, black and red alike: Where the law does not distinguish, neither ought we to distinguish? And contrary to the rule of interpreting all privileges' words, brought forward by the Jesuit, namely, When the words of a privilege are clear, they are neither to be restricted nor extended?

units.la: At nè forte quis objiciat, Necesse est ut eodem Privilegio Papa primo muniatur, respectu Ecclesiæ, nè videlicet, Possit unquàm aliquid docere & definire contra fidem, quia est Successor Petri: Respondeo, hanc Rationem, Primò, futilem esse, quia Pontifex non est genuinus & legitimus Petri Successor. Deinde falsam, quia (ut alia de Privilegijs Regula se habet) {o}Privilegium nunquàm est extendendum ad alias personas, vel alios Casus, propter similitudinem rationis, ut (fatente Jesuita) Doctores communiter tenent. Hàc arte defensionis labefactatà, refugis rursus ad humana Testimonia: pergis enim.
units.tr: But lest perhaps someone object that the Pope must first be fortified by the same privilege with respect to the Church, namely, that he could never teach or define anything against the faith, because he is the successor of Peter: I answer that this reason is, first, frivolous, because the Pope is not the genuine and lawful successor of Peter. Second, it is false, because (as the rule concerning privileges otherwise stands) a privilege is never to be extended to other persons or other cases on account of similarity of reason, as (the Jesuit admitting it) the teachers commonly hold. With this art of defence undermined, you again take refuge in human testimonies: for you go on.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Offic.

units.la: “ In sede Petri — fides non potist[?] habere defectum, ut scribit “ S.{*}Bernardus. — Pag.29.
units.tr: "In the seat of Peter ... faith cannot have a defect, as St Bernard writes." — p. 29.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Bernardi Iudicium ab ipsis Aduersarijs saepè contemni.
units.tr: Bernard's judgement is often scorned by the Adversaries themselves.

units.la: Hic fortassis parumper nobis hærendum esset, nisi Doctores Pontificij Nos expedirent, qui non ita penitus adorant hunc Sanctum, ut non interdum, quum eius testimonio urgentur, authoritatem eius parui faciant. Est enim vbi Bernardus docet B. Mariam Virginem originali peccato obnoxiam fuisse; festumque illum diem, in indicium contrariæ opinionis, annuatim celebratum, {p}Præsumptam nouitatem, matrem temeritatis, sororem superstitionis, filiam leuitatis vocat. Nunquid Bernardum iam mordaci vero vos acriter radentem libenter sustinebitis? {q}Respondemus (inquitis) totam devotionem ergà Dei genetricem non consistere in Bernardo, Bonaventurâ, & aliys Patribus. Negabat Bernardus mulierem absolui posse ab Ecclesiâ, quæ nubit intra tempus luctus. Ecquid probatis? Gregorius XIII. Pontifex, in margine Glossæ Decreti, Responsum hoc imprimi curauit; {r}Imò (inquit) Ecclesia potest, quicquid hic Bernardus dicat. Atque Inquisitores ipsi plusquam Pontificiâ authoritate respondent, {s}Deleantur hæc verba Bernardi. Nobis verò non licet adeò esse imperiosis. Quid quod ab errante Bernardo frequens illud Scriptorum errantium adagium originem suam traxerit, Bernardus non vidit omnia. Nec sanè mirum, cùm præsertim eo tempore (videlicet, Anno MDXXX) floruerit Bernardus, quando Rom. Ecclesia atrà quasi superstitionum nocte obducta fuit. Vir dignissimus meliori æuo; qui vel in tantis tenebris veritatis lucem salutarem aspexit, vicésque suas sæpè deplorabat, quòd inter Eos sibi necessariò viuendum fuerat, qui (inquit) {t}Ministri Christi, seruiunt ANTICHRISTO, nimirum, Præláti nostri Magistri Ecclesiarum. Tuum erit ex his Responsis seligere, quod Tibi maximè vsui fuerit, &, omisso Authore adeò recenti, ex primæuâ Antiquitate testem aliquem alium magis idoneum accersere. Tu pergis.
units.tr: Perhaps I should linger here a little, were it not that the Papist doctors relieve us of the task. They do not worship this Saint so deeply that they never, when he is pressed against them with his testimony, make light of his authority. For there is a place where Bernard teaches that the Blessed Virgin Mary was subject to original sin, and he calls the feast celebrated every year as a sign of the opposite opinion a presumptuous novelty, the mother of rashness, the sister of superstition, the daughter of levity. Will you willingly put up with Bernard, who scratches you so sharply with his truthful bite? We answer (you say) that all devotion towards the Mother of God does not rest on Bernard, Bonaventure and the other Fathers. Bernard denied that a woman who marries within the time of mourning can be absolved by the Church. What do you prove against him? Pope Gregory XIII had this reply printed in the margin of the gloss on the Decretum: Nay (he says) the Church can do whatever this Bernard says. And the Inquisitors themselves answer with more than papal authority: Let these words of Bernard be deleted. We, however, may not be so imperious. What of the common saying of erring writers, Bernard did not see everything, which surely took its origin from the erring Bernard? Nor is this surprising, especially since Bernard flourished at a time (namely in the year 1130) when the Roman Church was covered as if by a black night of superstitions. He was a most worthy man, born for a better age, who, even in such darkness, caught sight of the saving light of truth, and often lamented his lot, that he had to live among those who (he says) are ministers of Christ, yet serve ANTICHRIST, namely our prelates, the masters of the churches. It will be for you to choose from these replies what has been most useful to you, and, leaving aside so recent an author, to summon some other witness more fitting from primitive antiquity. On you go.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, de Offic.

units.la: "Et ad quam (nempè, Petri sedem) perfidia non potest habere accessum, ut loquitur {*}Cyprianus. pag.29.
units.tr: "And to that see (namely of Peter) perfidy cannot have access, as Cyprian says. p. 29.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Alibi verò clarius. {u}"Non solum Pontificem (inquis) sed etiam Ecclesiam Rom. non posse errare, asseruit, inter alios, S. Cyprianus lib. 1. Epist. 3. Navigare audent (inquit) ad Petri cathedram &c. nec cogitare eos esse Romanos, ad quos perfidia non potest habere accessum.
units.tr: Elsewhere, however, more clearly: "You assert that not only the Pope but also the Roman Church cannot err, as St. Cyprian asserts among others, in book 1, letter 3: they dare to sail (he says) to the chair of Peter, etc., nor do they consider that they are Romans, to whom perfidy cannot have access."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Cypriani authoritate, de more suo Rhetoricantis, abuti Bellarminum.
units.tr: Bellarmine abuses Cyprian's authority, rhetorizing in his usual manner.

units.la: QUoties Pontificii in isthæc Cypriani testimonia incidunt, mirum est quantos triumphos agant, ac si de Protestantium partibus actum penitus & conclamatum esset. Quorum hominum oscitantiam equidem satis mirari nequeo, qui eum pro se Advocatum adducunt, quo nullum habere possunt causæ suæ magis Adversarium; quod cùm hæc, tùm præcipuè subsequens Animadversio perspicuè demonstrabit. In loco iam citato Cyprianus sic inscribit Epistolam ad Pontificem Romanum; [Cornelio fratri salutem:] & in Epistolæ exordio; [Legimus tuas literas, charissime frater.] Res, inquies, non magni momenti. Sanè, nisi quod, ut nunc sunt mores, quivis Pontifex Rom. grandem sibi contumeliam factam ultrò expostularet, si quis minorum maiorumve gentium Episcopus eum FRATREM salutaret: nemini enim omnium nunc licet Pontificè, nisi inflatis ambabus buccis, tumidis & ventosis titulis compellàsse. Sed ad Rem.
units.tr: Whenever the Papists stumble upon those testimonies of Cyprian, it is remarkable what great triumphs they celebrate, as if the cause of the Protestants had been utterly finished and given up for lost. I truly cannot sufficiently wonder at the drowsiness of these men, who bring forward as their advocate one whom they could not have a greater adversary to their cause; as this, and especially the following remark, will plainly show. In the place already cited, Cyprian thus addresses his letter to the Roman Pontiff: [To Cornelius, his brother, greeting], and at the beginning of the letter: [We have read your letters, dearest brother]. The matter, you will say, is of no great moment. Certainly, were it not that, as customs now are, any Roman Pontiff would of his own accord complain of a great insult if any bishop of the lesser or greater nations greeted him as BROTHER: for nowadays no one at all may address the Pontiff except with puffed cheeks and swollen, windy titles. But to the matter.

units.la: Respondeo, Cyprianum, ubi negat [Perfidiam ad Romanos posse habere accessum] non tam suadendo laudare, aut astruere aliquam impossibilitatem errandi in Romana Cathedrâ; quàm, Rhetorum more, laudando admonere Cornelium Rom. Episcopum, nè patiatur Cathedram suam, hactenùs integram, fraudè aliquâ, aut Perfidiâ hominum schismaticorum circumuenìri. Et profectò Cyprianus Rhetor magnus fuit, {*}Qui in tantam eloquentiæ gloriam venit (inquit Hieronymus) vt publicè artem Oratoriam Carthagine doceret. Quam, si vsquàm, in hac Epistola Eum,& quidem egregiè præstitisse, tota eiusdem Epistolæ series videtur quodammodò profiteri.
units.tr: I answer that Cyprian, when he denies that [perfidy can have access to the Romans], does not so much praise, by way of persuasion, or assert some impossibility of erring in the Roman Chair; rather, in the manner of rhetoricians, by praising he admonishes Cornelius, the Roman bishop, not to allow his chair, hitherto intact, to be circumvented by some fraud or perfidy of schismatic men. And indeed Cyprian was a great rhetorician, who attained such glory in eloquence (says Jerome) that he taught the art of oratory publicly at Carthage. If he has done this excellently anywhere, it is in this letter; the whole sequence of the letter seems in some measure to profess as much.

units.la: Primo enim in loco mirari se dicit, quod obseruaret Cornelium quorundam Schismaticorum hominum minis atque terroribus nimis commotum fuisse; & docet Eum, à vero vigore, & diuinâ gubernandâ Ecclesiæ potestate alienum esse, vt Episcopi peraitorum hominum insidias pertimescant; apud quos manere debet fidei robur immobile, & stabilis, & inconcussa virtus contra omnes incursus atque impetus oblstrantium fluctuum. Progreditur Cyprianus, & Cornelium multis Argumentis, tanquàm armis, munit atque instruit, nè animum despondeat, aut oneri succumbat: & post allata Exempla Christi, & Patriarcharum addit & suum; suadetque nullam esse rationem cur Cornelius absentium horum hominum comminationes metueret, quas ipse apud eos præsens contempsisset. Laudat igitur hic diuinus Rhetor præteritam sedis Rom. constantiam, vt facilius hortetur ad animosè progrediendum; more Veterum, qui (vt egregiè quidam dixit) [illegible, ~10 letters] esse voluerunt, id est, in laudationibus commonefactiones contineri. Post, causam ipsam aggreditur Cyprianus, & ostendit, vnum ex illis Schismaticis antèa, ob multa & grauia eius delicta, Episcoporum XC. sententiâ condemnatum, Vnà cum aliis à Concilio exclusis, Romam postea (vt ipse loquitur) cum mendaciorum merce naufragasse.
units.tr: For first he says he marvels that he observes Cornelius to have been too much moved by the threats and terrors of certain schismatic men; and he teaches that it is foreign to the true vigour and to the divine power of governing the Church that bishops should fear the snares of wicked men, in whom there ought to remain an immovable strength of faith, and a steadfast and unshaken virtue against all the assaults and onsets of the opposing waves. Cyprian proceeds, and fortifies and equips Cornelius with many arguments, as with weapons, lest he lose heart or give way under the burden; and after adducing the examples of Christ and the patriarchs, he adds his own, and urges that there is no reason why Cornelius should fear the threats of these absent men, which he himself had despised when present among them. Therefore this divine rhetorician here praises the past constancy of the Roman see, so that he may the more readily exhort him to proceed boldly; following the custom of the ancients, who (as a certain writer excellently said) wished [illegible, about 10 letters], that is, that admonitions be contained in praises. Afterwards Cyprian takes up the matter itself and shows that one of those schismatics had earlier been condemned by the sentence of ninety bishops for many grave offences, and that, together with others excluded by the Council, he was afterwards shipwrecked at Rome (as he himself puts it) with his cargo of lies.

units.la: Postremò agitur de Cathedra, cuius authoritati Schismatici isti, nunc Romam provocantes, submittere se debuerint Carthaginensinè[?], an Romane? Hàc quæstione proposita, hodierni Papistæ pro Romana certarent strenuè. Quid autem Cyprianus? Carthaginensis Cathedræ ius asserit, atque defendit, tanquàm quod non modò humanâ diuinâque lege, sed etiam summâ æquitate nitatur. Humana; nam Statutum est (inquit) omnibus nobis. Diuina etiam, nam Pastoris est (inquit) vniuscuiusq; actus sui (adeoque Cypriani, de excommunicatione Schismaticorum) Domino (Deo; non Papæ) rationem reddere. Aequitate denique, nam eorum remotius subdola Schismaticorum temeritate decipitur: Carthagine verò, vbi Testes præsentes fuerint, rectiùs de Causâ decernitur. Addit (in quo æquitatis pars non minima consistit) nè Ecclesiæ Africanæ Iurisdictio, ex Schismaticorum Appellatione, aliquid detrimenti caperet: nam non minor (inquit) authoritas Episcoporum in Africa constitutorum, nempè, quàm Episcoporum Romanorum: id enim eleganti aposiopesi necessariò inuoluitur. Summa hùc rédit, docendo, [Non posse eò perfidiam habere accessum,] præmunit, & præparat Pontificis, Clericiq; Rom. animos, vt caveant sibi, nè impostura & Perfidia practica, vel fraus Schismaticorum posset ad Eos accessum habere: vt ipsi admittantur cum suâ mendaciorum mercé..
units.tr: Lastly, the question concerns the chair, to whose authority these schismatics, now appealing to Rome, ought to submit: Carthaginian or Roman? This question being proposed, the present-day Papists would strenuously contend for the Roman. But what does Cyprian do? He asserts and defends the right of the Carthaginian chair, as resting not only on human and divine law but also on the highest equity. Human: for it has been decided (he says) by all of us. Divine too: for it is the duty of each minister (he says) to give account of his own act (and so of Cyprian's excommunication of the schismatics) to the Lord (God, not the Pope). Lastly equity: for in more distant places one is deceived by the crafty rashness of schismatics, but at Carthage, where the witnesses are present, the matter is decided more rightly. He adds (in which no small part of equity consists) that the jurisdiction of the African Church should suffer no loss through the appeal of the schismatics; for the authority of the bishops established in Africa is not less (he says) than that of the Roman bishops: for this is necessarily implied by an elegant aposiopesis. The sum comes to this: by teaching [perfidy cannot have access there], he forewarns and prepares the minds of the Pontiff and the Roman clergy, that they may take care lest imposture and practised perfidy, or the fraud of schismatics, should be able to have access to them, so that they might be admitted with their cargo of lies.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Cyprianum dictis factisq; Romanæ Cathedræ acerrimum oppugnatorem fuisse.
units.tr: That Cyprian, in word and deed, was the most bitter opponent of the Roman See.

units.la: SEd quum ætas illa, quâ Cyprianus vixit; tùm primæva doctrina eius (si vnicum Rebaptizationis dogma excipiamus) tàm orthodoxa; tàm sancta & religiosa vita; & mors, Martyrii Corona, tàm gloriosa fuerit: certè Euius iudicium (præsertim in causa tanti momenti) apud verè Catholicos authoritate valere plurimùm debet. Hunc Patrem Pontificij ad partes suas obtorto collo trahunt; hunc à partibus suis stare Protestantes affirmant.Cypriano ipso Iudice, & teste vestro Binio lis omnis facile dirimitur. Conc. Carthaginense (cui etiam præfuit Cypria-nus) nus) decreuit in hunc modum : {a}Neque quisquam nostrum Episcopum se esse Episcoporum constituit, aut tyrannico terrore ad obsequendi necessitatem Collegas suos adigit. Quibus verbis Concilium (teste Binio) {b}Alludit ad decretum Stephani Papae, — qui aliter sentientibus pœnam Excommunicationis acriter comminatus est. Deinde, inter S.Cyprianum, & Stephanum Papam Rom. quæstio de Rebaptizandis Relapsis graviter agitatur. Quid Cyprianus? {c}Cyprianus (fatente Binio) cùm Concilio aliorum Episcoporum LXXXVII. ex Africa, & Numidia congregatorum, Stephano Papæ Rom aliter definienti se opposuit: Et (teste Bellarmino ipso) {d}putabat Cyprianus Pontificem perniciose erràsse. Sic causam egit Cyprianus; quàm verè, id non quæritur; constanter certè.
units.tr: But since the age in which Cyprian lived, his early teaching (if we except the single dogma of rebaptism) was so orthodox, his life so holy and religious, and his death, the crown of martyrdom, so glorious, surely his judgment (especially in a matter of such great moment) ought to carry great weight among truly Catholic men. The Papists drag this Father to their side by force; Protestants affirm that he stands on their side. With Cyprian himself as judge, and your own witness Binius, the whole dispute is easily settled. The Council of Carthage (over which Cyprian also presided) decreed as follows: {a}"None of us makes himself bishop of bishops, or by tyrannical terror forces his colleagues to the necessity of obeying." By these words the Council (according to Binius) {b}alludes to the decree of Pope Stephen, who sharply threatened excommunication against those who thought otherwise. Then, between St Cyprian and Pope Stephen of Rome, the question of rebaptizing the lapsed was hotly debated. What did Cyprian do? {c}Cyprian (as Binius admits), together with a council of 87 other bishops gathered from Africa and Numidia, opposed Pope Stephen when he defined otherwise; and (according to Bellarmine himself) {d}Cyprian thought the Pope had erred dangerously. Thus Cyprian pleaded his case; how truly is not the question; certainly firmly.

units.la: Si igitur ne Schismatici trans mare navigent, aut Romanam sedem appellent, interdicere; sit Pontificis Rom. Iurisdictionem asserere: si indignè ferre, quenquam vocari Episcopum Episcoporum; sit Pontificis titulo Vniuersalitatis patrocinari: si Episcopi Romani de Excommunicationis pœnà, contra suos Collegas, decretum Tyrannicum-terrorem vocare; sit Pontificis prærogatiuam in Episcopos alios confirmare: Si Concilium Papæ Concilio, velut pilum pilo, opponere; sit Cathedram Pontificis stabilire: Si denique iudicare Papam Stephanum perniciose erràsse; sit negare perfidiam ad eum habere accessum: tùm reuera S. Patrem Cyprianum Pontificiæ causæ Patronum acerrimum extitisse, sapiens nemo inficiabitur. Transfugis Tu aliò.
units.tr: If, therefore, to forbid schismatics to sail across the sea or appeal to the Roman See is to assert the jurisdiction of the Roman Pontiff; if to be indignant that anyone be called bishop of bishops is to defend the Pontiff's title of universality; if to call the Roman bishop's decree of excommunication against his colleagues a tyrannical terror is to confirm the Pontiff's prerogative over other bishops; if to set one council against the Pope's council, pile against pile, is to establish the Pontiff's chair; and if, finally, to judge that Pope Stephen erred dangerously is to deny that perfidy has access to him: then indeed no wise man will deny that St Father Cyprian was the most bitter champion of the papal cause. Go elsewhere, you deserter.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Offic.

units.la: “ Tale aliquid multò antea docuit Salomon, dicens; {*}[verba Sapientum sicut stimuli, & quasi clavi in altum defixi, quæ per Magistrorum consilium data sunt à Pastore uno: Eis amplius, fili mi, ne requiras.] — Pag.29.
units.tr: "Something of the kind was taught long before by Solomon, saying: {*}[The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed, which are given by the counsel of masters from one Shepherd. Beyond these, my son, do not seek.]" — p. 29.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Quid ex his? {e}Hoc loco docet Salomon (vt Tu alibi) non esse vlterius inquirendum, sed acquiescendum penitus, quando sententia data est à Summo Pastore, adiunctò praesertim consilio sapientium. Si haec dicuntur de Sacerdote veteris Testamenti, quanto magis dici possunt de Sacerdote Testamenti noui, qui longè maiores promissiones accepit? Quid concludis? {f}Dicimus Iudicem omnium controuersiarum esse Ecclesiam, id est, Pontificem cum Concilio, vt expressè habetur in Concilio Tridentino.
units.tr: What follows from this? {e}Here Solomon teaches (as you do elsewhere) that nothing further is to be inquired into, but that one must wholly acquiesce when a sentence has been given by the Chief Shepherd, especially with the counsel of the wise added. If these things are said of the priest of the Old Testament, how much more can they be said of the priest of the New Testament, who has received far greater promises? What do you conclude? {f}We say that the judge of all controversies is the Church, that is, the Pope with the Council, as is expressly stated in the Council of Trent.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Bellarminum, in interpretatione huius Scripturae (Eccles.12.) falli.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. That Bellarmine errs in his interpretation of this Scripture (Eccles. 12).

units.la: Quum nihil Amplius requirendum esse Salomon monuit, non proinde vetuit, nè abs Te quæramus amplius quis Pastor, quiuè Sapientes hanc Tibi doctrinam suggesserint; quod aut, hoc in loco, Pastor Sacerdotem veteris Testamenti designet, aut Concilio veteris Testamenti absolutè acquiescendum fuisse, aut denique summum omnium Controuersiarum iudicium infallibiliter Rom. Pontificis Concilio alligari?
units.tr: Since Solomon warned that nothing further is to be sought, he did not for that reason forbid us to ask you further who the Pastor is, or which wise men suggested this doctrine to you. Or does Pastor, in this place, designate the priest of the Old Testament? Or was the Council of the Old Testament to be absolutely acquiesced in? Or finally, is the supreme judgment of all controversies infallibly bound to the Council of the Roman Pontiff?

units.la: Primò, de Pastore. Sunt enim qui intelligunt, per dicta Sapientium, & Magistrorum consilium, Scripturas Diuinas, ore Prophetarum & Apostolorum traditas: per summum animarum Pastorem, Christum Iesum; & nihil amplius his requirendum à nobis tanquam ad salutem necessarium. [Ab uno Pastore,] id est, Christo, qui solus est animarum Pastor, Ioh.10. sic Hugo Card. sic Glossa Ordinaria. Pastor unus, hoc in loco, Christus est, sicut manifestè expositit Ezechiel cap.34. Suscitabo super eas Pastorem unum, qui pascat eas. sic Ribera Iesuita. Nec in hoc Textu Theologus quisquam, opinor, nisi praeiudicantis opinionis perspicillis tuis abusus, Tale aliquid cernere poterit.
units.tr: First, concerning the Pastor. For there are those who understand by the sayings of the wise and the counsel of the masters the Divine Scriptures, delivered by the mouth of the Prophets and Apostles; and by the chief Shepherd of souls, Christ Jesus; and that nothing further beyond these is to be sought by us as necessary to salvation. [From one Shepherd], that is, Christ, who alone is the Shepherd of souls, John 10. So Cardinal Hugo; so the Glossa Ordinaria. One Shepherd, in this place, is Christ, as Ezekiel plainly expounds in chapter 34: I will set up over them one Shepherd, who will feed them. So the Jesuit Ribera. Nor, I think, will any theologian see any such thing in this text, unless he has abused your spectacles of prejudiced opinion.

units.la: Secundo, Tu si vixisses sub Testamento veteri, quandò Pontifex vnà cum Sacerdotum ac Sapientium suorum Concilio publico verum & unicum Animarum Pastorem Iesum damnârunt ; an sententiæ Caiphæ penitus acquiescendum censuisses ; Nihilą[?], amplius requirendum?
units.tr: Second, if you had lived under the Old Testament, when the High Priest, together with the council of his priests and wise men, publicly condemned Jesus, the true and only Shepherd of souls, would you have thought that one must wholly acquiesce in the sentence of Caiaphas, and that nothing further was to be sought?

units.la: Tertiò, de Novo Testamento Responsum à Cypriano accepisti, qui Ecclesiæ primitivæ sententiam communem secutus, Pontificem Rom. unum Pastorem quidem, sed non unicum agnovit; & Inter, non Super alios Episcopos Iurisdictionem habuisse. Qui Pastor Carthaginensis, cum suorum Sapientum Consilio, vestri Pastoris, Sapientumque eius Consilio acquiescere recusavit. Affer, si sapis, istis aliquid clarius.
units.tr: Third, concerning the New Testament, you have received an answer from Cyprian, who, following the common opinion of the primitive Church, acknowledged the Roman Pontiff as one Shepherd indeed, but not the only one, and held jurisdiction among the other bishops, not over them. That Shepherd of Carthage, with the counsel of his wise men, refused to acquiesce in the counsel of your Shepherd and his wise men. Produce something clearer than these, if you have any sense.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officiis

units.la: “ Et clarius in lege definitum est à Sp. Sancto per Mosen dicentem, {*}[ Qui superbierit, nolens obedire Sacerdotis imperio, qui eo tempore ministrat Domino Deo tuo, ex Decreto Iudicis morietur homo ille, & auferes malum ex Israël ; cunctúsq; populus audiens timebit, ut nullus deinceps intumescat superbiâ.] Loquitur autem Moses de rebus dubiis in lege Domini, & doctrina. --- Pag.29.
units.tr: "And more clearly it is defined in the law by the Holy Spirit through Moses, who says: 'If anyone is proud and refuses to obey the command of the priest who then ministers to the Lord your God, that man shall die by the decree of the judge, and you shall take away the evil from Israel; and all the people, hearing it, shall fear, so that no one henceforth becomes puffed up with pride.' Moses, however, speaks of matters doubtful in the law of the Lord and in doctrine." --- Page 29.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Testimonium superius obscurum nimis; hoccinè verò Tibi adeò clarum videtur? {g}His verbis (ais alibi) valde clarè dubitantes non remittuntur ad Spiritum suum, sed ad Iudicem vivum, id est Summum Sacerdotem: nec sonant (ista verba) conditionem, sed assertionem & promissionem; vult enim Dominus securum reddere populum suum, & affirmat Sacerdotem iudicaturum secundùm legem: non enim voluit dicere, sta iudicio Sacerdotis, si iudicaverit secundùm legem, tunc enim fuissent homines magis dubij & perplexi, quàm antea: nec opus fuisset ire ad Sacerdotem, si ipsi potuissent de lege Domini iudicare. {h}Et Christus docuit, non obstante malâ Prælatorum vitâ, sequendam esse eorum doctrinam, Matth.23.[ Super Cathedram Mosis sedent Scribæ, & Pharisæi, quæcunque vobis dixerint, facite.] Notandum est, quid Dominus de Cathedra Mosis dixerit, intelligi à fortiori de Cathedra Petri.
units.tr: The earlier testimony is very obscure. But does this seem so very clear to you? "By these words," you say elsewhere, "those who doubt are very clearly not referred to their own spirit, but to the living judge, that is, the high priest. These words express not a condition but an assertion and a promise. For the Lord wishes to make his people secure, and affirms that the priest will judge according to the law. He did not mean, 'Stand by the judgment of the priest if he judges according to the law'; for then men would have been more doubtful and perplexed than before, and there would have been no need to go to the priest if they themselves could judge about the law of the Lord." And Christ taught that, despite the wicked life of the prelates, their doctrine is to be followed: Matt. 23: "The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat; whatever they tell you, do." It is to be noted that what the Lord said about Moses' seat is to be understood all the more of Peter's seat.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Sacerdotis veteris Testamenti iudicio, nisi iuxta legem, acquiescendum non fuisse.
units.tr: That one was not to acquiesce in the judgment of the priest of the Old Testament unless it was according to the law.

units.la: PApæ iudicium infallibile, tanquàm Rom. religionis arcem ipsam, duobus quasi propugnaculis munire satagis; quorum unum à Sacerdotis Testamenti veteris Tri-bunali, Alterum à Cathedra Mosis deducitur. De utrisque agemus.
units.tr: You are striving to fortify the infallible judgment of the Pope, as the very citadel of the Roman religion, with two bulwarks, as it were. One of these is derived from the tribunal of the priest of the Old Testament, the other from Moses' seat. We shall deal with both.

units.la: Si verba Scripturarum (ut Tu vis) affertiva & promissoria sint, tum (nam fateri oportet) nullo modo Iudicis veteris Testamenti sententiæ refragandum erat: sin verò Conditionalia, tum, quandoquidem statuis Iudicis illius Decretum omni exceptione maius fuisse, frustrà sanè es. Episcopus vester Abulensis Controuersiam hanc facilè dirimet. {i}Dicitur (inquit) in litera quòd Iudices illi duas constitutiones habere debent, prima est ut iudicent [Secundùm veritatem:] secunda, ut iudicent [iuxta legem.] Ergò videtur, quodsi iudicauerint contra veritatem, vel contra legem non est ijs assentiendum. Hæc ille. Etiamsi igitur, post, latam falsam {*} Iudicis sententiam, non manserit ius aliquod Appellandi ad forum vllum superius; nemini tamen in huiusmodi causa sublata fuit libertas non consentiendi. At debuit (inquis) populus Pontificum iudicio acquiescere, quia non poterant iudicare contra legem. Itané verò? non poterant Illi facere, quod etiam proculdubiò fecerunt? Nam Pontifex {k}Ananias permisit Paulum peruti contra legem: Pontifex Vrias Idololatricè, contra legem, {l}Infectebat se ad voluntatem Apostata Achaz: Pontifex {m}Aaron, contrà legem, vitulum conflabat, & diem festum celebrabat, in honorem Idoli.
units.tr: If the words of Scripture are, as you wish, assertive and promissory, then (for we must admit it) the sentence of the judge of the Old Testament ought by no means to have been opposed. But if they are conditional, then, since you maintain that the decree of that judge was greater than any exception, you are certainly labouring in vain. Your bishop Abulensis will easily settle this controversy: "It is said (he says) in the text that those judges ought to have two commands: the first, that they judge [according to the truth]; the second, that they judge [according to the law]. Therefore it seems that if they have judged against the truth or against the law, they are not to be assented to." So he. Even if, therefore, after the false sentence of the judge has been pronounced, no right of appeal to any higher court remained, yet in such a case freedom not to consent was never taken away from anyone. "But (you say) the people ought to have acquiesced in the judgment of the pontiffs, because they could not judge against the law." Really? Could they not do what they undoubtedly did? For the high priest Ananias permitted Paul to be struck against the law; the high priest Urijah, idolatrously and against the law, yielded to the will of the apostate Ahaz; the high priest Aaron, against the law, cast the calf and celebrated a feast day in honour of the idol.

units.la: Denique de Pontifice Caiphâ quid sentiendum putas? de quo scriptum est, [{n}Hoc dixit Caiphas, cùm esset Pontifex illius Anni.] Hinc vester Episcopus Roffensis Luthero falsè, vel insulsè potiùs insultans: {°}Mirum est, Luthere, (inquit) cùm hæc non ignoras, quòd tam parùm tribuis Pontifici Rom. cùm vel apertissimum sit ex Euangelio, Caipham ipsum verum iudicium protulisse. Et eâdem chordà oberrat vester Canus, {p}quia Ex ea re fit (inquit) ut nostrorum Pontificum iudicia vera sint, & quæ ad populi salutem diuinitùs instituta à Sp. Sancto, quia ij, qui ea præferunt, sunt Ecclesiæ Pontifices. Sic isti egregij scilicet iudicij Rom. Pontificis assertores, iudicio innixi blasphemi Caiphæ. Nam, {q}Renerà altera pars sententiæ Caiphæ (vt ait Bellarminus) blasphemia erat, quia sequitur in textu, Caiphas dixit quòd Christus blasphemasset. Ergo hic quoque Pontifex iudicium tulit contra legem. Hæc de Tribunali Sacerdotis veteris Testamenti.
units.tr: Finally, what do you think of the high priest Caiaphas, of whom it is written: [Caiaphas said this, since he was high priest that year.]? Hence your bishop of Rochester, insulting Luther falsely or rather foolishly: "It is strange, Luther (he says), that, since you are not ignorant of these things, you give so little to the Roman Pontiff, when it is most evident from the Gospel that Caiaphas himself pronounced true judgment." And your Canus strays on the same string: "because from this it comes about that the judgments of our Pontiffs are true, and those things which are divinely instituted by the Holy Spirit for the salvation of the people, because those who present them are the Pontiffs of the Church." Thus those distinguished asserters of the judgment of the Roman Pontiff, leaning on that judgment, are blasphemous like Caiaphas. For, "indeed the other part of Caiaphas' sentence (as Bellarmine says) was blasphemy, because it follows in the text that Caiaphas said Christ had blasphemed. Therefore this pontiff too gave judgment against the law." So much for the tribunal of the priest of the Old Testament.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Per [ Mosis Cathedram ] non propriam Iudicis sententiam, sed doctrinam Mosaicam indicari.
units.tr: That by [Moses' seat] is indicated not the judge's own sentence, but the Mosaic doctrine.

units.la: SECundum Propugnaculum Sedis Pontificiae in Cathedra Mosis positum fuit; vbi, per Cathedram, Bellarminus, Stapletonus, Sa, & Costerus{r} Authoritatem docendi, & praecipiendi interpretantur: quam statim traducunt ad Cathedram (id est, sententiam definitiuam in causis dubijs) absolutè, & nullâ{f} suppositâ conditione stabiliendam. At Pontificij alij quanto candidius, accuratius, verius? Nam vbi dicit Christus, Facite quod docent Pharisaei, Matth.23. Et rursus, Cauete à fermento Pharisaeorum, quae est eorum doctrina, Matth.16. Ad reconciliandam hanc (vt quis forte putet) verborum repugnantiam Iansenius Episcopus olim respondit;{ı} Proinde (inquit) docet Christus obediendum illis esse, quando recte praecipiunt, sedentes nimirum in Cathedra Mosis; non quando docent contra Cathedram, nempe doctrinam eius. Eodem modo Stella,{*} [a Super Cathedram Mosis sedent.] id est, (inquit) cum docent ea, quae Moses praedixerat, & docuerat, audiendi sunt; sed à falsa eorum doctrina cauendum est. est. Disertissime omnium Maldonatus Jef.{x} Dominus, per Cathedram Mosis, non de Pharisæorum doctrina (inquit) sed de doctrina legis, & Mosis loquitur: perinde enim est, ac si dixeris, Omnia quæ Lex, & Moses verbis dixerint, &c.
units.tr: The second bulwark was placed by the Papal See on Moses' seat. There Bellarmine, Stapleton, Sa and Costerus interpret "seat" as the authority of teaching and commanding, which they at once carry over to the seat (that is, a definitive sentence in doubtful cases) to be established absolutely and with no condition supposed. But other Papists, how much more candidly, accurately and truly! For where Christ says, "Do what the Pharisees teach," Matt. 23; and again, "Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is their doctrine," Matt. 16. To reconcile this apparent contradiction of words (as perhaps someone thinks), Bishop Jansenius once replied: "Accordingly (he says) Christ teaches that they are to be obeyed when they rightly command, sitting, of course, on Moses' seat; not when they teach contrary to the seat, that is, its doctrine." In the same way Stella: [they sit on Moses' seat], that is, "when they teach those things which Moses foretold and taught, they are to be heard; but one must beware of their false doctrine." Most clearly of all, Maldonatus the Jesuit: "The Lord, through Moses' seat, speaks not of the doctrine of the Pharisees (he says) but of the doctrine of the law and of Moses; for it is just as if you had said, All that the Law and Moses have said in words, etc."

units.la: Vides igitur hæc omnia præcepta, de parendo judicio Sacerdotum veteris legis, intertextam & involutam in se conditionem habere, quatenus legem & doctrinam Mosis tradant: Et per Cathedram non significari Judæis ipsius sententiam definitivam, sed ipsam doctrinam Mosis. Eodem modo Nos; Sedes Petri est fides Petri, hanc Cathedram Pontifex capessat, & nemo Christianus non bona fide spondebit obedientiam; sed Petro, vel potius Christo, non Papæ: qui postquam Apostolicam doctrinam pro derelicto habuit, novosq; fidei cudit Articulos, novam Papæ Cathedram constituit, non Petri. Et quid ni ego illam Erasmi Censuram usurpem, qui de ijs loquens, qui eo torquent hunc locum de Cathedra Mosis, ut suam {y}Exercent tyrannidem in populum; quasi tuo (inquit) & maiestate omnia metientes: non sedent in Cathedra Euangelica, sed Simonis Magi, aut ipsius Caiphæ?
units.tr: You see, therefore, that all these precepts about obeying the judgment of the priests of the old law have a condition woven and involved within them, insofar as they hand down the law and doctrine of Moses; and that by "seat" is signified to the Jews not the priests' own definitive sentence, but the doctrine of Moses itself. In the same way we say: "The seat of Peter is the faith of Peter." Let the Pontiff take hold of this seat, and no Christian would fail in good faith to pledge obedience; but the obedience is owed to Peter, or rather to Christ, not to the Pope. He, after he has regarded apostolic doctrine as abandoned and coined new articles of faith, has set up a new seat of the Pope, not of Peter. And why should I not borrow that censure of Erasmus, who, speaking of those who twist this passage about Moses' seat so that they "exercise tyranny over the people, measuring everything by their own will and majesty (he says): do they not sit in the evangelical seat, but in that of Simon Magus, or of Caiaphas himself?"

units.la: III ANIMADVERSIO. Expositiones Pontificiorum deliramentis Rabbinorum in- sulsorum perquam esse similes, ad cæcam Obedientiam inducendam.
units.tr: III ANIMADVERSION. The Papists' expositions are very like the foolish delusions of the rabbis, designed to induce blind obedience.

units.la: Scripturarum, quas ad efferendam amplificandamque Judicii vestri authoritatem produxti, sensum liquidum tenemus, quas itidem Scripturas Rabbini nimirum maleferiati Doctores, apud Judæos, crassis Glossematis suis tam nequiter impieque depravarunt: hi scilicet, ut Judæorum suorum authoritate firmarent, sicut se, ita etiam universos alios animorum judicio, communique sensu speliare[?] sategerunt. Nam de primo loco Deut. 17. ubi subiunxit Deus per Mosen, Quicquid docuerint secundum legem, sequeris sententiam eorum, nec declinabis ad dextram, neque ad sinistram. Inde Rabbini; {z}Si Iudex (inquiunt) forte dixerit quod sinistra manus sit dextra, talis sententia est tenenda. Quam blasphemam ac ridiculam Glossam Lyranus merito vellicat: Hoc manifeste falsum est (inquit) quia sententia nullius hominis, cuiuscunque authoritatis, est tenenda, si contineat manifestam falsitatem, vel errorem: hoc patet ex eo quod praemittitur in textu. [Et docuerit Tc[?] iuxta legem.] Ergo locum hunc non simpliciter, sed conditionaliter exponere necessario debet is, cui non collubitum est oculis priuari suis, & cæcâ obedientiâ ad aliorum arbitrium, quâdam affectatâ ignorantiâ, se pati in turpissimos errores abduci.
units.tr: We understand the plain sense of the Scriptures you have brought forward to magnify and enlarge the authority of your judgment. The rabbis, those wicked teachers among the Jews, have likewise corrupted these same Scriptures with their gross glosses, shamefully and impiously. Clearly they tried, in order to confirm their own authority among the Jews, to strip everyone else of their judgment and common sense just as they had stripped themselves. Take first the passage in Deut. 17, where God, speaking through Moses, adds: "Whatever they teach you according to the law, you shall follow their sentence, and you shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left." From this the rabbis say: "If the judge should perhaps say that the left hand is the right, such a sentence must be held." Lyranus rightly rebukes this blasphemous and ridiculous gloss: "This is manifestly false, because the sentence of no man, of whatever authority, is to be held if it contains manifest falsehood or error. This is clear from what precedes in the text: [and he teaches according to the law]." Therefore whoever does not wish to be deprived of his eyes, and to be led by blind obedience to the will of others, must necessarily explain this passage not simply but conditionally. Otherwise, by a deliberate ignorance, he suffers himself to be drawn into the most shameful errors.

units.la: Ad alterum Scripturæ locum accedo, de Cathedra Mosis, in qua Scribæ & Pharisæi sedisse dicuntur; in quos Christus, propter Cathedræ istius nefarium abusum, adeo vehementer est inuectus, Matth. 23. 2 Vae vobis Scribæ & Pharisæi, qui clauditis regnum Dei alys[?], neque ipsi intratis, neque alios intrare finitis. Ad hæc verba vester Arias Montanus, Theologus celebris, & de Ecclesia Christiana optimè meritus. {b}Multa fuerunt (inquit) in Scripturis mysteria, ad Regnum Dei pertinentia, — sed Pharisæi neque eis attendebant, neque alios ad hæc instruebant, aut instrui patiebantur, sed toti in illis erant, ut nudarum caeremoniarum observationem, sine explicatione significationum ipsarum, inculcarent; neq; permittebant ut quisquam de sacris Scripturis cogitaret, nedum doceret quicquam, nisi se consultis, & ex suarum interpretationum prescripto. Itaque illis claudebant regnum Dei ante homines; neque enim hominibus cæteris à se licebat de Scripturis agere: Sic enim dicebant Cæco illi restituto, in peccato natus es, & vis docere nos? Nolebant ut quisquam vel quam verissima illis afferret. Hæc ille. Vix ovum ovo tàm simile, tàm par, quàm cæca hominum obedientia, erga Pontificem, istis Rabbinicis, & Pharisaicis deliramentis.
units.tr: I come to the other passage of Scripture, about the Chair of Moses, on which the scribes and Pharisees are said to have sat. Christ inveighed so vehemently against them, because of their wicked abuse of that chair: Matt. 23. 2 Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, who shut up the kingdom of God against men; you neither enter in yourselves, nor allow those who would enter to go in. On these words your Arias Montanus, a famous theologian who deserved very well of the Christian Church, says: There were many mysteries in the Scriptures pertaining to the kingdom of God, but the Pharisees neither attended to them nor instructed others in them, nor allowed others to be instructed, but were wholly absorbed in urging the observance of bare ceremonies without explaining their meanings. They did not permit anyone to think about the holy Scriptures, much less to teach anything, unless he had consulted them and followed the prescription of their interpretations. So they shut the kingdom of God against men, for they did not allow other men to discuss the Scriptures. Thus they said to the man who had been healed of blindness: "You were born in sin, and do you want to teach us?" They did not want anyone to bring forward even the most true things. So far he. Scarcely one egg is so like another, so equal, as blind obedience towards the Pontiff is to these rabbinic and Pharisaical delusions.

units.la: Ad abusum Scripturæ huius quod attinet, de Cathedra Mosis, Erasmus, acerrimi vir iudicij, colophonem addet.
units.tr: As regards the abuse of this Scripture about the Chair of Moses, Erasmus, a man of the sharpest judgment, adds a final touch.

units.la: {1}Hunc locum de Cathedra Mosis quidam (loquitur de Ponti-sicis Episcopis, ipsisq; adeò Pontificibus) eo to quent, quassi parendum esset omnibus, quæ præcipiunt Episcopi, aut præpositi etiam impij, ob muneris authoritatem: cùm Christus de iis loquatur, qui rectè docent legem Mosaicam, non qui suis constitutionculis illaqueant homines. Hactenus de Scripturis obiectis, quas Tu tandem ad propositum tuum accommodaturus, de Principibus verba facis.
units.tr: Some people twist this passage about the Chair of Moses (he speaks of the Papal bishops, and of the Pontiffs themselves) as if everything that bishops, or even impious prelates, command were to be obeyed because of the authority of their office, whereas Christ is speaking of those who teach the Mosaic law rightly, not of those who ensnare men with their own petty constitutions. So far, concerning the Scriptures you have objected. You have at last set out to apply them to your purpose, and you speak about princes.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices

units.la: “ Hoc præceptum Sp. Sancti non obseruarunt Principes Germanie, quando surrexit Martinus Lutherus, & contra Sacerdotis imperium, qui eo tempore ministrabat Domino, neusu[?] doctrinas in populum seminare cæpit. — pag. 29.
units.tr: "The Princes of Germany did not observe this precept of the Holy Spirit when Martin Luther arose and began to sow new doctrines among the people against the authority of the priest, who at that time ministered to the Lord." Page 29.

units.la: 1. ANIMADVERSIO. Lutherum Pontificiorum partes, propter impiam Pontificium doctrinam; in novis fidei Articulis condendis, iure de- seruisse.
units.tr: 1. ANIMADVERSION. That Luther rightly abandoned the side of the Papists, because of their impious doctrine in framing new articles of faith.

units.la: Imò vero præceptum illud Sp. Sancti Deut. 17. conditionale fuisse, ex ipsius Sp. Sancti verbis, [Iuxta legem] iam {*}supra probauimus. At illud absolutum Pontificis ingum[?], ceruicibus suis imponi, seruiliter pati, Asellorum, non hominum esset: quod vel Reges vestri, quoties Illis collubitum est, excussisse constat. Quod ad Lutherum attinet. Nec eum adeò sibi Papam videri putamus, vt fas esse sibi crederet, nouum aliquam doctrinam seminare; nec, si fortè tantam sibi authoritatem arrogâsset, ita nos Papisti sumus, vt absolutè in illius verba iuremus. Vin' autem vt verum dicam? non aliam causam assignat Lutherus, cur Papatum deseruerit, quàm quia nouas Pontificum doctrinas ex animo sit execratus. Pontifex (inquit){e}quicquid illi rectum visum fuerit, in articulum fidei veritit. Certè quidem Lutherus, Lutheranique omnes vobis multò gratissimi forent, nisi hanc Pontificis insaniam repressissent. hoc vos satis testamini, quia {d}Cauédaest(inquitis) impia Luther anorum hæresis, qui dixerunt nullam esse in Ecclesia potestatem condendi novos articulos: Atque in Bulla Leonis inter Lutheri Hæreses (ut vos dicitis) numeratur hæc eius assertio; {e}Certum est (ait) in manu Ecclesiæ aut Papæ non esse statuere Articulos fidei: quùm tamen (Apostolo Iudice) nulla tetrior hæresis esse queat, quam hæc novos Articulos condendi professio; {f}Si vel nos, vel Angelus de cœlo prædicauerit aliquid, præter id quod accepistis, Anathema sit.
units.tr: Indeed that precept of the Holy Spirit in Deut. 17 was conditional, as we have already shown from the very words of the Holy Spirit: [according to the law]. {*}supra. But that absolute yoke of the Pontiff, to be placed on one's neck and endured like a slave, belongs to asses, not to men. Your own kings, as often as it pleased them, are known to have shaken it off. As for Luther: we do not think he so regarded himself as Pope that he would believe it lawful for himself to sow some new doctrine; nor, if he had perhaps arrogated such authority to himself, are we Papists so bound that we must swear absolutely to his words. But shall I tell you the truth? Luther gives no other reason why he deserted the Papacy than that he utterly detested the new doctrines of the Pontiffs. The Pontiff (he says), whatever seems right to him, he makes into an article of faith. Certainly Luther and all the Lutherans would be far more welcome to you, were they not to have checked this madness of the Pontiff. You yourselves bear sufficient witness to this, since you say that the impious heresy of the Lutherans is one that denied the Church any power of framing new articles. And in the Bull of Leo, this assertion of his is numbered among Luther's heresies (as you say): "It is certain that it is not in the hand of the Church or of the Pope to lay down articles of faith." Yet, by the judgment of the Apostle, no more foul heresy can exist than this profession of framing new articles: "If we, or an angel from heaven, should preach anything besides what you have received, let him be anathema."

units.la: Huc spectat antiquissima accuratissimi Vincentij Lirinensis præscriptio, in illum Apostoli locum, [Serua depositum:] {h}Id est, quod tibi creditum, non quod à Te inuentum; quod accepisti, non quod excogitasti; rem non ingenij, sed doctrinæ; in qua non Author esse debes, sed custos; non institutor, sed sectator; Aurum accepisti, aurum reddes, non plumbum; nolo auri speciem, sed naturam plane: præter id quod acceperit Catholicus, nunquàm licuit, nunquàm licebit annunciare aliquid. Anathematizare eos, qui aliquid, præterquàm quod acceperunt, ordinent, nunquàm non opportuit, nunquàm non oportebit. Addo, quod Te magis calumnie arguat, doctrinam illam, quam Lutherus seminare cœpit, cùm primùm Papali tyrannidi se opposuit, si tempus spectes, vetustissimam; si Scripturam diuinam, verissimam; si occasionem, quæ Lutherum ad eam propugnandam impulit; omnino necessariam fuisse, vestrorum hominum suffragijs facile {*}euincemus. Hæc de recentioribus Germanis Principibus, quos Tu antiquorum quorundam exemplis erudiendos putas; pergis enim.
units.tr: To this bears the very ancient rule of the most accurate Vincent of Lerins, on that Apostolic text, "Keep that which is committed to thee": that is, what has been entrusted to you, not what has been invented by you; what you have received, not what you have thought up; a matter not of talent but of doctrine, in which you ought to be not the author but the guardian, not the founder but the follower. You have received gold; you will hand back gold, not lead. I want the true substance of gold, not its outward appearance. Beyond what the Catholic has received, it has never been lawful, and never will be lawful, to announce anything. It has never not been necessary, and never will not be necessary, to anathematize those who set down anything other than what they have received. I add something that will convict you of calumny more strongly: the doctrine which Luther began to sow, when first he opposed himself to papal tyranny, if you look at the time, is most ancient; if you look at the divine Scripture, most true; if you look at the occasion which moved Luther to defend it, entirely necessary. This we shall easily prove with the support of your own men. So much for the more recent German princes, whom you think must be instructed by certain examples of the ancients; for you go on.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices

units.la: "Sedilli Principes vere pij seruarunt mandatu Dei, qui cum piissimis Gratiano & Theodosio seniore dixerunt, [Cunctos populos, quos Clementiæ nostræ regit imperium, in tali religione volumus versari, quam Diuum Petrum Apostolum tradidisse Romanum, religio usque adhuc ab ipso insinuata declarat; quamq; Pont. Damasum sequi claret.] pag 30.
units.tr: "Yet truly pious princes kept the command of God, who, with the most pious Gratian and the elder Theodosius, said: 'We wish all peoples whom the empire of our Clemency rules to dwell in that religion which the Apostle Peter handed down to the Romans, which the religion inserted by him until now declares, and which it is clear Pope Damasus follows.'" Page 30.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Hoc in loco Bellarminum Principes Protestantes vitupe- rando laudare.
units.tr: Here Bellarmine praises the Protestant princes by way of reproach.

units.la: Nescio an Tu Lutheri sectatores, quos levitatis ac novitatis arguis, vllo pacto commendare magis poteris, quàm ob oculos illis ponendo pijssimorum istorum Imperatorum exempla, quorum nunc premunt vestigia: siquidem Lutherus non novam hanc Pontificiam, de novis Articulis, doctrinam tradidit, sed antiquam illam, & verè Apostolicam, quàm Petrus & Paulus primò Romanos imbuerint; quamquè, post eos, Damasus, & foeliciorum temporum Pontifices secuti sunt. Grates igitur Tibi quam maximas Lutherus, ipsique adeò Principes Germaniae agere debuerunt pro hâc summâ Eorum laude; nisi quod gratiae causa hic nihil facias, pergis enim.
units.tr: I do not know whether you could recommend Luther's followers, whom you charge with levity and novelty, in any better way than by setting before their eyes the examples of those most pious emperors, whose footsteps they now follow. For Luther did not deliver this new Papist teaching, a new doctrine of new articles, but that ancient and truly Apostolic one, with which Peter and Paul first imbued the Romans; and after them Damasus and the Popes of the happier times followed it. Luther and the Princes of Germany therefore owe you the greatest thanks for this high praise. Except that you do nothing for the sake of gratitude here, for you go on:

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Offic.

units.la: Et sanè mirabile, quòd apud aliquos Principes plus fidei inuenerit, in rebus fidei, vna ouis errans ab Ouili, quàm summus Pastor, ab ipso Domino constitutus & Doctor, & & Iudex. — pag. 30.
units.tr: And indeed it is remarkable that among some princes one straying sheep from the fold has found more faith in matters of faith than the supreme Minister, constituted and appointed by the Lord himself as teacher and judge. — p. 30.

units.la: I. AINMADVERSIO
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Lutherum Ouem innocentem, & Pastorem probum agno- sci posse.
units.tr: That Luther may be recognised as an innocent sheep and an upright minister.

units.la: Mirari desine; nam quando Christus discipulis suis dixit, {i}Mitto vos tanquàm Oues inter Lupos, dùm vocat Eos oues, non negat esse Pastores. Si enim Apostolorum ipsorum innocentiam spectemus, reuera Oues; sin verò eorum munus Apostolicum, {k}Praedicandi Euangelium omni creaturae, certè quidem Pastores primarij fuere. Lutheri innocentiam vis? Erasmum audi, in Epistola ad Archiepiscopum Moguntinum. {l}Si Lutheo (inquit) favorem ut viro bono, quod fatentur & hostes; si ut reo, quod permittunt leges; si ut oppresso, quod dictat humanitas, quae tantandem esset invidia? non facile debacchandum in eum, cuius vita probatur ab omnibus. Ecce igitur verè Ouem Lutherum. Doctrinam porrò quæris? Erasmum ausculta denuò; {m} Impium fit (inquit) Lutherum in hic[?], quæ recte dixit, indefensum relinquere, ne posthàc non sit, qui verum audeat proloqui. Ecce Pastorem strenuum Lutherum nostrum. Hunc siue Pastorem, siue Ouem Leo Papa (vt vos {n} fatemini, voluptatibus deditus, maximè verò venationi) tanquàm innocuam Ouem venatur, & omnibus modis insectatur.
units.tr: Stop wondering. When Christ said to his disciples, {i}I send you as sheep among wolves, while he calls them sheep he does not deny that they are ministers. For if we look at the innocence of the Apostles themselves, they were indeed sheep; but if we look at their Apostolic office, of preaching the gospel to every creature, they were certainly the chief ministers. Do you want proof of Luther's innocence? Hear Erasmus again, in his letter to the Archbishop of Mainz: {l}If (he says) Luther is shown favour as a good man, which even his enemies admit; if as an accused man, which the laws allow; if as an oppressed man, which humanity dictates, what envy could there be? One should not rage against a man whose life is approved by all. Here, then, is Luther truly a sheep. Do you ask about his teaching? Hear Erasmus once more: {m} It is wicked (he says) to leave Luther undefended in those things which he has rightly said, lest there be no one hereafter who dares to speak the truth. Here is our Luther, a vigorous minister. Leo the Pope, who (as you admit) was given over to pleasures and especially to hunting, hunts this man, whether you call him minister or sheep, as an harmless sheep, and pursues him by every means.

units.la: Mirabile igitur Tibi videri non debuit, quòd Principes pietatis ac veritatis amantes Ouem istam, etiam minimè errantem, è faucibus Leonis eripuerint. De Pastore, & Doctore quod repetis satis superque {*} diximus. Tu pergis, & Lutheri doctrinam exagitas.
units.tr: It should therefore not have seemed strange to you that princes who love piety and truth snatched this sheep, who is not even straying at all, from the jaws of the lion. As for the minister and teacher, which you repeat, we have said enough and more than enough about that. {*} You go on, and attack Luther's teaching.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Offic.

units.la: At (inquies) Lutherus verbum Dei pro sua sententia proferebat. Itâ est, sed cum de intelligentia verbi Dei quæstio esset, cur non obseruandum est aliud Dei verbum, apertissime docens vt ad Sacerdotem iretur, qui eo tempore ministrabat Domino Deo suo? Et posteaquam de Concilio Sapientium Pastor primarius sententiam dixit, & Lutherum Hereticum pronunciauit, vbi est verbum Dei, quod apponi docet Hereticum declaratum ipsi Iudici summo, ab ipso Domino constituto? — Pag. 30.
units.tr: But (you will say) Luther brought forward the word of God in support of his own opinion. So he did; but when the question was about the understanding of the word of God, why was not another word of God observed, which teaches most clearly that one should go to the priest who at that time ministered to the Lord his God? And after the chief minister had given his opinion on the council of the wise, and had pronounced Luther a heretic, where is the word of God which teaches that a heretic declared by the supreme Judge himself, constituted by the Lord, is to be appealed to? — p. 30.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Alibi verò sic. {o} Nostro seculo Lutherus ab indulgentiarum reprehensione principium fecit sectæ suæ propagandæ, vt perspicuum est ex assertionibus articulorum à Leone X. damnatorum. {p} Quæ dixit Rex, de vsibus Indulgentiarum, & de cumulandis opibus per artificium Iubileorum & Indulgentiarum, satis ostendunt, eum plus fidei habuisse Luthero, & similibus Nouatoribus, quàm simplici veritati. {q} Quare à Rege, unde nouum illud lumen Anglis affulseris? ab Aquilone, respondebit, inde enim primus eorum Propheta Lutherus emersit. At nos Prophetam audimus dicentem, [{*}Ab Aquilone pandetur omne malum:] & si omne malum, certè tenebrae eorum, non lux veritatis.
units.tr: Elsewhere you say this: {o} In our century Luther began the propagation of his sect with a criticism of indulgences, as is clear from the assertions of the articles condemned by Leo X. {p} What the King said about the uses of indulgences, and about amassing wealth by the trickery of jubilees and indulgences, sufficiently shows that he trusted Luther and such innovators more than plain truth. {q} Therefore, you will answer, from which King did that new light dawn upon the English? From the north, for their first prophet Luther emerged from there. But we hear our Prophet saying, [{*}From the north all evil will be unleashed:] and if it is all evil, then surely theirs is darkness, not the light of truth.

units.la: Hæc Tu; sed confuse nimis complures quæstiones & perturbatè misces; quas Nos, methodi gratiâ, in sua genera dispertiemus: I. De Iudice vestro agemus: II. De Luthero Reo, & iudicato: III. De Causa ipsa: IV. De Prophetia illa Ab Aquilone; in qua non modò omnes Anglos, & præcipuè serenissimum Magnæ Britanniæ Regem satis insulsè subsannas: verùm etiam luculentissimis sacræ Scripturæ verbis caliginem offundis, & ad sensum tuum planè abuteris. Et quoniam hæc omnia abs Te eo animo dicuntur, ut Principes aduersus Lutheri doctrinam instiges, propterea, postremo in loco, orthodoxum iudicium Lutheri aduersus Papistas, de nequiter violata Eorum, erga Principes, obedientia attexemus.
units.tr: You say these things, but you mix together, rather confusedly and disorderly, a great many questions. For the sake of method we shall divide them into their proper kinds: I. We shall deal with your Judge. II. We shall deal with Luther as the accused and condemned. III. We shall deal with the cause itself. IV. We shall deal with that prophecy of the North, in which you not only mock with great folly all the English, and especially the most serene King of Great Britain, but also throw darkness over the most luminous words of Holy Scripture and abuse them completely to suit your own sense. And since all these things are said by you with the purpose of inciting princes against Luther's teaching, for that reason, in the last place, we shall add the orthodox judgment of Luther against the Papists concerning the wickedly violated obedience of their subjects towards princes.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Summam Regulam interpretandi Legem non esse absolutè penes Pontificem Romanum.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. The highest rule for interpreting the Law is not absolutely in the power of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: AD primam quæstionem, de obseruatione verbi Dei Deut.17. quoad Iudicem à Deo constitutum, eiusque Scripturæ expositionem, facilis est responsio. Principes Protestantes Scripturæ istius sensum, nempe Conditionalem vel maximè accipiunt, & simul prudenter admodùm animaduertunt vos sub Titulo Iudicis fucum Christianis facere. Primò, quia in N. Testamento Sacerdotem unum visibilem à Deo Ecclesia vniuersalis Iudicem constitutum esse, vniuersa Ecclesia vetus semper, tanquàm monstrum, & lymphaticum insomnium, execrata est. II. quià vix credibile est, vt Iudex vester (sicut verba Deut.17. monent,) Iuxta legem, exponat legem; quandoquidem profiteatur ipsum scriptum verbum, seu legem Dei,{a} Non perfectam aut sufficientem Regulam esse, iuxta quam Controuersia definiendæ sint. III. quia hic vester Iudex, in Interpretandis Scripturis, interdum cœcutit, & hallucinatur; quod Episcopus vester non negat, quia {b} In sanctarum Scripturarum expositione, & consequenter in inquisitione aliarum quarumlibet veritatum, Tractatores sacra Scriptura, ut Hieronymus, Augustinus, & caeteri sunt praeponendi Pontificibus. Certè ipse Hieronymus non Damasum Papam, sed Gregorium Nazianzenum vocabat Praeceptorem suum; {*} A quo didici (inquit) explanare Scripturas: & Rhemigius censuit non Pontificem Bonifacium, sed Augustinum Hipponensem Episcopum {*} Excellere omnes Theologos in exponendis Scripturis. Imò in hoc munere Interpretandi Scripturas quis non Bellarmini (vide quantum Tibi tribuimus) quàm Pauli Quinti Pontificis iudicium pluris faciet? IV. quia, ut vobiscum duplex verbum Dei esse demus, vnum [illegible, ~8 letters], seu scriptum, alterum [illegible, ~6 letters]; non scriptum; Iudicium tamen vestri Sacerdotis in Lutheri causa (de Indulgentijs) vtriusque verbi fundamento omni penitus destitutum fuit.
units.tr: As to your first question, concerning the observance of God's word in Deuteronomy 17 regarding the judge appointed by God and the exposition of that Scripture, the answer is easy. The Protestant princes understand the sense of that Scripture mainly as conditional, and at the same time they very wisely notice that you, under the title of judge, are deceiving Christians. First, because the whole ancient Church has always execrated, as a monstrous and frenzied dream, the notion that the New Testament appoints one visible priest by God as judge of the universal Church. Second, because it is hardly credible that your judge, as the words of Deuteronomy 17 direct, should expound the law "according to the law," since he professes that the written word itself, that is, the law of God, is not a perfect or sufficient rule by which controversies are to be decided. Third, because this judge of yours sometimes goes blind and wanders in interpreting the Scriptures; your bishop does not deny this, since in the exposition of the holy Scriptures, and consequently in the inquiry into any other truths, the expositors of Holy Writ, such as Jerome, Augustine and the rest, are to be preferred to the Popes. Certainly Jerome himself called not Pope Damasus but Gregory Nazianzen his teacher, "from whom I learned," he says, "to explain the Scriptures"; and Remigius judged that not Pope Boniface but Augustine, bishop of Hippo, surpasses all theologians in expounding the Scriptures. Indeed, in this office of interpreting the Scriptures, who would not value the judgment of Bellarmine (see how much we concede to you) above that of Pope Paul V? Fourth, because, granting with you that there are two words of God, one [illegible], or written, the other [illegible], not written, the judgment of your priest in Luther's case (concerning indulgences) was wholly destitute of the foundation of either word.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. De Luthero Reo; deq; occasione, & modo iniquissimo adver- sus Illum procedendi.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. On Luther as the accused; and on the occasion and the most unjust manner of proceeding against him.

units.la: Iacobus Augustinus Thuanus, vir non minùs erudi-tione, quàm officij dignitate nobilis, &, si quis alius, veri studiosus, Id, quod nunc docere conamur, fideliter copiosèque est prosecutus: cuius ego integrum Testimonium, in gratiam lectoris, referre minime gravabor.
units.tr: James Augustus Thuanus, a man as noble in learning as in the dignity of his office, and as devoted to the truth as anyone, has faithfully and at length set out what we are now trying to teach. For the reader's benefit I will not hesitate to quote his whole testimony.

units.la: {c} Peccatum, in sacris muneribus dispensandis, Leo (Pontisex) max longè graviore cumultuavit; nam cùm aliquos[?] ad omnem licentiam sponte suâ ferretur, Laurentij Puccy Cardinalis, hominis turbidi, cui nimium tribuebat, impulsu, ut pecuniam ad immensos sumptus undique corrogaret, missis per omnia Christiani orbis regna diplomatis, omnium delictorum expiationem ac vitam aeternam pollicitus est, constituto pretio, quod quisque pro peccati gravitate penderet: in eam rem per Provincias Quaestores & aerarii ordinaut, quibus additi Praecones, qui tanti beneficij magnitudinem apud populum commemcommendarent ; & orationibus artificiosè compositis , propositisque palam libellis rei efficaciam immoderatè extollerent. Quod licentia è nimis à Pontificijs Ministris passim , atque in Germania præcipuè fiebat ; vbi, qui redimendam pecuniam Romæ à Pontifice conduxerunt , lustra & popinas quotidie sine pudore, in aleæ lusum vsúsque turpissimos potestatem extrahendi animas functorum ex igne expiatorio profundebant. Tunc exortus Martinus Lutherus , Augustinianus , Vitembergæ in Saxonia Theologiam professus ; qui refutatis primùm, mox damnatis praconum concionibus , eò postremò deuenit, vt ipsam Pontificis potestatem , quam sibi per illa Diplomata arrogabat , in dubium revocaret , ac tandem ad doctrinæ examen, quam successu temporis libef[?]actam dicebat; crescentibus per contentionem animis , descenderet. Hæc Ille. Reum ipsum loquentem audiamus æquum est. "Clarè & diserte te- statí sumus" (inquit Lutherus) vt si non cogerent (nempè Pontificij) Nos ad Articulos palam impios, & blasphemos, nos bonâ ex parte eorum Iurisdictionem Episcopalem defensuros : sed reuerenter, & simpliciter ad eorum pedem prostratos ; & in causa publicæ æquissima petentes, Nos ad Satanica sua mendacia cogere volunt ; alto fastu me despicient, quod Indulgentias eorum, (bullæ enim erant) diffidàssem[?].
units.tr: Pope Leo committed a much graver sin in dispensing the sacred offices.
