For when he was himself inclined to every kind of licence, at the instigation of Cardinal Laurentius Pucci, a troublesome man on whom he relied too much, he set out to raise money on all sides for his immense expenses. Sending bulls throughout the kingdoms of the Christian world, he promised the expiation of all offences and eternal life, for a fixed price which each man would pay according to the gravity of his sin. For this purpose quaestors and treasurers were appointed in the provinces, with heralds added to commend to the people the greatness of so great a benefit; with artfully composed speeches and publicly displayed pamphlets they extolled the efficacy of the thing without measure. This licence was practised everywhere by the Papist ministers, and especially in Germany, where those who had contracted to redeem money from the Pope at Rome squandered brothels and taverns daily without shame, on gambling and the most shameful practices, with the power of drawing the souls of the dead out of the purgatorial fire. Then arose Martin Luther, an Augustinian who taught theology at Wittenberg in Saxony. He first refuted and soon condemned the sermons of the heralds, and at last came to call into question the very power of the Pope which he claimed for himself through those bulls; and finally, as tempers rose in the contention, he proceeded to the examination of the doctrine, which he said had been freed in the course of time. So far he. It is only fair that we hear the accused himself speaking. "We have clearly and plainly testified," says Luther, "that if they (the Papists) did not compel us to articles openly impious and blasphemous, we would in good part defend their episcopal jurisdiction. But when we humbly and simply prostrate ourselves at their feet, and in a most just public cause make our petition, they wish to compel us to their satanic lies; they will despise me with lofty pride, because I distrusted their indulgences (for they were bulls)."

units.la: Hactenùs de modo procedendi, qui in Luthero piùm sanè zelum, in Pontificijs verò egregium factum, imò etiam tyrannidem arguit. Nam, (teste Polydoro) Cùm Lutherus, Theologus apud suam gentem primarius, doctrinam Indulgentiarum improbaret, Procuratores (qui erant Institores Pontificis) eâ de re valdè commoti, primo quoque tempore nomen Lutheri Romam ad Magistratus detulerunt, is continuò Deorum contemptor accusatur ; causa agitur ; sed quia ad diem dictum non adfuit Romæ præsens, vt responderet, paulò post declaratur Haereticus. Hæc Ille. Quis hæc, (sic enim Lutherum appellas) tùm misella, quid faceret? Romæ coram Papæ Leonis tribunali non se sisteret? nihilominùs pro Haretico damnandus esset : sisteret verò se? Ad quæ confugeret, (tantùm) ora Leonis habuit. Consultius Illi videbatur, vt absens illis calamo, quàm præsens sanguine suo satisfaceret: præsertim vbi aut Rei (nisi veritatem proderet) vita periclitanda foret, aut Iudicis ipsius Errores turpissimi vniuerso orbi denudandi. Vtinam peregrinis, ex Inquisitionis vestræ faucibus, pateret reditus! Quantum verò Lutherus docendo disputandóque profecerit, Alphonsus vester non obscurè ostendit: quia,quòd Lipsiæ populum Ecchio Lutherum præstulerit, infert, non publicè disputandum esse cum Hæreticis pertinacibus, sunt enim (inquit) sæpè in disputando disertissimi.
units.tr: So far on the manner of proceeding, which shows in Luther a truly pious zeal, but in the Papists an outstanding deed, indeed even tyranny. For (as Polydore testifies) when Luther, the chief theologian among his people, disapproved of the doctrine of indulgences, the agents (who were the Pope's hawkers), greatly disturbed by this, at the first opportunity reported Luther's name to the magistrates at Rome; he is at once accused as a contemner of the gods; the case is pursued; but because he did not appear in person at Rome on the appointed day to answer, shortly afterwards he is declared a heretic. So he. What could that wretched man (for so you call Luther) do then? Would he not present himself before the tribunal of Pope Leo at Rome? Nevertheless he would have to be condemned as a heretic; and if he did present himself, to what could he flee, when he had only the jaws of Leo? It seemed wiser to him to make satisfaction to them with his pen while absent, rather than with his blood while present; especially where either the life of the accused would be endangered (unless he betrayed the truth), or the most shameful errors of the judge himself were to be laid bare to the whole world. Would that there were a way back for strangers out of the jaws of your Inquisition! How much Luther profited by teaching and disputing, your Alphonsus shows not obscurely: for because at Leipzig the people preferred Luther to Eck, he infers that one should not publicly dispute with obstinate heretics, for they are (he says) very often most eloquent in disputing.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Indulgentiarum doctrinam longè abesse à veritate, anti- quitate, pietate.
units.tr: The doctrine of indulgences is far removed from truth, antiquity and piety.

units.la: Lutherus duplicem Pontificiorum errorem, circa Indulgentias, exagitat; vnum in Praxi, quia Indulgentijs abutuntur ad conflandas pecunias: Alterum in doctrina, quia Indulgentias ad animas non solùm viuorum, verumetiam mortuorum subleuandas, & ex igne expurgatorio liberandas valere prædicant: Atq; hoc dogma verum, piumq; esse decernunt. Bellarminus praxin tàm turpiter quaestuosam negat; doctrinam verò nouitiam defendit. Io.[?] de de Praxi, respondet eam esse {g}Nouatorum calumniam, quà dicitur, Pontifices, per artificium Indulgentiarum, opes colligere atque corradere. Verecundiùs multò Conc. Tridentini Patres, qui reprehendentes {h}Quaestorum abusus, quorum (inquiunt) malitia ita quotidie magno fidelium omnium scandalo, & querela deprehenditur, vt de eorum emendatione spes nulla relicta videatur: Statuit Sancta Synodus, vt post hac in quibuscunque Christianæ religionis locis eorum nomen atque vsus penitus aboleatur.
units.tr: Luther attacks the Papists' double error concerning indulgences: one in practice, because they abuse indulgences to raise money; the other in doctrine, because they proclaim that indulgences are effective for the souls not only of the living but also of the dead, to relieve them and to free them from the purgatorial fire, and they decree that this doctrine is true and pious. Bellarmine denies that the practice is so shamefully profitable, but defends the doctrine as new. Io. (on the practice) replies that it is a calumny of the innovators, by which it is said that the Popes gather and heap up wealth through the device of indulgences. The Fathers of the Council of Trent speak far more modestly. In censuring the abuses of the questors, they say: Their wickedness is detected every day with great scandal and complaint from all the faithful, so that no hope of their amendment seems to remain. The holy Synod decrees that henceforth their name and practice be utterly abolished in whatever places of the Christian religion.

units.la: Anigitur tantùm in Quaestores, Pontificum seruos, culpam hanc transferendam putemus; & Dominos ipsos immunes, & nullius criminis affines esse censeamus?
units.tr: Shall we, then, think this fault is to be laid only on the questors, the servants of the Popes, and judge that the masters themselves are free and have no share in any crime?

units.la: De immanibus Pontificum Abusibus ab aliquot seculis, ante Concilium Tridentinum, omnes vbique locorum Historici grauiter {*}conquesti sunt: at, post Emendationem per SS.Synodum factam, vt omnis abusus in locis omnibus aboleatur, nihil non sanctum & syncerum expectandum fuit. At audi, quaeso, Massonium vestrum, hominem minimè Lutheranum (vtpote qui Lutherum Impia doctrinae praeconem haud pie vocet) nec tamen tam vndiquaque Pontificium, quin vera Pontificum vitia liberè fateatur. {i}Reuertar (inquit) ad Indulgentias, vt illud verissimè dicam, Rom. Pontifices adhuc nimium indulgentes suisse. Mittamus Praxin, doctrinam euentilemus.
units.tr: All historians everywhere have for some centuries, before the Council of Trent, grievously complained of the monstrous abuses of the Popes; but after the reform made by the holy Synod, so that every abuse be abolished in all places, nothing but holiness and purity was to be expected. Listen, I beg you, to your Massonius, a man by no means a Lutheran (since he does not piously call Luther a preacher of impious doctrine), and yet not so entirely Papist that he does not freely confess the true vices of the Popes. I shall return (he says) to indulgences, so that I may say the very truth: the Roman Popes were still too indulgent. Let us set aside the practice; let us examine the doctrine.

units.la: Indulgentiarum doctrinam ipsam tùm nouam, tùm etiam impiam, aut saltem impietatis nutricem esse, crebrae vestrorum Authorum confessiones testantur. De nouitate primùm citatur à {k}nonnullis Antonius, & Syluester Pierius liberè dicentes, Nihil expressè haberi de Indulgentiis nec ex Scripturis, nec ex dictis antiquorum Doctorum.
units.tr: Frequent confessions of your own authors testify that the doctrine of indulgences itself is both new and impious, or at least a nurse of impiety. As to its novelty, some cite first Antonius and Sylvester Prierias, who freely say: Nothing is expressly held about indulgences, either from the Scriptures or from the sayings of the ancient teachers.

units.la: Roffensis Episcopus, praecipuus Lutheri Antagonista, concedit vltrò; {l}In principio nascentis Ecclesiae nullum suisse Indulgentiarum vsum. Agrippa tum demùm Earum vsum coepisse affirmat, {m}Postquam (inquit) ad Purgatorij cruciatus aliquando trepidatum est: primùm autem, qui indulgentias ad Purgatorium extendit, Bonifacium octauum fuisse. Hic autem Bonifacius sedem Papalem occupauit circa Annum MCCXCIV. Alphonsus quandam antiquorum Indulgentiarum praxin, ab {n}Antiquis Stationibus emendicat; astutè Nos celans, quae fuerit illarum Stationum vera ratio. Hanc {o}Onuphrius accuratè copiosèque tradit, docetque fuisse solennes conuentus Christianorum in communibus precibus, ieiunijs, & ritibus Sacramentalibus celebrandis, in quibus ad populum alloquentem verbi diuini Ministri concionabantur. De Indulgentijs vero nè ꝑ quidem. Quod planè intelexisse Alphonsus videtur, quia quasi Stationes suas deserens, eò redactus est angustiarum, vt diceret, {p}Non ideò contemnendas esse indulgentias, quòd earum vsus in Ecclesia videtur serò receptus, quia multa sunt, (inquit) Pastoribus nota, quae vetustiores Scriptores ignorárunt. Sic Ille.
units.tr: The Bishop of Rochester, the chief antagonist of Luther, concedes readily: In the beginning of the rising Church there was no use of indulgences. Agrippa then affirms that their use began only after men had at some point grown anxious about the torments of purgatory; but the first to extend indulgences to purgatory was Boniface VIII. This Boniface occupied the papal see about the year 1294. Alphonsus begs from the Ancient Stations a certain practice of ancient indulgences, cunningly concealing from us what the true nature of those Stations was. Onuphrius sets this out accurately and fully: he teaches that they were solemn assemblies of Christians for celebrating common prayers, fasts and sacramental rites, in which the ministers of the divine Word preached to the people as they addressed them. But of indulgences there is not even a trace. Alphonsus evidently understood this clearly, since, abandoning his Stations, he was driven into such straits that he said: Indulgences are not to be despised because their use seems to have been received late in the Church, for there are many things, (he says), known to the ministers, which the more ancient writers did not know. Thus he.

units.la: Quod quid aliud est quàm praevaricari planissimè, causamque suam prodere, dum Indulgentiarum doctrinam nouam esse negare omninò non potest; nisi fingendo esse aliquam doctrinam antiquam, Antiquis Patribus penitùs incognitam? quae absona extra modum, absurdáque vox est, & in sanctos Patres proterve contumeliosa.
units.tr: What is this but to prevaricate most plainly and betray your cause, when you cannot altogether deny that the doctrine of indulgences is new, unless you pretend that there is some ancient doctrine entirely unknown to the Ancient Fathers? This is an absurd and unseemly expression beyond measure, and shamelessly insulting to the holy Fathers.

units.la: Verùm doctrina hæc facilius admitti posset, si tantùm vna, & non etiam impia esset: quam ex Scholasticis Authoribus quidam, multò ante Lutherum, (nisi quod piam adiunxerint) verè fraudem vocárunt: quam Thesauro Ecclesiæ spirituali satisfactionum (quem Vos Indulgentiarum fundamentum dicitis) carere dixerunt Doctores Lovanienses; &, ex Scholasticis, Maior & Durandus. His si nefarius Earum abusus accesserit, pietatis nouerca, vel carnificina esse videantur: Dicit enim Polydorus; dicit verò? imò verò dixit; nunc enim, né dicat, praui vestri Inquisitores Polydori sententiam deleri mandárunt, quae huiusmodi fuit. "Tempore cumprimis Bonifacij IX. Pontificis, quando huiusmodi venia plena manu non concedebatur modo, verumetiam (teste Platina) viti quadam merces vendebatur,— minus multi a malefactis abstinebant, & clavium authoritas multò vilior erat.
units.tr: Yet this doctrine could be admitted more easily if it were merely one that was false and not also impious. Some of the Scholastic authors, long before Luther (except that they added the word pious), truly called it a fraud: that it lacks the spiritual treasury of the satisfactions of the Church (which you call the foundation of indulgences), the Louvain doctors said; and among the Scholastics, Major and Durandus. If its wicked abuse be added to these, it may seem a stepmother of piety, or even its executioner. For Polydore says—or rather, said; for now, lest he say it, your wicked Inquisitors have ordered the opinion of Polydore to be erased, which was of this kind: "Especially in the time of Pope Boniface IX, when such indulgence was not granted in full measure, but (as Platina testifies) some kind of wine-merchandise was sold"—fewer men abstained from wrongdoing, and the authority of the keys was far cheaper.

units.la: His pensitatis, quis tàm excors, qui non planè intelligat; quis tàm effrons, qui neget Luthero iustam causam fuisse oppugnandi doctrinam hanc vestram; tùm haeretice nouam Ἀντιέργων[?]; tum blasphemè sacrilegam; tùm (ex abusu eius) impiè profanam? Si quis igitur cupiat Controuersiae inter Lutherum Oecum (sic enim appellas) & Leonem Pontificem, de turbandâ Ecclesiâ, statum liquidum perspicere; Apologum consulat, in contentione inter Oecem & Lupum, de turbandâ aquâ; & statim intelliget hanc de vobis narrari fabulam. Hæc de Causa, nunc ad sutile Bellarmini scomma reuertar.
units.tr: Having weighed these things, who is so dull as not to understand plainly, who so shameless as to deny that Luther had a just cause for attacking your doctrine, which was heretically new, [Ἀντιέργων] and blasphemously sacrilegious, and (through its abuse) impiously profane? If anyone therefore wishes to see clearly the state of the controversy between Luther, the Oecus (for so you call him), and Leo the Pope, over the disturbing of the Church, let him consult the fable of the contention between Oecus and the Wolf, over the muddying of the water; and he will at once understand that this tale is told about you. So much for the cause; now I return to Bellarmine's subtle jest.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Bellarmini, de Aquilone, farcasmate Prophetae mentem perperam depravari.
units.tr: Bellarmine's jibe about the North wrongly distorts the Prophet's meaning.

units.la: Quàm hoc insulum, & [illegible, ~8 letters], quaerenti ab Anglia Rege, unde lux Euangelij Anglis affulserit; responsurum eundem Regem, ab Aquilone? qua Tu voce Germaniam intelligis. Quasi vero ex Insula nostra Germaniam prospicienti oculi Septentrionem versus sint conuertendi. Sic, si non toto (quod aiunt) coelo, at certè dimidio errat Cardinalis. Multò verò etiam grauius errat, quòd nesciat Regem Angliae (quae est Eius, in caussis Diuinis, mentis perspicacitas) responsurum, Euangelium, quod Anglia profitetur, (quum non sit aliud, quam quod Christus Iesus sacrosanctis Noui Testamenti Scripturis consignari voluit) non magis Nouum dici, quàm est ipsum Nouum Testamentum Iesu: Nec ab Authore Luthero, sed à Lutheri Domino Christo: nec à Germania, vel Aquilone, sed (vndè salus ipsa, ceu sol) ab Oriente, nempè, à Iudea primò ortum habuisse: ex eodem verbo (inter maximas superstitionum vestrarum tenebras) lux illa Luthero affulsit, quae nunc adeò oculos vestros perstrinxit; vt quùm plerique vestrum coràm intueri, ac palàm profiteri non audeant, limis tamen oculis aspicientes, nonnulli tamen visae veritati testimonium haud obscurum subindè praebeant. Vix enim controuersia vlla est, inter Protestantes & Pontificios vehementiùs agitata, in qua, ex Ecclesia vestra, non aliqui Authores sanè grauissimi Causae nostrae Patroni disertissimi extiterint.
units.tr: How silly is this, and [illegible], when he asks the King of England where the light of the Gospel first shone on the English, and assumes the King will answer "from the North", which you take to mean Germany! As if those looking out from our island towards Germany had to turn their eyes to the North. So the Cardinal errs, if not by the whole heaven (as they say), at least by half of it. Far more serious is his error in not knowing that the King of England would answer (and this is the keen insight of that King in divine matters) that the Gospel which England professes is no newer than the New Testament of Jesus itself, since it is nothing other than what Christ Jesus willed to be set down in the holy Scriptures of the New Testament. It has its origin not from Luther as author, but from Luther's Lord Christ; not from Germany or the North, but (whence salvation itself comes, like the sun) from the East, that is, from Judea first. From that same word, amid the thickest darkness of your superstitions, that light shone upon Luther, and it has now so dazzled your eyes that, although most of you dare not look at it directly or openly profess it, nonetheless some of you, looking with squinting eyes, now and then give no faint testimony to the truth you have seen. For there is hardly any controversy between Protestants and Papists debated more vehemently in which some very grave authors of your Church have not stood up as most eloquent defenders of our cause.

units.la: Veruntamen ex Prophetiae verbis ioculariter insultas; {*}At Nos (inquis) Prophetam audimus dicentem, ab Aquilone pandetur omne malum. Ier.1. Et si omne malum, certè tenebrae eorum, non lux veritatis. Vbi per [omne malum] omne vitium; per [ab Aquilonem] Germaniam; per [Tenebras] haeresin in religione intelligis. Eodem prorsus ingenio Bozius vester; {a}In Protestantes (inquit) illud aptissimè cadit, [Ab Aquilone pandetur omne malum:] Vos namq; nobis ad Aquilonem, nos vobis ad Austrum sumus; quomodò igitur estis ab Ecclesia Dei? Hæc ille. Absurda omnia, & prorsus violenta. Nam primò Prophæta ipse satis explicat, quo de genere mali loquitur, vbi denunciat videre se {b}Ollam succensam à facie Aquilonis; ---- quia connocentur omnes cognationes Regnorum Aquilonis, aduersus vrbes Iudæ, & loquar (inquit) iudicia eorum ( nempe Iudæorum) qui dereliquerunt me. Loquitur tantùm de malo vindictæ, & iræ Dei. Id quod vestri Iesuitæ facilè perspiciunt; Per Aquilonem {c} (inquiunt) intelligit Prophæta Chaldæos, seu Babylonios; per ollam succensam, Dei iram; per Nebuchadonozorem, qui erat instrumentum iræ Dei, ad Ierusalem expugnandam à Babylone venturus, quæ erat Iudæa Aquilonaris, [loquar iudicia mea, ait Dominus] Id est, ostendam me iuste punire Vos Iudæos. Quæ malum! igitur hæc vestra oscitantia, seu potius peruersitas, quod tantùm de malo pœna dicitur [sicut & Amos.3. Non est malum in ciuitate, quod Deus non fecit] id de malo culpæ exponere & interpretari? Vos igitur infesto in Lutherum, Germanos, & Anglos odio, tanquàm præcipiti turbine abreptos fuisse; & in hoc, de Aquilone, Commento vestro, cùm faceti videri vultis, ridiculos esse quis non videat?
units.tr: But you mock the words of the Prophet with a jest: {*}"But we (you say) hear the Prophet saying, 'Out of the North all evil shall break forth.' Jer. 1. And if all evil, then certainly their darkness, not the light of truth." Here you understand by all evil every vice; by out of the North Germany; by darkness heresy in religion. With exactly the same cleverness your Bozius: "This saying, 'Out of the North all evil shall break forth,' (he says) fits the Protestants most aptly. For you are to us in the North, and we to you in the South; how, then, are you from the Church of God?" So he. All of this is absurd and wholly forced. For first, the Prophet himself explains clearly what kind of evil he is speaking of, when he announces that he sees {b}a boiling pot, its face turned away from the North; ... because all the families of the kingdoms of the North shall be gathered against the cities of Judah, and I will utter (he says) my judgments (namely, against the Jews) against those who have forsaken me. He speaks only of the evil of vengeance and the wrath of God. Your Jesuits readily see this: {c}"By the North (they say) the Prophet means the Chaldeans or Babylonians; by the boiling pot, the wrath of God; by Nebuchadnezzar, who was the instrument of God's wrath, coming from Babylon to storm Jerusalem, which was Northern Judea, [I will utter my judgments, says the Lord]. That is, I will show that I justly punish you Jews." What evil! So then, is it your carelessness, or rather perversity, that when it is said only of the evil of punishment [just as Amos 3 says: There is no evil in the city which the Lord has not done], you expound and interpret it of the evil of guilt? Therefore, while you wish to appear witty in your hostile hatred of Luther, the Germans and the English, as men swept away by a headlong whirlwind, and in this commentary of yours on the North, who does not see that you are ridiculous?

units.la: Quin dic, obsecro, nunquamnè legisti vbi scriptum est, {d}Ab Aquilone aurum? Hoc nisi Pontifices vestri experti olim fuissent, vbi miseros Germanos, & Anglos {e}Exactionibus, & Indulgentiarum artificio tantis pecuniis emunxissent, nunquam in doctrinam Lutheri tam immaniter sæuijssent. Denique quanto rectius Nobis in vos telum vestrum retorquere liceat, nimirùm, [Omne malum ab Aquilone] ait Propheta: vbi per Aquilonem Babylonem significat: at Roma (omnium ferè Pontificiorum consessione) est Babylon Apocalyptica, Ergò. Sed Nobis non vacat vobiscum in re seria nugas agere. Illud forte, Bellarmine, te male habet, quòd non sumus isti Boreales, de quibus Baronius vester tantopere gloriatur; qui
units.tr: Come, tell me, I beg you, have you never read where it is written, {d}"Gold from the North"? Had your Popes not once experienced this, emptying the wretched Germans and English of such great sums by {e}exactions and the trickery of indulgences, they would never have raged so savagely against the doctrine of Luther. Finally, how much more rightly may we turn your own weapon back upon you: the Prophet says, "All evil from the North", where by the North he signifies Babylon; but Rome (by the almost universal confession of the Papists) is the Babylon of the Apocalypse. Therefore... But we have no leisure to trifle with you in a serious matter. Perhaps this is what troubles you, Bellarmine, that we are not those Northerners of whom your Baronius boasts so much, who

units.la: V. ANIMADVERSIO. Lutheri doctrinâ Principum incolumitatem & dignitatem maximè muniri.
units.tr: V. ANIMADVERSION. The doctrine of Luther most strongly defends the security and dignity of princes.

units.la: NOn sum nescius Lutherô seditionis notam abs Te, saltem obliquè, fuisse inflatam: {g}Nam quis (inquis) Lutheri temporibus author fuit tot millibus rusticorum, ut adversus Principes arma sumerēt? nonne Ministri reformata, vel deformata potiùs religionis? Quàm Tu maligno hic in Lutherum animo hanc Anabaptistarum rabiem transtuleris, malim ex tua confessione, quàm ex aliqua coniecturâ meâ prudenti Lectori innotescat. {h}Potestatem politicam esse apud Christianos illicitam, est (inquis) opinio Anabaptistarum: quam non solùm Catholici omnes execrantur, sed etiam Lutherus in Saxonica visitatione, Philippus Melanchthon, Et Calvinus acerrimè oppugnant. Rectè. Non igitur Lutheri religio deformata (ut vir facetus loqueris) rabiosis Anabaptistarum fauit cohortibus; sed ingeniosa tua in istam religionem malitia has criminationes confinxit, ut Principum animos adversus Lutherum odio incenderes.
units.tr: I am not unaware that you have, at least obliquely, fixed the mark of sedition upon Luther: {g}"For who (you say) in Luther's time was the author of so many thousands of peasants taking up arms against the princes? Was it not the ministers of a reformed, or rather deformed, religion?" How you, with malicious spirit against Luther, have transferred this Anabaptist frenzy to him, I would rather let the prudent reader learn from your own confession than from any conjecture of mine. {h}"That political power is unlawful among Christians," you say, "is the opinion of the Anabaptists, which not only all Catholics execrate, but Luther in his Saxon visitation, Philip Melanchthon and Calvin also vigorously oppose." Rightly so. Therefore Luther's religion was not deformed (as you, a witty man, put it) and did not favour the frenzied bands of the Anabaptists; it is your ingenious malice toward that religion that has invented these accusations, so that you might inflame the minds of princes with hatred against Luther.

units.la: Qui tamen eò vobis odiosior videtur, quanto pro Principum maiestate pugnat acriùs, quantòque in Papam, propter violatam Eorum maiestatem, acerbiùs inuehitur. Sic enim Lutherus. {i}Jam vehementer piget pudetq;, imò miseret me (inquit) quoties cogito quot & quanta ludibria sibi ab Imperatoribus, Principibus, universaq; natione Germania Papa sibi fecerit. Deus bone! quanta libidine & fiducia in eis lusit? nonsecus eos ducens ac tractans quàm irrationabilia bruta, quibus tantùm ad cædes, dolos, rapinas, & quicquid Satan suggerere potuit Papisticarum artium abuteretur. Sanctus Petrus Papatum graphicè depinxit, 2. Pet. 2. [Dominationes spernunt:] tantùm abest ut Dominationem
units.tr: Yet he seems the more hateful to you, the more strongly he fights for the majesty of princes, and the more bitterly he attacks the Pope for violating their majesty. For thus Luther: {i}"Now I am greatly grieved and ashamed, indeed I pity myself, whenever I think of how many and how great mockeries the Pope has made of Emperors, Princes and the whole German nation. Good God! With what pleasure and confidence he has played with them, treating them no differently than irrational beasts, which the Papistical arts abuse only for slaughter, deceit, plunder, and whatever Satan could suggest. Saint Peter depicted the Papacy vividly, 2 Peter 2: [they despise dominions]; so far is it from the case that the dominion..."

units.la: {e} Quemcunque intelligerent nomine tenus sedentem in sede Romana, nulla habita discussione, eius ingressum ut Petrum colebant. agnoscat Papa, ut summos Principes egre ad osculapedum admittat; dein Monachum, & Sacrificulum stipite rudiorem, & lenone sceleratiorem, super universos mundi proceres eleuet, propter Characterem illum indelebilem. ita coguntur Dominationes contemptæ honorare idola, à quibus honorari debuerant; ignauissimum hoc animalium genus vix porcis alendis idoneum. Hæc Lutherus. Quæ verba Scopum Tractatus tui De officio Principis tam directè attingit, acsi propositum illi fuisset, eum diserte conuellere. Hactenus de Luthero: pergis Tu, & pari æquitate Caluinum inuadis.
units.tr: {e} Whoever they understood, by name alone, to sit in the Roman see, without any examination, they worshipped his entrance as if he were Peter. Let the Pope acknowledge that he admits the greatest princes with difficulty to kiss his feet; then he exalts a monk and a sacrificing priest, ruder than a stick and more villainous than a pimp, above all the nobles of the world, on account of that indelible character. Thus the contemned dominions are compelled to honour the idols by whom they ought to have been honoured; this most cowardly kind of animal is scarcely fit to feed pigs. So Luther. These words strike so directly at the aim of your treatise On the Office of the Prince that it would seem you had set yourself the purpose of openly overthrowing him. So much for Luther; you go on, and with equal fairness you attack Calvin.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office.

units.la: “ Hoc idem dici potest de Principibus illis, qui Johannem “ Caluinum, tanquàm nouum Apostolum receperunt. ―― Pag.31.
units.tr: "The same may be said of those princes who received John Calvin as a new apostle." ―― p. 31.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Titulum Apostoli Nos Caluino nullum tribuere; quewm[?] Pape[?] prærogatiuam esse adulatorie asseruant Pontificy[?].
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. That we do not attribute the title of Apostle to Calvin; the Papists assert that this is an arrogant prerogative of the Pope.

units.la: BEnè se res habet. si enim de Caluino idem dici potest, quod supra de Luthero; idem igitur, pro Caluino, responsum Tibi satisfacere debet. Imò, inquies, Principes Caluinum, tanquàm nouum Apostolum receperunt. Antiquum quidem obtines, dum calumnias in Caluinum congeris: ostende, si potes, ex omnium Protestantium scriptis, quæ sunt prope infinita, ubi vel quis Princeps Caluino nomen Apostoli tribuerit; aut ubi Caluinus ipse hunc Titulum sibi delatum approbauerit. Sed quid rei sit sen-tio. Tu scilicet dignitatis Papalis zelotes nimis hoc pacto cautum esse voluisti, nè quis Papam hac Arrogantiæ quasi prærogatiuâ priuaret: quem vos iactabundi commemoratis, ab Oratoribus Principum, {k}Apostolorum haredem; ab {l}Hayto (Anno Domini MCCCVII. in libro iussu Pontificis scripto) Apostolum vocari. Nec hoc solum, sed ipse Tu, Bellarmine, gestis non tantum {m}Rom. Pontificem. Sedis Apostolica Præsulem dici; sed etiam eius munus dici Apostolatum. Sed de hoc Titulo {*}infrà pluribus.
units.tr: Things stand well enough. For if the same can be said of Calvin as was said above of Luther, then the same answer, given for Calvin, ought to satisfy you. But, you will say, the princes received Calvin as a new Apostle. You are holding on to an old charge while you heap slanders on Calvin. Show me, if you can, from the writings of all the Protestants, which are almost countless, where any prince ever gave Calvin the name of Apostle, or where Calvin himself approved of this title being offered to him. But I know what your game is. You, a zealot for the Papal dignity, wanted to guard against the idea that anyone might strip the Pope of this arrogant prerogative, which you boastfully recall: that the orators of the princes called him heir of the Apostles, and that Hayton (in the year of the Lord 1307, in a book written by order of the Pope) called him Apostle. Not only that, but you yourself, Bellarmine, have no hesitation in calling the Roman Pontiff not merely the prelate of the Apostolic See, but also calling his office an apostolate. But I shall say more about this title below.

units.la: Quid multa? Inter Protestantes & Pontificios lata & grandis est differentia; nam Calvinum Illi tantùm vt Apostolicæ doctrinæ præconem colunt: hi verò Papam, vt purum putum [illegible, ~8 letters]: Illi Calvino credunt, propter verbum Evangelij (unde est quòd Evangelici sæpè audiant;) hi verbo Dei, propter Papam. Nec enim Eius Iudicium ex veritate verbi examinandum; sed verbi veritatem (saltem quoad Nos) ex Papæ iudicio pedere profitentur: inde fit vt verè ac proprie Papistæ appellentur; neque enim Sectariorum tesseram aut notam luculentiorem demonstrari vlla potest. Hæc de Titulo, quem Calvino affingis; sequitur de sigillo vocationis, quod ab Illo exigis.
units.tr: Why say more? There is a wide and great difference between Protestants and Papists. For the Protestants honour Calvin only as a herald of apostolic doctrine, but the Papists honour the Pope as a mere man. The Protestants believe Calvin on account of the word of the Gospel (which is why Evangelicals often listen to him), but the Papists believe the word of God on account of the Pope. For they openly profess that his judgment is not to be tested by the truth of the word, but that the truth of the word (at least as far as we are concerned) depends on the judgment of the Pope. Hence they are rightly and properly called Papists; for no clearer badge or mark of the sectarians can be shown. So much for the title which you attach to Calvin. Next comes the seal of vocation, which you demand from him.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic. Calvinum porrò insectans.
units.tr: Bellarmine, in De Officiis, attacking Calvin further:

units.la: “Calvinum tanquam novum Apostolum receperunt, cùm tamen nulla signa Apostolatus sui ostendere posset, nisi viventem hominem vere mortificatum, quem ex morte ad vitam falsò à se revocari credi voluerat.— pag.31.”
units.tr: “They received Calvin as a new Apostle, although he could show no sign of his apostleship, except a living man truly mortified, whom he wanted people to believe he had falsely called back from death to life.” —p. 31.

units.la: Sic Tu; sed hæc vestra pellucida calumnia est.
units.tr: So you say; but this is your transparent calumny.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Calvinum, ut miracula ederet, nunquam prorsus at- tentasse:
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. That Calvin never at all attempted to work miracles.

units.la: Calvinum verò miraculum edere vel tentâsse vnquam? falsò quoque? tale etiam Miraculum, quo ex vivo quis mortuus fiat? quodque illico in ludibrium verteret scilicet? Equis tanti tàmque stupendi facinoris testis idoneus? {o}Ex Bolseco hoc referre placuit. Placuit, ais? cui nihil non placet, quo Calvino conflctur odium. Ex Bolse-co verò? Ipsissimum expectabam; qui nimirum ex Eorum numero est, de quibus ipse Calvinus: {p}Multa ridicu[?]Iam & absurda nugati sunt famelici Errones, quibus nisi ventrem farcias, calumniarum plausibus[?] te obruent; partim nequam & scelerati homines, qui sua culpa à nobis dimissi, vel etiam ob maleficia abdicati, aliquo munere nouum pastum quaeritant[?], &c. Bolsecus (inquam) portentum hoc narrat, quod (uti mihi persuadeo) nemini sanae mentis, in Caluini scriptis versato, credibile videri potest; imo ne Bellarmino quidem: quippè tantùm semper abhorruit Caluinus ab hac curiositate affectandi miracula, vt, ad veritatem Euangelicam comprobandam, vel tentare miraculum edere cuiquam fas esse negaret. {q}Qui enim (inquit) veterum (viz. Apostolicorum) miraculorum oblitti, nouis inhiant, cum ita stupeant in aperta Dei veritate, & in clara luce caecutiant, non minora esse portenta dico, quàm si hominem in pecudem versum esse cernerem. Haec Caluinus, ac si non modò seipsum portenti loco haberi voluerit, verumetiam diceret, Tunc me quiuis existimet hominem conuersum esse in pecudem, quamprimum tentauero mortuum quemuis excitare ad vitam. Quid quòd ij, quibus Caluinus (dum in viuis erat) notissimus erat, nihil huiusmodi quicquam de illo cognouerunt? Bolsecus igitur tuus, Bellarmine, --- fingere qui non visa potest, prorsus niger est, propterea, ne Tibi imponat, --- Hunc tu Romane caueto. Si enim accusari sat est, quis innocens erit? si ab hoste iuratissimo, mendacissimo, mendicissimóque, quis vel erit tandem? nam hæc est ærugo mera.
units.tr: But did Calvin ever work a miracle, or attempt to? Is it even falsely claimed? Is it a miracle of such a kind, by which someone is made dead out of a living man, and which would at once be turned into mockery? Where is a witness fit for such a great and stupendous deed? You were pleased to report this from Bolsec. Pleased, you say? He to whom nothing is unpleasant, if it brings hatred on Calvin. From Bolsec? I expected exactly that; for he is certainly one of those of whom Calvin himself says: The famished vagabonds have babbled many ridiculous and absurd things, and they will overwhelm you with applause for calumnies unless you stuff their bellies; some of them are wicked and villainous men, whom we dismissed for their own fault, or even cast out for their crimes, and who seek some new livelihood by this means, etc. Bolsec (I say) tells this portent, which (as I am persuaded) can seem credible to no one of sound mind who has studied Calvin's writings; no, not even to Bellarmine. For Calvin always so shrank from this eagerness to seek miracles that he denied it was right for anyone even to attempt to work a miracle in order to prove the Gospel truth. For he says: Those who, forgetful of the miracles of the ancients (namely the apostolic ones), gape after new ones, when they are so dazed by the plain truth of God and grow blind in the clear light, I say that their portents are no less than if I saw a man turned into a beast. Thus Calvin speaks, as if he not only wished himself to be held as a portent, but also to say: Then let anyone think that I have been changed into a beast, as soon as I attempt to raise any dead man to life. Moreover, those to whom Calvin was very well known while he was alive knew nothing of any such thing concerning him. Your Bolsec, then, Bellarmine, who invents what cannot be seen, is utterly black; so, lest he deceive you, beware of him, Roman. For if it is enough to be accused, who will be innocent? If [the charge comes] from a most sworn, most lying and most beggarly enemy, who will ever be safe? For this is pure rust.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Pontificiorum miraculosa figmenta, seu fictitia Mi-racula.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. The miraculous fabrications of the Papists, or fictitious miracles.

units.la: POssem Ego (si animus mihi esset in hac speculatione diutius immorari) fabulam hanc, in odium Caluini confictam, nimis frequentibus vestrorum hominum praestigijs plurimis facilè compensare. Pauca tantùm libet ex vestrorum hominem confessionibus delibare.
units.tr: I could (if I had the mind to linger longer on this speculation) easily match this fable, invented out of hatred for Calvin, with very many of the frequent tricks of your men. I wish to draw only a few things from the confessions of your men.

units.la: I. {r}Maximam in Ecclesia deceptionem populi fieri in miraculis, eulis, fictis à Sacerdotibus, propter lucrum temporale.
units.tr: I. There is a very great deception of the people in the Church in regard to miracles, false ones, made up by priests for temporal gain.

units.la: II. {c}Quidam sunt, qui fabulis vanis, & fictis miraculis memoriam eorum, quibus fauent, studeant vulgo commendare; ea nonnunquam laudantes, quae laudatus nec fecit vnquam, nec probauit.
units.tr: II. There are some who, by empty tales and fictitious miracles, eagerly commend to the common people the memory of those whom they favour, sometimes praising things which the one praised never did or approved.

units.la: III. {t}Alij Diuorum construunt historias, pie nonnihil admentientes, supponunt reliquias, fabricant miracula, fingunt terribiles fabulas. &c.
units.tr: III. Others construct histories of the saints, lying a little in piety, they put forward relics, fabricate miracles, invent terrible tales, etc.

units.la: IV. {u}In hoc Capite (Augustini) non dubium (loquitur Viues de Miraculis) multa sunt addita ab ijs, qui omnia magnorum Authorum scripta spurcis suis manibus contaminarunt.
units.tr: IV. In this chapter (of Augustine) there is no doubt (Vives is speaking of miracles) that many things have been added by those who have defiled all the writings of the great authors with their filthy hands.

units.la: Hisce nimirum filiis Ecclesia vestra se pastam gestit. At verò nostra (fateor) perinde se iactitare nequit, aut quemquam praedicando fecisse vnquam vt {x}Pisces sonore laudarent Deum; aut praecipiendo coegisse, vt {y}Mulus adoraret Hostiam; aut vidisse aliquid {z}Spicæ Miraculum stramineum; aut {a}Domum per multa milliaria in in aere volitantem; aut {b}Apes Sacellum, cum astia, altari, fenestris, tintinnabulis construentes; aut {c}Muscas per excommunicationem interfectas; aut {d}Bufonem versum in caponem; vel (vt vester Cosmus, in hoc valdè [illegible, ~5 letters] ) {e}Damonē pod. crep. (quod me referre pudet) aut recentis stercoris faetore esse dupulsum; vel denique (nam abundè nimis fabularum habuimus) adeò quenquam nostrum foelicem, foecundumque miraculorum fuisse, vt {f}Necesse haberet interdictu, nè amplius miracula vlla faceret. Hæc de Calumnia tua; sequitur Hallucinatio.
units.tr: Your Church is clearly proud to be nourished on such children. But ours (I admit) cannot boast in the same way, that by preaching it has ever made anyone, as in the fish that loudly praised God; or by commanding, forced a mule to adore the Host; or seen any miracle of a straw ear; or a house flying through the air for many miles; or bees building a chapel with a shrine, altar, windows and bells; or flies killed by excommunication; or a toad turned into a capon; or (as your Cosmus, in this very [illegible] ) a demon farting (which I am ashamed to relate), or driven off by the stench of fresh dung; or finally (for we have had more than enough of fables) that any one of ours was so happy and fruitful in miracles that he had to be forbidden by interdict to work any more miracles. So much for your calumny; next comes the hallucination.

units.la: III ANIMADVERSIO. Aduersarios non sine summa peruersitate a Caluino, aut Pro- testantibus Miracula exigere.
units.tr: III ANIMADVERSIO. The adversaries, not without great perversity, demand miracles from Calvin or the Protestants.

units.la: IMportunius à Protestantibus Miracula exigere eò confidentius peruersitatem voco, quanto certius intelligo tùm vestram exigendi rationem instantijs appositissimis obtundi; tum etiam Vos, qui, tanquàm crediturí, miraculorum vicinia, iis [illegible, ~4 letters] (si forte fiant) obicem, ahenum[?] euia exigitis, ijs tamen (a forte nam) [?] oppositurus non credendi, obstinaciam. Instantia prima exemplum Iohannis Baptistæ proponitur: nam 1o. (vt obiectioiectiones Bellar. ipsorum Pontificiorum Confessionibus diluamus) Eius ministerium extraordinarium tuisse probatur, Quia (vt recte {h} Iansenius) Iohannes in deserto, non in templo praedicabat, exordium nouae legis docuit, & necesse esse vt homines se ad Euangelij gratiam pararent. Secundo, liquet Ipsum apud Scribas & Pharisaeos, qui tum erant praecipui Synagogae Doctores, in summo {i} odio fuisse, quia (Luc. 7.) Pharisaei spreuerunt consilium Dei, non baptizati ab eo, nempe, Iohanne: quem dixerunt habere Demonium, Id est, (Toleto Card. teste) {k} non credebant Iohannem missum à Deo, nec hoc solum, sed etiam obmurmurarunt contra eum, tanquam virtute Daemonis vitam austeram agentem. Et tamen idem {l} Toletus, & {m} Suarez, duo primarij Iesuitae, rationes multas attulerunt, cur conueniens fuerit, vt Iohannes miracula nulla faceret; iuxta quod scriptum est, Iohannes signa nulla fecit.
units.tr: I call it perversity, all the more confidently as I understand more clearly that your demand for miracles from the Protestants is refuted by the most fitting objections, and that you, who, as if ready to believe, demand miracles from close at hand, and who would set an obstacle against them (if by chance they happen) by your unbelief, are obstinate. The first instance offered is the example of John the Baptist. For first (to answer the objections of Bellarmine and of the Papists themselves), it is shown that his ministry was extraordinary, because (as Jansenius rightly says) John preached in the desert, not in the temple, taught the beginning of a new law, and it was necessary that men prepare themselves for the grace of the Gospel. Second, it is clear that he was held in the greatest hatred by the Scribes and Pharisees, who were then the chief teachers of the synagogue, because (Luke 7) the Pharisees rejected the counsel of God, not being baptized by him, namely John, whom they said had a demon, that is (as Cardinal Toledo testifies) they did not believe that John was sent by God, and not only this, but they also muttered against him, as one who lived a austere life by the power of a demon. And yet the same Toledo and Suarez, two leading Jesuits, have brought forward many reasons why it was fitting that John should do no miracles; according to what is written, John did no sign.

units.la: Altera Instantia petitur ab exemplo Ignatij Loyolae, primi Societatis Iesuiticae Patris, quem tandem Beatum deprædicant Romanenses; cuius missio extraordinaria fuit, vtpote qui discipulos suos voto extraordinario deuinxit, vt, nimirum {n} ad quascunque prouincias Orbis terrarum Pontifex pro tempore existens eos mitteret, sine cunctatione obtemperarent.
units.tr: The second instance is taken from the example of Ignatius Loyola, the first Father of the Society of Jesus, whom the Romanists at last proclaim Blessed. His mission was extraordinary, inasmuch as he bound his disciples by an extraordinary vow, so that, namely, whatever provinces of the world the Pontiff existing at the time should send them to, they would obey without delay.

units.la: Ecquibus vero miraculis Ignatium Societatem suam saltem testatum fecit? Imò (ait Bozius) Hominem, qui se suspenderat, precibus ad vitam revocavit. At Ribadeneira Iesuita, vitam Ignatij Loiola describens, in eodem Cap. quod De Miraculis instituit, introduxit Eum, tanquam Miracula faciendi virtute omnino destitutum; totusque in hoc est, vt eis satisfaciat, quibus proclive erat quaerere, Quid causa sit, cur Ignaty sanctitas non est demonstrata miraculis? Post ex S. Gregorio occurrens; Probatio Sanctitatis (ait) non est miracula facere, sed proximum vt se diligere. Et tandem; Itaque (inquit) Iohannes Baptista signum fecit nullum, vt ait Euangelista. Attende Lector; Iesuitae exemplum Iohannis Baptistae, pro Ignatio Loyola, vsurpare licuit; Protestantibus autem, pro Iohanne Calvino, non licuit: quo nemo quaeret Peruersitatis documentum insignius.
units.tr: But by what miracles did Ignatius make his Society at least attested? Indeed (says Bozius) he restored to life, by his prayers, a man who had hanged himself. But Ribadeneira, a Jesuit, describing the Life of Ignatius Loyola, in the same chapter which he entitled On Miracles, presented him as wholly destitute of the power of working miracles; and he is entirely intent on satisfying those who were inclined to ask, What is the cause why Ignatius' holiness was not shown by miracles? Afterwards, coming upon Gregory, he says: The proof of holiness is not to work miracles, but to love one's neighbour. And at last: Therefore (he says) John the Baptist did no sign, as the Evangelist says. Note this, reader: the Jesuits were permitted to use the example of John the Baptist for Ignatius Loyola, but the Protestants were not permitted to use it for John Calvin: in which no one will seek a more striking proof of perversity.

units.la: En vero (si fieri posset) expressius indicium peruersitatis, quia praesertim ij, qui à Protestantibus Miracula importunius efflagitant, ita comparati sint, vt fidem omnem Miraculis derogent, etiamsi signa omni exceptione maiora oculis suis videant. Qui vero hoc constet? Attendite. Synodo Tridentine[?] quidam Theologus selectissimus interfuit, cui pro concione in hunc modum perorare licuit. {q} Quid si Illi verbis suis (inquit, de Protestantibus agens) addant miracula? quid si strophis & artibus dicendi addant virtutem operandi? ---Vos videte ne seducamini: Ecce, inquit Christus, prædixi vobis, quantumuis mag-na mirabilia, naturæ & artis vim excedentia, prædicta tamen sunt nè citò moneamini; signum hoc est proxime desolationis imò ipsa est magna desolationis pars. Atque etiam Sedulius vester contra Protestantes (quos vir magnus scilicet Missallos[?] vocat) eodem planè ingenio Augustini testimonium citat. {r}Miracula non facitis (inquit) quæ si faceretis, etiam ipsa in vobis caueremus. Hæc illi. At verò ea requirere, atque adeò deposcere, atque efflagitare, tanquam sufficientia testimonia ad confirmandam doctrinam; sed tamen (vt docent alij) eâ tantùm lege, vt isthoc pacto nemo Illis persuadeat, etiamsi persuaserit. Quæ hæc vertigo? Ad Principes redeo, vt intelligamus tandem quo hæc pertinent, quæ de Luthero[?], & Caluino fabulati estis omnia.
units.tr: Indeed, here is an even clearer sign of perversity (if that could be), since especially those who most insistently clamour for miracles from the Protestants are so disposed that they detract from all faith in miracles, even when they see with their own eyes signs greater than any objection. But how is this established? Attend. A certain most select theologian was present at the Council of Trent, and he was allowed to hold forth in a sermon in this manner. What if they (he said, speaking of the Protestants) add miracles to their words? What if they add by flourishes and the arts of speaking the power of working? ---Take heed that you be not deceived: Behold, says Christ, I have foretold you; however great the wonders, exceeding the power of nature and of art, they are foretold so that you may not be quickly warned; this is a sign of the near desolation, indeed it is itself a great part of the desolation. And your Sedulius too, against the Protestants (whom that great man, of course, calls Missallos), cites the testimony of Augustine with the very same cleverness. You do not work miracles (he says), which, if you did, we would beware even of them in you. So he. But truly to require them, and indeed to demand and clamour for them, as sufficient testimonies to confirm doctrine; yet (as others teach) only on this condition, that by this means no one would be persuaded by them, even if they had persuaded. What vertigo is this? I return to the Princes, so that we may at last understand to what these things pertain, which you have fabricated about Luther and Calvin altogether.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office

units.la: “ Qui Principes, si fidem potius habere voluissent Doctori omnium Christianorum, à Christo ipso Ecclesiæ dato, pro cuius fide, vt non deficeret, orauerit, certè in improbam sensum dati non fuissent. ---- Pag.31.
units.tr: "Those Princes, if they had preferred to place faith in the teacher of all Christians, given to the Church by Christ himself, for whose faith he prayed that it might not fail, would certainly not have fallen into a wicked sense of the gift." ---- Page 31.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Hæc dictat splendida Bilis; sed deponamus affectus; Causa cum causa-, ratio cum ratione concertet. Vos unum visibilem Iudicem Pontificem Rom. nobis obtruditis, non quidem in Individuo Vago peregrinantem; sed in certa & signata aliqua persona consistentem, vtpote hunc Paulum V. Id Tu satis innuis, cùm Doctorem assignas in Cathedra collocatum; nempe, (vt Tu alibi) {f}Qui omnes Controversias, quacunque oriri possunt in negotio religionis, lucet solus definiat: vel, vt significantius tuus Salmeron; {t}Sicut (inquit) Iudaeo ad salutem non satis fuit credere Messiam quendam futurum, nisi singulariter crederet hunc signatum Iesum, à Iohanne demonstratum: ita requiritur, vt credas diuinâ fide non tantum Rom. Pontificem, sed in singulari hunc signatum Paulum IV. ab Electoribus acceptum; dummodò nullum vitium aut defectum in eius Canonicâ electione admissum fuisse constare possit.
units.tr: This is what splendid bile dictates; but let us lay aside passions: let cause contend with cause, reason with reason. You thrust upon us one visible Judge, the Roman Pontiff, not wandering vaguely in an unspecified individual, but standing in a certain and designated person, namely this Paul V. You indicate this well enough when you assign a Teacher placed in the Chair: namely (as you say elsewhere) who alone may define all controversies that can arise in any matter of religion; or, as your Salmeron says more pointedly: As (he says) it was not enough for a Jew to salvation to believe that some Messiah would come, unless he believed singularly that this designated Jesus, pointed out by John, was he; so it is required that you believe with divine faith not only the Roman Pontiff, but in the singular, this designated Paul IV, received by the electors; provided it can be established that no vice or defect was admitted in his canonical election.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Ex ipsius Pontificis Decreto, fidem Pontificibus plurimis abrogari, quos Ecclesia Romana tanquam Iudices suos venerata est.
units.tr: From the Pontiff's own decree, the faith owed to many popes is revoked, though the Roman Church has venerated them as its judges.

units.la: CErtam igitur aliquam & definitam personam, vtpote illum Clementem VIII. aut hunc Paulum V. Doctorem & Iudicem, in Romana Cathedra collocatum, diuinâ quidem fide credendum esse docetis: Cui, in omni fidei negotio, Christianis omnibus necessariò parendum sit; nisi existimari velint in reprobum sensum dari. Quodsi vnquam Deus graui aperto; iudicio summas potestates in reprobum sensum dederit; tum certè vel maximè eas, quae Regnum suum {*}Bestiae tradiderint. Vestrum me miseret, nec iniuriâ; nam (detis modò mihi veniam Causam hanc, de Iudice vestro, discutiendi accuratiùs) ostendam, non Protestantes Principes traditos esse in reprobum sensum, sed vos potiùs communi sensu penitùs excidisse: tum quòd hoc in loco tali signato Iudici tantum fidei habendum astruitis; tum verò magis, paulò post, vbi huic Iudici infallibile iudicium, & Rom. Cathedra constantiam inexpugnabilem tribuendam profitemini. Ab hac speculatione, de signato visibili Iudice, auspicabimur.
units.tr: You teach that we must believe with divine faith in some particular and defined person, namely Clement VIII or this Paul V, placed in the Roman chair as teacher and judge, to whom all Christians must necessarily submit in every matter of faith, unless they wish to think that God has given them over to a reprobate mind. But if God has ever, by a manifest and grave judgment, given the highest powers over to a reprobate mind, then surely he has done so most of all to those who have handed over their kingdom to the Beast. I pity you, and not without reason. For (if you will allow me to examine this question of your judge more carefully) I will show that it is not the Protestant princes who have been given over to a reprobate mind, but rather that you have utterly fallen from common sense. This is so, first, because in this place you claim that so much faith must be given to a designated judge; and still more so, shortly afterwards, where you profess that infallible judgment must be attributed to this judge and an unconquerable constancy to the Roman chair. We shall begin with this speculation about the designated visible judge.

units.la: Plurima sunt, quæ fidei vestræ tenebras offendunt. Primò, quoad Ordinationem, quià nullus est legitimus Episcopus, qui non est Sacerdos; nullius verus Sacerdos, qui non est "recta intentione ordinatus. At intentio ordinantis Sacerdotem quempiam nullâ infallibili evidentiâ vobis innotescere potest: quantò minùs hoc decernere licet in ipsis Pontificibus, quorum {x} Alij Episcopis, qui ab alijs ordinabantur, Sacerdotalem ordinationem abrogárunt? Secundò, Illegitimas Pontificum electiones consideremus, & in maiori caligine vos cœcos versari constabit. Quùm enim Iudex ille vester Romanus Pontifex decreuerit, vt {y}Si quis periurio, vel gratiâ humanâ, vel popularí, militariúe tumultu, & non concordi & Canonica electione Cardinalium Pontifex eligitur in thronum Petri; Is non Apostolicus, sed Apostaticus merito vocetur, liceatá, Cardinalibus, & Clericis Deum colentibus eum, vt prædonem, anathematizare, & quouis humano auxilio à sede Apostolicâ propellere. Hæc Pontifex; quem sequutus Bzouius, quantus quantus totus vir Pontificius: {z}Quifquis se (inquit) in Cathedram ingerit, neque per ostium, sed aliunde vi, corruptela, ambitione irrumpit, hominem talem oues Christi non sequuntur, filij Dei non agnoscunt, congregatio iustorum detestatur, velati ANTICHRISTUM. Sic ille.
units.tr: There are many things that darken your faith. First, concerning ordination: since no one is a legitimate bishop who is not a priest, and no one is a true priest who is not "ordained with right intention." But the intention of the one ordaining a priest can never become known to you by any infallible evidence, and much less may this be decided concerning the Pontiffs themselves, some of whom have denied priestly ordination to bishops who were ordained by others. Second, let us consider the illegitimate elections of the Pontiffs, and it will be clear that you are walking in still greater darkness, blind as you are. For when that judge of yours, the Roman Pontiff, decreed that "if anyone is elected to the throne of Peter by perjury, by human favour, or by popular or military tumult, and not by the unanimous and canonical election of the cardinals, he should rightly be called not apostolic but apostate; and the cardinals and clergy who worship God may anathematize him as a robber and drive him from the Apostolic See by any human aid." So said the Pontiff; and Bzovius, however much a Papist he was, followed him: "Whoever pushes himself into the chair, and breaks in not through the door but from elsewhere, by force, corruption or ambition, such a man the sheep of Christ do not follow, the sons of God do not acknowledge, the assembly of the just detests him, and he is clearly ANTICHRIST." So he.

units.la: His positis, Deus bone! Cathedra isthæc quot iamdiù Antichristos tenuit? Nam Onuphrius, Author vobis imprimis approbatus, refert{a} Iohannem X meretricis nobilissimæ (quæ eius amore flagrabat) Studio: Iohannem XXII à seipso: Bonifacium VII & Damasum II vi: Iohannem XI vi, & æstu: Silverium I. vi, & metu: Martinum II malis artibus; Papasque alios multos illegitimis modis Pontificatum adeptos esse. Hos tamen Ecclesia Rom. tanquam veros suos Iudices coluit: quemadmodum Iohanni XII, accidit, de quo Baronius;{b}
units.tr: With these things established, good God! How many Antichrists has this chair held for so long? For Onuphrius, the author you especially approve, reports: John X by the zeal of a most noble harlot who burned with love for him; John XXII by his own doing; Boniface VII and Damasus II by force; John XI by violence and heat; Silverius I by violence and fear; Martin II by wicked arts; and many other popes to have obtained the papacy by illegitimate means. Yet the Roman Church has venerated these men as its true judges, just as happened with John XII, concerning whom Baronius {b} writes:

units.la: {a} Hac apud Onuphrium de Creat. Pont.& Card. <| modo (inquit) dicendus fait legitimus Pontifex ; in cuius electione lex nulla est suffragata, sed omnia vi & metus impleuerint; cumq;[?] præ ætate, nec Diaconus esse potuit, & tamen hunc Rom. Ecclesia venerata est, minoris esse credens mali mortuum quantumlibet caput ferre, quam duobus capitibus infirmari, & unum in duo scindi. Hæc Ille. Quid igitur, lex Nicolaica dormis? Tertio in loco inter electos Antinalium consensu legitimè electus Papatu cedens, Honorium II. vi electum veneratus est: Quùmque Urbano VI. Cardinales tàm Itali quàm Galli, suis communibus suffragijs electo, Pontificatum abrogant, dicentes, sed falsò, metu populi Rom. se eum elegisse; Clementemq; VII. substituunt: in quo schismate Galli, Hispani, & Scoti Clementem; Germani verò, Hungari, & Angli Urbani partes sequuti sunt. Vti etiam accidit {b}Tempore Iohannis XXIII. quando tres erant, qui Pontifices haberi volebant, nec poterat facilè, iudicari quis eorum verus esset Pontifex: quia{i}Tres simul pro veris Papis haberentur. Iudicet nunc Lector vtrùm vel Ecclesia Rom. Catholica exi-stimanda sit, quæ Pontifices tot Apostaticos, tanquàm Doctores, & Iudices Apostolicos venerata est; an Principes toties in sensum reprobum coniecti, quoties Personam (in qua decernenda tam facilis & perniciis error est) in sede Pontificia collocatam, legitimum & indubitatum Iudicem suum diuinà fide credere recusauerint. Quod Reges & Iudices (vti spero) facilè perpendent; quos tu ad Intelligendum iam vehementer hortaris.
units.tr: {a} In the passage of Onuphrius on the Creation of Popes and Cardinals, he says, one must call him a legitimate Pope, in whose election no law gave support, but all things were carried out by violence and fear; and since, because of his age, he could not even be a deacon, yet the Roman Church venerated him, believing it a lesser evil to bear a dead head, however large, than to be weakened by two heads and to split one into two. So far he. What then, Nicolaitan law, are you asleep? Thirdly, in the place among the elected antipopes... [the text is garbled here] ...by the common consent of the cardinals, legitimately elected, yet resigning the papacy, the Church venerated Honorius II, who had been elected by violence. And when the cardinals, both Italian and French, abrogated the papacy of Urban VI, who had been elected by their common votes, saying (but falsely) that they had chosen him through fear of the Roman people, and set up Clement VII in his place, in that schism the French, Spanish and Scots followed Clement, but the Germans, Hungarians and English followed the side of Urban. This also happened {b} in the time of John XXIII, when there were three who wished to be held as Popes, and it could not easily be judged which of them was the true Pope, because three at once would be held to be true Popes. Let the reader now judge whether the Roman Catholic Church is to be regarded as holy, which has venerated so many apostate Pontiffs as its teachers and apostolic judges; or whether princes are to be cast into a reprobate mind whenever they refuse to believe with divine faith that a person (in whose appointment to the papal see so easy and so deadly an error is possible) is their legitimate and indubitable judge. Kings and judges (as I hope) will easily weigh this, and you now strongly urge them to understand.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: “ Ergò Reges intelligite, erudimini, qui iudicatis terram: “ illi Doctori fidem habete in controversiis fidei. — Pag.31.
units.tr: "Therefore, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth: give faith to that teacher in controversies of faith." — p. 31.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Pontifices Rom. subtractis omnibus Intelligendi medijs, Principes vt sapiant insulsè monere.
units.tr: The Roman Pontiffs, having removed every means of understanding, foolishly advise princes to be wise.

units.la: Præclari scilicet monitores Regum estis, vt intelligant, qui facitis næ dogmatizando & monèdo vt nihil quicquā intelligant: non Scripturarum voces, quas peregrina diæsecto editas, nè calleant, vos caucetis; docetis enim {k}Minimè expedire, vt in linguas vulgares vertantur; non sensum Scripturarum ex se, docetis enim {l}Scripturas esse velut nasum cereum, quæ horsum & illorsum trahi se permittunt, & quò traxeris non inuitas sequi: Non rationem Fidei suæ, quia docetis Eos {m}Implicitâ fide, & cæcâ obedientiâ Papæ Conclusionibus (absque Præmissis) tanquàm veris Oraculis credere: Non denique sese Reges esse internoscere, vtpote quos Papa, quotiescunque pecuniam aut præsidium ab illis exigit, pro Vasallis suis; quoties obsequium imperat, pro Mancipijs; quoties supplicium Illis infligit, pro pedum suorum scabellis habuit.
units.tr: You are clearly splendid advisers to kings, that they may understand, you who, by your teaching and your admonitions, make sure they understand nothing at all. You guard against the words of Scripture being understood, lest anyone become skilled in them, since they are published in a foreign tongue; for you teach that {k}it is by no means advisable for them to be translated into the common tongues. You deny the sense of Scripture to be clear in itself; for you teach that {l}Scripture is like a wax nose, which lets itself be dragged this way and that, and follows wherever you drag it, unwilling. You deny the reason for one's own faith, because you teach them to believe {m}by implicit faith and blind obedience, as true oracles, the conclusions of the Pope without the premises. Finally, you deny that kings know what they are: the Pope, whenever he demands money or support from them, treats them as his vassals; whenever he commands obedience, as his slaves; and whenever he inflicts punishment on them, as the footstools of his feet.

units.la: Hunc spiritum insolentiæ {n}Lutherus alicubi flagellat, quando agens de illis Apostoli verbis. 2. Cor. 11. [Si quis vos seruitutem redigit,sustinetis:] & [Si quis se extollit] nempè cùm cogit Principes omnem sibi honorem præbere, vsque ad exosculationem pedum. Postremò [si quis vos in faciem cædit] id est, viliores vos habeat quàm pecudes, & sœuissimam tyrannidem in peccantes, imò & in non peccantes exerceat. Hæc Lutherus. Proinde Principibus omnibus Psalmographi & Principis nobilissimi sententia etiam atque etiam tradenda & inculcanda est, [Reges intelligite, & erudimini, qui iudicatis terram;] nec imponi vobis patimini ab ijs, qui, cum oculos vobis aut effodiant aut occludant, nihilominus vos monent vt videre velitis. At, quid intelligere Principum maximè interest; Tu prudens Nos celas: Psalmista verò verbis proximis clarè docet, {o}[Seruite Domino in timore] viz. Domino omnium Dominantium immortali Deo; non Domino Papa, pro cuius
units.tr: {n}Luther somewhere lashes this spirit of arrogance, when treating of those words of the Apostle, 2 Cor. 11: [If anyone brings you into bondage, you endure it], and [If anyone exalts himself], namely when he forces princes to render every honour to him, even to kissing his feet. Lastly, [if anyone strikes you on the face], that is, he holds you in lower esteem than cattle, and exercises the most savage tyranny over sinners and even over those who do not sin. Thus Luther. Therefore the saying of the Psalmist and of the most noble Prince must be handed down and impressed again and again on all princes: [Be wise now, O kings; be instructed, you who judge the earth]; and do not allow yourselves to be imposed upon by those who, while they either gouge out your eyes or shut them, nevertheless advise you to wish to see. But what it is most in the interest of princes to understand? You, being wise, conceal this from us. The Psalmist, however, teaches clearly in the immediately following words: {o}[Serve the Lord with fear], namely the Lord of all lords, the immortal God; not the Lord Pope, for whose lordship you contend so eagerly only in the words immediately following.

units.la: {o} Psal.2,v.11. dominio tantùm verbis immediatè sequentibus ita gnaviter contendis.
units.tr: {o} Ps. 2:11. Only in the words immediately following do you contend so eagerly for his dominion.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: “ Illi Doctori fidem habete, in Controversijs fidei, cui veritas “ dixit,” [Orani pro te, vt non deficiat fides tua.] — pag.31.
units.tr: "Believe that Doctor in controversies of faith, to whom Truth said: [I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail]." — p. 31.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Quid veritas dixit, facilè intelligimus; at sensum, quem iam Christi verbis affingis, non perinde assequimur: quid verò aliàs docueris, satis meminimus. {e}Quarta sententia est (inquis) Pontificem, siue Haereticum esse possit, siue non, non posse definire aliquid Haereticum à tota Ecclesia credendum, quae est communissima opinio omnium fere Catholicorum — quae certissima est & asserenda: quaeq; vt facilius intelligi possit,—statuemus has propositiones. {f}Prima est, Summus Pontifex, quum Ecclesiam docet in his, quae ad fidem pertinent, nullo casu errare potest: 1o. quia Christus dixit, Luc.22. [Oravi pro Te &c.] 2o. quia dicitur S. Petro, [Porta inferi non praevalebunt adversus eam.] Nam vt supra ostendimus ad literam, Petra dicitur Petrus, & summus Rector Ecclesiae, & proinde quilibet eius successor dicitur similiter & Petra, nempe ratione constantiae: certè si Petra est, non frangetur.— {g}Quarta propositio est haec, Pontifex non solùm in Decretis fidei errare non potest, sed neq; in praeceptis morum, quae toti Ecclesiae praescribuntur, & quae in rebus necessarijs ad salutem, vel in iis, quae per se bona vel malasint, versantur. Dicimus quae toti Ecclesiae praescribuntur, nam in iudicijs particularibus non est absurdum eum posse errare. Dicimus etiam in necessarijs, nam in alijs legibus errare potest, superfluam & absurdam sententiam condendo: at non potest percipere aliquod vitium, aut prohibere aliquam virtutem, quia tunc erraret circa fidem, nam fides Catholica docet, virtutem esse bonam. Haec de Papa, quoad personam publicam, respectu Ecclesiae: nunc quoad personam eius privatam, respectu animae suae, quid anima tua apud se statuat, alijsque persuasum cupiat, explica. {c}Pie credi potest, Rom. Pontificem, non solum ut summum Pontificem errare non posse, sed etiam ut particularem personam non posse esse Haereticum, salsum aliquid pertinaciter credendo, quia Dominus dixit [Rogaui pro Te, ne fides tua deficiat.] --- At quomodo, quaeso [?], veram fidem semper praedicabit Pontifex Haereticus? potest quidem Deus ex corde Haeretico extorquere verae fidei confessionem, sicut quondam verbum posuit in ore Asinae Balaam: at violentum hoc erit, & non secundum prouidentiam Dei suauiter omnia disponentis. Hactenus Bellarminus. Instituti nostri est, primo Scripturae sensum aperire: deinde ostendere, ita eam Petram Petro proprium esse, vt Papae nullo modo conueniat, siue quoad priuatam, siue quoad publicam eius Personam. De testimonio ex Luc. 22. [Orauí pro Te, Simon] supra disseruimus; Secundum Matth.16. [Portae inferi non praeualebunt aduersus eam] nunc discutiendum occurrit.
units.tr: What Truth said we easily understand; but the sense you now attach to Christ's words we do not so readily grasp, and what you have taught elsewhere we remember well enough. {e}The fourth opinion is (you say) that the Pontiff, whether he can be a heretic or not, cannot define anything as heretical to be believed by the whole Church, which is the most common opinion of almost all Catholics — which is most certain and must be asserted; and so that it may be understood more easily, we will set out these propositions. {f}The first is: the Supreme Pontiff, when he teaches the Church in those matters which pertain to faith, can in no case err: (1) because Christ said, Luke 22: [I have prayed for you, etc.]; (2) because it is said to St Peter, [The gates of hell shall not prevail against it]. For, as we have shown above, taken literally, Peter is called Petra, and the supreme ruler of the Church, and therefore every successor of his is likewise called Petra, namely by reason of constancy: surely if he is a rock, he will not be broken. {g}The fourth proposition is this: the Pontiff can err not only in decrees of faith, but not even in precepts of morals, which are prescribed to the whole Church, and which concern things necessary to salvation, or those things which are in themselves good or evil. We say "which are prescribed to the whole Church", for in particular judgements it is not absurd that he may err. We say also "in necessary things", for in other laws he can err, by framing a superfluous and absurd judgement; but he cannot perceive any vice, or forbid any virtue, for then he would err concerning the faith, since the Catholic faith teaches that virtue is good. So much for the Pope as regards his public person in respect of the Church; now as regards his private person, in respect of his soul, explain what your soul holds within itself and wishes to persuade others of. {c}It may be piously believed that the Roman Pontiff, not only as supreme Pontiff cannot err, but also as a particular person cannot become a heretic by obstinately believing something false, because the Lord said: [I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail.] — But how, I ask, will a heretical Pontiff always preach the true faith? God indeed can wrest from a heretic's heart a confession of the true faith, just as he once put a word into the mouth of Balaam's ass; but this would be forced, and not in accordance with the providence of God, who disposes all things sweetly. Thus far Bellarmine. It is our purpose, first, to open up the sense of Scripture; then to show that it is so proper to Peter as Petra that it in no way fits the Pope, whether in respect of his private or of his public person. Concerning the testimony from Luke 22, [I have prayed for you, Simon], we have discussed above; the passage from Matthew 16, [The gates of hell shall not prevail against it], now falls to be examined.

units.la: I. AINMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. Animadversion.

units.la: Interpretationem Bellarmini, de Petrà, omne genus Testium nube obscurari.
units.tr: That Bellarmine's interpretation of the Rock is obscured by a cloud of every kind of witness.

units.la: Porta inferi non praeualebunt aduersus eam.] Id est, Petram, per quam ad literam Petrum (inquis) intelligi supra ostendimus. At nos per Petram, secundum sensum literalem, non intelligi Petrum, ex omni genere Authorum, siue Patrum antiquorum, tum Graecorum, tum etiam Latinorum; siue etiam Pontificiorum, tam Scholasticorum quam Glossatorum; disertissimis suffragijs probauimus: qui per Petram significari docent secundariò quidem Confessionem Petri, de Christo, cùm dixit, [Tues filius Dei viui,] non tamen in Concreto, id est, in Petro confitenti; sed in abstracto consideratum, quatenùs eandem audiri, scribi, intelligi, credi à quouis fideli possit. Primariò verò intelligunt Christum ipsum, quia Spiritu Dei toties in Scripturis fidei salutiferae lapis angularis, fundamentum, Petraq; dicitur. Nam Petrus non seipsum confitebatur, sed Christum. Indè est, quòd inter Patres (I) Chrysostomus; Christus dixit super hanc Petram, non super Petrum; non enim super hominem, sed super fidem aedificat Ecclesiam suam. (II) Augustinus; Super hanc Petram, quam confessus es: petra autem erat Christus. (III) Hilarius;[Super Petram] Petri ore confessam. (IV) Anselmus; Super Petrum, id est, Super me. (V) Beda; Nempe super me, à quo nomen tuum accepisti. Inter Glossatores (VI) Lyranus; Super hanc Petram, quam confessus es, id est super Christum: & (VII) Glossa Decreti; Non credo aliud Christum demonstrasse, quam Articulum, quem Petrus confessus est, dicens Christo, Tu es Filius Dei vivi. Inter Praedicatores (VIII) Ferus; Id est super fidem veram, id quod ex verbis Christi manifestè colligitur. Inter Episcopos (IX) Abulensis; Non verum est, quòd super Petrum fundata est Ecclesia: semel dixit Augustinus intelligi Petrum, saepius verò Christum; ubi etiam dicit, [Harum duarum sententiarum, quae sit probabilior, eligat Lector.] Augustinus ipse secundam tenet, ut patet ex verbis, quod primam dicit se tenuisse in quodam loco, secundam autem saepissimè posuit, & sic ipse istam tenet, & est probabilior. Inter Iesuitas (X) Pererius; Christus est Petra, super quam fundata est Ecclesia. Inter Cardinales (XI) Cusanus; Per Petram, Christus, quem Petrus confessus est. Inter Papas (XII) [illegible, ~12 letters] Inter Pontifices (XII) Gregorius Magnus, apud quem Petra & fundamentum idem sonant; In sacri-loquio (inquit) quando in singulari numero fundamentum dicitur, quia alius quàm Christus intelligitur, attestante Paulo 1. Cor. 10. Petra autem erat Christus & (XIII) Stephanus Papa; Super confessionem Petri. Inter Concilia, illud, quod apud Pontificios plerósque omnes est inster omnium (XIV) Conc. Tridentinum; Symbolum fidei: Credo in Deum omnipotentem &c. est fundamentum firmum & vnicum, contra quod (citatur in margine locus Matth. 16.) Portæ inferi non prævalebunt. Hæc in Thesi, nunc ad hypothesin descendamus; in qua Petrus & Papa inter se conferuntur, quoad certitudinem salutis: unde luculenter cernemus. Scriptura sensum genuinum putido Bellarmini commento quam insigniter depravari.
units.tr: "The gates of hell shall not prevail against it." That is, the Rock, which you say is literally Peter, as we have shown above. But we have proved from every kind of author, both the ancient Fathers, Greek and Latin alike, and also the Papists, Scholastics and Glossators, with the most distinguished support, that according to the literal sense the Rock is not Peter. They teach that it signifies, in a secondary way, Peter's confession concerning Christ, when he said, [Thou art the Son of the living God]. This is not taken in the concrete, that is, as Peter confessing, but in the abstract, insofar as it can be heard, written, understood and believed by any faithful person. Primarily, however, they understand Christ himself, since by the Spirit of God he is so often called in the Scriptures the cornerstone, the foundation and the Rock of saving faith. For Peter was not confessing himself, but Christ. Hence it is that among the Fathers (I) Chrysostom says: Christ said upon this Rock, not upon Peter; for he builds his Church not upon a man but upon faith. (II) Augustine: Upon this Rock which you confessed; but the Rock was Christ. (III) Hilary: [Upon the Rock] confessed by the mouth of Peter. (IV) Anselm: Upon Peter, that is, upon me. (V) Bede: Namely upon me, from whom you received your name. Among the Glossators (VI) Lyra: Upon this Rock which you confessed, that is, upon Christ; and (VII) the Gloss on the Decretum: I do not believe that Christ pointed to anything other than the article which Peter confessed, saying to Christ, You are the Son of the living God. Among the preachers (VIII) Ferus: that is, upon the true faith, which is clearly gathered from the words of Christ. Among the bishops (IX) Abulensis: It is not true that the Church is founded upon Peter. Augustine said once that Peter is meant, but more often Christ; where he also says: let the reader choose which of these two opinions is more probable. Augustine himself holds the second, as is clear from his words, since he says he held the first in one place, but very often he laid down the second, and so he himself holds it, and it is the more probable. Among the Jesuits (X) Pererius: Christ is the Rock upon which the Church is founded. Among the cardinals (XI) Cusanus: By the Rock, Christ, whom Peter confessed. Among the Popes (XII) [illegible, about twelve letters]. Among the Pontiffs (XII) Gregory the Great, for whom "rock" and "foundation" mean the same: In the sacred language (he says) when the foundation is mentioned in the singular, it is because someone other than Christ is meant, as Paul attests in 1 Cor. 10: "the Rock was Christ." And (XIII) Pope Stephen: Upon the confession of Peter. Among the councils, that one which is almost universally first among the Papists: (XIV) the Council of Trent: The creed of faith: "I believe in God Almighty," etc., is the firm and sole foundation, against which (the passage Matt. 16 is cited in the margin) the gates of hell shall not prevail. So much for the thesis; now let us descend to the hypothesis, in which Peter and the Pope are compared with one another as to the certainty of salvation. From this we shall see clearly how wretchedly Bellarmine's fancy has distorted the genuine sense of Scripture.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. Animadversion.
