units.tr: What monstrosity is this? The Pope the Prince of bishops; the Pope, too, embraces the whole world within his diocese? This matter is of too great moment to be touched on lightly by us. For I see that the diocese of the whole world is claimed for the Pope, not only (as here) with respect to bishops, but also to all princes. The former respect is treated here; the latter will perhaps have another place for discussion. Come, then, set out some account of this so universal diocese. {k} Of the names from which the primacy of the Pontiff is inferred, this is one: universal bishop, which is usually attributed to the Roman Pontiff. {l} For Pope Leo is styled Universal Bishop in the Council of Chalcedon, Act 3.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: First Observation.

units.la: Universum Orbem Pontificis esse Dioecesin totius Orbis omnium praxi, & suffragys refragari.
units.tr: That the whole world is the Pontiff's diocese is contradicted by the practice and votes of all.

units.la: Verum dicis, Bellarmine; sed non verè: Inscribitur enim Leo Universalis, at non (eo, quo Tu animo) absolutè, quasi in hoc Titulo Chalcedonensis Conc. Patres Pontificis Rom. Universalem Primatum & Iurisdictionem in totius Orbis Christiani Prouincias agnouerint: sed Oecumenicus, seu Universalis Episcopus dicitur (cum grandi restrictione hac) Magnae Romae, seu Romanae Ecclesiae. Quodsi ijdem Patres urbem Rom. metropolin universalem Europae appellarent, Ecquis indè colligeret, eius Metropolismū ad universas partes Orbis terrarum extendi atque diffundi? Rom. Ecclesiam certis & distinctis suis terminis antiquitus circumscriptam fuisse, nemo Theologus ignorat: vos igitur quod aperte vereq; non poteritis, id Distinctionum strophis efficere conamini. {m} Papam (inquitis) Patriarcham, & Primatem, & Metropolitam, & Episcopum esse fatendum est: Episcopum quidem urbis Romae, in qua Presbyteros solus ordinet, & reliqua munia obeat Episcopi; Metropolitam verò Prouinciae Romanae, in qua Episcopos consecrare, & Concilia convocare, caeteraq; praestare soleat, quae Metropolitae communi iure conueniunt. {n} At non solùm prouincia sua, hoc est, Romana, sed etiam Mediolanensis, & Italiarum omnium Prouinciarum Primas fuit. {o} Vt autem Patriarcha, speciali eius Diœcesis vniuersus Occidens fait quo nomine cum Alexandrino Patriarchâ in Nicena Synodo comparatur, ob speciale diœcesin. At, vt Papa est, & Princeps Pastorum, Diœcesis eius non tantùm Occidens, sed Orbis est vniuersus. Hæc Iesuita; & sic Tyber vester, veluti mare immensum, ambitione tanquam turbine turgescens, sæpe extra Totius Christiani Orbis ripas difluxisset, nisi Deus Opt. Maximus, vt illius elementaris, ita huius quoque Ecclesiastici maris superbis vndis certos quosdam fines posuisset, coercendo impetum eius, & dicendo: Hucusque, & non ultrà.
units.tr: You speak truly, Bellarmine, but not truly: for Leo is styled universal, but not (in the sense you intend) absolutely, as if in this title the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon had acknowledged the universal primacy and jurisdiction of the Roman Pontiff over the provinces of the whole Christian world. Rather he is called Oecumenical or Universal Bishop (with this great restriction) of Great Rome, or of the Roman Church. And if the same Fathers had called the city of Rome the universal metropolis of Europe, who would infer from that that its metropolitan authority extends and spreads to all parts of the earth? No theologian is ignorant that the Roman Church was from antiquity bounded by certain and definite limits. You, therefore, try by the twists of distinctions to do what you cannot openly and truly do. {m} You say: the Pope must be acknowledged as Patriarch, Primate, Metropolitan and Bishop: Bishop indeed of the city of Rome, in which he alone ordains presbyters and performs the other duties of a bishop; but Metropolitan of the Roman province, in which he is accustomed to consecrate bishops, convoke councils and perform the other things which metropolitans by common law owe. {n} But he was primate not only of his own province, that is, Roman, but also of Milan and of all the provinces of Italy. {o} As Patriarch, indeed, his special diocese was the whole of the West, by which name he is compared with the Patriarch of Alexandria in the Nicene Synod, on account of a special diocese. But as Pope and Prince of Pastors, his diocese is not only the West but the whole world. These are the words of the Jesuit. And so your Tiber, like an immense sea swelling with ambition as with a whirlwind, would often have overflowed beyond the banks of the whole Christian world, unless God Most Good and Greatest had set certain limits to its proud waves, both of that elemental sea and of this ecclesiastical sea, restraining its onrush and saying: Thus far, and no further.

units.la: Exempli causa; Vniuersalis, quam vendicat, authoritas, in {a}Vniuersalibus Concilijs congregandis, {b}Per octo prima Generalia Concilia, quæ erant ab Imperatoribus congregata, refutata fuit: vt & per Theodosium Imperatorem, à quo Leo Papa (quem dicis vocari Vniuersalem Episcopum) licet multâ supplicatione sæpius obnixè peteret, tamen vt Concilium celebraretur vel intra Italiam, non potuit obtinere. Authoritas Vniuersalis Decreti Conciliorum approbandi vel improbandi à Concilio Sardicensi repressa; vbi in {d}Forma præscribitur ne lideret Papa sententiam Synodi improbare. Authoritas & prærogatiua vniuersalis non labendi in Hæresin protrita per Tria * Concilia Generalia; in quibus Honorius Papa Anathema pronunciatur. Vniuersalis Papæ{e} Immunitas, vt nunquàm conciliùm potestatem vllâ deponatur, per Concilium etiam Romæ habitum {f}Contra Iohannem XII. Papam; post à Conc. Constantiensi, & Basileensi explosa. Vniuersalis Iurisdictio in excommunicandis alienis Ecclesijs primò ab {g}Alianis Episcopis, contra Victorem Papam; post à * Carthaginensibus, contra Stephanum Papam, tanquam Tyrannicus terror, & superbâ ambitio reiecta. Vniuersalis potestas {h}Appellationum in Conc. Africano, tanquam fumosus sæculi typhus, vel repugnante Papa Bonifacio, displosa. Vniuersale ius ordinandi aut constituendi Patriarchas alios in * Conc.Florentino à Græcis aduersus Eugenium denegatum. Vniuersalis præ-
units.tr: For example: the universal authority it claims, in convening universal councils, through the first eight general councils, which had been convened by the emperors, was refuted; likewise by the Emperor Theodosius, from whom Pope Leo (whom you say is called universal bishop), though he often earnestly sought by much supplication that a council might be held even within Italy, could not obtain it. The authority of universal approval or disapproval of councils was checked by the Council of Sardica, where a form is prescribed that the Pope should not venture to disapprove the sentence of a synod. The authority and universal prerogative of not falling into heresy was overthrown by the three general councils, in which Pope Honorius is pronounced anathema. The universal immunity of the Pope, that he should never be deposed by any council, was exploded by the council also held at Rome against John XII, Pope; afterwards by the Councils of Constance and Basel. The universal jurisdiction in excommunicating other churches was first rejected by the {g}African bishops against Pope Victor; afterwards by the Carthaginians, against Pope Stephen, as a tyrannical terror and proud ambition. The universal power of appeals in the African Council, as a smoky typhoon of the age, was dispelled, Pope Boniface opposing it. The universal right of ordaining or appointing other Patriarchs was denied by the Greeks against Eugenius at the Council of Florence. The universal pre-

units.la: h Apud.eund.Surium Tom.1.pag.591. præpotentia super alios Patriarchas, authoritate eiusdem Conc.{*} (Chalcedonensis, quod abs Te citatur (τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα [?], ἥ ἐστι, æqualia priuilegia & Patriarchatum Constantinopolitanum conferentis,) eodem Leone Papa reluctante, labefactata. Vniuersalis hæc extensio Diœceseos Romanæ {*} Hieronymi, Romani hominis, voce illa subbrutâ, quæ inter Romani Episcopi, & Ecclesiæ ipsius Iurisdictionem tantum interuallum ponit, quantum inter ORBEM & VRBEM.
units.tr: h Surius again, vol. 1, p. 591. Preeminence over the other Patriarchs, by the authority of the same council (Chalcedon, which you cite, [τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα], that is, equal privileges, conferring the Patriarchate of Constantinople), was weakened, Pope Leo himself resisting. This extension of the Roman diocese to universality is refuted by the voice of Jerome, a Roman himself, which sets as great a distance between the jurisdiction of the Roman bishop and that of the Church itself as there is between the WORLD and the CITY.

units.la: Denique quicquid est Vniuersalitatis, quod Ecclesia Rom. super Ecclesias alias vel olim assumpsit, vel hodierno die arrogare sibi possit, ipsius Basilij Magni hac vnâ censurâ concussum concidit. Quid vero ille, tàm sanctitatis, quàm doctrinæ laude vere magnus? Baronium auscultâ. {i}Basilius est ausus Occidentales erectis supercily insimulare, qui etiam in Epist. 10. dixit, Odi fastum illius Ecclesiæ. Hæc tot, tàmque grauia tantorum Patrum & Conciliorum testimonia totidem mihi tormenta & equulei esse videntur, quibus Aduersarij nostri confiteri cogantur, Papam nullam Vniuersalem, sed tantum specialem Diœcesin sortiri; Vniuersali Ecclesiæ subditam; & suis specialibus Iuribus atque prouincijs, veluti cancellis, definitam; extra quos Pontifex egressus aliarum Ecclesiarum Iura (veluti mare procellosum riparum muros, & claustra rumpens) non sine maxima Ecclesiæ perturbatione & schismate, quasi inundatione damnosâ, violauit.
units.tr: Finally, whatever universality the Roman Church has claimed over other churches in the past, or may presume to arrogate to itself today, is shaken and falls at this single censure from Basil the Great himself. And what of him, truly great in the praise of holiness no less than of learning? Listen to Baronius: Basil dared to charge the Westerners with haughty brows, and in Epistle 10 he said, I hate the arrogance of that Church. These many and weighty testimonies of such great Fathers and Councils seem to me so many torments and racks by which our opponents are forced to confess that the Pope has no universal diocese, but only a particular one, subject to the universal Church and bounded by its own particular rights and provinces, as by barriers. Beyond these, the Pontiff, going out like a stormy sea that breaks the walls of its banks and its barriers, has violated the rights of other churches, not without the greatest disturbance and schism in the Church, like a damaging flood.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Odiosum Oecumenici, seu vniuersalis Episcopi titulum à Gregorio Papa damnatum probari.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. That the odious title of Oecumenical, or universal, bishop was condemned by Pope Gregory is proved.

units.la: Quoniam verò Aduersarij nostri eò pertinaciæ processerint, vt terram cœlo misceant potiùs, quam ab eâ sententiâ, quam semel tenuerint, diuelli se sinant; qui reclamant & obstrepunt vsq; Papam suum urbe Romanam, vt Episcopum; Provinciam Romanam, vt Metropolitam; Italiam[?], vt Primatem; Partem Occidentem, vt Patriarcham; at k Vniuersam simul Ecclesiam [illegible, ~12 letters] uersalem Ecclesiae Pastorem, & Papam gubernare: iccirco hoc de suo Papa tam putidum Paradoxon maximi nominis Papae iudicio syncero & liquido conuellendum putaui. Gregorium Magnum hunc Titulum [illegible, ~10 letters] vel Vniuersalem Ecclesiae Episcopum, improbasse, extra controuersiam est, vtpote quod Vocabulum nouum, prophanum, sacrilegum, contra sensum Euangelij inuentum, nec ab ullo Praedecessorum suorum vsurpatum, in Patriarcha Constantinopolitano execratus est. Quo nunc Te subducis, Bellarmine? quo sensu ab hoc Vocabulo Gregorium abhorruisse autumas? 'Vt qui Episcopus Vniuersalis dicitur' (inquis) intelligatur esse solus Episcopus omnium aliorum Episcoporum, itaut alij non sint Episcopi, sed Vicarij illius, qui dicitur Vniuersalis Episcopus.'
units.tr: But since our opponents have gone so far in obstinacy that they would sooner mix earth with heaven than let themselves be torn from the view they once held, and since they cry out and protest that their Pope is Bishop of the city of Rome; the Roman province is his Metropolitan; Italy is his Primate; the Western part is his Patriarch, but at the same time universal Pastor of the Church, and governs the whole Church, I therefore thought this so foul a paradox of their Pope should be overturned by the sincere and clear judgment of the Pope of greatest name. That Gregory the Great rejected this title of universal Bishop of the Church is beyond controversy, since he execrated it as a new, profane, sacrilegious word, invented against the sense of the Gospel, never used by any of his predecessors, and applied it to the Patriarch of Constantinople. Where now do you slip away to, Bellarmine? In what sense do you claim that Gregory shrank from this word? 'So that he who is called Universal Bishop' (you say) 'is understood to be the sole bishop of all other bishops, so that the others are not bishops but his vicars, who is called Universal Bishop.'

units.la: Sic Tu, sed egregiè falleris: Vox enim, Vniuersalis Episcopi, sensu Gregoriano non substulit ordinem aliorum Episcoporum; sed Iurisdictionem eorum subuertit, vt Vniuersali vnius Imperio subiecti essent: nam (teste Azorio Iesuita) m Qui seipsum Oecumenicum Episcopum vocat, quamuis quidem ea ipsa appellatione non excludat caeteros Ecclesiarum Episcopos, vnum tamen ex duobus significat, vel eos esse inferiores, & sibi subiectos; vel se vna cum singulis Episcopis in corum Ecclesiis praesse, quorum vtrumque est absurdum. Haec Ille; cuius testimonio, tanquam acutissimo pugione, Caussae vestrae iugulum petit, atque confodit: quia Papa, dum se Episcopum Episcoporum, seu Vniuersalem ostentat, non modo alios omnes Episcopos (licet Eos Episcopatibus suis non exuat) Subiectos sibi esse prae se fert, sed etiam singulis Episcopis in eorum Ecclesiis praesit. Si enim Ecclesiae vniuersalis n Monarcha, cui vniuersae Ecclesiae orbis Christiani vna Diaecesis est; quomodo Is singulis non praesit? At alios omnes sibi subiectos habere, & alijs Episcopis in suis Ecclesiis praesse, vtrumque (ex sententia Azorij) est absurdum. Et reuerà hanc fuisse Gregorij mentem , ex confessione Cardin. Cufani constat; {o}Dicit Gregorius Epist. 22. (inquit) nullum Episcopum ita principatum gerere, vt omnis membra Ecclesiae sint ei subiecta. Sic ille. Omnia autem membra Dioecesano subiecta esse, cuiuis sano probe notum est. Maxime vero ex Gregorij ipsius Ratione lis tota dirimitur. Gregorius enim cur ab Ecclesia omni modo ad orcum, quasi, amandandum quemuis iudicaret, qui praesse omnibus vellet, hanc rationem reddit; {p}Quia tum vniuersa Ecclesia , quod absit , (inquit) à statu suo corruit , quùm is , qui appellatur Vniuersalis , cadit. Haec Gregorius.
units.tr: Thus you say, but you are grievously mistaken. For the expression Universal Bishop, in Gregory's sense, did not abolish the order of the other bishops, but overturned their jurisdiction, so that they would be subject to the rule of one universal man. For (as the Jesuit Azorius testifies), he who calls himself Oecumenical Bishop, although by that very title he does not exclude the other bishops of the Churches, nevertheless signifies one of two things: either that they are inferior and subject to him, or that he presides together with each bishop in their churches; and both are absurd. So he says. With his testimony, as with a most sharp dagger, he attacks and stabs the throat of your cause. For the Pope, while he displays himself as bishop of bishops, or universal, not only shows that all other bishops are subject to him (though he does not strip them of their bishoprics), but also that he presides over each bishop in their churches. For if he is the sole monarch of the universal Church, to whom the one diocese of the whole Christian world belongs, how does he not preside over each? Yet that he has all others subject to him and presides over other bishops in their churches, both are, by Azorius' judgment, absurd. And indeed, that this was Gregory's mind is established by the confession of Cardinal Cusanus: Gregory says in Epistle 22 that no bishop holds such a principate that all the members of the Church are subject to him. Thus he. But that all members are subject to the diocesan bishop is well known to anyone sane. Above all, the whole dispute is settled by Gregory's own reasoning. For Gregory, explaining why he judged that anyone who wished to preside over all should be utterly cast out of the Church, as though to perdition, gives this reason: because when he who is called Universal falls, the whole Church, which God forbid, falls from its state. Thus Gregory.

units.la: Quem Vocabuli huius [Vniuersalis Episcopi] sensum penitus Papalem reiecisse satis liquet: qualem admittere vellet. Tu nos docebas; {q}Quatenus Episcopus significat eum, qui debet curam totius Ecclesiae, sed generalem; hoc modo tribui potest Rom. Pontifici, ex mente Gregorij. Nihil agis; iam hic modus, quo non Iurisdictio aut regimen, sed Cura Vniuersalis significatur, nemini peculiaris, sed omnibus communis esse debet, quia {r}In Athanasio Magno laudat Basilius epist. 52. parem illi Ecclesiarum omnium curam esse, ac propriae; [illegible, ~50 letters]. Hoc sensu Nazianzenus dixit, eidem {f}Athanasio totius velut orbis praefecturam credidit esse, id est; sic praefuit, vt vniuersis prodesset, quia fides, quam Ille fartam sectam defendit, ad omnes spectat. Cyprianus (vt alios taceam) etiam ab eodem Nazianzeno dicitur, {t}Non soli Africanae Ecclesiae, sed etiam toti Occidenti praefuisse, imo Orienti fere ipsi, & meridiei, ac septentrioni, & quoquunque admiratione sui peruenit.
units.tr: It is quite clear that Gregory utterly rejected the sense of this expression, Universal Bishop, which you would wish to admit. You taught us that insofar as Bishop signifies one who ought to have care of the whole Church, but general care, in this way it can be attributed to the Roman Pontiff, according to Gregory's mind. You accomplish nothing. For this mode, in which not jurisdiction or rule but universal care is signified, belongs to no one in particular but must be common to all. For Basil, in his Epistle 52, praises Athanasius the Great, that he had a care of all the Churches equal to his own. In this sense Nazianzen said that to the same Athanasius was entrusted the governance, as it were, of the whole world; that is, he so presided as to benefit all, because the faith he defended as a firm sect pertains to all. Cyprian (to pass over others) is also said by the same Nazianzen not only to have presided over the African Church, but over all the West, indeed almost over the East, and the south, and the north, and wherever his admiration reached.

units.la: Quod vnicum superesset, dicas (quaeso) cur Gregorius hoc Vocabulum, tot nominibus odiosum, tantoperè sit aduersatus, si quidem bono vllo sensu (vt ais) conuenire sibi censuerit? {u}"Pronunciabat illud Gregorius (inquis) profanum & Sacrilegum vocabulum, quatenus tribuitur Constantinopolitano Episcopo, vt hac ratione facilius istius Episcopi superbiam comprimeret. Plane aut fucum facis, aut pateris : quasi vero Regem aut Monarcham vllum ita excordem esse vel mente fingere quis possit, qui Regis nomen Nouum, sacrilegium, à Prædecessoribus suis nunquàm vsurpatum, in se abominandum, sibique abrogandum, in animum inducat suum; vt hoc pacto facilius coerceat perduelles, & maiestatis reos, titulum istum falsò sibi vsurpantes. Quid quòd multo animosior fuerit Gregorius, quàm vt de dignitate suâ vel tantillum decerpi pateretur: Nam {x}Humilitatem (inquit) teneamus in mente, ita tamen vt ordinis nostri dignitatem seruemus in honore. Apagite igitur cum istis titulis inanibus Romani Episcopi, & Romanæ Diœceseos Vniuersalis, quos penè vniuersorum ordinum censuræ penitùs expunxerunt. Priusquàm ad ea, quæ sequuntur, progredi liceat, quæsitu indignum (mi Sirmonde) non videtur, quomodo Papa, [illegible, ~2 letters]ecialis Patriarcha Occidentis, passus sit{y} Auelli à Diœcesi Romana (id enim Te male habet) iamq; throno Constantinopolitano subiici Metropolitanus Prouinciæ, videlicet, Thessalonicensem, Corinthiam, Nicopolitanam, Atheniensem, Patrensem: siquidem Ille, vt totius orbis spiritualis & vniuersalis Monarchæ, Eas suo sibi iure, inuitis omnibus, retinere potuerat? Tu nunc perge Bellarmine.
units.tr: One thing remains. Tell me, please, why Gregory opposed this word so strongly, a word so odious on so many counts, if indeed (as you say) he thought it could fit him in any good sense. 'Gregory used to pronounce it (you say) a profane and sacrilegious word, insofar as it is given to the Constantinopolitan bishop, so that by this means he could more easily check that bishop's pride.' Plainly you either feign or suffer it. As if any king or monarch could be so witless, even in mind, that anyone could imagine him deciding that the name of King was a new, sacrilegious thing never used by his predecessors, abominable in himself and to be renounced, so that by this means he could more easily restrain rebels and those guilty of treason who falsely usurp that title for themselves! What more? Gregory was far too proud to suffer even a little of his dignity to be plucked away, for let us keep humility in mind, he says, yet so that we preserve the dignity of our order in honour. Away, then, with those empty titles of the Roman bishop and of the universality of the Roman diocese, which the censures of almost all the orders have utterly blotted out. Before it is permitted to go on to what follows, it does not seem an unworthy question, my dear Sirmond, how the Pope, as special Patriarch of the West, allowed the Roman diocese to be torn away (for that is what troubles you), and the metropolitan provinces, namely Thessalonica, Corinth, Nicopolis, Athens and Patras, to be subjected to the throne of Constantinople. For he, as monarch of the whole spiritual and universal world, could have kept them under his own right against everyone's will. You now go on, Bellarmine.

units.la: {y} Sirmundus Iof. quæ supra pag.63.
units.tr: Sirmond, Iof., as above, p. 63.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office [of the Pope].

units.la: “Debent Pontifices Verbo, & epistolis non tacere vitia Principum; sed, vt Apostolus loquitur, arguere, obsecrare, increpare opportunè, importunè, omni patientiâ, & doctrinâ.” --- Pag.34.
units.tr: "Pontiffs ought not to keep silent about the vices of princes, either in word or in letters, but, as the Apostle says, to rebuke, beseech and reprove, in season and out of season, with all patience and teaching." --- p. 34.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Pontifices nihil minùs quàm docendo Monitores agere.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO. The Pontiffs do almost nothing by teaching as admonishers.

units.la: Debent Pontifices (quis enim negat?) Principum vitia verbo arguere. sed huius muneris functionem nihil pensi habent, nam iamdiu {*}Verbum prædicare desierunt. Debent etiam Epistolis eos increpare: nemo inficias: at verò nesciunt, quià non ex Verbo Dei docendi principia petunt. Obsecrare verò? Imò Mandandi, iubendi, cogendiq; artem etiam, (non obtestandi) ad vnguem callent; obsecrandi, hortandiq; fere dedicerunt. Tu itaque,dum doces quatenùs debent Pontifices alios reprehendere; ipsos videris vel maximè reprehendisse. Quid prætereà?
units.tr: The Pontiffs ought (for who denies it?) to rebuke the vices of princes by the Word. But they take no trouble over the performance of this duty, for they have long since ceased to preach the Word. They ought also to rebuke them by letters: no one denies it; but they do not know how, because they do not derive the principles of teaching from the Word of God. To entreat, though? Indeed, they are thoroughly skilled in the art of commanding, ordering and compelling (not beseeching); they have almost forgotten how to entreat and exhort. So, while you teach how far the Pontiffs ought to reprove others, you appear above all to have reproved them yourself. What comes next?

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Duties (De Officiis).

units.la: Sed non minùs Principes debent præbere aures obedientes, & cogitare Pontificibus, & Episcopis molestissimè accidere, si quando ad huiusmodi reprehensiones venire cogantur: neque illos sponte hoc agere, sed coactos tum a comminatione diuinâ, quae sanguinem eorum de manu eorum requirendum clamat, nisi denuncient poenas peccantibus debitas; tum ab ipsa charitate paternâ, quae cogit medelas morbis adhiberi, quamuis amaras, nè filij eorum, & præsertim honorabiliores miserè pereant. Et certè si Principes Christiani libenter acciperent paternas admonitiones, præsertim ex vera charitate prodeuntes, multa fortasse discerent, quæ ignorant, & multis detrimentis futuris remedia adhiberent, quæ non adhibent, quià non est qui illos admonere audeat. --Pag.34.
units.tr: But princes ought no less to offer obedient ears, and to bear in mind that it is most distressing to Pontiffs and Bishops when they are compelled to make such rebukes; and that they do this not of their own accord, but are driven to it both by the divine threat, which cries out that the blood of such men is to be required at their hands unless they declare the punishments due to sinners, and by paternal charity itself, which compels remedies to be applied to diseases, however bitter, lest their sons, and especially the more honourable ones, perish wretchedly. And certainly, if Christian princes were willing to receive paternal admonitions gladly, especially those issuing from true charity, they would perhaps learn many things they do not know, and would apply remedies against many future harms which they do not apply, because there is no one who dares to admonish them. --Pag.34.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Pontificibus Rom. nimis adhærere, fatale Principibus non- nunquam fuisse.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO. That to cling too closely to the Roman Pontiffs has at times been fatal to princes.

units.la: I N hac Admonitione nulla vox est, quæ non summam pietatem spirare videatur: Impium enim esse oportet, & [illegible, ~12 letters], quisquis est inter mortales Deos, vel summus Monarcha, qui Pastorum Dei sacris monitis non paruerit, & ad eius comminationes non contremuerit; quando nimirum, in iis, non hominis, sed Dei immortalis Vox personat: quia scriptum est, {a}[Qui Vos audit, me audit &c.] Qui vero sacram illam vocem [{b}Non licet Tibi] præfracto & indignabundo animo audire renuerit, a deoque ministro Dei silentium imposuerit, facit quodammodo quod de sceleratissimo Herode scriptum segimus, {c}Adiecit hoc super omnia (peccata) quod Iohannem inclusit in carcere.
units.tr: IN this admonition there is no word which does not seem to breathe the highest piety. For it must be impious, and [illegible, about 12 letters], whoever he is among mortal gods, even the highest monarch, who has not obeyed the sacred admonitions of the ministers of God and trembled at their threats; since, clearly, in these it is not the voice of a man but of the immortal God that sounds forth. For it is written, {a}[He who hears you hears me, etc.] But whoever has refused to hear that sacred word, It is not lawful for you, with a stubborn and indignant mind, and has imposed silence on the servant of God, does in a certain way what we have read of the most wicked Herod: {c}He added this above all (sins), that he shut up John in prison.

units.la: De poenis vero quod addis, quas medelas amaras esse dicis, quibus Principum morbi curentur; vix dici potest quantas gratias Pontificis Paternitati Principes debeant, quod cum erga alios eius filios sese Patrem nimis indulgentem praebuerit per ipsas {*}Indulgentias (quibus pietatem omnem pene esse exhaustam ipsi Pontificij sint conquesti) ipsorum tamen Principum, tanquam honorabilium filiorum, curam praecipuam habuerint, ne praesertim hi miserè pereant; iccirco illas Amaras medelas adhibendas curauerit. neque enim, ex communi hominum sorte, quisquam a Pontifice coactus fuit unquam vel, ut {d}Henricus II. tergum suum verberandum percussoribus; vel, ut Henricus Imp. {c}Corpus in media hyeme, nudis pedibus, extremo frigori per dies aliquot excruciandum; vel, ut Fredericus Imperator, {f}Caput Pontificis pedibus conculcandum tradere. Et, ne quid {e}Amaritudinis deesse, cum opus est, possit, imprimis Basilicam venam incidendam esse praescribunt boni illi, scilicet, & benigni Medici: ex quà reuerà miserè perierunt duo Filij honorabilissimi Henricus Tertius, & Quartus Franciæ Reges.
units.tr: As to the punishments which you add, which you say are bitter remedies by which the diseases of princes are cured: it can scarcely be said how great thanks princes owe to the paternal care of the Pontiff. For although he has shown himself a Father too indulgent towards his other sons through the very {*}Indulgences (by which the Papists themselves have complained that almost all piety has been drained away), yet he has taken special care of the princes themselves, as honourable sons, lest especially these perish wretchedly; and for this reason he has seen to it that those bitter remedies are applied. For, by the common lot of men, no one was ever compelled by the Pontiff either, as {d}Henry II handed his back to be beaten by his assailants; or, as the Emperor Henry {c}was tormented for several days in the middle of winter, with bare feet, in the bitterest cold; or, as the Emperor Frederick {f}was made to hand over the Pontiff's head to be trampled underfoot. And lest any bitterness be lacking when it is needed, those good, kind physicians prescribe above all that the basilic vein be opened; from which, in truth, two most honourable sons, Henry III and Henry IV, Kings of France, wretchedly perished.

units.la: Nec hoc mirum vobis debet videri, quia (ut vester Historicus) {g}Haud aliud in causa fuisse dixerim, cur optimus Princeps Ludovicus XII. aquè magnitudine animi ac prudentiâ clarus, & tùm multis nominibus meliore utique fortunâ dignus, tot aduersitatibus in vita conflictatus sit, quàm quod tam artam cum Alexandro VI. Papa adfinitatem contraxisset, & impuri Patris (Papæ sc. Alexandri) omniq; scelerum genere cooperti filij (Borgiæ) crudelitates, libidines, fortunas deniq; fefuisset, & amplificássset. Hæc ille. Atque etiam cùm professionis Euangelicæ Regibus atque Principibus, ex quo Papæ imperio aduersati sunt, Dei beneficio felicius actum esse, (ut Scrip-
units.tr: Nor should this seem strange to you, because (to use the words of your own historian) {g}I would say there was no other reason why the excellent prince Louis XII, famous for his greatness of spirit and prudence, and in many respects certainly more deserving of good fortune, was buffeted by so many adversities in his life, than that he had contracted so close a marriage alliance with Pope Alexander VI, and that the cruelties, lusts and finally the fortunes of the impure father (namely Pope Alexander), and of his sons (the Borgias), who were covered with every kind of crime, had made him their helper and amplified them. So he. And likewise, since the Gospel profession has been opposed to the authority of the Pope, the Kings and Princes who opposed it have been dealt with more happily by the favour of God, (to use the words of Scripture) let our enemies be the judges; who rage and gnash their teeth most bitterly, because they see every day that all those harms which the power of the Pontiffs could inflict on the Protestants, or fraud could devise, or art contrive, or malice finally wish upon them, are by the divine will in vain.

units.la: {d} Matth.Paris.in Hen.2 An.1174.
units.tr: {d} Matthew Paris, on Henry II, year 1174.

units.la: {e} Ex Baronio, vid. supra.
units.tr: {e} From Baronius, see above.

units.la: {f} Ex Massonio, & alij supra.
units.tr: {f} From Masson, and others above.

units.la: {g} Thuanus hist.l.1. An.1505.pag.20. 21. {h}turæ verbis utar) Inimici nostri sint Iudices; qui fremunt atque frendent acerbissimè, quòd quotidiè videant illa Detrimenta, quæ adversus Protestantes vel Pontificum vis inferre, vel fraus effingere, vel ars excogitare, vel malitia denique imprecari illis potuerit, diuino nutu frustra esse omnia. Facilè nobis esset in huius argumenti latissimo lætissimóque campo expatiari, sed speculatio alia aliò nos vocat.
units.tr: {g} Thuanus, History, book 1, year 1505, pp. 20, 21. {h} (to use the words of Scripture) ... Our enemies be the judges; who rage and gnash their teeth most bitterly, because they see every day that all those harms which the power of the Pontiffs could inflict on the Protestants... are in vain by the divine will. It would be easy for us to range over the very broad and most joyful field of this subject, but another speculation calls us elsewhere.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. REMARK.

units.la: Pontifices ipsos omnium maximè ad sana monita aures, & pectora obturare.
units.tr: The Popes themselves, above all, stop their ears and hearts against sound warnings.

units.la: DUo adhuc restant; I. Votum est, ut Principes Episcoporum admonitiones audirent, — ut multa discerent quæ ignorant: II. Quærela, Heu! Non esse, qui Eos admonere audeat. Ad primum in promptu est responsio, non esse expectandum, Reges ut quicquam fere discant ab illis, qui omnia penè, scitu digna, densâ implicitate fidei nube inuoluunt; quiq; ita Eos scire docent, ut fere nihil sciant. His Magistris si Rex noster Sereniss‍. in disciplinam se tradidisset, nunquam pulcherrimis genuinæ Theologiæ exercitationibus suis Pontificiæ professioni plagas mortiferas inflixisset.
units.tr: Two points remain. (1) It is a wish that princes would hear the admonitions of bishops, so that they might learn many things which they do not know. (2) The complaint: Alas! there is no one who dares to admonish them. To the first, the answer is ready: kings should not expect to learn much from those who wrap almost everything worth knowing in a thick cloud of implicit faith, and who teach them to know in such a way that they know almost nothing. If our most serene King had submitted himself to such teachers as a pupil, he would never have dealt deadly blows to the Papist profession with his most excellent exercises in genuine theology.

units.la: Quod subinde quæreris, non esse qui Principes admonere audeant, equidem non credo: quid enim Papa adversus Principes non audet? Ecquis verò Rex tàm deploratí & perditi animi, ut piè monentem non sustineat? nihil profectò in Rege impio miserius ipsâ felicitate viuendi ut velit; nec ullus Dæmon legitur humano generi infestior, quam ille {i}Spiritus furàrs, qui, ubi maximè dominetur, res ipsa declarat. Monet enim Iesuita, {k}Papam, etiam in Casu intoleràbilis erroris, ut in Causa nimiæ Incõgentiæ, non esse publicè reprehendendum: & dicit hanc suam Assertionem magis ad prudentiam pertinere, quam ad doctrinam. Ratio; Quia (inquit) cauendum est, ne cum Hæreticis in verbis aut factis, quæ Pon-tificis tificis imminucre authoritatem videantur, etiam apparenter conueniamus. Hæc ille. Nimirum , Ut vulpes olim ægroto cauta Leoni; ita per omnia Iesuita Papæ se accommodat : at ægroti Leonis huius ingenium ita comparatum esse, vt nihil ægriùs ferat, quàm vitiorum suorum reprehensionem, docet Ipsius {1}Confirmatio Decreti illius, quo statuitur, quòd Papa licet fraternæ salutis ita negligens deprehendatur, vt innumerabiles populos cateruatim secum ducat ad gehennam, tamen eius culpas redarguere præsumit Mortalium nullus. Glossa etiam in Extrauag. peræquè adblanditur Papæ, vbi in negotio, vel potiùs negotiatione dispensationum Papalium cautetur hisce verbis; {m}Nec est qui audeat dicere , Domine cur ita facis? Et nè quis fortè parùm attentus, non animaduersa hàc Glossa,incautiùs transeat,nota marginali, tanquam Mercuriali digito, dirigitur ijsdem verbis, Non est qui audeat discere, Cur ita facis?
units.tr: As for the complaint you repeat, that there is no one who dares to admonish princes, I do not believe it. For what does the Pope not dare against princes? Indeed, what king is of so desperate and lost a mind that he will not put up with a godly admonisher? Certainly nothing is more wretched in an impious king than to wish to live in his own happiness, and no demon is read of as more hostile to the human race than that spirit of the Furies, which, where it rules most, the thing itself makes plain. For the Jesuit warns that the Pope, even in the case of intolerable error, or in the case of excessive ignorance, is not to be publicly rebuked; and he says that this assertion of his pertains more to prudence than to doctrine. His reason: because (he says) we must take care not to appear even apparently to agree with heretics in words or deeds which seem to diminish the authority of the Pope. So he says. Plainly, like the fox of old, cautious towards the sick lion, the Jesuit accommodates himself in everything to the Pope. But that the disposition of this sick lion is such that he bears nothing more badly than the rebuke of his own faults, is shown by the confirmation of that decree of his, by which it is laid down that although the Pope may be found so negligent of the brothers' salvation that he leads innumerable peoples in droves with him into hell, yet no mortal presumes to refute his faults. The Gloss on the Extravagants also flatters the Pope in the same way, where, in the matter, or rather the trafficking, of papal dispensations, it is warned in these words: Nor is there anyone who dares to say, "Lord, why do you act thus?" And lest anyone, being somewhat inattentive, should pass by this Gloss without noticing it, it is directed by a marginal note, as if by a Mercurial finger, in the same words, There is no one who dares to learn, "Why do you act thus?"

units.la: Huius tàm stupendæ pernicaciæ documentum dedit Paulus II. Pont. qui, quùm tentarent viri Diuini & humani iuris peritissimi ab iniustâ sententia Eum dimouere, respondet {o}Toruis oculis, An me ad Iudices reuocatis? as si nesciatis omnia iura in scrinio pectoris nostri collocata esse: sic fiat sententia &c.Nec igitur mirum, si ex ore eximij Concionatoris vestri aliquando eruperit isthæc vox vera;
units.tr: Paul II, the Pope, gave proof of this amazing obstinacy. When men most skilled in divine and human law tried to move him from an unjust sentence, he replied with stern eyes: "Do you summon me before judges? As if you did not know that all laws are stored in the chest of our breast. Let the sentence be passed, etc." Nor is it surprising, then, if that true saying once burst from the mouth of your outstanding preacher:

units.la: {p}Impij Pontifices nunc (inquit) non ab Ecclesia argui, & in ordinem cogi volunt; quasi sint Domini, non ministri. Quùm igitur Pontifices, Patresfamilias[?], & Speculatores vestri tàm sint omnium bipedum maximè intractabiles, & innumerabiles populos secum ad infernum caternatim ducant potiùs, quàm se argui patiantur: ipsa si Salus maximè cupiat, an seruare poterit hanc familiam? Bellarminus (vt verissimè est) diffisus ingenijs Principum, ad preces se recipit, quibus attentionem præbere æquum est.
units.tr: "Impious Popes now (he says) wish not to be refuted by the Church, nor to be brought into order; as if they were lords, not ministers." Since, then, your Popes, heads of families, and Overseers are the most unmanageable of all two-footed creatures, and rather than suffer themselves to be corrected, lead innumerable peoples with them in droves to hell, could Salvation, even if it most desired it, preserve this household? Bellarmine, as is most true, distrustful of the dispositions of princes, betakes himself to prayers, to which it is fitting to give attention.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Offic.

units.la: “ Vtinam multos Laberemus[?] Theodosios, & multos simul “ Ambrosios; Ille enim ex Charitate nihil utile tacebat, & “ Ille ex obedientia libentissime omnia audiebat, & executio- “ ni mandabat. ---pag.35.
units.tr: "Would that we had many Theodosiuses and many Ambroses at the same time! For the one, out of charity, kept silent about nothing useful, and the other, out of obedience, most willingly heard everything and carried it out." pag.35.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. REMARK.

units.la: Bellarmini Precationem hanc neq; hic vndequaq; veram; & eius generis aliam tantum non blasphemam esse.
units.tr: That Bellarmine's prayer here is not wholly true, and that another of its kind is hardly short of blasphemous.

units.la: ETsi pia admodùm hæc Precatio; licebit tamen mihi illud in os tibi retorquere, Nescis quid petis: vt scilicet Pontifici tuo, si huic voto pondus inesset; tùm quia Theodosius Pontificem Rgm. postposuit Ambrosio, quem nouit {*}[illegible, ~18 letters], id est, (Comparatiuè dictum) solum Episcopi nomine dignum; tum etiam quia Ambrosius vim omnem aduersus Principes temporalem infregit, atque interemit, quandò vltrò professus est, Nos in omnibus nostris cùm seculari potestate dissidijs, vbi ad extremum deuentum, tantùm Precum & lachrymarum armis pugnare debere. Te verò hoc in loco Ambrosium excommunicantem, & Theodosium pœnitentem innuere satis intelligo; de quibus Exemplis {*}infra, vbi Ea premiis arctiùs.
units.tr: Although this prayer is very pious, I may nevertheless turn it back upon you with the words, You do not know what you ask: namely, that if this wish had any weight for your Pope, then, first, because Theodosius placed the Pope of Rome behind Ambrose, whom he knew to be worthy of the name of bishop alone (said in a comparative sense); and then also because Ambrose broke and destroyed all force against princes, the temporal power, when he himself openly professed that we ought, in all our disputes with the secular power, when things have come to the last extremity, to fight with the weapons of prayers and tears alone. Indeed, I understand well enough that in this place you hint at Ambrose excommunicating and Theodosius doing penance; of these examples more below, where I will deal with them more closely.

units.la: Interea loci per hoc tuum [UTINAM] ansam nobis tui reprehendendi præbes, atque ostendendi quàm parum apud pios fidei mereatur huiusmodi tua Precatio. “ Est enim vbi dicis ; {q}Utinam Sp. Sancto placuisset per Mo-sen Sanctum Prophetam suum huius (nempe Iosephi Patriarchæ) sapientissimi atq; optimi Principis res omnes gestas, in illa tam longa octoginta annorum gubernatione describi; plura enim in eius vita, & rebus gestis legendis Principes Christiani, de ratione regni bene administrandi, didicissent. Quæ precatio videri potest cùm nonnullam in se falsitatem continere, tùm non procul abesse à blasphemia. Falsitatis eam arguit Pererius Iesuita, qui tres causas reddit, cur (sic enim loquitur) “{r}Solium omnium Iacob filiorum, Iosephi copiosè ac diligenter perscripsit historiam Mosis; 1º. est, vt ostenderet quà causa, & quo eueneuentu Populus Dei in Aegyptum venerit; tot, tantisque miraculis inde liberandus. Secunda, quòd Ea historia Iosephi (inquit) omne genus virtutum referta sit exemplis, ideoque solus inter fratres suos dignus fuit Ioseph, ut vita eius omnibus veri Dei, & verarum virtutum cultoribus multùm commendaretur; & in exemplum omnibus ad imitandum propinaretur. Tertia, quod Ioseph multis rebus insignem atque illustrem Christi typum & figuram gessit; quocirca eius mores, (inquit) actus, virtutes, & casus distinctè & expresse declarare oportuit. Hæc ille. At verò deindè precari Te, ut Spiritus Sanctus melius quam Ei placuerit Christianos milites pleniori historia instituerét, videsis annon nimis affine sit vestræ illi blasphemæ Glossæ, quæ, in gratiam Pontificis, falso supponit,{f} Deum non satis discretum fuisse, si---Non igitur mirum, quòd Spiritus Sancti oracula, per se absolutissima, Tu {t}Tantùm partialem, & insufficientem regulam, seu normam esse ausus es profiteri. Vtinam Te aliquando Errorum tuorum Bellarmine, poeniteat.
units.tr: Meanwhile, by this your [UTINAM] you give us an occasion to rebuke you and to show how little such a prayer of yours deserves credit among the godly. For you say: "Would that it had pleased the Holy Spirit, through Moses his holy Prophet, to describe all the deeds of this most wise and best of princes (namely, of the Patriarch Joseph) in that so long government of eighty years; for Christian princes would have learned more about administering the kingdom well from reading about his life and deeds." This prayer may be seen to contain some falsehood, and not to be far from blasphemy. Pererius the Jesuit charges it with falsehood, giving three reasons why (for so he speaks) "the history of Moses wrote out at full length and with care the story of Joseph alone among all the sons of Jacob": (1) the first is, that he might show by what cause and by what outcome the People of God came into Egypt, to be delivered thence by so many and so great miracles. (2) The second, because that history of Joseph (he says) is filled with examples of every kind of virtue, and therefore Joseph alone among his brothers was worthy, so that his life might be strongly commended to all the worshippers of the true God and of true virtues, and be offered as an example to all for imitation. (3) The third, that Joseph bore the notable and illustrious character of a type and figure of Christ in many things; wherefore it was fitting to declare distinctly and expressly his manners, actions, virtues, and fortunes. So he says. But then, that you pray that the Holy Spirit should have instructed Christian soldiers with a fuller history than it pleased him to give: see whether this is not too closely related to that blasphemous Gloss of yours, which, to please the Pope, falsely supposes that God would not have been sufficiently discreet, if---. It is no wonder, then, that you have dared to profess that the oracles of the Holy Spirit, in themselves most absolute, are only a partial and insufficient rule or norm. May you someday repent of your errors, Bellarmine.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Reges Christianos, quoad curam Subditorum, Speculatores habendos esse.
units.tr: II. Animadversion. That Christian kings are to be regarded as overseers (speculatores) with respect to the care of their subjects.

units.la: Pontifices Speculatores sunt (inquis:) quid Tibi autem de Principibus videtur? Principes in terris (inquis) sunt quasi specula & exemplaria, in quæ Subditi omnes respiciant, seq; eorum moribus accommodare satagunt. Quasi verò Principes Speculorum tantùm, & non Speculatorum pariter munere fungantur, quos super omnes Mortales {u}[ὑπερεχούσαις [?]] eminentiâ constitutos esse Apostolus docet; vt potè qui omnium Subditorum suorum Episcopi sint, quorum mores obseruent, & moderentur. Vocem hanc, Episcopum, idem atque Speculatorem significare, {*}ostendimus: indeque esse quòd, apud Ethnicos, {y}Reges, honoris gratiâ, à Poëta Episcopi vocentur: nam quùm ἐπισκοπεῖν [?] ni-hil sit aliud quàm Speculari; vel, vt Ambrosius, super-inspicere ; Vt Augustinus ,super-intendere, quod est Subditorum saluti prospicere: certè Spiritus Sanctus, qui vocat Regem [illegible, ~8 letters], à voce Episcopi, seu Speculatoris minimè abhorreret, præsertim si sensum eum teneamus, quem habuit Eusebius, quando Constantinum Magnum dixit communem quendam Episcopum diuinitùs constitutum, Episcoporúmque quasi confortem factum, ac quæ ad pacem Dei stere vniuersis dispensantem.
units.tr: The Popes are overseers (you say). But what do you think of princes? Princes on earth (you say) are as it were mirrors and examples, in which all subjects look, and strive to accommodate themselves to their manners. As if princes performed only the office of mirrors, and not equally the office of overseers (speculatores), whom the Apostle teaches are set above all mortals in eminence; since they are bishops of all their subjects, whose manners they watch over and regulate. We have shown that this word bishop means the same as overseer; and hence it is that among the heathen kings are called bishops by the poet, as a mark of honour. For since to oversee (episkopein) is nothing other than to watch over (speculari), or, as Ambrose puts it, to look over from above; and as Augustine puts it, to superintend, which is to look out for the welfare of the subjects: surely the Holy Spirit, who calls the king [illegible, about eight letters] by the name of bishop, or overseer, would not shrink from it, especially if we hold to the sense which Eusebius had, when he called Constantine the Great a common bishop appointed by God, made a sort of co-bishop of the bishops, and dispensing to all things that pertain to the peace of God.

units.la: Talem se Speculatorem præbuit Ecclesiæ Dei Otho Imperator (Te confitente) Vir Imperatoris honore, ob celebrem pietatem dignus: Qui tamen Papam (propter mores flagitiosos) venatorem, lubricum, atque incorrigibilem [?] deposuit. Itá vt Ecclesiæ Rom. nonnunquàm plurimùm interfit (vt voto Bellarmini paria reponamus) in hunc modum precari: Vtinam, ad Pontificum nostrorum perditos mores reprehendendos, multos Bernardos, multosque pariter Othones haberemus. Atque itá huic Speculationi, de hoc tertio Titulo, finem imponimus; sequitur Quartus.
units.tr: Otho the Emperor showed himself such an overseer of the Church of God (as you yourself confess), a man worthy of the honour of the Emperor on account of his celebrated piety. He nevertheless deposed the Pope, a hunter (venator) on account of his shameful morals, a slippery and incorrigible man [?]. So that it sometimes greatly concerns the Roman Church (to match the wish of Bellarmine with one of our own) to pray in this manner: Would that we had, to rebuke the depraved morals of our Popes, many Bernards, and likewise many Ottos. And so we bring this consideration of the third title to an end; the fourth follows.

units.la: CAP. V. DE QVINTO, ET POSTREMO NOMINE PAPÆ, VIDELICET, SACERDOS MAGNVS, SIVE PONTIFEX MAXIMVS.
units.tr: CHAP. V. Concerning the fifth and last name of the Pope, namely, Great Priest, or Supreme Pontiff.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices (De Officiis).

units.la: "Postremum nomen Pontificis est Sacerdos magnus, siue Pontifex maximus, quod est nomen honorificentissimum: quæ causa fuit vt, apud gentes, Cæsares Augusti Pontifices etiam maximi nominari voluerint. — Pag.35.
units.tr: "The last name of the Pontiff is Great Priest, or Supreme Pontiff, which is a most honourable name; for this reason among the nations the Caesars Augustus also wished to be called Supreme Pontiffs." — p. 35.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: An hoc igitur Rom. Episcopo proprium? Ad hoc Tu alibi; "Quo titulo (inquis) vtitur Gregorius I. cap. 4. Dial. quemque Anselmus, & B. Bernardus Episcopi Rom. tribuebant: & Hieronymus Damasum Papam vocat summum Sacerdotem.
units.tr: Is this, then, proper to the Roman bishop? To this you say elsewhere: "By what title (you say) does Gregory I, in chapter 4 of the Dialogues, use, which Anselm and Saint Bernard attributed to the Roman bishops, and Jerome calls Pope Damasus the chief priest."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. Animadversion.

units.la: Hisce titulis, [Summus, & Maximus Pont.] aliorum Episcoporum ordinem & dignitatem æqualem non imminui.
units.tr: These titles, [Summus and Maximus Pontifex], do not diminish the equal order and dignity of the other bishops.

units.la: Enecca, vt Lectori suo ambitiosi ingenij vanitatem deridendam propinaret, nescio cuius male-sani hominis exemplum producit, vsque adeo magnitudinis & celsitudinis cupiditate flagrantis, vt si Arbor esset, magnam arborem; si mons, magnum montem; imò si vel matula, matulam magnam se esse optaret. Iam verò nobis ante oculos obuersatur Is, qui magna parui faciens, sibi nunquàm satisfacit, nisi, quùm Pater salutandus, Pater Patrum; quùm Pastor, Pastorum Princeps; quùm Doctor, omnium Christianorum Doctor; quùm Speculator, totius mundi Speculator; quùm denique Sacerdos, aut Pontifex, summus, & maximus dici haberique possit. quos tamen ità ampullosos titulos Illi minimè inuideret quispiam; verum modò, istorum, ac sanum sensum amplecti, neque nouum nomen vetustatis fuco colorare, neque commune aliis, tanquàm sibi proprium, arrogare vellet. Qui enim nunc Papa appellantur (vt de nouitate primùm dicam) Eos Episcopus vester Balbus agnoscit antiquitus{b} Nec Papas, nec Pontifices, sed tantùm Romanos Episcopos vocatos fuisse.
units.tr: Enecca, in order to offer his reader the vanity of an ambitious mind to be mocked, produces the example of I know not what ill-minded man, so burning with the desire of greatness and loftiness that if he were a tree he would wish to be a great tree; if a mountain, a great mountain; indeed, if he were even a jar, he would wish to be a great jar. Now there is set before our eyes the man who, making little of great things, is never satisfied with himself unless, when he is to be greeted as Father, he is Father of Fathers; when he is Pastor, Prince of Pastors; when he is Doctor, Doctor of all Christians; when he is Speculator, Watchman of the whole world; and finally, when he can be called and held Priest or Pontiff, supreme and greatest. Indeed, no one would grudge him these bombastic titles, provided he would embrace them in their sound sense, and would neither colour a new name with the varnish of antiquity nor claim for himself as his own what is common to others. For those who are now called Popes (to speak first of the novelty), your bishop Balbus acknowledges that they were formerly called not Popes nor Pontiffs, but only Roman bishops.

units.la: Ad proprietatem vocis quod attinet; nec vocabulum [Summus] Papam solum facit; nec vox [Pontifex] eiusue adiunctum [Maximus] alium æqualem negat. De primo vocabulo [Summus] Azorius Iesuita perappositè sanè distinguere videtur. {c}Dico (inquit) in vnoquoque genere posse esse summa per negationem, id est, quorum singulis nihil est superius; sed non per affirmationem, vnumquodque sit omnium superius. Hæc Ille. Priore modo Pontificem [summum] Sacerdotem dici posse minimè repugnamus, videlicet, per negationem, Id est; Eum nullum in ordine Ecclesiastico Superiorem habuisse: non tamen per affirmationem, vt alios vniuersos ab huiusmodi Superioritate excludat: quia, vt de egregijs Oratoribus Cicero, {d}Isti summi (inquit) fuerunt in suo genere; ita Nos in genere Patriarchitum[?], Episcopos Alexandrinum, Antiochenum, Hierosolymitanum, Constantinopolitanum (quoad Iurisdictionem) iuxtà cum Rom. Episcopo, in suo genere, Summos fuisse agnoscimus: Id quod Iura Eorum, ex vniuersalium Conciliorum Decretis, distincta demonstrant. Imò verò in acerbissima illa contentione, quæ inter Episcopum Rom. & Constantinopolitanum intercessit, non tam de Iurisdictionis, quàm de Tituli & Dignitatis amplitudine agebatur.{a} Ambo Episcopi (Rom.vz.& Constant.) à Græcis (hoc autem idem est quod summi) Oecumenici, id est, Vniuersales dicebantur, hic in Oriente, illè in Occidente. Inspicio etiam hodiernas Patriarcharum literas, quarum fronte Inscriptio hæc, quâ ipsi à se,& à toto Oriente semper insigniuntur, OIKOTMENIKOΣ: sic enim non ita pridem Patriarcha Alexandrinus in literis ad GEORGIVM multis nominibus apprimè colendum Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem, [?]κηρύττει ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιστολῶν ἐν τῇ πατριαρχικῇ ἀξίᾳ [?] μεγάλης τῆς Αλεξανδρείας καὶ πρὸς τὴν Οἰκουμένην &c. Quod autem obiciunt Pontificij dicentes; {f} Constantinopolitanos titulum Oecumenici vsurpâsse, conniuentibus Episcopis Romanis: leuis illa quidem & friuola responsio est. Quid enim? vt {g} Totius Ecclesiæ Monarcha (nam ad Papalem Monarchiâ stabiliendam vos animorum & corporum vestrorum neruos omnes contenditis) in diuiso imperio, & in abrepti sibi Prærogatiuæ suæ honorificentissimis titulis connniueret?
units.tr: As far as the propriety of the word goes: neither does the word Summus make a Pope alone, nor does the word Pontifex, or its addition Maximus, deny another equal. Concerning the first word, Summus, the Jesuit Azorius seems to distinguish very aptly. I say (he says) that in every kind there can be a summit by negation, that is, things to which nothing is superior; but not by affirmation, that each thing be superior to all. So he. In the former sense we by no means deny that the Pontiff may be called chief priest, namely by negation, that is, that he had no superior in the ecclesiastical order; but not by affirmation, so as to exclude all others from such superiority. For, as Cicero says of the distinguished orators, those chiefs (he says) were chiefs in their own kind; so we acknowledge that the bishops of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem and Constantinople (as to jurisdiction) were, alongside the Roman bishop, chiefs in their own kind; which their rights, distinctly shown by the decrees of the universal councils, demonstrate. Indeed, in that bitter contention which arose between the Roman bishop and the Constantinopolitan, the matter at issue was not so much jurisdiction as the breadth of title and dignity. Both bishops (the Roman and the Constantinopolitan) were called by the Greeks (and this is the same as summi) Oecumenical, that is, universal, the one in the East, the other in the West. I also look at the present-day letters of the Patriarchs, on whose front this inscription, by which they and all the East always designate themselves, appears: OECUMENICAL [οἰκουμενικός]. For thus not long ago the Patriarch of Alexandria, in his letters to GEORGE, the Archbishop of Canterbury, to be honoured in many ways, proclaims from the letters, in the patriarchal dignity, of great Alexandria and to the Oecumene, etc. [κηρύττει ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιστολῶν ἐν τῇ πατριαρχικῇ ἀξίᾳ μεγάλης τῆς Αλεξανδρείας καὶ πρὸς τὴν Οἰκουμένην]. As for the objection the Papists make, saying that the Constantinopolitans usurped the title of Oecumenical while the Roman bishops connived, that answer is indeed slight and frivolous. For why, pray, should the Monarch of the whole Church (for you strive with all the sinews of your minds and bodies to establish the Papal monarchy) in a divided empire connive at others seizing his own prerogative with the most honourable titles?

units.la: At nomen [Pontifex] fortasse plus in se momenti habet, præsertim si cum cognomine [Maximus] copuletur. Pontificis nomen, si originem eius spectemus, non adeò per se honorificum, vt non aliis etiam Episcopis conueniat, quippe (teste Maffonio) {b}Pontifex à ponte appellatur; pons enim sublicius à Pontificibus primò factus, & sæpè restitutus — Hanc igitur vocem mutuati veteres, ad Ecclesiastica munia transtulere, & sacris præpositos Pontifices dixerunt. An verò ideò cuiquam Præposito veluti propria assignanda? Nec (vt ex testibus tuis te refellam) Gregorius Magnus Papa, nec Sanctus Bernardus hoc vobis concederet: Illeenim {i}Fundensis Ecclesiæ Episcopum, Pontificem vocabat; hic pariter ad Archiepiscopum Senonensem scribens, {k}Nihil suum (inquit) Episcopus quærat, sed tantum Dei gloriam, ac salutem proximorum, hoc enim faciens implet non solum Pontificis officium, sed & Etymologiam nominis, Pontem utique seipsum faciens inter Deum & proxi[illegible, ~3 letters] : pertingit pons iste ad Deum eâ fiduciâ, quâ non suam, sed illius gloriam quærit ; pertingit usque ad proximum illâ pietate, quâ & ipsi, non sibi prodesse desiderat &c. Nihil igitur in hoc nomine non commune Episcopis alijs videmus.
units.tr: But the name Pontifex perhaps carries more weight in itself, especially when it is joined with the surname Maximus. If we look at its origin, the name of Pontiff is not so honourable in itself that it does not also suit other bishops; for (on the testimony of Maffei) Pontifex is so called from a bridge; for the sublician bridge was first made, and often restored, by the Pontiffs. The ancients therefore borrowed this word and transferred it to ecclesiastical duties, and called those set over sacred things Pontiffs. But is it therefore to be assigned to any one overseer as if it were his own? Nor (to refute you from your own witnesses) would Gregory the Great, the Pope, nor Saint Bernard concede this to you. For the former called the bishop of the church of Fondi Pontiff; the latter likewise, writing to the Archbishop of Sens, says: The bishop should seek nothing of his own, but only the glory of God and the salvation of his neighbours; for by doing this he fulfils not only the office of a Pontiff but also the etymology of the name, indeed making himself a bridge between God and his neighbour [illegible]. That bridge reaches to God with the confidence by which he seeks not his own glory but God's; it reaches to the neighbour with that piety by which he desires to profit them and not himself, etc. Therefore we see nothing in this name that is not common to other bishops.

units.la: Cognomen verò [Maximus] quomodò (inquies) pluribus conueniet? aduorte animum tuum parumper, & Baronius tuus Te docebit. {1}Pontifex Maximus (inquit) apud Gentiles quinto in loco (ergò non erat illud honorificentissimum) positus est. {m}Iccirco, ne, quùm alij Maximi dicerentur, iste Pontifex maximus alios suprà se, vel sibi æquales videretur habere Pontifices ; Pontificis Maximi nomine amplitudini iure iunctius est titulus, EPISCOPUS EPISCOPORUM. Hæc ille. Sentin' igitur, Bellarmine, in istis tuis magnificis Titulis quàm Tu nihil quicquam profeceris?
units.tr: But how, you will ask, will the surname Maximus suit more? Pay attention for a moment, and your Baronius will teach you. The Supreme Pontiff (he says) was placed among the Gentiles in the fifth place (therefore that title was not most honourable). Hence, lest, when others were called Maximi, this Supreme Pontiff should seem to have other Pontiffs above him or equal to him, the title BISHOP OF BISHOPS is rightly joined with the name of Supreme Pontiff for dignity. So he. Do you perceive, then, Bellarmine, how in those magnificent titles of yours you have achieved nothing at all?

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. Animadversion.

units.la: Immodica Pontificiorum, de Papâ, Elogia & Christianis ho- minibus horrori, & ipsi Christo dedecori esse.
units.tr: The immoderate eulogies of the Papists concerning the Pope make him a horror to Christian men and a dishonour to Christ himself.

units.la: AIn?Sacerdotum summum, siue Pontificem maximum Titulum Papæ honorificentissimum esse? id primo certè aspectu non mediocri nos quoque affecit voluptate : nihil enim gratius nobis, aut optatius quàm nomen aliquod dignitatis vllo modo tolerabile audire, quo, tanquàm honorificentissimo Titulo, exsuperans Pontificum ambitio saturari posset. Sed, ô curuas hominum mentes! quibus in fœdissimis ergà Pontificem adulationibus nihil nisi immensum, diuinum, Christoq, ferè proprium satisfacere queat. Aures igitur arrigere (Lector,) vel potiùs obstrue; nam Ea producturus sum Pontificiorum de Papâ Elogia, quæ nec sine horrore referre, nec absq; stupore & execratione audire pius cuiusquam animus aut possit, aut debeat. viz. PAPA, I. Totius gregis Dominici unicus Pastor. II. Cuius dignitate nulla alia non modo non inueniri, sed nè excogitari potest in terris maior. III. De cuius potestatis viribus disputare, sacrilegium est. IV. Unctione, & regno Chri-flus. stus[?][* præ participibus suis.] V. Cùm cuius cœlesti maiestate nullum Diadema comparctur : cui [* claudere cœlos, & aperire, detrudere ad inferos, & eruere] quoscunque velit concessum est. VI. Cui à Deo rerum omnium potestas tributa est. VII. [* Sponsus Ecclesiæ] Catholicæ; Præpositus [* supra Gentes & Regna, vt euellat] &c. VIII. A cuius nutu pendent leges; cuius voluntas pro lege; vox pro oraculo. IX. Sanctæ & vniuersalis Ecclesiæ Pastor, iuxta Apostolum, [* Super omnem principatum & potestatem, & omne quod nominatur siue in hoc, siue in futuro seculo] à Deo constitutus. X. Christi, & Dei Vicarius, in quo illud Propheticum rursus impleatur, [* Adorabunt eum omnes Reges, omnes Gentes seruient ei.] XI. Quo nihil maius videt Luna globus. Hæc omnia Narratore Authorum, quos citat, omnium prodigiosissimo adulatore Abrahamo Bzovio Polono. Pergunt Alij. XII. Cuius non sufficit amplitudini nomen hoc Pontifex Max. nisi adiuncto hoc titulo, Episcopus Episcoporum. XIII. Est [* lapis positus in Sion, probatus, pretiosus, angularis, fundamentum summum.] XIV. Sub cuius plane supremi in terris numinis tutela opus meum in lucem emissum. XV. In consortium induuidue vnitatis assumptus. XVI. DOMINVS NOSTER DEVS PAPA.
units.tr: Is the title "chief priest" or "high priest" (Pontifex Maximus) the most honourable title for the Pope? At first sight this too gave us no small pleasure, for nothing is more welcome or more desired than to hear some name of dignity that is tolerable in any way, by which the overweening ambition of the Pontiffs might be satisfied as with a most honourable title. But, O crooked minds of men! With what most shameful flatteries toward the Pope can anything satisfy them except what is immense, divine, and almost proper to Christ? So prick up your ears, reader, or rather stop them; for I am about to set out the Papists' eulogies concerning the Pope, which no pious mind can or should either repeat without horror or hear without astonishment and execration. Namely: POPE: (I) the sole Pastor of the whole flock of the Lord. (II) Than whose dignity no other, not only is found, but cannot even be imagined, greater on earth. (III) To debate the powers of whose authority is sacrilege. (IV) Christ, anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. (V) With whose heavenly majesty no diadem can be compared; to whom it is granted to shut and open the heavens, to cast down to the depths and to snatch away whomever he wishes. (VI) To whom power over all things has been given by God. (VII) The Bridegroom of the Catholic Church; Governor [over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up and destroy] etc. (VIII) On whose nod the laws depend; whose will is law, whose voice is an oracle. (IX) The Pastor of the holy and universal Church, according to the Apostle, [above every principality and power, and every name that is named, in this age or in the age to come], constituted by God. (X) The Vicar of Christ and of God, in whom that prophetic word is fulfilled again: [All kings shall adore him, all nations shall serve him]. (XI) Than whom the globe of the moon sees nothing greater. These things are all related by the author whom he cites, Abraham Bzovius the Pole, the most monstrous flatterer of all. Others go on: (XII) To whose dignity this name "Chief Pontiff" is not enough unless this title is added, Bishop of Bishops. (XIII) He is [the stone laid in Zion, tried, precious, the corner stone, the chief foundation]. (XIV) Under whose protection, plainly that of the highest divinity on earth, my work has been brought to light. (XV) Taken into the fellowship of an individual unity. (XVI) OUR LORD GOD THE POPE.

units.la: Hæc illi Oratores, Theologi, Glossatores, Episcopi, Cardinalesq; Pontificij (post quæ tam monstrosa Papārum[?] encomia vix quicquam CHRISTO IESV relictum est integrum) blasphemis suis dictis scriptisque Pontificibus tribuerunt; quæ Pontifices ipsi ita auidis auribus oculisque hauserunt, vt hæc instar Apocalypseos esse possint, quibus spiritus Antichristianus manifeste detegatur, & deprehendatur. Hæc vero vt Te nihil moueant? Tu enim progrederis.
units.tr: These are the things which the Papist orators, theologians, glossators, bishops and cardinals have ascribed to the Pontiffs in their blasphemous sayings and writings (after such monstrous eulogies of the Popes scarcely anything has been left whole to CHRIST JESUS); and the Pontiffs themselves have drunk them in with such greedy ears and eyes that they may serve as an Apocalypse, by which the Antichristian spirit is plainly uncovered and detected. But do these things not move you at all? For you go on.

units.la: Quæstio, de authoritate & dig- nitateque Regum & Pontificum, sub lege veteri, cuentilatur[?].
units.tr: The question, concerning the authority and dignity of kings and popes under the old law, is discussed.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officiis.

units.la: In Testamento veteri quùm primùm à Mose, qui simul erat Princeps & Pontifex, diuisa sunt ista potestates, & Pontificatus Aaroni, post eum Eleazaro collatus fuit, & Principatus Iosue; ab eo tempore semper præpositus fuit Pontifex Principi, ut ex libro Numerorum, & Iosue potest intelligi.—pag.35.
units.tr: In the Old Testament, when these powers were first divided by Moses, who was at the same time prince and priest, the priesthood was conferred on Aaron, and after him on Eleazar, and the principate on Joshua; from that time the high priest has always been placed above the prince, as can be understood from the book of Numbers and from Joshua. —p. 35.

units.la: At aliquanto post explicatius. Legimus quando Deus praedixerit Mosi, quòd brevi erat moriturus, dixisse Deum ad Mosen, [Tolle Iosue filium Nun, virum in quo est Spiritus Dei, & pone manum tuum super eum; qui stabit coram Eleazaro Sacerdote, & omni multitudine; & dabis ei præcepta, cunctis videntibus, & partem gloriæ tuæ, ut audiat eum omnis Synagoga filiorum Israël. Pro hoc si quid agendum erit, Eleazar Sacerdos consulet Dominum: Ad verbum eius egredietur, & ingredietur ipse, & omnes filij Israël cum eo.] Ex hac narratione Scripturæ diuinæ non pauca discere possumus; primùm in hac electione Iosue diuisam esse potestatem temporalem à spirituali, siue politicam ab Ecclesiastica. Moses enim utramque potestatem à Deo ipso acceperat; sed ab hoc tempore spiritualis data est Eleazaro, temporalis data est Iosue Duci; Atque hæc est causa cur Deus Mosi dixerit, ut daret Iosue Duci [unam partem gloriæ suæ,] id est, unam potestatem, non utramque. Discimus porrò potestatem spiritualem esse præstantiorem Temporali; siquidem semper videmus Eleazarum Sacerdotem anteponi Iosue Duci, ut in Num. 28. [Præcepit, ergo Moses Eleazaro Sacerdoti, & Iosue.] Denique Num. 27. Ad verbum eius [Eleazari] ingredie“tur & egreditur ipse [Iosua] & omnes filij Israël. Hactenus Bellarminus pag.231.232.
units.tr: But somewhat later he explains it more fully. We read that when God had foretold to Moses that he was shortly to die, God said to Moses, [Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of God, and lay your hand upon him; he shall stand before Eleazar the priest and all the multitude; and you shall give him charge in the sight of all, and give him some of your glory, that all the congregation of the sons of Israel may hear him. If anything is to be done, Eleazar the priest shall consult the Lord for him; at his word he shall go out and come in, he and all the sons of Israel with him.] From this narrative of Holy Scripture we can learn not a few things. First, that in this election of Joshua the temporal power was divided from the spiritual, that is, the political from the ecclesiastical. For Moses had received both powers from God himself; but from this time the spiritual power was given to Eleazar, and the temporal power was given to Joshua the leader. And this is the reason why God told Moses to give to Joshua the leader [one part of his glory], that is, one power, not both. Furthermore, we learn that spiritual power is more excellent than temporal; since we always see Eleazar the priest placed before Joshua the leader, as in Num. 28. [Moses therefore commanded Eleazar the priest and Joshua.] Finally, in Num. 27: at the word of him [Eleazar] he [Joshua] and all the sons of Israel go in and go out. So far Bellarmine, pp. 231–232.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Formam regiminis politici, sub Veteri Testamento, Princi- pibus Novi Testamenti exemplo proponi posse.
units.tr: That the form of political government under the Old Testament can be set before the princes of the New Testament as an example.

units.la: Quòd in causa Regia ex Veteri Testamento ratiocinari coeperis, rem facis, Bellarmine, ut in se solidam, ita Protestantibus longè gratissimam; quippe (ut nostis) Isti praescribenti Tertulliano facile subscribunt, ut scilicet, {a}Cogantur Haeretici ad sacras Scripturas opiniones suas sistere. At verò Sanderus, & Stapletonus (quorum alteri quae de authoritate Ecclesiae, & de Iustificatione; alteri, quae de authoritate Pontificis in Controversiis tuis cumulâsti, debes plurima) indolem quandam Eorum, qui scripturis veteris Testamenti se cogi posse renuunt, satis prodiderunt. Nam, quùm Illis à Protestantibus obijcitur, Ius idem manere Principes Noui Testamenti, quod Principes Veteris Testamenti habuerunt; qui Sacerdotibus interdum praescripserunt, quid in causis Ecclesiasticis agere deberent; tum-etiam Ipsos officium suum negligenter obeuntes, à Ministerio abdicârunt: Respondet Sanderus, {o}Abuti eos sacris Scripturis, quòd ad asserendam Authoritatem Regiam in novo Testamento illa vrgeant, quae in Testamento veteri gerebantur. In eodem luto haeret Stapletonus; {p}Quia regimen (inquit) Veteris Testamenti imperfectius. Quam rationem nulla vnquàm non modò Antiquitas, sed (ante ortos nostro in seculo Anabaptistas) nè novitas quidem somniauit: {q}Anabaptistae enim (fatente Bellarmino) dicunt Iudaeis permissos fuisse Magistratus, propter imperfectionem; sed aliam rationem esse Noui Testamenti.
units.tr: When you began to reason about the royal cause from the Old Testament, Bellarmine, you did something that is solid in itself and very welcome to the Protestants. As you know, they readily subscribe to Tertullian's prescription, namely that heretics must be compelled to confine their opinions to the holy Scriptures. But Sanderus and Stapleton (to one of whom you owe much on the authority of the Church and on justification, and to the other much on the authority of the Pope in your controversies) have sufficiently revealed the character of those who refuse to be bound by the Scriptures of the Old Testament. For when the Protestants object to them that the same right remains for the princes of the New Testament that the princes of the Old Testament had, who sometimes prescribed to the priests what they ought to do in ecclesiastical causes, and who also removed them from the ministry when they carried out their duty negligently, Sanderus replies that they abuse the holy Scriptures, since they press into service, to assert royal authority in the New Testament, the things that happened in the Old. Stapleton sticks in the same mud: "Because the government of the Old Testament was more imperfect," he says. No antiquity, let alone novelty (before the Anabaptists arose in our century), ever dreamed up this reasoning. For the Anabaptists, as Bellarmine admits, say that magistrates were permitted to the Jews because of their imperfection, but that the New Testament has a different reason.

units.la: Horum duorum obiectiunculis satis erit impraesentiarum tuam, in his libris, confessionem, ceu victricem clypeum opponere. “{r}Antequam (inquis) ad vitas “Principum veteris Testamenti describendas accedam, vi“ detur mihi obex quidem esse remouendus, qui fructum lectionis eiusmodi vitarum impedire facilè posset. Dicent “ enim Christiani Principes, superuacaneum videri, velle “ cognoscere quid in Repub. Hebraica Testamenti veteris egerint Principes, siue Reges, quùm nos ad Remp. noui Testamenti, per Dei gratiam, pertineamus. Sed hic obex facilè “ remoueri potest; docet enim S. Augustinus in epist. ad Honoratum, de gratia noui Testamenti, & alibi frequenter, “ sanctos viros Testamenti veteris, quales imprimis fuerint “ sancti Principes Moses, Iosua, Dauid, & aly, floruisse “ quidem tempore Testamenti veteris, sed reuerà pertinuisse “ ad Testamentum nouum; nempe quatenus bona temporalia “ contemnentes spiritualibus inhærebant. Eiusmodi fuisse “ sanctos Principes veteris Testamenti, quorum vitas legendæ[?] proponimus, usque adeo verum est, ut rarissimi Christiani Principes inveniantur, qui veteribus illis in virtutibus & vitæ sanctitate non cedant. Hæc Bellarminus. Hoc igitur obice, vt ais, remoto, facilior de reliquis differendi Ratio nobis proponitur: hoc enim iam Nobis incumbit, ut Reges in veteri Testamento Sacerdotibus imperasse probemus.
units.tr: To these two little objections it will be enough, for the present, to oppose your own confession in these books, as a victorious shield. "Before (you say) I come to describe the lives of the princes of the Old Testament, it seems to me that an obstacle must be removed, one which could easily prevent the fruit of reading lives of this kind. For Christian princes will say that it seems superfluous to want to know what the princes or kings did in the Hebrew commonwealth of the Old Testament, since we, by the grace of God, belong to the commonwealth of the New Testament. But this obstacle can easily be removed. For St Augustine teaches in his letter to Honoratus, on the grace of the New Testament, and often elsewhere, that the holy men of the Old Testament, such as especially the holy princes Moses, Joshua, David and others, flourished indeed in the time of the Old Testament but in truth belonged to the New Testament, namely insofar as, despising temporal goods, they clung to spiritual ones. That the holy princes of the Old Testament, whose lives we propose to be read, were of this kind is so true that very few Christian princes are found who do not yield to those ancients in virtue and holiness of life." Thus Bellarmine. "This obstacle, then," as you say, "being removed, an easier way of dealing with the rest is set before us; for it now falls to us to prove that kings in the Old Testament ruled over priests."

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Mosen, & Iosuam, quâ Principes, Sacerdotibus præfuisse.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. That Moses and Joshua, as princes, were set over the priests.

units.la: HOc vel quadruplici Exemplorum Collatione facilè effectum dabimus; I. inter Mosen Principem, & Aaronem Sacerdotem: II. inter Iosuam, & Eleazarum: III. inter Salomonem, & Abiatharum: IV. inter Iosiam, & Sacerdotum tribum instituitur; de quibusfingulis comminus disceptabimus.
units.tr: I will bring this about easily by a fourfold comparison of examples: I. between Moses the prince and Aaron the priest; II. between Joshua and Eleazar; III. between Solomon and Abiathar; IV. between Josiah and the tribe of the priests. We shall dispute each of these face to face.

units.la: I. Dicimus Mosen praefuisse Aaroni: Respondet Sanderus, {f}Hoc inepte obiici, quia Moses erat Sacerdos, testante Dauid, Psal 98. Moses & Aaron in Sacerdotibus eius. Argutè; quasi verò Moses non (ipso testante Bellarmino){t} Simul Princeps & Pontifex fuerit; qui licet docendi, sacrificandi, consecrandi, & Pontificem inungendi munera exercuerit, nihilominus tamen Politici Magistratus personam gessit, & exequutus est gnauiter. Præfuit igitur Aaroni Moses, vtrum vero vt Princeps, an vt Sacerdos, subinde quæritur; "Vt Sacerdos, (ait Bellarminus) sed extraordinarius: Nos autem, vt Princeps, (inquimus) liquidóque ostendimus. Nam (teste vestro Abulensi) {x}Postquam Sacerdotes isti consecrati sunt a Mose, & ministrare poterant, Moses desiit esse Sacerdos, & nunquam minis-trauit. At Mosen, quùm iam non Sacerdos extraordinarius, sed ordinarius Princeps fuit, Aaroni præfuisse, Aaronem testem adhibemus; qui à Mose de conflato aureo vitulo grauiter reprehensus, respondet (Sacerdos licet, & iure primogenituræ præcellens) {y}Ne indignetur mihi Dominus meus. &c. Quod Responsum dedit Aaron (vt Author vester asserit) {z}Non vt Maior, sed vt subditus. Cuius subiectionis reuera duplicem Rationem suggerit; Prima est, quia Moses Propheta erat, ad quem solum Deus specialiter loquebatur, vt Exod.cap.4. [Ipse loquetur pro Te (nempè Aarone) ad Populum.
