Secunda, quia Moses erat constitutus Dux populi, & Iudex, quantum ad omnia. Atque etiam Mosen in Causa de Idololatria, per Vitulum, non Prophetæ, sed Iudicis partes exequutum esse, Res ipsa loquitur, nam Multa millia eorum, qui adorabant vitulum, occidebat. Nec abest Coniectura, Mosen in Scripturis Regem appellari Deut. 35.5. vt {b}Abulensis obseruat; qui locus ex Hebræo redditur, [Quod erit Rex apud rectissimum:] vbi de solo Mose agi videtur.
units.tr: I. We say that Moses was set over Aaron. Sanderus replies: "This is objected foolishly, because Moses was a priest, as David testifies, Psalm 98: Moses and Aaron among his priests." Clever! As if Moses, by Bellarmine's own testimony, were not at the same time prince and high priest, who, although he exercised the offices of teaching, sacrificing, consecrating, and anointing the high priest, nevertheless bore the person of a political magistrate and carried out that role vigorously. Moses therefore was set over Aaron. But whether he was set over him as priest or as prince is then asked. "As priest," says Bellarmine, "but extraordinary." We, however, say as prince, and we shall clearly show it. For (on the testimony of your Abulensis) "after those priests had been consecrated by Moses and were able to minister, Moses ceased to be a priest and never ministered again." But that Moses, when he was no longer an extraordinary priest but the ordinary prince, was set over Aaron, we take Aaron himself as witness. Sharply rebuked by Moses over the molten golden calf, he replies (though a priest, and excelling by right of the firstborn): "Let not my lord be angry with me," etc. That answer Aaron gave (as your author asserts) "not as a greater, but as a subject." Indeed, he suggests a twofold reason for this subjection. The first is that Moses was a prophet, to whom God alone spoke specially, as in Exodus, chapter 4: "He himself [Aaron] will speak for you to the people." The second is that Moses was appointed leader of the people and judge in all matters. And the thing itself shows that Moses, in the case of the idolatry with the calf, performed the part not of a prophet but of a judge, for he killed many thousands of those who worshipped the calf. Nor is conjecture lacking that Moses is called king in the Scriptures, Deut. 35.5., as Abulensis observes. That passage is rendered from the Hebrew, "He shall be king over the most upright," where it seems to speak of Moses alone.

units.la: II. Collatio instituta est inter Iosuam Principem, & Eleazarum Sacerdotem. Tu Eleazarum Iosuæ præpositum, nos Subditum fuisse dicimus. In hac Controuersia, vel nobis tacentibus, Episcopus Abulensis per omnia Tibi satisfaciet, qui docet, Potestatem à Deo in Iosuam collatam plusquam Iudicis fuisse: {c}Quia Iudices habebant potestatem in aliis bell.cis, in alijs parùm poterant, Iosua autem authoritatem exercebat in criminalibus, quùm occidebatur Achan. Deinde, Magnam esse differentiam inter Iudices & alios Principes; quia alij Reges possunt, quicquid lex non prohibet, Iudices autem solum quod lex iubet.
units.tr: II. A comparison was made between Joshua the prince and Eleazar the priest. You say Eleazar was set over Joshua; we say he was subject to him. In this controversy, even if we kept silent, Bishop Abulensis would satisfy you completely. He teaches that the power conferred by God on Joshua was greater than that of a judge: "Because judges had power in some wars, but in others could do little; Joshua, however, exercised authority in criminal matters, when Achan was put to death." Then: "There is a great difference between judges and other princes; for other kings can do whatever the law does not forbid, but judges only what the law commands."

units.la: Nunc manus secum conferant Bellarminus, & Abulis. Primò, BELLAR. {*} Praecepit Deus Mosi, dicens, Dabis Iosua partem gloriae tuae; In hoc diuisa est potestas publica ab Ecclesiastica: Moses enim, qui utramque potestatem acceperat à Deo, tantum temporalem dat Iosuae, & hac est causa, cur Deus dixit Mosi, ut daret [Partem gloriae suae] id est, unam potestatem, non utramque. ABVL. {d}Moses iam non erat Sacerdos. {e}Et dicitur [In partem gloriae, ut audiat omnis Synagoga filiorum Israel:] id est, ut post mortem Mosis praeciperetur praecipiendo [ut omnis Synagoga audiat,] id est, ut Iosuam loquentem auscultet, & obediat praeceptis Mosis. BELLAR. At dicit Moses, [pro hoc si quid agendum erit, Eleazar consulet Dominum.] Ergò &c. ABVL. {f}Id est, ad petitionem Iosuae Eleazarus Sacerdos inquiret à Domino responsionem de his, quae facere deberet Iosua; & sic obligabatur Eleazarus consulere Dominum quodcunque Iosua diceret ut consuleret. BELLAR. At dicitur, quòd consulente Eleazaro, [ad verbum eius ingredientur, & egredientur omnes filij Israel.] Ergò &c. ABVL. {g}Id est, Eleazarus Sacerdos; praeceptum Iosuae faciendo, quicquid ipse iusserit.
units.tr: Now let Bellarmine and Abulensis join hands. First, BELLARMINE: "God commanded Moses, saying, 'You shall give Joshua part of your glory.' In this the public power is divided from the ecclesiastical: for Moses, who had received both powers from God, gives only the temporal to Joshua. And this is the reason why God told Moses to give [part of his glory], that is, one power, not both." ABULENSIS: "Moses was no longer a priest." "And it is said [in part of his glory, that all the synagogue of the sons of Israel may hear]: that is, that after the death of Moses it might be commanded, by a command, [that all the synagogue hear], that is, that they listen to Joshua speaking and obey the precepts of Moses." BELLARMINE: "But Moses says [if anything is to be done for this, Eleazar shall consult the Lord]. Therefore etc." ABULENSIS: "That is, at Joshua's request Eleazar the priest shall inquire of the Lord for an answer about what Joshua ought to do; and so Eleazar was bound to consult the Lord whatever Joshua told him to consult about." BELLARMINE: "But it is said that, at Eleazar's consultation, [at his word all the sons of Israel shall go in and go out]. Therefore etc." ABULENSIS: "That is, Eleazar the priest; by doing the command of Joshua, whatever he himself shall order."

units.la: Quod addit Bellarminus, in ipsa historia {*}Nomen Eleazari anteponi nomini Iosuae: id certè, ad authoritatis praecellentiam aut praepotentiam indicandam, nullarum virium est, quia Sp. Sanctus, in historica rerum narratione, interdum Personarum dignitatis rationem habet; interdum rei gestae, seu gerendae ordinem seruat; nonnunquàm de industria curiositatem ordinis euitat. Primò enim ubi praeponitur {h}Moses Aaroni, in hoc dignitatis ratio discerni potest. Secundò, ubi Eleazarus Iosuae, ibi rei gerendae ordo seruatur; quia Eleazari munus erat priùs indicio Urim Dominum consulere, quid gerendum fuit, quàm poterat Iosua praestitutum & mandatum Dei obire & exequi. 3°. In recensendis nationibus Parthorum, Medorum, Elamitarum &c. quæ per primam Euangelij promulgationem ad fidem conuertebantur, Spiritus Sanctus dignitatis ordinem non præcisè tenet, sed curiositatem in illo Cathalogo datâ opera euitans, Elamitas inhabitantibus Iudeam præponit; Romanos, rerum Dominos, etiam Lybiæ, & Ægypti Incolis postponit. Qui his responsis non acquiescet, reddat sodes rationem, cur S. Lucas narrans historiam de Aquila, & uxore eius Priscilla Act. 18. & v. 2. præponens virum uxori; in v. 18. eundem postposuerit? Deinde si in præponendis nominibus ea Consequetia insit, quam hoc in loco comminisceris, reddas (obsecro) Tu nobis rationem in hoc loco(pag. 212.) vbi dicis, Philonem Iudæum iure vocare Mosen Regem, Legislatorem, Pontificem, & Prophetam. Cur ex his quatuor Attributis Regem Pontifici, Legislatorem Prophetæ præposuerit?
units.tr: As for what Bellarmine adds, that in the narrative itself the name of Eleazar is placed before the name of Joshua, this has no force for showing a preeminence of authority or power. The Holy Spirit, in the historical narration of events, sometimes takes account of the dignity of persons, sometimes keeps the order of the deed done or to be done, and sometimes deliberately avoids the curiosity of order. First, where Moses is placed before Aaron, the reason of dignity can be discerned in this. Second, where Eleazar is placed before Joshua, the order of the deed to be done is kept, because it was Eleazar's office to consult the Lord by the judgement of the Urim about what was to be done, before Joshua could carry out and execute the command of God that had been laid down. Third, in listing the nations of Parthians, Medes, Elamites and so on, which were converted to the faith at the first promulgation of the Gospel, the Holy Spirit does not strictly keep the order of dignity. Deliberately avoiding curiosity in that catalogue, he places the Elamites inhabiting Judea first, and puts the Romans, lords of affairs, after even the inhabitants of Libya and Egypt. Whoever is not satisfied with these answers, let him kindly give a reason why St Luke, narrating the history of Aquila and his wife Priscilla (Acts 18), places the husband before the wife in v. 2, but in v. 18 puts him after her. Further, if there is in the placing of names that consequence which you invent in this place, please give us a reason here (p. 212) where you say that Philo the Jew rightly calls Moses king, lawgiver, high priest, and prophet. Why did he place king before high priest, and lawgiver before prophet, among these four attributes?

units.la: Quid multa? quatenùs dignitas Sacerdotalis & Regia, quoad materiam, circa quam versantur, inuicem distinguuntur (quarum hæc Temporalis, illa Spiritualis) Eleazarum (cum vestro Albulensi) Honorificentiorem: At verò, quoad externam omnium rerum curam atque regimen, Iosuam merito Excellentiorem vocabimus: quia (vt idem Episcopus monet) {l}Considerandum est quod Iosua Princeps secularis summo sacerdoti directè, ita ut teneretur Eleazarum obedire Iosuæ in omnibus quæ iuberet, sicut cæteri de populo; Sic enim fuit tempore Mosis, quando ipse non fuit Sacerdos. Nec sanè in hac suâ opinione Author vester præceps aut deuius, neque hominis, sed Spiritus Sancti instinctu ductus; nam Iof.3. [Deus dixit Iosue, magnificabo Te hodiè, in conspectu Israël, sicut fui cum Mose, itâ ero tecum, & Tu præcipies Sacerdotibus portare Arcam &c.] Pergit Episcopus: ⁿ Quamuis Iosua (inquit) non esset de tribu Sacerdotum, mandabat tamen non modò minoribus Sacerdotibus, siue Leuitis (vt hic,) sed etiam magno Sacerdoti, Num. 27. quùm dicitur, [Pro hoc si quid agendum erit, erit, Eleazar Sacerdos consulet Dominum.] Hæc de Iosuâ.
units.tr: What more need be said? Insofar as the priestly and royal dignities differ from each other in the matter with which they are concerned (the one being temporal, the other spiritual), we shall call Eleazar more honourable (with your Albulensis). But as to the external care and government of all things, we shall rightly call Joshua more excellent, because (as that same bishop warns) It must be considered that Joshua, the secular prince, was directly over the high priest, so that Eleazar was bound to obey Joshua in all things he commanded, just as the rest of the people did; for so it was in the time of Moses, when he himself was not a priest. Nor indeed in this opinion is your author rash or wandering, nor is he led by human instinct but by the Spirit of the Holy Spirit; for Josh. 3. [God said to Joshua, I will magnify you today in the sight of Israel, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you, and you shall command the priests to carry the ark, etc.] The bishop goes on: Although Joshua (he says) was not of the tribe of the priests, he nevertheless gave orders not only to the lesser priests or Levites (as here) but also to the high priest, Num. 27., where it is said, [If anything is to be done for this, Eleazar the priest shall consult the Lord.] So much for Joshua.

units.la: SECT. V. III. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: SECT. V. III. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Idem ius Salomoni in Abiathar; Iosiæ in Sacerdotum tribum vindicari.
units.tr: The same right over Abiathar is claimed for Solomon; for Josiah, over the tribe of the priests.

units.la: Tertia Collatio erit inter Principem Salomonem, & Abiatharum Sacerdotem. I°. Abiathari Sacerdotis crimen vultis? Reus erat (fatente Stapletono) lasæ maiestatis, & conspirationis contra Salomonem cum Adoniâ ad regnum aspirante, vt patet 3. Reg. cap. 2. II°. An verò pœnam? hanc Salomon satis explicat, quia mortem, tanquam pœnam debitam, denunciat, verf. 26. [Homo mortis est;] id est (ait Iesuita) Dignus morte. At Pœna, quam exigit, Exilium fuit, [vade in Ariathot &c.] Cur hanc ei gratiam Salomon indulserit, ipse Causam reddit; Quoniam portasti arcam coram Patre meo, non Te interficiam. III°. An demùm iustitiam Iudicis quæritis? Sp. Sanctus vobis satisfaciet, quia dicitur in eâdem historiâ, Salomon ambulauit in præceptis Dauid Patris sui, nisi quòd immolabat in excelsis. Et (iuxta regulam Iuris) vbi aliquid excipitur, alia integratur.
units.tr: The third comparison will be between the Prince Solomon and the priest Abiathar. First, do you want to accuse the priest Abiathar of a crime? He was guilty (as Stapleton admits) of treason and of conspiracy against Solomon with Adonijah, who aspired to the kingdom, as is clear from 3. Reg. cap. 2. Second, do you want the punishment? Solomon explains this well enough, since he pronounces death as the penalty owed, verse 26 [he is a man of death]; that is (says the Jesuit) worthy of death. But the penalty he imposed was exile [go to Anathoth, etc.]. Why Solomon granted him this favour, he himself gives the reason: Because you carried the ark before my father, I will not put you to death. Third, do you finally ask for the justice of the judge? The Holy Spirit will satisfy you, since it is said in the same history: Solomon walked in the precepts of David his father, except that he sacrificed in the high places. And (according to the rule of law) where something is excepted, the rest stands.

units.la: IV°. An Personam intueamur, quam nunc Salomon sustinuit? (nam hoc vnum restat, de quo nobis Pontificij litem intendunt) Salomon (inquitis) non vt Rex, sed vt Propheta, & exequutor diuinæ Iustitiæ Abiathar depositit: quia in textu dicitur, [Id eum fecisse, vt impleretur verbum Domini.] Cui obiectioni Episcopus vester Iesuita iam anteà respondit; Vocabulum [vt] non ponere causam finalem, sed consequentiam; quia non eiecit Eum Salomon in eum finem, vt impleretur verbum Domini, sed ad alium finem; sic tamen vt consequens ad istud opus Salomonis sit, quod impleretur verbum Domini. Quem sensum vester Iesuita sequutus est; sic enim exponit: Ita impletum est quòd Deus fuerat comminatus Heli, 1. Reg. 2. Qui quidem vsus eiusdem vocabuli [vt] in sacris literis est frequentissimus. Quùm milites Ethnici, Christi vestes inter se partientes, nihil minùs quàm de verbo Dei cogitabant, dicitur tamen, {t}Id factum esse, vt impleatur Scriptura. Superiùs, Bellarmine, dixeras, Salomonem in deponendo Abiathar non Regem, sed Prophetam, & executorem diuinæ iustitiæ egisse.
units.tr: Fourth, shall we look at the person Solomon then sustained? (for this is the one point left, over which the Papists press their dispute with us.) Solomon (you say) deposed Abiathar not as king but as prophet and executor of divine justice, because the text says [He did this that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled.] To this objection your Jesuit bishop has already replied: the word [that] does not mark a final cause but a consequence; for Solomon did not cast him out with the end that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled, but for another end; yet in such a way that it was a consequence of that work of Solomon that the word of the Lord was fulfilled. Your Jesuit followed this sense; for he explains: Thus it was fulfilled that God had threatened Eli, 1 Reg. 2. Indeed this use of the same word [that] is most frequent in the sacred letters. When the Gentile soldiers, dividing Christ's garments among themselves, were thinking nothing less than the word of God, it is nonetheless said: that this was done that the Scripture might be fulfilled. Earlier, Bellarmine, you had said that Solomon in deposing Abiathar acted not as king but as prophet and executor of divine justice.

units.la: Adeòne coecutis, vt pugnantia Te loqui nõ sentias? Etenim Propheta est praedicere tantùm iudicia diuina; Regum autem exequi; Ille iustitiæ Dei Index quasi; hic vindex esse solet. Ita Elizæ Propheta praenunciauit mortem Iehoram; Iehu Princeps exegit, {u}iuxta verbum Domini. Eodem modo de fatali hac Abiathari abdicatione generaliter Propheta praedixit, 2.Sam.2. quam Princeps Salomon hoc in loco effectam dedit: non tamen ex intentione exequendi illud Decretum Dei? qui enim potuit, qui nullum eâ de re mandatum Dei acceperat?
units.tr: Are you so blinded that you do not notice you are saying contradictory things? For it is the office of a prophet only to foretell the divine judgments, but of kings to carry them out; the one is, as it were, the judge of God's justice, the other is usually its avenger. Thus the prophet Elisha foretold the death of Jehoram; the prince Jehu carried it out according to the word of the Lord. In the same way the prophet generally foretold this fatal removal of Abiathar, 2 Sam. 2., which Prince Solomon in this place brought about. Yet was it not with the intention of carrying out that decree of God? For how could he have done so, if he had received no command of God in that matter?

units.la: Quarta Collatio est inter Iosiam Regem, & Sacerdotum tribum. Iehosaphat, Ezechiæ, Iosiæ, præcellentissimorum Regum res præclarè gestæ neminem fugiunt; qui in reparando Templo, indicendis Ieiunijs, Idololatriæ monumentis demoliendis, vero Dei cultu stabiliendo, alijsque religionis officijs exequendis toti fuerunt. Ex quibus singulis illud cum hac Causa coniunctissimum mihi semper est visum, quod Iosiam præstitisse legimus, quando {x}officium colligendi pecunias, ad Templum instaurandum, Sacerdotibus impositit; {a}Eosque, vnà cum Iehoida summo Pontifice, coram se sisti iussit; & neglecti officij, quòd muneri suo defuerint, postulauit. De qua re diserte ingenuéque vester Episcopus. {b}Sacerdotes (inquit) in duobus peccabant, 1o. quod non discurrerent per loca Iudea, ad colligendam pecuniam sicut Rex iubebat: 2o. quia receperunt pecuniam aliquam, nihil tamen reparârunt. Dato igitur quòd Rex aliquod auferret de iure Sacerdotum, tamen non peccabat, quia propter culpam suam priuabantur iure suo: Et Rex ipse potestatem super Sacerdotes habuit, & potuit eos occidere, pro crimine, sicut cæteros Laicos; & a fortiore priuare eos officij dignitate. Hæc
units.tr: The fourth comparison is between King Josiah and the tribe of the priests. The famous deeds of the most excellent kings, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah, are known to everyone; they devoted themselves wholly to repairing the Temple, proclaiming fasts, tearing down the monuments of idolatry, establishing the true worship of God, and performing the other duties of religion. Of these particulars, the one that has always seemed to me most closely connected with this cause is what we read Josiah did when he imposed on the priests the office of collecting money to restore the Temple; he ordered them, together with Jehoiada the high priest, to be brought before him, and demanded an account of their neglected duty, because they had failed in their office. On this matter your bishop speaks clearly and ingenuously. The priests (he says) were at fault in two respects: first, because they did not go through the places of Judea to collect money as the king commanded; second, because they received some money but repaired nothing. Granting, then, that the king took something from the right of the priests, he was not doing wrong, because they had been deprived of their right on account of their own fault. And the king himself had power over the priests and could put them to death for a crime, as he could other laymen; and, a fortiori, deprive them of the dignity of their office. These things

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Ius idem Principum, in Sacerdotes veteris Testamenti, Confessionibus aliorum Aduersariorum confirmari.
units.tr: The same right of princes over the priests of the Old Testament is confirmed by the confessions of other adversaries.

units.la: Hæc veritas tantâ, támque diuinâ exemplorum luce coruscans, Confessionem sui ab Aduersarijs nostris extorsit: Concedit enim Stapletonus{c}Reges ipsos in veteri Testamento non solùm piè, sed & necessario rebus Ecclesiasticis nonnihil se immiscuisse. Cuius veritatis Assertorem adducit secum Scholasticorum facilè Principem{d}Thomam Aquinatem, in hæc verba; In veteri Testamento Regnum præseminebat Sacerdotio. Ex Loyolensi Schola Testem habemus Salmeronem Iesuitam, absque omni ambage asserentem{e}Summos Sacerdotes subditos fuisse Regibus (in veteri Testamento) sicut apud Gentiles. Cui {f}Carerius, {*}Aculensis, aliíque plurimi accedunt. Bellarminus ab hoc propugnaculo depulsus, ingenij sui viribus fretus, aliunde præsidium petit. . . . “Ratio huius excellentia est, quia Pontifex praeest rebus diuinis, & Princeps rebus humanis; cui & addi potest, quòd regiones Principum terrae definitae sunt certis Prouincys; Regio autem subiecta Pontifici Maximo omnes Prouincias, & omnia Regna Christianis Principibus subiecta complectitur. Hinc ille pius Episcopus Patarensis, quùm vidisset sanctum Pontificem Siluerium ab Imperatore Haeretico parum honesté habitum, exclamauit, multos esse Reges in terris, sed nullum talem, qualis est ille Pontifex Rom. qui praeest Ecclesiis totius mundi. ---pag.35.36.
units.tr: This truth, shining with so great and so divine a light of examples, has extorted a confession from our adversaries. Stapleton concedes that kings themselves in the Old Testament not only piously but also necessarily meddled somewhat in ecclesiastical affairs. As the champion of this truth he easily brings forward the prince of the Schoolmen, Thomas Aquinas, who says: In the Old Testament the kingdom was pre-eminent over the priesthood. From the school of Loyola we have the Jesuit Salmeron as a witness, who asserts without any ambiguity that the high priests were subject to kings (in the Old Testament), as among the Gentiles. Carerius, of Aculum, and very many others agree with him. Bellarmine, driven from this bulwark, relying on the strength of his own wit, seeks help elsewhere: "The reason for this excellence is that the Pontiff presides over divine things and the Prince over human things. To this may be added that the regions of princes are defined by fixed provinces, but the region subject to the Supreme Pontiff embraces all the provinces and all the kingdoms subject to Christian princes. Hence that pious Bishop of Patara, when he had seen the holy Pontiff Silverius treated rather dishonourably by a heretical Emperor, exclaimed that there are many kings on earth, but none like that Roman Pontiff, who presides over the Churches of the whole world." ---pp. 35, 36.

units.la: Quod Patarensis Episcopi dictum & obiecisti non semel.
units.tr: This is the saying of the Bishop of Patara, which you have objected more than once.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Bellarminum Liberati testimonium pro libitu suo accipere, & rejicere.
units.tr: Bellarmine takes and rejects the testimony of Liberatus as he pleases.

units.la: EN rationes duas, certè quidem ludicras; quarum Alteri fusè admodum {*}respondimus; De Altera mox {*}videbimus. Nunc Obiectioni, ex dictis Patarensis Episcopi, occurrendum est. Dixitne verò Patarensis Pontificem Rom. Ecclesiis totius mundi praesse? Imò, exclamavit, (inquis) Teste {*}Abbate Liberato in Breviar. cap. 22. At idem tuus Liberatus in eodem Cap. refert Vigilium Papam scripsisse Epistolam, quâ Monothelitarum haeresin confirmabat. Ecquid Tibi arridet? Respondes, {b}Pos-set dici[?], Epistolam illam Vigilij, cuius meminit Liberatus, suisse confictam ab Haereticis; Liberatum autem credidisse falso rumori, quem Haeretici sparserant. Candorem tuum, Bellarmine.
units.tr: Behold two arguments, certainly frivolous, of which we have answered the first at considerable length; the second we shall presently examine. Now the objection drawn from the words of the Bishop of Patara must be met. Did the Bishop of Patara really say that the Roman Pontiff presides over the Churches of the whole world? "Indeed he cried out," you say, "as Abbot Liberatus witnesses in the Breviarium, chapter 22." But this same Liberatus, in the same chapter, reports that Pope Vigilius wrote an epistle by which he confirmed the heresy of the Monothelites. Does that please you? You reply that it could be said that that epistle of Vigilius, which Liberatus mentions, was forged by the heretics, and that Liberatus believed a false rumour which the heretics had spread. Such is your candour, Bellarmine.

units.la: Abbas Liberatus, si quid afferat, quod ad amplificandam Papae Sylverij Diœcesin faciat, audiendus est: sin quid narrauerit, quo Papae Vigilio haeresEos[?] nota inuratur, tum (quæ est vestra authoritas) Rumusculus deditus, testis levis, & nimis credulus reijiciendus est illico. Porrò ais; Possit autem dici, illam epistolam Vigilij, cuius meminit Liberatus, corruptam ab Haereticis. Quod si itidem & Nos; Posset responderi, Narrationem de Patarensi Episcopo à Monachis quibusdam, in honorem Pontificis, fuisse corruptam; æqui Tu Responsum hoc bonique consuleres? quod tamen Vivi vestro non incredibile videretur, qui graviter questus est, 'Magnorum authorum scripta istiusmodi{} male-feriatorum hominum manibus contaminari. Hæc de Testimonio.
units.tr: If Abbot Liberatus says anything that tends to magnify the diocese of Pope Silverius, he is to be heard; but if he relates anything by which a stain of heresy is burned into Pope Vigilius, then (such is your authority) a gossip addicted to rumours, a light witness and too credulous, is to be rejected at once. Moreover you say: "It could be said that that epistle of Vigilius, which Liberatus mentions, was corrupted by the heretics." But if we too should say: "It could be answered that the account of the Bishop of Patara was corrupted by certain monks, out of honour for the Pontiff," would you take that answer fairly and in good part? Yet this would not seem incredible in the case of your Vives, who complained bitterly that the writings of great authors of this kind are defiled by the hands of worthless men. So much concerning the testimony.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Patarensem Episcopum, sensu minimè Pontificio, totius Ecclesiae praefectu- ram Pontifici concessisse.
units.tr: That the Bishop of Patara, in a sense by no means Papal, conceded to the Pontiff the governance of the whole Church.

units.la: Sed Liberatum tamen fidei integrae Testem amplexantes, Testimonium ipsum discutiamus. Dixit Patarenfis Episc. Pontificem Rom. præsse Ecclesiis totius mundi. Esto. Si verò hoc Græcus Episcopus id dixit solus, [illegible, ~5 letters]; sin vnà cùm aliis, Aliorum pariter totius Græce Ecclesiæ Antistitum [illegible, ~5 letters] est secutus, qui quidem Rom. Episcopo præfecturam ordinis per vniuersum mundum (Ecclesiastico tamen iure acquisitam) facilè concesserunt; Iurisdictionis, aut authoritatis nunquàm. Fac enim (quod iam supra ex Veterum monumentis probauimus ) Alexandrinam, Constantinopolitanam, Carthaginensem, Asianam, Antiochenam, aliasque Græcas Ecclesias (vt olim fuerunt) sanè celeberrimas sua Iura, Dioeceses, priuilegia Concilijs Nicæno, Chalcedonensi, Carthaginensi, Africano, Constantinopolitanóque, in præiudicium Romanæ Ecclesiæ, sibi vendicare; & sine dubio Ecclesia hæc facilè mouebit risum fucatis & ementitis nudata coloribus.
units.tr: But, embracing Liberatus as a witness of sound faith, let us examine the testimony itself. The Bishop of Patara said that the Roman Pontiff presides over the Churches of the whole world. Granted. But if the Greek bishop said this alone, [illegible]; but if he followed others together with him, [illegible] of the other bishops of the whole Greek Church, who indeed readily conceded to the Roman bishop a precedence of order throughout the world (acquired, however, by ecclesiastical law), but never jurisdiction or authority. For suppose (as we have already proved above from the monuments of the ancients) that the Alexandrian, Constantinopolitan, Carthaginian, Asian, Antiochene and other Greek Churches (as they once were, and most famous indeed) claimed for themselves their own rights, dioceses and privileges, in the Councils of Nicaea, Chalcedon, Carthage, Africa and Constantinople, to the prejudice of the Roman Church; then without doubt this Church would easily move to laughter, stripped of its painted and counterfeit colours.

units.la: Nam (vt alia multa præteream) Conc. Niceni Canon (quo instituitur vt Alexandrinus Aegypti, & aliarum quarundam Prouinciarum Priuilegia seruaret [ιπωπ ꝸ] Quoniam Episcopus Rom. itâ consueuit) satis declarat, quòd Episcopus Rom. seculis antiquioribus non tantùm Atlas habebatur, qui mundi totius oneri sustinendo esset. Quibus verbis Sirmondus Ief. ex vi particulae [ꝸ] Institutam esse comparationem inter Alexandrinum & Episcopum Romanum fateri coactus est, etiam reluctante Bellarmino; cui tamen [ιπωπ] suapte sponte accesserat. Ex qua consessione tollitur Bellarmini refugium, quùm itâ Canonem exponit; Quoniam Episcopus Romanus id (nempè Alexandrino Episcopo) permisit: quo interpretamento nota illa Comparationis [ꝸ] exulare oportet, vt nullus eruditus non videat. Hoc igitur Canone Vniuersalis illa Papæ Dioecesis euertitur. Ad Historiam Liberati reuertamur.
units.tr: For (to pass over many other things) the canon of the Council of Nicaea (by which it is ordained that the Alexandrian bishop should keep the privileges of Egypt and certain other provinces [ἐπειδή], since the Roman bishop has been accustomed to do so) sufficiently declares that in more ancient ages the Roman bishop was regarded not merely as an Atlas who would sustain the burden of the whole world. Sirmond the Jesuit, from the force of the particle [ꝸ], was compelled by these words to admit that a comparison was instituted between the Alexandrian and the Roman bishop, even though Bellarmine resisted; yet the [ιπωπ] had come to him of its own accord. From this admission Bellarmine's refuge is removed, when he explains the canon thus: since the Roman bishop permitted this (namely, to the Alexandrian bishop). By that interpretation the well-known force of the particle of comparison [ꝸ] must be banished, as every learned man sees. By this canon, therefore, that universal diocese of the Pope is overthrown. Let us return to the history of Liberatus.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO. Iustinianum in causa Sylverÿ (non obstante Patarensis Epi- scopi reclamatione) de iure suo neutiquam cessisse.
units.tr: III. Animadversion. That Justinian, in the case of Silverius (despite the protest of the bishop of Patara), by no means gave up his right.

units.la: CArd. Baronius eiusdem historiae meminit, & ex ipsissimo Liberati loco ea repetit, quae sicco pede minime praetereunda videntur. Ex Graecis Episcopis unum Patarensem magno animo in defensionem Sylverij Papae surrexisse aduersus Imp. Iustinianum, verum quidem est; Eumque de iniuria in Sylverium perpetrata, redarguisse, verbis supra citatis; videlicet, Papam Sylverium unum esse supra Ecclesiam mundi totius. Addit vero Liberatus, in verbis immediate sequentibus; Quum audiens Imperator, revocari Romam Sylverium iussit, & de literis illius iudicium fieri, ut si probaretur ab ipso fuisse scriptas, degeret in quacunque civitate Episcopus: si autem falsae fuissent probatae, restitueretur suae sedi. Haec Liberatus. At cuius tandem criminis suspicione laborabat Papa Sylverius? Fertur Monachum Scholasticum (ait Liberatus) fictas in nomine Sylverij composuisse literas, Regi Gothorum scriptas, ex quibus conuinceretur Sylverius Romanam prodere velle civitatem. Haec ille.
units.tr: Cardinal Baronius also mentions this history and repeats from Liberatus's very words what seem not to be passed over lightly. That one of the Greek bishops, the bishop of Patara, rose with great courage in defence of Pope Silverius against the Emperor Justinian is true; and that he rebuked the wrong done to Silverius, in the words quoted above, namely that Pope Silverius alone is above the whole Church of the world, is also true. But Liberatus adds, in the words immediately following: When the Emperor heard this, he ordered Silverius to be recalled to Rome, and an inquiry to be made into his letters, so that if it were proved that he had written them, the bishop should live in whatever city he pleased; but if they were proved to be forged, he should be restored to his see. So Liberatus. But of what crime was Pope Silverius then suspected? It is reported (says Liberatus) that a monk named Scholasticus had composed letters falsely in Silverius's name, written to the king of the Goths, by which Silverius might be convicted of wishing to betray the city of Rome. So he.

units.la: Hic amabo Te siste paululum gradum, Lector; & disce ex hoc unius orthodoxi Imperatoris facto, quanta omnium super Papas appareat esse authoritas. Primo Papam in ius vocari, reum proditionis postulari aduersus Imperatorem; secundo, exilio multari; tertio, (vbi, monente Episcopo Patarensi, suspicatus est Imperator testes falsos, criménque confictum fuisse) reuocari in patriam, eâ tamen lege, vt Causa eius inferioribus Iudicibus rursus examinanda mandetur; vt ipse, si innocens & innoxius esset, sedi suae restitueretur; sin Reus deprehendatur, quacunque alia civitate degens, à sede amotus, iudicio acquiescat. Hisce singulis adijciamus ipsum Episc. Patarensem, qui tanto animo Sylverij patrocinum suscepit, hinc Catholici Imperatoris mandato minimè repugnasse.
units.tr: Here, I beg you, Reader, pause a little, and learn from this one deed of an orthodox Emperor how great the authority of the Popes is over all things. First, the Pope was summoned to trial and charged with treason against the Emperor; second, he was punished with exile; third, when the Emperor, at the warning of the bishop of Patara, came to suspect that the witnesses were false and the charge invented, he was recalled to his homeland, on the condition, however, that his case be remitted to inferior judges for re-examination; so that if he were innocent and blameless, he should be restored to his see, but if he were found guilty, he should be removed from his see and abide by the sentence, living in whatever other city. Let us add to each of these points that the bishop of Patara himself, who took up Silverius's cause with such courage, did not on this account oppose the command of a Catholic Emperor.

units.la: Nè mihi succensèat Card. Bellarminus, quòd Iustinianum Imperat. Catholicum vocauerim, quùm (testante Card. Baronio ) Decreta de fide sanciuerit: & Rursus; {o} Iustiniani sanctio aduersus Haereticos: Denùo, {p}Iustiniani Contestatio aduersus Haereticos: Imò quòcum Patrensi Episcopo de facta Syluerio iniuria, non de Haresi expostulauerit. Non est igitur verisimile, Sanctum Episcopum, qui tam animosè Papæ causam egit, vt Eum crimine proditionis liberaret, Causam Christi suo silentio prodidisse. Quid quòd Iustinianus Syluerium Pont. (modò ille se suspicione criminis laesæ maiestatis expurgauit) in sedem restituì decreuerat? Istnè[?] Haeretici partes fuerunt? Sed pergis, vti soles, præcipitanter agere.
units.tr: Let Cardinal Bellarmine not be angry with me for calling Justinian a Catholic Emperor, since (as Cardinal Baronius attests) he enacted the decrees concerning the faith; and again, Justinian's sanction against heretics; and once more, Justinian's protestation against heretics; indeed, he complained to the bishop of Patara about the wrong done to Silverius, not about heresy. It is therefore not probable that the holy bishop, who defended the Pope's cause so boldly, and freed him from the charge of treason, betrayed the cause of Christ by his silence. What of the fact that Justinian had decided to restore Pope Silverius to his see, once he had cleared himself of the suspicion of treason? Was that the part of a heretic? But you go on, as you always do, acting rashly.

units.la: Causa Regia ex iudicio Patrum expenditur.
units.tr: The Royal Cause weighed by the judgement of the Fathers.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: "Quanta verò sit eminentia potestatis Pontificiæ super potestatem Regum, & Principum terrenorum, docent multi Patres: sed ego contentus ero testimonio S. Bernardi." Pag.36.
units.tr: "How great the eminence of the Pontifical power is over the power of kings and earthly princes, many Fathers teach; but I shall be content with the testimony of St Bernard." Page 36.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Tantum verò Eminentiam potestatis Pontificiæ (sed Alibi) asseris, vt {q}Principes deponat: & alioqui Ecclesiam non esse sufficientem & perfectam, nisi id posset in ordine ad finem spiritualem. — Quòd verò tempore Neronis, Iuliani, & aliorum Ethnicorum Principum Christiani eos non deposuerint, id fuit, (inquis) quia deerant illis vires temporales.
units.tr: You assert so great an eminence of Pontifical power (but elsewhere) that it deposes princes; and otherwise that the Church is not sufficient and perfect unless it could do this in relation to the spiritual end. — But that in the time of Nero, Julian and other pagan princes, the Christians did not depose them, was (you say) because they lacked temporal powers.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. Animadversion.

units.la: Non defectum virium, sed diminutum mandatum anti- quos Christianos in subiectionis officijs, erga Ethnicos Principes continuisse; contra quam blasphemè decent Pontifices.
units.tr: That the ancient Christians lacked not strength but a restricted command in the duties of subjection toward pagan princes; against which the Pontiffs blasphemously teach.

units.la: Hancinè in Ecclesia potestatem multi Patres docuerunt? annon uniuersi antiquioris notæ planè potius contrarium? In hanc rem Eum ego testem dabo, qui ausit de se hisce verbis profiteri;{r} Testis est mihi Deus, nihil me voluisse, cogitâsse, aut scripsisse, quod vel minimâ ex parte posset Decretis SS. Catholicæ, Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ, religioni, & fidei directè vel per obliquum retorqueri, aut referri in odium inimicitiamque alicuius potestatis spiritualis aut temporalis. Testem integriorem quis requirat? testimonium ipsum attendamus. ' A Christo passo (inquit) per internallum trecentorum Annorum, etsi innumera crudelisque tormenta Christiani passi fuerint, & clades atrocissimas, nusquam tamen legitur eos adversus Reges rebellasse. + sed hoc fere argumento ostenderunt se, suamque religionem omnibus anteferri debere, quod in ea sententia ita pertinaciter & obnixè perdurant, ut unico amore Dei, & divini cultus Christianos se ab eo dicerent appellari, cuius sit hoc pussimum[?] dogma, ut MAGISTRATIBUS PAREANT. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Is this the power that many Fathers taught in the Church? Is it not rather the plain opposite of what the most ancient and well-known writers say? To witness on this matter I will call the man who dared to profess of himself in these words: God is my witness that I have never willed, thought or written anything which could in the smallest part be turned directly or indirectly against the decrees of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, its religion and faith, or be referred to the hatred or enmity of any power, spiritual or temporal. Who could ask for a more complete witness? Let us consider his testimony itself. From the passion of Christ (he says), through the space of three hundred years, although the Christians suffered countless and cruel torments and most atrocious defeats, yet nowhere do we read that they rebelled against kings. + But by this argument they showed that their religion ought to be preferred to all others, since they persist so stubbornly and resolutely in that opinion that, by the sole love of God and of divine worship, they called themselves Christians from him; and the most important dogma of which is this: that they OBEY THE MAGISTRATES. Thus he.

units.la: Nulli jam protritis distinctiunculis vestris est locus: non cum dicitis, jam non Voluntatem Illis, sed vires ad resistendum defuisse: aut (ut schola vestra loquitur) Christianos quoad temporalia, si non actu, attamen habitu Superiores fuisse: non quod scribis, Ecclesiam Christi non per se esse sufficientem, nisi potestatem illam habeat: non quum Glossa Bonifacy VIII. Papæ, obstrepit & dicit; {t}Non videri Dominum (Christum) satis disertum fuisse (ut cum reuerentia, inquit, loquar) nisi unicum posset se Vicarium reliquisset; "{u}qui posset in Imperatores & quoscunque alios depositionis sententiam ferre." Quæ enim malum? illa Reuerentia, quæ coniuncta est cum tam insigni blasphemia? Blasphemiam dico, quòd cùm negare non possunt, antiquis perfectissimisq; (Christianis vires defuisse, ad deponendos Ethnicos Principes, qui pertraxerunt Subditos suos à fide Christi; nihilominus tamen dicant, Ecclesiam non sufficientem fuisse, in ordine ad finem spiritualem: quo vix potest quisquam satis demirari istorum hominum insaniam; eoque magis, quod orthodoxam veritatem Subiectionis erga Principes infideles (etiam licet Christiani viribus essent superiores) Antiqui {x}Patres in Apologys suis suae aetatis Christianis omnibus testatissimâ fecerint. quod Bellar. non negâsset, nisi contra omnem Authoritatis historicae fidem animum suum obstinâsset; qui, omnibus antiquis praetermissis Patribus, ad recens natum Bernardum duntaxat conuolat, unicâ eius in unum S. Pauli locum expositione fretus.
units.tr: There is now no room for your worn-out little distinctions: not when you say that it was not their will but their strength to resist that was lacking; or (as your school puts it) that Christians were superior in temporal matters, if not in act, yet in habit; not what you write, that the Church of Christ is not sufficient in itself unless it has that power; not when the Gloss of Pope Boniface VIII murmurs and says: that the Lord (Christ) did not seem sufficiently eloquent (to speak with reverence, as it says) unless he had left a single Vicar who could "pronounce a sentence of deposition against emperors and any others." What, then, is that reverence worth, that is joined with so notable a blasphemy? Blasphemy I say, because, when they cannot deny that the most ancient and most perfect (Christians lacked the strength to depose the pagan princes, who drew their subjects away from Christ), nevertheless they say the Church was not sufficient in relation to the spiritual end. Scarcely anyone can sufficiently marvel at the madness of these men; and all the more because the Ancient Fathers, in their Apologies written for the Christians of their own age, have set out most clearly the orthodox truth of subjection to unbelieving princes (even though the Christians were superior in strength). Bellarmine would not have denied this, unless he had obstinately set his mind against all trust in historical authority; who, passing over all the ancient Fathers, flies only to the recently born Bernard, relying on a single exposition of one passage of St Paul.

units.la: Causa inter Principes & Pontifices, de praestantia Authoritatis, agitur ex ce- lebri illo Canone Apostolico, [OMNIS ANIMA &c.] Rom. 13.
units.tr: The dispute between princes and popes over the superiority of authority is conducted from that famous apostolic canon, [EVERY SOUL, etc.] Rom. 13.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Duties (de Officiis)

units.la: Bernardus sic loquitur ad Imperatorem Conradum; Legi (inquit) Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit, & qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit: Quam tamen sententiam vobis, & omnimodis moneo custodire, in exhibenda reuerentia summa & Apostolica Sedi, & B. Petri Vicario, sicut ipsam vobis vultis ab vniuerso seruari Imperio. Hæc Ille. — pag. 36.
units.tr: Bernard speaks thus to the Emperor Conrad: "Read (he says) 'Let every soul be subject to the higher powers,' and 'whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God.' I warn you, however, and in every way I urge you to keep this opinion, by showing the highest reverence to the Apostolic See and to the Vicar of St. Peter, just as you wish the same to be observed throughout the whole Empire." Thus he. — p. 36.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Et hæc ex Illo Tu, sed quo animo nondum satis assequimur: nos enim hebetes Protestantes semper credidimus ex hoc loco Apostoli Rom. 13. [Omnis anima &c.] omnem omnino animam, tâm Ecclesiasticam, quam Laicam politicis Magistratibus subijci; maximè verò ijs, qui in summa eminentia constituti sunt. Nec Te hoc latuit; {a}Protestantes (inquis alibi) obyciunt hunc locum Pauli, & 1. Pet. 2. Subiecti estote omni humanæ creaturæ propter Deum, siue Regi tanquam præcellenti &c. In quibus locis sermo est (inquit) de secularibus potestatibus, & nullus excipitur, non Clericus, non Episcopus, nō Papa, quùm dicatur [Omnis anima.] Respondeo (inquis) tàm Petrum, quàm Paulum loqui generaliter, & hortari omnes subditos, vt suis superioribus pareant, tàm spiritualibus quam temporalibus: ex qua sententia non potest deduci Papam [subiectum esse Regi, nec Regem Papæ; sed sententiæ sunt generales. Probatur; nam Paulus ait, [Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit,] vbi non restringit sermonem ad potestatem secularem, sed de omni potestate loquitur. Nec, obstat exemplum de Regibus, qui gladium portant: nam diligentius voluit Paulus de Rege loqui, quia eo tempore accusabantur Christiani seductionis & rebellionis à Calumniatoribus. Pari ratione Petrus generaliter loquitur, — Itaque S. Bernardus in epist. 183. ad Conradum Imperatorem, Legi (inquit) Omnis anima &c. Hæc Tu. Protestantes igitur interpretantur hunc locum specialiter intelligi de potestate politica; qui, te interprete, sumitur communiter & generaliter tàm pro Ecclesiastica potestate, quàm politica. Illi ex sensu speciali inferunt, Episcopos ipsos Principibus subijci: Tu ex tuo generali colligis, Ex hoc loco deduci non posse, vel Regi Papam subijci, vel Papam Regi. Ad opinionem tuam astruendam, ais, Te [?]posse multos nempe Patres producere, sed vnius Bernardi testimonio contentum esse; ipse mox non modò ab ipso Bernardo, sed & a multis Patribus, nec hoc solùm, sed etiam à Tuis, imò à Teipso refutandus.
units.tr: You say this in your own words, but we do not yet fully grasp with what intention. For we dull Protestants have always believed that from this passage of the Apostle, Rom. 13, [Every soul, etc.], every soul whatsoever, the ecclesiastical as well as the lay, is subject to the political magistrates, and above all to those who are placed in the highest eminence. Nor was this hidden from you: {a}Protestants (you say elsewhere) object to this passage of Paul and to 1 Pet. 2, "Submit yourselves to every human creature for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme," etc. In these places (you say) the discussion is about secular powers, and no one is excepted: not the clergyman, not the bishop, not the Pope, since it is said [Every soul.] I answer (you say) that both Peter and Paul speak generally and exhort all subjects to obey their superiors, spiritual as well as temporal. From this statement it cannot be deduced that the Pope is subject to the king, nor the king to the Pope; but the statements are general. This is proved: for Paul says, [Let every soul be subject to the higher powers,] where he does not restrict the discourse to secular power, but speaks of every power. Nor does the example of kings who bear the sword stand in the way: Paul wished to speak more carefully of the king, because at that time Christians were accused by their calumniators of sedition and rebellion. By the same reasoning Peter speaks generally. — Thus St. Bernard, in Epistle 183 to the Emperor Conrad: "Read (he says) 'Every soul,' etc." Thus you. The Protestants therefore interpret this passage as understood specially of political power; which, on your reading, is taken commonly and generally for ecclesiastical power as much as for political power. They infer from the special sense that the bishops themselves are subject to princes; you gather from your general sense that it cannot be deduced from this passage either that the Pope is subject to the king, or the king to the Pope. To establish your opinion, you say that you could produce many Fathers, but that you are content with the testimony of Bernard alone; yet he himself is at once to be refuted, not only by Bernard himself, but by many Fathers, and not only by these but even by your own men, indeed by yourself.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: FIRST REMARK.

units.la: Bernardum ipsum, vbi accuratius Textum hunc penfitâssel, sensum & explicationem Protestantium confirmâsse.
units.tr: That Bernard himself, had he weighed this text more carefully, would have confirmed the sense and explanation of the Protestants.

units.la: {B}ernardus in Epist. 183. reuera ex hoc loco Apostoli [Omnia anima] Conrado Duci suadet Pont. Romano Reverentiam exhibere; qui idem {b}Bernardus (teste etiam vestro Espencæo) in Epist. 42. ad Henricum Senonensem Archiepiscopum ex ijsdem Apostoli verbis [Omnis anima &c.] sic colligit; Si omnis anima subdita sit supereminentibus authoritatibus, tum vestra, quis vos excipit ab vniuersitate? si quis tentat excipere, tentat decipere. Nolite acquiescere consilijs eorum &c. Hæc ex Bernardo: cætera, quæ apud Bernardum sequuntur, quæq; Espencæus omisit, huiusmodi sunt. Qui quum sint Christiani, Christi tamen vel sequi facta, vel obsequi dictis opprobria dicunt: ipsi sunt qui dicere solent, Audite Pontifices, seruate vestra sedu[?] honorem, si non crescat per vos, non decrescat per vos. hæc ipsi; sed Christus aliter iussit, & gessit: Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, & quæ sunt Dei Deo: quod ore loquutus est, mox opere implere curauit, conditor Cæsaris Cæsari non cunctatus est reddere censum. Exemplum enim dedit vobis, vt & vos idem faciatis. — plurimum se vobis deferre isti putant, quùm vos Christo præferre conantur; sed Ioh. 13. Non est seruus maior Domino suo, neque Apostolus eo qui misit eum. Hactenus Bernardus.
units.tr: {B}ernard, in Epistle 183, indeed from this passage of the Apostle, [Every soul], urges Conrad the Duke to show reverence to the Roman Pontiff; and the same {b}Bernard (as your own Espencaeus also attests), in Epistle 42 to Henry, Archbishop of Sens, draws the following conclusion from the same words of the Apostle, [Every soul, etc.]: "If every soul is subject to the higher authorities, then who excepts you from the universal rule? If anyone tries to except you, he tries to deceive. Do not give assent to their counsels," etc. These are Bernard's words. The rest that follows in Bernard, which Espencaeus left out, is of this kind: "Although they are Christians, they say that to follow the deeds of Christ or to obey his words is a reproach. They are the ones who are accustomed to say, 'Hear, Pontiffs, preserve your seat's honor; if it does not grow through you, let it not decline through you.' These are their words;" but Christ ordered and acted otherwise: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." What he spoke with his mouth he soon took care to fulfil in deed; the founder did not hesitate to render the tribute to Caesar. For he gave you an example, that you too should do the same. — These men think they show you great deference when they try to put you before Christ; but John 13: "The servant is not greater than his lord, nor the apostle greater than him who sent him." Thus far Bernard.

units.la: An iam contentus eris testimonio vnius Bernardi tui; vel potius nihil minus quam tui? ipsius enim Lutherus, aut Caluinus, si reuiuiscerent, non possent Pontificum causam magis conuellere; non, primo, Pontificiorum ingenium describere peritius; quibus nihil est solennius quam Papis & Episcopis suadere, vt in contemptum Principum Honorem suum seruent; secundo non subiectionem, Principibus ab Episcopis debitam, fortius probare aut neruosius, quam demonstrando Christum hanc Subiectionem Apostolis præcepto exemploque suo imposuisse atque iniunxisse; Tertiò non Pauli sententiam enucleatius explicare, quam docendo in vniuersali signo [Omnis anima] Archi-episcopi, adeoque etiam Pontifices, etiam Apostolum comprehendi; Quartò non deniq; Bellarminum ipsum acrius corripere, quam afferendo Eos, qui Ecclesiasticas personas ab hac vniuersalitate, vz.[Omnis anima subdita &c.] excipere tentant, tentare decipere.
units.tr: Will you now be content with the testimony of your one Bernard; or rather with nothing less than your own? For if Luther or Calvin were to come back to life, they could not overthrow the cause of the Pontiffs more thoroughly: not, first, could they describe the character of the Papists more skilfully, for nothing is more customary for them than to urge Popes and bishops to keep their honor by scorn of princes; second, could they prove more forcefully or vigorously the subjection owed by bishops to princes than by demonstrating that Christ imposed and enjoined this subjection on the Apostles by his precept and his example; third, could they explain the sentence of Paul more clearly than by teaching that in the universal sign [Every soul] the archbishops, and therefore also the Pontiffs, even the Apostle himself, are included; fourth, and finally, could they rebuke Bellarmine himself more sharply than by asserting that those who try to except ecclesiastical persons from this universality, namely [Every soul is subject, etc.], try to deceive.

units.la: Hic fortasse quispiam haesitabit, quaeretque quum unus hic Bernardus non unus sit, sed tam dispar sibi, & plane diversus, cui potius fides habenda? dicam, potius Bernardo Textum defixis, quam obliquis oculis intuenti: nam in Epistol. ad Conradum Bernardus Textum obiter tantum aspiciens, praetermisso sensu, ad verba tantum allusit: At in illa, ad Archiepiscopum Senonensem, in versando tractandoque Textu sedulo immoratur: Addo, non Bernardo tantum dicenti, sed facienti quoque, & sententiam suam {*}factis comprobanti. Ut taceam, ex priore expositione Bernardum exigere a Principibus Reverentiam erga Episcopos, quam nos quoque deberi confitemur: at ex posteriori sensu ab Episcopis erga Principes obedientiam & subiectionem efflagitat. Haec de uno Bernardo, nunc de multis illis Patribus.
units.tr: Here perhaps someone will hesitate, and will ask, since this one Bernard is not one but is so unlike himself and plainly inconsistent, to which of him credit should rather be given. I shall say: rather to the Bernard who looks at the text with fixed eyes than to the one who looks at it with sidelong glances. For in the Epistle to Conrad, Bernard, glancing at the text only in passing, neglecting the sense, merely alludes to the words; but in that to the Archbishop of Sens he lingers diligently over the handling and treatment of the text. I add that he is not only speaking as Bernard, but also acting, and confirming his opinion by his deeds. To say nothing of this: by the former explanation Bernard demands from princes reverence towards bishops, which we too confess ought to be owed; but by the latter sense he demands from bishops obedience and subjection towards princes. So much for this one Bernard; now for the many Fathers.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Patres illos multos, quos citari posse ait Bellarminus, in contrarium plane sententiam abiisse.
units.tr: That the many Fathers whom Bellarmine says can be cited have plainly gone over to the opposite opinion.

units.la: AD probandam Eminentiam Pontificiu[?] super Reges, ais, praeter Bernardum, Patres multos produci posse: sed qui illi fuerint, prudenter nos celas, vel astutè potius. nam quotquot in expositionem istius Apostolici Canonis [Omnis anima] &c. (de quo supra Bernardus) inciderunt, Ecclesiasticos universos, adeoque Pontifices ipsos saecularibus potestatibus subiici uno quasi ore conclamarunt. Hoc verius esse, quam ut negari queat, testabitur Espencaeus vester. {c}Turbulenti quidam, (inquit) motâ inter regnum & Sacerdotium controversiâ, mirum quot quantasq; turbas utrinque dederunt: atqui tot post Paulum, tot ante hanc Camarinam annorum centenarijs, & Chrysostomus ut nihil unquam futurum tale suspicans, simpliciter illud, [Omnis anima subdita sit &c.] enarrat; Omnè, inquit, etiamsi sine Apostolus, siue Propheta, siue Sacerdos, siue Monachus. quem illic sequuntur Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, & qui non Graeci? Deinde (reste Pererio Iesuitâ) {d}Augustinus in epist. ad Macedonium hoc loco, atque omnes fermè veteres intellexerunt Paulum hic loqui TANTVM de seculari potestate. Haud aliter Ambrosius; nec, quod sciam, antiquioris notæ Pater quispiam. Nemo igitur non videat haud temerè esse, quod ex omnibus veteribus Patribus Bellarminus in Vno duntaxat etiam sequioris ætatis (quanquàm hoc quoque satis infeliciter) Patre Bernardo instet atque insistat.
units.tr: You say that, besides Bernard, many Fathers can be brought forward to prove the pre-eminence of the Pontiff over kings. But you prudently, or rather craftily, keep quiet about who they are. For all who have come upon the exposition of that famous apostolic canon, Omnis anima etc. (which Bernard discussed above), have with one voice declared that all churchmen, and the Pontiffs themselves, are subject to secular powers. That this is truer than can be denied will be attested by your own Espencaeus. "Some troublemakers," he says, "when the controversy between kingdom and priesthood was stirred up, caused wonderful and great disturbances on both sides. Yet so many centuries after Paul, and so many centuries before this Camarina, Chrysostom, as if suspecting nothing of the kind would ever happen, expounds that passage simply: Omnis anima subdita sit etc. 'Every soul,' he says, 'whether it be an apostle, or a prophet, or a priest, or a monk.'" Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius and all the other Greeks follow him. Then (rightly, says your Jesuit Pererius) "Augustine in his letter to Macedonius, and almost all the ancients, understood that Paul is speaking here ONLY of secular power." Ambrose understood it in no other way, and, so far as I know, no Father of older standing did either. Therefore no one can fail to see that it is not without reason that Bellarmine, out of all the ancient Fathers, insists and persists on the one Father Bernard, who is only of a later age, and even he, as it happens, quite unluckily.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Spiritus Sancti Præcepto, de subiectione Omnis animæ, omnes etiam Ecclesiasticos necessario constringit.
units.tr: The precept of the Holy Spirit, that every soul be subject, binds necessarily all churchmen as well.

units.la: QUùm sint ex Aduersarijs, qui licet concedant Apostolum eo in loco loqui {e}Tantùm de potestate seculari, idque contextum disputationis, & verborum Apostoli seriem indicare; respondent tamen {f}Rationem, ob quam vult Apostolus parendum esse potestati seculari, multò maximè competere in Ecclesiasticam potestatem: nempè hanc, [Non est potestas nisi à Deo,] vt hoc pacto vim Obiectionis eneruent. Arctius igitur à nobis vrgendi sunt, & validioribus viribus ad confessionem veritatis cogendi.
units.tr: Among your side there are some who, although they grant that the Apostle is speaking there only of secular power, and that the context of the discussion and the sequence of the Apostle's words show this, nevertheless reply that the reason why the Apostle wants obedience paid to secular power applies much more strongly to ecclesiastical power: namely this, [There is no power but of God], so that in this way they may blunt the force of the objection. We must therefore press them more closely, and compel them with stronger arguments to confess the truth.

units.la: In disputatione Apostoli tria potissimùm veniunt consideranda; occasio, propositio, conclusio. Pererius Ief. occasionem fusè explicauit, {g}Fuisse nimirùm nonnullos primis illis Ecclesiae Catholicae temporibus, qui falsò arbitrantes & docentes exemptos esse homines Christianos seculatibus & ciuilibus legibus, & liberos ab obedientiâ & subiectione magistratuum & Principum secularium, quòd Dominus dixisset, [si filius vos liberauit, verè liberi eritis] Iohan.8. & rursus, de tributis loquens, ait; [filij sunt liberi] Matth.17. hanc paucorum hominum falsam[?] sententiam & doctrinam Christianorum vniuersam gentem reddidisse Ethnicis omnibus inuisam & exosam, & maledictis atque conuitijs obnoxiam: Quinetiam (Chrysostomo authore) parùm[?] rumorem percrebuisse, Apostolos ipsos, & praedicatores Euangelij esse nona-
units.tr: In the Apostle's argument three things chiefly must be considered: the occasion, the proposition, and the conclusion. Pererius the Jesuit has explained the occasion at length. "There were, namely, in those first times of the Catholic Church, some who falsely supposed and taught that Christian men were exempt from secular and civil laws, and free from obedience and subjection to magistrates and secular princes, because the Lord had said, [If the Son has made you free, you will be free indeed] (John 8), and again, speaking about tribute, he said, [the children are free] (Matt. 17). This false opinion and teaching of a few men made the whole Christian people hated and detested by all the heathen, and exposed to curses and insults. Indeed (according to Chrysostom) a rumour spread that the apostles themselves, and the preachers of the gospel,

units.la: {g} Idem ibid. nonatores, atque ad euertendas leges ciuiles omnia dicere & facere. Ut itaque hoc scandalum auferrent tum in Concionibus, tum in Epistolis suis valde laborabant in docendo & persuadendo homines Christianos, propter fidem & religionem à Christo suscepta, non esse immunes ac liberos à praestando obedientiam, & tributa Regibus, & Principibus. Haec ille. Ratio igitur, cur Apostolus hortatus est omnes Christianos obedientiam & subiectionem Politicis Magistratibus praestare, haec fuit, nè Eorum sibi odium conflarent, quasi essent ab Illorum Dominio liberi atque immunes. At (nam hac Ratione Aduersarij è latebris, velint nolint, extrahantur) Ethnici aequè in Christianos Ecclesiasticos atque in Laicos authoritatem sibi suo iure vendicabant. {h}Apostoli igitur argumentum ordinem vtrumque necessitate subiectionis pariter deuinxit.
units.tr: were innovators, and said and did everything to overthrow the civil laws. Therefore, in order to remove this scandal, both in their sermons and in their letters they worked hard to teach and persuade Christian men that, on account of the faith and religion received from Christ, they were not immune and free from paying obedience and tribute to kings and princes." So he. The reason, then, why the Apostle exhorted all Christians to pay obedience and subjection to the political magistrates was this: lest they should incur the hatred of these rulers, as if they were free and exempt from their dominion. But (for by this reasoning the adversaries must be dragged out of their hiding places, whether they like it or not) the heathen claimed authority by their own right over Christian churchmen as well as over laymen. The Apostle's argument therefore bound both orders equally by the necessity of subjection.

units.la: Sequitur Propositio [Non est potestas nisi à Deo] quam occasio ipsa satis per se interpretatur, nempè (vt erudite admodum Caietanus) {i}Licet sententia haec solitaria vera sit, vniuersalissimè accepta; ad propositum tamen Pauli non est, nisi arctata ad potestatem, de qua est sermo, hoc est, ad praecellentem; nempè Principum secularium. Haec ille, Quibus Principum potestatem simpliciter praecellentem vocat, etiam tum cum cõferatur in æquilibrio alia potestas quæcunque. Ad Conclusionem descendamus.
units.tr: There follows the proposition, [There is no power but of God], which the occasion itself sufficiently explains by itself, namely (as the learned Cajetan says): "Although this statement taken by itself is true and is understood in the most universal sense, nevertheless it is not, for Paul's purpose, except as restricted to the power of which he is speaking, that is, to the pre-eminent power, namely that of secular princes." So he. He calls this the power of princes that is simply pre-eminent, even when some other power is weighed against it on equal terms. Let us come to the conclusion.

units.la: Conclusio ipsa, [Omnis anima potestatibus subdita sit:] ad quam enucleandam, ex Societate Iesuitarum, Expositorem Salmeronem intromittamus. {k}Ad hunc Pauli locum (inquit), & Expositorum sensum praedictum dicendum est quòd potestas Ethnici principatus, nondum Ecclesiæ incorporata, subditos habet omnes, quia ad eam Remp. cui praesident, tanquàm membra pertinent, siue Ethnici, siue Christiani, siue Clerici, siue Episcopi, siue Apostolici: & hoc ex iure naturæ, vt modo Turcarum Principes supra Christianos, & Principes, qui suis locis resident. Eodem modo {l}Costerus Iesuita. Et Conclusionem nostram de Subiectione Sacerdotum erga Principes {m}Espencæus multis persequitur.
units.tr: The conclusion itself, [Let every soul be subject to the powers], is to be unfolded, and for this we shall bring forward as expositor Salmeron of the Society of Jesus. "On this passage of Paul (he says), and on the sense of the expositors mentioned, it must be said that the power of a heathen princedom, not yet incorporated into the Church, has all its subjects, because they belong to the commonwealth over which they preside, as its members, whether they are heathen, or Christian, or clergy, or bishops, or apostolic men. And this is by the law of nature, as is the case now with the princes of the Turks over Christians, and with princes who reside in their own places." In the same way "Costerus the Jesuit." And our conclusion, concerning the subjection of priests to princes, Espencaeus pursues at length.

units.la: Deinde per hunc locum obstructus est vobis omnis aditus ad commune illud {*}vestrum ἀποστασίου[?], nefariarum seditionum, proditionum, praefidiaeque plenum: quo docetis, vestros Catholicos teneri quidem Obedire Infidelibus, & haereticis Principibus, Subditos suos à fide abstrahentibus, sed tantum DONEC RESISTENDI VIRES HABUERINT. Siccine Paulum fuisse, & tam doctos dolos in sancto pectore versasse? siccine Petrum fuisse versipellem? absit à nobis haec vecordia, vel blasphemia potius. Paulus, [Omnis anima, inquit, superioribus potestatibus subdita sit;] vocem, Animam, per synecdochen, pro homine poni, nemo ignorat: at Ratio, cur hoc in loco Anima pro homine sumatur (ut vestrum Thomam consulamus) haec est, " Quia subiectionem debemus ex animo{n}: vel (ut plenius Card. Caietanus) ut intelligeremus non solum res nostras, aut corpora nostra, sed etiam Animas debere subiici Principibus secularibus, in iis, quae possunt legitime imperare. Quod distertius docet Apostolus, vbi addit, [Necesse est subiici, non tantum ob iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam.] {p}Nomen conscientiae (inquit Pererius) vsurpat Scriptura, vbi agit de peccato mortali, non autem vbi de veniali. ---- Ambrosius exponit, non solum timore praesentis poenae, sed propter conscientiam futuri iudicij.
units.tr: Furthermore, through this passage every access is blocked to your common apostasy [ἀποστασίου], full of wicked seditions, treasons and ambushes, by which you teach that your Catholics are indeed bound to obey unbelieving and heretical princes who draw their subjects away from the faith, but only as long as they have the strength to resist. Was Paul really like this, and did he harbour such skilful deceit in his holy breast? Was Peter really so crafty? Far be it from us, this madness, or rather blasphemy. Paul says, "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers". That the word soul is put for the man, by synecdoche, no one is ignorant. But the reason why soul is taken here for the man (to consult your Thomas) is this: "Because we ought to pay subjection from the heart"; or (as Cardinal Cajetan says more fully) "so that we might understand that not only our goods or our bodies, but also our souls, ought to be subject to secular princes, in those things which they can lawfully command." The Apostle teaches this more plainly where he adds: "It is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath, but also for conscience' sake." "The name of conscience" (says Pererius) "Scripture uses where it deals with mortal sin, but not where it deals with venial sin." ---- Ambrose explains it: not only from fear of present punishment, but for conscience' sake, from fear of future judgement.

units.la: Quibus autem decretum est, quamprimum vires nacti fuerint, in rebellionem erumpere, Illi profecto (qui aduersarium virium maiorum metu duntaxat, non Conscientiae religione repressi) Principibus suis non humanam, nedum Christianam, sed prorsus belluinam subiectionem exhibent. Hoc enim certe ferarum est; quae conclusae nimirum & constrictae parcunt seque submittunt, rupto autem repagulo in Dominos involant. At Psalmista prohibet Nos similes esse bestiis, quae fræno chamoq;[?] cohibende: & S. Paulus, ut huiusmodi occultae simultatis ac dissimulationis suspicionem omnem ex Principum Ethnicorum animis radicitus evelleret, universos Christianos ad subiectionem praestandam Conscientiarum (quo nullum est arctiùs, nullum sacratiùs) vinculo obstrinxit : [ Omnis anima &c. ] ⁴Id est, ac si diceret {*} sanctus Paulus (ait Salmeron Ief.) non turbentur Principes, Reges, aut Imperatores, neque seuiant in Christiani nomine Professores, quia nihil innouauit præceptor meus Christus, quo ladat eorum potestatem, cælestia prædicans, terrens contemnens ; nec eripit mortalia, qui regna dat cælestia. Hæc Ille.
units.tr: But as for those who have decided to break out into rebellion as soon as they have gained strength, such men (who are restrained from resisting greater powers only by fear, not by religious conscience) render to their princes not a human subjection, let alone a Christian one, but a utterly brutish one. For this is truly the way of wild beasts, which, when shut in and bound, spare and submit themselves, but when the barrier is broken, fly at their masters. The Psalmist forbids us to be like beasts, which must be restrained with bit and bridle. And St Paul, so that every suspicion of such hidden enmity and pretence might be torn up by the roots from the minds of heathen princes, bound all Christians to the paying of subjection by the bond of conscience (than which nothing is tighter, nothing more sacred): [Omnis anima etc.] "That is, as if he said: 'Let not princes, kings or emperors be troubled, and let not the professors of the Christian name rage, because my teacher Christ has introduced nothing which harms their power; he preaches heavenly things, he does not frighten or despise earthly ones, nor does he snatch away mortal things, he who gives heavenly kingdoms.'" So he.

units.la: Antequam aliò pergamus, Bellarminus rursus compellandus est, sæpè à nobis monitus, multùmque monendus vt suis præsidiis diffidat, nec ea testimonia obijciat, in quibus plerunque non solùm ab Authoribus, quos citat, sed etiam à seipso citante refutatur. Cuius ofcitantiæ specimen iam præbet, dicit enim {+}Paulum Eiuverbis [Omnis anima potestatibus præeminetibus subditi sit] generaliter loqui hortarique vt omnes subditi suis Superioribus pareant tàm spiritualibus quàm temporalibus : ex qua sententia (inquit) non potest deduci Papam subiectum esse Regi, nec Regem Papæ. Hæc Bellarminus. Disputo. Hæc Apostoli Propositio de subiectione erga sublimiores potestates vel generaliter accipienda est, de quauis potestate sublimiori ; vel spiritualiter de subiectione erga potestatem secularem. Si generaliter, & tamen (vt ais) Regem Papæ subiectum esse non probat ; tùm erras planissimè, dum afferis ex hoc {*}Docerì eminentiam potestatis Pontificiæ super potestatem Regum & Principum terrenorum : nam verba Apostoli disertissima sunt, [Omnis anima sublimioribus potestatibus subdita sit.] Sin verò Paulus specialiter intelligit Potestates seculares, tùm Papa subijcitur Impp. quia dicitur, [Omnis anima sublimioribus potestatibus subdita sit :] nisi forsan exanimem faciatis Papam. Annon vtroque cornu confoderis? Hactenùs de loco Pauli; ad Bernardum reuertor.
units.tr: Before we proceed further, Bellarmine must be addressed again, often warned by us, and much to be warned that he should distrust his own defences, and not bring forward those testimonies in which he is for the most part refuted, not only by the authors whom he cites, but also by himself while citing them. He already gives a sample of this carelessness, for he says: "Paul in these words, [Let every soul be subject to the higher powers], speaks generally and exhorts that all subjects obey their superiors, both spiritual and temporal; from this opinion (he says) it cannot be deduced that the Pope is subject to the king, nor the king to the Pope." So Bellarmine. I argue. This proposition of the Apostle concerning subjection to higher powers must be taken either generally, of any higher power; or spiritually, of subjection to secular power. If generally, then, though (as you say) it does not prove that the Pope is subject to the king, you are quite plainly in error when you assert from this that the eminence of the papal power over the power of kings and earthly princes is taught: for the Apostle's words are most explicit: [Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.] But if Paul means specifically secular powers, then the Pope is subject to the emperors, because it is said: [Let every soul be subject to the higher powers], unless perhaps you make the Pope soulless. Have you not impaled yourself on both horns? So far concerning Paul's passage; I return to Bernard.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: « Dixit (inquis) Bernardus; [Exhibendam esse reuerentiam summa & Apostolicæ Sedi, & B. Petri Vicario, sicut (inquit) ipsam vobis vultu ab vniuerso serua[?]ri Imperio.] Quorsum hæc? Ex his docetur quæ sit eminentia potestatis Pontificum super potestatem Regum.. — pag. 36.
units.tr: « You say Bernard said: "The reverence due to the supreme and Apostolic See and to the Vicar of St Peter is to be shown, as he says, by the whole empire, in your sight." To what purpose are these things? From these things it is taught what is the eminence of the power of the Pontiffs over the power of kings. » Page 36.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: {p}Quatenus vero? Vt deponant eos (inquit alibi) quamprimum vires habeant. Sic Bellarminus; ubi personas quatuor commemorat, tanquàm partim Authores, partim Patronos, aut saltem assertores & vindicatores istius. (uti {*}dixit) Eminentis Pontificiæ potestatis supra potestatem Principum terrenorum: Bernardum, Pontificem Petri successorem, Petrum Vicarium Christi, & Petri Dominum: Christum Iesum. A quibus singulis (si accuratius paulo res ipsa pensitetur) Causam Regiam propugnari, Pontificiam verò penitus profligari facilè videbimus.
units.tr: To what extent, though? That they depose them, he says elsewhere, as soon as they have the strength. So Bellarmine, where he names four persons as partly authors and partly patrons, or at least assertors and defenders, of the eminent papal power over the power of earthly princes (as he puts it): Bernard, the Pontiff, successor of Peter; Peter, the Vicar of Christ; and the Lord of Peter, Jesus Christ. If we weigh the matter a little more carefully, we shall easily see that the royal cause is defended by each of these, and the papal cause utterly overthrown.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: S. Bernardum Potestatis Regiæ Assertorem esse satis lu- culentum.
units.tr: That St Bernard is a sufficiently clear assertor of royal power.

units.la: Bernardum ut virum {f}Mirabilem, & veluti quoddam in terris Sydus merito agnoscimus: nam in atra quasi nocte Rom. Ecclesiæ ferè solus effulsit Bernardus, qui tam doctrinæ, quam vitæ suæ lumine, cum in aliis multis, tum in hoc, de fidelitate ergà Reges, dogmate tenebras vestras dispulit. De doctrina {**}accepimus; Praxin experiamur. De hac Baronius historiam prolixam habet. Summa est, {t}Honorium Pont. ob persecutionem à Ludovico Francorum Rege illatam Episcopo Parisiensi, Sanctum Bernardum è Claustro protraxisse, qui de Causa illa inquireret, & de causa cum Rege pugnaret; ut patet ex
units.tr: We rightly acknowledge Bernard as a wonderful man and, as it were, a star on earth. For in the dark night of the Roman Church he almost alone shone forth, who by the light of his teaching and of his life, both in many other matters and in this one, concerning the doctrine of fidelity toward kings, dispelled your darkness. We have received his teaching; let us test his practice. Baronius has a lengthy account of this. The sum is that Pope Honorius, because of the persecution inflicted by Louis, King of the Franks, on the Bishop of Paris, drew St Bernard out of his cloister, to inquire into that cause and to contend with the King over it, as appears from

units.la: Epist. 46. Bernardus igitur, re explicata, aduersus Regem Ludouicum literas declaratorias dedit ad Papam Honorium, in quibus significat {a}Regem illum non tàm Episcopos, quam in ipsis iustitiae zelum persequi; &, veluti {x}alterum Herodem, Christum non in incunabilis, sed in Ecclesiis inuidere exaltatum. Nunc quo genere Pugnæ aggressus sit Regem (Baroni) explica. Bernardus (inquis) consurgit in Regem Ludouicum scribens ad eum literas (Epist. 221) vbi ait, Profecto stabimus, & pugnabimus vsque ad mortem, si ita opportuerit, pro matre nostra, ARMIS QVIBVS LICET, NON SCVTIS ET GLADIIS, SED PRECIBVSQVE APVD DEVM. Haec omnia apud Baronium; qui quùm multis paginis, à Bernardo exsumptis, sua volumina infarserit, Epistolam tamen eius CLXX. ad eundem Regem Ludouicum prudens sciensque omisit: in qua Bernardus, {y}Si totus Orbis (ait) aduersus me coniuraret, vt quippiam molirer aduersus Regiam maiestatem, ego tamen Deum timerem, & ordinatum ab eo Regem offendere temerè non auderem: nec enim ignoro vbi legerim, ] QVI POTESTATI RESISTIT, DEI ORDINATIONI RESISTIT.] Post multa, perorans dicit; Hoc sentite de nobis, hoc sentite de nostris, non infringetur veritas in nobis, non imminuetur honor Regis Regnique vtilitas per nos. Haec Bernardus. Quid verò hac Bernardi Apologià, pro Regis temporali honore & securitate, etiam quùm maximum Pontificis in Regem odium exarserat, liberius, disertius, constantiusque dici potuit? Quotusquisque (Bellarmine) vestrorum Abbatum, Episcoporum, Cardinalium, hac præsertim tempestate, tale aliquid vel hiscere audeat? vae illi, si auferit. Haec de Bernardi sententia; nunc de Pontificum iudicijs.
units.tr: Epist. 46. Bernard therefore, having explained the matter, gave a declaratory letter against King Louis to Pope Honorius, in which he signifies that that king persecutes not so much the bishops as the zeal for justice in them; and, like another Herod, envies Christ exalted not in the cradle but in the churches. Now, Baronius, explain with what kind of fight he attacked the king. Bernard (you say) rises up against King Louis, writing him a letter (Epist. 221), where he says: "Surely we shall stand and fight, even to death if need be, for our mother", WITH WHATEVER ARMS ARE LAWFUL, NOT WITH SHIELDS AND SWORDS, BUT WITH PRAYERS BEFORE GOD.
