All this is in Baronius; but although he has stuffed his volumes with many pages taken from Bernard, he knowingly and deliberately omitted Bernard's letter CLXX to the same King Louis. In it Bernard says: "If the whole world were to conspire against me, so that I should devise anything against the royal majesty, I would nevertheless fear God, and would not rashly dare to offend the king he has ordained. For I do not forget where I have read: WHOEVER RESISTS THE POWER RESISTS THE ORDINANCE OF GOD." After much, concluding, he says: "Think this of us, think this of ours: the truth will not be broken in us, nor will the honour of the King or the good of the kingdom be diminished through us." These are Bernard's words. But what could be said more freely, more clearly, or more steadfastly, in defence of the king's temporal honour and security, than this apology of Bernard, even when the Pontiff's hatred against the king had blazed most fiercely? Which of your abbots, bishops or cardinals, Bellarmine, would dare to whisper anything of the kind, especially in these times? Woe to him if he should. So much for Bernard's opinion; now for the judgements of the Pontiffs.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: {u} Bernardus Pontificem Petri Vicarium nominat, non quod non sit Christi Vicarius, sed quòd Vicarium pro successore acceperit: nam in secundo libro de Consideratione aperte vocat eundem Pontificem potestate Petrum. — pag. 36.
units.tr: Bernard calls the Pontiff the Vicar of Peter, not because he is not the Vicar of Christ, but because he took "Vicar" to mean successor: for in the second book of De Consideratione he openly calls the same Pontiff Peter in power. Page 36.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Ex undecim Titulis (ut Tibi videntur) Papæ proprijs hic Vicarius Christi sextus ponitur; unde Primatum Pontificis in Episcopos & Principes universos colligi existimas.
units.tr: Of the eleven titles proper to the Pope (as they seem to you), the Vicar of Christ is placed here as the sixth; whence you think the primacy of the Pontiff over all bishops and princes is to be inferred.

units.la: I. AINMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Pontifices Rom. Petro meritis ac doctrinâ dispares atq; dis- cordes, eidem Successores haut aptè constitutus.
units.tr: The Roman Pontiffs, unlike and discordant with Peter in merits and doctrine, are not aptly set up as his successors.

units.la: QUòd Bernardus vocaverit Pontificem Petri Vicarium, Bellarmino ægre est; proinde Bernardus (interprete Bellarmino) Vicarium pro Successore accepit: fortasse quia nimirum Bernardus non vidit omnia. Cui Tu facilè ignosces, qui nosti Illum canonicè errasse: nam {a}In Canone (inquis) Ego Ludovicus, distinct. 63. Romanum Pontifex Petri Vicarius dicitur. Quatenus verò Petri Successorem Papam esse Bernardus censuerit? Vocat (inquis) Pontificem potestate Petrum: Et Papam, licet inferiorem meritis, tamen iure successionis potestate Petro parem esse, tanquam Pontificiæ Eminentiæ basis{b} proponitur. Hoc tamen simpliciter verum vix credidit, opinor, Baronius tuus, qui ex suis historiis refert{c} Sanctum Petrum in forma terribili Papæ cuidam apparuisse, atque ei (quod Balsamum suo altari destinatum vendidisset) elato brachio colaphum vehementer incussisse. quod si inter dispares bellum incidat, ut contigit Diomedi cum Glauco, hos Tu potestate pares dixeris?
units.tr: That Bernard called the Pontiff the Vicar of Peter is grievous to Bellarmine; so, on Bellarmine's reading, Bernard took "Vicar" to mean successor. Perhaps Bernard, of course, did not see everything. You will readily pardon him, since you know that he erred by the canon law: for "In the canon, Ego Ludovicus, distinction 63, the Roman Pontiff is called the Vicar of Peter," you say. But as for whether Bernard judged the Pope to be the successor of Peter? He calls the Pontiff Peter in power, you say; and the Pope, though inferior in merits, is put forward as equal to Peter in power by right of succession, as the basis of papal eminence. Yet I suppose your Baronius scarcely believed this to be true without qualification, he who relates from his histories that St Peter appeared to a certain Pope in a terrible form and, with his arm raised, struck him a violent blow on the cheek, because he had sold a balsam destined for his altar. But if a battle breaks out between unequals, as happened to Diomedes with Glaucus, would you call these two equal in power?

units.la: De Successionis iure quanta est Adversariorum nostrorum deliratio, qui semper in Petro Papam, & vicissim in Papa Petrum se videre iactitant? quùm præsertim ex multiplici collatione satis constet; Petro Papam (si mores Eorum quis respiciat, vtpote animam reprehensionis patientem) {d}Humili {e}Tetricum: si quotidianam vitæ consuetudinem, Sancto {f}Flagitiosum: si erga Principes obedientiam, Subiecto {g}Tyrannum: si munus Pastoritium, siue in Conc. Generalibus comparendo, {h}Ambidanti {i}Claudum; siue in disceptandis fidei causis, accuratè & maturè {k}Considerati {l}Precipitem: siue etiam enunciationem Euangelij (quod est præcipuum Pastoris officij:) {m}Loquenti {n}Mutum: si denique potestatem non errandi in fide, aut quoad personam publicam, {o}Orthodoxo {p}Hæreticum; aut quoad priuatam, {q}Beato {r}Damnatum successisse. Vt nihil hic dicam de Labyrinthis difficultatum, quibus Successionis huius Assertores (sed heri) se extricabant.
units.tr: What great folly is it among our adversaries, who keep boasting that they always see Peter in the Pope and, conversely, the Pope in Peter! This is especially so since from many comparisons it is quite clear that the Pope has succeeded Peter in the following ways. If one looks at their morals (for the soul is open to reproof), Peter was humble and the Pope stern; if one looks at daily life, Peter was holy and the Pope shameful; in obedience to rulers, Peter was subject and the Pope a tyrant; in the pastoral office, whether one looks at appearing in general councils, Peter was ambidextrous and the Pope lame; or in deciding questions of faith, Peter was accurate and mature in considering, the Pope precipitate; or again in the proclamation of the Gospel (which is the chief duty of a pastor), Peter spoke and the Pope is mute; and finally, if one considers the power of not erring in faith, whether as a public person or as a private one, Peter was orthodox and the Pope heretical, or Peter was blessed and the Pope damned. Not to mention here the labyrinths of difficulties in which the defenders of this succession (only yesterday) were entangling themselves.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Papæ potestatem neque quà unctus, neque qua Vicarius vl- lo modo stabiliri.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSIO. That the power of the Pope cannot be established in any way, either as anointed or as Vicar.

units.la: Nulla vspiam honoris syllaba ab vllo Patre Pontifici cuiquam attributa est, quam non Tu, tanquam ad supremam illam Pontificis eminentiam super omne genus Christianos stabiliendam, arripis statim obuijsque vlnis ampleCteris[?]: atque hoc animo Papam simul Vicarium Christi, simul Unctione Christum autumas; sed quam non apte? Si enim apud Te reputares, quibus hominum ordinibus, quàmque vario respectu Vicarius conueniat, facilè intelligeres Eminentioris potestatis Pontificiæ Argumentum nullum ex his elici posse. Non ex titulo hoc [Vicarius Christi,] qui enim potest? Papa est (inquis) Successor Petri. Quasi vero aut Petrus inter Apostolos solus Christi Vicarius fuerit (hoc veter Aquinas negabit, apud quem Apostoli omnes & Discipuli erant Christi Vicarij:) Aut Christi (Qui ad mortem suam nunquam cessauit prædicare) Vicarius Papa sit, qui iamdiu prædicare desijt. Verius
units.tr: No syllable of honour that any Father has ascribed to any Pope is left unseized by you, and you rush to embrace it with open arms, so as to establish that supreme eminence of the Pope over every kind of Christian. In this spirit you claim that the Pope is at once Vicar of Christ and Christ by anointing. But how aptly? If you considered within yourself which orders of men a vicar may belong to, and in how many different respects, you would easily see that no argument for a higher papal power can be drawn from these titles. Not from this title, [Vicar of Christ], for who can it fit? The Pope is, you say, the successor of Peter. As if Peter alone among the Apostles were Christ's Vicar (Aquinas will deny this, for in his view all the Apostles and disciples were Christ's Vicars); or as if the Pope were the Vicar of Christ, who never ceased to preach until his death, while the Pope has long ceased to preach. More truly

units.la: bat.
units.tr: ...was speaking.

units.la: {n} Papa iamdiu penitus siluit.
units.tr: The Pope has long been wholly silent.

units.la: {o} Talis Petrus imbutus spiritu veritatis.
units.tr: Such was Peter, filled with the Spirit of truth.

units.la: {p} Qualis Papa Honorius, & alij.
units.tr: Such was Pope Honorius, and others.

units.la: {q} Beatus Simon, Mat.16.
units.tr: Blessed Simon, Matt. 16.

units.la: {r} Non-nullus Papa. Verius multò Eius Vicarij, qui munere suo funguntur, Principes haberi debent. quippe ni? Imperator Christianorum (vt ait Cusanus Cardinalis) in sua praesidentia Christi Vicarius, qui Rex Regum, & Dominus Dominantium, exiit: unde sicut Christus est Rex Regum, ita omnes Reges in potestate regnantis domini quid Divini habent; quapropter Reverentia & Obedientia eis debetur. Necnon Bellarminus Cardinalis; Considerauimus (inquit) Principem Christianum, vt Vicarium in temporalibus Dei Regis magni. Haec ille.
units.tr: Not any Pope. Far more truly, his Vicars, who discharge his office, ought to be regarded as princes. For indeed, the Emperor of the Christians (as Cusanus the Cardinal says) in his presidency is the Vicar of Christ, who came forth as King of kings and Lord of lords; hence, just as Christ is King of kings, so all kings have something divine in the power of the reigning lord; therefore reverence and obedience are owed to them. Likewise Cardinal Bellarmine: We have considered the Christian prince as Vicar of God the great King in temporal matters. So he.

units.la: Secundo Titulo, quo nimirum Pontifex à Bernardo Vnctione Christus dicitur, forsan plus praesidij inest; vel potius multò minus: non enim vocauit Pontificem potestate Christum: absit! imò distinctionis vigore hoc negat; Potestate Petrum (inquit,) Vnctione Christum: non tamen quoad Diuinam illam Eminentiam Vnctionis, & Supra mensuram, quam Christus habuit; sed quoad participationem & similitudinem. Quà quidem significatione Sacerdotes legis veteris Prophetas; sub lege Euangelica Apostolos, Episcopos, Sacerdotes, Reges, & Regeneratos Christianos quoslibet Christos dicere licuit. In quo Iesuitas, aliosque Doctores Pontificios nobis assentientes habemus. Exempli causa, Primò, de Lege Veteri. Moses Aaronem Pontificem primus Christum nominauit. — Externae Vnctiones notae erant, vt sciremus eos, qui Divino Spiritu afflati essent, sine terrestri Vnguento Christos appellari: vnde Propheta Dauid Psal. 104. agens de Abraham, Isaac, & Iacob, qui ante Mosen fuerant, & ante indicatam ab eo Vnctionem (videlicet externam) eos propter Divini Spiritus, cuius participes erant, influentiam Christos appellauit. [Nolite tangere Christos meos.] Ita Sacerdotes, & Prophetae, & Reges non à visibili oleo, sed ab inuisibili, ante Vnctionem olei visibilis, Christi dicti sunt. Ad nouum Testamentum spectat illud, Psal 45. 7. de Christo dictum, [Vnxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo exultationis prae participibus tuis:] Vbi Participes, iuxta Hieronymum, Apostolos, credentes significat,
units.tr: In the second title, by which the Pontiff is called Christ by Bernard in respect of anointing, there is perhaps more support, or rather far less: for he did not call the Pontiff Christ in power; far from it. Indeed, by the force of a distinction, he denies this: Peter in power, he says, Christ in anointing; yet not with respect to that divine eminence of the anointing, and beyond measure, which Christ had, but with respect to participation and likeness. In this sense it was permitted to call the priests of the old law and the prophets, and under the Gospel law the Apostles, bishops, priests, kings, and any Christians who have been born again, Christs. On this point we have the Jesuits and other Papist teachers agreeing with us. For example, first, from the Old Law: Moses first named Aaron, the high priest, Christ. External anointings were known, so that we might understand that those who were inspired by the Divine Spirit are called Christs without earthly ointment; hence the prophet David, Psalm 104, speaking of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who lived before Moses and before the anointing enjoined by him (that is, the external one), called them Christs because of the influence of the Divine Spirit of which they were partakers. [Touch not my Christs.] So priests, prophets and kings were called Christs, not from visible oil but from invisible oil, before the anointing of visible oil. To the New Testament belongs that passage, spoken of Christ in Psalm 45:7, [God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows], where Fellows, according to Jerome, signifies the Apostles, the believers,

units.la: {u} Cusan. Concord. Cath. lib. 3. cap. 5. pag. 787. c.ut[?], quibus Vnctionis sua vocabulum tribuit, vt ab vncto vncti[?], a Christo Christiani. Quippè{b} Nomen Christi, ex vi significationis, commune est, Reges & Sacerdotes significans, qui oleo vngebantur; & inde deductum est, ad significandos iustos & sanctos, quos gratia Dei vngit. Hæc de Papa, quatenus communiter vel potiùs æquiuocè Christi Vicarius. Atque hactenus de Titulo; nunc ab eis Sacerdotibus, quos dicitis Vicarios Christi, Reuerentiam atque obsequium deberi Christi Pro-regibus & Vicarijs secularibus, probandum, Primò, ex Testimonijs ipsorum Vicariorum tàm spiritualium, quàm etiam Temporalium. Primò de Pontificibus.
units.tr: Cusanus, Concordantia catholica, book 3, chapter 5, p. 787, to whom he attributes the name of anointing, so that from the anointed come the anointed, and from Christ the Christians. For the name of Christ, by the force of its meaning, is common, signifying kings and priests who were anointed with oil; and from this it was derived to signify the just and holy, whom the grace of God anoints. So much for the Pope, insofar as he is commonly, or rather equivocally, the Vicar of Christ. And so far concerning the title. Now, that reverence and obedience are owed to those priests whom you call Vicars of Christ, and to the secular vice-kings and vicars of Christ, is to be proved first from the testimonies of the vicars themselves, both spiritual and temporal. First, from the Popes.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO. Causam Regiam demonstrari ex suffragijs Pontificum (per .xxx. Annorum curriculum) qui Reuerentiam Impe- ratoribus vltrò professi sunt.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSIO. That the royal cause is demonstrated from the votes of the Popes (over the course of three hundred years), who freely professed reverence toward the emperors.

units.la: Pontificijs in hac Controuersia sumus nos, fateor, verè Aduersarij, sed tamen tàm æquo erga illos animo sumus, & in Causæ nostræ firmitatem tàm fideliter incumbimus, vt totam hanc quæstionem, de Eminentia & potestate Pontificum in Principes sanctissimorum, Pontificum ipsorum iudicijs dirimendam desinendámque libentissimè permittamus; sed tamen antiquorum illorum, qui vitæ iuxta doctrinæque integritate claruerunt. Quorum examen Pontificij effugere non debent, siquidem (vt præ se ferunt) veri Catholici esse velint. Duo sunt, quæ authoritate horum efficere conamur; Primum est, Imperatoribus fidelitatem, reuerentiam, obedientiam à Pontificibus deberi. Alterum, potestatem Imperatoriam ad negotia etiam Ecclesiastica necessariò se extendere.
units.tr: I admit that with the Papists we are truly adversaries in this controversy; yet we are so fair-minded toward them, and so faithfully devoted to the firm establishment of our cause, that we most willingly allow the whole question, concerning the eminence and power of the Popes over princes, to be settled and ended by the judgments of the most holy Popes themselves; but of those ancient ones who were distinguished for the integrity of their life and doctrine. Papists ought not to escape their scrutiny, since (as they profess) they wish to be true Catholics. We try to establish two things by their authority. The first is that fidelity, reverence and obedience are owed by the Popes to the emperors. The second is that imperial power must necessarily extend even to ecclesiastical affairs.

units.la: Primis post Christum Annis trecentis inter Pontifices à S. Petro, vsque ad Miltiadem Papam, fuerunt numero viginti septem, qui sub Nerone, Domitiano, Decio, Diocletiano, alijsque immanissimis Tyrannis exquisitissimis tormentis trucidati Martyrij gloriam consequuti, {c}Nibil vnquàm studio nouarum partium contra infideles Principes quacunque moliti sunt, etiam quùm (vt aliquando accidit) pares viribus erant. Tunc illi, ex toto ordine Monachorum, nullum Iacobum Clementem; ex genere Clericorum, nullum Garnettum; ex Laicorum turba, Rauilliacum, Catesbeyum, aut Fauxium omnino nullum ad Imperatorum atrocissimam rabiem vel ferro, aut flammâ, aut vllâ machinatione coërcendam concitârunt: quippè dogma hoc pijssimum, vt veluti Christianæ religioni proprium professi & venerati sunt, quod Petrus & Paulus Omni anime præceperunt, necessario subjici oportere potestatibus secularibus. Hæc de Fidelitate.
units.tr: In the first three hundred years after Christ, from Saint Peter to Pope Miltiades, there were twenty-seven Popes. Under Nero, Domitian, Decius, Diocletian, and other most savage tyrants, they were slaughtered with the most exquisite torments and obtained the glory of martyrdom. They never, by any zeal, attempted any novel scheme against unbelieving princes, even when (as sometimes happened) they were equal in strength. Then they stirred up from the whole order of monks no James Clement; from the class of clergy no Garnet; from the crowd of laymen no Ravaillac, no Catesby, or no Fawkes at all, to check the most atrocious rage of the emperors either by sword, or fire, or any device. For they professed and venerated this most pious doctrine as if it were proper to the Christian religion: that Peter and Paul, in Let every soul, commanded that it is necessary to be subject to secular powers. So much for fidelity.

units.la: Post inclytam hanc sanctissimorum Pontificum cohortem, qui sub Christo Imperatore in militia Christiana de mundanis hostibus beatam victoriam reportantes, fidelitatem suam erga Ethnicos Imperatores vitâ, morteque sua testatissimam fecerunt; sequitur aliorum Pontificum veluti Sacro-Sancta Synodus, qui in suis ad Imperatores literis summam erga illos reuerentiam obedientiámque professi sunt. In quorum testimoniis recensendis temporum ordinem obseruabimus, prout à vestro Seuerino Binio difertissimè traditur.
units.tr: After this famous band of most holy Popes, who under Christ as Emperor, in the Christian warfare, won a blessed victory over worldly enemies, and by their life and death bore the most convincing witness to their loyalty toward the heathen emperors, there follows a long line of other Popes, as it were a most holy synod, who in their letters to the emperors professed the highest reverence and obedience toward them. In reviewing their testimonies we shall observe the order of time, as it is most clearly set out by your Severinus Binius.

units.la: Anno ccclii. Liberius I. Papa ad Constantium Imperatorem; {d}Opto, (inquit) tranquillissime Imperator, vt benignas aures mihi Clementia tua tribuat, quo possim mansuetudini tuae mentis meae propositum aperire: in eo me laborare intelligo, quòd repetitâ satisfactione animam tuam in gratiam meam reuocare non possum; firmo enim tamen me quidem, quem PACIENTER OMNIA FERRE NECESSE EST, plurimùm lacerat. Nisi igitur ad exorandam mansuetudinem vestram Lucciferum Coepiscopum meum &c.
units.tr: In the year 352, Liberius I, Pope, to the Emperor Constantius: I wish, most tranquil Emperor, that your clemency would grant me kindly ears, so that I may open to your gentleness the purpose of my mind: I understand that I am labouring in this, that by repeated satisfaction I cannot bring your soul back into my favour; for I am firmly held, whom it is necessary to bear everything patiently, and who is grievously torn. Unless, therefore, to beg your gentleness, my fellow bishop Lucifer etc.

units.la: Anno ccccxl. Leo I. Papa, Pastoralis Iurisdictionis, quoad ista ætas tulit, assertor vehementissimus, in Epist.26.ad Pulcheriam Augustam; SUPPLICATIONEM NOSTRAM (inquit) ad clementiss. Principem digneris afferre. Et rursus, Epist. 35. ad Eudoxiam Augustam; SUPPLICITER (inquit) postulauí &c. Deinde Epist.65.{1} idem Leo literas dat ad Leonem Augustum. En! Leones duo congrediuntur; alter spiritualis, politicus alter, quis cui cedat, si quis ambigat, ex formula praefationis coniecturam faciat, in qua sic Leo Papa; Literas Clementiae tuae veneranter accepi, quibus cuperem OBEDIRE, sed magis id vobis arbitror placiturum. &c. Obserua, Obedientiam non detrectat, qui magis vult obedire Ei, cui potiore ratione placere satagit.
units.tr: In the year 440, Leo I, Pope, the most vehement champion of pastoral jurisdiction as far as that age allowed, in Epistle 26 to Pulcheria Augusta: OUR SUPPLICATION, he says, you would deign to bring before the most merciful Prince. And again, Epistle 35 to Eudoxia Augusta: HUMBLY, he says, I have asked, etc. Then Epistle 65, the same Leo writes to Leo Augustus. Behold! Two Leos meet: one spiritual, the other political. If anyone doubts which yields to which, let him make a guess from the form of the preface, in which Pope Leo writes thus: I have received your Clemency's letters with reverence, by which I would wish to OBEY, but I think it will please you more. etc. Observe: he does not refuse obedience who is more eager to obey him whom he strives to please on stronger grounds.

units.la: Anno cccclxvii. Simplicius I. Papa Epist. 4. ad Leonem Imp.{f} Ea devotione, qua Principes Christianos iugi veneratione suscipio, cupio debita Pietati vestrae officia deferre, — ut simul Honorificentiam vestram promptâ mente persoluam. — Clementiae vestrae propensius Coepiscopus meus Acatius meâ vice supplicabit.
units.tr: In the year 467, Simplicius I, Pope, Epistle 4 to Leo, Emperor: With the devotion with which I receive Christian princes in continual reverence, I desire to offer the duties owed to your Piety, — so that at the same time I may pay your Honour with a ready mind. — My fellow bishop Acacius will beg on my behalf more earnestly of your Clemency.

units.la: - Anno ccccxxciii. Felix III. Papa Epist. 2. ad eundem Imp.{g} Honorificentiam tuam precor, ut SUPPLICATINEM MEAM Princeps Christianus benigne accipias auribus.
units.tr: In the year 493, Felix III, Pope, Epistle 2 to the same Emperor: "I beg your Honour that, as a Christian Prince, you kindly lend your ears to MY SUPPLICATION."

units.la: Anno cccxcii Gelasius I. Papa Epist. 5. Anastasio Imp.{h} Legibus tuis ipse quoque PARENT religionis Antistites.
units.tr: In the year 392, Gelasius I, Pope, Epistle 5, to Anastasius the Emperor: "The bishops of religion themselves also OBEY your laws."

units.la: Anno cccxcvi Anastasius I.Papa 78.ad Epist.Anastasium Imp.{i} Humilis pietati tuae PRECATOR occurro. — praecelsum PIETATIS tuae vocabulum per vniuersas gentes toto Orbe prefulget. Et deinde Epist. 5.{k} Ad literas vestras, & MANDATA respondi. Et rursus Epist. 78. ad Iustinum Imp.{l} Ipsam tibi Ecclesiam Deimecum SVPPLICARE.
units.tr: In the year 396, Anastasius I, Pope, Epistle 78, to Anastasius the Emperor: "I come before your piety as a humble SUPPLICANT. Your exalted name of PIETY shines throughout all nations in the whole world." Then, Epistle 5: "I have answered your letters and COMMANDS." And again, Epistle 78, to Justin the Emperor: "The Church of God itself SUPPLICATES you together with me."

units.la: Anno Domini Ilv[?]. Pelagius I. Papa Epist. 16. ad Childericum Francorum Regem; {m}Regibus Nos (vz. Episcopos) SUBDITOS esse Sacra Scripturae praecipiunt. Quibus verbis {n}Pelagium Subiectionem suam Regibus debitam esse testari, vester Tholosanus asseuerat.
units.tr: In the year 511 (?), Pelagius I, Pope, Epistle 16, to Childeric, King of the Franks: "Sacred Scripture commands that we (that is, the bishops) be SUBJECT to kings." Your Tholosanus asserts that by these words Pelagius testified that the subjection owed to kings was his own.

units.la: Anno Domini Ixc[?]. Gregorius I. Papa lib. 4. Epist. 31. ad Mauritium Imp.{o} In Serenissimis IUSSIONIBUS DOMINORUM meorum pietas vestra mihi minimè pepercit. Et lib. 4. Epist. 32. Serenissime Domine, quod quidem ad me attinet, Serenis. IUSSIONIBUS OBEDIENTIAM praebeo.
units.tr: In the year 590 (?), Gregory I, Pope, book 4, Epistle 31, to Maurice the Emperor: "In your most serene COMMANDS to my lords, your piety has not spared me at all." And book 4, Epistle 32: "Most serene lord, as far as I am concerned, I render OBEDIENCE to your most serene COMMANDS."

units.la: Anno DCXLIX. Martinus I. Papa Epist. 3. ad Constantinum Imp. {p}Domino pissimo, & Serenissimo Martinus Episcopus, seruus seruorum Dei, & uniuersa Synodus in hac urbe Romae congregata. Nos ad pietatem vestram confugientes, ORANTES, atque hortantes vestram Serenitatem, ut hac diligenter legere dignetur.
units.tr: In the year 649, Martin I, Pope, Epistle 3, to Constantine the Emperor: "To the most pious and most serene lord, Martin, bishop, servant of the servants of God, and the whole synod gathered in this city of Rome. We, fleeing to your piety, ENTREATING and exhorting your Serenity, that you deign to read these things diligently."

units.la: Anno DCCXIX. Agatho I. Papa ad Heraclium, & Tiberium Augg. {q}Domini Serenissimi, secundum pissimam missionem vestram pro OBEDIENTIA, quam debuimus, praesentes confamulos nostros curauimus demandare, proquibus FLEXO MENTIS POPLITE SUPPLICITER vestram mansuetudinem & Clementiam deprecamur.
units.tr: In the year 719, Agatho I, Pope, to Heraclius and Tiberius Augusti: "Most serene lords, in accordance with your most pious mission, and for the OBEDIENCE we owe, we have taken care to send our fellow servants who are present, and for whom, with MINDS BOWED ON BENDED KNEE, we humbly beseech your gentleness and clemency."

units.la: Anno DCCXXCI[?]. Hadrianus I. Papa Epist. ad Constantinum, & Irenen. {r}Domini pissimi, deprecantes Clementiam vestram, tanquam praesentialiter HUMO STRATUS, ET VESTRIS VESTIGIIS PROVOLUTUS, QUAESO &c.
units.tr: In the year 791 (?), Hadrian I, Pope, Epistle to Constantine and Irene: "Most pious lords, entreating your clemency, as if present, PROSTRATE ON THE GROUND, and FALLEN AT YOUR FEET, I ask, etc."

units.la: Anno DCCXCVI. Leo III. Papa (ut vult Aimonius) {f}Postquam Carolum coronauerat, & Imperatorem creauerat, spectante populo ipsum voluit ADORARE, ut agnosceret scilicet populus quanti esset Imperatoria maiestas.
units.tr: In the year 796, Leo III, Pope (as Aimonius says): after he had crowned Charles and made him Emperor, he wished to ADORE him in the sight of the people, so that the people might know how great the imperial majesty was.

units.la: Hucusque, Lector, septingentorum plusquam annorum spacium percurri; nec maiorem cohortem Testimoniorum mihi referre nunc visum, ut satietati tuae occurram; nec tamen minorem libuit, ne utilitati tuae desuisse viderer. Quorum scribendi stylum,& formulam, qua Obedientiam suam tantâ cum humilitate,& Reverentia erga Imperatores, tanquam Dominos suos, profitentur, si cum formulis succedentium Papārum comparaueremus (in quibus isti Imperatoribus ipsis, veluti Vasallis suis, minabundi, mandantes volentesq; sese Imperatores & Dominos esse oftentarunt) Ex hac una Nota, veluti ex infallibili Shibboleth, decernere est, quantum posteri Pontifices à Decessoribus suis, hâc in parte, degenerârint. Haec de TestiTestimonijs Pontificum antiquorum, quoad Reverentiam,& Obedientiam Imperatoribus debitam;sequuntur alia Eorum testimonia, quoad Causas, in quibus ius Regium exerceatur.
units.tr: Thus far, Reader, I have run through a span of more than seven hundred years. I have not thought it right to bring forward now a larger troop of testimonies, lest I weary you; nor did I wish to give fewer, lest I seem to have failed to serve your interest. If we compare the style and formula of their writing, in which they profess their obedience with such humility and reverence towards emperors as their lords, with the formulas of the popes who came after (in which those men, threatening and commanding the emperors themselves as if they were their vassals, showed themselves to be the emperors and lords), one may judge from this single mark, as from an infallible Shibboleth, how far the later popes have degenerated from their predecessors in this respect. These are the testimonies of the ancient Pontiffs concerning the reverence and obedience due to emperors. What follows are their other testimonies, concerning the causes in which royal right is exercised.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. REMARK.

units.la: Eosdem Pontifices, in Causis Ecclesiasticis, eandem obedientia- m Imperatoribus facitis quoque praestitisse.
units.tr: The same Pontiffs, in ecclesiastical causes, also rendered the same obedience to emperors.

units.la: QVum ipsis formulis Supplicationum Pontificum tanta vis insit, ut Lectorem non pertinaciter obstinatum ad subiectionem obedientiamque Eorum Imperatoribus debitam agnoscendam cogat; tum sane multo magis Adversarij nostri ex Causis Supplicandi revincuntur. Causarum vero Ecclesiasticarum duplex est genus, alterum merum, alterum autem mixtum. Merum nos dicimus, quod Ordini Sacerdotali ita proprium est, ut à seculari Principe, absq; sacrilegio, exerceri aut contrectari nequeat; cuius generis est munus publicum verbum Dei praedicandi, Sacramenta administrandi, Sacerdotes ordinandi, fidei Causam iudicandi,& Sacerdotaliter ligandi, solvendiq;. Mixtum autem illud est, quod non proprie spirituale, sed spirituali annexum atq; adiunctum vocamus; nec in munere ipso Ecclesiastico, sed tantùm circa illud versatur. Ad hoc Caput reducuntur omnia illa Christiani Principis negotia publica, quae ad curam religionis (quod locum, tempus, personas tàm Ecclesiasticas, quàm seculares) pertinent; de quibus, ut instituti nostri ratio postulat, atque [?] fidei Pontificum iudicium consulere aequum censeo.
units.tr: Since the very formulas of supplication used by the Pontiffs carry such force that they compel a reader, unless he is stubbornly obstinate, to acknowledge the subjection and obedience due to emperors, then our adversaries are far more clearly refuted by the causes in which they supplicated. Now there are two kinds of ecclesiastical causes: one pure, the other mixed. We call a cause pure when it is so proper to the sacerdotal Order that it cannot be exercised or handled by a secular prince without sacrilege. Of this kind is the public office of preaching the Word of God, administering the sacraments, ordaining ministers, judging the cause of faith, and binding and loosing in a sacerdotal manner. But that is mixed which we call not properly spiritual but attached and joined to the spiritual; it is concerned not with the ecclesiastical office itself, but only with what lies about it. To this head are reduced all those public affairs of the Christian prince which pertain to the care of religion (whether as to place, time, or persons, both ecclesiastical and secular). Concerning these, as the plan of our undertaking requires, I think it fair to consult the judgment of the Pontiffs' faith.

units.la: Liberius I. Papa supplicabat, ut {t}iuberet Imperator, sicut ei placuerit, Conc. Aquilonense congregari: vtq; authoritate sui exulem Liberium Tristitiâ magnâ liberaret.
units.tr: Liberius I, Pope, begged that the Emperor would order, as he pleased, the Aquileian council to be gathered, and by his authority free Liberius, who was exiled, from great sadness.

units.la: Leo I. Papa Epist. 7. laudat Imperatorem, quod {a}“Non solum Regiam, sed etiam Sacerdotalem animam effenderet, quia nimirum, praeter Imperiales curas, piissimam curam religionis haberet. Idem etiam {z}semel, iterum, ac tertio Imperatoris beneuolentiam vehementer obtestatur, ut Is Vniuersale Concilium Sacerdotum haberi (etiam) intra Italiam iubeat. Et tandem, vbi intellexit præsentiam suam ad Synodum orientalem ab Imperatore requiri, rescribit Pontifex se Illius {y}MANDATIS OBEDIRE VELLE.
units.tr: Leo I, Pope, Epistle 7, praises the Emperor because he showed "not only a royal but also a sacerdotal soul, since, besides his imperial cares, he had a most pious care of religion." The same pope "once, twice, and a third time" earnestly entreats the Emperor's goodwill, that he would order a universal council of priests to be held (even) within Italy. And finally, when he understood that his presence was required by the Emperor at the eastern synod, the Pontiff replies that he is willing to OBEY his COMMANDS.

units.la: Bonifacius I. Papa ab Honorio Aug. petit vt in vrbe Roma nunquàm quis per ambitum Antistes ordinetur; rationémque subdit, quà Imperator, {z}Deo fauente, in humanis rebus diuinæ cultor religionis præsideat: subindeq, precatur, vt Is in perpetuum statui vniuersalis Ecclesiæ CONSVLAT.
units.tr: Boniface I, Pope, asks Honorius Augustus that no one be ordained bishop in the city of Rome by ambition. He adds the reason why the Emperor, with God's favour, presides over human affairs as a worshipper of divine religion; and then he prays that he would CONSULT for the perpetual state of the universal Church.

units.la: Celestinus I. Papa agnoscit Theodosium iuniorem, dum vniuersali Ecclesiæ consuleret, omnibus animarum suarum salutem reddidisse.
units.tr: Celestine I, Pope, acknowledges that Theodosius the younger, while he was providing for the universal Church, had rendered salvation to the souls of all.

units.la: Simplicius I. Papa Imp. Zenonem obnixè obsecrat {a}vt nefanda præsumptionis operarios (loquitur de quibusdam Episcopis) Regiâ censeat potestate COHIBERI.
units.tr: Simplicius I, Pope, earnestly beseeches the Emperor Zeno that the workers of unholy presumption (he speaks of certain bishops) be RESTRAINED by royal power.

units.la: Gelasius I. Papa, quamuis Imperatorem moneat, Eum {b}Subdi debere Præsulibus Ecclesiæ Religionis ordine in spiritualibus; tamen, quantum ad ordinem pertinet publicæ disciplinæ, agnoscit Imperium Ei Superna dispensatione collatum, EIVSQVE LEGIBVS PARERE RELIGIONIS ANTISTITES.
units.tr: Gelasius I, Pope, although he admonishes the Emperor that he ought to be subject to the prelates of the Church in spiritual matters, in the order of religion, yet, as far as the order of public discipline is concerned, he acknowledges that the empire was conferred on him by heavenly dispensation, and that the bishops of religion OBEY his laws.

units.la: Hormisda I. Papa Anastasio Imp. gratulatur. Primò, quòd {c}Curam principalis acuminis (sic enim loquitur) non tantùm in administranda Reip. exercere officio; sed melioribus eum nobilitaret institutis per curam redintegrandæ vnitatis. Secundò, FVTVRAM SYNODVM (inquit) Scriptis tuis Sacratissimis indicari MANDASTI, CVI Nos (viz. Papa) INTERESSE DEBERE eisdem paginis, Deo vt credimus Tibi imperante, commonuisti. Postremò Eum ad curam religionis obeundam hortatur sedulò; Assume FIDEI CVRAM, & sicut alter Ezechias exurge, ille simulacra contriuit, Tu dura infidelium corda confringe; ille memoriam serpentis æneí sustulit, Tu virus præsentis effunde &c. Hoc vult, vt Acatij Hæretici superbiam pessundaret.
units.tr: Hormisdas I, Pope, congratulates the Emperor Anastasius. First, because he exercises the care of his princely wit (for so he speaks) not only in the office of administering the commonwealth, but also ennobles it with better institutions through care for restoring unity. Secondly, "you COMMANDED the future synod to be announced by your most sacred writings, at which we (that is, the Pope) ought to be present, as you reminded us in the same pages, God, we believe, commanding through you." Lastly, he earnestly urges him to undertake the care of religion: "Take up the CARE OF FAITH, and, like another Hezekiah, rise up. He broke the images; you break the hard hearts of unbelievers. He removed the memory of the brazen serpent; you pour out the poison of the present age, etc." He does this to crush the pride of the heretic Acacius.

units.la: Gregorius I. Papa Mauritij Imp. legem, opinionę suâ iniustam, promulgat, hàc ratione adhibitâ; {d}Ego IUSSIONI VESTRAE SUBIECTUS, legem per diuersas terrarum partes transmitti feci: & quia ipsa omnipotens Deo minimè concordat, ecce sereniss. MEIS DOMINIS nunciaui; vtrobique igitur quod debui exsolui, qui & IMPERIO OBEDIENTIAM PRAEBUI, & quod sensi minimè tacui. Et, ad Theodosium, fatetur Deum concessisse Eum {e}Non solum militibus, sed etiam SACERDOTIBUS DOMINARI. Eodem ferè modo {f}Martinus I. & {g}Agatho I. PP.
units.tr: Gregory I, Pope, promulgates for the Emperor Maurice a law which in his own opinion is unjust, using this reasoning: "I, subject to your command, have caused the law to be sent through various parts of the lands; and because it in no way agrees with almighty God, behold, I have announced it to my most serene LORDS. So on both sides I have paid what I owed: I have rendered OBEDIENCE to the empire, and I have not kept silent about what I felt." And to Theodosius he confesses that God granted him to rule "not only over soldiers but also over PRIESTS." In almost the same way, Martin I and Agatho I, Popes.

units.la: Vt hæc omnia summatim perstringam. Concilium Episcoporum res quidem spiritualis est; At locum designare, aut Conc. congregare, siue particulare, vt Aquileiæ; siue vniuersale, vt Italiæ, Imperatoris est, qui authoritate suâ Iuberet; nec modo minorum gentium Episcopos; sed & summos Pontifices, Imperatoris iussa capessere parere[?] est, pròut ipsi Pontifices disertè fatentur. Exempli gratiâ, Obedientiam, sic Leo: Interesse debemus, sic Pelagius: Promulgando legem, iniquam licet, parere debeo, sic Gregorius: Quibus etiam, quoad externæ disciplinæ dispensationem; Antistites parere tenentur, sic Gelasius.
units.tr: To sum up all these things briefly: a council of bishops is indeed a spiritual matter, but to designate a place, or to convene a council, whether particular, as at Aquileia, or universal, as for Italy, belongs to the Emperor, who by his authority commands. And not only bishops of the lesser nations but also the supreme Pontiffs must carry out and obey the Emperor's commands, as the Pontiffs themselves plainly confess. For example: obedience, thus Leo; we ought to be present, thus Pelagius; in promulgating the law, though unjust, I ought to obey, thus Gregory. To these may be added Gelasius, who says that bishops are bound to obey as regards the dispensation of external discipline.

units.la: Nec sanè mirum, si Religiosi omnes Imperatoribus aliquo modo subijciantur, nisi Religione ipsâ religiosores existimari velint: nam Imperatoribus Religionis cura à Deo demandata est, vnde est, quòd in Christiano Principe Sacerdotalem animum Leo cerneret: quod ad Imperatorem idem Leo Religionis; Hormisda totius fidei; Celestinus omnium animarum Salutis curam pertinere confitentur.
units.tr: Nor indeed is it surprising that all religious persons should in some way be subject to emperors, unless they wish to be thought more religious than religion itself. For the care of religion has been committed to emperors by God; hence it is that Leo perceived a sacerdotal soul in a Christian prince; and that Leo, Hormisdas and Celestine acknowledge that religion, the care of all faith, and the care of the salvation of all souls, pertain to the Emperor.

units.la: Res hæc clarior est, quàm vt negari; & cum hàc Causa coniunctior, quàm vt vllâ Ingenij subtilitate eludi possit: quia quùm iam de summi Pontificis Eminentiâ super Reges (quod, vt nunc sunt mores, apud Pontificios Controuersiarum omnium caput summum est) disferatur; nos ad ipsos quoque Pontifices prouocare maximè cupimus. Ex quo ordine Aduersarij exempla obijciunt Eorum, qui potestatem suam[?] deponendis Principibus exercentes, in Repub. Christiana miras miseriasque tragœdias excitarunt: quibus Nos gloriosissimorum Christi Martyrum quasi agmen opponimus, ab exemplis eorum Pontificum, qui, inter atrocissimas persecutiones, nè tantillum moliti contrà Principes seculares res , {*}pijsimum hoc dogma tenentes parendi Magistratibus; atque ita suam in Christum fidem, simul & erga Reges fidelitatem sanguine suo obsignârunt. Illi Innocentium IV. Gregorium VII. Clementem VI. Bonifacium VIII. Leonem X. & huiusmodi Regum hostes infensissimos, & improbitatis notis maximè insignes nobis obtrudunt: Nos Liberium I. Leonem I. Anastasium I. Gregorium I. Gelasium I. & priscæ ætatis quoscunque alios, omnium iudicio, sanctissimos Pontifices produximus. Illi, pro Pontificia eminentia, in Pontificibus vilioris Notæ ac nominis Quartis, Sextis, Septimis, Octavis, & nonnunquàm Decimis; Nos, ad Regiam authoritatem asserendam in Pontificibus Primis institimus: ita vt, de veritate amplius dubitare, nihil aliud sit, quàm in clarissima luce cœcutire. Hæc de Papa-rum ipsorum iudicijs.
units.tr: This matter is clearer than to be denied, and so closely bound up with this cause that no subtlety of wit can evade it. Since the eminence of the supreme Pontiff over kings is being debated (which, as things now stand, is the chief of all the controversies among the Papists), we are especially eager to call the Pontiffs themselves to account. From this same line of argument, our opponents cite examples of those who, exercising their power to depose princes, stirred up wondrous and wretched tragedies in the Christian commonwealth. Against these we set, as it were, the glorious host of the most glorious martyrs of Christ, and against the Papists' examples we set those Pontiffs who, amid the most savage persecutions, attempted nothing at all against secular princes, holding fast to this most pious doctrine of obedience to magistrates, and so sealed with their blood both their faith in Christ and their fidelity to kings. The Papists thrust upon us Innocent IV, Gregory VII, Clement VI, Boniface VIII, Leo X, and others of this kind, the most bitter enemies of kings and especially notorious for wickedness. We have brought forward Liberius I, Leo I, Anastasius I, Gregory I, Gelasius I, and whatever other most holy Pontiffs of earlier times, by the judgment of all. The Papists, in the name of "papal eminence," press Pontiffs of lesser repute and name, the Fourths, Sixths, Sevenths, Eighths, and sometimes Tenths; we, in asserting royal authority, insist on the First Pontiffs. So that to doubt the truth any further is nothing else than to be blind in the clearest light. So much for the judgments of the Popes themselves.

units.la: V. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: V. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Imperatorum authoritatem tam ex nominum, in Decretis, præscriptione; quàm ex Eorum, in Concilijs præsi- dentia[?] demonstrari.
units.tr: The authority of emperors is shown both from the order of their names in the Decrees and from their presidency in the councils.

units.la: QVùm quæcunque hactenùs à Bellarmino prolata fuerè, ad {*}Eminentiam potestatis Pontificiæ super Reges probandam, tanquàm ad scopum proprium collimént omnia; idcirco operæ-pretium duximus (postquàm à Sanctissimorum Pontificum Generalis, quasi, Synodi suffragijs Causam obtinuimus) postremo in loco, veluti ad Cæsaris tribunalia provocantes, vtrum hæc dignitatis authoritatisque Eminentia Principibus tribuenda sit; id est, vtrùm Principibus Reuerentia ac obedientia à Pontificibus debeatur, ex Principum Christianorum rebus gestis [illegible, ~3 letters] experiri.
units.tr: Since everything that Bellarmine has so far put forward aims, as at its proper target, at proving the eminence of papal power over kings, we have thought it worth the effort (having won the cause, as it were, by the votes of the most holy Popes and their general synod) to take up, last of all, as though appealing to Caesar's tribunal, the question whether this eminence of dignity and authority is to be attributed to princes; that is, whether the Pontiffs owe reverence and obedience to Christian princes, and to test this by the deeds of Christian princes [illegible].

units.la: Ad Pontificæ dignitatis Eminentiam efferendam, duobus imprimis Argumentis veteris; I. Sacerdotis (inquis) nomen præponitur nomini Principis. II. Præsidentia Loci in Concilijs Episcopis concedebatur. Pro priore in Iosuæ cùm Eleazari Sacerdotis; pro posteriore, in Constantini Magni cùm Conc. Niceni Episcoporum collatione infisitis: & in utroque exemplo videris Tibi Eminentiam Pontifici debitam, non tantùm Reverentiæ, sed & Authoritatis intueri. Quibus ipsissimis Argumentis (vt sint per se validissima) Te iam, Bellarmine,à fronte adoriemur.
units.tr: To raise up the eminence of the pontifical dignity, Bellarmine relies chiefly on two arguments from the Old Testament: (1) "the title of priest," you say, "is placed before the title of prince"; (2) "the place of presidency in the councils was granted to the bishops." For the former you cite Joshua together with Eleazar the priest; for the latter, the arrangement of the bishops at the Council of Nicaea with Constantine the Great. In both examples you see an eminence due to the Pontiff, not only of reverence but of authority. We shall now attack you, Bellarmine, head on with these very arguments, strong as they are in themselves.

units.la: Pro Iure præpositurae hominis, contenti esse debemus exemplo Honorÿ Imp. in scriptione literarum ad Bonifacium Papam: præsertim quùm omnes Pontifices Rom. (inter quos Alij erant honoris sui importuni nimis atque molesti exactores) illud decretorum suorum monumentis dignum censuerint. Inscriptio est hujusmodi, Victor HONORIVS, inclytus, Triumphator, semper Augustus Sancto venerabili BONIFACIO Papæ. Unde Glossa; Præmisit Imperator nomen suum, quia fortè hæc consuetudo erat olim. Spissum verbum hoc [fortè,] nam Imperatores in Inscriptionibus nomina sua præponere certè quidem consueuerunt: sic Valentinianus, & Martianus Impp. VALENTINIANVS, & MARTIANVS gloriosi Triumphatores, semper Augg.— LEONI Reuerendissimo Archiepiscopo gloriosæ civitatis Romæ. Sic Iustinus Hormisdæ. Sic Iustinianus Iohanni. Nusquam etiam apud veterum Imperatorum vllum (quantum recordatione vltimâ repetere possum) exemplum aliquod contrarium memini. Ita vt Consuetudo, in nominibus suis præponendis, facilè significet Imperatores Pontificibus, si non superiores, at saltem minimè inferiores fuisse.
units.tr: As for the right of precedence belonging to the man, we ought to be content with the example of the Emperor Honorius in the address of his letters to Pope Boniface, especially since all the Roman Pontiffs (among whom there were some overly troublesome and burdensome exactors of their own honour) thought it worthy of a place in the records of their decrees. The inscription runs as follows: Victor HONORIUS, inclytus, Triumphator, semper Augustus Sancto venerabili BONIFACIO Papae. Hence the Gloss: "The emperor placed his own name first, because perhaps this was the custom of old." The word fortè ("perhaps") is a thin one here, for emperors certainly were accustomed to put their own names first in inscriptions: so Valentinian and Martian, emperors: VALENTINIANUS and MARTIANUS, glorious triumphers, ever Augusti; to Leo, most reverend archbishop of the glorious city of Rome. So Justin to Hormisdas; so Justinian to John. Nowhere among the ancient emperors, so far as I can recall from my most recent reading, do I remember any contrary example. So the custom of placing their own names first readily shows that the emperors were, if not superior to the Pontiffs, at least in no way inferior.

units.la: Multò maioris momenti est Consuetudo præsidentiæ in Concilijs, præsertim Episcoporum. Exemplorum accumulatione hic nihil est opus, habemus enim Bellarminimum hoc non obscurè confitentem : à quo quùm quæritur, quare Papa Rom. antiquis Conc. generalibus personaliter interesse noluerit, Ille ( siste, quæso te, Lector, & vel ad punctum temporis auscul ta) respondet ; {e}Vna ratio fuit, (inquit) quia in Conc. orientalibus, ubi semper interfuit Imperator, Graci Imperatorem in summo loco collocabant ; ergo, ad vitandum tumultum, ipse Papa non ibat, sed tantùm Legatos mittebat. Hæc ille. Nihil profectò cordatus quispiam quæret amplius, præsertim si quibus, & quantis in Concilijs, per quot Patres, per quos Principes in summo loco supra Pontifices, collocandi potestas fuerit, diligentius expendatur.
units.tr: The custom of presidency in the councils, especially of the bishops, is of far greater weight. There is no need here for a pile of examples, for we have Bellarmine himself not obscurely confessing this. When he is asked why the Roman Pope was unwilling to attend the ancient general councils in person, he answers (stop here, I beg you, Reader, and listen for a moment): "One reason was that in the eastern councils, where the emperor was always present, the Greeks placed the emperor in the highest place; therefore, to avoid tumult, the Pope himself did not go, but sent only legates." So he says. Surely no thoughtful person will ask anything further, especially if one weighs more carefully in what and how great councils, through how many Fathers, and through which princes, the power to place someone in the highest place above the Pontiffs was exercised.

units.la: Primò Concilia illa Orientalia, nempè Nicænum I. Constantinopolitanum I. Ephesinum I. Chalcedonense I. si ætatem quis velit, Antiquissima fuerunt ; si solemnitatem, Generalissima ; si authoritatem, reverà ea, quæ Gregorius I. Papa, & post Eum Pontifices, & Patres vniuersi, veluti Quatuor Dei Oracula, venerati sunt. Hæc sunt Concilia, in quibus Papa ipse, (si præsens adfuisset, & præsidentiam affectâsset) proculdubiò grandem tulisset repulsam. Secundo istorum Conciliorum Patres Nicæa cccxviii. Constantinopoli cl. Ephesi cc. Chalced. Ioexxx. [?] ex omnibus orbis Christiani accersiti, imprimis Orthodoxi Episcopi ; qui primum & summum locum Imperatoribus deferendum esse censuerunt. Postremo Imperatores, qui sese Pontificibus præponendos duxerant, non erant (vt Bozius fronte perfricta, linguaque quasi mercede astricta, & ad calumniam conducta loquitur) {f}Rebus Christianis nondum bene constitutis, nimio fastu inflati, & adhuc Gentium superbam spirantes : sed, qui tunc rerum potiebantur, numerantur Constantinus, Theodosius, Valentinianus, Martianus, Principes!( post hominum memoriam) religiosissimi ; quorum potissimùm cura & authoritate Resp. Christiana statim post profligatam atrocissimorum Ethnicorum tyrannidem, & perditissimorum Hæreticorum reticorum frastam [?] contusamque audaciam, cùm in summa pacis felicitate, tùm salutaris fidei integritate constituta est. Hæc de suprema Principum dignitate; sequitur de authoritate tàm Eorum, qui priscis ; quàm Illorum, qui posterioribus seculis regnárunt.
units.tr: First, those eastern councils, namely the First Council of Nicaea, the First of Constantinople, the First of Ephesus, and the First of Chalcedon. If anyone looks to their age, they were the most ancient; if to their solemnity, the most general; if to their authority, they are truly those which Pope Gregory I, and after him the Pontiffs and all the Fathers, venerated as the Four Oracles of God. These are the councils at which the Pope himself, had he been present and aspired to the presidency, would undoubtedly have met with a great rebuff. Second, the Fathers of these councils: 318 at Nicaea, 150 at Constantinople, 200 at Ephesus, 630 at Chalcedon, summoned from the whole Christian world, above all orthodox bishops, who judged that the first and highest place was to be granted to the emperors. Finally, the emperors who thought themselves set before the Pontiffs were not, as Bozius speaks with a brazen forehead, with a tongue bound as if for hire and enlisted for calumny, "Christian affairs not yet well established, puffed up with excessive pride, and still breathing the haughtiness of the Gentiles." Rather, those who then held power are counted: Constantine, Theodosius, Valentinian, Martian, princes (within human memory) most religious, by whose chief care and authority the Christian commonwealth was established, immediately after the overthrow of the most savage tyranny of the heathens and the audacity of the most abandoned heretics had been crushed, both in the highest felicity of peace and in the soundness of saving faith. So much on the supreme dignity of princes; there follows an account of the authority of both those who reigned in earlier ages and those who reigned in later ages.

units.la: VI. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: VI. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Priscos Imperatores Pontificibus ipsis authoritate & potest- ate eminuisse, ijsque [?] leges imposuisse.
units.tr: That earlier emperors excelled the Pontiffs themselves in authority and power, and imposed laws upon them.

units.la: INter Imperatores, qui priscis seculis Rempublicam Christianam sanctissimè felicissimèq; administrárunt, commemorari solent Constantinus, Theodosius, Honorius, Valentinianus, Gratianus, Iustinianus. Horū primus Constantinus Christianus Imp. idemq; verè Magnus, {*}Caussam Donati authoritate suâ Miltiadi Papæ examinandam commisit; cui alios quoque Episcopos, in eodem iudicio, Socios assignauit; &, post latam ab Illis sententiam, eandem Caussam Arelatensi Episcopo determinandam delegauit. In hac historia quot sunt Circumstantiæ totidem fere Argumenta occurrunt Eminentiæ Imperatoriæ super ipsum Pontificem.
units.tr: Among the emperors who governed the Christian commonwealth most holily and happily in earlier ages, the usual examples are Constantine, Theodosius, Honorius, Valentinian, Gratian and Justinian. The first of these, Constantine, a Christian emperor and truly the Great, committed the case of Donatus by his own authority to Pope Miltiades for examination, and assigned to him other bishops as assessors in the same judgment. After their sentence was pronounced, he delegated the same case to the bishop of Arles to be decided. In this history there are almost as many arguments for the imperial pre-eminence over the Pontiff himself as there are circumstances.

units.la: Theodosius, & Iustinianus de personis Ecclesiasticis omnibus (nec enim Papa excipitur) & de Eorum bonis & disciplinâ leges & Canones conscripserunt. hoc Bellarminum malè vrit, atque peturbat; Cui propterea videtur istos sanctissimos Imperatores {g}Hac in re seculariu, id est ,suæ potestatis limites egressos esse. At istis sanctiss. Imperatoribus, atque eiusdem ævi Pontificibus aliter videbatur, quandò {*}Leo Papa (frustrà licet) ab eodem Imperatore tàm obnixè humiliterque rogauit, vt Concilium(etiam) intra Italiam connocari authoritate Imperatoriâ mandaret.
units.tr: Theodosius and Justinian drew up laws and canons concerning all ecclesiastical persons (for the Pope is not excepted), and concerning their goods and discipline. This troubles and disturbs Bellarmine, and so he thinks these most holy emperors went beyond the limits of secular power, that is, of their own authority, in this matter. But to those most holy emperors, and to the Pontiffs of the same age, it appeared otherwise, when Pope Leo, though in vain, asked the same emperor so earnestly and humbly to order, by imperial authority, that a council be convened even within Italy.

units.la: Porrò Valentinianum, Gratianum, & Honorium, in præscribendis legibus, (nullâ habir'à [?] ratione Iuris Pontificij) viris Ecclesiasticis obedie.ndi necessitatem imponendo, parem authoritatem o[?]stendisse satis constat. In quorum rebus gestis non est quòd quis Authoritatis Eorum documenta insigniora expectet; quibus praesertim (excipiamus modò{*} exemplum illud Iustiniani, qui Siluerium Papam exilio mulctauit) ad Papas in ordine cogendos authoritate suam exercere tunc necesse non fuit, quùm adhùc Pontifices, vt viros verè Apostolicos decuit, religionem Euangelicam, pacemque politicam religiosè coluerint. At quam primum alia aetas mores alios inuexerat, tùm Principes ius suum saepè vindicâsse, & Coactiuam protestatem in Pontifices exprompsisse explorate cognoscimus; quod Exempla sequentia demonstrant.
units.tr: Moreover, it is quite clear that Valentinian, Gratian and Honorius, in prescribing laws (with no regard to Pontifical law), imposed on churchmen the necessity of obedience and showed equal authority. In their deeds there is no reason to expect the more striking proofs of their authority. Indeed, Pontiffs of that time had no need to exercise their authority to bring the Popes into line, since they still cultivated the Evangelical religion and political peace devoutly, as truly apostolic men ought. But as soon as a later age introduced other customs, we know well that princes often asserted their right and brought forth coercive power against the Pontiffs, as the following examples show.

units.la: VII. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: VII. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Eandem authoritatem succedentes Imperatores super Pon- tifices exercuisse.
units.tr: That the emperors who succeeded exercised the same authority over the Pontiffs.

units.la: Inter Imperatores familiam ducit Carolus Magnus Imp. in quo Baronius Card: videtur sibi {b}Dignum virtutum exemplar intueri, & religionis omnibus absolutum numeris simulachrum:---quem Paschalis Papa in numerum Sanctorum asciscit. Quid autem Carolus Imperator? Iter (inquis) Romam direxit; de inuestigandis criminibus, quae tùm Leoni III. obiiciebantur.---Tum in Ecclesia D. Petri fecit congregari Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, Abbates, omnesque nobiles; vbi sedentes pariter tàm magnus Rex, quàm beatissimus Pontifex, residebant etiam Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, Abbates: atque itâ crimina, quae aduersus Pontificem fuerant, examinantur. &c. Haec ille. In hoc igitur exemplo elucet & eminet Imperatoria Maiestas & authoritas super Pontificem, quem multis criminibus oneratum iudicij examen subire Imperator cogere potuit, imò debuit; vt Exemplum proximum demonstrat.
units.tr: Among the emperors, Charlemagne leads the way. Baronius the cardinal seems to regard him as a worthy pattern of virtues and a likeness completely perfect in every point of religion, whom Pope Paschal enrolled among the saints. But what did the emperor Charlemagne do? He went to Rome (you say) to investigate the crimes that were then charged against Leo III. Then he had the archbishops, bishops, abbots and all the nobles gathered in the church of St Peter, where, seated together, the so great king and the most blessed Pontiff presided, and the archbishops, bishops and abbots were also present; and thus the crimes that had been alleged against the Pontiff were examined, etc. So he writes. In this example, therefore, the imperial majesty and authority over the Pontiff shines out and stands forth: the emperor could, indeed ought to, compel him, burdened with many crimes, to undergo the examination of a court, as the next example shows.

units.la: Maius enim quiddam aggressus est Otho Imp. Anno domini IDccc.[?] qui Iohannem XII. Pont. deposuit, & Leonem VIII. substituit. Hoc (quo non occurrit ex omni historia Exemplum illustrius) Vos non mediocriter torquet: à quibus quaerimus, quid de Personis istis, Imperatore nimirùm deponente, & Pontifice deposito vobis videatur? I. de Imperatore. {i}Otho Germanorum primus (ait Bellar.) coronam Caesaream legitimè sibi traditam in Germaniam intulit; vir illo honore, ob celebrem pietatem, & raram in bellis felicitatem non indignus. II. Pontificem verò quo vos dignamini elogio? Tu; {k}Fuit iste Iohannes (inquis) omnium Pontificum fere deterrimus. Et Baronius tuus; {l}Iohannes Papa impiissimus, (inquit) quem omnes boni iure detestantur. Et cui iam ambigendum, iure-nè Imperator tàm pius (nam de facto constat) Pontificem tàm flagitiosum deposuerit? Haec, haec Causa est, in quà vnà summa ista Eminentia Pontificiae potestatis, super Principes, in discrimen adducitur. Tu igitur Bellarmine, Tuque Baroni, nobilissimum par Cardinalium, adeste Pontifici vestro, & Respondete; Rectenè, an secus Imp. vobis fecisse videatur? Age, Bellarmine, nam Responsum tuum, ut par est, priore loco deposcimus. {m}Constat bono zelo, sed non secundùm scientiam depositum fuisse Iohannem: fuit enim iste Iohannes omnium Pontificum fere deterrimus. Nec igitur mirum est, si pius Imperator, qualis fuit Otho primus, sed minùs peritus rerum Ecclesiasticarum, iudicaverit eum potuisse deponi, quàm multi Doctores idem senserint. {n}Sed sciendum est, quòd Otho non propriâ authoritate Iohannem deposuit, sed authoritate Concilij deponendum curavit; quod Conc. in multis erravit, nec tàm Concilium, quàm Conciliabulum fuit, & ideò paulò post abrogatum. Vide Baron. Tom. Annal. 10. ad Annum Domini 963. Vidi equidem (Bellarmine) Baronium vestrum, &, pro virili, perpendi, nec (vt verè fatear) responsis vestris calumniosius, futilius, repugnantius quicquam esse video.
units.tr: For the emperor Otto undertook something greater still, in the year 963, when he deposed Pope John XII and put Leo VIII in his place. This (for no more striking example occurs in all history) troubles you not a little. We ask you what you think of these persons: the emperor, namely, who deposed, and the Pontiff who was deposed? I. Concerning the emperor: Otto the First of the Germans (says Bellarmine) brought the imperial crown, lawfully handed to him, into Germany; a man not unworthy of that honour, on account of his famous piety and his rare good fortune in war. II. But what praise do you award the Pontiff? You (you say): This John, you say, was almost the worst of all the Pontiffs. And your Baronius: Pope John, most impious (he says), whom all good men rightly detest. And who can now doubt whether the emperor, so pious (for that is established as fact), was right to depose a Pontiff so disgraceful? This, this is the case in which alone that supreme eminence of papal power over princes is brought into danger. You, then, Bellarmine, and you, Baronius, most noble pair of cardinals, come to the aid of your Pontiff and answer: does the emperor seem to you to have acted rightly or otherwise? Come on, Bellarmine, for we demand your reply first, as is fitting. John was deposed with good zeal, but not according to knowledge; for this John was almost the worst of all the Pontiffs. Nor is it therefore surprising if a pious emperor, such as Otto the First, but less skilled in ecclesiastical affairs, judged that he could be deposed, as many teachers have thought the same. But it must be known that Otto did not depose John by his own authority, but took care that he be deposed by the authority of a council; which council erred in many things, and was less a council than a conciliabulum, and therefore was soon annulled. See Baronius, Tom. X of the Annals, at the year of the Lord 963. I have indeed looked at your Baronius (Bellarmine), and weighed him as far as I can; and (to speak truly) I see nothing more calumnious, more frivolous or more self-contradictory than your answers.

units.la: Tu videsis igitur, Baroni (nam Te huc BelIarminus[?] accersi voluit) quid de facto Othonis sentiendū statuas.{n} Indignum[?] Iudicium, & insolens factum! (inquis:) quid rei est? Canonum iura violantur. quo modo, obsecro? Concilium congregatum erat contra Pontificem, absque eius consensu. Nempe, hominem reum, etiam Impussimum[?], inuitum de Tribunali citare (Aduocato Baronio) facinus hui! insolens est: quo quid, quæso, futilius? Ecquid præterea? secundum est paucitas Testium {p}vbi enim(inquis) sufficiens Testium contra Pontificem numerus, quem septuaginta duorum esse oportet? Septuaginta duos testes in causa Papæ Marcellini adhibitos fuisse, non mirum, Is enim in Ethnicorum templis, dijs gentium thura adolendo, Idololatriæ crimen publicè ac ex professo perpetrabat. At in omnibus omnium Episcoporum causis, de tanto Spectatorum numero, Canonem sanciri, quæ Theologia docuit? quæ dictauit ratio? quæ necessitas postulauit? Quanquàm horum Aduocatorum vafritiam quis iure reprehendat, quòd talè Canonem exigant, quo posito atque sancito, Episcoporū, præcipuè vero Pontificum suorum existimationi probè consultū, vel potius improbitati itā præclarè indultū sit; vt nisi, veluti alter Rabsecha, in frequenti astantium corona, blasphemias suas eructent, religiosissimi; nisi, sicut Simon Magus, publicè pactione Simoniacam agant, integerrimi; nisi, tanquàm porci & sues, in luce meridiana, communique (saltem Septuaginta duorum) hominum conspectu cùm Scortis suis volutentur, omnium mortalium castissimi, sanctissimique haberi debeant. Exegit igitur hunc Canonem Baronius; quem deinde in illo iudicio Othonis violatum fuisse queritur. In qua assertione insignem futilitatem cum egregia falsitate coniunctam cernimus.
units.tr: See then, Baronius (for Bellarmine wanted you summoned here), what you judge should be thought of the deed of Otto. An unworthy judgment and an outrageous act! (you say). What is the matter? The laws of the canons are violated. In what way, I beg you? The council was convened against the Pontiff without his consent. Indeed, to cite an accused man, even the most wicked, against his will from the tribunal (with Baronius as advocate), what a crime! It is outrageous. What, I ask, could be more frivolous? Anything further? The second point is the paucity of witnesses: for where (you say) is the sufficient number of witnesses against a Pontiff, which ought to be seventy-two? That seventy-two witnesses were used in the case of Pope Marcellinus is no wonder, for he committed the crime of idolatry publicly and openly, burning incense in the temples of the heathen to their gods. But in all the causes of all bishops, what theology has taught, what reason has dictated, what necessity has demanded that a canon be enacted requiring so great a number of spectators? Yet who could rightly blame the cunning of these advocates, that they demand such a canon, by which, once it is laid down and sanctioned, the reputation of bishops, and above all of their Pontiffs, is well protected, or rather their wickedness is so splendidly indulged, that unless, like another Rabshakeh, they belch out their blasphemies before a crowd of bystanders, they are not to be held the most devout; unless, like Simon Magus, they publicly carry on simoniacal bargains, they are not to be held the most upright; unless, like pigs and swine, they wallow in broad daylight, in the sight of at least seventy-two people, with their whores, they are not to be held the most chaste and holy of all mortals. Baronius therefore demanded this canon, which he complains was violated in that trial of Otto. In this assertion we see remarkable frivolity joined with outstanding falsehood.

units.la: Nam Concilium illud, aduersus Iohannem Papam, abundè testium habuisse, testis est Luitprandus; ex quo constat {q}Episcopos, Diaconos, clerum, & cunctum populum Romanum, quasi vnum virum, dirâ obtestatione sese obstrinxisse, petentes ut nunquàm ipsi suis peccatis absolverentur, Nisi isthac, qua tunc obiecta erant, & multò turpiora Iohannes Papa facinora admiserit. Sic Luitprandus, Author omni exceptione maior. Pergit Baronius. {r}Auli (inquit) monstrosiora; in quânam Synodo petitum est ab Episcoporum consensu Imperatorem condemnare Episcopum, vel Clericum aliquem; & non potius ab Imperatore postulatum, ut Synodus ipsa hominem Ecclesiasticum damnet? Sic ille. Viden', Bellarmine, Baronium tuum, ad quem Videndum Lectorem tuum reiecceras? fatetur ille Episcopos illius Concilij petijsse ab Imperatore; vt ipse Pontificem damnaret: in quo Episcopi non obscure fatentur, penes Imperatorem authoritatem esse Pontificem deponendi. quod nè quis agnosceret, Tu respondisti Othonè non suâ authoritate Ioh. Papam deposuisse, sed authoritate Concilij deponendum curâsse: & obseruationem hanc inter Recognitiones.i.e. secundas, adeoque (vt quis arbitretur) saniores cogitationes reposuisti.
units.tr: For that council against John the Pope had plenty of witnesses; Liudprand is the witness, from whom it is established that the bishops, deacons, clergy and the whole Roman people, as one man, bound themselves by a dreadful oath, asking that they themselves never be absolved of their sins unless John the Pope had committed the deeds that were then charged against him, and much more shameful deeds besides. So Liudprand, an author beyond all exception. Baronius goes on: Look (he says) at the more monstrous things: in what synod was it asked, by the consent of the bishops, that the emperor should condemn a bishop or some cleric, and not rather that the emperor should demand that the synod itself condemn the churchman? So he writes. Do you see, Bellarmine, your Baronius, to whom you had sent your reader to look? He confesses that the bishops of that council asked the emperor to condemn the Pontiff himself; in which the bishops openly admit that the authority to depose a Pontiff rests with the emperor. Lest anyone recognise this, you replied that Otto did not depose John by his own authority, but took care that he be deposed by the authority of a council; and you have put this observation among your Recognitions, that is, your second thoughts, and so (as one might judge) more sensible reflections.

units.la: Deinde, {f}Tu Papam malè viuentem admonendum, nullo modo iudicandum, sed iudicio Dei referendum esse dicis: Baronius vero Clericum, quamuis non Imperatoris, at Concilij authoritate damnari approbat. Quid his repugnantibus?
units.tr: Next, you say that a Pope who lives wickedly must be admonished, not judged, and that the matter must be referred to the judgment of God. Baronius, however, approves of a cleric being condemned, though not by the authority of the Emperor, but by the authority of a Council. What are we to make of these contradictions?

units.la: Postremò,huic {t}Concilio interfuerunt (vt ait Luitprandus) prope omnes Italiae Episcopi; quorum consensu Otho pio zelo (vt dixit Bellarminus) Iohannem deposuit: nec tamen potuit vel Bellarminum Concilium illud, per contumeliam, Conciliabulum vocitare; vel Baronij {a}Othonis factū audax & insolens appellare: vti etiam nuperrimè à Bzouio {b}Iudicium execrandum, tyrannicâ authoritate latum dicitur.
units.tr: Finally, nearly all the bishops of Italy took part in this Council (as Luitprand says); and with their consent Otto, out of pious zeal (as Bellarmine put it), deposed John. Yet Bellarmine could not refrain from insultingly calling that Council a conciliabulum (a sham council), and Baronius could not refrain from calling Otto's deed bold and insolent, just as, most recently, Bzovius says it was an execrable judgment, passed by tyrannical authority.

units.la: Ex his Aduersariorum nostrorum ingenia perspicere est, qui expectant tribus tantùm Italis, herìque natis plus fidei adhiberi, quàm multò antiquioris aetatis Italiae Episcopis proè omnibus: quiq; veluti suis iudicijs damnati, eum Papam perperàm iudicari queruntur, quem tamen Impijssimum, & merito ab omnibus detestandum esse, ipsi libere confitentur. Quùm enim Iohannem Pontificem iniquisimum quissimum vocas, Baroni; vel ætatis illius Testibus fidem habes, vel non: si habes, cur aduersus Testes ipsos debaccharis? si testibus fidem derogas, cur ipsum Pontificem detestaris? Francisci de victoria, ordinis Prædicatorum, & sacræ theologiæ in Academia Salmanticensi Professoris, iudicio accuratissimo Causam hanc examinandam determinandamq; libenter deferemus. {c} Propter iniustas (inquit) dispensationes, & alia mandata insolentia, quæ in perniciem Ecclesiæ procederent, posset convocari, ut congregari Concilium generale contra voluntatem Papæ, ut ei resisteret, & obviaret eius insolentiæ. Hoc expresse tenet Sylvester, atque etiam Turrecremata, assertor vehementiss. Pontificiæ dignitatis, lib. 3. cap. 10. [Ad refranandas, inquit, quorundam Pontificum exorbitantias, qui Pontificatum extra sanctorum Patrum regulas pro voluntate exercent, aut Simoniaca pactione dehonestant, aut seculi vanitate, & vita scandalosa confundunt; hac de causa legitur congregatum Concilium Episcoporum Italiæ Romæ per Imperatorem, contra Iohannem Papam XII. qui venator lubricus & incorrigibilis erat.] Quod factum laudat & approbat Card. Turrecremata; & hoc est valde utile. Hæc Ille, quo testimonio Aduersariorum (fremant ipsi licet) calumnia detegitur atque diluitur.
units.tr: From this one can see the ingenuity of our opponents. They expect that more faith should be given to three Italians, who were born only yesterday, than to the bishops of Italy, who lived much earlier, almost all of them. And although they themselves openly admit that John was most impious and rightly abhorred by all, they complain that the one who judged him, like a judge of their own, has judged him wrongly. When you call John a most wicked man, Baronius, do you give credit to the witnesses of that age or not? If you do, why do you rage against those very witnesses? If you deny them credit, why do you condemn the Pope himself? We will gladly refer this case to be examined and decided by the most accurate judgment of Francisco de Victoria, of the Order of Preachers and Professor of sacred theology at the Academy of Salamanca. On account of unjust dispensations, he says, and other insolent mandates which tended to the ruin of the Church, a general Council could be convened and gathered against the will of the Pope, in order to resist him and oppose his insolence. Sylvester holds this expressly, and so does Turrecremata, the most vehement champion of papal dignity, in book 3, chapter 10. [To check the excesses of certain Popes, he says, who exercise the papacy beyond the rules of the holy Fathers, at their own will, or disgrace it by simoniacal bargains, or confound it by worldly vanity and a scandalous life, for this reason we read that a Council of the bishops of Italy was gathered at Rome by the Emperor against Pope John XII, who was a slippery and incorrigible hunter.] Cardinal Turrecremata praises and approves this deed, and says that it is very useful. So far he. By this testimony of our opponents (let them rage as they will), the calumny is exposed and refuted.

units.la: Anno MXLVI Henricus III. Imp. Gregorium VI. Papam exuit Pontificatu. huic Imperatori Aduersarij hæreseos, aut schismatis, vel (quod equidem sciam) criminis omnino nihil obiiciunt; tantum {d} dicunt Eum periculose nimis Ecclesiastica iudicia sibi arrogasse.
units.tr: In the year 1046, Henry III, Emperor, deprived Gregory VI of the papacy. Our opponents charge this Emperor with no heresy or schism at all, nor, as far as I know, with any crime whatever; they only say that he presumed too dangerously to take to himself the judgments of the Church.

units.la: VIII. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: VIII. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Francorum etiam Reges, contra violentiam Pontificis, le- gem Pragmaticam Ianxiuisse, obseruåsseque.
units.tr: The Kings of France, too, enacted and observed the Pragmatic Sanction against the violence of the Pope.

units.la: FRancorum Reges salutemus; semperne & tranquillitas in Gallia? tùm sanè vel maximè tempore Lodovici IX. Regis, cui Tu, in tuo Catalogo, inter "Sanctos Principes" locum honorificum tribuisti. {e} Beatus “ (inquis) Lodouicus, pessimus Francorum Rex à Bonifa-“ cio VIII. Pont. in Sanctos relatos est. Hæc Tu. Idem tamen Ludouicus, Pontificis authoritati cœteroquin deditissimus, Pragmaticam Sanctionem edidit, contra exactiones & onera grauissima per Curiam Romanam Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ impolita; Quæ (inquit) deinceps nullatenus colligi volumus, nisi pro rationabili causa de spontaneo consensu nostro, &c. Respondens {f}dubitas, an S. Ludovicus istas Papales exactiones edicto suo prohibuerit: perinde quasi sancti Imperatoris nihil interfuerit improbissimi papæ rapinis obsistere. Coniecturas, quas affers, Reuerendiss. Episcopus Elien sis[?] diffluit singulas. Ego, vt {g}praeterea constet quàm sis iniquus & malignus æstimator Regiæ authoritatis, Bzouium vestrum oppono Tibi, virum (nè forte nescias) PONTIFICE ipso plenum; vtpote qui nuper satis grande volumen Pontifici Romano nuncupauit, ROMANVS PONTIFEX inscriptum: in quo quantus quantus est, totus est Papalium Titulorum turgidus ventosusque ostentator. Ille; {h}Hoc mense (inquit) Sanctus Lodouicus promulgauit pragmaticam Sanctionem, quâ statuit, vt Prælati Ecclesiarum, & Patroni Beneficiorum ordinarij ius suum plenarie habeant; eliminare quoque voluit crimen Simoniæ, omniaque fieri ex determinatione iuris communis: Nec voluit impositas exactiones colligi per quamcunque curiam, --sed mandauit vt libertates à maioribus concessæ integræ maneant. Hæc de Lodouico.
units.tr: Let us greet the Kings of France. Was there ever tranquillity in Gaul? Certainly, above all, in the time of King Louis IX, whom you, in your Catalogue, have honoured with a place among "the Holy Princes". "Blessed", you say, "Louis, the worst King of the French, was enrolled among the saints by Pope Boniface VIII." So you say. Yet this same Louis, otherwise most devoted to the authority of the Pope, issued the Pragmatic Sanction against the heavy exactions and burdens which the Roman Curia had imposed on the Gallican Church. These, he says, we wish from now on to be collected in no way, except for a reasonable cause and by our own free consent, etc. In reply you doubt whether St Louis forbade those papal exactions by his edict, as if the holy Emperor had had no part in resisting the plunderings of the most wicked Pope. The most reverend Bishop of Ely dissolves each of the conjectures you bring forward. But so that it may further be clear how unfair and malicious a judge you are of royal authority, I set against you your Bzovius, a man (lest perhaps you not know it) full of the POPE himself, since he recently dedicated a rather large volume to the Roman Pontiff, entitled ROMAN PONTIFF. In it, whatever he is, he is wholly a boastful and windy display of papal titles. He says: This month St Louis promulgated the Pragmatic Sanction, by which he decreed that the prelates of the churches and the ordinary patrons of benefices should have their right fully; he also wished to eliminate the crime of simony, and that everything be done according to the determination of the common law. Nor did he wish the imposed exactions to be collected by any curia whatever, but ordered that the liberties granted by our ancestors remain whole. So much concerning Louis.

units.la: Lodouicus I. Philippi Pulchri Regis Francorum auus fuerat; {i}Illum (vt refert Maffonius) inter Divos retulit Papa Bonifacius: hic autem (viz. Philippus) quùm Bonifacius non Galliæ solùm, sed mundi Dominum se esse prædicaret, monet eum, nè eo loquendi genere, in Regni sui perniciem, vteretur: quùm id facere Pontifex recusaret, vetuit Rex pecuniam à Gallia Romam deferri; & admonitus ab Episcopo Rom. vt interdictum solueret, mutare sententiam noluit, Nunciumq; Gallie finibus statim excedere iussit. Tunc Pontifex Regem, vt Romà proficisceretur, publicè citauit: Rex ad Concilium futurum prouocauit aduersus Bonifacium, quasi hæresis reum. Sic se gessit Ludovici Nepos, Pragmatica Sanctionis acerrimus defensor.
units.tr: Louis I was the grandfather of Philip the Fair, King of the French. Pope Boniface placed him among the divine (as Maffei reports).
