But this Philip, when Boniface declared himself lord not only of Gaul but of the world, warned him not to use that way of speaking to the ruin of his kingdom. When the Pope refused to do so, the King forbade money to be carried from Gaul to Rome; and when the Bishop of Rome admonished him to lift the interdict, he refused to change his decision, and ordered the Nuncio to leave the borders of Gaul at once. Then the Pope publicly summoned the King to go to Rome. The King appealed against Boniface to a future Council, as a man guilty of heresy. Thus behaved the grandson of Louis, the most fierce defender of the Pragmatic Sanction.

units.la: Succedentes Francorum Reges eiusdem Sanctionis Ius semper sibi vendicasse, Galliæ Regis Orator {k} in Concil. Tridentino locupleti oratione palam fecit; quâ docet Primò, legem à Ludovico IX. contra Pontifices latam, qui potestate suâ abutentes, auare in Ecclesia grassarentur, posteà peruincente Pontificum seu astu, seu potentiâ, eadem, quæ priùs, mala inualuisse; quæ tamen postmodò Conc.Basileensis decreto sublata sunt, & Annalia vectigalia ex beneficijs exigi vetita. Quam Synodum, quòd Pontificum nimiam potentiam coercere videretur, ab ipsis pro falsâ habitam, Carolus VII. posteà in Regni comitijs confirmauit, edicto, quod vulgò Pragmaticam Sanctionem nuncupauit. At Bellarminus hic aurem vellit, Nosque facti Pij II. admonitos cupit, quem ait, misso ad Ludovicum XI. legato, petijsse vt Sanctio illa aboleretur.{1} Sed quod Pius II. efficere non potuit tempore Ludovici XI. effecisse posteà Leonem X. Francisco I. regnante, in Conc.Lateranensi Sess II. in qua Sanctio illa publico Decreto sublata est. Dixti Bellarmine, nunc Oratorem Regium, si placet, reliqua persequentem, audiamus. {m}Schola Parisiensis (inquit) Pij II. Pontificis Legato reclamauit.-- quas autem inimicitias, eam ob rem, posteà Julius III. Pont. cum Ludovico XII. optimo Principe exercuerit, vosscitis; & vtinam non adeo recens memoria esset. Posteà Leo X. cum Rege Francisco transegit; sed quamuis instrumenta ea de re confecta fuerint, Sanctio tamen illa adeò apud Nos in omnibus Regni curijs, & Theologorum nostrorum collegijs religiosè etiam hodie colitur, vt eam seruaturos se etiam iureiurando promittant. Hæc de pristinis Francorum Regibus.
units.tr: That the Kings of France who succeeded always claimed the right of this same Sanction, the orator of the King of France made plain with a rich speech at the Council of Trent. In it he teaches, first, that the law enacted by Louis IX against the Popes, who, abusing their power, were rampant with greed in the Church, was afterwards, when the Popes prevailed either by craft or by power, overcome by the same evils as before. Yet these were later removed by the decree of the Council of Basel, and the annates were forbidden to be exacted from benefices. This Synod, because it seemed to restrain the excessive power of the Popes, was regarded by them as false; afterwards Charles VII confirmed it in the assembly of the realm, by an edict which commonly he called the Pragmatic Sanction. But Bellarmine here pulls our ear, and wants us to be admonished by Pius II, whom he says, after sending a legate to Louis XI, asked that the Sanction be abolished. But what Pius II could not bring about in the time of Louis XI, Leo X later accomplished under Francis I, in the Lateran Council, Session II, in which that Sanction was removed by public decree. Let us hear, Bellarmine, now the King's orator, if you please, pursuing the rest: The Parisian school (he says) protested against the legate of Pius II. As for the enmities which Pope Julius III afterwards carried on with Louis XII, the best of princes, for that reason, you know; and would that the memory of it were not so recent. Afterwards Leo X came to terms with King Francis; but although documents were drawn up about the matter, that Sanction is still today so religiously observed among us in all the courts of the realm and in the colleges of our theologians, that they promise even under oath to keep it. So much concerning the former Kings of France.

units.la: Idem Orator vela pandit orationis, & Domini sui Caroli Regis (qui tempore Conc.Tridenti regnabat) Causam agit strenuè in hunc, qui sequitur, modum. {g}Pontifex sive fraude circumuentus, sive spe & pollicitationibus inductus, aut (quod verisimilius est) vi, metuq. adactus, abiectâ pastorali curâ, & depositâ arbitri persona, ipse in partes transfiit: Rex, qui præcipuum locum inter Christianos Reges obtinet, omni ope & Industria nixus est, ut ius cuique suum seruetur, atq; ante omnia ut Ecclesiae libertas illibata maneat. Sed Pont. Iulius III. praecipiti irâ incensus, bellum Octauio indixit, & in Mirandulae oppidanos, qui in eius manus inciderant, omnia crudelitatis exempla (à quibus alieni à nostra religione abhorrent) nullo sexus respectu exercuit. An hoc eum decent, qui se Agni pacifici Vicarium in terris prositetur? — Haec Rex Christianissimus per me dicit, atque denunciat, nec cum inanes in ista causa minas ac censuras extimescere, quas alioqui, si causam iniquam foueret, pius Princeps merito perhorresceret: multò minus praescriptiones reformidare, qui sciat quid olim vniuersi ordines Regni Lutetiæ sub Philippo Pulchro, & Schola Parisiensis contra Bonifacium VIII. decreuerint. Haec Iacobus Aretus, Legatus Regis Galliæ in Conc.Trid. Quùm Francorum Reges Christianissimi. Maiestatem suam aduersus Pontifices tàm acriter propugnauerint, creditunè facilè est, Catholicissimos Reges Hispaniæ de suo iure libenteer vnquàm decessisse?
units.tr: The same orator spreads the sails of his speech, and vigorously pleads the cause of his lord, Charles, the King (who reigned at the time of the Council of Trent), in the following manner. The Pope, whether circumvented by fraud, or led on by hope and promises, or (what is more likely) compelled by force and fear, having cast off his pastoral care and laid down the role of arbiter, himself passed over to a party. The King, who holds the foremost place among Christian kings, has striven with every effort and diligence that each one's right be preserved, and above all that the liberty of the Church remain unharmed. But Pope Julius III, kindled with headlong anger, declared war on Octavio, and against the townsmen of Mirandola, who had fallen into his hands, he practised every example of cruelty (from which those who are alien to our religion shrink in horror), sparing no sex. Does this become one who professes himself the Vicar of the peaceable Lamb on earth? — These things the Most Christian King says and declares through me, nor does he fear empty threats and censures in this cause, which a pious Prince would rightly dread if he were supporting an unjust cause; much less does he fear prescriptions, since he knows what the whole orders of the realm at Paris decreed under Philip the Fair, and the Parisian school decreed, against Boniface VIII. These are the words of Jacques Amyot, Legate of the King of France at the Council of Trent. Since the Most Christian Kings of France have defended their majesty so fiercely against the Popes, is it easy to believe that the Most Catholic Kings of Spain have ever willingly given up their right?

units.la: IX. ANIMADVERSIO. Parem Sanctionem Hispaniæ, & Lusitaniæ Reges, in simili Causa, aduersus Pontifices tulisse.
units.tr: IX. Animadversion. That the Kings of Spain and Portugal, in a similar cause, likewise issued a decree against the Popes.

units.la: HIspaniæ Regnum, ex antiquis Constitutionibus, Gregorius VII. Papa sibi, quasi suo iure, vendicauit; Quod nimirum hactenus (inquit) praeteritorum temporum{o} incommoda, & aliquot Antecessorum nostrorum occultauit negligentia. Sic Paterfamilias totius Ecclesiæ, scilicet; sic Ouilis Dominici Pastor, sic Orbis Christiani Iudex summus, sicipsus Christi Vicarius, ante Annos plus minùs sexcentos, Reges Hispaniæ admonitos voluit, Regnum illud totum ad Rom. Pontificem pertinere. Quid verò Hispaniæ Reges, quos ipsi Pontifices summo paternæ pietatis assectu complexi, benevolentiæque suæ erga Eos meritis maximis prosecuti sunt? nnnquid non omni hereditarij iuris sui praetextu penitùs abiecto, Paparum monitis concedere? Concedere verò? nonne potiùs Eos falsi convincere, atq; si etiam opus esset, armis (nam Belli inter Papam
units.tr: The kingdom of Spain, on the strength of ancient constitutions, Pope Gregory VII claimed for himself as though by his own right. He said that the troubles of past times, and the negligence of some of our predecessors, had hitherto concealed this. Thus the Father of the whole Church, the Chief Shepherd of the Lord's flock, the supreme Judge of the Christian world, and Christ's own Vicar, about six hundred years ago, wished the kings of Spain to be warned that the whole of that kingdom belonged to the Roman Pontiff. But what did the kings of Spain do, whom the Pontiffs themselves had embraced with the greatest fatherly affection and rewarded with the greatest favours for their goodwill? Did they not, having wholly cast aside every pretext of hereditary right, yield to the warnings of the Popes? Yield, indeed? Did they not rather prove those claims false and, if it were necessary, repel so great an injury by arms (for the war waged between the Pope

units.la: & Philippum II. Regem Hispaniae suscepti, {*}Rabadineira Ief.meminit) iniuriam tantam propulsare?
units.tr: and Philip II, King of Spain, which Rabadineira the Jesuit mentions)?

units.la: Card. Barony{p} Dissertatio contra Monarchiam Siculam Orbis Christiani quas oras non salutauit? in qua Regnū Siciliæ Dolo malo, audaci sacrilegio, & Tyrannica inuasione Rom. Pontificibus abreptum esse queritur, & vociferatur: tandem Causa non tàm verè, quàm vehementer agitatà, apud Philippum III. Hispaniæ Regem Serenisf. precibus obnixè contendit, vt Is, tanquàm alter{q} Zorobabel, templum incensum quasi restituere velit. Quid interea loci Rex iustitiae obseruantissimus? an istis fucis os sibi sublini passus est? imò Causa communicatà, & in Consistorijs suis in deliberationem vocatà, Edicto, & Pragmatica sua sanctione decreuit atque constituit,{r} Nè cui in ditione suâ Dissertationem illam (Baronij) aduersus dictam Monarchiam habere liceret. Nempè—& habent sua fata libelli.
units.tr: Cardinal Baronius's Dissertatio contra Monarchiam Siculam did not reach what corners of the Christian world? In it he complains and loudly protests that the kingdom of Sicily, by treachery, bold sacrilege, and tyrannical invasion, was snatched away by the Roman Pontiffs. At last, in a cause not so much truly as vehemently pressed, he earnestly sought by prayers from the most serene Philip III, King of Spain, that he would, like another Zerubbabel, seem to restore the burnt temple, as it were. And meanwhile, what of the King, most observant of justice? Did he allow his face to be smeared with such paint? On the contrary, the matter was communicated to him and brought under deliberation in his councils, and by his edict and his own pragmatic sanction he decreed and ordained that no one in his dominions should be allowed to hold that Dissertation (of Baronius) against the said monarchy. Indeed, books have their own fates.

units.la: Postremò in loco obuersatur Nobis ante oculos Lusitania Regnum, cuius Rege extincto,{s} Pontifex (vt Thuanus vester testatur) suas partes interposuit, & illud Regnum Rom. fedi beneficiarum dicitans, Regis in eo constituendi ius sibi vendicauit. — quod tanquàm ridiculum prorsus ab omnibus habitum, & a Philippo ipso postea omnino explosum. Hæc Ille. Facessat igitur isthæc tua, Bellarmine, eminentia potestatis Pontificiæ super Principes euanida & commentita venditatio iam toties à Nobis non solum vtriusque Testamenti præscripto; doctrinàque, & Apostolorum, Apostolicorumque Episcoporum; totiusque adeò primitiuæ Ecclesiæ consentienti constantique praxi damnata; verumetiam Pontificiorum Confessione ingenuâ labefactata; imò & ipsorum Pontificum, atque etiam Imperatorum, & Principum, opinione vestrâ, Catholicissimorum luculentis Exemplis, documentisque explosa, protrita, & conculcata.
units.tr: Lastly, there is before our eyes the kingdom of Portugal, whose king having died, the Pontiff (as your Thuanus attests) interposed his claims and, calling that kingdom a fief of the Roman see, claimed for himself the right of setting up a king in it — a thing regarded by all as utterly ridiculous, and afterwards completely exploded by Philip himself. So far he. Let then that vaunted, feigned and empty boast of yours, Bellarmine, of the eminent power of the Papacy over princes, depart; a boast already so often condemned by us, not only by the prescription of both Testaments, by the teaching of the Apostles and apostolic bishops, and by the consistent and unanimous practice of the whole primitive Church, but also overthrown by the candid confession of the Papists themselves; indeed, by the splendid examples and proofs of the Popes themselves and of the Emperors and Princes, most Catholic in your opinion, exploded, trampled and crushed.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: Abeat igitur Pontifex ille tuus, indignus prorsus qui in Pastorum choro compareat; suus cuique Principi proprius Episcopus & Pastor prodeat tandem; & quid iuris in ipsos Principes sibi vendicet, palàm proferat ac prositeatur.
units.tr: Let that Pontiff of yours go away, utterly unworthy to appear in the choir of ministers. Let each prince's own bishop and minister finally step forward, and let him openly state and profess what right he claims over the princes themselves.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarminus de Offic.

units.la: “Beata ciuitas, cui ex magno dono Dei contigit, vt haberet Principem pium, & Episcopum sanctum; & qui inter se coniuncti animis & studijs toti essent populo sibi commisso regendo [?] gubernando occupati. Sed vtinam non quotidie audiremus Principes cum Episcopis rixantes vel de præcedentia, vel de emolumentis temporalibus, quasi non essemus Christiani. ---pag. 37.”
units.tr: "Happy is the commonwealth that, by a great gift of God, has been granted both a pious prince and a holy bishop, who, joined together in mind and zeal, are both wholly occupied in ruling and governing the people committed to them. But would that we did not hear every day princes and bishops quarrelling, either over precedence or over temporal advantages, as if we were not Christians." ---p. 37.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Inconsulto Bellarminum Principes pios rixarum, aduersus Episcopos, insimulare.
units.tr: Bellarmine accuses pious princes of quarrelling with bishops without good reason.

units.la: Beatam esse illam Rempublicam, quæ summo Dei beneficio Principem pium, & Episcopum sanctum, ceu Mosen & Aaronem, mortalibus simul duces nacta est (quo genere consortij nullum in hac vita sacratius aut auspicatius) iuxta Tecum[?] sentimus. Valeant igitur viri contentionum, qui inter
units.tr: That commonwealth is blessed which, by the highest gift of God, has obtained at once a pious prince and a holy bishop, like Moses and Aaron, as leaders for mortals (a partnership than which none in this life is more sacred or auspicious). We agree with you accordingly. Farewell, then, to men of strife, who

units.la: [?] Reading of the word aster "iuxta" is uncertain; the initial letter is decorative. inter Episcopos & Principes dissidium cupiunt. Sed in tàm disparibus Romanensium officiis tàm arctum vinculum, tàm stabile & irruptum animorum coniugium optandum magis quàm sperandum videtur. hinc illa tua tàm grauis querimonia, UTINAM &c. in qua {*}Principes vestros, opinione tua non ita pridem {**}Egregios omnino, & singulari pietate ac iustitiâ conspicuos; nunc tanquàm importunos & iniquos Rixatores traducis. Vel in Principibus vestris, hoc in loco, vituperandis accusator falsus; vel ibi laudandis praedicandisque assentator haud quidem verax. Subindè verò utriusque ordinis Rixatores variis modis ad humilitatem informare conaris. “ Ne quotidie audiremus in templo magistrum Deum nobis “ dicentem Matth. 23.12. Qui se humiliat exaltabitur, qui “ se exaltat humiliabitur: & Luc. 18.14. Discite à me, qui “ mitis sum & humilis corde: & Luc. 22.26. Qui maior est “ inter vos fiat sicut minor, & qui praecessor est sicut qui Mi- “ nister. —— pag. 37.
units.tr: between bishops and princes desire discord. But in such unequal Romanist duties, so close a bond and so stable and unbroken a union of minds seems to be wished for rather than hoped for. Hence that so grave complaint of yours, UTINAM &c., in which you present your {*}princes, who in your opinion not long ago were {**}altogether outstanding and conspicuous for singular piety and justice, now as troublesome and unjust brawlers. Either you are a false accuser in belittling your princes here, or a not truthful flatterer in praising and extolling them there. Yet at other times you try in various ways to shape the brawlers of both orders to humility: "Lest we hear every day in the temple God, our Teacher, telling us: Matt. 23.12. Whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled; and Luke 18.14. Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and Luke 22.26. Let the greatest among you become as the least, and the one who is first as the one who serves." ---p. 37.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Ex Scripturis sacris, à Bellarmino praeter scopum detortis, Principes superbia denotari.
units.tr: That princes are denoted by pride from the holy Scriptures, which Bellarmine has wrongly twisted beside the point.

units.la: IN his Euangelistarum testimonijs Christus non modò discipulorum suorum leuitatem, sed & multò etiam magis Scribarum & Pharisaeorum crassam ambitionem redarguit: quibus ex locis si Episcopos vestros perstringi voluteris, vix potuisti Illorum mores rectius depingere. Nam Luc. 22. reprehenduntur Discipuli, quòd dignitatis praeeminentias ambitiosius prensarent. Matth. 23. b Legis Doctores (vnà cum Pharisaeis) quòd honoris titulos, salutationum gestus, atque [?]id est, accubitus primas aucuparent. Luc. 18. c Pharisaei ipsi, quòd Iustitia & Sanctitatis opinionem plausumque captarent. quas sanè singulas ambitionis species & formas plerique Episccopi vestri (quâ nunc tument superbiâ) nimis exprimunt & præ se ferunt. Qui enim aliter fieri potest, quamdiù Illi istius Capitis membra sint, qui est omnium Episcoporum non tam prælaturæ dignitate, quàm elationis fastu {*}Summus. Tunc, inquam, hanc incudem quantum potes minis præceptisque diuinis, citiùs tamen aquam è pumice, quàm ex ea liquidæ humilitatis guttulam vnam expresseris. Quodsi verò propositum Tibi fuit ex his Scripturis, (quibus vel Scribarum, qui erant [illegible, ~8 letters], id est, legis interpretes; aut Pharisæorum, {d}qui legilum rituum cognitionem profitebantur, fastus & arrogantia damnatur) Principum duntaxat insolentiam reprimere: hoc esset Theologi officio (Cui incumbet maximè {e}verbum veritatis [illegible, ~10 letters]) non parùm abuti, etiam tum, quùm veritatem crepas maximè: pergis enim.
units.tr: IN these testimonies of the Evangelists, Christ rebukes not only the levity of his disciples but much more the gross ambition of the Scribes and Pharisees. If you wished to aim these passages at your bishops, you could hardly have depicted their manners more accurately. For in Luke 22 the disciples are reproved because they grasped more ambitiously at pre-eminence of dignity. In Matt. 23 b the teachers of the law (together with the Pharisees) are reproved because they hunted after titles of honour, salutations, and the first couches at table. In Luke 18 c the Pharisees themselves are reproved because they sought the reputation and applause of righteousness and holiness. Indeed, most of your bishops, in the pride in which they now swell, express and display each of these forms and kinds of ambition far too much. For how can it be otherwise, as long as they are members of that Head, who is the highest of all bishops, not so much in the dignity of prelacy as in the haughtiness of pride? Then, I say, you may hammer this anvil as much as you like with threats and divine precepts; yet you will sooner squeeze water from a pumice stone than one little drop of clear humility from it. But if it was your purpose to restrain only the insolence of princes from these Scriptures (by which the arrogance and haughtiness of the Scribes, that is, the interpreters of the law, or of the Pharisees, who {d}professed knowledge of the legal rites, is condemned), this would be to abuse, not a little, the office of the theologian (to which the word of truth {e}chiefly belongs [illegible]), even when you most loudly cry out the truth. For you go on.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarminus de Offic.

units.la: “Hæc autem veritas est (quicquid introduxerit in variis locis vel ambitio vel consuetudo) Episcopus est Pater, & Pastor, & Doctor tam Principis quàm reliqui populi: & secundum hæc nomina Princeps subiectus esse debet Episcopo, non Episcopus Principi. Quamuis enim illa nomina magis conueniant summo Pontifici, quàm particularibus Episcopis; tamen nemo negare poterit, quin Pater sit honorabilior filio, & Pastor ouibus, & Doctor discipulis: & Episcopo cuicunque nomina illa recte conuenire ergo eos omnes, qui ad eius curam & prouidentiam pertinent.”
units.tr: "This truth is (whatever ambition or custom may have introduced in various places) that the bishop is father, pastor, and teacher both of the prince and of the rest of the people; and according to these names the prince ought to be subject to the bishop, not the bishop to the prince. For although those names apply more to the supreme Pontiff than to particular bishops, yet no one will be able to deny that a father is more honourable than a son, and a pastor than sheep, and a teacher than disciples; and that those names rightly apply to any bishop, and therefore to all who belong to his care and oversight."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Vt Principes deprimantur, Relatiuorum (vt pote Pasto- ris, Patris, Doctoris &c.) æquè & habitudi- nes inuerti.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. That Princes are lowered by the inversion of relatives (such as shepherd, father, teacher, and so on) and of their relations alike.

units.la: Argumentum hoc specie quidem neruosum, reuerà elumbe est, & ex quo consequutio planè contraria eliciatur: quià Rex (quoad regimen temporale, de quo tantum nostra instituta est quæstio) Pater patriæ, Dux, Rectórque omnium, qui Eius sese tutelæ atque patrocinio dederunt. At Rex, Tutor, & Protector tam Episcoporum, quàm populi sui; proindè secundùm hæc nomina Episcopus Regi subditus esse debet: nec enim (vt Relata suis Correlatiuus pari ratione respondeant) filius patre, ouis pastore, pupillus Tutore & Vindice suo præstantior. Errat igitur in hac sua ratiocinatione Cardinalis, quòd posthabitâ collatione duplici & geminatâ, tantùm in simplici insistat. Verbi causâ. Mater est superior filio: Beersheba est mater Salomonis: Ergò vna illa mulier erat tanto Rege superior. Hæc Consequentia, quæ videtur quoad simplicem collationem valere, quoad reciprocam dissoluitur. Sic Rex est subdito suo superior: Regi Salomoni mater Eius Beersheba subijcitur: Ergò filius est superior matre suâ.
units.tr: This argument is vigorous in appearance but in fact feeble, and from it the exact opposite conclusion follows. For the King (as far as temporal rule goes, which alone is the subject of our question) Father of his country, Leader, and Ruler of all who have given themselves into his guardianship and patronage. But the King is Guardian and Protector of his bishops no less than of his people; therefore according to these names the bishop ought to be subject to the King. For (so that correlatives may answer to their correlates in the same way) a son is not superior to his father, a sheep to its shepherd, a ward to his guardian and defender. The Cardinal therefore errs in this reasoning of his, in that, setting aside the double and twofold comparison, he dwells only on the single one. For example: a mother is superior to her son; Bathsheba was the mother of Solomon; therefore that woman was superior to so great a king. This inference, which seems to hold for the simple comparison, is dissolved when the comparison is reciprocal. Thus the king is superior to his subject; to King Solomon his mother Bathsheba is subject; therefore the son is superior to his mother.

units.la: Deteximus Aduersarij errorem, nodum tamen ipsum nondùm explicuimus. Hoc vt expeditiùs fiat, peritus veritatis indagator debet inuestigare quid sit in omni geminata Collatione præstantius; quod ex habitudinis præstantia facilè emergit: quùm enim, quoad externum honorem, habitudo Regis ad Subditum præcellentior sit habitudine matris ad filium; non quidem respectu interna[illegible, ~4 letters] & affectus naturalis, sed respectu externi dominij; ideoque Rex matri honore est præferendus. Similis est inter Principem & Episcopum suum Collatio, in qua habitudo Pastoratus Regij excellit Episcopalem, quamuis non quoad spirituale, attamen quoad temporale & externum dominium, cui ipsi Episcopi divino iure subduntur; quùm præsertim præstantia externi honoris ab externo & generali regimine æstimetur.
units.tr: We have exposed the adversary's error, but we have not yet untied the knot itself. To do this more quickly, the skilled seeker after truth must investigate what is more excellent in every double comparison, and this readily emerges from the excellence of the relation. For since, as regards outward honour, the relation of king to subject is more eminent than that of mother to son (not indeed with respect to inward love and natural affection, but with respect to external dominion), the king is therefore to be preferred to the mother in honour. Similar is the comparison between the Prince and his bishop, in which the relation of royal pastorate surpasses the episcopal one, though not as to the spiritual, yet as to temporal and external dominion, to which the bishops themselves are subject by divine right; especially since the eminence of outward honour is judged by outward and general government.

units.la: Sed præcedentiam Regis ante Episcopum vir humilis Ambitionem vocas; ratione vnicâ, eâque ad nauseam vsque repetitâ fretus: quoniam Episcopus est Pater,& Pastor scil. Exiliter atque ieiunè. De qua Nos suprà copiosè disseruimus. Deinde quùm (vt nomina hæc Pater & Pastor
units.tr: But you call the King's precedence before the bishop "ambition," relying on a single reason, repeated to the point of nausea: that the bishop is Father and Pastor, meagrely and feebly so. Of this we have spoken at length above. Then, since (as these names Father and Pastor

units.la: {f} Rom.13. Pastor, vt ais, magis conueniant summo Pontifici, quàm particularibus Episcopis) si cum animo tuo agitares, quis prisca ætatis Summorum Pontificum mos fuerit, qui Apostolorum vestigia prementes, omnem externi honoris {*}praeminentiam Principibus tribuerunt: ex hoc Argumento, à Maiore, facilè discernes, Antiquos Pontifices Romanos in nulla re magis ab hodiernis Episcopis particularibus quàm ambitione superari. Ecquid præterea?
units.tr: Rom.13. Pastor, as you say, belong more fittingly to the supreme Pontiff than to the particular bishops. If you were to consider with an open mind what the custom of the Supreme Pontiffs of old was, who, treading in the footsteps of the Apostles, attributed to princes every pre-eminence of external honour, you would easily discern from this argument a fortiori that the ancient Roman Pontiffs were surpassed by today's particular bishops in nothing more than in ambition. What else?

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officiis.

units.la: “ Prætera Episcopus in Ecclesia sedet in throno, & ad altare Sacerdotio fungitur ; quæ Principi nullâ ratione conueniunt. — pag.38.
units.tr: "Moreover, the bishop sits in the Church on a throne and performs the priestly office at the altar, which in no way belong to a prince." — p. 38.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Celsiorem in Ministerio locum externam dignitatis celsitu- dinem non probare.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. That a higher place in the ministry does not prove a greater external height of dignity.

units.la: QUid igitur? Ergonè (quod paulò ante præmiseras) Princeps Episcopo subditus, & præcedentia Episcopo, vt honorabiliori debetur? Argutè verò. quasi Sacerdotio fungi dominij nota sit, & non potiùs ministerij. Et quùm ex Decreto Conc. Tridentini. præcipuum Episcopi munus sit Verbum Dei prædicare; certè verò Ambo, vbi ille Concionatoris munus præstat, Episcopi thronus augustissimus merito haberi debet. {§}Pulpitum etiam, quo Lector fastus est plebi conspicuus, Ecclesiæ tribunal dicitur. In suis muneribus defungendis exercendisque Orator rostrum, Philosophus sublime aliquod subsellium, tanquam thronum suum occupat: æquumnè propterea Tibi videtur Sacerdotem Aaronem cum Mose ; Episcopum Oftiensem, iam concionantem, cum Cæsare ; Aristotelem in ludo suo cum Alexandro de honoris dignitate & præcedentia, ex loci sublimitate, rixari & contendere? Distædet sanè me istarum næniarum ; eóque magis, quià hac ratione ipse etiam Pont. Max. quouis sacrificulo, ad Altare Sacerdotis fungente, omnino minor erit. præterea etiam quid?
units.tr: What then? Is the Prince, therefore (as you had said just before), owed subjection to the bishop, and precedence before the bishop as the more honourable? Cleverly indeed, as if to serve in the priesthood were a mark of dominion and not rather of ministry! And since, by the Decree of the Council of Trent, the chief duty of the bishop is to preach the Word of God, surely the pulpit, where he performs the office of preacher, ought rightly to be regarded as the bishop's most august throne. The pulpit, too, from which the reader is conspicuous to the people, is called the tribunal of the Church. In discharging and exercising their duties, the orator takes the rostrum and the philosopher some high seat as his throne. Does it therefore seem fair to you that Aaron the priest should quarrel and contend with Moses, or the bishop of Ostia, when preaching, with Caesar, or Aristotle in his school with Alexander, about honour, dignity and precedence, on account of the loftiness of the place? I am truly weary of such trifles, and all the more so because on this reasoning even the Supreme Pontiff will be altogether inferior to any little sacrificer serving at the altar. What else, moreover?

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officiis.

units.la: “ Habemus praterea multos grauissimos Authores qui de excellentia dignitatis Episcopalis ita disputant, vt ostendant Principum terrenorum eminentiam cum Episcopali fastigio nulla ratione comparari posse. Hi sunt Sanctus Gregorius Nazianzenus, S. Ioh. Chrysostomus, Graci; S. Ambrosius, & S. Gregorius Latini. — pag.38.
units.tr: "We have, moreover, many most weighty authors who discuss the excellence of episcopal dignity in such a way as to show that the eminence of earthly princes cannot in any way be compared with the episcopal height. These are St Gregory Nazianzen and St John Chrysostom among the Greeks, and St Ambrose and St Gregory among the Latins." — p. 38.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Ex speciosis Patrum nominibus Bellarminum velitari.
units.tr: Bellarmine skirmishes with the showy names of the Fathers.

units.la: Testes hosce si spectemus, eos Authores, ac par est, multò grauissimos, & praeclara orbis Christiani lumina agnoscimus; sin testimonia ipsa, adeò sunt per se obscura, & à causa ipsa penitùs abhorrentia, acsi[?] cordi Tibi fuisset, potius in verborum Patrum vmbratili obscuritate delitescere, quam liquidum lucidùmque eorum sensum agnoscere. Agedùm verò faxis ex Gracorum[?] testimoniis ita disputetur, vt Causa Graeca[?] fide non agatur; neue quod Tu verbis ponis, re postea prodas.
units.tr: If we look at these witnesses, we acknowledge them, as is right, to be far the most weighty authors and brilliant lights of the Christian world. But if we look at the testimonies themselves, they are so obscure in themselves and so utterly alien to the cause that you would seem to have preferred to lurk in the shadowy obscurity of the Fathers' words rather than to recognise their clear and plain meaning. Come now, see to it that the Greek testimonies are so argued that the cause is not pursued with Greek faith (that is, treachery), and that you do not afterwards betray in deed what you set down in words.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Offic.

units.la: “ S. Gregorius Nazianzenus in oratione ad cives suos timore perculsos, & Principem irascentem; An me (inquit) aequo animo feretis? nam vos quoque mea potestati, meisque subselliis lex Christi subiecit: Imperium enim ipsi quoque gerimus; addo etiam praestantius, atque perfectius, nisi verò aequum sit spiritum carni fasces submittere, ac caelestia terrenis cedere. — pag.39. Quid Tu ex his elicias scire cupio.
units.tr: “S. Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration to his fellow citizens, terrified and with the prince angry: "Will you (he says) bear me with an even mind? For the law of Christ has placed you too under my power and my benches. For we also bear rule, and what is more, a higher and more perfect rule: unless perhaps it is fair for the spirit to yield the rods to the flesh, and for heavenly things to give way to earthly." — p. 39. I want to know what you draw from these words.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Ex hoc testimonio Nazianzeni Bellarminum palmarium quasi argumentum depromp[?]fisse sibi videtur, quo authoritas Regia enertatur, per VII. Conclusiones.
units.tr: From this testimony of Nazianzen, Bellarmine seems to have drawn what is, as it were, his chief argument, by which royal authority is weakened, through seven conclusions.

units.la: I. Vt probes potestatem Ecclesiasticam & Politicam constituere vnam Remp. {h}Pulcherrima (inquis) est similitudo Greg. Nazianzeni, quam fere omnes Theologi amplexi sunt, [sicut in homine est ratio & corpus &c.] quae duo coniuncta hominem constituunt: ita in Ecclesia potestatem esse Ecclesiasticam sive spiritualem, & civilem, seu politicam; ex quibus duabus partibus mysticum corpus conflatur. Alibi etiam sic; Vt se habent in homine spiritus & caro; ita se habent in Ecclesia duae illae potestates caro & spiritus: nam non caro & spiritus separati (ut est caro in brutis sine spiritu, & spiritus in Angelis sine carne) sed coniuncti unum hominem efficiunt.
units.tr: I. To prove that the ecclesiastical and the political power together constitute one commonwealth. {h}"The most beautiful (you say) is the similitude of Gregory Nazianzen, which almost all theologians have embraced: [just as in man there is reason and body, etc.], two things which, joined together, make up a man; so in the Church there is an ecclesiastical or spiritual power, and a civil or political power; from these two parts the mystical body is compounded. Elsewhere too he says it thus: as spirit and flesh stand in man, so those two powers, flesh and spirit, stand in the Church: for flesh and spirit, separated (as flesh is in brutes without spirit, and spirit in angels without flesh), but joined, make one man."

units.la: II. Vt ostendas ex his duabus potestatibus Politicam subordinatam esse Ecclesiasticae, non autem Deo immediate subiectam; adeoque Sacerdotibus Regibus, Reges autem neutiquam praeesse Sacerdotibus, ad eandem recurris Similitudinem. {i}Aptior est (inquis) similitudo Nazianzeni de carne & spiritu, habet enim caro sensum & appetitum, quibus respondent actus & obiecta proportionata, & quorum omnium finis immediatus est sanitas & bona constitutio corporis: habet spiritus intellectum & voluntatem, & actus atque obiecta proportionata, & pro fine animae sanitatem & perfectionem: quae cum in homine unam personam efficiunt, necessario habent subordinationem, caro enim subest, spiritus praest; & licet spiritus non se immiscear actionibus carnis, sed sinat eam exercere omnes suas actiones, ut in brutis; quando ea officiunt fini ipsius spiritus, carni imperat. {k}Si igitur Barclaius Christianus dici velit, admittere debet Pontificem & Regem non esse duos Magistratus immediate sub Christo, sed Regem Pontifici, Pontificem vero soli Christo subiectum esse debere.
units.tr: II. To show from these two powers that the political power is subordinate to the ecclesiastical and not immediately subject to God; and so that priests rule over kings, but kings by no means rule over priests, you have recourse to the same similitude. {i}"The similitude of Nazianzen about flesh and spirit is more apt (you say). For the flesh has sense and appetite, to which correspond proportionate acts and objects, and the immediate end of all of which is the health and good constitution of the body. The spirit has intellect and will, with proportionate acts and objects, and for its end the health and perfection of the soul. When these are joined in one person, as in man, they necessarily have subordination: the flesh is subject, the spirit presides. And although the spirit does not interfere in the actions of the flesh, but allows it to carry out all its own actions, as in brutes, yet when these hinder the end of the spirit itself, it commands the flesh. {k}If therefore you wish Barclay to be called a Christian, you must admit that the Pontiff and the King are not two magistrates immediately under Christ, but that the King must be subject to the Pontiff, and the Pontiff alone must be subject to Christ."

units.la: III. Vt doceas totum ordinem Ecclesiasticum exemptum esse ab omni authoritate seculari, eodem refugis. {l}Haec similitudo (inquis) ostendit secularem potestatem spirituali nulla ratione praeferri, quam neque dirigere, neque punire possit, nisi rebellionem tyrannidemque instituat sicut nonnunquam Gentiles, & haeretici Principes ausi sunt.
units.tr: III. To teach that the whole ecclesiastical order is exempt from all secular authority, you take refuge in the same. {l}"This similitude (you say) shows that secular power can by no means be preferred to spiritual power, which cannot direct or punish it, unless it institutes rebellion and tyranny, as Gentile and heretical princes have sometimes dared to do."

units.la: IV. Vt concludas penes Ecclesiasticam potestatem esse Principes pro suo arbitrio tàm spiritualibus quàm temporalibus (indirectè saltem) poenis coërcere, adeandem Te recipis Similitudinem. {m}Vt spiritus (inquis,) quando fini spirituali caro officit, ei imperat & castigat, & si opus est indicit ieiunia, aliasq; afflictiones, etiam tum detrimento aliquo & debilitate ipsius corporis; & cogit linguam ne loquatur, & oculos ne videant &c. deinde etiam si ad finem spiritus obtinendum necessaria sit aliqua carnis operatio, & ipsa etiam mors, spiritus imperare potest, vt se, & sua exponat, vt in Martyribus videmus. Ita prorsus politica potestas habet suos Principes, leges, iudicia, &c. Et similiter Ecclesia suos Episcopos, canones iudicia: illi habent pro fine temporali pacem, ista salutem aeternam. — Si carnalis obest fini spirituali, spiritualis potest, ac debet coërcere temporalem omnem rationem & viâ, quae ad id necessaria esse videbitur. {n}Vt possit spiritus disjungere de sensibus & membris corporis, indicendo illis ieiunia, flagella, vigilias: potest Pontifex mutare regna, & uni Regi auferre, & alteri conferre, si id necessarium est ad animae salutem.
units.tr: IV. To conclude that the power of the Church holds princes to restrain both spiritual and temporal persons with penalties at its own discretion (at least indirectly), you again take refuge in the same similitude. {m}"As the spirit (you say), when the flesh hinders the spiritual end, commands it and chastises it, and if necessary appoints fasts and other afflictions, even with some loss and weakening of the body itself; and it compels the tongue not to speak and the eyes not to see, etc.; then also, if some operation of the flesh, even death itself, is necessary for attaining the end of the spirit, the spirit can command that it expose itself and its own, as we see in the martyrs. So altogether the political power has its princes, laws, judgments, etc., and similarly the Church has its bishops, canons and judgments: the former have peace as their temporal end, the latter eternal salvation. If the carnal hinders the spiritual end, the spiritual can and ought to restrain every temporal matter, by whatever way shall seem necessary." {n}"That the spirit may separate itself from the senses and members of the body, by appointing to them fasts, scourgings and vigils: the Pontiff can change kingdoms, and take them away from one King and confer them on another, if this is necessary for the salvation of the soul."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Argumentum, à similitudine ductum, illustrare magis quàm probare.
units.tr: I. REMARK. An argument drawn from a similitude illustrates rather than proves.

units.la: TAccant (ait {*}Apostolus) mulieres in Ecclesia. hinc eleganter Lutherus; Humani (inquit) ingenij ratio sola in diuinis minimè audiatur. Huiusmodi Tu nobis mulierem obtrudis, nempè Similitudinem hanc Carnis & Spiritus, fœcundam nimis, sed non fœlicem satis; vtpote quæ contra mentem Authoris; contra sacræ Scripturæ doctrinam, contra Catholicæ Ecclesiæ praxin, contra Pontificum Rom. constantem professionem multiplici dissimilitudine laborat: cò quod non satis discernis, seculares & spirituales potestates in Repub. Christiana per se difdiscretas esse & disparatas. Et quamuis ratio, à Similitudine ducta, sit omnium maximè imbellis, quae non robur, sed solum lumen disputationi adferat; in hac tamen totus es, nec Rationem ullam uspiam urges vehementius. Rectius Dialectici, qui Similitudinem ad genus docendi exotericum & populare accommodant, Cuius in acroamatico & accurato arguendi genere rarus ac ferè nullus est usus; sic enim Princeps Philosophorum, [illegible, ~10 letters]. Haud igitur in tam coacta Similitudine adeò acriter Tibi insistendum fuit, in qua (quod de Sabinis dicitur) quod voluisti somniasti.
units.tr: Let women keep silence (says the Apostle) in the Church. Hence Luther elegantly says: human reason alone should by no means be heard in divine matters. Such a woman you thrust upon us, namely this similitude of flesh and spirit: too fruitful, but not happy enough. For, against the author's mind, against the teaching of Holy Scripture, against the practice of the Catholic Church, and against the constant profession of the Roman Pontiffs, it labours under many dissimilarities, because you do not sufficiently distinguish that secular and spiritual powers in the Christian commonwealth are by themselves distinct and disparate. And although an argument drawn from a similitude is the weakest of all, bringing not strength but only light to a dispute, you are entirely given over to it here, and you press no argument anywhere more vehemently. Dialecticians rightly adapt the similitude to the exoteric and popular kind of teaching, whose use in the acroamatic and exact kind of argument is rare and almost nil; for thus the Prince of Philosophers [illegible in the scan]. It was therefore not necessary to press so sharply on so forced a similitude, in which (as is said of the Sabines) you have dreamed what you wished.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Celebrem illam [CARNIS, & SPIRITVS] aduersus Prin- cipes detortam Similitudinem ab ipso Nazianzeno membratim refutari.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. That the famous similitude of [FLESH AND SPIRIT], twisted against princes, is refuted piece by piece by Nazianzen himself.

units.la: Similitudinem hanc Carnis & Spiritus semel in libris de Pontifice obijcis; rursus repetis in Torto; in Responso ad Apologiam inculcas denuò; post contra Barclaium ingeris; atq; etiam insuper eam Lectori obtrudis in Epistola ad Anonymum: quam cramben quinquies iam recoctam in hoc de Principum officio Tractatu reponis; ac si omnes fortunae vestrae, & totius Causae vestrae aedificiu hoc potissimum fundamento niteretur. Dabis (uti spero) mihi veniâ, quùm sis in urgenda hac Similitudine impendio prolixior atque impor-tunior, si ego in ea refellenda maiorem operam insumam.
units.tr: You bring forward this similitude of flesh and spirit once in your books on the Pope, repeat it in Torto, press it again in the reply to the Apologia, throw it at Barclay afterwards, and even force it on the reader in the letter to Anonymous. Now you put this crumb, already reheated five times, into this treatise on the duty of princes, as though all your fortunes and the whole structure of your cause rested chiefly on this foundation. I hope you will pardon me, since you are so very long-winded and importunate in pressing this similitude, if I take more pains in refuting it.

units.la: spiritualem quidem Sacerdotū potestatem supra Principum anthoritatem, in merè spiritualibus, hon minus quàm spiritum carni (nec sanè imerito) praeferendam esse iudicauit. At Principes, quoad exernam dignitatem, aut temporalem coercionem potestati Ecclesiasticae ncutiquam subiecit: tantum enim abest vt Gregorius, cognomento Theologus, tàm tetram [illegible, ~8 letters] Christianis propinaret, vt planè contrariam Illi mentem fuisse, vel mores ipsius demonstrent.
units.tr: He did judge that the spiritual power of the priests is to be preferred above the authority of princes in purely spiritual matters, no less than the spirit is preferred to the flesh (and not without good reason). But as for external dignity or temporal coercion, he never subjected princes to ecclesiastical power. Indeed, Gregory, surnamed the Theologian, was so far from offering such a foul [...] to Christians that his own conduct shows his mind to have been plainly the opposite.

units.la: I. Tu quemuis Principem, sanctissimum licet, si cum Episcopo vel nequissimo comparetur, stricto tamen iure Carnis loco habendum censes: quae si fuisset Nazianzeni sententia, non vehementius Theodosium Imp. hortatus esset, ut glisceentia[?] iam acerbissima inter Episcopos odia authoritate sua reprimeret. Esto finis invidiae (inquit) pacem colant Antistites, idque tua potissimum opera; sedato tu Sacerdotum bellum, quo barbaram (id est, Barbarorum) audaciam compescuisti. En tibi Episcopes carnales, sic enim Apostolus; Quam inter vos sit liuor, contentio, dissidia, nonne carnales estis? Ecce Theodosium Principem spiritualem, siquidem spiritus est actiones carnis moderari.
units.tr: I. You think that any prince, however holy, if compared with a most wicked bishop, must nevertheless be held, by strict right, to stand in the place of the flesh. If this had been Nazianzen's opinion, he would not have urged the Emperor Theodosius more vehemently to restrain by his authority the most bitter hatreds, now flaring up, between the bishops. "Let there be an end to envy," he says, "let the prelates cultivate peace, and let it be chiefly your work. Settle the war of the priests, you who have checked the barbarian (that is, the barbarians') audacity." Here you have carnal bishops, for so the Apostle calls them: "Since there is envy, strife and dissension among you, are you not carnal?" Behold Theodosius, a spiritual prince, since indeed the spirit is what governs the actions of the flesh.

units.la: II. Principem secularem minime imperare Episcopis, nec Ecclesiasticis negotiis se immiscere debere, inde concludis, quia Caro spiritus imperio & throno subjicitur. At {q}Greg. Nazianzenus, Vir (ut ait Ruffinus) per omnia incomparabilis, verbo & operibus clarus; hoc Tuum commentum verbis operibusq; redarguit, qui Thronum, id est, sacram aedem, sibi a Theodosio Imp. traditum post aliquot annos eidem Imperatori resignat, in haec verba. Vicem tibi reddat, Imperator, Christus in die remunerationis pro beneficijs eis, quibus Ecclesiam affecisti. --- Nunc te supplex peto, ut laboribus hisce liberer. Idcirco potestas conferendi alicui aedem Episcopalem iure quodam Regali Imperatori competit: quod a vobis inter Ecclesiastica negotia censetur. Eodem modo se gessit erga Principem irascentem, in eadem, quam allegas, oratione, dicens, Praclarissime praeses (Utinam liceat dicere, Mitissime) supplicationis loco causiciem meam Tibi offero. Sic Nazianzenus. Nec igitur absolute se habet Princeps ad Episcopum, ut caro ad spiritum; quando enim fando auditum est, spiritum carni supplicasse?
units.tr: II. You conclude from the fact that the flesh is subject to the rule and throne of the spirit that a secular prince ought in no way to command bishops, nor to meddle in ecclesiastical affairs. But Gregory Nazianzen, "a man (as Rufinus says) incomparable in all things, famous for word and deed", refutes this fiction of yours by his words and deeds. After some years he gave back to the same Emperor the throne, that is, the sacred church, which Theodosius had entrusted to him, in these words: "May Christ repay you, Emperor, on the day of reckoning, for the benefits you have bestowed on the Church. --- Now I beg you as a suppliant that I may be freed from these labours." Therefore the power of conferring an episcopal church on someone belongs to the Emperor by a certain royal right, which among you is counted as an ecclesiastical matter. He behaved in the same way toward a prince who was angry, in the same oration you cite, saying: "Most distinguished governor (would that I could say, most gentle), I offer you my pillow as a suppliant." So Nazianzen. Therefore the prince does not stand toward the bishop absolutely as the flesh stands toward the spirit; for when has it ever been heard that the spirit supplicated the flesh?

units.la: III. In hac tua sententia [vz. Sicut caro & spiritus unum hominem, sic potestas Ecclesiastica & politica unam constituunt Remp. in qua politica Ecclesiastica, sicut caro spiri-
units.tr: III. In this your view [namely, that as flesh and spirit make one man, so ecclesiastical and political power make one commonwealth, in which the ecclesiastical, as the flesh to the spirit,

units.la: {q} In vita eius per Greg.Presb. tui subordinatur.] Aduersarium habes S. Nazianzenum, etiam vbi cum Tibi Aduocatum asciscis. {r}Subiecti sumus (inquit) tum Deo, tum inuicem alijs alij, tum eis, qui cum Imperio in terris nobis praesunt: Deo quidem propter omnes causas, alij alijs propter fraternum amorem, Magistratibus propter ordinis conseruationem. — Etiam haec in legum nostrarum numero est, & quidem laudabilium, praeclarissimè promulgaturum à spiritu, nimirum, vt quemadmodum heris serui, vxores maritis, Ecclesia Domino, discipuli pastoribus & doctoribus obtemperant, ita nobis etiam praescribitur, cunctis potestatibus eminentibus subiecti sumus, non tantùm ob iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam, vt qui pendendo Tributo sumus obnoxij.
units.tr: {q} In his life by Gregory the Presbyter, is subordinated to the political.] You have Nazianzen as an opponent, even when you take him as your advocate. "We are subject," he says, "both to God, and to one another in turn, and to those who are set over us on earth with authority: to God indeed for all causes, to one another for brotherly love, to the magistrates for the preservation of order." And this too is among our laws, and indeed a praiseworthy one, most splendidly promulgated by the Spirit, namely, that just as servants obey their masters, wives their husbands, the Church the Lord, and disciples their ministers and teachers, so we too are commanded: "let every soul be subject to the higher powers", not only for wrath's sake but also for conscience's sake, since we are liable to pay tribute.

units.la: Tu ex Nazianzeno in Repub. Christiana nonnisi vnam subordinationem, nempè, politicae potestatis spirituali odorari & peruestigare potuisti: Nazianzenus verò aliam notat, Ecclesiasticae scilicet Seculari; sed quasi in sphaera diuersa. Quodsi enim sphaeram coelestem, id est, Res meré spirituales contemplemur, Princeps Episcopo subijcitur, quia (teste Nazianzeno) Lex Christi Imperium subiecit Sacerdotio. Sin Res temporales, seu terrestrem sphaeram intueamur, Potestas Ecclesiastica Politicae subordinatur, sic enim Nazianzenus; Nos eminentioribus potestatibus & magistratibus subiecti sumus. Quam etiam Subiectionem abundè praestitit erga Tyrannum vel immanissimum, veluti rancidissimam & putridissimam carnem, Iulianum Apostatam; quem (fatentibus Iesuitis) idem Nazianzenus, quoad in vinis egit, seu legitimum Imperatorem reueritus est.
units.tr: From Nazianzen you could sniff out and track down, in the Christian commonwealth, only one subordination, namely that of the political power to the spiritual. Nazianzen, however, notes another, that of the ecclesiastical to the secular; but he treats them as if in different spheres. For if we contemplate the heavenly sphere, that is, purely spiritual things, the prince is subject to the bishop, because (as Nazianzen testifies) the law of Christ made the empire subject to the priesthood. But if we look at temporal things, or the earthly sphere, ecclesiastical power is subordinated to the political; for so Nazianzen says: "We are subject to the higher powers and magistrates." He also rendered this subjection fully toward a tyrant, even the most savage, like rancid and putrid flesh, Julian the Apostate; whom (as the Jesuits admit) Nazianzen himself, as long as he lived, revered as the lawful emperor.

units.la: Quid quod denique ais Episcoporum esse Principes coercere, vt castigare solet spiritus carnem, quoties haec sini [?] spirituali officit: At Ecclesiasticis omnes, quantumuis sacrilegij aut parricidij scelere inquinatos, ab omni coactiua Principum potestate esse exemptos. Hoc monstrum Nazianzenus planè iugulat, vbi {*}*hortatus est Theodosium Imp. vt eâdem authoritate quorundam Sacerdotum audaciam reprimeret, qua ante Barbarorum Ethnicorum compescuerat. Proinde S. Nazianzeno magistro (vt cum Hieronymo loquar) gloriòr atque exulto, cuius si fletur iudicio, certè quidem vicimus.
units.tr: As for your saying, finally, that it is the office of bishops to coerce princes, as the spirit is wont to chastise the flesh whenever the flesh hinders the spiritual: but that all ecclesiastics, however defiled by the crime of sacrilege or parricide, are exempt from every coercive power of princes. Nazianzen plainly cuts the throat of this monster, when he urged the Emperor Theodosius to restrain by the same authority the audacity of certain priests, by which he had earlier restrained the audacity of the heathen barbarians. Therefore, to use Nazianzen as my teacher (to speak with Jerome), I glory and exult; and if the judgment is to be weighed, certainly we have won.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO. Eandem Similitudinem & rationibus, & Pontificiorum principijs manifestò conuelli.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION. That the same similitude is manifestly overturned both by reasons and by the principles of the Papists.

units.la: Quùm de mente Nazianzeni satis iam constet, mens Bellarmini pertractanda accuratiùs atque exagitanda videtur, vt Lector intelligat, quot ille dissimilitudines, quámque vafrá subtilitate ex vna Similitudine conflauerit. Similitudinem hanc, [Vt spiritus imperat carni, itá Ecclesiastica potestas politica;] Nos valdè probamus: at indè colligere, Primò, Ergò, Sicut caro & spiritus in vnum hominem, itá has duas potestates in vnam Rempublicam coalescere, dissimile omninò est: quia Caro destituta spiritu inanime & informe cadauer iacet; at status politicus separatus ab Ecclesiastico per se viuit & viget, muneribúsque suis singulis satis liberè defunguntur. Hoc testantur Iuliani secula, quandò nefarius Apostata, ciurato Christianismo, idolomaniae Ethnicae se addixit; cuius tamen imperio Nazianzenus, & Ecclesia ipsa, quoad regimen temporale, absque omni seditiosa molitione semper paruit.
units.tr: Now that the mind of Nazianzen is sufficiently established, the mind of Bellarmine seems to need to be examined more carefully and scrutinised, so that the reader may understand how many dissimilarities, and with what crafty subtlety, he has built up out of the single Similitude. We strongly approve this similitude, [As the spirit rules the flesh, so the ecclesiastical power rules the political one;] but to infer from it, first, therefore, just as flesh and spirit coalesce into one man, so these two powers coalesce into one commonwealth, is wholly dissimilar. For flesh destitute of spirit lies as a lifeless and shapeless corpse; but the political state, separated from the ecclesiastical, lives and thrives by itself, and its several offices are discharged quite freely. The ages of Julian bear witness to this, when the wicked Apostate, though Christianity was in place, devoted himself to heathen idolatry; yet to his rule Nazianzen, and the Church itself as far as temporal government went, always submitted, without any seditious undertaking.

units.la: II. Ergò Politicum magistratum Carnem prorsus indigitari; Ecclesiasticum quemlibet purum putum Spiritum; dissimile etiam, "Quia (iuxta Hieron.) quiuis Laicus, cùm baptizatur, Sacerdotium accipit Laici, id est, Baptismum, scriptum enim est, Reges nos & Sacerdotes Deo patri suo fecit. Nec desunt {x}Doctores Pontificij, qui infanti vnius diei, modò sit baptizatus, characterem cuiuslibet ordinis sacri imprimi tenent. Hoc docuit Guil.de monte Laudano, communiter receptus ibi à Cardinali, & aliis, & à Bonifacio. Et Thomas part.3.63.art.16.ad 1. per omnia Sacramenta (inquit) fit homo particeps Sacerdotij Christi, vtpote particeps Sacerdotij Christi, utpote participans aliquem effectum eius. Haec Nauarrus. Vos igitur insigni contumelia Magistratum & populum Christianum afficitis, dum eos Carni (quae est pars hominis bruta) assimilatis: vobis autem ipsis semper Spiritualis cognomen arrogatis.
units.tr: II. Therefore the political magistrate is wholly designated as the flesh, and each ecclesiastical man as pure spirit. Also dissimilar: "because" (according to Jerome) "every layman, when he is baptised, receives the priesthood of the laity, that is, baptism; for it is written, He has made us kings and priests to God his Father." Nor are there lacking Papist teachers who hold that an infant of one day, provided only that he has been baptised, has the character of any sacred order imprinted on him. William of Montlaudun taught this, commonly received there by the Cardinal and others, and by Boniface. And Thomas, part 3, question 63, article 16, reply 1: "through all the sacraments" (he says) "a man is made a partaker of the priesthood of Christ, as one who shares in some effect of it." So Navarrus. You therefore inflict the greatest insult on the magistrate and the Christian people, while you liken them to the flesh (which is the brutish part of man), but for yourselves you always claim the name Spiritual.

units.la: III. Ergo Populum, ac Magistratum Laicum se causis Ecclesiasticis immiscere non magis debere, quàm solet caro spiritus negotia tractare; Dissimile: primò quia Magistratus politicus praescribit leges, quae, quamuis politicae sint, nihilominus spirituales haberi possunt; hisce enim Christianorum subditorum conscientiae obligantur. Hic Te, Bellarmine, testem appello. {y}Lex (inquis) civilis non minùs obligat in conscientia quàm lex diuina, etsi minùs firma sit hæc, quàm illa. {z}Et licet lex politica dicatur temporalis, ratione obiecti, quia versatur circa temporalia & externa, tamen in se est res spiritualis. {a}Et obligat ad poenam aeternam, non quatenus lex hominis, sed quatenus lex Ministri Dei: {b}ut Rom. 13. qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Deinde quia tàm Magistratus politicus, quàm populus negotijs Ecclesiasticis nonnunquàm inseruiunt. De Populo {c}Bellarminus negare non potest, eum ex authoritate Conc. Nicaeni se electioni presbyterorum admisceuisse; Eumque ex testimonio Cypriani, Sacerdotes eligendi potestatem & suffragium ferendi habuisse, licet more testis, non iudicis. Deinde (ut Tolosanus vester) {d}Reges ipsos Pastores esse non tantum corporum Subditorum, sed etiam, per consequentiam, animarum; pro quarum salute non minùs quàm pro corporum incolumitate, laborare debent, & auxilium Ecclesiae contra Haereticos & contemptores praebere. Iccirco Tu Carni spiritus actiones decernendi, curandi, dirigendi, & quodammodò eligendi vim & potestatem aliquam inesse probes oportet, priusquam illa tua de Carne & Spiritu analogia rite cohereat aut consistat.
units.tr: III. Therefore the people and the lay magistrate ought no more to meddle in ecclesiastical causes than the flesh is accustomed to handle the affairs of the spirit. This is dissimilar. First, because the political magistrate prescribes laws which, although they are political, may nevertheless be regarded as spiritual; for by these the consciences of Christian subjects are bound. Here I call you as witness, Bellarmine. "Civil law (you say) binds in conscience no less than divine law, although it is less firm than that." "And although political law is called temporal, by reason of its object, because it is concerned with temporal and external things, yet in itself it is a spiritual thing." "And it binds to eternal punishment, not as the law of man but as the law of God's minister," as in Romans 13: "whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God." Then, because both the political magistrate and the people sometimes serve ecclesiastical affairs. Bellarmine cannot deny that the people, by the authority of the Council of Nicaea, mixed themselves into the election of presbyters; and that, from the testimony of Cyprian, the people had the power of choosing priests and of giving a vote, though in the manner of a witness rather than a judge. Then, as your Tolosanus says, "kings themselves are shepherds not only of the bodies of their subjects but also, by consequence, of their souls; for whose salvation they ought to labour no less than for the safety of their bodies, and to give aid to the Church against heretics and contemners." Therefore you must prove that the flesh has some force and power to decree, to care for, to direct, and in some measure to choose the actions of the spirit, before your analogy of flesh and spirit can properly hold together or stand.

units.la: IV. Vt ad subordinationem venianus) Ergo, sicut anima non immiscet se actionibus carni proprys, nisi indirecte uitatis suæ : Nec enim piscantur homines in aere, nec venantur leporem in medio Mari, vt ait Comicus. Quippè operatio omnis facultati suæ proportionata esse debet, nec pertingit vltrà obiectum debitum ac homogeneum. Itâ non est Regis Sacramenta administrare, nec Pontificis gladium distringere : sed, vt est apud Gratianum{1}, Regum est corporalem irrogare poenam, Sacerdotum spiritualem inferre vindictam. Præclarum imprimis documentum in Othone{*} habuimus, qui Pius imperatur Ioannem Papam fere omnium Pontificum deterrimum deposuit. Nè longior sim,{m} Pelagij Papæ dictū probamus; Patricium (is erat ab Imperatore quasi Prorex constitutus) fuisse Patrem Papæ in temporalibus, sicut Papa est eius pater in spiritualibus : eandemque professionem Romanæ Pontifices (vt{*} liquet) per multorum seculorum seriem posteritati testatissimam reddiderunt. De Episcopis alijs post{‡} videbimus.
units.tr: IV. To come to subordination. Therefore, just as the soul does not mix itself in the actions proper to the flesh, except indirectly, in respect of its own life: for men do not fish in the air, nor hunt hares in the middle of the sea, as the comic poet says. Every operation ought to be proportioned to its faculty, nor does it reach beyond its proper and homogeneous object. So it is not the king's business to administer the sacraments, nor the pontiff's to draw the sword; but, as is found in Gratian, it belongs to kings to inflict bodily punishment, and to priests to inflict spiritual vengeance. We had a notable proof of this above all in Otto, who, called Pious as emperor, deposed John, almost the worst of all popes. That I may not be too long, we approve the saying of Pope Pelagius: that the patrician (who had been appointed by the emperor as a kind of viceroy) was father of the pope in temporal matters, just as the pope is his father in spiritual matters; and this profession the Roman pontiffs, as is clear, have rendered most attested to posterity through a long series of centuries. About other bishops we shall see later.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Offic.

units.la: “ Sanctus Chrysostomus lib. 3. de Sacerdotio sic loquitur, [Sacerdotium regno tanto est excellentius quantum spiritus & carnis interuallum esse potest,] & hoc multis argumentis probat : loquitur autem de summo Sacerdotio, id est, de Episcopatu. Ex multis rationibus vnam praeterire nolo ; Habent (inquit) & terrestres Principes vinculi potestatem, verum corporum solum : id autem, quod dico, Sacerdotis vinculum ipsam animam contingit, atque ad coelos vsque perusdit. Et infra ; nam quasi iam in coelum translati, & supra humanum naturam positi, atque à nostris affectibus exempti, sic illi ad principatum istum perducti sunt. Quid multa ? Rex aliquis, si cui ex subditis honorem hunc detulerit, vt potestatem habeat quoscunque volet in carcerem coniciendi, eosdemque rursus laxandi, beatus ille & admirandus iudicio omnium fuerit. At verò qui à Deo tanto maiorem accepit potestatem, quanto etiam anima corporibus praestant, hic vilem dignitatem accipisse videri potest.”
units.tr: “St Chrysostom, in book 3 of On the Priesthood, speaks thus: [The priesthood is as much more excellent than kingship as the interval between spirit and flesh can be], and proves this by many arguments; but he is speaking of the highest priesthood, that is, of the episcopate. Among the many reasons I do not wish to pass over one: earthly princes (he says) also have the power of binding, but only of bodies; what I say, however, is that the priest's bond touches the soul itself and pierces right through to the heavens. And below: for as if already translated into heaven, and placed above human nature, and freed from our affections, so they have been led to that principate. What more? If some king had conferred this honour on one of his subjects, so that he had power to throw into prison whomever he wished, and again to release them, that man would be thought blessed and admirable in the judgment of all. But he who has received from God a power as much greater as souls surpass bodies, can seem to have received a vile dignity.”

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Sacerdotes Regibus externâ potestate non praecellere, licet Sacerdotium Regno, obiecto & fine, praeminet.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO. The priests do not surpass the kings in external power, although the priesthood is superior to the kingdom in its object and end.

units.la: VNÀ cum S.Nazianzeno S.Chrysostomum producis, nobile sanè par Praesulum integerrimorum; qui quum ferè quasi συγγενεῖς[?] essent, eandem sententiam eisdem penè verbis, adeoq; unà, sine dubio, eâdemq; mente promulgârunt: quâ quidem praestantiam ordinis spiritualis plurimum illustrant, itâ tamen, ut dignitati & authoritati Regiæ in temporalibus nihil quicquam detractum velint. Sacerdotium Regno praecellere, quantum carni spiritus, quantum terrae coelum, quantum corpori anima, & (addo ex {a}Chrysostomo) multò etiam magis, nemo Christianus insiciabitur: huius tamen tantae tamque admirabilis potestatis, quam Deus (sic enim idem Chrysostomus) nec Angelis nec Archangelis datam voluit, excellentia quibus claudetur limitibus, & quousq; se extendat, dispiciendū Tibi fuerat. An vero ad Temporalia, itâ ut Episcopi (quod passim inculcas) {o}praecedentiam ubiq; & praesidentiam supra Principes; aut etiam ius vel castigandi, vel Regnis suis exuendi; & {p}Quàuis ratione coercendi sibi vendicent? longè à nobis ablit, ut tribuamus tantam tàm incomparabili Theologo vecordiam, qui planè χωρισμῶς[?] minimè εὐπρεπῶς[?] fuit; cultor, non contemptor Regum.
units.tr: WHEN you bring forward S. Nazianzen and S. Chrysostom, you cite a noble pair of most upright prelates. Since they were almost like kinsmen [συγγενεῖς], they proclaimed the same opinion, in almost the same words, and so surely in agreement and with the same mind. By this they greatly illustrate the excellence of the spiritual order, yet in such a way that they wished nothing at all to be taken from the dignity and authority of kings in temporal matters. The priesthood excels the kingdom as much as the spirit excels the flesh, as much as heaven excels earth, as much as the soul excels the body, and (I add from {a}Chrysostom) much more besides. No Christian will deny this. But you ought to have considered what limits would enclose the excellence of this great and admirable power, which God (for so the same Chrysostom says) willed to give neither to angels nor to archangels, and how far it extends. Or do they claim for themselves, in temporal matters, so that the bishops (as you press everywhere) have {o}precedence and presidency everywhere over princes; or even a right to punish or strip kings of their kingdoms, and to restrain them by any means? Far be it from us to attribute such madness to so incomparable a theologian, who was altogether far from such things and by no means seemly. He was a worshipper of kings, not their despiser.

units.la: Comparatione inter Sacerdotiū & Regnum, de muneris excellētia, institutā, vtriusq; praestantia, ex obiecti & finis dignitate æstimanda est. Mysterium Euangelij, seu pacis gratuitae in Christo finis, est salus æterna per Christum Iesum, in gloriam Patris: Regni politici obiectum, publica res; finis, pax civilis: non potest igitur Sacerdotalis potestas Regiam non infinitis modis excellere. At propterea in civili hominum consortio, quoad praecedentiam, & honorem externum, Sacerdotem Regi praeponendum esse, nihil est minus consectarium. v. g. Astronomia, tanquàm ars nobilior, in perscrutandis coeli plagis;
units.tr: In a comparison between the priesthood and the kingdom, their excellence in function, their institution, and the superiority of each must be judged from the dignity of their object and end. The mystery of the Gospel, or the end of the free peace in Christ, is eternal salvation through Jesus Christ, to the glory of the Father. The object of the political kingdom is public affairs, its end is civil peace. Therefore the priestly power cannot fail to excel the royal power in countless ways. But it is by no means a consequence that, in the civil fellowship of men, the priest should be placed before the king in precedence and external honour. For example, astronomy, as the nobler art, deals with searching the regions of heaven.

units.la: {a} Chrysost. in 2 Cor. 7. hom. 15.
units.tr: {a} Chrysostom, on 2 Cor. 7, homily 15.

units.la: {o} Bellar. resp. ad Apolog. c. 4.
units.tr: {o} Bellarmine, reply to the Apology, ch. 4.

units.la: {p} Bellar. supra. uitatis suæ : Nec enim piscantur homines in aëre, nec venantur leporem in medio Mari, vt ait Comicus. Quippè operatio omnis facultati suæ proportionata esse debet, nec pertingit vltrà obiectum debitum ac homogeneum. Itâ non est Regis Sacramenta administrare, nec Pontifici gladium distringere : sed, vt est apud Gratianum, Regnum est corporalem irrogare pœnam, Sacerdotum spiritualem inferre vindictam. Præclarum imprimis documentum in Othone habuimus, qui Pius imperatur Ioannem Papam fere omnium Pontificum deterrimum deposuit. Nè longior sim, Pelagÿ Papæ dictū probamus; Patricium (is erat ab Imperatore quasi Prorex constitutus) fuisse Patrem Papæ in temporalibus, sicut Papa est eius pater in spiritualibus : eandemque professionem Romani Pontifices (vt liquet) per multorum seculorum seriem posteritati testatissimam reddiderunt. De Episcopis alijs post videbimus.
units.tr: {p} Bellarmine, as above. Of its own kind. For, as the comic poet says, men are not fished for in the air, nor is a hare hunted in the middle of the sea. Indeed every operation must be proportioned to its faculty, and it does not reach beyond its due and homogeneous object. So it is not for the king to administer the sacraments, nor for the Pontiff to draw the sword. Rather, as Gratian has it, the kingdom is to inflict bodily punishment, the priesthood to inflict spiritual vengeance. We had a striking proof of this above all in Otto, who, as a pious emperor, deposed John, almost the worst of all the Pontiffs. Not to be too long, we approve the saying of Pope Pelagius, that the patrician (who had been appointed by the emperor as a kind of viceroy) was the father of the Pope in temporal matters, just as the Pope is his father in spiritual matters. The Roman Pontiffs, as is clear, have made this profession very well attested to posterity through a long series of centuries. We shall see about other bishops later.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, on the Offices.

units.la: “ Sanctus Chrysostomus lib. 3. de Sacerdotio sic loquitur, [Sacerdotium regno tanto est excellentius quantum spiritus & carnis interuallum esse potest,] & hoc multis argumentis probat : loquitur autem de summo Sacerdotio, idest, de Episcopatu. Ex multis rationibus unam praeterire nolo ; Habent (inquit) & terrestres Principes vinculi potestatem, verum corporum solum : id autem, quod dico, Sacerdotis vinculum ipsam animam contingit, atque ad coelos usque perusdit. Et infra ; nam quasi in coelum translati, & supra humanum naturam positi, atque à nostris affectibus exempti, sic illi ad principatum istum perducti sunt. Quid multa? Rex aliquis, si cui ex subditis honorem hunc detulerit, ut potestatem habeat quoscunque volet in carcerem coniiciendi, eosdemque rursus laxandi, beatus ille & admirandus judicio omnium fuerit. At verò qui à Deo tanto maiorem accepit potestatem, quanto etiam animae corporibus praestant, hic vilem dignitatem accipisse videri potest.
units.tr: "Saint Chrysostom, in book 3 of On the Priesthood, speaks thus: [The priesthood is as much more excellent than the kingdom as the interval between spirit and flesh can be], and he proves this by many arguments. He speaks, however, of the highest priesthood, that is, of the episcopate. Among many reasons I do not want to pass over one: (he says) earthly princes also have the power of binding, but only of bodies; but what I say is that the priest's binding touches the very soul and penetrates even to the heavens. And below: for as if translated into heaven, and placed above human nature, and freed from our passions, they have been brought to that principate. Why say more? If a king were to confer this honour on one of his subjects, so that he might have power to throw into prison whomever he wished and to release them again, that man would be called blessed and admirable in the judgement of all. But he who has received from God a power so much greater, as souls surpass bodies, may seem to have received a base dignity.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Sacerdotes Regibus externa potestate non praecellere, licet Sacerdotium Regno, obiecto & fine, praemineat.
units.tr: The priests do not surpass the kings in external power, although the priesthood is superior to the kingdom in its object and end.

units.la: VNà cum S.Nazianzeno S.Chrysostomum producis,nobile sanè par Præsulum integerrimorum; qui quum ferè quasi ἀρχιερεῖς[?] essent, eandem sententiam eisdem penè verbis, adeoq; vnà, sine dubio, eàdemq; mente promulgàrunt: quà quidem præstantiam ordinis spiritualis plurimum illustrant, itâ tamen, vt dignitati & authoritati Regiæ in temporalibus nihil quicquam detractum velint. Sacerdotium Regno præcellere, quantum carni spiritus, quantum terræ cœlum, quantum corpori anima, & (addo ex {n}Chrysostomo) multò etiam magis, nemo Christianus insiciabitur: huius tamen tantæ tamque admirabilis potestatis, quam Deus (sic enim idem Chrysostomus) nec Angelis nec Archangelis datam voluit, excellentia quibus claudetur limitibus, & quousq; se extendat, dispiciendū Tibi fuerat. An vero ad Temporalia, itâ vt Episcopi (quod passim inculcas) {o}praecedentiam vbiq; & præsidentiam supra Principes; aut etiam ius vel castigandi, vel Regnis suis exuendi; & {p}Quauis ratione coercendi sibi vendicent? longè à nobis abest, vt tribuamus tantam tàm incomparabili Theologo vecordiam, qui planè [illegible, ~8 letters] minimè [illegible, ~8 letters] fuit; cultor, non contemptor Regum.
units.tr: WHEN you bring forward S. Nazianzen and S. Chrysostom, you cite a noble pair of most upright prelates. Since they were almost like high priests [ἀρχιερεῖς], they proclaimed the same opinion, in almost the same words, and so surely together, with the same mind. By this they greatly illustrate the excellence of the spiritual order, yet in such a way that they wished nothing at all to be taken from the dignity and authority of kings in temporal matters. The priesthood excels the kingdom as much as the spirit excels the flesh, as much as heaven excels earth, as much as the soul excels the body, and (I add from {n}Chrysostom) much more besides, no Christian will deny. But you ought to have considered what limits would enclose the excellence of this great and admirable power, which God (for so the same Chrysostom says) willed to give neither to angels nor to archangels, and how far it extends. Or do they claim for themselves, in temporal matters, so that the bishops (as you press everywhere) have {o}precedence everywhere and presidency over kings; or even a right to punish or strip kings of their kingdoms, and to restrain them by any means, {p}? Far be it from us to attribute such madness to so incomparable a theologian, who was [illegible, about 8 letters] and by no means [illegible, about 8 letters]; a worshipper, not a despiser, of kings.

units.la: Comparatione inter Sacerdotiū & Regnum, de muneris excellētia, institutā, vtriusq; præstantia, ex obiecti & finis dignitate æstimanda est. Mysterium Euangelij, seu pacis gratuitæ in Christo finis, est salus æterna per Christum Iesum, in gloriam Patris: Regni politici obiectum, publica res; finis, pax ciuilis: non potest igitur Sacerdotalis potestas Regiam non infinitis modis excellere. At propterea in ciuili hominum consortio, quoad præcedentiam, & honorem externum, Sacerdotem Regi præponendum esse, nihil est minus consectarium. v. g. Astronomia, tanquàm ars nobilior, in perscrutandis coeli plagis ; Geographia tantùm in terræ climatibus , & dimensionibus rimandis versatur ; Ethicus excolit animum virtutum præceptis, vitámque instituit atque informat ad bene beateque viuendum ; Politicus verò Reipub. bono externo consulit. An igitur Ptolomæum Archimedi, Alexandrum Aristoteli potestate & honore cedere æquum est ? Ad Rem propius accedam.
units.tr: In a comparison between the priesthood and the kingdom, their excellence in function, their institution, and the superiority of each must be judged from the dignity of their object and end. The mystery of the Gospel, or the end of the free peace in Christ, is eternal salvation through Jesus Christ, to the glory of the Father. The object of the political kingdom is public affairs; its end is civil peace. Therefore the priestly power cannot fail to excel the royal power in countless ways. But it is by no means a consequence that, in the civil fellowship of men, as regards precedence and external honour, the priest should be placed before the king. For example, astronomy, as the nobler art, deals with searching the regions of heaven; geography deals only with the climates and measurements of the earth; the ethicist cultivates the mind with precepts of virtue and shapes and forms life for living well and happily; but the politician looks after the external good of the commonwealth. Is it therefore right that Ptolemy should yield power and honour to Archimedes, or Alexander to Aristotle? Let me come closer to the matter.
