units.la: Infidelem Christus (quo quid abiectius) {q}Canem appellat ; Herodem item {*}Vulpem : Fidelem verò, honoris caussâ, {r}filium Abrahæ nuncupat ; Iudas etiam quùm iam Apostolus erat, quià tamen tantùm nomine tenùs Christianus{f}, Diabolus dicebatur: quanquam quiuis verè sanctus, laicus licet, inter Eos numeratur, qui hujusmodi Regni coelestis hæredes censentur,{t} quibus mundus non est dignus: quales diuinus noster Rhetor Chrysostomus dixit, dùm sacris mysterijs interfuit, quodammodò ad coelum rapi. "An censes te (inquit) in terris consistere ? annon potius euectigiò in coelos transferri? Quod non multùm abludit ab illo Apoc. 1. Reges nos fecit, & Sacerdotes Deo. An quia vir verè Christianus infidelem & impium non minùs quàm Spiritus carnem, coelum terram, filius canem, hæres æternæ gloriæ Diabolum nobilitate & dignitate spirituali superat ; ideone quis virum Sanctum quàlibet cuiuis Regi non sancto, aut Imperatori Ethnico honore ciuili præferendum esse duxerit? Tantum abest vt præcellentia ordinis, aut potestatis Spiritualis, ex respectu præstantiæ obiecti aut finis, aliquam, inferat præcedentiam ciuilis honoris aut authoritatis super Eos, qui in politico regimine Supremi constituti sunt.
units.tr: Christ calls the unbeliever (what could be more abject?) a dog, and likewise calls Herod a fox. But the believer, for the sake of honour, he calls a son of Abraham. Even Judas, when he was already an apostle, was called a devil, because he was a Christian only in name. Yet any truly holy man, though a layman, is counted among those who are reckoned heirs of the heavenly kingdom, men of whom the world is not worthy. Such, our divine rhetorician Chrysostom said, when he was present at the sacred mysteries, is in some way caught up to heaven: "Do you think (he says) that you stand on earth? Are you not rather carried up to the heavens?" This does not differ much from that in Revelation 1: He has made us kings and priests to God. But because a man truly Christian surpasses the unbeliever and the impious in spiritual nobility and dignity, as spirit surpasses flesh, heaven surpasses earth, a son surpasses a dog, and an heir of eternal glory surpasses the Devil, shall anyone therefore think that a holy man ought to be given civil honour before any non-holy king or heathen emperor? So far is the excellence of the spiritual order or power, judged by the object or end, from implying any precedence of civil honour or authority over those who are set in supreme place in the political government.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Veram Chrysostomi sententiam, de Regum suprematu, omnes Sophistarum Strophas confundere.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. That Chrysostom's true opinion on the supremacy of kings confounds all the sophists' tricks.

units.la: DEindè iure quis miretur abs Te citari testem Chrysostomum quo nullum habes in hac Causa acriorem Aduer-
units.tr: Then who could rightly be surprised that you cite as a witness Chrysostom, whom you have no fiercer opponent than

units.la: {q} Mat.7.27. Aduersarium. Nec enim solos laicos, sed & Monachos, & Sacerdotes, atque etiam Apostolos saecularibus Magistratibus subditos esse Chrysostomus diserte {x}asserit. Id quod satis (inquit) declarat Apostolus, cum dixit in exordio, [Omnis anima potestatibus subdita sit, etiamsi Apostolus sit, vel Prophēta, siue (audiat hoc Papa, & nisi omnem pudorem abster-serit, erubescat) Quisquis tandem fuerit. Etiam (non itaque tantum ex {y}discretione) Ex debito obedire iubentur, non gratiam illis, sed debitum praestantes. Nec obedire solum, verum-etiam seu subordinari Regibus infidelibus: nec modo (tanquam tempori seruientes) {a} Donec vires ad resistendum comparauerint; sed ex intimis animi votis, iuxta illud Apostoli, [Orationes facientes pro omnibus hominibus, pro Regibus, & omnibus in sublimitate constitutis. 1. Tim.2.] Unde Chrysost. {b}Quid sibi vult quòd ait primò {z}omnium[ pro Regibus &c.] In obsequio-quotidiano, perpetuoque diuinae religionis ritu, quando diebus singulis mane vespere orationes fundantur ad dominum: quomodo? an pro fidelibus tantum? id verum non esse, ostendunt quae sequuntur, [pro Regibus,] neque enim tunc Reges Deum colebant, sed multis postea temporibus in infidelitate perstiterunt. — Et nè adulationis causâ Apostolum ita scripsisse putarent, vide quid adiunxit, [ ut quietam vitam agatis ] Haec Chrysost. quae verisimiles Iesuitas plane iugulant, qui latronum & perduellionum lege freti, parendi infidelibus Regibus fidem dant, cùm hac perfida mentis reseruatione ac restrictione, Donec vires habuerint. Et nè Sanderus, & alij ogganniant, Eos, qui obligabantur obtemperare infidelibus magistratibus, non perinde teneri subesse Regibus Christianis, ratione {*}Pacti & foederis in Baptismo initi; huic Paradoxo oppidò scitè occurrit Chrysostomus. {c}Sicut[?] Principibus(inquit) & potestatibus, de quibus Apostolus, quanto magis religioso Principi parendum?
units.tr: Mat.7.27. adversary in this cause. For Chrysostom plainly asserts that not only laymen but also monks, priests, and even apostles are subject to secular magistrates. As the Apostle makes clear (he says) at the beginning: [Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, even if he be an apostle or a prophet, or (let the Pope hear this, and unless he has wiped away all shame, let him blush) whoever he may be. They are commanded to obey not merely out of discretion but out of obligation, rendering not a favour to them but what is owed. And they must obey and be subordinate not only to unbelieving kings, nor only as serving the times, until they have gathered strength to resist, but from the innermost desires of the heart, according to the Apostle's saying, [Making supplications, prayers, and intercessions for all men, for kings and all who are in high place, 1 Tim. 2.] Hence Chrysostom: What does it mean that he says first of all, [for kings, etc.]? In the daily, constant observance of divine worship, when prayers are offered to the Lord each morning and evening, how is it done? Is it only for believers? That this is not true is shown by what follows, [for kings,] for at that time the kings did not worship God, but afterwards for many ages they remained in unbelief. And lest they think the Apostle wrote this out of flattery, see what he added: [that you may lead a quiet life]. These are Chrysostom's words, which plainly slaughter the Jesuits, who, relying on the law of robbers and traitors, pledge obedience to unbelieving kings, with this treacherous mental reservation and restriction, until they have strength. And lest Sanders and others grumble that those who were bound to obey unbelieving magistrates are not equally bound to be subject to Christian kings by reason of the pact and covenant entered into at baptism, Chrysostom meets this paradox very neatly: To princes (he says) and powers, of whom the Apostle speaks, must obedience be rendered; how much more to a religious prince?

units.la: Ergone igitur ut has Chrysostomi sententias à Bellarmino (qui unam, & ab hac causa valdè seiunctam praeterire nolit) praetermissas esse mirer? forte sentiebat vir sagax, Exceptiones suas singulas à Chrysostomo in hac Caussa, prorsus dilui. I. nimirum, Episcopum obedire debere Principi secularibus; II. etiam Ex debito; III. Infidelibus Ethnicis; IV. adeoque magis Christianis: quæ omnia ex diametro Bellarmini exceptionibus repugnant. Quid multa? Bellarminus Chrysostomum, & alios Græcos Patres crepat, deus bone! quâ fronte? quum præsertim Sacerdotes Regibus subesse, & subordinatos esse (teste ipso {*}Espencæo) ex loco illo Apostoli [Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit] docuerint non modò Chrysostomus, sed etiam Theodoretus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus, Et QUI NON GRÆCI? Hucusque de Græcis; Latinos consulamus. Bellar. ex Latinis Patribus Ambrosio. Gregorio.
units.tr: Must I then wonder that Bellarmine, who will not pass over one opinion that is quite remote from this cause, has passed over these sayings of Chrysostom? Perhaps that shrewd man saw that his exceptions, one by one, are utterly dissolved by Chrysostom in this cause: namely, (I) that a bishop must obey secular princes; (II) that this is owed; (III) to unbelieving heathens; (IV) and therefore much more to Christians. All these things flatly contradict Bellarmine's exceptions. Why say more? Bellarmine scorns Chrysostom and the other Greek Fathers, good God! With what face? Especially since not only Chrysostom but also Theodoret, Oecumenius and Theophylact, and (as Espencaeus himself testifies) priests, have taught from that passage of the Apostle, Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, that priests are subject to and subordinate to kings. And what of the Latins? So far, the Greeks; let us consult the Latins. Bellarmine cites from the Latin Fathers Ambrose and Gregory.

units.la: I. Ex Ambrosio.
units.tr: I. From Ambrose.

units.la: “S. Ambrosius in lib de dignitate Sacerdotali cap.2. Honor (inquit) & sublimitas Episcopalis nullis poterit compara-tionibus adæquari; si Regum fulgori compares, & Principum diademati, longè erit inferius, quàm si plumbi metallum ad auri fulgorem compares: quippè cùm videas Regum colla & Principum submitti genibus Sacerdotum, & exosculatis eorum dextris, orationibus eorum credant se commaniri.--- Pag. 40.
units.tr: "St Ambrose, in his book On the Dignity of the Priesthood, chapter 2: The honour and eminence of a bishop (he says) cannot be matched by any comparison. If you compare it with the splendour of kings and the diadem of princes, it will be far inferior, as if you compared lead with the lustre of gold; since you see the necks of kings and princes bowed at the knees of priests, and, kissing their right hands, they believe themselves strengthened by their prayers." — p. 40.

units.la: Cùm sæpe alibi, tùm præcipuè in hoc Tractatu Ambrosium Advocatū accersis; semel, {d}Hinc S. Ambrosius in Epist. ad Theodosiū &c. Rursus; {e}Utinam haberemus plures Ambrosios, &c. Post, {f}Inter grauissimos Authores, præexcellentia dignitatis Episcopalis supra Reges, habemus Ambrosium &c. Nec non, {g}Ambrosius divino zelo accensus. Tandem,{h} Si multos haberemus Ambrosios.
units.tr: Although you often summon Ambrose as your advocate elsewhere, especially in this Treatise: once, "Hence St Ambrose in his letter to Theodosius, etc."; again, "Would that we had more Ambroses, etc."; afterwards, "Among the most weighty authors, for the pre-eminence of episcopal dignity above kings, we have Ambrose, etc."; and again, "Ambrose, kindled with divine zeal." Finally, "If we had many Ambroses."

units.la: Pontificij etiam alij omnes (quotus Papale fastigium suffulcire student) de Ambrosio omnia bona dicere, eius nomen decantare, dicta facta celebrare solet, quasi qui in uno Ambrosio (utinam sano palato) ambrosiam ipsam degustâsse videantur. Quid rei sit avemus scire.
units.tr: All the other Papists too, as many as strive to prop up the papal eminence, are wont to say all good things of Ambrose, to sing his name, to celebrate his sayings and deeds, as if they seemed to have tasted the very ambrosia itself in the one Ambrose (would that their palate were sound). We long to know what the matter is.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Ambrosii, De Auro, Similitudinem Bellarminum mi-serè adulterásse.
units.tr: Of Ambrose, On Gold, that Bellarmine has wretchedly corrupted the comparison.

units.la: IN hac obiectione, cùm Ambrosii verba audiuimus, tum-etiam facta Eius vidimus, quæ utraque adversus iura Principum an quid ponderis habeant, accuratiùs, discutiendum: necesse tamen non est ut de verbis liticulam vobis intendamus. Quanquàm cùm potestatem spiritualem seculari præstare (iuxtà cum Nazianzeno) ut spiritum carni, & (secundùm Chrysostomum) ut cælum terræ, iam suprà concessimus, certè quidem non est cur de Ambrosii Similitudine laboremus. Damus igitur Diadema Regum Episcopali sublimitate multò esse inferius, quàm si plumbi metallum cum auri fulgore comparetur; nempe, si simpliciter, & non secundùm quid inter se conferantur. Exempli causâ. Aurum est non plumbo modò, sed & ferro omni præstantius, sive fulgorem, sive durabilitatem eius spectemus; at respectu usus bellici tam ad ferendos ictus, quàm ad hostes feriendos, ferro cedit.
units.tr: In this objection, when we have heard Ambrose's words and also seen his deeds, both of which must be examined more carefully to see whether they carry any weight against the rights of princes, it is not necessary, however, to wage a petty quarrel with you over words. Although we have already conceded, along with Nazianzen, that spiritual power surpasses secular power as spirit surpasses flesh, and (according to Chrysostom) as heaven surpasses earth, there is certainly no reason for us to labour over Ambrose's comparison. We therefore grant that the diadem of kings is far inferior to episcopal eminence if the metal of lead is compared with the lustre of gold; namely, if they are compared simply and not in some respect. For example: gold is more excellent not only than lead but than all iron, whether we look at its lustre or its durability; yet in respect of military use, both for bearing blows and for striking enemies, it yields to iron.

units.la: Eodem modo potestas spiritualis licet propter tum obiecti splendorem, nempè gratiam cœlestem; tum-etiam propter finem, quæ est vita æterna, Auro assimiletur, nihil tamen hoc impedit, quominùs Supremus Magistratus politicus, ad pacem externam sartam tectam conservandam, cuiuslibet ordinis Christianis regimine temporali dominetur. Ad quod significandum Dominus huius potestatis ferrum insigne esse voluit, ut patet Rom.13. Non enim frustrà gladium gestat, quia Minister Dei est, &c. In quo Textu, quùm Patres consulimus, Ecclesiasticis nullis (nisi ex Principum indulgentia) immunitatis est locus; non à subiectione, quia præmisit vers.3. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit. Nec à pœna, si forte contra pacem publicam deliquerint, quia attexit vers.4. Minister Dei est, & vindex [illegible, ~18 letters] adversus eum, qui malum operatur. Cui doctrinæ omnis antiquitas suffragata est. tuat[?] sicut nonnunquam Gentiles, & hæretici Principes ausi[?] sunt.
units.tr: In the same way, although spiritual power is likened to gold because of the splendour of its object, namely heavenly grace, and also because of its end, which is eternal life, this does not prevent the supreme political magistrate, for preserving external peace safe and sound, from ruling in temporal government over Christians of every rank. To signify this, the Lord wished iron to be the mark of this power, as is plain from Romans 13: For he does not bear the sword in vain, since he is God's minister, etc. In this text, when we consult the Fathers, no place for immunity is left to ecclesiastics (except by the indulgence of princes): not from subjection, because it is said in verse 3, Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; nor from punishment, if perhaps they have offended against the public peace, because it is added in verse 4, He is God's minister and an avenger [illegible] against him who does evil. All antiquity has supported this doctrine, as sometimes heathen and heretical princes have dared to do.

units.la: IV. Vt concludas penes Ecclesiasticam potestatem esse Principes pro suo arbitrio tàm spiritualibus quàm temporalibus (indirectè saltem) poenis coercere, adeandem Te recipis Similitudinem. {u}Vt spiritus (inquis,) quando fini spirituali caro officit, ei imperat & castigat, & si opus est indicit ieiunia, aliasq; afflictiones, etiam tum detrimento aliquo & debilitate ipsius corporis; & cogit linguam nè loquatur, & oculos nè videant &c. deinde etiam si ad finem spiritus obtinendum necessaria sit aliqua carnis operatio, & ipsa etiam mors, spiritus imperare potest, ut se, & sua exponat, ut in Martyribus videmus. Ità prorsus politica potestas habet suos Principes, leges, iudicia, &c. Et similiter Ecclesia suos Episcopos, canones iudicia: illi habent pro fine temporalis pacem, ista[?] salutem aeternam. — Si carnalis obest fini spirituali, spiritualis potest, ac debet coërcere temporalem omnis ratione & viâ, quæ ad id necessaria esse videbitur. {n}Vt posset spiritus disponere de sensibus & membris corporis, indicendæ illis ieiunia, flagella, vigilias: potest Pontifex mutare regna, & vni Regi asserre, & alteri conferre, si id necessarium est ad animæ salutem.
units.tr: IV. To conclude that the ecclesiastical power has it in its own judgment to punish princes, both spiritual and temporal, at least indirectly, you take refuge in that same comparison. As the spirit (you say), when the flesh hinders its spiritual end, commands and chastises it, and if need be appoints fasts and other afflictions, even with some loss and weakening of the body itself; and it compels the tongue not to speak and the eyes not to see, etc.; then also, if for attaining the spirit's end some action of the flesh, or even death itself, is necessary, the spirit can command it to expose itself and its own, as we see in the martyrs. Just so, political power has its princes, laws, judgments, etc.; and likewise the Church has its bishops, canons, and judgments: the former have peace as their temporal end, the latter eternal salvation. If the carnal hinders the spiritual end, the spiritual can and ought to restrain the temporal by every means and way that shall seem necessary for this. Just as the spirit can dispose of the senses and members of the body, appointing for them fasts, scourgings, and watchings, so the Pontiff can change kingdoms, assign them to one king and confer them on another, if this is necessary for the salvation of the soul.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Argumentum, à similitudine ductum, illustrare magis quàm probare.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. An argument drawn from a similitude serves to illustrate rather than to prove.

units.la: TAiunt[?] (ait {*}Apostolus) mulieres in Ecclesia, hinc elegantèr Lutherus; Humani (inquit) ingenij ratio sola in divinis minimè audiatur. Huiusmodi Tu nobis mulierem obtrudis, nempè Similitudinem hanc Caro & Spiritus fœcundam nimis, sed non fœlicem satis; vtpotè quæ contra mentem Authoris; contra sacræ Scripturæ doctrinam, contra Catholicæ Ecclesiæ praxin, contra Pontificum Rom. constantem professionem multiplici dissimilitudine laborat: eò quod non satis discernis, seculares & spirituales potestates in Repub. Christiana per se discretas esse & disparatas. Et quamuis ratio, à Similitudine ducta, sit omnium maximè imbellis, quæ non robur, sed solùm lumen disputationi adferat; in hac tamen totus es, nec Rationem vllam vspiam vrges vehementiùs. Rectiùs Dialectici, qui Similitudinem ad genus docendi exotericum & populare accommodant, Cuius in acroamatico & accurato arguendi genere rarus ac ferè nullus est visus; sic enim Princeps Philosophorum, [illegible, ~20 letters] Haud igitur in tàm coacta Similitudine adeò acriter Tibi insistendum fuit, in qua (quod de Sabinis dicitur) quod voluisti somniasti.
units.tr: Women should keep silence in the Church, as the Apostle says; hence Luther nicely remarks: "Human reason alone is by no means to be heard in divine matters." You thrust such a woman upon us: this comparison of flesh and spirit, too fruitful but not fortunate enough. It is at odds with the author's intention, with the teaching of Holy Scripture, with the practice of the Catholic Church, and with the constant profession of the Roman Pontiffs, and it suffers from many dissimilarities, because you do not sufficiently distinguish that the secular and spiritual powers in the Christian commonwealth are separate and distinct in themselves. And although an argument drawn from similitude is the weakest of all, which brings not strength to a dispute but only light, you nevertheless rely wholly on it, and you press no other reason more vehemently anywhere. The dialecticians are more correct, who adapt similitude to the exoteric and popular manner of teaching; in the esoteric and exact manner of arguing it is rarely or almost never seen. For thus the Prince of the Philosophers [illegible]. There was therefore no need to press so sharply upon so forced a similitude, in which (as is said of the Sabines) you dreamed what you wished.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Celebrem illam [CARNIS, & SPIRITVS] aduersus Prin- cipes detortum Similitudinem ab ipso Nazianzeno membratim refutari.
units.tr: That the famous similitude of [FLESH AND SPIRIT], twisted against princes, is refuted limb by limb by Nazianzen himself.

units.la: SImilitudinem hanc Carnis & Spiritus semel in libris de Pontifice obijcis; rursus repetis in Torto; in Responso ad Apologiam inculcas denuò; post contra Barclaium ingeris; atq; etiam insuper eam Lectori obtrudis in Epistola ad Anonymum: quam crambeh quinquies iam recoctam in hoc de Principum officio Tractatu reponis; ac si omnes fortunæ vestræ, & totius Causæ vestræ ædificiū hoc potissimum fundamento niteretur. Dabis (uti spero) mihi veniā, quùm sis in vrgenda hac Similitudine impendio prolixior atque impor tunior, si ego in ea refellenda maiorem operam insumam.
units.tr: You put forward this similitude of flesh and spirit once in your books on the Pope; you repeat it in The Tort; in the Response to the Apology you press it again; afterwards you hurl it against Barclay; and you even thrust it upon the reader in the Letter to Anonymous. Now you set this cabbage, already reheated five times, before us again in this treatise on the Duty of Princes, as if the whole of your fortune and the structure of your whole Cause rested chiefly on this foundation. You will (I hope) pardon me, since in pressing this similitude you are more lavish and more importunate, if I expend greater effort in refuting it.

units.la: Greg. Nazianzenus spiritualem quidem Sacerdotū potestatem supra Principum anthoritatem, in merè spiritualibus, hòn minūs quàm spiritum carni (nec sanè imeritò) præferendam esse iudicauit. At Principes, quoad externam dignitatem, aut temporalem coercionem potestati Ecclesiasticæ neutiquam subiecit: tantum enim abest vt Gregorius, cognomento Theologus, tàm tetram [illegible, ~8 letters] Christianis propinaret, vt planè contrariam illi mentem fuisse, vel mores ipsius demonstrent.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen did judge that the spiritual power of the priests is to be preferred, in purely spiritual matters, to the authority of princes, no less than spirit is preferred to flesh (and not without reason). But as to external dignity or temporal coercion, he by no means subjected princes to ecclesiastical power. Indeed, so far is Gregory, surnamed the Theologian, from offering the Christians so foul a [illegible], that his own conduct and character show his mind to have been quite the opposite.

units.la: I. Tu quemuis Principem, sanctissimum licet, si cum Episcopo vel nequissimo comparetur, stricto tamen iure Carnis loco habendum censes: quæ si fuisset Nazianzeni sententia, non vehementius Theodosium Imp. hortatus esset, vt gliscentia iam acerbissima inter Episcopos odia authoritate sua reprimeret. Esto finis inuidiæ (inquit) pacem colant Antistites, idque tua potissimum operâ; sedato tu Sacerdotum bellum, quis barbaram (id est, Barbarorum) audaciam compescuisti. En Tibi Episcopes carnales, sic enim Apostolus; Quam inter vos sit liuor, contentio, dissidia, nonne carnales estis? Ecce Theodosium Principem spiritualem, siquidem spiritus est actiones carnis moderari.
units.tr: I. You judge that any prince, however holy, if compared with a bishop, even the most wicked, must nonetheless be regarded in the strict sense of law as flesh. Had this been Nazianzen's opinion, he would not have urged the Emperor Theodosius more vehemently to restrain by his authority the most bitter hatreds now blazing among the bishops. Be an end to envy, (he says), let the prelates cultivate peace, and this especially by your effort; you who have checked the war of the priests, and who have restrained the barbarous (that is, of the barbarians) audacity. Behold, Bishops, carnal men; for thus the Apostle: "Since there is among you envy, strife, and divisions, are you not carnal?" Behold Theodosius the spiritual prince, since it belongs to the spirit to moderate the actions of the flesh.

units.la: II. Principem secularem minimè imperare Episcopis, nec Ecclesiasticis negotijs se immiscere debere, inde concludis, quia Caro spiritus imperio & throno subijcitur. At Greg. Nazianzenus, Vir (vt ait Ruffinus) per omnia incomparabilis, verbo & operibus clarus; hoc Tuum commentum verbis operibusq; redarguit, qui Thronum, id est, sacram ædem, sibi à Theodosio Imp. traditum post aliquot annos eidem Imperatori resignat, in hæc verba. Vicem tibi reddat, Imperator, Christus in die remunerationis pro beneficijs eius, quibus Ecclesiam affecisti. ---- Nunc te supplex peto, vt laboribus hisce liberer. Idcirco potestas conferendi alicui ædem Episcopalem iure quodam Regali Imperatori competit: quod à vobis inter Ecclesiastica negotia censetur. Eodem modo se gessit erga Principem irascentem, in eadem, quam allegas, oratione, dicens, Præclarissime præses (Vtinam liceat dicere, Mitissime) supplicationis loco cauiciem [?] meam Tibi offero. Sic Nazianzenus. Nec igitur absolutè se habet Princeps ad Episcopum, vt caro ad spiritum; quando enim fando auditum est, spiritum carni supplicasse?
units.tr: II. You conclude that a secular prince must not rule over bishops, nor interfere in ecclesiastical affairs, because the flesh is subjected to the rule and throne of the spirit. But Gregory Nazianzen, a man (as Rufinus says) incomparable in all things, famous for word and deed, refutes this fiction of yours by his words and deeds, when he gives back to the same Emperor, some years later, the throne, that is, the sacred church, which Theodosius the Emperor had given him, in these words: May Christ, on the day of recompense, repay you, Emperor, for the benefits by which you have blessed the Church. ---- Now I humbly ask you to free me from these labours. Therefore the power of granting a bishop's church to someone belongs to the Emperor by a certain royal right, which you count among ecclesiastical affairs. In the same way he behaved towards a prince who was angry, in the same oration which you cite, saying: Most distinguished governor (would that I might say, most gentle), I offer you my petition as a supplication. Thus Nazianzen. Therefore the prince is not absolutely related to the bishop as the flesh to the spirit; for when has it ever been heard, to speak plainly, that the spirit has begged the flesh?

units.la: III. In hac tua sententia [vz. Sicut caro & spiritus vnum hominem, sic potestas Ecclesiastica & politica vnam Remp. in qua politica Ecclesiastica, sicut caro spiritui subordinatur.] Adversarium habes S. Nazianzenum, etiam ubi eum Tibi Advocatum asciscis: {r}Subiecti sumus (inquit) tùm Deo, tùm invicem aliys aliy, tùm eis, qui cum Imperio in terris nobis praesunt: Deo quidem propter omnes causas, aliy aliys propter fraternum amorem, Magistratibus propter ordinis conservationem. — Etiam hoc in legum nostrarum numero est, & quidem laudabilium, praeclarissimè promulgaturum à spiritu, nimirum, ut quemadmodum heris servi, uxores maritis, Ecclesia Domino, discipuli pastoribus & doctoribus obtemperant, ita nobis etiam praescribitur, cunctis potestatibus eminentibus subiecti simus, non tantùm ob iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam, ut qui pendendo Tributo sumus obnoxi.
units.tr: III. In this your opinion [namely, just as flesh and spirit make one man, so ecclesiastical and political power make one commonwealth, in which the political is subordinate to the ecclesiastical, as flesh is to spirit], you have Saint Nazianzen as an opponent, even where you enlist him as your advocate: We are subject (he says) both to God, and to one another, to one another in turn, and to those who in the earth stand over us with authority: to God indeed on account of all things; to one another on account of brotherly love; to magistrates on account of the preservation of order. ---- This also is among our laws, and indeed a praiseworthy one, which the Spirit has most splendidly promulgated: that, just as slaves obey their masters, wives their husbands, the Church the Lord, disciples their ministers and teachers, so we also are commanded to be subject to all eminent powers, not only because of wrath, but also for conscience' sake, as those who are bound by the paying of tribute.

units.la: Tu ex Nazianzeno in Repub. Christiana nonnisi unam subordinationem, nempè, politicae potestatis spiritualis odorari & pervestigare potuisti: Nazianzenus vero aliam [illegible, ~10 letters] notat, Ecclesiasticæ scilicet Secularis; sed quasi in sphæra diuersa. Quodsi enim sphæram cœlestem, id est, Res meræ spirituales contemplemur, Princeps Episcopo subijcitur, quia (teste Nazianzeno) Lex Christi Imperium subiecit Sacerdotio. Sin Res temporales, ceu terrestrem sphæram intueamur, Potestas Ecclesiastica Politicæ subordinatur, sic enim Nazianzenus; Nos eminentioribus potestatibus & magistratibus subiecti sumus. Quam etiam Subiectionem abundè præstitit erga Tyrannum vel immanissimum, veluti rancidissimam & putridissimam carnem, Iulianum Apostatam; quem (fatentibus 'Iesuitis) idem Nazianzenus, quoad in vinis egit, ceu legitimum Imperatorem reueritus est.
units.tr: From Nazianzen you have been able to sniff out and track down in the Christian commonwealth only one subordination, namely of political power to spiritual. Nazianzen, however, notes another [illegible], namely of the ecclesiastical to the secular; but as if in a different sphere. For if we contemplate the heavenly sphere, that is, purely spiritual things, the prince is subject to the bishop, because (as Nazianzen bears witness) the law of Christ has subjected the empire to the priesthood. But if we look at temporal things, as at the earthly sphere, ecclesiastical power is subordinated to the political, for thus Nazianzen: We are subject to the higher powers and magistrates. He also showed this subjection fully towards a tyrant, even the most savage, as towards a rancid and putrid flesh, Julian the Apostate; whom (as the Jesuits confess) the same Nazianzen, so long as he acted in the vineyards, revered as a lawful Emperor.

units.la: Quid quod denique ais Episcoporum esse Principes coercere, vt castigare solet spiritus carnem, quoties hæc fini spirituali officit: At Ecclesiasticis omnes, quantumuis sacrilegij aut parricidij scelere inquinatos, ab omni coactiua Principum potestate esse exemptos. Hoc monstrum Nazianzenus planè iugulat, vbi {*}hortatus est Theodosium Imp. vt eâdem authoritate quorundam Sacerdotum audaciam reprimeret, qua ante Barbarorum Ethnicorum compescuerat. Proindè S. Nazianzeno magistro (ut cum Hieronymo loquar) glorior atque exulto, cuius si fletur iudicio, certè quidem vicimus.
units.tr: What is more, you finally say that it is for bishops to restrain princes, just as the spirit customarily chastises the flesh whenever it stands in the way of the spiritual end; yet all ecclesiastics, however defiled by the crime of sacrilege or parricide, are exempt from every coercive power of princes. Nazianzen clearly strangles this monster, when he urged the Emperor Theodosius to check the audacity of certain priests by the same authority with which he had restrained that of the heathen Barbarians before. Therefore, in Saint Nazianzen, my master (to speak with Jerome), I glory and exult; and if the verdict is judged by his, certainly we have won.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO. Eandem Similitudinem & rationibus, & Pontificiorum principijs manifesto connectti.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION. That the same Similitude is clearly connected both with the arguments and with the principles of the Papists.

units.la: QVùm de mente Nazianzeni satis iam constet, mens Bellarmini pertractanda accuratius atque exagitanda videtur, ut Lector intelligat, quot ille dissimilitudines, quámque vafra subtilitate ex vna Similitudine conflauerit. Similitudinem hanc, [Ut spiritus imperat carni, ita Ecclesiastica potestas politica;] Nos valdè probamus: at indè colligere, Primò, Ergò, Sicut caro & spiritus in vnum hominem, ita has duas potestates in vnam Rempublicam coalescere, dissimile omninò est: quia Caro destituta spiritu inanime & informe cadauer iacet; at status politicus separatus ab Ecclesiastico per se viuit & viget, muneribusque suis singulis satis liberè defungitur. Hoc testantur Iuliani secula, quando nefarius {a}Apostata, ciurato Christianismo, idolomaniae Ethnicae se addixit; cuius tamen imperio Nazianzenus, & Ecclesia ipsa, quoad regimen temporale, absque omni seditiosa molitione semper paruit.
units.tr: Since the mind of Nazianzen is now sufficiently clear, the mind of Bellarmine seems to need a more careful examination and scrutiny, so that the reader may understand how many dissimilarities, and with what crafty subtlety, he has drawn out of this one Similitude. We greatly approve this Similitude, [As the spirit rules the flesh, so the ecclesiastical power rules the political]. But to infer from it, first, therefore, just as flesh and spirit grow together into one man, so these two powers should coalesce into one commonwealth, is entirely unlike. For the flesh, deprived of spirit, lies as a lifeless and shapeless corpse; but the political state, separated from the ecclesiastical, lives and thrives by itself and discharges its individual duties quite freely. The age of Julian bears witness to this, when the wicked Apostate, having cast off Christianity, devoted himself to heathen idolatry. Yet Nazianzen, and the Church itself, so far as temporal government went, always obeyed his rule without any seditious attempt.

units.la: II. Ergò Politicum magistratum Carnem prorsus indigitari; Ecclesiasticum quemlibet purum putum Spiritum; dissimile etiam, "{b}Quia (iuxta Hieron.) quiuis Laicus, cùm baptizatur, Sacerdotium accipit Laici, id est, Baptismum, scriptum enim est, Reges nos & Sacerdotes Deo patrisuo fecit. Nec desunt {x}Doctores Pontificij, qui Infanti vnius dici, modò sit baptizatus, characterem cuiuslibet ordinis sacri imprimi tenent. Hoc docuit Guil. de monte Laudano, communiter receptus ibi à Cardinali, & aliys, & à Bonifacio. Et Thomas part.3.63.art.16. ad 1. per omnia Sacramenta (inquit) fit homo particeps Sacerdotij Christi, vtpotè particeps Sacerdotij Christi, utpote participans aliquem effectum eius. Hæc Nauarrus. Vos igiter insigni contumelia Magistratum & populum Christianum afficitis, dum eos Carni (quæ est pars hominis bruta) assimilatis: vobis autem ipsis semper Spiritualis cognomen arrogatis.
units.tr: II. Therefore the political magistrate is entirely designated as the flesh, and any ecclesiastic as pure spirit. This is also unlike: "Because (according to Jerome) every layman, when he is baptized, receives the priesthood of the laity, that is, Baptism; for it is written, He has made us kings and priests to God his Father." Nor are there lacking Papist teachers who hold that the character of any holy order is imprinted on an infant of a single day, provided only that he has been baptized. William of Mont-Laudun taught this, and it was commonly received there by the Cardinal, and by others, and by Boniface. And Thomas, part 3, q. 63, art. 16, ad 1: "Through all the sacraments," he says, "a man becomes a partaker of the priesthood of Christ, inasmuch as he participates in some effect of it." So says Navarrus. You therefore inflict a great insult on the Magistrate and the Christian people when you liken them to the flesh (which is the brutish part of man), while you always arrogate to yourselves the name of Spiritual.

units.la: III. Ergo Populum, ac Magistratum Laicum se causis Ecclesiasticis immisçere non magis debere, quàm solet caro spiritus negotia tractare; Dissimile : primò quià Magistratus politicus præscribit leges, quæ, quamuis politicæ sint, nihilominus spirituales haberi possunt; hisce enim Christianorum subditorum conscientiæ obligantur. Hic Te, Bellarmine, testem appello. {y}Lex (inquis) ciuilis non minùs obligat in conscientia quàm lex diuina, etsi minùs firma sit hæc, quàm illa. {z}Et licet lex politica dicatur temporalis, ratione obiecti, quia versatur circa temporalia & externa, tamen in se est res spiritualis. {a}Et obligat ad pœnam æternam, non quatenus lex hominis, sed quatenus lex Ministri Dei: {b}ut Rom. 13. qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Deinde quia tàm Magistratus politicus, quàm populus negotijs Ecclesiasticis nonnunquàm inseruiunt. De Populo {c}Bellarminus negare non potest, eum ex authoritate Conc. Nicæni se electioni presbyterorum admisçuisse; Eumque ex testimonio Cypriani, Sacerdotes eligendi potestatem & suffragium ferendi habuisse, licet more testis, non Iudicis. Deinde (ut Tolosanus vester) {d}Reges ipsos Pastores esse non tantùm corporum Subditorum, sed etiam, per consequentiam, animarum; pro quarum salute non minùs quàm pro corporum incolumitate, laborare debent, & auxilium Ecclesiæ contra Hæreticos & contemptores prabere. Iccircò Tu Carni spiritus actiones decernendi, curandi, dirigendi, & quodammodò eligendi vim & potestatem aliquam inesse probes oportet, priusquam illa tua de Carne & Spiritu analogia rite cohæreat aut consistat.
units.tr: III. Therefore the people and the lay magistrate ought not to meddle in ecclesiastical causes any more than the flesh is accustomed to manage the affairs of the spirit. This is unlike: first, because the political magistrate prescribes laws which, although they are political, may nevertheless be regarded as spiritual; for by these the consciences of Christian subjects are bound. Here I call you, Bellarmine, as witness. A civil law (you say) binds in conscience no less than divine law, although it is less firm than that. And although political law is called temporal by reason of its object, because it is concerned with temporal and external things, yet in itself it is a spiritual thing. And it binds to eternal punishment, not insofar as it is human law, but insofar as it is the law of God's Minister, as in Rom. 13: whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God. Then, because both the political magistrate and the people sometimes serve ecclesiastical affairs. As for the people: Bellarmine cannot deny that by the authority of the Council of Nicaea the people was admitted to the election of presbyters; and that, from the testimony of Cyprian, the people had the power and the right of voting in choosing priests, though in the manner of a witness, not a judge. Then (like your Tolosanus) kings themselves are shepherds not only of the bodies of their subjects but also, by consequence, of their souls; for whose salvation they ought to labour no less than for the safety of their bodies, and to afford help to the Church against heretics and despisers. Therefore you must prove that the flesh has some power of deciding, overseeing, directing, and in some measure choosing the actions of the spirit, before your analogy of flesh and spirit can properly hold together or stand.

units.la: IV. Vt ad subordinationem venianus) Ergo, sicut anima non immisçet se actionibus carni proprijs, nisi indirectè in ordine ad spiritualia, quatenus nimirum obsunt fini spirituali, qui est vita aeterna: itaque Papa directè negotiis temporalibus politici magistratus praesit, ut praesit Episcopus: sed quatenus necessaria videantur ad finem spiritualem. Dissimile; quia anima regit & moderatur carnis actiones directè omninò, haud aliter atq; Papa Episcopus praeesse assolet: potest enim imperare corpori ut edat, vel non edat, &c. Quod ex eadem similitudine ipse Papa Bonifacius sibi iam olim persuaserat: nam (teste Tolosano) {a}Quod omnis potestas, etiam temporalis, est à Papa, sibi aliquando persuasit Bonifacius VIII. in quodam Decretali, [ut anima dominatur in corpus:] posse igitur summos Pontifices transferre regna. Potestne igitur Papa Christianis Principp. regna auferre, & in alios transferre? Potest, inquitis; Ecqua ratio? [Sicut carnem anima, &c.] Quomodo autem istā authoritatem in Principes exerceat Pontifex? Bellarminus Papista, Indirectè, ait: Papa ipse Bonifacius, Imò (inquit) Directè. Eandem similitudinem dissimili & dispari iudicio vrgent; alter alteri, vterque verò magis veritati contrarius: quippè istam similitudinem in temporalibus obtinere iactant nequitèr. Quanquam hoc posito, quod in Temporalibus valeat, certè Papae Directum dominium indè colligi (& quidem rectius) Canonistae uno ore concluderent: id quod Caeterus Iurisconsultus contra Bellarminum demonstrat. {1}Vnica est anima in homine(omnium Thee-elozorum consensu) per quam homo omnia munia agit, vegetat, generat, &c. Ergo directè agit in omnibus, nisi velimus impropriè loqui, & plures animas in nobis ponere subiectas distinctas. ---- Nec dicere Papam habere potestatem in temporalibus, in ordine ad spiritualia, probat eum hanc indirectè habere magis quàm Regem indirectè authoritatem suam exercere, quia temporale quid facit in ordine ad iustitiam administrandam. V. Ergo, sicut ratio dominatur in corpus, non corpus in rationem; ita potestas spiritualis politica praesit, non autem ab caregitur. Dissimile, quia quoad Temporalia Deus Sacerdotes Principibus substituit, & subordinauit, tàm sub veteri, quam sub nouo Testamento. De veteri Pontificios Authores plurimos Testes * habuimus. De nouo Canon diuinus expressis verbis decreuit,§ Omnis anima potestatibus eminentioribus, [illegible, ~8 letters] subdita, vel subordinata sit. & rursus, h Necesse est [illegible, ~10 letters] subjici, non solum ob irã[?], sed etiam propter conscientiam. Quibus verbis Sacerdotes Regibus subjici, qui Patres Graeci non tenent? dixit * Espencaeus: quibus etiam Latini Patres astipulantur; & his accedit luculenta praxis cùm aliorum omnium, tùm Romanorum Episcoporum, qui Ethnicis infidelibus subiectionem fideliter praestiterunt. Multò igitur potiùs Regibus Christianis parere tenentur. Consequentia inexpugnabilis. b Si enim (ratiocinante Bellarmino) Christianis licet Regi subesse Ethnico, cur non potiùs Regi Christiano? Duplex enim subordinatio, & quasi reciproca in sacra pagina traditur; vna iuxta quam saeculares Principes Ecclesiasticis subduntur, [Obedite Praepositis vestris,] nempè in merè spiritualibus: de quibus Gregorius VII. Pont. i Quis Regum aut Imperatorum ex imposito sibi officio valet aliquem Christianum baptizare, vel corpus Domini conficere, vel (spiritualiter) ligare, & soluere? Altera est quoad Temporalia, quà Sacerdotes Regibus subijciuntur, Rom. 13. Omnis anima subdita sit, &c. respectu cuius reponere fas erit, Quis Sacerdotum, ex imposito sibi Sacerdotali officio, valet vel custodem carceris designare; vel k Meum ac Tuum definire; vel, ubi de Patrimonio litigatur, unum assem diuidere; vel in familia herciscenda legem figere; ne dùm quenquam, nè quidem indirectè, exilio multare; aut Magistratum de loco summouere ?
units.tr: IV. As to subordination: therefore, just as the soul does not interfere with the actions proper to the flesh except indirectly, in relation to spiritual things, insofar as they hinder the spiritual end, which is eternal life, so the Pope presides directly over the temporal affairs of the political magistrate, as a bishop presides, but insofar as they seem necessary for the spiritual end. This is unlike, because the soul governs and regulates the actions of the flesh altogether directly, just as the Pope and bishop are wont to preside; for it can command the body to eat or not to eat, and so on. From this same similitude Pope Boniface himself had long ago persuaded himself: for (according to Tolosanus) Boniface VIII once persuaded himself, in a certain Decretal, that all power, even temporal, is from the Pope, [as the soul rules the body]; therefore the supreme Pontiffs can transfer kingdoms. Can the Pope therefore take kingdoms away from Christian princes and transfer them to others? He can, you say. On what ground? [As the soul the flesh, etc.] But how does the Pontiff exercise this authority over princes? Bellarmine the Papist says indirectly; Pope Boniface himself, nay, says directly. They urge the same similitude with unlike and disparate judgment, each against the other, and both more contrary to the truth; for they wrongly boast that this similitude holds good in temporal matters. Yet granting that it holds good in temporal matters, the Canonists would with one voice conclude from it a direct dominion of the Pope (and indeed more rightly), as the other jurist demonstrates against Bellarmine. "There is one soul in man (by the consent of all the Peripatetics), by which man performs all his functions, is nourished, generates, and so on. Therefore it acts directly in all things, unless we wish to speak improperly and to posit several distinct souls in us, subject to one another." Nor does saying that the Pope has power in temporal matters in relation to spiritual ones prove that he exercises it indirectly any more than a king exercises his authority indirectly, since the temporal thing does its work in relation to the administration of justice. V. Therefore, just as reason rules the body and not the body reason, so the spiritual power presides over the political and not vice versa. This is unlike, because in temporal matters God has set priests under princes and subordinated them, both under the Old and under the New Testament. About the Old we have had very many Pontifical authors as witnesses. In the New, the divine Canon decreed in express words: Every soul be subject to the higher powers ... And again: It is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath, but also for conscience's sake. By these words, which Greek Fathers do not hold that priests are subject to kings? Espencaeus said so, and the Latin Fathers also agree; and to this is added the clear practice both of all others and of the Roman bishops, who faithfully rendered subjection to heathen infidels. Much more, therefore, are they bound to obey Christian kings. The consequence is unassailable. For if (reasoning as Bellarmine does) it is lawful for Christians to be subject to a heathen king, why not rather to a Christian king? For a double and, as it were, reciprocal subordination is handed down in Sacred Scripture. One, according to which secular princes are subject to ecclesiastics [Obey your rulers], namely in purely spiritual matters, concerning which Pope Gregory VII: What king or emperor, by the office imposed on him, is able to baptize any Christian, or to consecrate the body of the Lord, or to bind and loose spiritually? The other concerns temporal matters, in which priests are subject to kings, Rom. 13: Let every soul be subject, etc. In regard to this it will be right to reply: What priest, by the priestly office imposed on him, is able either to appoint the keeper of a prison, or to define Mine and Thine, or, where there is litigation over a patrimony, to divide a single penny, or to lay down a law in the division of an inheritance; not even indirectly to punish anyone with exile, or to remove a magistrate from his place?

units.la: VI. Ergo, Sicut spiritus castigat carnem, quoties obesse fini spirituali, ita potest spiritualis seculares Principes quacunque ratione coercere; ipsi autem spirituales à Coactiua Principum potestate sunt exempti. Dissimile; nam, secundùm Decreta Philosophorum, Nihil agit extra sphæram activitatis suæ : Nec enim piscantur homines in aëre, nec venantur leporem in medio Mari, ut ait Comicus. Quippè operatio omnis facultati suæ proportionata esse debet, nec pertingit ultrà obiectum debitum ac homogeneum. Itâ non est Regis Sacramenta administrare, nec Pontificis gladium distringere : sed, ut est apud Gratianum,{1} Regum est corporalem irrogare pœnam, Sacerdotum spiritualem inferre vindictam. Præclarum imprimis documentum in Othone{*} habuimus, qui Pius imperator Ioannem Papam feré omnium Pontificum deterrimum deposuit. Nè longior sim,{m} Pelagij Papæ dictū probamus; Patricium (is erat ab Imperatore quasi Prorex constitutus) fuisse Patrem Papæ in temporalibus, sicut Papa est eius pater in spiritualibus: eandemque professionem Romani Pontifices (vt{*}liquet) per multorum seculorum seriem posteritati testatissimam reddiderunt. De Episcopis alijs post{‡} videbimus.
units.tr: VI. Therefore, just as the spirit chastises the flesh whenever the flesh hinders the spiritual end, so the spiritual power can restrain secular princes in whatever way; but the spiritual themselves are exempt from the coercive power of princes. This is unlike. For, according to the decrees of the philosophers, nothing acts outside the sphere of its activity: for men are not fished for in the air, nor is a hare hunted in the middle of the sea, as the comic poet says. Indeed every operation must be proportioned to its faculty, nor does it reach beyond its due and homogeneous object. Thus it is not the King's business to administer the sacraments, nor the Pontiff's to draw the sword; but, as it stands in Gratian, it is for kings to inflict bodily punishment, and for priests to inflict spiritual vengeance. We had an outstanding proof of this in Otto, a pious emperor, who deposed John the Pope, almost the worst of all pontiffs. Not to be too long: we approve the saying of Pope Pelagius, that the patrician (who had been appointed by the emperor almost as his viceroy) was the father of the Pope in temporal matters, just as the Pope is his father in spiritual matters; and the Roman Pontiffs (as is clear) have handed down this profession to posterity, most amply attested through a long succession of centuries. Concerning other bishops we shall see later.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officiis

units.la: Sanctus Chrysostomus lib. 3. de Sacerdotio sic loquitur, [Sacerdotium regno tanto est excellentius quantum spiritus & carnis interuallum esse potest,] & hoc multis argumentis probat: loquitur autem de summo Sacerdotio, id est, de Episcopatu. Ex multis rationibus unam præterire nolo; Habent(inquit) & terrestres Principes vinculi potestatem, verum corporum solum: id autem, quod dico, Sacerdotis vinculum ipsam animam contingit, atque ad cælos usque perusdit[?]. Et infra; nam quasi iam in cælum translati, & supra humanum naturam positi, atque à nostris affectibus exempti, sic illi ad principatum istum perducti sunt. Quid multa? Rex aliquis, si cui ex subditis honorem hunc detulerit, ut potestatem habeat quoscunque volet in carcerem coniiciendi, eosdemque rursus laxandi, beatus ille & admirandus iudicio omnium fuerit. At verò qui à Deo tanto maiorem accepit potestatem, quanto etiam anima corporibus præstant, hic vilem dignitatem accipisse videri potest.
units.tr: Saint Chrysostom, in book 3 of On the Priesthood, speaks thus: [The priesthood is as much more excellent than kingship as the distance between spirit and flesh can be.] He proves this by many arguments, and he is speaking of the highest priesthood, that is, the episcopate. I do not want to pass over one of his many reasons. Earthly princes, he says, have power over bodies only, but the bond of the priest touches the soul itself and penetrates even to heaven. And a little further on: for they are, as it were, already translated into heaven, placed above human nature, and freed from our passions, and so they are raised to that dignity. What more? If a king were to confer on one of his subjects the honour of having the power to cast anyone into prison and to release them again, that man would be thought blessed and admirable in everyone's judgement. But he who has received from God a power as much greater as souls are greater than bodies, this man may seem to have received a trivial dignity.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Sacerdotes Regibus externa potestate non praecellere, licet Sacerdotium Regno, obiecto & fine, praemineat.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. Priests do not surpass kings in external power, although the priesthood excels kingship in its object and its end.

units.la: VNà cum S.Nazianzeno S.Chrysostomum producis, nobile sanè par Praesulum integerrimorum; qui quum feré quasi συγχωρι[?] essent, eandem sententiam eisdem pene verbis, adeoq; vnà, sine dubio, eàdemq; mente promulgárunt: quà quidem praestantiam ordinis spiritualis plurimum illustrant, itá tamen, vt dignitati & authoritati Regiae in temporalibus nihil quicquam detractum velint. Sacerdotium Regno praecellere, quantum carni spiritus, quantum terrae coelum, quantum corpori anima, & (addo ex Chrysostomo) multò etiam magis, nemo Christianus insiciabitur: huius tamen tantae tamque admirabilis potestatis, quam Deus (sic enim idem Chrysostomus) nec Angelis nec Archangelis datam voluit, excellentia quibus claudetur limitibus, & quousq; se extendat, dispiciendū Tibi fuerat. An vero ad Temporalia, itá vt Episcopi (quod passim inculcas) praecedentiam vbiq; & praesidentiam supra Principes; aut etiam ius vel castigandi, vel Regnis suis exuendi; & {p}Quaúis[?] ratione coercendi sibi vendicent? longè à nobis absit, vt tribuamus tantam tàm incomparabili Theologo vecordiam, qui planè κυσίσιμος[?], minimè αὐτοφυσίμος[?] fuit; cultor, non contemptor Regum.
units.tr: Together with Saint Gregory Nazianzen you cite Saint Chrysostom, a noble pair of most upright prelates, who, being almost in agreement, proclaimed the same opinion in nearly the same words, and so, without doubt, with one and the same mind. Indeed, they greatly illustrate the excellence of the spiritual order, yet in such a way that they wish nothing whatever to be taken away from the royal dignity and authority in temporal matters. That the priesthood excels kingship as spirit excels flesh, as heaven excels earth, as the soul excels the body, and (I add from Chrysostom) by much more besides, no Christian will deny. But you ought to have considered by what limits the excellence of this so great and so admirable power, which God (for so the same Chrysostom says) wished to be given neither to Angels nor to Archangels, is bounded, and how far it extends. Do Bishops (as you repeat everywhere) claim precedence and presidency over princes in all places, in temporal matters, or even the right to punish them, or to strip them of their kingdoms, or to restrain them by any means? Far be it from us to attribute such madness to so incomparable a theologian, who was altogether a lover of order, not a self-seeker, and a worshipper, not a despiser, of kings.

units.la: Comparatione inter Sacerdotii & Regnum, de muneris excellētia, institutā, vtriusq; praestantia, ex obiecti & finis dignitate aestimanda est. Mysterium Euangelij, seu pacis gratuitae in Christo finis, est salus aeterna per Christum Iesum, in gloriam Patris: Regni politici obiectum, publica res; finis, pax civilis: non potest igitur Sacerdotalis potestas Regiam non infinitis modis excellere. At propterea in ciuili hominum consortio, quoad praecedentiam, & honorem externum, Sacerdotem Regi praeponendum esse, nihil est minus consectarium. v. g. Astronomia, tanquàm ars nobilior, in perscrutandis coeli plagis ; Geographia tantùm in terræ climatibus , & dimensionibus rimandis versatur ; Ethicus excolit animum virtutum præceptis, vitámque instituit atque informat ad bene beateque viuendum ; Politicus verò Reipub. bono externo consulit. An igitur Ptolomæum ⌣[?]Archimedi, ⌣[?]Alexandrum ⌣[?]Aristoteli potestate & honore cedere æquum est ? Ad Rem propiùs accedam.
units.tr: A comparison between the priesthood and kingship, regarding the excellence of their office, must be judged by the dignity of their object and end, and by the superiority of each. The mystery of the Gospel, or the end of the gratuitous peace in Christ, is eternal salvation through Jesus Christ, to the glory of the Father; the object of political government is the public good, and its end is civil peace. Therefore the priestly power cannot fail to excel the royal power in infinite ways. Yet it is by no means a consequence that, in civil human society, a priest should be placed before a king as regards precedence and external honour. For example, astronomy, as the nobler art, is occupied with searching out the regions of the heavens; geography is concerned only with examining the climates and measurements of the earth; the moral philosopher cultivates the mind with the precepts of the virtues, and forms and shapes life for living well and happily; but the statesman looks to the external good of the commonwealth. Is it therefore fitting that Ptolemy should yield in power and honour to Archimedes, or Alexander to Aristotle? I shall come closer to the matter.

units.la: Infidelem Christus (quo quid abiectius)q Canem appellat ; Herodem item * Vulpem : Fidelem verò, honoris caussa,r filium Abrahæ nuncupat ; Iudas etiam quùm iam Apostolus erat, quia tamen tantùm nomine tenùs Christianusf, Diabolus dicebatur: quanquam quiuis verè sanctus, laicus licet, inter Eos numeratur, qui hujusmodi Regni coelestis hæredes censentur,ε quibus mundus non est dignus: quales diuinus noster Rhetor Chrysostomus dixit, dùm sacris mysterijs interfuit, quodammodò ad coelum rapi. "An censes te (inquit) in terris consistere ? annon potius euectigiò in coelos transferri ? Quod non multùm abludit ab illo Apoc. 1. Reges nos fecit, & Sacerdotes Deo. An quia vir verè Christianus infidelem & impium non minùs quàm Spiritus carnem, coelum terram, filius camem, hæres æternæ gloriæ Diabolum nobilitate & dignitate spirituali superat ; ideone quis virum Sanctum quaelibet cuiuis Regi non sancto, aut Imperatori Ethnico honore ciuili præferendum esse duxerit ? Tantum abest vt præcellentia ordinis, aut potestatis Spiritualis, ex respectu præstantiæ obiecti aut finis, aliquam, inferat præcedentiam ciuilis honoris aut authoritatis super Eos,qui in politico regimine Supremi constituti sunt.
units.tr: Christ calls the unbeliever a dog, than which nothing is more abject; likewise he calls Herod a fox. But the believer he calls, out of honour, a son of Abraham. Judas, even when he was already an apostle, was called a devil, because he was a Christian only in name. Yet any man who is truly holy, even if he is a layman, is counted among those who are regarded as heirs of the heavenly kingdom, of whom the world is not worthy; such a man our divine orator Chrysostom described, when he was present at the sacred mysteries, as being in some measure caught up to heaven. "Do you think," he says, "that you are standing on the earth? Are you not rather carried up into the heavens?" This does not differ much from that saying in Revelation 1: He has made us kings and priests to God. Or because a man who is truly Christian surpasses an unbeliever and an impious man in spiritual nobility and dignity, no less than spirit surpasses flesh, heaven earth, the son of God the son of man, the heir of eternal glory the Devil, has anyone therefore thought that a holy man should be preferred in civil honour to any king who is not holy, or to an heathen emperor? So far is the excellence of the spiritual order or power, judged by the superiority of its object or end, from implying any precedence of civil honour or authority over those who are set in supreme place in political government.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Veram Chrysostomi sententiam, de Regum suprematu, omnes Sophistarum Strophas confundere.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. Chrysostom's true opinion on the supremacy of kings confounds all the sophists' tricks.

units.la: DEindèiure quis miretur abs Te citari testem Chrysostomum quo nullum habes in hac Causa acriorem Aduer-
units.tr: Why should anyone be surprised that you cite Chrysostom as a witness, when you have no fiercer opponent in this cause than he is? Your adversary...

units.la: ε [?] Hebr.2.;8. Adversarium. Nec enim solos laicos, sed & Monachos, & Sacerdotes, atque etiam Apostolos secularibus Magistratibus subditos esse Chrysostomus diserte asserit. Id quod satis (inquit) declarat Apostolus, cùm dixit in exordio, [Omnis anima potestatibus subdita sit, etiamsi Apostolus sit, vel Propheta, sive (audiat hoc Papa, & nisi omnem pudorem abstersit, erubescat) Quisquis tandem fuerit. Etiam (non itaque tantum ex {y}discretione) Ex debito obedire subentur[?], non gratiam illis, sed debitum praestantes. Nec obedire solùm, verùm etiam seruiri[?], seu subordinari Regibus infidelibus: nec modo (tanquam tempori seruientes) {a}Donec vires ad resistendum comparaverint; sed ex intimis animi votis, iuxta illud Apostoli, [Orationes facientes pro omnibus hominibus, pro Regibus, & omnibus in sublimitate constitutis. 1.Tim. 2.] Unde Chrysost. {b}Quid sibi vult quòd ait primò{z} omnium [pro Regibus &c.] In obsequio-vz. quotidiano, perpetuoque divinae religionis ritu, quando diebus singulis mane vespere orationes fundantur ad dominum: quomodo? an pro fidelibus tantùm? id verum non esse, ostendunt quae sequuntur, [pro Regibus,] neque enim tunc Reges Deum colebant, sed multis postea temporibus in infidelitate perstiterunt. — Et ne adulationis causa Apostolum ita scripsisse putarent, vide quid adiunxit, [ut quietam vitam agatis] Haec Chrysost. quae versipelles Iesuitas plane iugulant, qui latronum & perduellionum lege freti, parendi infidelibus Regibus fidem dant, cùm hac perfida mentis reseruatione ac restrictione, Donec vires habuerint. Et ne Sanderus, & alij oggan-niant, Eos, qui obligabantur obtemperare infidelibus magistratibus, non perinde teneri subesse Regibus Christianis, ratione *Pacti & foederis in Baptismo initi; huic Paradoxo oppido scite occurrit Chrysostomus. {c}Sicut Principibus (inquit) & potestatibus, de quibus Apostolus, quanto magis religioso Principi parendum?
units.tr: Hebr. 2.8. Adversary. For Chrysostom clearly asserts that not only laymen but also monks, priests, and even apostles are subject to secular magistrates. The Apostle, he says, makes this sufficiently plain when at the outset he says, [Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, even if he is an apostle or a prophet, or (let the Pope hear this, and if he has not wiped away all shame, let him blush) whoever he may be. Indeed, not only out of respect, but of obligation, they owe obedience, rendering not a favour but a debt. And they must not only obey but also serve, or be subordinate to, even unbelieving kings; and not merely for as long as they are serving the moment, until they have gathered strength to resist, but with the sincere desires of the heart, according to the Apostle's words, [Making supplications, prayers, and intercessions for all men, for kings and all who are in high place, 1 Tim. 2.] Hence Chrysostom asks: What does he mean by saying first, "for all", [for kings, etc.]? In the daily obedience and constant worship of the divine religion, when prayers are offered to the Lord every morning and evening, how is it done? Only for the faithful? That this is not true the words that follow show: [for kings]; for in those days kings did not worship God, but in later times they remained in unbelief. And lest they think the Apostle wrote this out of flattery, see what he adds: [that we may lead a quiet life.] These are Chrysostom's words, which utterly slay the slippery Jesuits, who, relying on the law of brigands and traitors, give their pledge to obey unbelieving kings, with this treacherous mental reservation and restriction: until they have strength. And lest Sanders and others murmur that those who were bound to obey unbelieving magistrates are not equally bound to be subject to Christian kings, by reason of the pact and covenant entered into at baptism, Chrysostom meets this paradox most neatly: Just as the princes and powers of whom the Apostle speaks (he says), how much more ought one to obey a pious prince?

units.la: Ergo igitur ut has Chrysostomi sententias a Bellarmino (qui vnam, & ab hac caussa valdè seiunctim[?] praeterire nolit) praetermissas esse minime mirer? forte sentiebat vir sagax,Exceptionesfuas singulas à Chrysostomo in hac Caussa, prorsus dilui. I. nimirum, Episcopum obedire debere Principi secularibus; II. etiam Ex debito; III. Infidelibus Ethnicis; IV. adeoque magis Christianis: quae omnia ex diametro Bellarmini exceptionibus repugnant. Quid multa?Bellarminus Chrysostomum, & alios Graecos Patres crepat,deus bone! quâ fronte? quum praesertim Sacerdotes Regibus subesse,& subordinatos esse (teste ipso {*}Espencaeo)ex loco illo Apostoli [Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit] docuerint non modo Chrysostomus, sed etiam Theodoretus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus, ET QVI NON GRÆCI? Hucusque de Græcis; Latinos consulamus. Bellar. ex Latinis Patribus Ambrosio. Gregorio.
units.tr: Therefore, I am not surprised that these sentences of Chrysostom have been passed over by Bellarmine, who would not want to omit this one and is very far removed from this cause. Perhaps the shrewd man saw that each of his exceptions was utterly dissolved by Chrysostom in this cause: namely, I. that a bishop must obey a secular prince; II. even by right; III. unbelieving heathens; IV. and so much more Christians. All of these are in direct contradiction to Bellarmine's exceptions. What more is there to say? Bellarmine rails against Chrysostom and the other Greek Fathers, good God! With what face? Especially since not only Chrysostom but also Theodoret, Oecumenius, and Theophylact have taught, from that passage of the Apostle [Let every soul be subject to the higher powers], that priests are subject to and subordinate to kings (as Espencaeus himself testifies), and AND WHAT OF THE NON-GREEKS? So far concerning the Greeks; let us consult the Latins. Bellarmine, among the Latin Fathers, [cites] Ambrose and Gregory.

units.la: I. Ex Ambrosio.
units.tr: I. From Ambrose.

units.la: “S. Ambrosius in lib. de dignitate Sacerdotali cap.2. Honor (inquit) & sublimitas Episcopalis nullis poterit comparationibus adaequari; si Regum fulgori compares, & Principum diademati, longè erit inferius, quàm si plumbi metallum ad auri fulgorem compares: quippè cùm videas Regum colla & Principum submitti genibus Sacerdotum, & exofculatis eorum dextris, orationibus eorum credant se communiri.” — Pag.40.
units.tr: "St. Ambrose, in his book On the Dignity of the Priesthood, chapter 2: The honour and sublimity of a bishop (he says) can be compared with nothing at all; if you compare it with the splendour of kings and the diadem of princes, it will be far inferior, as if you compared lead with the lustre of gold: since you see the necks of kings and the knees of princes bowed before the priests, and, after kissing their right hands, they believe they are protected by their prayers." — p. 40.

units.la: Cùm sæpe alibi, tùm præcipuè in hoc Tractatu Ambrosium Aduocatû accersis; semel, {d}Hinc S.Ambrosius in Epist. ad Theodosiû &c. Rursùs; {e}Vtinam habueremus plures Ambrosios,&c. Post, {f}Inter grauissimos Authores, praeexcellentia dignitatis Episcopalis supra Reges, habemus Ambrosium &c. Nec non, {g}Ambrosius diuino zelo accensus. Tandem, {h}Si multos haberemus Ambrosios.
units.tr: You often cite Ambrose as your advocate elsewhere, but especially in this Treatise: once, Hence St. Ambrose in his letter to Theodosius, etc. Again, Would that we had more Ambroses, etc. Afterwards, Among the most weighty authors, we have Ambrose, etc., on the pre-eminence of episcopal dignity over kings. Nor again, Ambrose, kindled with divine zeal. Finally, If we had many Ambroses.

units.la: Pontificij etiam alij omnes (quotis Papale fastigium suffulcire student) de Ambrosio omnia bona dicere, eius nomen decantare, dicta facta celebrare solet, quasi qui in uno Ambrosio (vtinam sano palato) ambrosiam ipsam degustâsse videantur. Quid rei sit auemus scire.
units.tr: The other Papists, all of whom strive to prop up the papal eminence, are accustomed to say all good things about Ambrose, to sing his praises and celebrate his words and deeds, as though those who seem to have tasted ambrosia itself in the one Ambrose (I wish they had a sound palate). What the matter is, we wish to know.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Ambrosii, De Auro, Similitudinem Bellarminum mi-serè adulterâsse.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. Bellarmine has wretchedly corrupted the comparison of Ambrose, taken from gold.

units.la: IN hac obiectione, cùm Ambrosii verba audiuimus, tum-etiam facta Eius vidimus, quæ vtraque aduersus iura Principum an quid ponderis habeant, accuratiùs discutiendum: necesse tamen non est vt de verbis liticulam vobis intendamus. Quanquàm cùm potestatem spiritualem seculari præstare (iuxtà cum Nazianzeno) vt spiritum carni, & (secundùm Chrysostomum) vt cœlum terræ, iam suprà concessimus, certè quidem non est cur de Ambrosii Similitudine laboremus. Damus igitur Diadema Regum Episcopali sublimitate multò esse inferius, quàm si plumbi metallum cum auri fulgore comparetur; nempe, si simpliciter, & non secundùm quid inter se conferantur. Exempli causâ. Aurum est non plumbo modò, sed & ferro omni præstantius, siue fulgorem, siuè durabilitatem eius spectemus; at respectu vsus bellici tam ad ferendos ictus, quàm ad hostes feriendos, ferro cedit.
units.tr: IN this objection, since we have heard Ambrose's words and also seen his deeds, both must be examined more carefully, to see whether they have any weight against the rights of princes. Yet it is not necessary that we bring a quarrel against you over the words. Although, since we have already granted above (with Nazianzen) that spiritual power surpasses secular power as spirit surpasses flesh, and (according to Chrysostom) as heaven surpasses earth, there is certainly no reason for us to labour over Ambrose's comparison. We grant, then, that the diadem of kings is far inferior to episcopal sublimity, as lead compared with the lustre of gold; namely, if they are compared simply and not in some respect. For example: Gold is more excellent not only than lead but than all iron, whether we look at its brilliance or its durability; yet in respect of military use, both for bearing blows and for striking enemies, it yields to iron.

units.la: Eodem modo potestas spiritualis licet propter tum obiecti splendorem, nempè gratiam cœlestem; tum-etiam propter finem, quæ est vita æterna, Auro assimiletur, nihil tamen hoc impedit, quominùs Supremus Magistratus politicus, ad pacem externam sartam tectam conseruandam, cuiuslibet ordinis Christianis regimine temporali dominetur. Ad quod significandum Dominus huius potestatis ferrum insigne esse voluit, vt patet Rom. 13. Non enim frustrà gladium gestat, quia Minister Dei est. &c. In quo Textu, quùm Patres consulimus, Ecclesiasticis nullis (nisi ex Principum indulgentiâ) immunitatis est locus; non à subiectione, quia præmisit vers. 3. Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit. Nec à pœna, si forte contra pacem publicam deliquerint, quia attexit vers.4. Minister Dei est, & vindex [τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι,?] aduersus eum, qui malum operatur. Cui doctrinæ omnis antiquitas suffragata est.
units.tr: In the same way, spiritual power, although it may be likened to gold on account of the splendour of its object, namely heavenly grace, and also on account of its end, which is eternal life, nevertheless this does not prevent the supreme political magistrate, for preserving external peace secure and safe, from ruling the temporal government of Christians of every order. To signify this, the Lord wished that iron be the emblem of this power, as is plain from Rom. 13. For he does not bear the sword in vain, for he is God's minister, etc. In this text, when we consult the Fathers, there is no place for any ecclesiastical immunity (except by the indulgence of princes): not from subjection, since it begins at verse 3: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. Nor from punishment, if they should happen to offend against the public peace, since it adds at verse 4: He is God's minister and an avenger [τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι] against him who does evil. All antiquity has supported this doctrine.

units.la: Porrò si Papa (egregius scilicet rerum æstimator) Sacerdotio Imperium omni modo inferius esse iudicaret, non, ad maiorē dignitatis splendorem conciliandum,{i} (Coronam insigne Imperij cum mitra (vt solet) consociaret. Hæc de Ambrosii verbis, & Similitudine, ab Auro ductâ, quo oculos lectores perstringere conatus es. Iam facta expendamus, quæ ad tria Capita reducuntur; I. Ambrosius Theodosium excommunicauit. II. Legem præscripsit. III. Templi cancellis semouit.
units.tr: Moreover, if the Pope (a fine judge of affairs, no doubt) judged that the empire is in every way inferior to the priesthood, he would not, to bring greater splendour to his dignity, have joined the crown, the emblem of empire, with the mitre (as he is accustomed to do). These are the words of Ambrose and the comparison, drawn from gold, with which you have tried to dazzle the eyes of your readers. Now let us weigh the deeds, which are reduced to three heads: I. Ambrose excommunicated Theodosius. II. He prescribed a law. III. He removed him from the chancel of the temple.

units.la: Bellarminus alibi.
units.tr: Bellarmine elsewhere.

units.la: {k}Non potuit Ambrosius excommunicare Imperatorem Theodosium propter eadem illam, nisi priùs causam illam cognouisset, & adiudicâssset, & nisi etiam in foro externo legitimus Iudex Theodosij fuisset. Post cogebat Imperatorem ad legem politicam ferendam; at prescribere ei formam legis nonne manifeste ostendit, posse Episcopum interdùm temporali potestate uti, etiam in eos, qui potestatem super alios acceperunt? Et si Episcopus id potest, quanto magis (Papa) Episcopus Episcoporum? Et in hoc Tract. Deinde quùm post pœnitentiam aliam ingressus est Theodosius cancellos templi, Ambrosius non conticuit, sed locorum differentiam eum docens, iubet ei vt exeat, & cum reliquis Laicis consistat. --- pag.334. Sic Tu.
units.tr: Ambrose could not have excommunicated the Emperor Theodosius for that act unless he had first investigated the case and passed judgment on it, and unless he had also been a lawful judge of Theodosius in the external forum. Next, he compelled the Emperor to enact a civil law; but does not prescribing the form of the law to him clearly show that a bishop may sometimes use temporal power, even against those who have received power over others? And if a bishop can do this, how much more can the Pope, the bishop of bishops? And on this point, the treatise. Then, when Theodosius, after his other penance, entered the chancel of the church, Ambrose did not keep silent but, teaching him the difference of places, ordered him to leave and stand with the other laymen. --- p. 334. Thus you.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Ambrosium aduersus Imperatorem nullum processum fe- rensem tentasse.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. That Ambrose attempted no legal proceeding against the Emperor.

units.la: ERgonè Temporali potestate vsus est Ambrosius? Conclusio lubrica, nè dicam perfida. Quid enim (vt ab Excommunicatione auspicemur) absurdius, quàm Citationes, Testificationes, & Adiudicationes, in foro spirituali, Temporalis potestatis partes proprie dictas censere? Enimvero Ambrosius aduersus Theodosium processu forensi non est vsus; non citatur Reus; non pro tribunali sistitur; nulli accersuntur testes; sed nè nominantur quidem; non dicta Causa; non sententia in Eum, ad formam externi iuris, fertur. Nihil horum historia meminit. Sed Thessalonicae quidam, è comitatu Caesaris, per populi tumultum interfectus est: Theodosius, ira dissimulata, plebem ad ludos Circenses inuitat: ibi repente à militibus in inermes, noxios iuxta & innoxios, sæuitum: non ex meritis, sed ex furore pœna grassata est. Nihil hic inquisitione opus erat, facinus omnium oculis expositum, cuius tot Testes, quot in isthac clade ceciderant, cadauera mortuorum; imò verò etiam ipsi Ambrosio (per Theodosij minas) cognitum antequam designatum: Factum (inquit Ambrosius) quod revocari non potuit, imò quod atrocissimum fore dixi. Ambrosius igitur nullum adhuc Temporale munus obiisse cernitur; Imperatore superior, sed in propria specie potestatis, eiusque non forensis aut coactiuæ, sed tantùm spiritualis.
units.tr: Did Ambrose therefore use temporal power? A slippery conclusion, not to say treacherous. For what could be more absurd (to begin with excommunication) than to count citations, testimonies and judgments in the spiritual forum as the proper parts of temporal power? Indeed Ambrose did not use a forensic process against Theodosius: the defendant is not summoned; he is not brought before a tribunal; no witnesses are called, not even named; the case is not heard; no sentence is pronounced against him according to the form of external law. History records none of this. But at Thessalonica a certain man from the Caesar's retinue was killed in a riot of the people. Theodosius, hiding his anger, invited the common people to the Circus games; there, suddenly, the soldiers fell upon the unarmed, the guilty and the innocent alike, and raged against them. The punishment spread not according to merits but according to fury. Here there was no need of inquiry: the deed lay open to everyone's eyes, and of its witnesses there were as many as there were corpses of the dead who had fallen in that slaughter; indeed the deed was known even to Ambrose himself (through Theodosius' threats) before it was carried out. "The deed," says Ambrose, "could not be undone; indeed, I said it would be most atrocious." Ambrose, therefore, is seen to have performed no temporal office; he is superior to the Emperor, but in the proper kind of power, and that not forensic or coercive, but purely spiritual.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Frigidum & ieiunum esse, quod Bellarm. de lege condenda, & de cancellis interdicendis obiicit.
units.tr: What Bellarmine objects concerning the enacting of a law and the forbidding of the chancels is cold and pointless.

units.la: ATque cogebat Imperatorem (inquis) legem politicam condere: hoc manifeste ostendit, posse Episcopum interdum Temporali potestate uti. Sic Tu, quasi Theodoreto innixus; "sed cedo nobis verba Theodosij. " "Quoniam (inquit Ambrosius) irato animo obsecutus contra innoxium populum sententiam pronunciasti, conscribe legem, quâ deinceps sententia, per iracundiam pronunciata, irrita sint, & cognitiones Causarum de cæde deinceps ad triginta dies scriptæ maneant." ---- Istud consilium Imperator, quoniam prudentissimum esse censebat, libenter amplexatus, iubet exemplo conscribi legem, suâque subscriptione confirmat. Bene habet, erat Theodosius ad iram præceps natura, & concitatior; hoc in Epistola ad Eum ostendit Ambrosius: " Quod habes (inquit) fidei studium, non possum negare; quod Deus Timorem, non diffiteor: sed habes naturam impetum, quem si quis lenire velit, cito vertis ad misericordiam; & si quis stimustimulet, in maius exsuscitas, ut eum revocare vix possu: vtinam si nullus mitiget, nullus accendat. Hæc Ambrosius.
units.tr: "And he compelled the Emperor (you say) to enact a political law: this clearly shows that a bishop can sometimes use temporal power." Thus you, as if leaning on Theodoret. "But let me give you the words of Theodosius." "Since (says Ambrose), having yielded to an angry mind, you pronounced sentence against an innocent people, draw up a law by which sentences pronounced thereafter in anger shall be void, and the records of cases of bloodshed shall remain written up for thirty days." The Emperor, thinking this counsel most prudent, gladly embraced it, ordered the law to be drawn up accordingly, and confirmed it with his signature.
