Well, Theodosius was by nature headlong into anger and rather impetuous; Ambrose shows this in his letter to him: "The zeal of faith that you have, I cannot deny; that you fear God, I do not deny: but you have a nature of impetuosity, which if anyone wishes to soothe, you quickly turn to mercy; and if anyone stimulates it, you rouse it to greater heights, so that it can hardly be recalled: would that no one either soothed it or inflamed it." Thus Ambrose.

units.la: Posteà ira seu furor iste in horrendam stragem illam {o}Thessalonicensem irrupit, in qua septem millia hominum interfecta fuere. dat tandem Ambrosius (sic enim vocatur) {p}Consilium conscribendæ legem illam, tanquam pœnitentiæ non fucatæ testimonium certissimum; non tamen ut pro præterito peccato satisfaceret, sed ut de futuro sibi caveret: quod medicamentum (ita enim appellatur) nemo Temporale fuisse dixerit, sed quale Ethnicus Philosophus Augusto adhibuit, quem (quòd Eum sensit ingenio in iracundiam præcipitem fuisse) monuit imperare sibi, ut {q}viginti quatuor Græcas literas repeteret, priusquam iracundiæ flammâ præsenti exardescens, aliud quicquam diceret aut faceret; ut isthoc pacto morbum animi, quem ratio non poterat, mora sanaret. Unica restat, de discessione è Cancellis, Obiectio. Inter Templi Cancellos Imp. exire iubetur, locum cedit. Respondeo; {r}Ritus ipse si spectetur, [illegible, ~5 letters] fuit, in Ecclesia Mediolanensi prohibitus, in Constantinopolitana obtinuit; sin eventum consideremus, hunc quis felicem magis existimet, quam necessarium, & non tam prudentiæ Ambrosy (nisi forte Imperatoris indolem satis perspectam, & exploratam habuerit) quam Theodosij facilitati & humilitati tribuendum. Nullus autem est facilior quam zeli excessus: sed & nullus venia dignior; id quod in Ambrosio Bellarminus fateri debet, siquidem principijs suis constare velit: ipse enim Iudaeorum patrocinium in se suscepit, quorum {f}Sectam tolerandam esse docet. At Ambrosius apud Imperatorem defensionem facti sustinet cuiusdam Episcopi, aliorumque Christianorum, qui Synagogam Iudaeorum incenderant: pro quibus in hunc modum orditur {s}Ambrosius; Poposci Imperator, ut in me magis vindicares; & hoc, si crimen putares, mihi ascriberes; quid manimandata in absentes iudicium? habes praesentem, habes consitentem reum, proclamo quòd ego Synagogam incenderem, quòd ego illis mandauerim, nè esset locus, in quo Christus negaretur.—Non est causa, vt propter aedificij exustionem in populum tàm seuerè vindicetur, multò autem minus, quia Synagoga incensa est perfidiae locus, impietatis receptaculum, quod Deus damnauit ipse, {u}"Ierem. 7." Haec Ambrosius aduersus Iudeos. Quodsi pari zelo contra eosdem, quos hodie Pontifex placidâ quiete frui mediâ Româ permittit, bonus senex æstuaret, Deus bone! quas turbas daret? vtcunque Ambrosij zelus non invasit Regum tribunalia, nec egressus est parietes Templi sui. Haec ad Ambrosium; nunc ex Ambrosio.
units.tr: Afterwards that same anger or fury burst out into that horrible slaughter at Thessalonica, in which seven thousand men were killed. Ambrose at last gives (as he is called) counsel for drawing up that law as the most certain evidence of a repentance that was not feigned; yet not so that he might make satisfaction for a past sin, but so that he might guard himself against the future. No one would say that this remedy (for so it is called) was temporal; it was like the remedy the heathen philosopher applied to Augustus. Knowing that Augustus was headlong into anger, the philosopher advised him to command himself to recite the twenty-four Greek letters before he said or did anything while flaring up with the present flame of anger, so that by this delay the disease of the mind, which reason could not cure, might be healed. One objection remains, concerning withdrawal from the chancels. It is said that the Emperor is ordered to go out from among the chancels of the Temple, and he yields the place. I answer: if the rite itself is considered, [illegible] was forbidden in the Church of Milan but prevailed at Constantinople; if we consider the outcome, who would judge this more fortunate than necessary, and to be attributed not so much to the prudence of Ambrose (unless perhaps he had a sufficiently clear and tested knowledge of the Emperor's disposition) as to the facility and humility of Theodosius. Yet no fault is easier than an excess of zeal; and none is more worthy of pardon. Bellarmine must concede this in Ambrose if he wishes to remain consistent with his own principles, for he himself has taken up the defence of the Jews, whose sect he teaches ought to be tolerated. But Ambrose, before the Emperor, defends the deed of a certain bishop and other Christians who had set fire to the synagogue of the Jews. On their behalf Ambrose begins in this manner: "I demanded, Emperor, that you should rather take vengeance on me; and if you thought it a crime, you should have ascribed it to me. What is the point of a judgment against absent men? You have me present, you have a defendant who confesses. I declare that I set fire to the synagogue, that I ordered it, so that there would be no place in which Christ would be denied." "There is no reason that such severe punishment should be inflicted on the people on account of the burning of a building, much less because the synagogue was a place of unbelief and a refuge of impiety, which God Himself has condemned," {u}"Jer. 7." "Thus Ambrose against the Jews." But if the good old man had been seething with the same zeal against those whom the Pontiff today permits to enjoy peaceful quiet in the middle of Rome, good God! what uproars would he cause? However, the zeal of Ambrose never invaded the tribunals of kings, nor did it go beyond the walls of his own Temple. So much for Ambrose; now from Ambrose.

units.la: III ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. Remark.

units.la: Ambrosium, rectè intellectum, sublimitatis Regiae propugnatorem fortissimum, cultoremque humilli- mum fuisse.
units.tr: That Ambrose, rightly understood, was the most courageous champion of royal dignity and the most humble servant of it.

units.la: Pontificij, quoties superiora Ambrosij facta commemorant, dici vix potest quantis clamoribus & vociferationibus excipiant; Nos vero tantum abest vt quicquam de Ambrosij iusta laude decerpamus, vt nomen Ambrosij (id quod significat) immortale esse cupiamus: qui si meritis, iurisdictione, debito erga Principes obsequio, aliisque virtutibus cum Papa Romano comparetur, in omnibus æqualis, in pluribus certè quidem superior reperietur. Ecquid egregium in Ambrosio quaerat quis? si accuratum iudicium, {x}vocabatur Arx fidei: si zeli vtriusque præstantiam? Ambrosium nouì, (inquit Imperator Theodosius) solum dignum qui Episcopus nominetur. Itaque si omnes omnium literae obliteratae essent, tamen hic vir vnus optimus, prudentiae, grauitatis, ac pietatis laude florentissimus, omniúmque seculorum memoria merito celeberrimus, præ Alijs in hac Causa à nobis consulendus esset, & Aduersariorum ingenia ad eius iudicium, tanquàm ad amussim exploranda.
units.tr: Whenever they recall Ambrose's earlier deeds, the Papists cannot be described as receiving them with enough shouting and clamour. We, for our part, are so far from detracting anything from Ambrose's well-deserved praise that we wish his name, which means immortal, to be indeed immortal. If he is compared with the Roman Pope in merit, in jurisdiction, in the due obedience he showed to princes, and in his other virtues, he will be found equal in all respects and certainly superior in many. What outstanding quality in Ambrose would anyone seek? Is it his sound judgment, which was called the citadel of faith? Or the excellence of his zeal on both fronts? I have known Ambrose, says the Emperor Theodosius, to be the only man worthy to be called bishop. So even if all the writings of all men had been lost, this one excellent man, flourishing in the praise of prudence, gravity and piety, and deservedly most famous in the memory of all ages, would still have to be consulted by us in this cause before others, and the wits of our opponents tested against his judgment as against a rule.

units.la: I. Illi; Non debent Principes in caussis Ecclesiasticis authoritatem suam interponere. At Hic, ({y}Auxentio Episcopo Mediolanensi ex humanis abeunte, & Ecclesia iam vacante, populóque Ambrosium adhuc virum Consularem unà voce Episcopum postulante) cùm ad Imperatorem relatum esset populi desiderium, & omni maturitate iuberetur impleri; Imperatoris authoritati obtemperandum duxit.
units.tr: I. They say: Princes ought not to interpose their authority in ecclesiastical causes. But he, when Auxentius, bishop of Milan, had departed this life and the Church was now vacant, and the people, with one voice, were demanding Ambrose, still a man of consular rank, as their bishop, when the people's wish was reported to the Emperor and he ordered it to be carried out with all speed, thought that he must obey the authority of the Emperor.

units.la: II. Illi; {a}Bona Clericorum tàm Ecclesiastica, quàm secularia libera sunt à tributis Principum secularium. Ambrosius verò; {b}Magnum quidem & speciale documentum est, quo Christiani viri sublimioribus potestatibus docentur debere esse subiecti, Lex, quæ nullum Christianum excipit omnes includit. quin & insuper Ambrosius; {c}Agri Ecclesiæ soluunt tributum.
units.tr: II. They say: The goods of clerics, both ecclesiastical and secular, are free from the taxes of secular princes. But Ambrose says: It is indeed a great and special proof by which Christian men are taught that they ought to be subject to higher powers: a law which excludes no Christian but includes everyone. Moreover, Ambrose also says: The fields of the Church pay tribute.

units.la: III. Illi; {d}Penes Pontificem Rom. seu Christi Vicarium est Clericos eximere. Quid Ambrosius? {e}Si Censum Dei filius soluit, quis tu es qui putas non esse soluendum? Quasi dixerit Ambrosius; Quisquis homo es, seruus es, [nec est seruus maior Domini suo.] Nec valet Responsum; {f}Christum soluisse tributum, quia voluit, non quia debuit; quia actio ex parte Christi, quamuis liberrima, Eis tamen, quibus loco documenti praescribitur, necessitatem imitationis imponit. unde est quòd Ambrosius ex hoc Christi exemplo confirmauerit Magnum illud & speciale (ut vocat) documentum, quo Christiani docentur debere Principibus esse subiecti; Et rectè, nam [Christus etiam oblatus est, quia voluit,] Actio liberrima, habens in se [potestatem ponendi animam suam:] Et tamen Christianis necessitatis incumbit, quoties Causa subest, patiendi; {f}[Qui non accipit crucem suam, & sequitur me, non est me dignus, qui seruat vitam suam, perdet eam &c.
units.tr: III. They say: It belongs to the Roman Pontiff, that is, Christ's Vicar, to exempt clerics. What does Ambrose say? If the Son of God paid the census, who are you to think it should not be paid? It is as if Ambrose had said: whoever you are, you are a servant, [nor is a servant greater than his lord.] Nor does the reply hold good that Christ paid tribute because he willed to, not because he was obliged to; for an action on Christ's part, however entirely free, nevertheless imposes a necessity of imitation on those for whom it is set forth as a pattern. That is why Ambrose, from this example of Christ, confirmed that great and special proof (as he calls it) by which Christians are taught that they ought to be subject to princes; and rightly so, for [Christ was also offered up because he willed it,] a most free action, having in itself [the power of laying down his life]. Yet Christians are under a necessity, whenever the cause requires it, of suffering: [He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me; he who saves his life will lose it, etc.

units.la: IV. Ille; {g}Clerici non subiiciuntur legibus politicis obligatione coactiua, sed solùm directiua. Ambrosius verò; {b}Vbi dicit Apostolus [Iccirco tributa pendimus, Ministri enim Dei sunt] ideo dicit Tributum pendi, ut subiectionem præstent, quùm sciant se non esse liberos, sed SVB POTESTATE eius, qui vicem Dei agit, sicut Deo.
units.tr: IV. They say: Clerics are not subject to civil laws with a coercive obligation, but only with a directive one. But Ambrose says: Where the Apostle says [Therefore we pay tribute, for they are ministers of God], he says that tribute is paid so that they may render subjection, since they know that they are not free but UNDER THE POWER of him who acts in God's place, as to God.

units.la: Quibus verbis docet, ex necessitate soluendi tributum necessariam obligationem Subiectionis, & subordinationis demonstrari; quæ quidem quùm præstanda sit Magistratui politico, Vicem Dei agenti, sicut Deo, non potest Pseudo-vicarii Christi vllo iure dissolui.
units.tr: By these words he teaches that from the necessity of paying tribute there is demonstrated a necessary obligation of subjection and subordination. Since this is owed to the political magistrate, acting in God's place, as to God, it cannot by any right be dissolved by the pseudo-vicar of Christ.

units.la: V. Illi; {*}Si Principes vel hæresin defenderint, vel tyrannidem exercuerint, penes Papam & Ecclesiam est, Principibus prius excommunicatis Subditos eorum fidelitatis iuramento absoluere, & quamprimùm viribus valuerint, ad arma contra eos consistare, imò etiam pœnas Principibus infligere, & quàuis ratione eos regnis suis spoliare. An sacrum Ambrosii pectus tam tetrum in se monstrum aleret? Absit! qui soluit Imperatorem resipiscentem Excommunicationis vinculo, soluturusne erat subditos eius vinculo & sacramento fidelitatis, si forte contra sua monita tyrannicè animum obfirmâsset? Si regnum (inquit) flectit in tyrannidem, en me paratum mori. Rursus, quùm {i}Ariani vnam de Mediolanensis Ecclesiæ basilicis (Imp. Valentiniano annuente) occupare vellent; {k}Rogamus, Augustæ, (inquit) non pugnamus. Quibus igitur armis Episcopo contra immanem Principum tyrannidem se defendere liceat? Habeo (inquit) defensionem, sed in orationibus pauperum. {l}Dico paratum[?] me esse, vt si ill: fecerit, quod solet esse Regiæ Maiestatis, ego subirem quod Sacerdotis esse consueuit. Dolere potero, potero flere, potero gemere. Aduersus Arma, milites, Cothofque LACHRYMAE MEA ARMA SVNT; TALIA ENIM MVNIAMENTA SVNT SACERDOTIS, ALITER NEC DEBEO RESISTERE. Ambrosius non debuit resistere: At Papa forsan debet; cuius est contumeliosos Principes, seu Arietes, QVACVNQVE RATIONE coercere. Imò etiam, {m}Sacerdotum tyrannis infirmitas est, Cum infirmor (ait Apostolus) tum potens sum; aliter Sacerdotes nunquàm tyranni fuerunt, sæpe tyrannidem passi. Postremò Dauid cecinit Deo, [Tibi soli peccavi.] Hinc Ambrosius; {n}Rex utique erat (inquit) nullius ipse legibus tenebatur, quia liberi sunt Reges vinculis delictorum. Quæ Ambrosij Apologia, aduersus Pontificios, [illegible, ~5 letters] & accusatio esse posset. In his & alijs, de Theodosij potestate, quanto nos rectius, UTINAM multos Theodosios haberemus? &c. Hæc de primo Patre Latino; sequitur secundus.
units.tr: V. They say: If princes either defend heresy or exercise tyranny, it is for the Pope and the Church, after first excommunicating the princes, to absolve their subjects from their oath of fidelity, and as soon as they have the strength, to take up arms against them; indeed even to inflict punishments on princes, and by whatever means to strip them of their kingdoms. Could the sacred breast of Ambrose have nourished so hideous a monster? Far from it! He who absolved the repentant Emperor from the bond of excommunication, would he have been about to release his subjects from the bond and oath of fidelity, had the Emperor perhaps hardened himself tyrannically against his admonitions? If the kingdom (he says) turns to tyranny, behold me ready to die. Again, when the Arians wished to seize one of the basilicas of the Milanese Church, with the consent of the Emperor Valentinian: We ask, Augustus (he says), we do not fight. By what arms, then, may a bishop be permitted to defend himself against the savage tyranny of princes? I have a defence (he says), but it is in the prayers of the poor. I say that I am ready, so that if he did what is customary for royal majesty, I would undergo what is customary for a priest. I can grieve, I can weep, I can groan. Against arms, soldiers and Goths MY TEARS ARE MY ARMS; FOR SUCH ARE THE FORTIFICATIONS OF A PRIEST, OTHERWISE I OUGHT NOT TO RESIST. Ambrose ought not to have resisted: but perhaps the Pope ought; whose office it is to restrain insolent princes, or battering-rams, BY WHATEVER MEANS. Moreover, the tyranny of priests is weakness: "when I am weak, then I am strong," says the Apostle; otherwise priests were never tyrants, but often suffered tyranny. Lastly, David sang to God, [Against thee only have I sinned.] Hence Ambrose: He was indeed a king; no one bound him by their laws, since kings are free from the chains of their offences. This would be Ambrose's apology, and an accusation, against the Papists, [illegible, ~5 letters]. In these and other matters, concerning the power of Theodosius, how much more rightly we would act, if only we had many Theodosiuses! etc. These things are said of the first Latin Father; the second follows.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic. ex Gregorio I. Pont.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices, from Gregory I, Pope.

units.la: “ Sanctus Gregorius in Epistola &c. ---- pag.40.
units.tr: "Saint Gregory in the Epistle," etc. ---- p. 40.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Siste gradum parumper, Bellarmine, & de Gregorij testimonio dicturus hunc ordinem obserua, vt primo in loco quam in Principes authoritatem; deinde quantam ab eis, erga Sacerdotes, Reuerentiam exigat Gregorius Lectoribus innotescat. Incipe. ° Si quis Antistitum, (inquit Greg.) {p}Iudicum, vel quarumcunque secularium personarum nostræ præceptionis Decretum violauerit, cuiuscunque sublimitatis, aut dignitatis sit, honore suo priuetur. Quem locum Gregorius VII. Papa adducit ad probandum iure à sede depositum fuisse Henricum Imp. Eodem planè ingenio Cardinalis Baronius. {q}Vides (Lector) Pontificis Rom. esse sancire leges, quibus si Reges ipsi non parent, Regno suo priuentur: considerat hoc Gregorius VII. Romanus Pontifex; Si (inquit) B.Gregorius Doctor utique mitissimus hoc dixit. &c.
units.tr: Pause a moment, Bellarmine, and before you speak of Gregory's testimony, observe this order, so that readers may learn first what authority he claims over princes, and then how much reverence he requires from them toward priests. Begin. "If anyone of the bishops," says Gregory, "or of the judges, or of any secular persons, violates the decree of our precept, whatever his sublimity or dignity, let him be deprived of his honour." Pope Gregory VII cites this passage to prove that Henry the Emperor was rightly deposed from his see. Cardinal Baronius reasons in exactly the same way. "You see, reader, that it belongs to the Roman Pontiff to enact laws, and if kings themselves do not obey them, they are deprived of their kingdom. Gregory VII, the Roman Pontiff, considered this: 'If,' he says, 'Blessed Gregory, a most gentle teacher, said this...'" etc.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Citatam Gregorij, de Medardi Monasterio, Epistolam spuriam esse, & indignam Gregorio prolem.
units.tr: That the cited Epistle of Gregory, concerning the monastery of Medardus, is spurious and unworthy of Gregory's offspring.

units.la: GRegorij Magni nomen Nos (vt par est) magno honore prosequimur, Vobis vero iustè succensemus, quòd piam mentem non modò scriptis spurijs & supposititijs, sed etiam fucatis & inhonestis interpretamentis perperàm adulterastis. Primo enim Epistolam hanc, quam Gregorio I. affingitis, Gregorius VII. Papa, nisi mente male-fanâ legisset, supposititiam iuxtà & impiam esse facilè agnouisset. Supposititiciam eò confidentiùs voco, non modò quod ipse Baronius fatetur Subscriptionem eius {r}Non posse congruere cùm istis temporibus, siquidem complures (inquit) Episcopi, qui subscripti reperiuntur, post aliquot abhinc Annos creati noscuntur : verum multò etiam magis, quià id probat noster Iamesius Protobibliothecarius Oxoniensis (si quisquam alius) inexhaustae industriae vir, & in Patrum monumentis peruoluendis versatissimus; qui cum aliis quibusdam viris eruditis hanc prouinciam sustinens, Sanctorum Patrum scripta, & imprimis Gregorij, a maleferiatorum hominum corruptelis, tanquam ab infestissimis blattis & tineis, vindicandi; tandem hanc Epistolam, de Monasterio S.Medardi, in septem manu-scriptis Gregorij operibus minimè haberi obseruauit.
units.tr: We honour the name of Gregory the Great with great respect, as is right, but we are justly angry with you, because you have corrupted that pious mind, and not only with spurious and supposititious writings but also with disguised and dishonest interpretations. For first, Gregory VII, the Pope, had he not read with an evil mind, could easily have recognised that this Epistle, which you attribute to Gregory I, is supposititious and impious. I call it supposititious with more confidence, not only because Baronius himself admits that its subscription cannot agree with those times, since (he says) several bishops who are found among the subscribers are known to have been created some years later; but much more because our James, Chief Librarian of Oxford (if anyone), a man of inexhaustible industry and most versed in turning over the monuments of the Fathers, proves it. He, undertaking with certain other learned men the task of vindicating the writings of the holy Fathers, and especially of Gregory, from the corruptions of wicked men as from the most hostile moths and worms, at last observed that this Epistle, concerning the Monastery of St Medardus, is by no means found in seven manuscript works of Gregory.

units.la: Quid ni verò Epistolam illam parùm piam esse dixerim, quae tota Imprecatoria est, quùm praesertim summam {f}Crudelitatem esse, (si quis imprecetur cuiquam, vt ad aeternas poenas damnetur, fatetur Bellarminus; qui propterea Eam Interminatoriam tantùm & decretum Excommunicationis esse interpretatus est. At verba Epistolae expendamus [Si quis huius praeceptionis decreta violauerit, omnium maledictionum anathemate, quibus infideles & haeretici ab initio seculi vsque in praesens damnati sunt, cùm Iudâ traditore Domini in inferno inferiori damnetur ; nisi digna poenitentiâ praefatorum Sanctorum sibi propitiauerit clementiam, & fratrum communem reconciliauerit concordiam..] Vah ! ut intonat ? iam verò communem fratrum concordiam reconciliare ingentis molis esset; subit enim recordatio veteris Erasmi querelae, de mutuis Fratrum vestrorum inter se odijs ; {t}Dispeream si inter mille Fratres inueneris vel vnum : salutem igitur vllius ex huiusmodi hominum communi Concordia pendere, aut alioquin aeternum perire velle, quantum (quaeso) ab execratione distat ?
units.tr: Why should I not call that Epistle very impious, when it is entirely imprecatory, especially since Bellarmine admits that it is cruelty to pray that anyone be damned to eternal punishments? For this reason he interpreted it as merely a threatening and a decree of excommunication. But let us weigh the words of the Epistle: [If anyone violates the decrees of this precept, let him be damned with the anathema of all the curses by which infidels and heretics have been condemned from the beginning of the age until now, together with Judas the traitor of the Lord in the lowest hell; unless by fitting repentance he win the clemency of the aforesaid Saints, and reconcile the common concord of the brothers.] Oh, how it thunders! Indeed, to reconcile the common concord of the brothers would be a huge undertaking, for there comes to mind the old complaint of Erasmus about the mutual hatreds of your Brothers among themselves: [May I perish if among a thousand brothers you find even one.] So to make anyone's salvation depend on such a common concord of men, or otherwise to wish him to perish eternally: how far (I ask) is that from execration?

units.la: Secundo reclamare videtur ipsius Gregorij sanctitas, quem vos elogijs vestris virum coelestem praedicatis.--Tantane (vero) animis coelestibus ira? Imo, vt Sanctum coelestemque decuit, Gregorius{a}: "Deus (inquit) maledicere possit, homo autem in scripturis prohibetur, quia quod homo agit, malitiâ vindictâ, Deus facit virtute, iustitiæ. Verum, vt vt est de Execratione, nihilominus nulla ratione ab impietate excusari potest: quia nemo temerè, nisi insignitèr impius, Anathema denunciandus est. At ex Decreti huius atroci stylo, quisquis de isthoc decreto vel negligenter dixerit, vel fratres inquietauerit, aut contumax biuerit, nisi in gratiam redierit, vel (quod fieri posset fortasse in melius) aliter ordinauerit, honore primandus, & vt Catholicæ fidei depravator, vt Sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ destructor, consortio Christianitatis sequestrandus, omnium maledictionum anathemate, cum Iudâ traditore damnandus censetur. Quæ verba--- Non sani esse hominis non Janus iuret Orestes. Facessat igitur Cardinalis cùm suo insulso & impio Decreto, quod tàm indignum S.Gregorio I. quam Gregorio VII. dignum. Hæc de potestate Papali in Principes. Nunc (vt eo redeat vnde digressa est Oratio) de Reuerentia à Principibus erga Sacerdotes debita ex Gregorio agendum.
units.tr: Secondly, the holiness of Gregory himself seems to cry out against it, he whom you proclaim by your eulogies a heavenly man. "Can such anger (truly) be in heavenly minds?" Indeed, as became a holy and heavenly man, Gregory says: "God can curse, but man is forbidden in the Scriptures, because what man does through malice and the desire for vengeance, God does through the power of justice." However, be that as it may about Execration, it cannot in any way be excused from impiety, because no one should rashly be denounced with anathema unless he is notably impious. But from the savage style of this Decree: whoever shall have spoken carelessly about this decree, or disquieted the brothers, or lived obstinately, unless he returns to favour, or (which perhaps might be done for the better) orders otherwise, is to be deprived of honour, and, as a corrupter of the Catholic faith and a destroyer of the holy Church of God, is to be cut off from the fellowship of Christians, and is judged to be damned with the anathema of all curses, together with Judas the traitor. As for these words: "No sane man would swear by Janus, not even Orestes." Let the Cardinal then depart with his silly and impious Decree, which is as unworthy of Gregory I as it is worthy of Gregory VII. These things concern papal power over princes. Now (to return to where the oration digressed) we must treat, from Gregory, the reverence owed by princes to priests.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: "Gregorius in epist. ad Mauritium Imp. Quid mirum (inquit) si illos vestra pietas dignetur honorare, quibus in suo eloquio honorem tribuens, eos aut Angelos, aut Deos ipse appellat Deus?" --- Pag.40.
units.tr: "Gregory, in his letter to the Emperor Maurice: What wonder if your piety deigns to honour those whom God himself, granting them honour in his own speech, calls either angels or gods?" — p. 40.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Hæc Gregorius. sed quid ex his Bellarminus? Quid si Gregorius à Principibus Sacerdotes (nam de appellatione illa [Dy estiu][?] post * dicemus) honorandos esse censuerit? "Etsi Gregorius seruum se Imperatoris vocet, tamen addit, Debere Imperatorem Sacerdotibus reuerentiam exhibere: quod certè inferioris est, non superioris.
units.tr: So far Gregorius. But what does Bellarmine make of this? What if Gregory thought that Sacerdotes (for I will deal with that title [Dy estiu]? after the asterisk) should be honoured by princes? "Although Gregory calls himself the servant of the Emperor, he nevertheless adds that the Emperor ought to show reverence to priests; which is certainly the mark of an inferior, not a superior."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Inanissimam Bellarmini Rationem esse, discentis, solus esse Inferioris Reuerentiam alicui exhibere.
units.tr: Bellarmine's reasoning is most empty, learner: that only an inferior owes reverence to someone.

units.la: Certè quidem falleris: nam (S.Petro monitore){b} Debet maritus honorem exhibere uxori (sed) tanquam inferiori: tenetur etiam Episcopus (Doctore S.Paulo){c} viduas honorare: & Cuilibet Christiano, ut{d} Alius alij honore praeeat, praecipitur. An iccirco Vxores imperitare viris; Viduas ab Episcopis exigere obsequium; & plebeium quemlibet aequis cum Principibus incedere passibus Catechismo suo instituet Bellar.? Non opinor. Nihil enim aliud est Reuerentia quàm exhibitio boni respectus externi, cùm discreta quādam significatione excellentiae. Et quia excellentia Mariti, quae in dominio est fita, maior est quàm vxoris; ergò Maior Marito reuerentia debetur: & iuxta Excellentiae discrimen Abrahamus maiorem respectum habuit ergà Saram vxorem, quàm ergà Hagar concubinam.
units.tr: You are certainly mistaken. For (at the prompting of St Peter) a husband ought to show honour to his wife, though as to one who is inferior; the bishop too is bound (by the teaching of St Paul) to honour widows; and it is commanded to every Christian that one should go before another in honour. Will Bellarmine therefore teach in his catechism that wives rule their husbands, that bishops exact obedience from widows, and that any common man walks with princes on equal footing? I think not. For reverence is nothing other than the showing of a good external regard, with a certain distinct sign of excellence. And because the excellence of the husband, which lies in dominion, is greater than that of the wife, therefore greater reverence is owed to the husband; and in proportion to the difference of excellence, Abraham had greater regard for his wife Sarah than for his concubine Hagar.

units.la: Non igitur omnis excellentia in Superioritate consistit: {e}honoramus enim Medicum, propter necessitatem; Amicos, propter necessitudinem; Parentes, propter pietatem; Peregrinos, propter humanitatem; & diuersorum generum homines diuerso honoris gradu [illegible, ~6 letters] ex more & lege patriâ prosequimur. A Sacerdotibus igitur & reliquis Christianis supremus in terris honos Regibus debetur, propter impressam in Illis supremam diuinae Maiestatis & excellentiae imaginem, ratione externi dominij, cui subesse & parere tenetur{f} OMNIS ANIMA.]
units.tr: Not all excellence, then, consists in superiority. For we honour a physician on account of necessity, friends on account of close bond, parents on account of duty, strangers on account of humanity; and we pay men of different kinds different degrees of honour according to custom and the law of the land. Therefore the highest honour on earth is owed by priests and all other Christians to kings, on account of the supreme image of the divine majesty and excellence stamped upon them, and by reason of the external dominion to which every soul is bound to submit and obey.

units.la: Debent & Principes eximium gradum honoris Sacerdotibus Christi, propter ordinis & muneris praestantiam. Iccirco Gregorius, quùm sensit se ab Imperatore {g}Simplicem (id est, vt ipse interpretabatur) Fatuum appellari; iure potuit ab Imp. Reuerentiam deposcere; Cuius erat Dei Ministros ab omnium aliorum contumelia & contemptu vindicare. Hactenus [illegible, ~4 letters].
units.tr: Princes too owe a special degree of honour to the ministers of Christ, on account of the eminence of their order and office. Hence Gregory, when he perceived that he had been called by the Emperor a "simpleton" (that is, as he himself interpreted it, a fool), could rightly demand reverence from the Emperor; for it was his task to defend the ministers of God against the insult and contempt of all others. Thus far [illegible, ~4 letters].

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Gregorium Mauritii Iussionibus obtemperasse, non solum ex necessitate, aut humilitate; sed ex Conscientiae vinculo.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. That Gregory obeyed the commands of Maurice not only from necessity or humility, but from the bond of conscience.

units.la: SAnctum Testem haud bona fide adduxisti Gregorium I. Pont. quem nos, in hac lite dirimenda, Iudicem deposcimus; quoties nimirum dicit (dicit autem saepissime) se Imperatorum, tanquam DOMINORVM suorum, iussionibus paruisse. Ad quod nullum adhuc à Vobis potuimus responsum vel verisimile exprimere, duo licet summae eruditionis Cardinales (viz. Bellarminus, & Baronius) omnes ingeniorum suorum nervos torserint versauerintque, ut Gregorii tàm clara testimonia, tanquam amentatas hastas, è manibus nostris excuterent. I. Bellarminus. {b}Non sine causa dixi (inquit) S.Gregorium partim ex humilitate, partim ex necessitate se Imperatori subiecisse, siquidem adeò tyrannicè (Mauritius) Ecclesiam Rom. premebat, ut ipse {a}Gregorius, quamvis mitissimus esset, Eum cùm Diocletiano & Neronè comparaverit; deplorans durissimum iugum, quod sub Mauritio ferre coactus fuerat. Ex quo sequitur, ut obedientia, quam Gregorius Mauritio exhibuerat, non debita fuerat, sed coacta. Haec Bellarminus. Ain' verò? Coactam obedientiam praestitisse Gregorium; deplorantem nimirum durissimum iugum tyrannidis Imperatoris in ipsam Ecclesiam Romanam?
units.tr: You have not in good faith cited the holy witness Gregory I, Pontiff, whom in this dispute we ask to be our judge; for he says, as often as he speaks (and he speaks of it very often), that he obeyed the commands of the Emperors as of his own LORDS. To this we have as yet received from you no answer, nor even a plausible one, though two Cardinals of the greatest learning (namely Bellarmine and Baronius) have strained and wrenched every sinew of their wits, that they might shake from our hands Gregory's so clear testimonies, as if they were javelins with thongs attached. I. Bellarmine: "I did not speak without cause," he says, "when I said that St Gregory submitted himself to the Emperor partly from humility, partly from necessity, since Maurice so tyrannically oppressed the Roman Church that Gregory himself, though he was most gentle, compared him with Diocletian and Nero, lamenting the very harsh yoke which he had been forced to bear under Maurice. From which it follows that the obedience which Gregory showed to Maurice was not owed but extorted." So Bellarmine. Is that so? Gregory rendered an extorted obedience, bewailing, of course, the very harsh yoke of tyranny of the Emperor over the Roman Church itself?

units.la: Responsum hoc deploratae caussae est, nè dicam Conscientiae, argumentum. Est enim ubi Gregorius, in suis ad Mauritium literis, eidem Imperatori Eius, in conseruanda Ecclesia, fidem ac diligentiam gratulatur. {c}Piissimus Dominus noster, ad compescendos bellicos motus, pacem quaerit Ecclesiae, atque ad huius compagem Sacerdotii dignatur corda reducere. Ecquid hic tetricum Mauritius exprompsit? ecquid violentum? ecquod Nerone aliquo, aut Diocletiano, & non potius Constantino Imp. dignum? Et tamen Gregorius verbis immediatè sequentibus; Quod quidem Ego (inquit) opto, atque, quantum ad me attinet, ferenissimis iussionibus obedientiam prabeo. Quia autem non Causa mei, sed dei est, quia non solus Ego, sed tota turbatur Ecclesia (Intelligit per Episcopum Constantinopolitanum qui se universalem Ecclesiae Episcopum appellari voluit) --- pijssimus Dominus locum fecit vulneris, atque resistentem agrum Augustae authoritatis vinculi constringat. Rursus sub finem Epistolae; Pijssimus Dominus dignetur negotium indicare: si iudicio vestrae pietatis cesserit (vz. Episcopus Constantinopolitanus,) omnipotenti Deo gratias referimus, sin autem, &c. Ego autem Dominorum IUSSIONIBUS obedientiam prabens, Illi scripsi, &c. Haec Gregorius. Quibus verbis non modo agnoscit penes Imperatorem esse, Iudicium exercere in Episcopum Constantinopolitanum; verum etiam Imperatoris iussionibus suam quoque obedientiam liberrime atque ex animo profitetur.
units.tr: This answer is the argument of a cause that is already lost, not to say of a conscience. For there is a passage where Gregory, in his letters to Maurice, congratulates the same Emperor on his faith and diligence in preserving the Church: "Our most pious Lord seeks peace for the Church, to quell the movements of war, and deigns to bring back the hearts of this priesthood to the unity of its body." Did Maurice here bring out anything harsh? Anything violent? Anything worthy of some Nero or Diocletian, and not rather of the Emperor Constantine? And yet Gregory, in the words immediately following: "Which indeed I (he says) desire, and, so far as concerns me, I render obedience to the most gentle commands. But since the matter is not mine but God's, since not I alone but the whole Church is troubled" (he means by the Bishop of Constantinople, who wished to be called bishop of the universal Church) "— may our most pious Lord make room for the wound, and bind the resisting field with the bond of Augustan authority." Again near the end of the letter: "May our most pious Lord deign to indicate the affair: if it shall have yielded to the judgment of your piety" (namely the Bishop of Constantinople) "we give thanks to almighty God; but if otherwise, etc. For I, rendering obedience to the COMMANDS of my Lords, have written to him, etc." So Gregory. In these words he not only acknowledges that it lies with the Emperor to exercise judgment over the Bishop of Constantinople, but also most freely and sincerely professes that his own obedience is rendered to the commands of the Emperor.

units.la: At Gregorium, dixti, partim ex necessitate, partim ex humilitate se Imperatori subiecisse; ut quamvis pateat Eum sponte Obedientiam exhibuisse Imperatori, id saltem humilitati Eius tribuendum putemus. Mus pusillus quam sapiens est bestia, aetatem qui vni foramini nunquam committit suam? hanc bestiolam imitatur Cardinalis, sed frustra; primum enim foramen, de Necessitate, occlusimus; alteri, de Humilitate, aditum nullo negotio praestruemus. Bellarminus totus est in hoc, ut probet Sacerdotum personas non debere subijci Principibus; imo vero etiam diuino iure debere non subijci, quasi talis subiectio non posset (scilicet) non Ecclesiasticam dignitatem laedere atque subuertere. At vero Gregorium, ex Subiectione illa, quam Imperatori exhibuit, nihil quicquam Sacerdotali aut Papali authoritati detractum sensisse, ipse oppido lubens responsurus est. Nam {k}Dum (inquit) praedicator Gentium (S.Paulus) dicat, [Quamdiu sum Gentium Apostolus, ministerium meum honorificabo:] Ita docet (Apostolus) humilitatem teneri in mente, ut tamen ardinis[?] nostri dignitatem feruemus[?] in honore: quatenus in Nobis nec Humilitas timida, nec erectius superba. Necnon Alibi: solerter nitendum est, ne dum inornatius custoditur virtus humilitatis, soluantur iura regiminis, & dum Prælatus quisquam plusse deiecit, subditorum vitam distringere sub disciplina vinculo non possit. Sic Gre-gorius.
units.tr: But you say that Gregory submitted himself to the Emperor partly from necessity, partly from humility; so that, although it is plain that he rendered obedience to the Emperor of his own accord, we may at least think this should be attributed to his humility. How wise is the little mouse, which never entrusts its life to a single hole! The Cardinal imitates this little beast, but in vain; for we have first closed the hole of necessity, and the approach by way of humility we shall block with no trouble at all. Bellarmine is wholly intent on proving that the persons of priests ought not to be subject to princes; indeed, that by divine right they ought not to be subject, as if such subjection could not (to be sure) fail to injure and overturn ecclesiastical dignity. But Gregory himself will very gladly answer that he did not perceive from that subjection, which he showed to the Emperor, anything at all taken away from sacerdotal or papal authority. For (he says) when the preacher of the Gentiles (St Paul) says, [As long as I am an apostle of the Gentiles, I will honour my ministry], he teaches (the Apostle) that humility is to be held in the mind, yet so that we also keep up the dignity of our order in honour; so that in us there is neither timid humility nor a haughtiness too lofty. And elsewhere: It must be laboured at diligently, lest, while virtue of humility is kept too meanly, the rights of rule are dissolved, and while some prelate has cast himself down too far, he cannot restrain the life of his subjects under the bond of discipline. So Gregory.

units.la: Denique fatemur Gregorium obedientiam & subiectionem Imperatori præbuisse ex Humilitate quidem, sed omninò debitâ, propter tremendam Eius authoritatem, qui vult {m}Omnem animam subiici sublimioribus istis (nempè secularibus) potestatibus. Deinde etiam ex necessitate; sed non humanâ, aut metu{n} irae Imperatoris; sed prorsus diuinâ, & Conscientiæ causâ, vi præcepti Eius, qui per Apostolum dicit, Necesse est subiici: non, vt Bellarminus voluit; partim ex humana coactione, partim ex humilitate; quasi nobis hominem versipellem, astutum, qui faro vt nouerat, depingeret; qui descendit vt ascendat; repit humi, vt volet per aerem; subijciat se Seruus obedies Iusionibus, vt postea cuadat (quemadmodum Gregorius VII) Dominus Dominorum. Hucusque ad Card. Bellarminum respondimus ex Gregorio.
units.tr: Finally, we confess that Gregory rendered obedience and subjection to the Emperor out of humility, indeed, but wholly due humility, on account of his tremendous authority, who wills that every soul be subject to those higher (namely secular) powers. Then also from necessity; but not a human necessity, nor a fear of the wrath of the Emperor; rather one altogether divine, and for the sake of conscience, by virtue of the precept of him who says through the Apostle, It is necessary to be subject; not, as Bellarmine wished, partly from human compulsion, partly from humility; as if he were painting for us a crafty, cunning man, who knew how to play the fox; who stoops that he may rise, who creeps on the ground that he may fly through the air, who subjects himself as an obedient servant to commands, so that afterwards he may rule (as Gregory VII did) as Lord of lords. Thus far we have answered Cardinal Bellarmine from Gregory.

units.la: VII. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: VII. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Nullum omnium Pontificum Maiestatis Regiae hostem fuisse tam infensum, quam fuit Gregorius Propugnator feruidus.
units.tr: No one among all the Popes was as hostile to the royal majesty as Gregory, the fervent champion.

units.la: Superest aliud longè apertissimum Gregorij testimonium, ex alia ad Mauritium Imperatorem Epistola; à quo Gregorius in mandatis habuit, vt legem Eius, opinione suâ valdè iniquam, promulgaret; de qua tamen in hunc, qui sequitur, modum Gregorius. {o}Ego (inquit) indignus famulus vester, vestrae iussioni subiectus, eandem legem per diuersas terrarum partes transmitti feci: & quia lex ipsa omnipotenti Deo minimè concordat, ecce hoc per suggestionis mea paginam Serenissimo Domino meo (Mauritio) significavi. Ubicunque igitur quae debui exsolui, quae & Imperatori obedientiam praebui, & pro Deo quod sensi minimè tacui. Hactenus Gregorius. Cui testimonio, meridiana luce clariori, Cardinalis Baronius quasi noctem quandam conatur offundere. {P}Gregorius (inquit) in eadem epistola contestatus est, se non ut Episcopum ista scribere, sed iure privato loqui, quod satis ad excusationem Gregorij esse potest, quum aliam agit personam tanquam in scena, ubicunque quis personam induit, ut verbis debet. Sic Ille. Dignum equidem nugaci histrione potius quam stupendo Congregationis Oratorij Presbytero, & Cardinale Commentum; risu certè non plausu excipiendum.
units.tr: There remains another, by far the clearest, testimony of Gregory, taken from another letter to the Emperor Maurice. Gregory had been instructed by him to promulgate his law, which Gregory judged to be very unjust. Yet he wrote about it in this manner: "I, your unworthy servant, subject to your command, have had this same law sent through various parts of the lands; and because the law itself by no means agrees with almighty God, behold, I have signified this by the page of my letter to my most serene lord Maurice. Wherever, therefore, I have paid what I owed, and have shown obedience to the Emperor, I have also, for God's sake, not kept silent about what I thought." Thus far Gregory. Cardinal Baronius tries to cast a kind of night over this testimony, which is clearer than noon sunlight. "Gregory (he says) declared in the same letter that he was writing these things not as a bishop but speaking by private right, which can be enough to excuse Gregory, since he plays another part, as on a stage, and wherever anyone puts on a character, he ought to speak in accordance with it." Thus he. This is a thing worthy of a jesting actor rather than of a Presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, and of a Cardinal's invention; surely it should be met with laughter, not applause.

units.la: Verba enim Gregorij huiusmodi sunt: Omnipotenti Deo reus, qui serenissimo Domino, in omni quod agit & loquitur, purus non est. Hiccine hominis vafri & dissimulatoris personam in scena sustinentis prologus est? annon potius religiosa animi simplicis & candidi pectoris professio? huius igitur verba immediatè sequentia auscultemus. Ego autem indignus famulus neque ut Episcopus, neque ut servus Reipublicae, sed iure privato loquor: quia (serenissime Domine) ex illo iam tempore Dominus meus fuisti, quando Dominus non omnium erat. Sic Ille. Quibus verbis, ut se facilius in gratiam Imperatoris insinuaret, revocat in memoriam necessitudinem illam, quae inter se & Mauritium olim intercesserat, quum nec Mauritius adhuc Imperator erat (quod significat illis verbis, [Quando Dominus omnium non fuisti,] nec Gregorius ipse Episcopus; ad quod alludit verbis illis [Neque ego ut Episcopus] sed utrumque iure privato fruebatur. Nunc autem Mauritio rerum potiente, Gregorius palàm profitetur, se ergà Imperatorem tàm boni ciuis, quàm veri Episcopi numeros omnes expleuisse: illud, quòd in lege promulganda obedientiam Imperatori praebuit; hoc, quòd non fecit, sed aperte significavit, legem illam omnipotenti Deo minimè concordare.
units.tr: For the words of Gregory are of this kind: "Guilty before almighty God, he who is not pure towards the most serene lord in everything he does and says." Is this the prologue of the persona of a crafty and dissembling man playing a part on the stage? Is it not rather a religious profession of a simple mind and a sincere heart? Let us hear, then, the words that immediately follow. "But I, your unworthy servant, speak neither as a bishop nor as a servant of the commonwealth, but by private right: because (most serene lord) you have been my lord from that time on, when he was not yet lord of all." Thus he. In these words, in order to insinuate himself more easily into the Emperor's favour, he recalls to mind that close bond which had once existed between himself and Maurice, when Maurice was not yet Emperor (which he signifies by those words, "when you were not lord of all"), nor was Gregory himself yet a bishop (to which he alludes in the words "neither as a bishop"); both enjoyed that private right. But now, with Maurice holding power, Gregory openly professes that he has fulfilled every part, both of a good citizen and of a true bishop, towards the Emperor: the first, in that in promulgating the law he showed obedience to the Emperor; the second, in that he did not carry it out, but plainly declared that that law by no means agrees with almighty God.

units.la: Icircò[?] ignoscere Nobis debent Cardinales, si Ipsos potiùs in Scena Pseudolos egisse putemus, quàm S. Gregorium aut ergà Imperatorem, cui Subiectionem exhibuit, perfidiæ; aut etiam ergà Sacerdotum ordinem, per nimiam abiectionem, sacrilegij crimine se obstrinxisse. Multò verius atque candidius vester Espencæus; {q}Gregorius primus, idem & Magnus (inquit) lib. 2. Epist. 64. ingenuè agnoscebat Imperatori à Deo concessum, non militibus solùm, sed Sacerdotibus quoque dominari. Gregorium autem I. qui Anno MXC. cum Gregorio VII. qui Anno MLXXIII. viguit, in hac Causa {*} coniungere; quid aliud est quàm serenitatem cum fulmine, aut cum pace bellum consociare? I. enim ille Primus; {r}Hoc verbum Ivssionis (inquit) à meo auditu remouete: non ego iussi. At Septimus; {t}Mandamus (inquit) ne quisquam sit vel Rex, vel alius, qui nostris Legatis resistere audeat. {u}Alioquin intelligant, quid sit Ivssionem Ecclesiae parui facere: & passim imperiosissimè Mandata, & Iussiones crepat. II. Primus Imperatoris {*}Iussionibus obedientiam spospondit. Septimus autem {*}Iussiones suas Imperatoribus imponit, & Authoritatibus Eorum vbique detrectat. III. Primus {*}Subiectionem Mauritio suam iuramento obstrinxit. At Septimus, acsi iusiurandum Illi iocus esset, Imperatorum subiectos Iuramenti sui religione exsoluit. IV. Primus Deum timens (sic enim ait) in morte cuiusquam Longobardorum miscere se reformidauit: sed septimus Arma impia contra Imperatorem mouit, & veluti terram caelo miscens, orbem caede & sanguine cruentauit. Ne longior sim, S. Gregorius (honoris causa) huius nominis Primus cluit: Septimus vero {x}Primus omnium Pontificum dici meruit; sed (vt est apud Frisingensem) qui Imperatorem regno priuauit. Quod vero ad Sanctitatem attinet; Gregorius VII. Maiestatis laesae, aliorumque scelerum crimine in quatuor {y}Concilijs (quae Aduersarij Conciliabula vocant, quòd Papa, nimirum pars rea, in illis Index esse prohibebatur) Papiensi, Wormatiensi, Brixiensi, Moguntinensi damnatus est. Hactenus de praecipuis Gregorij testimonijs disseruimus; eo iam redeat unde deflexit oratio.
units.tr: Therefore our Cardinals ought to pardon us if we think they have played a deceitful part in a comedy, rather than that St. Gregory was guilty of treachery towards the Emperor, to whom he showed submission, or else, through excessive abasement, bound himself by the crime of sacrilege towards the order of priests. Your Espencaeus speaks far more truly and frankly: "Gregory I, the same also the Great (he says, book 2, Epistle 64), frankly acknowledged that the Emperor was granted by God to rule not only over soldiers but also over priests." But to join Gregory I, who flourished around the year 590, with Gregory VII, who flourished in the year 1073, in this cause: what else is this than to combine serenity with thunderbolt, or war with peace? For that first Gregory said: "Remove this word 'command' from my hearing: I did not command." But the seventh says: "We command that no one, whether king or any other, dare to resist our legates." "Otherwise let them understand what it is to hold the command of the Church cheap," and everywhere he thunders most imperiously with commands and orders. II. The first promised obedience to the Emperor's commands. The seventh, however, imposes his own commands on the Emperors and everywhere flouts their authority. III. The first bound himself by oath to submission to Maurice. But the seventh, as if an oath were a joke to him, released the subjects of the Emperors from the obligation of their oath. IV. The first, fearing God (for so he says), shrank from taking part in the death of any Lombard; but the seventh raised impious arms against the Emperor and, as if mingling earth with heaven, stained the world with slaughter and blood. To be brief: St. Gregory earned renown under this name First (as an honour); but Seventh deserved to be called the first of all the Popes; yet (as it is in Frisingensis) he who stripped the Emperor of his kingdom. As for holiness, Gregory VII was condemned for the crime of injured majesty and other wickedness in four Councils (which the adversaries call conciliabula, because the Pope, namely the guilty party, was forbidden to be judge in them): at Pavia, Worms, Brixen and Mainz. Thus far we have discussed the principal testimonies of Gregory; let the discourse now return to where it turned aside.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: “ S. Gregorius in lib. 4. epist. 30. ad Mauritium Imp. Quid mirum (inquit) si illos vestra pietas dignetur honorare, quibus in suo eloquio Honorem tribuens, eos aut Angelos, aut Deos ipse etiam appellat Deus. — pag. 40.
units.tr: "St. Gregory, in book 4, epistle 30, to the Emperor Maurice: What wonder (he says) if your piety deigns to honour those to whom, in his own speech, God himself gives honour, calling them even angels or gods." — p. 40.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Gregorium, honorem ab Imperatore postulando, nihil minus quam Superiorem fuisse.
units.tr: That Gregory, in asking the Emperor for honour, was by no means a superior.

units.la: VErba Gregorij satis per se manifesta sunt; involutus autem sensus tuus aliunde eruendus, vbi supra {*}contendis, Sacerdotes Principibus praeesse, & honore praecedere: quo nihil Gregorij menti repugnantius dici potest. Nam haec verba illi animi eius dolor & indignatio ipsa expressit, quòd Imperator Eum mordaci sarcasmo Simplicem, id est, (vti diximus, Gregorio ipso Interprete,) Fatuum vocâsset, & falsò nimis contumeliosèque inter Stultos numerâsset; propterea petit vt Pietas eius dignetur ipsum honorare. Quae formula loquendi planè ostendit, Gregorium ipsum Imperatorem Superiorem & Digniorem agnoscere, Cui supplicando hanc authoritatem tribuit, vt ipsum honorare dignaretur; quod & facta Gregorij abundè demonstrabunt. At Sacerdotes (inquis) Deos vocat; Ergò &c. Hoc, si placet, Argumentum persequere.
units.tr: Gregory's words are clear enough in themselves. Your reading of his meaning, which you must draw from elsewhere, is that, as you argue above, priests take precedence over princes and outrank them in honour. Nothing could be more contrary to Gregory's mind. These words were forced from him by his own grief and indignation, because the Emperor had mocked him with a biting sarcasm, calling him "simple" (that is, as we have said, in Gregory's own words, "foolish"), and had counted him among the fools, and that falsely and too insultingly. For this reason he asks that the Emperor's piety deign to honour him. This form of speech plainly shows that Gregory himself acknowledged the Emperor as his superior and worthier, to whom he gives, by way of supplication, the authority to deign to honour him; and Gregory's deeds will also amply demonstrate this. But (you say) he calls priests gods. Therefore, etc. If you like, pursue this argument.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, on the Offices (De Officiis).

units.la: “ Ecclesiasticaque testatur historia, quia quum pia memoria Constantino in scripto oblata accusationes contra Episcopos fuissent: Libellos quidem accusationis accepit, & eosdem, qui accusati fuerant, Episcopos convocans, in eorum conspectu libellos, quos acceperas, incendit, dicens; Vos Dij estis à vero Deo constituti, ite, & inter vos causas vestras discutite, quia dignum non est ut nos iudicemus Deos. --- pag. 40.
units.tr: "Ecclesiastical history bears witness that when accusations against bishops had been presented in writing to the Emperor of pious memory, Constantine indeed received the written charges, and, summoning the bishops who had been accused, burned in their sight the documents he had received, saying: 'You are gods, appointed by the true God; go and examine your causes among yourselves, for it is not fitting that we should judge gods.'" --- p. 40.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Honorificum Decorum appellationem non primario Sacer- dotibus, sed Principibus supremè ascribi.
units.tr: That the honourable title of "gods" is ascribed chiefly not to priests but to supreme princes.

units.la: DIxit Constantinus Sacerdotes Deos esse: deinde Libellos eorum incendit: quos Iudicare recusauit. Dicta à factis secernamus. Dixit Sacerdotes Deos esse: hinc Tu; Ergò Regibus superiores. I. Ad Antecedens olim Caluinus; {b}Constantinus adhuc catechumenus, & non valde in Scripturis exercitatus, hanc vocem [Deos] errore ad Sacerdotes transtulit. Nè hoc Responsum vobis absonum aut insolens videatur, Baronium vestrum attendite. {c}Constantini (inquit) tyrocinio condonandum, quòd Petrum & Paulum Deos vocauerit. II. Consequentiam retorqueo; nam {d}In Scriptura sacra (etiam de politicis Magistratibus, Te constitente) Iudices populi à Deo ipso vocantur Dij, Psal.81. Deus stetit in Synagoga Deorum, in medio autem Deos diudicat: cuius vocabuli rationem explicat Iehosaphat 2. Paral.19. vbi dicit, Iudices non hominum, sed Dei iudicium exercere: & Deut.1. Monet Moses vt iuste iudicent, quia Dei iudicium est: & Christus Ioh.10. Si illos dixerit Deos, ad quem Dei sermo factus est &c. Haec Bellarminus. Insurgo. Quùm Deus Principes Deos dixerit; quod idem de Sacerdotibus (quod sciam) in sacra pagina nusquam legitur: sunt igitur Reges Sacerdotibus superiores.
units.tr: Constantine said that priests are gods; then he burned their petitions, which he refused to judge. Let us separate his words from his deeds. He said that priests are gods; therefore you conclude that they are superior to kings. I. To the antecedent, Calvin once replied that Constantine, still a catechumen and not well versed in the Scriptures, carelessly transferred the word "gods" to priests. Lest this answer seem to you absurd or unusual, consider your own Baronius, who says that Constantine's inexperience must be pardoned for calling Peter and Paul gods. II. I turn the inference back upon you. For in Holy Scripture (speaking also of the civil magistrates, you being the witness) the judges of the people are called gods by God himself: Psalm 81, "God stood in the congregation of the gods; he judges among the gods" [Psal. 81]. Jehoshaphat explains the reason for this term in 2 Chronicles 19, where he says that judges exercise not the judgement of men but of God. And Deuteronomy 1 Moses warns that they should judge righteously, because the judgement is God's. And Christ in John 10: "If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came," etc. So far Bellarmine. I press the point: since God has called princes gods, and so far as I know nowhere in the sacred page is the same said of priests, kings are therefore superior to priests.

units.la: Vt tamen non negem hanc Appellationem Sacerdotibus sensu aliquo commodè competere; nihilominùs Eos Regibus externo honore & authoritate praeesse, nullâ ratione efficient: quià Deus ipse, qui ordinis est Deus, & non [illegible, ~4 letters], inter istos [illegible, ~6 letters], id est, mortales Deos, quemadmodum inter Angelos, ordines constituit. {e}Nam [illegible, ~12 letters] sunt, inter quos vnus regit, {f}[illegible, ~10 letters] excellentiam, vt Rex; alius [illegible, ~8 letters] vt Dux à Rege mis{g}su. Eodem modo in hac Causa accidere nullus dubito. Hanc rem illustrabimus illo exemplo (in quod supra tantum digitum intendi) {h} Salomonis, & Beersheba; qui duo in eodem hominum coetu versantur, ille Regis simul & filij personam gerit; haec vicissim Matris & Ciuis. Inter Eos (vt hoc fingamus) de officij iure certatur; Beersheba Salomonē adit, sed Illi supplicans, vt potè dignoscens in filio Regem: similiter Salomon matrem salutat Corpore inclinato, ita tamen (Causæ indignitate commotus) vt Supplicanti prorsus adnuerit: Ex vna parte in Ciuem matrem, ex altera in Matre Ciuem & Subditum discernens.
units.tr: Yet, although I do not deny that this title can fittingly belong to priests in some sense, they will by no reasoning prove that they rule over kings in external honour and authority. For God himself, who is the God of order, has established an order among these [illegible], that is, mortal gods, just as he has established orders among the angels. For there are [illegible] among whom one rules, [illegible] excellence, as a king does; another [illegible], as a leader sent by the king. I have no doubt that the same happens in this cause. We will illustrate this matter with the example to which I merely pointed above: Solomon and Beersheba. These two move in the same company of men: he bears the person of king and at the same time of son; she in turn of mother and citizen. Let us imagine that between them a dispute arises over the right of office: Beersheba approaches Solomon, but supplicating him, since she rightly recognises the king in the son. Likewise Solomon greets his mother with a bowed body; yet, moved by the unworthiness of the cause, he nonetheless grants the suppliant's request in full, discerning on the one side a citizen in a mother, and on the other a citizen and subject in a mother.

units.la: Eodem modo inter Sacerdotes & Principes se res habet; Sacerdos vt Pastor spiritualis honorandus est à Rege; vt vero Reip. ciuis Regem, vt Dominum suum temporalem, tenetur honorare. Quùm autem huiusce quæstionis status in eo ponatur, vtri ab altero maior vel magis debeatur honor externus ciuilis, siue præcedentia; proculdubio pensitatâ vtrinque hac genuinâ & duplicatâ relatione, præponderabit maiestatis Principis. Licet enim, propter obiectum & finem Sacerdotij supernaturalem, ac cœlestem, redundet in Sacerdotis personam reuerentia quædam interna, sacra, spiritualis, sublimis, quam in eodem genere nunquam pertingit Maiestas Regia; in externa tamen ciuili prælatione anteibit illa, quæ in externis ciuilibus pollet suprema potestas, tantùm ratione ordinationis diuinæ. Cuius luculentissimum documentum in Gregorio habemus, qui (vt Ciuem decet) crebris supplicationibus & officijs Imperatoris Iustionibus[?] obsequium & obedientiam suam testatus est. Ratio est in promptu, quia Princeps (vt iuxta cum Tertulliano Bellarminus fatetur) est à Deo secundus: qui autem Papam vel directè vel indirectè Principi in Temporalibus præponit; facit ille profectò Principem Tertium post Deum. Hæc de verbis Constantini, nunc Facta trutinemus.
units.tr: The matter stands in the same way between priests and princes. As a spiritual shepherd, the priest is to be honoured by the king; but as a citizen of the commonwealth he is bound to honour the king as his temporal lord. Since, however, the question at issue is which of the two is owed greater or more civil external honour, or precedence, from the other, undoubtedly, when this genuine and twofold relation is weighed on both sides, the majesty of the prince will prevail. For although, on account of the supernatural and heavenly object and end of the priesthood, a certain inward, sacred, spiritual and lofty reverence pours into the person of the priest, which royal majesty never reaches within the same kind, yet in external civil pre-eminence that supreme power which is strong in external civil matters will go before, and this only by reason of divine ordinance. We have a most clear proof of this in Gregory, who (as a citizen should) bore witness to his obedience and submission by frequent supplications and services to the Emperor. The reason is at hand, because the prince (as Bellarmine agrees, along with Tertullian) is second from God. But whoever places the Pope before the prince in temporal affairs, directly or indirectly, surely makes the prince the third after God. So much for the words of Constantine; now let us weigh his deeds.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Constantinum Magnum, ex maturo iudicio, in Episcoporum causis praefuisse.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. That Constantine the Great, on mature judgment, presided over the causes of bishops.

units.la: NOn est vt de voce [Deos;?] quam Sacerdotibus tribuit Constantinus, Lectorem vltra fatigemus. Historiam ipsam, de factis, aggredimur; in qua nulla fere vox occurrit, quae non Suprematus Imperatorij in Sacerdotes luculentissimum testimonium adferat: si modò Generale {k}Concilium convocasse; Episcopos undique per literas accersisse: Concilii locum Niceam destinasse: Congregatorum Libellos accepisse: igni comburi iussisse; Flammisq; mandasse: & finito tandem Concilio singulos ad gregem suum redire iussisse; supremae in Eos authoritatis demonstratio videri possit. At noluit (inquis) Constantinus Episcoporum causas iudicare. Verum est; quid ergò? an proinde omninò non illud Ei licuit? vel id non adeò expedire visum est? An quia non nunc in tyrocinio, iccirco nunquam immiscuit se in Sacerdotum negotijs? Operae sanè pretium erit haec expedire singula.
units.tr: There is no need to tire the reader further over the word [gods?] which Constantine gave to priests. We turn to the history itself, to his deeds, in which there is almost no statement that does not supply the most striking evidence of the emperor's supremacy over the priests, provided that he convened a General Council; summoned the bishops from every quarter by letter; appointed Nicaea as the place of the Council; received the libels of the assembled bishops; ordered them burned in the fire and had them consumed by flames; and, when the Council was finished at last, ordered each one to return to his flock. You may say these things show his supreme authority over them. But (you object) Constantine was unwilling to judge the causes of the bishops. That is true. What follows? Was it therefore altogether unlawful for him, or did it not seem altogether expedient? Or is it because he was not then in his apprenticeship that he never once meddled in the affairs of the priests? It will certainly be worth our while to take these points one by one.

units.la: Primum potuit, imò (nisi Temporis istius necessitas aliud suasisset) Iudicem se interponere debuit Constantinus, quid ni verò debuerit? Episcopi inter se litigant; Criminationum suarum Libellos non Imperatoris statuæ, sed ipsi Imperatori offerunt; Episcopi Causas suas Imperatori iudicandas tradunt: Imperatorem igitur iudicium suum interponere erit nefas? Cui potiùs in hac Causa habeda est fides? frequentinè Episcoporum coronæ, an vni Imperatori? Si Imperatori, tùm dignus is videri debet, qui de Episcoporum causis iudicaret; praesertim eorum, quibus iudicij & sapientiae laude ipse antecelluit. Sin Episcopis, tùm multò etiam magis dignus, quem ipsi Episcopi etiam in Causa sua sibi Iudicem asciscunt.
units.tr: First, Constantine could, indeed (unless the necessity of that time had suggested otherwise), and ought to have interposed himself as judge. Why should he not have been obliged to do so? Bishops quarrel among themselves; they offer their libels of accusation not to some statue but to the emperor himself; the bishops hand over their causes to the emperor to be judged. Will it therefore be wrong for the emperor to interpose his judgment? To whom ought greater credit to be given in this cause: a crowd of bishops, or the one emperor? If to the emperor, then he ought to seem worthy to judge the causes of the bishops, especially of those whom he himself surpassed in the praise of judgment and wisdom. If to the bishops, then he is worthy much more, since the bishops themselves take him as their judge even in their own cause.

units.la: Secundum sensit reverà Imperator, minimè expedire hisce Causis se implicare. Si (quatenùs coniec[?]rauit) quaestiones merè fuissent spirituales, de fide, rectè fecit; quia hoc genus Causarum Concilio Generali tradendum est : sin ideò iudicandi prouinciam recusabat , quod Accusatores Eorum mixtos esse suspicatus est,ne sic quidem male;nec enim mirum si Constantinus,(quae erat illius verè Christiani pectoris ergà Episcopos pietas) qui dixit velle se {1}Episcopum stuprum aliena uxori inferentem paludamento suo obtegere, ne aspectus alios laederet; si Criminationum Libellos Eorum, quos vidit mutuis odijs , iam, & dissidijs flagrantes,sigillo suo obsignatos,quasi paludamento obscoenos, ad sopiendam inuidiam , infamiámque extinguendam igne comburi iusserit. In hanc sententiam praeclarè Caluinus contra Paulum III. Pont. qui ex hoc Constantini facto immunitatis suae patrocinium mutuatus est:{m}Alioqui (inquit) prudenter egisse Constantinum fatcor , qui cùm Episcopos cerneret fatali quadam rabie in mutuam laceratione inflammatos , Ario parcere , & deserere Christi causam, vt sua cupiditati morem gererent , probrosos Eorum libellos concidesse. Sic Ille.
units.tr: Second, the emperor in fact judged that it was by no means expedient for him to become entangled in these causes. If (as I conjecture) the questions had been purely spiritual, concerning the faith, he acted rightly, because this kind of cause must be handed over to a General Council. But if he refused the office of judge because he suspected that their accusers were of mixed motives, not even then did he act badly. Nor is it strange that Constantine, whose piety towards bishops was that of a truly Christian heart, who said that he wished to cover with his military cloak a bishop who was defiling another man's wife, lest he offend other eyes, should have ordered their libels of accusation, which he saw were burning with mutual hatreds and dissensions, sealed with his own seal, and, as though they were obscene under his cloak, consigned to the fire to quench envy and extinguish infamy. Calvin wrote excellently to this effect against Pope Paul III, who borrowed from this deed of Constantine a defence of his own immunity: "Otherwise (he says) I grant that Constantine acted prudently, who, seeing the bishops inflamed by a certain fatal rage in mutual laceration, and that they would spare Arius and abandon the cause of Christ in order to indulge their own greed, burned their shameful libels." Thus he.

units.la: Tertium.Facta Constantini,quum iam haberent suam quandam maturitatem, & quasi senectutem, intuearnur; vt quàm procul à mente Pontificiorum abfuerint (nè salso amplius Eius nomen obtendant)Lector intelligat, & habeat quod sibi satisfaciat. Primò cùm {n}Factio seditiosa (Episcopos) Aegyptios mutuò distraxit, ita vt Imperatori Constantino nonnihil negotij facesserent, quos tamen vt Patres,imò vt Dei Prophetas reuerebatur; illos secundò accersere dignatus est,& se rursùs non inuitum Arbitrum eorum controuersijs imponere, & demùm arbitrium suum,& sententiam per Epistolam significare, atque Concilij Decreta sigillo suo rata facere. Deindè ad Tyrensis Synodi Patres. {o}Quodsi quis (ait,) reiecto ac spreto mandato nostro adesse Synodo noluerit , delegabimus aliquem , qui Regia illum authoritate exilium eiectum docebit , hominem minimè decere summi Imperatoris praeceptionibus ad tuendam veritatem repugnare. Postremò ad Nicomedienses Episcopos. {p}Si cassos (inquit) habemus & orthodoxos Episcopos, gaudemus; quod si quis audaciter & inconsulte ad fovendas pestes exarserit, Ministri Dei (Meipsum dico) executione audaciae suae poenas dabit. Haec Constantinus. Ut multa paucis complectar. Constantinus Imp. Episcopos à se iudicandos esse non censuit: at Episcopi ipsi censuerunt. Illis non in Causis dogmaticis, at in Criminalibus; nec in tempore non suo, at in opportuno, quùm sedata omnia; nec tunc in tyrocinio suo Niceae, at post, animo maturus & aevo, Aegypti, Tyri, Nicomediae, iudicium authoritatemque suam interposuit. Hactenus de testimonijs ipsis; quibus ad extremum Coronidis loco additur à Bellarmino, vz.
units.tr: Third, let us look at the deeds of Constantine, when they already had their own maturity and, as it were, old age, so that the reader may understand how far they were from the mind of the Papists (lest they put forward his name any longer with false pretence), and may have something to satisfy himself. First, when a seditious faction tore the bishops of Egypt apart from one another, so that they gave the Emperor Constantine no little trouble, whom nevertheless he revered as Fathers, indeed as prophets of God, he deigned to summon them, and again, not unwillingly, to set himself up as arbiter of their controversies; and finally to signify his judgment and sentence by letter, and to make the decrees of the Council valid by his own seal. Then to the fathers of the Synod of Tyre: "But if anyone (he says), having rejected and scorned our command, is unwilling to attend the Synod, we shall send someone who, by royal authority, will teach that he has been cast out into exile, a man who ought by no means to resist the commands of the supreme Emperor in defence of the truth." Last, to the bishops of Nicomedia: "If we have bishops who are sound and orthodox, we rejoice; but if anyone has boldly and rashly flared up to foster pestilences, a minister of God (I mean myself) will pay the penalty for his audacity in carrying out the sentence." Thus Constantine. To embrace many things in few words: the Emperor Constantine did not judge that the bishops were to be judged by him, but the bishops themselves did judge so. He interposed his judgment and authority not in dogmatic causes but in criminal ones; not at a time that was not his own, but at a fitting time, when all was calmed; and not then in his apprenticeship at Nicaea, but afterwards, mature in mind and age, at Egypt, Tyre and Nicomedia. So far concerning the testimonies themselves; to which, as a final crown, Bellarmine adds, namely:

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De officiis

units.la: “Si haberemus Sanctos Episcopos, non egeremus huiusmodi testimonijs, ipsa enim sacra potestas, cum vera sanctitate coniuncta, cogit ad sui veneration em non solum Principes minores, sed etiam summos. — pag. 41.
units.tr: "If we had holy bishops, we would not need testimonies of this kind, for sacred power itself, joined with true holiness, compels reverence not only from lesser princes but even from the highest." — p. 41.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Bellarminum, in urgendis Testimonijs, non quicquam profecisse.
units.tr: FIRST REMARK. That Bellarmine has gained nothing by pressing his testimonies.

units.la: Cuiusmodi, obsecro, testimonijs? nam quae hactenus protulisti Nazianzenum, Chrysostomum, Ambrosium, Gregorium Authores & testes sanctos, & plane divinos habuerunt, & Caussae Regiae Patronos disertissimos: quos tamen producere soletis, ut Episcopis, si forte in summa Sacra via Reges conveniant, locum honorificentiorem; si palatia ingrediantur, praecedentiam deberi probetis; & posse Eos Principibus non excommunicatis Subiectionem suam negare; Excommunicatis Coronam detrahere. Hæc hæc est hodierni Papismi Arx præcipua. Proh hominum væcordiam! longè aliter Nazianzenus; {*}Magistratus, inquit, nobis praesunt. {*}Episcopi (inquit) Regibus subditi. Ambrosius, {*}Sacerdotes (inquit) secularibus potestatibus debent esse subiecti. Gregorius, {*}Imperatori (inquit) concessum est, Sacerdotibus dominari. Hæc sunt genuinæ & expressæ istorum Testium assertiones, quibus Bellarminus nihil nisi coactas & umbratiles Similitudines opposuit. Heu miseram Causam, quæ eget huiusmodi testimonijs! Testimonia excussimus; nunc Exemplis agis.
units.tr: What testimonies, I beg you? For the authorities you have so far produced, Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Gregory, are holy and plainly divine witnesses, and the most eloquent advocates of the royal cause. Yet you usually bring them forward so that, if bishops happen to meet kings on the sacred highway, you may prove that the bishops are owed the more honourable place; that if they enter palaces, precedence is due to them; and that they may deny their submission to princes who are not excommunicated, and strip the crown from those who are. This is the chief citadel of today's Papism. What madness of men! Nazianzen speaks quite differently: "Magistrates," he says, "are set over us." "Bishops," he says, "are subject to kings." Ambrose: "Priests," he says, "ought to be subject to secular powers." Gregory: "It has been granted to the emperor to rule over priests." These are the genuine and express assertions of these witnesses, against which Bellarmine has set nothing but forced and shadowy similitudes. Alas for a cause that needs testimonies of this kind! We have shaken out the testimonies; now you press us with examples.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De officiis

units.la: “ Certè magnus Constantinus cùm Concilio Episcoporum interesse vellet, non solium sublime erigi voluit, sed paruam sedem; neque ante sedit, quàm Episcopi illi annuissent vt sederet. Vide Eusebium de vita Constantini lib.2. cap.10. —pag.41.
units.tr: "Certainly, when the great Constantine wished to take part in the council of bishops, he wished not only to have a high seat raised for himself, but a low one; and he did not sit until those bishops had given their assent that he should sit. See Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book 2, chapter 10." — p. 41.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: FIRST REMARK.

units.la: Adversarios, pro libitu suo, Historicos veteres nunc repudiare, nunc amplecti.
units.tr: Our opponents, at their pleasure, now reject the ancient historians and now embrace them.

units.la: Lectorem tuum mones, Eusebium vt videat de vita Constantini; sed quibus oculis videat, id verò non doces: vtrùm quibus Eusebium Baronius tuus vehementer accusator; an quibus Ipse in Constantinum Imp. apud Theodoretum egregius subsannator. Ille, vbi agitur de loco, & tempore baptismi Constantini, primùm quaerit, {q} Sitne vera historia Eusebij; & ipse mentiens concludit tandem, Eusebium esse mentitum. Tu verò, vbi obijcitur{r} ex Theodoreto Constantinum in Conc. Nicaeno petiisse, vt tantùm Scripturarum testimonijs res in quaestionem addu-ctæ dissoluerentur, & determinarentur, (quo nihil dici potuit pro Scripturarum plenitudine augustius) Tu primam hanc Conditionem Iniquam vocas: deindè ipsum Constantinum perstringis, {f} Erat (inquis) Constantinus magnus Imperator, sed non erat magnus Ecclesiae Doctor. Quod responsum propius abest à contumelia, quasi Ille aut Doctoris munus suscepisset, aut sacrae Synodi Patres Orthodoxi non eius voci ac voluntati suffragati fuissent.[illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: You warn your reader to see Eusebius on the Life of Constantine, but you do not tell him with what eyes he is to see him: whether with those of your Baronius, who vehemently accuses Eusebius, or with those of the excellent mocker of the emperor Constantine found in Theodoret. Baronius, where he treats of the place and time of Constantine's baptism, first asks whether the account of Eusebius is true, and then, himself lying, concludes that Eusebius lied. You, when it is objected from Theodoret that Constantine at the Council of Nicaea asked that the matters brought into question should be resolved and settled by the testimonies of Scripture alone (nothing could be said more worthy of the fullness of Scripture), you call this first condition unjust. Then you assail Constantine himself: "Constantine was (you say) a great emperor, but he was not a great teacher of the Church." This answer comes close to insult, as if he had assumed the office of a teacher, or as if the orthodox fathers of the holy synod had not supported his voice and will. [illegible]

units.la: Sequitur enim apud Theodoretum verbis immediatè seqq. {c}Ista aliaq, de eodem genere, dum doctrinæ Apostolicæ consensum stabilire moliretur Constantinus, tanquam filius amantissimus, Episcopis & Sacerdotibus veluti Patribus propositi; maxima pars Concilij eius verbis obtemperauit. Hæc Theodoretus. Ex quo liquet, præcipuum nostræ religionis propugnaculum non tam magni Imperatoris, quàm maximi Concilij Niceni authoritate confirmatum esse; nam, vt Nicæa (quod Eusebius habet) à Victoria nomen suum traxerit, sic auspicato Protestantium Articulus, pro Scripturarum sufficientia, Nicæa obtinuisse videatur. Hæc [illegible, ~4 letters] omnino; nisi quatenus ad fastidiosam Aduersariorum nostrorum indolem, in allegandis Authoribus, denudandam vel maximè faciant. Ad Caussam reuertor.
