units.tr: For immediately afterwards in Theodoret the words follow: "These and other things of the same kind, while Constantine was labouring to establish agreement with apostolic teaching, were put forward to the bishops and priests as to fathers, as a most loving son; and the greater part of the council obeyed his words." So says Theodoret. From this it is clear that the chief bulwark of our religion was confirmed not so much by the authority of the great emperor as by that of the most great Council of Nicaea. For just as Nicaea (as Eusebius has it) took its name from victory, so the auspicious article of the Protestants, that of the sufficiency of Scripture, seems to have prevailed at Nicaea. [illegible] altogether; except insofar as they very much help to strip bare the tiresome disposition of our adversaries in citing authors. I return to the cause.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Singulis, de sella Constantini, Circumstantijs Bellarmini rationem labefactari.
units.tr: SECOND REMARK. That, with regard to each of the circumstances of Constantine's seat, Bellarmine's reasoning is weakened.

units.la: Vidi equidem Eusebium, in loco abs Te citato; vbi tamen Constantinum non video: non rectè citas, quo nullus est error facilior; in hoc Nos veniam pesumus, damnus, vicissim. Historia habetur Lib.3.cap.10. vbi video Constantinum non voluisse sedere, antequam Episcopi sedissent, & vt ipse sederet, annuissent. At inter nos minimè ambigitur, num non voluerit Constantinus; sed an non Ei licuerit, nondum sedentibus Episcopis, sedere: nec enim quicquid noluit vir prudens, id nolle ex officio necessario debebat. Tu integrum hoc Caput inscribis De officio Principis erga Episcopum proprium; Episcopum etiam proprium quemlibet Principe suo superiorem esse astruis, quod nunc demum, ex hoc facto Constantini confirmare voluisti; quasi illi non licuerit sellam oblatam capessere, antequam Episcopi omnes sedissent. Hanc Conclusionem Te docuit {u}Summus tuus Doctor Papa {w}Gregorius VII. Constantinus Magnus (inquit) non praemum Sessionis, sed ultimum inter Episcopos elegit locum; sciuit enim quia superbis Deus resistit, humilibus dat gratiam. Vah[?] ut se ventosus Papa, tanquam utrem, inflat! qui ex hoc Exemplo iactat se & alios Episcopos omnes ipsis Imperatoribus Superiores esse, quos (nimirum) humiles esse oportet; acsi imprimis Pontificibus superbis esse licuerit. Nos Imperatores ab hac Contumelia vindicabimus.
units.tr: Indeed I have looked at Eusebius in the place you cite, where, however, I do not see Constantine. You cite incorrectly, and nothing is an easier error. In this matter we, in turn, may pardon you: "The account is found in book 3, chapter 10, where I see that Constantine did not wish to sit until the bishops had sat down, and had given their assent that he should sit." But between us there is no doubt whether Constantine was unwilling; the question is whether it was not lawful for him to sit before the bishops had sat down. For a prudent man is not bound by duty to be unwilling to do whatever he was unwilling to do. You entitle this whole chapter "On the duty of a prince toward his own bishop," and you assert that every bishop is superior to his own prince, which you now at last wished to confirm from this deed of Constantine, as if it were not lawful for him to take the seat offered, before all the bishops had sat down. Your Supreme Teacher, Pope Gregory VII, taught you this conclusion: "Constantine the Great (he says) chose not the first place of session but the last among the bishops; for he knew that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble." Oh, how the windy Pope puffs himself up like a bellows! From this example he boasts that he and all the other bishops are superior to the emperors themselves, who (of course) ought to be humble; as if it were allowed above all to proud pontiffs. We emperors will vindicate ourselves from this insult.

units.la: {*}Alibi Constantinus Synodum {y}Episcoporum coegit, in quorum medio congressu [illegible, ~28 letters] non dedignatus est adesse; & una considere; rerumque in deliberationem vocatarum se participem facere. Vide Eusebium. Hic non expectato ullo Episcoporum motu, unà cum Episcopis consedit Constantinus; idque ex Dignatione fecit, non igitur ex debito. quidni Illi ius idem Nicæ fuerit? eò nunc (si placet) pergamus, & historiam ipsam penitius introspicianus.
units.tr: Elsewhere, Constantine gathered a synod of bishops, in whose midst he did not disdain to be present, and to sit together with them, and to make himself a participant in the matters brought up for deliberation. See Eusebius. Here, without waiting for any movement of the bishops, Constantine sat down together with the bishops; and he did so out of courtesy, not out of obligation. Why should it not have been the same right at Nicaea? Let us now, if you please, proceed there, and look more deeply into the history itself.

units.la: Sequitur apud {*}Eusebium; In Concilio Nicano sedem, quae quemque decebat, capiebat quisque:—in universo Ministrorum Dei conventu, propter Imperatoris adventum, qui jam erat in expectatione [illegible, ~20 letters] omnes egere silentium;—signo dato, quod Imperatoris adventum indicabat, [illegible, ~22 letters] omnes consurrexerunt:— per medium confessum intrat (Imperator,)—& postquam [illegible, ~24 letters] ad locum summum venit, [illegible, ~20 letters] primus in medio conventu stetit; & cum parua sella, [illegible, ~18 letters] ex auro fabricata, propositâ ei esset, non, priusquam Episcopi annuissent, consedit; [illegible, ~30 letters] idemq; omnes post Imperatorem factitarunt. Ex his constat, primò Episcopos, honoris causâ, Imperatoris adventum expectâsse; deindè jam ingressum eius expectantes, altum egisse silentium; post, ad primum quoque conspectum Eius, universum Chorum assurrexisse; tùm sellam auream ei obtulisse, & quùm ei praecipuam (proculdubio ob magnificentiam) sedem deberi significarunt, an & Sessionem in primam negarent? postremò nullum omnium ante Con·stan-tinum sedisse. Sic Episcopi. Constantinus dein quid? priusquam quidem Episcopi annuissent, sedere omnino noluit; attamen post ingressum in {a}Synodum [τόπον] ad sustinendum locum transsit, ubi rectus stetit. Licuit illi haud dubie in medio prius sedere, cui licuit stare in supremo. Denique vel Episcopos ipsos, etiam annuendo, ut prius Imperator sederet, satis significasse Praesidentiam Imperatori deberi, manifeste patet; tum quòd omnes Episcopi (iuxta Eusebium) post Imperatorem sedebant, tum etiam quià non sederunt prius, (ut est apud Sozomenum) quàm Imperator, ut consederent, manifestet; atque adeo gestu, nutu, & sessu suo Imperatorem sibi superiorem Episcopi agnoverunt. Vt{b}PRIMVS igitur historiam de Constantino, quà visa, quis non videat stupendam vecordiam vestram, qui ex illa historia illud Praesidendi ius Imperatori detractum voluerit, quod singuli ferè historiae illius apices penes illum fuisse, quodammodo clamitare videntur.
units.tr: It follows in Eusebius: "In the Council of Nicaea each one took the seat that befitted him;" "in the whole assembly of the ministers of God, because of the emperor's arrival, which was already awaited, all kept silence;" "at a signal given, which announced the emperor's arrival, all rose;" "the emperor entered through the midst of the assembly," and "after he came to the highest place, he stood first in the middle of the gathering; and when a small seat, made of gold, was set before him, he did not sit down until the bishops had given their assent;" and "all did the same after the emperor." From these things it is clear: first, that the bishops, out of honour, waited for the emperor's arrival; then, awaiting his entrance, they kept a deep silence; afterwards, at the first sight of him, the whole chorus rose; then they offered him a golden seat, and when they indicated that the chief seat (doubtless on account of his magnificence) was owed to him, did they also deny him the first session? Lastly, none of them had sat before Constantine. So the bishops. What did Constantine do next? Before the bishops had given their assent, he was altogether unwilling to sit; yet after entering the synod, he moved to [τόπον] place to take up the position where he stood upright. Without doubt it was lawful for him to sit in the middle first, to whom it was lawful to stand in the highest place. Finally, it is plain that the bishops themselves, even by nodding assent that the emperor should sit first, sufficiently signified that the presidency is owed to the emperor: both because all the bishops (according to Eusebius) sat after the emperor, and because they did not sit down before the emperor, as Sozomen has it, made it clear that they should sit. And so by their gesture, nod, and posture the bishops acknowledged the emperor as their superior. Therefore, first, who would not see your stupendous madness, who from that history wished to draw away from the emperor that right of presiding, when almost every detail of that history seems, in a manner, to cry out that it lay with him?

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. REMARK.

units.la: In facto Constantini non Maiestatis eius diminutio- nem, sed mansuetudinis eluxisse.
units.tr: That Constantine's action showed not a diminishing of his majesty but his gentleness.

units.la: IN hoc facto Constantini examinando Historicos nostros duces sequamur, qui sine dubio Magistros fideliter sequuti sunt suos; & sentiemus {c}Eusebium hoc Eius Modestiae, {d}Nicephorum Callistum Animi submissionis attribuisse. Modestia autem, secundum Philosophos, nihil aliud est quàm debiti honoris moderatio, quae est voluntaria remissio, & infra debitum depressio dignitatis propriae; non necessaria agnitio alienae. Tantum igitur abest vt Ius praesidendi Imperatori detrahat, vt magis illud demonstret, quum praesertim idem de Constantini modestia verè dici possit, quod de Eius mansuetudine fatetur {e}Baronius, qui ait: Eum tam studiosum mansue-
units.tr: In examining this action of Constantine, let us follow our own leading historians, who without doubt faithfully followed their masters. We shall find that Eusebius ascribes it to his modesty, and Nicephorus Callistus to his submissiveness of spirit. Modesty, however, according to the philosophers, is nothing other than the moderation of due honour: a voluntary withdrawal and a lowering of one's own dignity below what is due, not a necessary acknowledgement of another's. So far is it from taking away the right of presiding from the emperor that it rather shows it, especially since the same can truly be said of Constantine's modesty as Baronius confesses of his gentleness. He says: he was so devoted to gentleness

units.la: {a} Eufeb. quo supr. & Sozom. l. 1 hist. cap. 18.
units.tr: {a} Eusebius, loc. cit., and Sozomen, Historia ecclesiastica, book 1, ch. 18.

units.la: {b} Sozom. ibid.
units.tr: {b} Sozomen, ibid.

units.la: {c} Euseb. lib. 3. de [?]vita Constantini, c. 37
units.tr: {c} Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book 3, ch. 37.

units.la: {d} Nicephor. Callist. lib. 8. cap. 16.
units.tr: {d} Nicephorus Callistus, book 8, ch. 16.

units.la: {e} Baron. Anno 316 num. 65. mansuetudine fuisse, ut se Imperatorem fuisse interdum vi- deretur oblitus. Quid autem? an propterea hanc tantam sui demissionem in vitij partem interpretabimur? Abest enim, vt orationis, ita & moris quaedam quasi ... & sicut illa orationis non reddit sermonem falsum, sed figuratum; ita zeli & humilitatis huiusmodi excessus interdum non vitiant aut deturpant hominum actus, sed commendant potius atque cohonestant, ipsaque virtutes illustriores faciunt, modo ne affectati nimium sint, aut absoni atque abiecti. Fallitur enim sua opinione quisquis existimat mediocritatem ipsam, qua virtus definitur, in puncto consistere; quia huius medij latitudo quaedam est, quae, ex Analogia Circumstantiarum, maior minorue existimatur. Hyperbolicae humilitatis exempla & documenta habemus in sacris literis {f}Dauids saltantis; {g}Domini lauantis Discipulorum pedes; & {h}Patru redeunti filio obuiam properantis. Quid multa? in hoc facto Constantini non iustitiae, acsi debuerit non absque Episcoporum venia sedere; sed prudentiae laus maxima elucet, quod cum vidit Episcopos grauissimis opinionum dissidijs miserè distractos, Eorum animos hisce sanctissimis mansuetudinis, modestiae, & humilitatis quasi lenocinijs ad se pellexit.
units.tr: {e} Baronius, Annales, year 316, no. 65. that he sometimes seemed to forget that he was emperor. But what then? Shall we therefore interpret so great a self-abasement as a fault? For just as there is a certain excess of speech, which does not make the statement false but figurative, so excesses of this kind in zeal and humility do not always spoil or disfigure men's actions, but rather commend and adorn them, and make the virtues more illustrious, provided only they are not too affected, or out of tune and abject. He is mistaken in his opinion who thinks that the mean itself, by which virtue is defined, lies at a point; for this mean has a certain breadth, which, according to the analogy of circumstances, is judged to be greater or less. We have examples and instances of hyperbolic humility in Holy Scripture: David dancing; the Lord washing the disciples' feet; and the father hastening to meet his returning son. Why say more? In this action of Constantine there shines not a justice, as if he ought not to have sat without the bishops' permission, but a great praise of prudence: when he saw the bishops miserably torn apart by the gravest disagreements of opinion, he drew their minds to himself by these most holy enticements of gentleness, modesty and humility.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. REMARK.

units.la: Dignitatem Imperatoriam supra Pontificiam in confesso haberi.
units.tr: That the imperial dignity is admitted to stand above the papal.

units.la: Card. Cusanus, testis omni exceptione maior, ex antiquis Conciliorum Codd. exempla florentissimae quondam Ecclesiae perquirens, & quid Imperatore cum suis Patritijs in Conc. agere maxime decuit, perpendens; Reperio (ait) Imperatorem in sui persona existentem semper praesedisse. In sexta vero Synodo Constantinus praesedit in medio, cum decem de maioribus Patritijs, & ad laevam eius vicarij seniores Romae, vt Hierosolymorum; ad dextram vero Patriarcha alij primo Constantinopolitanus, deinde Alexandrinus, qui in eodem scamno consungebatur. Testes alios omitto, quià in re perspicua, non opus est testimonijs non necessarijs. Nè moleste feras, lector, si in hac Aduersariorum obiectiuncula refutanda prolixior fuerim, quo illi solent lætius liberiusque huiusmodi Exemplis premendis immorari. Pergunt enim.
units.tr: Cardinal Cusanus, a witness beyond all exception, searching the ancient records of the Councils for examples of the once flourishing Church, and weighing what the emperor with his patricians ought most of all to do in a council, says: I find that the emperor, when present in person, always presided. In the sixth Synod, Constantine presided in the middle, with ten of the greater patricians; and on his left the vicars of the elders of Rome, as of Jerusalem; on his right the patriarchs, first of Constantinople, then of Alexandria, who sat on the same bench. I omit other witnesses, since in a plain matter there is no need of unnecessary testimonies. Do not be annoyed, reader, if I am rather long in refuting this little objection of our opponents, since they are accustomed to dwell more gladly and freely on such examples in order to press them. For they go on.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officiis.

units.la: “ Et quum alias ad concionem in templo interesse voluit Constantinus, ubi solus Episcopus, qui concionabatur, fedebat in throno, & populus de more illius temporis stabat; oblata est Sedes Imperatori; sed recusavit, & cum reliquo populo stare voluit. Vide Eusebium in vita Constantini lib. 4. cap. 33. ----Pag. 41.
units.tr: "And when at another time Constantine wished to be present at a sermon in the temple, where only the bishop who was preaching sat on a throne and the people stood according to the custom of that time, a seat was offered to the emperor; but he refused and wished to stand with the rest of the people. See Eusebius, Life of Constantine, book 4, ch. 33. ---- p. 41."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. REMARK.

units.la: Constantinum inter concionandum non sedisse, ut maiorem animi attentionem ostenderet, non ut authoritatem suam exereret[?].
units.tr: That Constantine did not sit during the sermon in order to show greater attentiveness of mind, not to exercise his authority.

units.la: Libentissime[?] quidem; quem tamen Te vix dum vidisse quivis facile credet, qui Eusebij verba penitius pauló introspexerit, sic enim sequitur apud Eusebium, qui Concioni tunc interfuit. {k}Quùm flagitaremus (inquit) ut Constantinus in Regali folio, quod ibi sessionis causa positum erat, sederet, ----minimè cessit nostris precibus. Post (nempè magnà iam parte Concionis consumptà) deposcentibus Nobis ut sederet, subtristi vultu respondit, nefas esse institutum de Deo disputationibus negligentes aures præbere; sibi verò hoc esse imprimis utile, præsertim quum pium est de divinis rebus differentes erectos videre. Hæc Eusebius. Hæc altera historia est, ex qua colligit Bellarminus, Sacerdotes Imperatoribus esse superiores: in quo planissimè à scopo aberrat, utinam memoriæ aut inscitiæ lapsu magis quàm noxà quàdam Conscientiæ. Quà enim ratione hoc tàm inauditum paradoxum effutiret? Sedente (inquit) Concionatore[?] in Throno suo, Imperatori in suo Regali folio sedere non licuit. Consequentia sanè subagrestis, & (nisi Bellarmino Srni honorem haberem) explodenda magis quàm refellenda. Quæ enim, sodes, isthæc Ratio est, quam cùm omnis omnium temporum per universas Ecclesias recepta consuetudo, (nec enim Romanam ipsam excepio) tùm ipsa historia, unde desumpta est, apertissimè refutat.
units.tr: Most willingly indeed; yet anyone who looks a little more carefully into Eusebius's words will hardly believe you have even seen them, for this is what follows in Eusebius, who was present at that sermon. When we begged (he says) that Constantine should sit on the royal seat, which had been placed there for the purpose of sitting, he by no means yielded to our prayers. Afterwards, when much of the sermon had already been spent, and we pressed him to sit, he answered with a sad face that it was wrong to give ears negligent of the disputations about God; and that for himself this was especially useful, particularly since it is pious to see those who discourse on divine things standing upright. This is Eusebius. This is the other story from which Bellarmine gathers that priests are superior to emperors: in which he wanders quite plainly from the mark, and I wish it were by a lapse of memory or ignorance rather than from some guilt of conscience. For by what reasoning would he utter so unheard-of a paradox? With the preacher (he says) sitting on his throne, it was not allowed for the emperor to sit on his royal seat. The consequence is certainly rather rustic, and (unless I held Bellarmine Srni in honour) to be hissed off rather than refuted. For what kind of reasoning, pray, is this, which the universal custom of every age, received through all the Churches (nor is even the Roman Church excepted), and the very history from which it is drawn, most clearly refutes?

units.la: In Historia personæ duæ loquentes introducuntur, Imperator, & Episcopi. Dixit vero Imp. sibi nefas videri sedere inter concionandum; numquid verò [illegible, ~5 letters] & absolutè? minimè, sic enim Episcopis ipsis sedere nefas esset, nefas item Imperatori Sedem offerre. An igitur solum quatenus Auditor Sedendo in institutis de Deo disputationibus negligentiùs redditur; stando verò attentior? omnino, hæc enim ipsissima Imperatoris Ratio fuit. Atque utinam omnes Christiani, negligentiæ aut torporis sui consci, eandem (quatenus vere utilis & conducibilis) legem non sedendi sibi statuerent. Eusebius autem, alijque, quitùm aderant, sanctissimi Episcopi nunquam profectò Constantinum, ut in Regio solio sederet, semel flagitarent, atque etiam rursus (tanquam excessum zeli Ipsius stantis moderaturi) officiosissimè deposcerent, nisi id non modò licuisse, sed & maximè illum decuisse credidissent.
units.tr: In the history two speaking persons are introduced, the emperor and the bishops. The emperor said that it seemed to him wrong to sit during the sermon; but was it said [illegible, ~5 letters] and absolutely? By no means; for in that case it would be wrong for the bishops themselves to sit, and likewise wrong for the emperor to offer a seat. Is it then only in so far as a hearer, by sitting, is made more negligent of the disputations about God, but by standing more attentive? Entirely so; for this was the very reason of the emperor. And would that all Christians, conscious of their negligence or torpor, would set for themselves this same law of not sitting (so far as it is truly useful and advantageous). Eusebius, moreover, and the others who were present, the most holy bishops, would certainly never have begged Constantine so often to sit on the royal throne, and again, as if to moderate the excess of his own zeal while standing, would not have most dutifully pressed him, unless they had believed that this was not only permitted but also especially fitting for him.

units.la: Ut igitur suprà in solemni Concilio Patres {*}Niceni suo nutu (quo reverentiam Constantino exhibuerunt) ità nunc in hoc Templo Episcopi interpellatione suâ evanidum hoc & inconditum Bellarmini Paradoxon dis-sipârunt, quo docuit oportere Imperatorem in Conc. non Dedere, nisi Episcopis annuentibus, in Templo verò hè Sedere quidem. Hic subindè Nos è Templo ad Convivium invitat; sequemur, observaturi quas dapes adferat.
units.tr: Therefore, just as above, at the solemn Council of Nicaea, the Fathers dispersed by their nod (by which they showed reverence to Constantine), so now in this temple the bishops by their interruption dissipated this empty and absurd paradox of Bellarmine, by which he taught that the emperor ought not to sit in council except with the bishops nodding assent, but in the temple indeed to sit. Here he invites us from the temple to a banquet; we shall follow, intending to observe what dishes he sets before us.

units.la: Sanctus Martinus Episcopus Tarraconensis sic honoratus est ab imperatore Maximino, ut in comuniu ipse etiam Imperatore praepositus fuerit. — Pag.41.
units.tr: Saint Martin, bishop of Tarragona, was so honoured by the emperor Maximinus that he was placed even above the emperor at table. — p. 41.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: {l} Maximus Imp. quum in comuniu sederet, assidente quoq; B. Martino, & pincerna primum calicem Imperatori, ut omnium nobilissimo, velle offerre, illo ad episcopum misit, qui non recusauit, sed primus bibit; et postea non Imperatori sed Presbytero suo calicem tradidit, multum scilicet existimans dignorem, qui post se biberet; nec integrum sibi fore, aut Regum, aut eos, qui a Rege erant proximi, Presbytera pratulisset[?], ut scribit Sulpitius in vita S Martini. {m} Vides, Rex, quale fuerit iudicium Martini de dignitate Presbyterorum? quod si quicunque Presbyteri solum, quia Presbyteri, tales ac tantisunt[?], uti etiam Regibus praeferantur, quis iure mirabitur si Cardinales aequales Regibus non nulli aiicantur[?]? Haec Tu imperite ac inepte satis quod etiam Martini factum{n} Baronius,{o} Biniusque lectoribus observandum propinant affatim.
units.tr: When the Emperor Maximus was sitting at table, with blessed Martin also seated beside him, the cupbearer wished first to offer the cup to the Emperor as the most noble of all, and sent it to the bishop. Martin did not refuse, but drank first. Afterwards he handed the cup not to the Emperor but to his own presbyter, evidently thinking him worthier to drink after him. Nor would it have been right for him to have preferred his presbyter to kings or to those nearest the king, as Sulpicius writes in the life of St Martin. You see, King, what Martin's judgment was about the dignity of presbyters? But if any presbyters, simply because they are presbyters, are so great that they are preferred even to kings, who will rightly be surprised if some cardinals are set on a level with kings? These things, as you (Bellarmine) foolishly and clumsily enough, along with Martin's deed, Baronius and Binius serve up to their readers in abundance for them to note.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Sulpitij historiam à Bellarmino ipso in dubium vocatam esse.
units.tr: That Sulpicius's account has been called in doubt by Bellarmine himself.

units.la: IN hac historia tria veniunt potissimum discutienda; I. Sulpitij fides; II. S. Martini authoritas; III. & exillo facto Bellarmini, aduersus Principes, ridicula sane (in re tam seria) & odiosa collectio. Sulpitius Seuerus, Author omnino verus atque syncerus haud quidem ipsi Bellarmino fuisse videtur, cum alibi (Cuius propterea {p} Libros de sacra Historia caute legendos esse monet) tum vero insuper in Eius de Martino narratione, quem Bellarminus ideo reprehendit, qua tradidit {q} S. Martinum sensisse Neronem cum Antichristo venturum; & Antichristum ipsum ex malo spiritu concipiendum. Iam vero Martini dogma falso retulit Sulpitius; quidni pariter & factum Ejus?
units.tr: In this story three things chiefly need to be examined: I. the trustworthiness of Sulpicius; II. the authority of St Martin; III. Bellarmine's ridiculous and, in so serious a matter, spiteful inference against princes drawn from that deed. Sulpicius Severus does not seem to have been altogether a true and sincere author in Bellarmine's own eyes, both elsewhere (for which reason he warns that the author's books of sacred history are to be read with caution) and especially in his account of Martin, which Bellarmine rightly criticises. There Sulpicius reports that St Martin thought Nero would come together with Antichrist, and that Antichrist himself would be conceived from an evil spirit. Now Sulpicius misreported Martin's doctrine; why not his deed as well?

units.la: Nec sane abest Conjectura, etiam ex re nata, ipso quoque Sulpitio narratore; ex qua constat Regem Maximum apud se decreuisse ingentem hominum cladem in Hispania edere, Martinum vero obstitisse, quantumque potuit saluti hominum consuluisse, quorum cervicibus gladius imminebat: Regem, ferocis ingenii hominem, ira propterea accensum, quod Martinus non in ipsius partes se inclinaret; proinde Martinum, diu licet saepius rogatum, a Regis convivio abstinuisse: tandem vero ad diem festum invitatum adfuisse: ibi sumpto poculo, & Rege, aliisque Proceribus praetermissis, Praebibisse Presbytero suo, tanquam (ut ipse dicebat) aliis omnibus dig-niori. Quid? an vero ut omnino honore illo dig-niori? non est verisimile; sed tantum ut hoc symbolo significaret, Regem, aliosque viros illustres, qui cum Rege ad tantam hominum cladem conspirassent, indignos prorsus fuisse, quibus salutem de more bibendo gratularetur. Atque ita non aliter inter Regem & Presbyterum, quam inter virum noxium & innocentem, facta est collatio: & Martinus non de praeeminentia authoritatis, sed de sanctitatis praestantia contendit; nec iam Presbyteri aut suipsius, sed dei Causam egit.
units.tr: Nor is a conjecture lacking, drawn from the circumstances, and from Sulpicius's own narrative, from which it is clear that the Emperor Maximus had resolved within himself to inflict a huge slaughter of men in Spain, while Martin opposed him and cared as much as he could for the safety of men whose necks the sword was hanging over. The Emperor, a man of savage temper, was therefore angered because Martin did not incline to his side. Accordingly Martin, although he was often asked, abstained from the king's banquet; at last, however, invited to a feast day, he attended. There, having taken the cup and passed over the king and the other nobles, he drank to his presbyter, as (he himself said) worthier than all the others. What then? Was he really saying that the presbyter was worthier of that honour? That is not likely. Rather, he meant by this gesture that the king and the other illustrious men who had conspired with him in so great a slaughter of men were utterly unworthy to be wished health by a drink, as custom required. And so the comparison between the king and the presbyter was made not otherwise than between a guilty man and an innocent one. Martin contended not about pre-eminence of authority but about the excellence of holiness; and he was now pleading not the cause of a presbyter or of himself, but the cause of God.

units.la: Ita S. Martini factum symbolicos peractum potius quam cum Sulpitio (qui ipse 'Sanctitatis nomine illustris apud probatos, Authores nusquam legitur) interpretari libuit: a quo [illegible, ~3 letters] & crasso modo Martinus (tanquam insoliti vini odore turbatus adeo officii immemor) Presbytero praebibere, omissis Alijs, introducitur. Haec de Sulpitio; ad Martinum accedo propius.
units.tr: So I have preferred to interpret St Martin's deed as a symbolic act, rather than in line with Sulpicius, who is nowhere read as an author illustrious for his reputation for sanctity among approved writers. In Sulpicius's version Martin is introduced, in a crude manner, as though disturbed by the smell of unusual wine and so forgetful of his duty, drinking to his presbyter while passing over the others. So much for Sulpicius. I now come closer to Martin himself.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Quaedam Sanctorum facta non esse sancta; nec in exem- plum trahenda.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. Some deeds of saints are not holy, nor are they to be drawn into example.

units.la: Martinus vero (inquis) vir Sanctus fuit; quid tum postea? an vt propterea quodlibet Martini factum Sanctum dici mereatur? Nego equidem Consequentiam, quod ante me negauit vester Durandus; {t}Gregorius Magnus (inquit) Sanctus fuit, sed quum non fuit Deus, errare potuit vt homo: Negauit Salmeron Iesuita; {u}Bernardus (inquit) Sanctus fuit, tamen tota devotio erga Dei genetricem non consistit in Bernardo: Negauit denique Bellarminus, qui {x}Victorium sanctum Martyrem fuisse fatetur; eundemque, quod Eruditio illi defuit, erroris incusat. Imò, quem tandem omnium Sanctorum dabis, qui, si cum ipsa perfectione, tanquam cum Angelo luctari velit, non statim (Cuius rei symbolum in {y}Iacob exprimitur) in actionibus suis Claudicare deprehenditur? quod nunc S. Martino (si factum Eius non indulgenter nimis interpretemur) accidisse facile credimus, quum praesertim exempla Sanctorum omnium, quae sunt sacris Bibliis consignata, palàm docent, non decere divinitatis Praecones humanitatis ciuilitatisque esse expertes. Tertio in loco Bellarmini Consequentia exagitanda est.
units.tr: But Martin (you say) was a holy man; what follows from that? Is any deed of Martin's to be called holy for that reason? I deny the inference, as your Durandus denied it before me. Gregory the Great (he says) was a saint, but since he was not God, he could err as a man. Salmeron the Jesuit denied it; Bernard (he says) was a saint, yet the whole devotion towards the Mother of God does not rest in Bernard. Lastly Bellarmine denied it, who admits that Victorinus was a holy martyr, and charges him with error because learning was lacking in him. Indeed, which of all the saints will you produce who, if he were to wrestle with perfection itself as with an angel, would not at once be found limping in his actions (the symbol of this is expressed in Jacob)? We readily believe that this has now happened to St Martin, if we do not interpret his deed too indulgently, especially since the examples of all the saints recorded in the sacred Scriptures plainly teach that it does not befit the heralds of divinity to be without humanity and courtesy. In the third place, Bellarmine's inference must be assailed.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO. Martini factum à receptis & probatis moribus paulo fuisse alienius.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION. Martin's deed was somewhat foreign to accepted and approved customs.

units.la: S. Martinus primus habuit Presbyterorum suum, quàm ipsi Regi; inde Bellarminus, Quilibet Presbyter, quà Presbyter, in conuiuio, & extra conuiuium Regi cuius est praeferendus. Consequentia, si vel historiam spectes, improbabilis¹; sin vero Episcoporum aliorum, ergà Reges, mores, improba & immodesta videbitur. I°. enim Collectio Bellarminiana, ex circumstantijs facti Martini; II. factum etiá ipsum, ex sua nouitate refellitur. Circumstantia prima; Martino iam sessuro posita est sellula iuxta Regem; an igitur supra? somnium: imo verò infrà; nam quùm Pincerna officij sui esse duxerit, Regi prius quàm Martino paterem offerre, dubium non est, quin & alter Minister, in collocandis sellulis, eandem legem [illegible, ~3 letters] observauerit. Secundò, vbi Martini Presbyterum inueniam? en! Inter fratrem & patruum Regis medius collocatur. O facinus indignum! cur enim non supra Regem positus, Rege dignior? nisi forte in istiusmodi sympositiacis congressibus alia præsidendi, Præbibendi autem lex alia fuerit.
units.tr: St. Martin had his presbyter placed before the king himself; hence Bellarmine: any presbyter, as a presbyter, at table and away from table, is to be preferred to the king. This inference is improbable if you look at the history alone; if you look at the customs of the other bishops towards kings, it will seem shameless and immodest. First, Bellarmine's conclusion is refuted by the circumstances of Martin's deed; second, the deed itself is refuted by its novelty. The first circumstance: a little stool was set for Martin, about to sit down, next to the king. Was it then above him? Far from it, it was below. For since the cupbearer judged it his duty to offer the cup to the king before Martin, there is no doubt that the other minister, in arranging the stools, observed the same rule [illegible, about 3 letters]. Second, where do I find Martin's presbyter? Look! He is placed between the king's brother and uncle. O unworthy deed! Why was he not placed above the king, being more worthy than the king? Unless perhaps in such convivial gatherings the rule of precedence at seating is one thing, and the rule of drinking another.

units.la: Ad Martini factum quod attinet. {a}istud à Pincerna, qui calicem primò Regi obtulit, nouum & insolens habebatur, uti etiam ab ipso Rege, & Nobilium aliis, Qui omnes admirati sunt, & hoc ipso facto se contemptos existimabant. Obserua, Lector; non Rex solùm, sed & alij Nobiles hoc facto se contemptos existimabant: quid deinde aulæ Regiæ, aliisque Episcopis videbatur, attende. {b}Aula tota clamabat, fecisse Martinum in Regis prandio, quod in inferiorum Iudicum conuiuijs Episcoporum nemo fecisset. Nemo igitur non cernat, Consequentiam Bellarmini, tum propter Circumstantiarum aliarum [illegible, ~6 letters]; tum-etiam propter facti ipsius insolentiam penitùs esse luxatam. Quantò verò magis, si hoc Martini factum ex communi Christianæ Reip. consuetudine & vsu æstimetur? itàut hæc sola excusatio superfit, — Simplicitas digna fauore fuit.
units.tr: As for Martin's deed: that the cupbearer, who offered the cup first to the king, was regarded as something new and unusual, and likewise by the king himself and the other nobles, who all wondered, and by this very deed believed themselves to be held in contempt. Note, reader: not only the king but also the other nobles believed themselves to be held in contempt by this deed. Now consider what seemed right to the royal court and to the other bishops. The whole court cried out that Martin had done at the king's banquet what none of the bishops would have done at the banquets of lesser judges. Therefore no one can fail to see that Bellarmine's inference is completely out of joint, both because of the other [illegible, about 6 letters] circumstances and because of the very unusualness of the deed. How much more so if this deed of Martin is judged by the common custom and practice of the Christian commonwealth? So that only this excuse remains: it was a simplicity worthy of favour.

units.la: IV. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: IV. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Summas Imperatorum prærogatiuas præsidendi, præcedendi, & præscribendi vnico Martini poculo præponderare.
units.tr: The highest prerogatives of emperors, of sitting first, of going first, and of prescribing, are outweighed by Martin's single cup.

units.la: PRimò, Idem Martinus pro vita quorundam (qui iamiam neci tradendi erant) Regi supplicare debuit, tamen {c}Imperauit ille potius quàm rogauit. Submissius se gerebant non solùm (opinione vestrà) sanctitate Martino nihilo inferiores {*}Episcopi antiquissimi; verùmetiam authoritate longè maiores, Martinus I. Agatho I. Hadrianus I.alijque plurimi primæ classis {*}Pontifices Rom.qui Orantes, hortantes, supplicantes obsequium & obedientiam suam Imperatoribus humillimè præstiterunt.
units.tr: FIRST, the same Martin ought to have begged the king for the life of certain men who were about to be put to death; yet he commanded rather than asked. The most ancient bishops, who were not only (in your opinion) no inferior to Martin in holiness, but far greater in authority, behaved more humbly: Martin I, Agatho I, Hadrian I, and many other popes of the first rank, praying, exhorting, and entreating, most humbly rendered their obedience and submission to the emperors.

units.la: II. Si in Concilijs Sedendi ius supremum penes Principem esse primæuæ antiquitatis Exempla confirmârint, quia Orientales Patres parati erant Imperatori supremum locum concedere, (nam hanc causam reddidit {d}Bellar. cur octo primis Conc. Generalibus Papa interesse noluit:) Dein si Anno MDCCCCXXXIX[?]. in Concil. Florentino (dominante tunc Papatu) {e}Imperatori Graeco, super omnes Episcopos Orientales; Germano Imp. supra Episcopos Occidentales sedes collocata est, quando acerrima contentio inter Galliæ & Hispaniæ Reges orta est, quis eorum proximus Imperatori sederet: Sanè importuna & dura collatio est, ex vnico hoc conuiuali & (vt ita loquar) poculari potiùs quàm populari Martini facto concludere, Principes ad ima subsellia esse detrudendos.
units.tr: SECOND, if the examples of the earliest antiquity confirm that the supreme right of sitting in the councils rests with the prince, that is because the Eastern Fathers were ready to give the supreme place to the emperor (for this is the reason Bellarmine gives why the pope did not wish to attend the first eight general councils). Then, if in the Council of Florence in the year 1439 (when the papacy was then dominant), the Greek emperor was placed above all the eastern bishops, and the German emperor above the western bishops, and when a very bitter dispute arose between the kings of France and Spain as to which of them should sit next to the emperor, it is surely a hasty and harsh inference to conclude from this single banquet-and-cup deed of Martin, rather than from public custom, that princes must be thrust down to the lowest benches.

units.la: III. Si de nomenclatura quæratur, Quùm Basilius Imp. in Concilio VIII. in subscriptione nomen suum {f}Ex humilitate nominibus Episcoporum postposuit, tota Synodus rogarunt, vt se præponeret: id tantæ Synodi tot Patres (erant enim numero {g}ccc.) nunquam precibus ab Imperatore contendissent, si Episcopos, nedùm Presbyteros iure Ei præferendos existimâssent.
units.tr: THIRD, if the question is one of nomenclature: when the emperor Basil at the Eighth Council, in signing, out of humility placed his name after the names of the bishops, the whole Synod asked him to put himself first. Such a great synod of so many fathers (for there were 300 of them) would never have urged the emperor with entreaties to do this, if they had thought that bishops, not to mention presbyters, ought by right to be placed before him.

units.la: IV. Si in publicis plateis incedendum est, obseruari possit, quòd in Imperatoris Inauguratione nuperà Imperator ipse diademate, sub umbella, quam Senatores Francofurtenses gestabant, medius ibat; post Moguntinus & Coloniensis Episcopi agmen claudunt: Vbi licet locum occupárunt Principum Imperij; secuti tamen sunt, in honorem Imperatoris.
units.tr: FOURTH, if one must go in public streets, it may be observed that at the recent inauguration of the emperor, the emperor himself, wearing the diadem, walked in the middle under the canopy which the Frankfurt senators carried; after him the bishops of Mainz and Cologne brought up the rear. Although they occupied the place of the princes of the empire, they nevertheless followed out of honour to the emperor.

units.la: Postremò ( vt de Conuiuio par pari referam ) {b}Constantinus, Nicænæ Synodi negotijs feliciter transactis, Iussit sedes in palatio suo parari multas, quo illis Pastoribus omnibus epulum daret: qui autem erant illustriores, mensæ suæ fecit participes; alios autem ad alias dimisit mensas. Hæc Historicus. Attamen è toto illo sacro ( tot enim erant) trecentorum & octodecim Episcoporum coetu nullus omninò, quasi Cardinalitio fastu tumidus, cum Imperatore expostulauit, se, quem ante Imperatorem de patera bibere, aut cibos praegustare oportuit, ad inferiores mensas dimissum fuisse.
units.tr: Finally (to speak of the banquet on equal terms): Constantine, after the business of the Synod of Nicaea had been happily concluded, ordered many seats to be prepared in his palace, where he might give a feast for all those bishops; those who were more distinguished he made sharers of his own table, and the others he sent away to other tables. So the historian. Yet out of that whole sacred assembly (for there were so many) of three hundred and eighteen bishops, not one, puffed up as if with cardinalitial pride, complained to the emperor that he, who ought to have drunk from the cup and tasted the food before the emperor, had been sent away to the lower tables.

units.la: Sed quid Ego bonas horas contero in tanta futilitate refellenda; qua Bellarminus, in gratiam ordinis Cardinalitij, ex Martini prebibentis exemplo vnico & plane enormi, regulam generalem extrahit eminentioris dignitatis omne genus Sacerdotum supra Reges & Imperatores, in omnibus, contra omnium antiquorum Pontificum mores; contra vetustissimorum Conc. consensum; contra testatissimam praxin omnium temporum, omniumque Imperatorum, qui à primis vsque Regum exordijs Praesidendi, praescribendi, praecedendi ius obtinuerunt? Prebibendi igitur factum hoc nihil moror, quia (quod proverbij loco dicitur) Anima sicca est sapientissima. Mitto itaque [illegible, ~10 letters]; nè videar, vna cum illis, [illegible, ~8 letters] qui (si caute exponatur) ex Sanctitatis ac sobrietatis poculo Sacerdotibus arrogantiam & petulantiam propinare solent. Haec de S. Martino. Sed Sanctes etiam alios conquiris.
units.tr: But why do I waste good hours refuting such triviality, by which Bellarmine, for the benefit of the cardinalitial order, draws from the single and plainly outrageous example of Martin drinking first a general rule that every kind of priest of higher dignity is above kings and emperors in everything, against the custom of all the ancient popes, against the consensus of the most ancient councils, against the most attested practice of all times and of all emperors, who from the earliest beginnings of kings held the right of presiding, prescribing and going first? As for the deed of drinking first, therefore, I make nothing of it, because (as is said by way of proverb) a dry soul is the wisest. So I pass over [illegible, about 10 letters], lest I seem to be pouring out, together with those men who (if it is interpreted cautiously) are wont to pour out arrogance and insolence to priests from the cup of holiness and sobriety. Enough about St. Martin. But you seek other Saints as well.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarminus de Offic.

units.la: ‘‘ Et Sanctus Patritius Episcopus Hibernorum sic Regibus imperabat, acsi vere parens ac Dominus ipsorum esset. — pag.41.
units.tr: ‘‘ And Saint Patrick, bishop of the Irish, so commanded kings as if he were truly their father and lord. — p. 41.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Patritij factum in obscuro latitare, tanquam in specu ipsius subterraneo.
units.tr: Patrick's deed lies hidden in darkness, as though in his own subterranean cave.

units.la: Episcopum Patritium fuisse Sanctum facile credo, atque etiam (nam Septem Reges baptizasse legitur) Regum parentem: sed et pariter parentem obsequentemque Regibus: hoc quà Ciuem; illud quà Episcopum; utroque modo ut Sanctum decuit, siue Pastorem solicitum, siue etiam fidum Subditum. At, sensu Bellarminiano, Patritium Regum Dominum in temporalibus suisse, ecquis idoneus Testis? Haud temere, nullus enim (quòd sciam) Patritii vitam conscripsit nisi Henricus de Herfordia, Scriptor qui narrat Patritium, dauinitus admonitum, humi (miraculi causa) circulum designasse, atque inibi terra penitus subsidente, hiatum ingentem apparuisse. — hunc hiatum adhuc extare, & occulto quodam ac fumoso meatu ad nescio qua Purgatorij loca deducere. Hæc Ille; cuius historiae verba illa [Nescio qua Purgatorij loca] imprimis amplector; eoque magis, quia quæcumque loca ex Scripturis, ab Aduersarijs, pro Purgatorio, adduci solent, non plus (scio) pro illo faciunt, quàm hic Patritii specus Purgatorialis, qui iamdiù in fabulam vulgi abijt. Non expectabit Lector ut Testem (quisquis tandem fuerit) alio digner responso, quem Bellarminus dignum censet, qui alto prematur silentio. Sanctum alium salutemus.
units.tr: I readily believe that Patrick, bishop of the Irish, was a saint, and also (for he is said to have baptized seven kings) a father of kings; but equally he was a parent and an obedient subject to kings: the first as a citizen, the second as a bishop, in both ways as becomes a saint, whether as a diligent shepherd or as a faithful subject. But that, in Bellarmine's sense, Patrick was lord of kings in temporal matters, what competent witness is there? Hardly any, and rightly so. For no one (as far as I know) wrote Patrick's life except Henry of Hereford, a writer who tells how Patrick, warned by God, drew a circle on the ground (for the sake of a miracle), and how, when the earth sank away entirely within it, a huge chasm appeared. He says this chasm still exists and leads by some hidden, smoky passage down to I know not what places of Purgatory. So he writes. I especially embrace those words of his story, "I know not what places of Purgatory"; all the more so because whatever places the Papists are wont to bring forward from the Scriptures for Purgatory do no more to support it (I know) than this Purgatorial cave of Patrick, which long ago passed into the common folk's fable. The reader will not expect me to honour this witness (whoever he may be) with another answer, one which Bellarmine thinks worthy to be buried in deep silence. Let us greet another saint.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: De Sancto Dunstano Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi scriptum est, in vita ipsius, id, quod non meis verbis, sed Authoris historiae referre volo. Quadam vice Rex in monasterium virginum venit, ibique captus amore cuiusdam puellae, quae, quae inter Moniales non velata nutriebatur, eam ad suum colloquium adduti[?] secretius voluit. Illa, quum duceretur, timens pudori suo, raptum ab una Sanctimonialium capiti suo velum imposuit, eo modo se protegi sperans, si forte Rex quid inhonestè ab ea exigere vellet. Quam ipse velatum intuens, Quàm subitò (inquit) Sanctimonialis effecta es? ereptum ā[?] velum ab ea detraxit; illa conatu quo poterat frustrà obnitente; sic illa abusus est. Ubi verò res Dunstano innotuit, acerbo mœrore perculsus est: igitur quùm in re non segnis ad Regem veniret, & ille venienti promptè occurreret, eumque per manum ad solium suum perducere vellet; manum Dunstanus turbato vultu retraxit, nec eam ab homine contigi passus est. Ad
units.tr: Concerning Saint Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, it is written in his life what I wish to report not in my own words but in those of the author of the history. On one occasion the king came to a convent of virgins, and there, captivated by love of a certain girl who was being brought up among the nuns without a veil, he wished to bring her to a more private conversation. She, as she was being led away, fearing for her modesty, had a veil placed on her head by one of the nuns, hoping in this way to be protected, should the king perhaps wish to demand something dishonourable from her. When he saw her veiled, he said: "How suddenly have you become a nun?" and he snatched the veil from her; she, struggling as hard as she could but in vain, was violated by him. When the matter became known to Dunstan, he was struck with bitter grief: so, not sluggish in the affair, he came to the king, and when the king promptly met him as he came and wished to lead him by the hand to his throne, Dunstan with a troubled countenance drew back his hand and did not allow the man to touch it. Ad

units.la: « quod ille attonitus (non enim illum scire putabat, quod clanculo à se factum existimabat) cur manum sibi non daret interquirebat. Sed Dunstanus ad eum ait; Tu postposito omni pudore adulterium commisisti; Tu despecto Deo, signum castitatis non veritus, nunc virgini suam integritatem praeripuisti: & cur manum, sumo Patri virginis filium immolantem, impuris manibus tuis non tradam quaeris? Lava prius per poenitentiam manus tuas à sordibus tuis, & tunc demum quò gratiæ reconcilieris, honora & amplectere manum Pontificis. Territus ille ad hæc, in terra procumbit, pedes Antistitis pe-tit, se peccâsse, gemitu verba interrumpente, contestans. Quod Dunstanus videns tantum in Rege humilitatis exemplum, eum amplectitur, & erigit, & quæ ad salutem animæ operrentur[?] loquens, septennem ei poenitentiam iniunxit.»
units.tr: "at which the king, astonished (for he did not think Dunstan knew what he believed had been done secretly), asked why he would not give him his hand. But Dunstan said to him: 'Having cast aside all shame, you committed adultery; having scorned God, not respecting the sign of chastity, you have now snatched away a virgin's integrity; and do you ask why I will not hand my hand, which immolates the Son of the highest Father, to be touched by your impure hands? First wash your hands of your filth through repentance, and then at last, that you may be reconciled to grace, honour and embrace the hand of the bishop.' Terrified at these words, he fell to the ground, sought the feet of the prelate, confessing that he had sinned, his groans interrupting his words. Seeing in the king such an example of humility, Dunstan embraced and raised him up, and speaking of those things which work toward the salvation of the soul, he imposed on him a penance of seven years."

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Leuiusculi Dunstani historiæ similibus narratiunculis elevari.
units.tr: Dunstan's history is lightened by similar little tales.

units.la: IN superiore Paragrapho, pro Patritio, historiam adduxti sine Authore: hoc in loco (nam scriptum, inquis, est) Authorem innuis sine nomine: ut Tibi iure illud tuum reponere possem, Author sine nomine est sine authoritate. Sed Anonymus hic, ni fallor, {1}Osbertus est: sapienter authorem celas, cuius historia nihil quidquam putidius: In qua nimirum Dunstanus recusavit Missæ solennia agere, priusquam Tres monstra corruptores (ô noster misericors!) Capitis poenam sustinuissent. Ibi ex Dæmoniacu-iusdam ante se saltantis gesticulationibus Regis Angli obitum agnovit. (Non equidem existimarem Diabolum viro Sancto adeo fuisse familiarem.) Ibi Edgarus Rex die Dominico, venationi intentior, orauit ut Missa, usque dum rediret, differretur: Cui bonus ille Episcopus libenter morem gessit. Idem Dæmonem ignito forcipe per nasum arripit Dunstanus, lepidè irridens. Quod & Delrius, non obesæ naris Iesuita, arridens approbânsque retulit: de quo tamen Dunstani forcipe quid nos aliud sentiamus, quàm quod de Dominici candela
units.tr: In the preceding paragraph, for Patrick, you brought forward a history without an author; here (for it is "written", you say) you hint at an author without a name, so that I might rightly return your claim: an author without a name is without authority. But this anonymous writer, unless I am mistaken, is Osbert; you wisely hide the author, whose history is nothing more foul. In it Dunstan, forsooth, refused to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass until three monstrous corrupters (O our merciful man!) had undergone the penalty of death. There, from the gestures of a demoniac dancing before him, he learned of the death of the English king. (I would not have thought the Devil so familiar with so holy a man.) There King Edgar, more intent on hunting on the Lord's day, asked that the Mass be postponed until he returned; that good bishop willingly gratified him. The same Dunstan seizes a demon by the nose with a red-hot pair of tongs, mocking him wittily. Delrio, a Jesuit with no small nose, also related this with a smile and approval; yet as to what we think of this "tongs of Dunstan", what else do we think than what we think of the "candle of the Lord"

units.la: {1} Hunc Dunstani vitam scripsisse, testatur Tossanus; Quem Baronius citat, vbi de Dunstano meminit.
units.tr: {1} That Osbert wrote this life of Dunstan is attested by Tossanus, whom Baronius cites where he mentions Dunstan.

units.la: {k} De his singulis vide Baronium Annal.Tom.10. vester Canus? Dominicum (inquit) Dæmonis obstrepentis sibi manum candelâ combussisse dicere, perridiculum est. At non possunt huiusmodi exempla numero comprehendi, quae diuinorum Christianorum historias obscurârunt. Hæc Canus. Istiusmodi ego in leviculis historiis subnotanda duxi, ut facilius intelligas, Lector, Bellarminum senem nunc vapidum ex fæce haurire, quoties ex istiusmodi historiis Tibi aliquid observandum propinat.
units.tr: {k} On each of these matters see Baronius, Annals, vol. 10. Your Canus says that it is "most ridiculous" to say that the Lord's candle burnt the hand of a demon who was disturbing him. "But such examples cannot be counted, which have obscured the histories of the divine Christians." So says Canus. I thought such things should be noted in these trifling histories, so that you may more easily understand, reader, that Bellarmine, now an old man and insipid, draws from the dregs whenever he offers you anything to be observed from histories of this kind.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: “ Hic Lector primum observet, Episcopo veniente, Regem non in cubiculo eum expectâsse, sed illi occurrisse, manum porrexisse, atque ad solium deducere voluisse : deinde Regem ad reprehensionem publicam non iratum excanduisse.” — pag. 43.
units.tr: "Here the reader should first observe that when the bishop came, the king did not wait for him in his chamber, but went out to meet him, held out his hand, and wished to lead him to the throne; then that the king, when publicly rebuked, did not flare up in anger." — p. 43.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Bellarminum in Circumstantijs ludere ; Caussam ipsam non attingere.
units.tr: Bellarmine trifles with the circumstances and does not touch the cause itself.

units.la: Quid igitur Bellarmine? an propterea (nam hoc est [illegible, ~6 letters]) Dunstanus Episcopus Rege suo absolutè superior fuit? hic admonitus Lector Bellarminum non minus oscitanter & ieiunè disseruisse, quàm Regem piè humiliterque hactenus se gessisse facilè observabit. Primò enim Rex Episcopo venienti occurrit: ita, apud Euangelistam, {n}Pater filio. 2°. Manum ei porrigit: ita {o}Christus Malcho, tangens aurem eius, & sanans eam. 3°. Ad solium deducere vult: nempe etiam {p}Salomon Rex Beersheba suam Matrem ad solium perduxit suum. 4°. Rex ad reprehensionem publicam non iratus excanduit: similiter & {q}Petrus, publicè à Paulo reprehensus, ne mussitat[?] quidem. Annon verò iners planè Sophista, & ridiculus nugator esset, qui indè Filium Patre, Beersheban Salomone, Malchum Christo, (& quod vos mordeat) Paulum Petro Superiorem esse colligeret? Ecquid præterea Tibi observatu dignum occurrit?
units.tr: What then, Bellarmine? Is it for this reason (for this is [illegible, ~6 letters]) that Dunstan the bishop was absolutely superior to his king? Here the reader, once warned, will easily see that Bellarmine has argued no less drowsily and meagrely than the king has hitherto conducted himself piously and humbly. First, the king went out to meet the bishop as he came: so the father to the son, in the Evangelist. Second, he stretched out his hand to him: so Christ to Malchus, touching his ear and healing it. Third, he wishes to lead him to the throne: indeed King Solomon also led his mother up to his throne at Beersheba. Fourth, the king, not angered, did not flare up at public rebuke: likewise Peter, publicly rebuked by Paul, did not so much as mutter. Would he not be a plainly inert sophist and a ridiculous trifler who from this inferred that the son is superior to the father, Solomon to Beersheba, Malchus to Christ, and (which should sting you) Paul to Peter? What else occurs to you as worth observing?

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: “ Obseruet Lector Regem humi stratum pedes Episcopi cum lachrymis & singultibus apprehendisse; poenitentiam sep-
units.tr: “ Let the reader observe that the king, lying prostrate, seized the bishop's feet with tears and sobs, and most willingly accepted a penance of seven years. — p. 44.

units.la: “ tem Annorum libentissimè acceptâsse. —pag. 44.
I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Poenitentiae indictionem Regiae eminentiae nihil detrahere.
units.tr: The imposition of penance does not detract from royal eminence.

units.la: POenitentiam, & cor contritum gratissimum Deo sacrificium, Angelis, hominibúsque iucundissimum spectaculum esse, libenter agnoscimus: Dunstano igitur, septuennem poenitentiam indicenti, talem seueritatem; & Regi acceptanti talem obedientiam gratulamur. At multò mitiores vestri Pontificij, quos scimus r Tenui animi dolore, & t Attritione; seu c Imperfectâ & remissâ contritione, atque adeò leui poenitentiâ esse contentos: quùm contra Ministri Protestantes u Magnam animi concussionem: x Acrem & vehementem contritionem: y Conscientiam vulneratam: nec Septuennes modò, sed etiam in poenitentialibus homilijs (cum Baptista) quoad aetas humana ferat, perennes poenitentiae fructus exigunt à suis; & fideles qui sunt conditionem amplectuntur. Nihilominùs haec Poenitentia indictio Regiae eminentiae nunquàm fraudi fuit.
units.tr: We gladly acknowledge that repentance and a contrite heart are a most pleasing sacrifice to God and a most delightful spectacle to angels and men. So we congratulate Dunstan on imposing such a seven-year penance, and the king on accepting it with such obedience. But your Papists, whom we know to be content with a slight sorrow of mind and attrition, or imperfect and remiss contrition, and therefore with a light penance, stand in contrast: Protestant ministers demand a great shaking of the spirit, sharp and vehement contrition, a wounded conscience. Nor do they demand seven years only; in their penitential sermons (like the Baptist) they require perpetual fruits of repentance from their own people for as long as human life endures, and the faithful embrace that condition. Nevertheless this imposition of penance has never been a disadvantage to royal eminence.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Offices.

units.la: “ Et in historia sequitur, Regem multis bonis operibus super-
units.tr: “ And in the story it follows that the king, by adding many good works, expiated that sin.

units.la: “ additis peccatum illud expiâsse. pag.44.
I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSIO.

units.la: Dunstanum ipsum, in hoc certamine, Bellarmino aduersari.
units.tr: Dunstan himself opposes Bellarmine in this contest.

units.la: BOna quæcunque Rex fecit, nos iuxtà Tecum laudamus; Dunstani erga Regem facta non perindè laudanda: siquidem Pontificio fastu Regem contempserit. Quòd enim (nam Superbiam aegritudinem esse Philosophi definiunt) pedes suos à Rege procumbente suppliciter tangi permiserit, podagra: quod autem manum suam à Rege contingi passus non est, hæc chiragra fuit. At Dunstanus (inquies) non gloriæ suæ studio, sed detestatione peccati Regis (qui Virginis integritatem præripuit) itâ se gessit. Prona equidem mente hoc crederem, nisi quòd Card. Baronius aliud quiddam Lectori suo observandum commendauit; quùm nimirùm {2}Dunstanus (Archiepiscopatus Cantuariensis) pallium à Iohanne XIII. Pontifice Româ acceperat, Vidisti (inquit) extrema duo, Episcopum sanctissimum, Pontificem verò perditissimum: attamen illum hunc (videlicet, Pontificem) reuereri & colere obseruantissimè. Hæc ille, Obseruantissimè autem Pontificem reuereri & colere est (vobis definitoribus) Eius pedes exosculari. Obseruet igitur Lector, Dunstanum sui muneris esse, perditissimi Pontificis pedes exosculari, existimâsse; lasciui Regis manum vel attingere probro sibi duxisse. Ecquis Rex tam fungus, qui in his [illegible, ~3 letters] non sentiat?
units.tr: Whatever good deeds the king did, we praise along with you; but Dunstan's acts toward the king are not equally to be praised, since he showed contempt for the king with Papal haughtiness. For that he allowed his feet to be touched suppliantly by the king lying prostrate (for philosophers define pride as a sickness) is gout; but that he did not allow his hand to be touched by the king is gout in the hand. But Dunstan (you will say) acted thus not from desire for his own glory but from detestation of the king's sin, for the king had robbed a virgin of her integrity. I would gladly believe this, were it not that Cardinal Baronius commended something else for his reader to observe: namely that Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, had received the pallium from Pope John XIII at Rome. "You have seen," he says, "the two extremes: a most holy bishop, but a most depraved pope; yet he revered and cherished the latter most dutifully." So he. But to revere and cherish a pope most dutifully means, by your own definition, to kiss his feet. Let the reader observe, then, that Dunstan judged it his office to kiss the feet of a most depraved pope, but counted it a disgrace even to touch the hand of a lustful king. What king is so dull that he does not feel this in these [illegible, ~3 letters]?

units.la: Quanquam Dunstanus Archiepiscopus (vt quod verum est fatear) interdum tam æquum se erga Regem suum præbuit; vt, exemplo eius, Bellarmini, aliorumque Monarchomachorum omnium dogma conuelli & labefactari videatur. Quamprimùm enim Rex Eadmundus Regni fastigium est consequutus, Archiep. Dunstanum ad se accersi iubet, eius prudentiæ atque fidei regni gubernacula demandat: quid ad hoc Dunstanus? Baronium vestrum auscultemus, ex Osberto in Dunstani vita. {a}Dunstanus (inquit) Regi quasi præcellenti, secundùm Apostoli præceptum, obediendum esse perpendens, Regem adiit, & salua in omni reuerentia ordinis sui, eius imperio se subiecit. Hæc Ille. Archiepiscopum & Cardinalem committamus, nihil quis sentiet repugnantius. Nam Card. {*}Proprius Episcopus Regi, vt spiritus carni, omni modo superior: At Archiep. Regi, vt præcellenti, obediendum censuit. Rursus Card. passim negat hanc Subiectionem cum Sacerdotali dignitate posse consistere. Archiepisc.verò, Salvâ ordinis sui reverentiâ, Regis imperio se subiecit. Denique Archiep. cur Regi obediendum sit, diuino oraculo praeceptum Apostolicum allegat. Card. verò, cur Episcopi obedire non debeant, undè habeat, apud se amplius deliberet: quae enim aduersus Reges hactenus adducta sunt, Lector (scio) non tam obseruatione quam explosione digna existimabit. Ad exitum festino.
units.tr: Yet Archbishop Dunstan (to confess what is true) sometimes showed himself so fair toward his king that by his example the doctrine of Bellarmine and of all the Monarchomachs seems to be overthrown and shaken. For as soon as King Edmund had attained the summit of the kingdom, he summoned Archbishop Dunstan to himself and entrusted to him the reins of government for his prudence and faith. What did Dunstan do in response? Let us listen to your Baronius, quoting Osbert in the life of Dunstan: "Dunstan, considering that the king is to be obeyed as one who excels, according to the Apostle's precept, approached the king and, saving all reverence due to his order, submitted himself to his command." So he. Let us set the Archbishop and the Cardinal side by side; no one will find anything more contradictory. For the Cardinal holds that a bishop is in every way superior to the king, as spirit is to flesh; but the Archbishop judged that the king, as one who excels, is to be obeyed. Again, the Cardinal everywhere denies that this subjection can coexist with sacerdotal dignity, while the Archbishop, saving the reverence of his order, submitted himself to the king's command. Finally, the Archbishop cites the apostolic precept, a divine oracle, as the reason why the king is to be obeyed; but as for why bishops ought not to obey, the Cardinal must deliberate further as to where he gets his reason. As for the arguments so far brought against kings, the reader (I know) will think them worthy not so much of observation as of rejection. I hasten to the end.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio

units.la: “Multa eiusmodi adduci possent de Sanctis Episcopis, quos “Reges & Principes terrae, ut par erat, in HONORE MAXIMO habebant: quos, si temporis nostri Episcopi imitari velint, non erit cur de Principibus saeculi conquerantur; verè “enim non deessent multi Theodosij, si multos haberemus Ambrosios.---- Pag.44.
units.tr: “Many such things could be adduced concerning the holy bishops, whom the kings and princes of the earth, as was fitting, held in the greatest honour. If the bishops of our time were willing to imitate them, there would be no reason for them to complain about the princes of the world; for indeed there would not be lacking many Theodosiuses, if we had many Ambroses.----” Pag. 44.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Quid sit tandem, quod Episcopos vestros malè habeat, cùrue de Principibus saeculi conquerantur, nè nos celes obsecro. b Principes (inquis) cùm Episcopi de praecedentia rixantur. Graue crimen scilicet; quùm praesertim Episcopi(ut Tu vis) sint ipsis superiores. Ad quod probandum Ambrosium & Theodosium denuò introducis, & praeter Exempla Episcoporum (quae suprà citâsti) aliorum Episcoporum eiusmodi multa alia adduci posse dicis: quos si vestri (nimirum) imitari velint (nempe supra Reges ipsos) In HONORE MAXIMO habeantur. Haec singula paucis perstringam.
units.tr: What, I beg you, is it that troubles your bishops, and why do they complain about the princes of the world? Do not hide it from us. “The princes,” you say, “quarrel when bishops dispute about precedence.” A grave crime indeed, especially since bishops (as you would have it) are superior to them. To prove this you bring forward again Ambrose and Theodosius, and, besides the examples of bishops (which you cited above), you say that many other such examples of other bishops can be adduced, whom, if your men were willing to imitate (namely, above the kings themselves), they would be held in the greatest honour. I shall touch on these points briefly, one by one.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Causam Regiam perspicuè satis ex antiquorum Episcopo- rum testimonys definiri.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION. That the royal cause is defined clearly enough by the testimonies of the ancient bishops.

units.la: SI forte quæstio oriatur, an ab Episcopo grauiter reprehendendus Rex sit? c{c}Ambrosium appellas: si an honore Sacerdotibus postponendus ? rursus testem accersis {d}Ambrosium: si an ad legem politicam ferendam cogendus; aut è Templi concessis remouendus ? Ambrosium nobis regetis denuo: si denique an Episcopus longe maximo honore sit praeferendus, ipsum Ambrosium crepas; acsi vigilans dormirensue vnum somniares Ambrosium. Qui tamen Ambrosius palàm docet, {*}Sacerdotes, adeoque Pontifices omnes, qui Tributa accipiunt à Regibus, soluere; qui dominium iactant, Subyci; qui tyrannidem exercent,pati potius debere: atque bella, quae aduersus Principes excitant, in Supplicationum libellos; hastas in orationes; & hostiles minas in miserantium Lachrymas conuertere. In quibus, si Sacerdotes omnes Ambrosium imitarentur, non haberent reuera Episcopi vestri cur de Principibus seculi, imò nec Principes cur de Episcopis tantopere conquererentur.
units.tr: If by chance the question arises whether a king may be severely rebuked by a bishop, you appeal to Ambrose. If whether he should be placed below the priests in honour, you again summon Ambrose as witness. If whether he should be compelled to enact a civil law, or be expelled from the precincts of the Temple, you tell us once more, Ambrose. Finally, if whether a bishop is far to be preferred to the greatest honour, you rattle off Ambrose himself, as though, waking or sleeping, you dreamed of nothing but Ambrose. Yet this same Ambrose openly teaches that priests, and indeed all pontiffs, who receive tributes from kings, must pay them; that those who boast of lordship must be subject; that those who exercise tyranny ought rather to suffer; and that the wars they stir up against princes they should turn into petitions of supplication, their spears into prayers, and their hostile threats into tears of pity. If all priests imitated Ambrose, your bishops would really have no reason to complain about the princes of the world; nor would the princes have reason to complain so greatly about the bishops.

units.la: Theodosius Imp. vnà cùm Episcopo Ambrosio prodijt; nobile par, pietatis iuxtà & verae religionis sta-bili [?] quasi connubio coniunctissimum: quorum vt hic Episcopos subesse Regibus, ità ille Reges Episcopis praeesse [?] factis suis celebertrimis demonstrauit. Aduersarij vero Theodosium ad partes Pontificias pertrahere conantur, ipsi responsis [?] suis iam iugulandi. Primò cùm Theodosius dicit, se Episcopo Dioscoro Authoritatem, & Primatum dedisse, quanta satis ad Synodum moderandam esse potuit: Respondetur; {e}Theodosius (inquiunt) das, quod non habet, nisi ex vsurpatâ authoritate, idque ex imperitia Ecclesiastici Canonis. Deinde Theodosius & Iustinianus Imp. de personis Ecclesiasticis, deque eorum bonis ac disciplinis leges conscripserunt. Respondetur, eos hac in re {f}Potestatis suae limites egressos esse; sic Bellar. Ex quibus Responsis quis non satis percipiat, in Aduersarijs nostris, non tàm scientiam quàm conscientiam desiderari: tùm quòd in hac Causa Theodosium Patronum {*}ascisci, quem (vt nunc con-stat) flat ) Aduersarium, sibi nōrunt; quemque imperitiae in-iustitiaeque calumniose condemnant.
units.tr: Theodosius the emperor went forth together with Bishop Ambrose: a noble pair, most closely joined as in a firm marriage of true piety and true religion. Of these, the one showed by his famous deeds that bishops are subject to kings, and the other that kings are over bishops. Our opponents, however, try to draw Theodosius over to the Papist side, though they are themselves already to be throttled by their own answers. First, when Theodosius says that he gave Bishop Dioscorus authority and primacy, as much as was enough to govern the synod, the reply is: “Theodosius, you give what you do not have, except from usurped authority,” and that out of ignorance of the ecclesiastical canon (they say). Next, Theodosius and Justinian the emperors drew up laws concerning ecclesiastical persons, and concerning their goods and discipline. The reply is that in this matter they overstepped the limits of their power; so Bellarmine. From these replies who would not perceive well enough that in our opponents there is wanting not so much knowledge as conscience? This is shown partly by the fact that in this cause they take on Theodosius as their patron, whom (as is now plain) they know to be an adversary to themselves, and whom they calumniously condemn for ignorance and injustice.

units.la: II. ANIMADVERSIO. Episcoporum antiquorum subiectionem potestati seculari, testantibus Aduersarijs confirmari.
units.tr: II. ANIMADVERSION. That the subjection of the ancient bishops to secular power is confirmed by the testimony of our opponents.

units.la: DE Episcoporum suffragijs vestrum Binium testem adhibere liber, apud quem Episcopi in Conc. Aquileiensi Theodosium rogant, ut Concilij decretum ratum esse {g}iubeat. Et deinde Cyrillus Alexandrinus Theodosium, tanquam supremum humana gloria culmen, & longe maximo discrimine caeteris omnibus antecellens agnoscit: in quo divinae coelestitudinis symbolum omni terreno fastigio sublimius extat; cuiusque maiestatis nutibus nemo non ad iustam vivendi rationem provocetur. Haec ille. Qui neminem excipit, quomodo non omnes complectitur? imo & seipsum quidem inuoluit. Idem enim Archiepiscopus, in alteris eius ad Theodosium literis (quem antea offenderat, quod ad Eum tanquam ad hominem fide nutantem scripsisset;) {h}Vos (inquit) soli in omnes imperium sortiti, timore & mansuetudine subditos vestros in officio continentes:
units.tr: Concerning the votes of the bishops, you bring forward your Binius as witness, in whose work the bishops at the Council of Aquileia ask Theodosius to order that the council's decree be ratified. Then Cyril of Alexandria acknowledges Theodosius as the supreme summit of human glory, excelling all others by a far greater distance, in whom the symbol of divine heavenly majesty stands higher than every earthly height, and at whose nod no one is not summoned to a just manner of living. So he. Since he excepts no one, how does he not embrace everyone? Indeed he even entangles himself. For the same archbishop, in his other letter to Theodosius (whom he had previously offended, because he had written to him as to a man wavering in faith), says: “You alone, having obtained the empire over all, keep your subjects in duty by fear and gentleness:

units.la: Quare ego quoque impulsus sum, ut laesam vestram pietatem modesta quadam defensione placandam existimarem, ubi unum praetermittere duxi, propter obseruantiam, quae vestra Maiestati ab omnibus debetur: qui Sacerdotibus praecepistis Templum Dei sanctificare; & blasphemam (Theodori) linguam compescere. Ephesini quoque Conc. Episcopi ducenti literis pluribus {i}Theodosium obnixe rogant in hunc modum, Religiosissimo Deoque dilectissimo Theodosio semper Augusto sacra Synodus, quae per Dei gratiam, & vestra maiestatis nutum ac voluntatem in Ephesiorum Metropoli congregata est. SUPPLICAMUS ut literas vestras &c. — Et ORAMUS, & ante maiestatis vestrae vestigia prouoluimur, ut cum longanimitate suscipere &c. Et rursus; Nunc per piissimos Episcopos Legatos nostros nostros precesq; manibus pietatis vestrae genua complecti-mur, enixè precantes, vt quae per subreptionem acta sunt, omnino sint nulla. Haec apud Binium; ex quibus satis liquet, Aduersarios nostros vanius quam verius Theo-dosii imperiale crimen impegisse. Cuius authoritati priscae antiquitatis Episcopi sapientissimi subiectionem praebuerunt.
units.tr: Therefore I too was moved to think that your wounded piety should be soothed by a modest defence, when I judged it right to pass over one thing, on account of the reverence which is owed by all to your Majesty: you who ordered the priests to sanctify God's Temple, and to restrain the blasphemous tongue (of Theodore). The bishops of the Council of Ephesus, two hundred in number, also earnestly beg Theodosius with several letters in this manner: “To the most religious and to God most beloved Theodosius, ever Augustus, the holy Synod, which has been assembled in the metropolis of Ephesus by the grace of God and by the nod and will of your majesty. WE BEG that your letters etc. — And we PRAY, and prostrate ourselves before the feet of your majesty, that you receive with patience etc.” And again: “Now through our most pious bishops, our legates, we embrace the knees of your piety with our hands, earnestly praying that whatever has been done through misrepresentation be entirely void.” Haec apud Binium. From these passages it is clear enough that our opponents have charged the emperor Theodosius with a crime more vainly than truly. To his authority the bishops of the most wise antiquity gave their subjection.

units.la: III. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: III. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Eandem Subiectionem historica narratione, multifariam probari.
units.tr: That the same subjection is proved many ways from historical narrative.

units.la: SI omnes omnium temporum Episcopos memoratem, qui Principibus obseruantiam obsequiumque suum officiosissimè testati sunt, Tractatus hic vtiq; in immensum excresceret: modum itaque mihi statuam, delectumque faciam sanctissimorum Episcoporum, qui Valentiniano, Martiano, Leonique Impp. religiosissimis fideliter obtemperantes, in florentissimis felicissimisque Reip. Christianae temporibus viguerunt. De quibus ex Binio, Teste (opinione vestra) religiosissimo, constat I.k Episcopos Archimandritas Nouendecim Imperatori SVTPICASSE[?], vt per eum fides eorum firmaretur: professosq;, esse, se Dominissimi[?] Imperatoris (in Concilio constituendo) intentionem sequi. II.l Episcopos Europae Sacras eius literas relegisse, quibus Praecepit &c. III. Secundae Stiriaem Episcopos, in eo quod dignatus erat pijs eius syllabis indicare illius finem, dilatione eius Sanctioni obediuisse. IV.n Mesopotamiae alios septem eius Consilio Obedientes, sententiam suam declarasse. V. Necminus sese Obedientes praestitisseo Duodecim Phoenicie Episcopos, quia Cor Regis (sic enim aiebant) in manu Dei, & cor Dei in manu Regis VI. Isauriae prouinciae alios p Sexdecim, in ijs, quae Imperator illis Praecepit, legibusque quas pro rebus diuinis Sacerdotibus imposuit, se Subiectos agnouisse, nutuque illius inseruisse. VII. Episcopos (vt acervo premam) q Antiochiae, riachi, Pisidia, Selenciae, Pandesp[?]olcos, Adrianopolcos, Metro-polcos, Trojodolopolcos, Philomeli, Sozopolcos, Mulinopolcos, Limenopolcos, Sanctioni eius zelo divino completa, & subiectis per disciplinam quae ad salutem pertinent providenti parui[?]se. VIII. Epiphanium Pergensem vna cum aliis tredecim Reuerendis Episcopis {r}Pamphyliae, Prout divinus syllabus eius Pietas PRAECEPIT, quid sentirent de Timotheo Episcopo, cuius causa omnis de iudicio & probatione Imperatoriu & Sanctorum Patrum integritate pendebat, obtemperarasse. IX. {s}Prouincia Lyciae Episcopos viginti, in Marena Metropoli congregatos (quibus Imperator, vt aiunt, per syllabus sacras clamare visus est, sicut Moses, [Qui, est Domini veniat ad me) precatos esse; vt nulli aliy subiiciantur; vtque is Inimicos Ecclesiae nullo modo sineret, tanquam toram eo prostratos supplicasse. X. Hellespontica Regionis octodecim simul congregatos {t}Iussionibus eius velociter paruisse. XI. Quinque Episcopos Armeniae Secundae, agnoscentes {u}Deum prabuisse illi super omnes homines sine prohibitione potestatem, seque, qui pro abiectione sua nihil in terris sunt, in eius receptos curas, Iussos esse sententiam illi suam significare. XII. (ne longior sim) Alios {x}Iubenti & praecipienti obedientes fuisse: Alios, {y}vt Ille Sacerdotes iuberet pro incolumitate Imperij preces celebrare, exorasse.
units.tr: If I were to set out every bishop of every age who has dutifully testified his observance and obedience to princes, this treatise would certainly swell beyond measure.
