I will therefore set a limit for myself and select the most holy bishops who, faithfully obeying the most religious emperors Valentinian, Martian and Leo, flourished in the most prosperous and happy times of the Christian commonwealth. Concerning them, it is established from Binius, a witness (in your opinion) most religious, that: I. bishops, nineteen archimandrites, supplicated the emperor so that their faith might be confirmed through him, and they professed that they were following the intention of the most lordly emperor (in convening the council). II. the bishops of Europe read over his sacred letters, in which he commanded, etc. III. the bishops of Second Syria, bishops, because he had deigned to make known to them by his pious letters the purpose of the council, obeyed his sanction by deferring to it. IV. seven others of Mesopotamia, obedient to his counsel, declared their opinion. V. no less did twelve bishops of Phoenicia show themselves obedient, because the heart of the king (as they said) is in the hand of God, and the heart of God in the hand of the king. VI. sixteen others of the province of Isauria, acknowledged that they were subject to him in the things which the emperor commanded them and in the laws which he imposed on priests for divine matters, and yielded to his nod. VII. the bishops (to press the heap down) of Antioch, Pisidia, Selencia, Pandespolcos, Adrianopolcos, Metropolcos, Trojodolopolcos, Philomeli, Sozopolcos, Mulinopolcos and Limenopolcos, having fulfilled his sanction with divine zeal, and having provided for their subjects through discipline what pertains to salvation, obeyed. VIII. Epiphanius of Perga, together with thirteen other reverend bishops {r}of Pamphylia, as his divine and pious letter commanded, obeyed in declaring what they thought about Timothy the bishop, on whose case the whole matter of judgment and proof depended, with the integrity of the imperial and holy Fathers. IX. The bishops of the province of Lycia, twenty, gathered at Marena the metropolis (to whom the emperor, as they say, seemed through his sacred letter to cry out, like Moses, "Whoever is on the Lord's side, let him come to me"), prayed that they be subject to no other, and that he by no means permit enemies of the Church; having prostrated themselves, as it were, at his feet, they entreated. X. Eighteen bishops of the Hellespontine region, gathered together at once, quickly obeyed his commands. XI. Five bishops of Armenia Secunda, acknowledging that God had granted him power over all men without restriction, and that they, who in their abjection are nothing on earth, had been received into his care, were ordered to declare their opinion to him. XII. (not to be too long) others obeyed his command and order; others entreated that he would order those priests to offer prayers for the safety of the empire.

units.la: Possent huiusmodi fere mille priscae antiquitatis testimonia afferri Episcoporum eorum qui (quemadmodum de LXX. Interpretum diversis cellulis fertur) dissitis regionibus plerique degentes, in hanc unam sententiam quasi unanimiter conspirarunt, ut concluderent Imperatorie Pietatis, Maiestatis, Pra-potentiae sacris syllabis, iussionibus, oraculis, sanctionibus, atq; praeceptis obedientiam & subiectionem ab omnibus Sacerdotibus deberi. Elogia igitur, quibus Episcopi Reges ornarunt; testimonia, quibus eorum Praeceptis & Iussionibus subiectione sua exhibuerunt, tam clara sunt, ut nisi Aduersarij nostri eo ineptitudinis & peruersitatis venerint, ut quemadmodùm ex illis Alij dixerint, *Exornauit. i. e. ornamentis nudauit; & Statuimus. i. e. abrogamus; itâ illi Imperatorum IVSSISSE per SUPPLI[?]CASSE; & Episcoporum OBTEMPERASSE per IMPERASSE interpretentur: certè quidem Eos Nazianzeni, Chrysostomi, Ambrosii, Gregorii, aliorumque antiquissimorum Episcoporum (quos adduximus) suffragiorum perspicuitate, multitudine, pondere obrui necesse est. Hactenùs de Episcopis.
units.tr: Almost a thousand such testimonies of ancient bishops could be brought forward, of those who (as is told of the separate cells of the Seventy translators) mostly lived in distant regions and yet conspired almost unanimously in this one opinion, namely that obedience and subjection are owed by all priests to the sacred syllables, commands, oracles, sanctions and precepts of imperial piety, majesty and power. The praises, therefore, with which bishops adorned kings, and the testimonies by which they showed their subjection to his precepts and commands, are so clear that, unless our opponents have come to such a pitch of folly and perversity that, as some of them have interpreted from those texts, Exornauit, i.e. stripped of ornaments; and Statuimus, i.e. we abrogate; so they would interpret that the emperors commanded by entreating, and that the bishops obeyed by commanding, it is certain that the clarity, number and weight of the votes of those (we have cited) Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Gregory, and other most ancient bishops must overwhelm them. So much concerning the bishops.

units.la: CAP. VII. DE OFFICIO PRINCI- PIS CHRISTIANI ERGA SUUM CONFESSARIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. ON THE DUTY OF A CHRISTIAN PRINCE TOWARDS HIS CONFESSOR.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: “ Sacerdos Principis Confessarius non sine ratione ponitur à nobis inter eos, quos ut suos superiores Princeps Christianus venerari debet.----Pag. 44.
units.tr: "The priest who is a Christian prince's confessor is not without reason placed by us among those whom a Christian prince ought to honour as his superiors.----Page 44.

units.la: Explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation.

units.la: Etsi hoc in loco sermonem ad Sacerdotem proprium astringas, supra tamen magis generaliter omnium Sacerdotum causam strenuè agis; totus in hoc, ut probes Sacerdotibus praecedentia praeminentiam deberi, quia scilicet {*}Sacerdotium regno politico, quantum spiritus carni, quantum aurum plumbo, quantum coelum terrae praestat: praecipuè verò ubi de praebibitione illa S. Martini triumphas, & ex liquido firmum, & humido solidum Te putas argumentum colligisse. {a}Quod si quicunque Presbyteri (inquis) solum quia Presbyteri tali ac tanta dignitate praediti sunt, ut Regibus praeferantur, quis iure mirabitur si Cardinales (Presbyteri * aut Diaconi) aequales Regibus dicantur. {b}Quod dici solet, equiparari Cardinales Regibus; de externo cultu & honore intelligendum videtur: usus enim abtinuit, ut quemadmodum Principes omnes Regibus, sic etiam cedant Cardinalibus. Haec Tu. Propterea quae dicenda erant de Presbyteris aut Cardinalibus, in hoc Capite (sed parcius) expedienda sunt.
units.tr: Although in this place you narrow your discussion to the priest in particular, you nevertheless argue more generally the cause of all priests. Your whole aim is to prove that priority and pre-eminence are owed to priests, because, of course, {*}the priesthood surpasses the political realm as much as the spirit surpasses the flesh, as much as gold surpasses lead, as much as heaven surpasses earth. You especially exult over that drinking-cup of St Martin, and you think you have drawn a firm argument from the liquid and a solid one from the moist. {a}But if (you say) any elders whatever, merely because they are elders and endowed with so great a dignity that they are placed above kings, then who would rightly wonder if cardinals (elders {*}or deacons) are said to be equal to kings? {b}What is commonly said, that cardinals are equated with kings, seems to be meant with regard to outward worship and honour: for custom has prevailed that, just as all princes yield to kings, so they also yield to cardinals. So you. Therefore what has to be said about elders or cardinals will be dealt with in this chapter, though more sparingly.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Hodiernorum Presbyterorum arrogantiam priscorum Episcoporum subiectione refelli.
units.tr: FIRST ANIMADVERSION. The arrogance of present-day elders is refuted by the subjection of the ancient bishops.

units.la: INgenium tuum, Bellarmine, externae gloriae satis cupidum prodidisti, dum Presbyteros tuos effers ad caelum, ut Tu cum illis supra omnes Reges ambitiosis alis volitare possis. Non est ergo quod de Presbyteri istius [illegible, ~8 letters] tantopere glorieris; nam {c}Gloriatio vestra non est bona. Deponite infulas, Deus enim ipse (propter impressam in illis supremae Maiestatis imaginem) Reges Deos dixit; illos inter mortales {d}[illegible, ~12 letters] constituit; Illosque [illegible, ~12 letters] i. e. supereminentes potestates appellavit; {e}quibus aliam Omnem animam subjici mandavit: Illis denique non modo omnes (quos etiam {*}Deos dicendos autumas) Catholicae Ecclesiae Episcopi per mille Annorum seriem obedientiam exhibuerunt; verum etiam (vobis confitentibus) Episcoporum Episcopi, Summi Pontifices pene universi, ex omnium seculorum memoria, usque ad Hildebrandi[?] Papae aetatem, Suprematum {*}tribuerunt. Quum igitur vestros, ut ita dicam, summos Ioves Imperatoribus subiectos videmus, aequumne ut istos Presbyteros aliós, ceu minutulos Deos, illis superiores esse concedamus? minime vero, nedum Cardinales.
units.tr: YOUR disposition, Bellarmine, you have revealed to be keenly eager for outward glory, while you extol your elders to the skies, so that with them you may soar on ambitious wings above all kings. There is therefore no reason for you to glory so much in that [illegible, ~8 letters] of the elders; for {c}your boasting is not good. Lay aside your mitres! For God himself (on account of the image of supreme majesty stamped upon them) called kings gods; he set them among mortals; and he called them {d}[illegible, ~12 letters], that is, supereminent powers; {e}to whom he commanded every other soul to be subject. Lastly, to them not only have all the bishops of the Catholic Church (whom you also claim are to be called gods) paid obedience through a series of a thousand years; but also (as you yourselves confess) almost all the chief bishops, the Popes, from the memory of every age down to the time of Pope Hildebrand, have ascribed supremacy to them. Since, then, we see your, so to speak, chief Jupiters subject to emperors, is it right that we should concede that those other elders, as if they were little gods, are superior to them? By no means, much less cardinals.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, De Officio.

units.la: Siquidem sacerdos audiendis confessionibus poenitentium, quicunque illi sunt, siue Principes, siue privati, Index est loco Dei, & potestatem habet in fori conscientia ligandi & soluendi.
units.tr: For the priest who hears the confessions of penitents, whoever they are, whether princes or private persons, is a judge in the place of God, and has power in the forum of conscience to bind and to loose.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO. Confessiones Papistarum variis erroribus, atque foedis & horridis abusibus inquinari.
units.tr: FIRST ANIMADVERSION. The confessions of the Papists are polluted by various errors and by foul and horrid abuses.

units.la: Confessionem non modò publicam, sed & privatam; nec tantum generalium, sed etiam quorundam particularium peccatorum ( quatenus quis itâ angitur & affligitur peccatorum sensu, ut se explicare absque alieno adjutorio nequeat) coràm Sacerdote, à Protestantibus ipsis admitti, vel {f}Aduersarij nostri confitentur: sed tamen cùm hac moderatione admitti, ut huiusmodi Confessio nec omnibus hominibus, nec de omnibus peccatis, (interclusâ aliàs omni salutis spe) exigatur. Quos tamen certum est à Romana Ecclesia [?] confitendi deterreri tùm propter multiplices errores, tùm etiam propter abusus foedissimos, quibus mos Romanus scatet.
units.tr: Confession, not only public but also private, and not only of general sins but also of certain particular sins (inasmuch as someone is so troubled and afflicted by a sense of sin that he cannot explain himself without another's help), made before a priest, is admitted by the Protestants themselves, or our opponents confess it. But it is admitted with this moderation: that such a confession is demanded neither of all men nor for all sins (otherwise all hope of salvation would be cut off). Yet it is certain that they are deterred from confessing by the Roman Church, both on account of manifold errors and also on account of the most foul abuses with which Roman custom teems.

units.la: Inter Errores merito numeramus tàm {g}Canonem illum Tridentinum, qui definit Confessionem omnium particularium peccatorum necessariam esse iure divino; sine qua peccatorum remissio nulla: quàm {h}Innocentij II. Papæ decretum, quo fideles omnes, ad annos discretionis pervenientes, viventes ab ingressu Ecclesiæ arcendos, & mortuos sepulturâ Christianâ privandos, nisi saltem semel in Anno peccato proprio Sacerdoti confiteantur; Contra nubem quandam Testium, qui liberè ingenuèque fatentur {i}Propositum confitendi non fuisse necessarium in veteri lege;
units.tr: Among the errors we rightly count both that Tridentine canon which defines that {g}confession of all particular sins is necessary by divine law, without which there is no remission of sins; and {h}the decree of Pope Innocent II, by which all the faithful who have reached the years of discretion are to be kept from entering the Church while living, and deprived of Christian burial when dead, unless at least once a year they confess their own sin to a priest; against that cloud of witnesses who freely and candidly admit that {i}the intention of confessing was not necessary under the old law;

units.la: Quandò {k}Sacerdos non omnia populi peccata sciebat, sed tantùm in generali: Etiam {a}Nullo iure diuino imperatum; neque in communi vsu {b}Antiquæ Ecclesiæ fuisse: nec hactenùs {c}Ad Græcos manâsse. Addo, non rectè dici Sacerdotem vt proprie Iudicem esse loco Dei, potestatem habere soluendi & ligandi: {d}Quia aliter Deus soluit & ligat, aliter Ecclesia; Deus per se dimittit peccatum, mundans animam ab interiori macula; Sacerdos autem offendendo homines ligatos aut absolutos esse, vt Sacerdos offendebat leprosum esse mundum: Quemadmodùm solet accidere (vt vetter [?] mos est) aliquem {e}Post mortem absolui; quæ ratio Absolutionis propriè Iudicialis dici non potest. Transeo ad Abusus.
units.tr: when {k}the priest did not know all the sins of the people, but only in general; {a}not commanded by any divine law; nor was it {b}in common use in the ancient Church; nor has it hitherto {c}spread to the Greeks. I add that it is not rightly said that the priest, as a judge properly so called, holds the place of God and has the power of loosing and binding: {d}because God looses and binds in one way, the Church in another; God forgives sin by himself, cleansing the soul from inward stain; but the priest, by declaring men bound or absolved, is like the priest who declared the leper clean. Just as it commonly happens (as is customary) that someone is {e}absolved after death; and this manner of absolution cannot properly be called judicial. I pass on to the abuses.

units.la: Abusum voco illam {f}Enumerationem omnium peccatorum, & circumstantiarum eorum, quatenùs peccatum notabiliter aggrauant (eiusmodi Septem recensetis, quas cuiuis peccato adhærere possibile est;) & id genus documenta alia, quibus {g}Arguti homines Confessionem impossibilem reddi iierunt: & veluti {h}Ignari & importuni Medici conscientijs hominum, quas extricare & leuare debent, laqueos iniiciunt. Nec mirum, quùm præsertim ipse Aquinas {i}Circumstantiarum torturas sensisse videtur, & arbitrabatur candido Christi pectori confirmationem esse Confessionem, quæ tranquillo animo sine circumstantijs bonâ fide facta est, quàm quæ his sit animo scrupuloso & inquieto. Deindè Formulas illas Confessionum, {k}quibus (loquitur de Iesuitis) sancti illi Pneumatici circa peccatorum differentias obscœna quædam & impudica exquiruut, quæ sine interrogati (cuius auribus inaudita tumpitudines & lasciuiæ instillantur) rubore, & interrogantis inhonesti appetitus titillatione vix vllis verbis aut ne vix quidem enunciari possint. Istiusmodi eas dixerim, de quarum Polutionibus {l}Toletus Iesuita meminit.
units.tr: I call an abuse that {f}enumeration of all sins and their circumstances, insofar as they notably aggravate sin (you list seven such circumstances, which can attach to any sin), and that kind of other devices by which {g}clever men have made confession impossible; and like {h}ignorant and meddlesome doctors, they cast snares upon men's consciences, which they ought to disentangle and relieve. Nor is this surprising, since {i}Aquinas himself seems to have felt the torments of circumstances, and thought that confession made in good faith with a calm mind, without circumstances, is a confirmation to the candid breast of Christ, rather than one made with a scrupulous and restless mind. Then those formulas of confession, {k}by which (he speaks of the Jesuits) those holy pneumatics inquire about certain obscene and immodest matters concerning the differences of sins, which can scarcely be uttered in any words without blushing on the part of the one questioned (into whose ears unheard-of filthiness and wantonness are instilled) and without arousing the dishonourable appetite of the questioner. Such, I would call them, are those whose pollutions Toletus the Jesuit mentions.

units.la: Quamuis hi Abusus sint omninò execrabiles, à quibus Ecclesia abhorruisse certum est: ille tamen mihi omnium maximè horrendus semper est visus, quo sic statuunt, quòd etsi Confitens significauerit so iam insigne aliquod facinus mente secum agere atque anhelare, tamen
units.tr: Although these abuses are altogether execrable, and the Church has certainly shrunk from them, that one has always seemed to me the most horrendous of all, by which they lay down that, even if the one confessing has indicated that he is mentally planning and longing for some notable crime, nevertheless

units.la: Tantum esse sigillū confessionis religionem, vt in nullo casu, propter nullum finem, etiam pro tuendā totā Repub. ab ingenti malo temporali aut spirituali violare illud liceat. Sic Illi. Tantum religio potuit suadere malorum. Atque hoc modo nefandam illam, & quasi Achroniticam Prodirionem Pulverem, (quà prodigiosissimi post homines natos perduelles, Iesuitarum pleni, Regem nostrum & Regnum totum repræsentatiuum vno quasi camino devorare voto se obstrinxerant;) hoc Sigillum obtendentes, silentio contra ius falsque premebant. Si totus legis Decalogi finis Charitas sit, quanto magis Euangelij? Poenitentiæ Sacramentum (quod dicitis) tantum in gratiam poenitentis, quatenus est poenitens, instituitur; cuius semper vox esse solet, Peccavi; Peccabo vero nunquàm: quippe Confessio tantum praeteritorum peccatorum agnitio est, non autem professio futurorum; hæc contritio animi, illa obfirmati. Sigillum autem Sacramenti nunquid Sacramento ipso sacratius, cuius tamen tantam esse Religionem putatis, vt non ad facinus futurum reuelandum, pro salute aliorum vel Temporali vel Spirituali, vobis infringere illud liceat; etiam tunc cum ipsius consitentis anima silentio vestro Satanæ magis mancipatur?
units.tr: So great is the seal of confession as a matter of religion, that in no case, for no end, not even to defend the whole commonwealth from a great temporal or spiritual evil, is it lawful to violate it. Thus they. So much could religion persuade to evils. And in this way, concealing that unspeakable and, as it were, timeless Gunpowder treason (by which the most monstrous traitors ever born, full of Jesuits, had bound themselves by a vow to devour, as if in one furnace, our King and the whole representative kingdom), they pressed it down in silence, against law and truth, holding up this seal. If charity is the whole end of the law of the Decalogue, how much more is it the end of the Gospel? The sacrament of penance (as you call it) is instituted only for the sake of the penitent, insofar as he is penitent; its voice is always wont to be, I have sinned; but never, I will sin. For confession is only an acknowledgment of past sins, not a profession of future ones; the one is the contrition of the mind, the other of a hardened one. But is the seal of the sacrament more sacred than the sacrament itself, whose religion you think is so great that it is not lawful for you to break it in order to reveal a future crime for the salvation of others, whether temporal or spiritual, even when the very soul of the confessor is, by your silence, more surrendered to Satan?

units.la: Sed quid ego tàm portentosum Paradoxon discutio, æterna execratione potius quàm ratione refutandum? Summa est, Confessionem auricularem per multiplices Pontificiorum Abusus sæpe factam iam esse, ex necessitate, & Circumstantiarum perplexitate, Conscientiarum carnificinam; ex formulis interrogationum, illecebram & lenocinium voluptatis; ex isthac lege non prodendi futura peccata, proditionum flagitiosorum latebram atque Sigillum. Hæc de Confessione; ad CONFESSARIVM reuertor.
units.tr: But why do I discuss so monstrous a paradox, which ought to be refuted with eternal execration rather than with reason? The sum is this: auricular confession, through the manifold abuses of the Papists, has often become, from its necessity and the perplexity of its circumstances, a torture-chamber of consciences; from its formulas of questioning, an allurement and enticement of pleasure; from that law of not disclosing future sins, a hiding place and seal for shameful treasons. So much for confession; I return to the CONFESSOR.

units.la: Bellarminus de Offic.
units.tr: Bellarmine, On the Office.

units.la: "Cuius potestatis signum euidens est, quòd in eo iudicio Sacerdos sedet capite tecto; poenitens autem, quicunque ille sit,
units.tr: "The sign of this power is evident in that, in this judgment, the priest sits with his head covered, while the penitent, whoever he is,

units.la: etiamsi Rex aut Imperator, genibus flexis, & capite detecto. pag. 454
units.tr: even if he is a king or emperor, kneels and bares his head. p. 454

units.la: Episcopi (inquis Alibi) maiores sunt Regibus. De Presbyteris eadem est ratio: nam Presbyteri, licet sint maioris ordinis Sacerdotes, tamen potestatem ipsi quoque habent ligandi atque soluendi, Reges & Principes benedicendi; quod Angelicas virtutes longe superat.
units.tr: Bishops (you say elsewhere) are greater than kings. The same reasoning applies to presbyters: for presbyters, although they are priests of the higher order, also have the power of binding and loosing, and of blessing kings and princes, which far surpasses the angelic virtues.

units.la: I. ANIMADVERSIO.
units.tr: I. ANIMADVERSION.

units.la: Argumento, quo Reges Confessario subdi volunt, ipsum Pontificem necessario constringi.
units.tr: By this argument, by which they want kings made subject to the confessor, the Pope himself is necessarily bound.

units.la: Iam tandem ad exitum perducta est quaestio; nam in comparatione Regiae dignitatis cum Sacerdotali Eadem est (inquis) ratio Presbyteri & Episcopi; eadem item Episcopi & summi Pontificis: Nec enim Pontifex quisquam ita summus, ut non Angelicis virtutibus inferior sit. Ergo quacunque hactenus ad Regum dignitatem infringendam deprimendamque accumulasti, ea in hoc Principis erga Confessarium suum officio complexus es omnia. Siue igitur in Templis conueniendum, siue in Conciliis sedendum, siue in Palatiis bibendum, siue in publicis plateis incedendum sit, praecipuus honos externus à Regibus est Presbyteris ipsis deferendus. Euidens est signum, scilicet, quod in Absolutionis negotio Sacerdos sedet tecto capite, Rex vero, aut Imperator flexis genibus, & capite detecto absolutionem petit. Respondeo paucis, Antecedens non necessarium esse, Consequens vero (ne quid grauius dicam) debile prorsus & infirmum. Non equidem vllis Sacerdotibus, praesertim in tam sacris, tantum honorem omnino inuideremus, nisi solum ijs, qui eum necessario sibi deberi iactitant; quia (vti vos optime noftis) Ritus iste non modo nullo iure diuino impositus est, sed ne quidem vsu Ecclesiastico vniuersaliter receptus, vtpote qui ad {*}Graecos nondum dimanauit. Rituum, quam experimur, differentia corum eorum in se ἀδιαφορίαν[?] & indifferentiam satis probat, nisi vbi Ritus est à Deo præscriptus, vt (exempli causa) Exod. 28. Summus{°} Sacerdos nudis pedibus & tecto capite sacrificium perficiebat. At Contra nunc fieri à Sacerdotibus solet, vbi pedibus calceatis, aperto capite sacrificiû peragitur, quia caput Christus iam nobis manifestatur, 1.Cor.11. vir Propheticus debet esse sine velamine. Iudæis vero *mos est (vt ait Epiphanius) adhuc tectum & velatum caput in sacris habere; quòd nondum ablatum sit cordis velamen, quibus non est revelatus Christus. Si tamen, vt ille apud Ethnicos dixit, Non Tibi sed Isidi; aut ad Pontificem Imperator, Non Tibi sed Petro: ita dicamus honorem hunc non Sacerdoti sed in sacro officio proprie Deo haberi; (haud secus atque apud Nos fit, quando in Administratione Eucharistiæ ab Episcopo stante Rex noster flexis genubus Sacramentum accipit, quod est profectò maximè consentaneum) nihil erit reliquum quod contra opponat Cardinalis.
units.tr: At last the question has been brought to its conclusion. For in comparing royal dignity with priestly dignity, you say: "The reasoning is the same for a presbyter and a bishop; likewise the same for a bishop and the supreme Pontiff." For no Pope is so supreme that he is not inferior to the angelic virtues. Therefore, whatever you have hitherto piled up to weaken and lower the dignity of kings, you have gathered it all into this duty of a prince towards his confessor. So whether one must gather in churches, sit in councils, drink in palaces, or walk in public squares, the chief outward honour must be paid to the presbyters by kings. It is an evident sign, namely, that in the business of absolution the priest sits with covered head, while the king or emperor, with knees bent and head bared, asks for absolution. I reply briefly: the antecedent is not necessary, and the consequent (not to say anything harsher) is wholly weak and feeble. We would indeed not grudge any priests so great an honour, especially in such sacred matters, except those who boast that it is owed to them by necessity. For, as you very well know, this rite is not only imposed by no divine law, but is not even universally received by ecclesiastical usage, since it has not yet spread to the Greeks. The variety of rites that we experience proves well enough that they are in themselves indifferent [ἀδιαφορίαν], unless the rite is prescribed by God, as for example in Exod. 28, where the high priest performed the sacrifice with bare feet and covered head. On the contrary, now it is commonly done by priests where the sacrifice is performed with shod feet and uncovered head, because Christ is now manifested to us as our head. Cor. 11: the prophetic man ought to be without a veil. Among the Jews, however, it is (as Epiphanius says) still the custom to have the head covered and veiled in sacred things, because the veil of the heart has not yet been removed from those to whom Christ has not been revealed. Yet if, as that man said among the heathen, "Not to you but to Isis"; or the emperor to the Pope, "Not to you but to Peter": so let us say that this honour is not paid to the priest but properly to God in the sacred office (no differently from what happens among us, when in the administration of the Eucharist our king, with knees bent, receives the sacrament from the bishop standing, which is surely most consistent), then nothing will remain that the Cardinal can set against it.

units.la: Consequentiam quod attinet, Sacerdotem Ego vestrum ad Papam mittendum censeo, quocum expostulet, cur (quùm P Summus Pontifex debeat abijcere se ad pedes infimi Sacerdotis, dum sua peccata confitetur; & quùm venit in conspectum Sacerdotis caput nudat, saltem dum Missa celebratur) ipsum extra istas sacri Ministerij functiones sibi præesse non sinat. Sic enim Ratio tua retorquebitur. Esse Capite detecto Euidens est signum potestatis superioris. At summus Pontifex, coram Sacerdote sedente capite tecto, flectit genua, & caput detegit: Ergo Confessarius Sacerdos est summo Pontifice Superior. Nec sufficiet objicere, Papam iam non vt Pontificem considerari, sed communiter vt Christianum: quia similiter quiuis de Rege affirmabit, Eum non vt Regem Christianum respici.
units.tr: As to the consequence, I think your priest should be sent to the Pope, to complain with him why (since the supreme Pontiff must cast himself at the feet of the lowest priest while he confesses his sins, and when he comes into the sight of a priest he bares his head, at least while Mass is being celebrated) he does not allow the priest to be set above him outside those functions of the sacred ministry. For in this way your argument will be turned back on you. To have the head bared is an evident sign of superior power. But the supreme Pontiff, before a priest sitting with covered head, bends his knees and bares his head. Therefore the confessor priest is superior to the supreme Pontiff. Nor will it suffice to object that the Pope is now considered not as Pontiff but commonly as a Christian, because in the same way anyone will affirm of a king that he is not regarded as a Christian king.

units.la: Denique quis tam excors qui non intelligit in hoc negotio Sacerdotem non iam omninò dominij, sed ministerij partes agere. At Iudex est (inquis;) esto, quasi verò qui est ex vno ministerio quodammodo Iudex,non possit esse in se Subditus. Hunc ego ad Papam remitto denuò: nam {q}Papa (vt vester Episcopus asserit) cum seipsum absoluere non potest, absoluitur à subdito. Audin'? à Subdito quum itaque huic ministerio se Papa subdit, nonnon interea Summus agnosci debeat? Exemplo res fiet dilucidior.
units.tr: Finally, who is so dull as not to understand that in this matter the priest no longer plays the part of lordship at all, but of ministry? But he is a judge, you say. Granted; as if one who is in some respect a judge by virtue of one ministry could not himself be a subject. I send this back to the Pope again: for the Pope (as your bishop asserts), since he cannot absolve himself, is absolved by a subject. Do you hear? By a subject. Since therefore the Pope submits himself to this ministry, ought he not meanwhile to be acknowledged as supreme? The matter will become clearer by an example.

units.la: {r}Confessarius (inquis) duas gerit personas, & Iudicis, & Medici. Papa itaque fidem curámque Corporis sui Medico dat; quando igitur Medicus Papae tangit venas, palpat latera, vrinam explorat, & velut in statera ægrotantis humores expendit; deinde ægroto medicamenta præscribit, iubet insolita, consueta prohibet, arguit oblata, execratur exhibita, authoritate & arbitrio suo omnia ordinat, atque disponit; cui Papa, si sanus esse velit, suâ sponte obtemperat; quasi esset Medicus [illegible, ~8 letters]: si vero se ille nimis Medicum esse meminerit, & ministerij oblitus Pontifici se vestro Superiorem iactitaret; quis non ipsum Medicum, (quod pari ratione de Confessario dicendum) tanquàm Medico egentem, ad Anticyras ocyus ablegandum duxerit? Viden', Lector, quàm effoeta & languida sint hæc, quæ Cardinalis affert?
units.tr: The confessor (you say) bears two persons, both of judge and of physician. The Pope therefore entrusts the care and keeping of his body to the physician. When therefore the physician touches the Pope's veins, feels his sides, examines his urine, and as if on a balance weighs the humours of the sick man; then prescribes medicines for the invalid, orders unusual things, forbids customary ones, finds fault with what has been offered, condemns what has been supplied, and orders and arranges everything by his own authority and will; to which the Pope, if he wishes to be well, obeys of his own accord, as if the physician were [illegible]. But if that man, remembering himself too much a physician and forgetting his ministry, were to boast that he is superior to your Pope, who would not think the physician himself (and what is said of the confessor must be said by the same reasoning), as one in need of a physician, to be sent off quickly to Anticyra? Do you see, reader, how feeble and languid are these things which the Cardinal brings forward?

units.la: Quanquam quem toto itinere hactenùs vacillantem & hæsitantem experti sumus, mirandum non est, si eundem videamus in extremo actu deficere.
units.tr: Yet since we have found him wavering and hesitating throughout the whole journey hitherto, it is no wonder if we see him failing in the last act.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: SOLI DEO GLORIA.
units.tr: GLORY TO GOD ALONE.
